The Court relied on Ambika Prasad v. U.P. State, [1980] 3 SCR 1159, which had concluded that the scheme did not create tangible sex discrimination.
members.conclusion: The provisions did not discriminate between men and women as such, and the challenge under Article 14 failed.

predicates.article_14_equality_challenge: The proceeding challenges a statutory family definition as discriminatory on grounds of sex.
predicates.adult_daughters_excluded_from_family_def: The statutory scheme excludes adult daughters from the family unit used for calculating a landholder’s ceiling area.
predicates.no_property_taken_from_daughter_or_confe: The scheme neither takes property from a daughter that it leaves with a son nor grants the son a right to land retained by the holder.

members.legal_issue: Treating a husband as the tenure holder for administrative purposes when his wife owns land does not violate equality guarantees if her ownership and compensation rights are preserved.
material_facts: The law treated the husband as the tenure holder even where the wife owned the land.
The Court found that this treatment simplified dealings and did not affect ownership or enjoyment of land within the permissible limit.
If the wife’s land was taken as surplus, compensation was payable to her, and the law protected her in selecting land to be declared surplus.
members.legal_principle: Articles 14 and 15 do not invalidate a procedural device that treats the husband as tenure holder where it does not diminish the wife’s ownership or rights to compensation. The Court relied on Sections 3(17) and 12A and the compensation provisions in Chapter III of the land-ceiling law.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the tenure-holder definition was not discriminatory and rejected the challenge.

predicates.sex_discrimination_challenge_to_land_cei: The proceeding alleges sex discrimination in a land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.husband_is_used_as_procedural_representa: The scheme treats a husband as the tenure holder for dealings concerning land owned by his wife.
predicates.wife_ownership_and_compensation_are_pres: The wife retains ownership and is entitled to compensation if her land is taken as surplus.

members.legal_issue: Giving the husband authority to make the family's land-retention selection does not discriminate against the wife when retained land remains owned in the same proportions as before selection.
material_facts: The husband was authorized to make the family declaration and select the land to be retained as permissible area.
The land retained for the family and separate unit had to be owned or held by their members in the same proportions as before the selection.
The challenge alleged that the husband could select his own land and cause the wife's land to be treated as surplus.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 14 together with the statutory requirement that ownership of the retained permissible area remain in the same proportions as before selection.
members.conclusion: The selection arrangement did not discriminate against the wife because the retained land had to preserve the members' prior ownership proportions.

predicates.family_land_selection_case: The proceeding challenges a land-retention selection made for a family under a ceiling scheme.
predicates.one_spouse_selects_retained_land: One spouse is authorized to submit the family's declaration and select which land is retained.
predicates.retained_land_preserves_prior_ownership_: The members' ownership shares in the retained land remain proportionate to their ownership shares before selection.

members.legal_issue: Delivery of compensation bonds satisfies the compensation claim even though the bonds have not yet been encashed.
material_facts: The taxpayer had received compensation bonds under the statutory compensation scheme.
The bonds were payable in installments and could not be cashed before their due dates.
The taxpayer argued that compensation remained payable until the bonds were encashed.
members.legal_principle: Section 68 of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, provided for compensation to be paid in cash, bonds, or a combination of both. Rules 62 to 65 governed the bonds' issuance, interest, installments, and payment on presentation. Delivery of bonds in accordance with that scheme constituted payment of compensation.
members.conclusion: The compensation claim was satisfied when the bonds were delivered in accordance with the compensation scheme; compensation did not remain payable until encashment.

predicates.compensation_payment_dispute: The dispute concerns whether compensation remains payable after bonds have been issued for it.
predicates.bonds_delivered_as_compensation: The recipient has been delivered bonds as payment of compensation under the applicable compensation scheme.

members.legal_issue: Delivery of compensation bonds satisfies the government's obligation to pay compensation, so the compensation does not remain payable until the bonds are encashed.
material_facts: The compensation bonds had been delivered to the respondent as payment of compensation for his former rights.
The bonds were payable in instalments and could not be cashed before their due dates.
members.legal_principle: Section 68 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, provides for compensation to be paid in cash, bonds, or partly in each. The rules governing the bonds provide for payment of principal and interest in instalments and permit earlier redemption at the government's option. Delivery of bonds under that arrangement constitutes payment of compensation.
members.conclusion: The compensation claim was satisfied upon delivery of the bonds and did not continue to be payable until they were encashed.

predicates.compensation_payment_proceeding: The government is paying compensation to a person whose rights have been acquired or extinguished.
predicates.government_delivered_bonds_as_compensati: The government delivered bonds to the person as payment of that compensation.

members.legal_issue: The negotiability of a bond does not make it legal tender or require a recipient to accept it in payment of a debt.
material_facts: The taxpayer argued that the bonds were negotiable instruments and therefore had to be accepted for payment of tax.
The bonds could be transferred to a person willing to purchase them, but they were not cashable at the time they were tendered.
members.legal_principle: A negotiable instrument may be transferred to a willing purchaser, but negotiability alone does not make it legal tender or compel anyone, including the Government, to accept it for a debt.
members.conclusion: The bonds' negotiability did not make them legal tender or oblige the authorities to accept them in payment of the tax arrears.

predicates.payment_tender_dispute: The matter concerns whether a recipient must accept an instrument tendered to pay a debt.
predicates.instrument_is_negotiable: The instrument can be transferred to another person.

members.legal_issue: The negotiability of compensation bonds does not make them legal tender or require a creditor, including the government, to accept them for a debt.
material_facts: The respondent argued that the bonds were negotiable and therefore had to be accepted for his tax debt.
The bonds were not cashable at the time he offered them.
members.legal_principle: Negotiability allows the owner to transfer an instrument to a person willing to purchase it; it does not make the instrument legal tender or impose a duty on anyone, including the government, to accept it for payment of a debt.
members.conclusion: The bonds' negotiability did not oblige the government to accept them in payment of the tax arrears.

predicates.payment_tender_dispute: A debtor offers an instrument to a creditor as payment of a debt.
predicates.negotiable_bonds_offered: The instrument offered is a bond that can be transferred by its owner.

members.legal_issue: An identification parade is not substantive evidence, and defects in its conduct can make it unworthy of reliance even as corroboration.
material_facts: The identification parade was conducted in the presence of police officers.
Although the parade record stated that three lungis were presented, the identifying witness said he was shown only one.
The witness said similar lungis were worn by many people in the village, and no distinguishing feature linked the identified lungi to the accused.
members.legal_principle: Under Musheer Khan v. State of Madhya Pradesh, an identification test is not substantive evidence and may only corroborate identification in court. Under Section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Ramkishan Mithanlal Sharma v. State of Bombay, communications made by identifiers to police during investigation are barred; police presence at the identification exercise brings those communications within that bar.
members.conclusion: The identification parade was unworthy of acceptance in support of the prosecution.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution and identification_parade_used and (police_present_at_identification or (parade_record_lists_multiple_items and only_one_item_shown) or no_distinguishing_identification_feature)

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the prosecution relies on evidence to establish guilt.
predicates.identification_parade_used: The prosecution relies on an identification parade to support the identification of an accused or an exhibit.
predicates.police_present_at_identification: Police officers are present while identifiers participate in the identification exercise.
predicates.parade_record_lists_multiple_items: The record of the identification exercise states that multiple comparable items were presented.
predicates.only_one_item_shown: The identifying witness is shown only one item despite the record stating that multiple items were presented.
predicates.no_distinguishing_identification_feature: The identifying witness provides no distinctive feature separating the accused or identified item from others of the same kind.

members.legal_issue: Identification-parade evidence is corroborative and cannot repair unreliable testimony when the identifying witness does not testify about the identification.
material_facts: An officer testified that the child witness identified the accused at an identification parade.
The child witness did not testify that he had identified the accused at the parade.
The child’s substantive testimony suffered from serious infirmities.
members.legal_principle: Ordinarily, the person said to have identified the accused at a parade must give evidence about that identification so the defence can cross-examine the witness about any opportunity to see the accused beforehand. Identification at a parade is corroborative evidence; it cannot cure unreliable substantive testimony. The judgment cites no specific statutory provision or earlier case for these principles.
members.conclusion: The identification-parade evidence could not improve the prosecution case.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding concerns whether the accused committed a criminal offence.
predicates.identification_witness_did_not_testify_a: The person said to have identified the accused at a parade did not testify about that identification.
predicates.substantive_identification_testimony_unr: The identifying witness’s substantive testimony about identifying the accused was unreliable.

members.legal_issue: A decades-old document may be presumed duly executed when the statutory conditions for the presumption apply and the presumption is not rebutted.
material_facts: A power of attorney executed more than thirty years earlier bore the owner’s signatures.
The owner acknowledged being taken to the relevant office after her father’s death but gave evasive answers when confronted with the document.
The parties acted on the document’s terms from the time it was made, and the owner did not lead evidence to rebut the presumption of due execution.
members.legal_principle: Section 90 of the Evidence Act permits a court to presume due execution and attestation of a document that is thirty years old when produced from proper custody. Under Section 4, a ‘may presume’ presumption is rebuttable; the court may regard the fact as proved unless disproved or call for proof. The owner’s failure to rebut the presumption, together with the parties’ conduct under the document, supported treating it as genuine.
members.conclusion: The older power of attorney was properly treated as genuine and binding on the owner.

predicates.civil_document_validity_dispute: A party to a civil dispute challenges the validity of a document.
predicates.document_is_at_least_thirty_years_old: The document was at least thirty years old when produced in court.
predicates.document_is_produced_from_custody_the_co: The document was produced from custody that the court accepted as proper in the circumstances.
predicates.party_challenging_document_does_not_rebu: The party challenging the document did not produce evidence rebutting due execution.

members.legal_issue: A court may presume the genuineness of a document that is more than thirty years old and produced from proper custody, and an unsupported allegation of fraud does not rebut that presumption.
material_facts: The defendants produced a patta issued in 1929 from their custody.
The document’s contents and endorsements referred to government-record entries made pursuant to official orders.
The plaintiffs alleged that the patta was forged but produced no evidence proving forgery.
members.legal_principle: Section 90 of the Evidence Act permits, but does not require, a court to presume the genuineness of a document that is at least thirty years old and produced from custody the court considers proper. Mere allegations of fraud are insufficient to rebut the presumption.
members.conclusion: The patta qualified for a presumption of genuineness, and the plaintiffs did not rebut that presumption.

rule.if: civil_evidence_issue and document_is_over_thirty_years_old and document_produced_from_proper_custody and fraud_allegation_is_unsubstantiated

predicates.civil_evidence_issue: A court must determine the evidentiary status of a document in a civil proceeding.
predicates.document_is_over_thirty_years_old: The document was made more than thirty years before it is produced in court.
predicates.document_produced_from_proper_custody: The document is produced from custody that the court considers appropriate in the circumstances.
predicates.fraud_allegation_is_unsubstantiated: A party alleges that the document is fraudulent but provides no evidence sufficient to establish that allegation.

members.legal_issue: A petition dismissed in limine should be remitted for consideration where additional issues remain to be decided and the petitioner may be able to establish entitlement under the governing order.
material_facts: The appeal arose from a High Court order dismissing a petition in limine.
The appellant had been allotted a demarcated plot but had not executed a sale deed.
Additional legal points remained, and whether the appellant qualified for the benefit depended on proof that it fell within the governing order.
members.legal_principle: The Court had already determined the interpretation of the government order in the connected appeals, but held that the petition should not have been dismissed in limine because additional legal points remained and the appellant’s qualification depended on proof. No earlier case was cited for this procedural ruling.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed and the matter remitted to the High Court to readmit and decide the petition according to law, with the appellant required to establish that it qualified under the governing order.

predicates.appeal_from_petition_dismissed_in_limine: A party appealed from an order dismissing its petition without a full hearing.
predicates.additional_issues_remain: Legal or factual issues material to the petition remain undecided.
predicates.entitlement_depends_on_facts_not_yet_pro: The petitioner’s entitlement depends on facts that have not yet been established.
predicates.petition_should_be_remitted_for_hearing_: The petition should be restored and sent for consideration and decision after the remaining issues are addressed.

members.legal_issue: An estoppel ground raised in a petition but not decided by the High Court must be remitted for the High Court to consider.
material_facts: One petitioner asserted estoppel based on expenditure incurred in laying out land and payment accepted by the improvement board for its sanction.
The High Court had not decided that estoppel ground.
members.legal_principle: The Court left the estoppel issue for the High Court because it had not been decided there; the judgment states no further substantive rule on estoppel.
members.conclusion: The petition raising estoppel was remanded to the High Court for consideration of that ground.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_petition: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a writ petition in which a ground was raised.
predicates.estoppel_ground_was_raised: A petitioner asserted that the opposing side was estopped based on conduct or expenditure relating to the land.
predicates.high_court_did_not_decide_estoppel_groun: The High Court did not determine the estoppel ground raised in the petition.

members.legal_issue: The valuation method prescribed by municipal bye-laws governs property-tax assessments made after those bye-laws take effect, rather than earlier judicial principles developed for assessments constrained by rent-control legislation.
material_facts: The municipal corporation had enacted bye-laws prescribing how annual rent and rateable value were to be determined.
The assessments in issue concerned periods after those bye-laws came into force.
The earlier judicial principles relied on by the taxpayers had been developed in cases involving premises governed by rent-control legislation.
The High Court had applied those earlier principles despite the existence of the municipal corporation’s valuation bye-laws.
members.legal_principle: Section 116(1) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act sets the general measure of rateable value, while bye-law 3 of the 1994 Bye-Laws prescribes how annual rent is determined. Where the municipal legislation itself provides a method for determining annual value, that method governs rather than a rent-control statute’s fair-rent or standard-rent limit. The Court relied on Assistant General Manager, Central Bank of India v. Commissioner, Municipal Corporation for the City of Ahmedabad, East India Commercial Company Private Limited v. Corporation of Calcutta, and The Commissioner v. Griha Yajamanula Samkhya; it distinguished The Corporation of Calcutta v. Padma Debi, Dr. Balbir Singh v. Municipal Corporation, Delhi, and Lt. Col. P.R. Chaudhary v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi, which concerned assessments in the context of rent-control legislation. It also noted that Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Delhi Urban House Owners’ Welfare Association had upheld the bye-laws.
members.conclusion: Assessments made after the 1994 bye-laws came into force must be governed by those bye-laws, and the principles in the earlier rent-control cases do not govern those assessments.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment: The proceeding concerns the assessment of property tax on land or a building by a municipal authority.
predicates.assessment_after_valuation_bylaws: The assessment concerns a period after the municipal authority’s valuation bye-laws took effect.
predicates.bylaws_prescribe_valuation_method: The municipal authority’s bye-laws prescribe how the relevant annual value or rent is to be determined.

members.legal_issue: Property tax rateable value must be assessed under the current municipal statute rather than an inconsistent valuation method preserved under earlier municipal rules.
material_facts: The assessments concerned property tax under the current municipal statute, which provided a method for determining annual rent and rateable value.
The lower court relied on an earlier municipal by-law to assess owner-occupied property, although the current statute contained its own valuation procedure.
The earlier enactment had been repealed, and only by-laws consistent with the current statute were preserved.
members.legal_principle: Sections 60 and 63 of the New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994 provide for property-tax assessment and rateable value based on the annual rent at which property might reasonably be expected to be let, less the specified deduction. Section 416(2) preserves earlier by-laws only insofar as they are consistent with the Act; the specific statutory valuation method therefore displaces an inconsistent earlier by-law.
members.conclusion: The earlier by-law could not be used where it was inconsistent with the current statute; rateable value had to be determined under the statute by reference to the rent the property could reasonably be expected to command, subject to the statutory deductions.

predicates.property_tax_assessment_appeal: A party appealed a decision concerning the assessment of property tax.
predicates.current_law_has_specific_rent_valuation_: The law governing the assessment provides a specific method for valuing property by reference to rent it could reasonably command.
predicates.earlier_valuation_rule_conflicts_with_cu: An earlier valuation rule would produce an assessment inconsistent with the method provided by the current law.

members.legal_issue: The power to declare local areas as grams or nagars under section 9(1) is not an excessive delegation of legislative power.
material_facts: The statute set population ranges for gram and nagar areas and authorized prescribed inquiries into population, land revenue, and whether areas could conveniently be grouped.

The statute's stated purpose was democratic decentralization through a system of local panchayats, and the court found that it contemplated establishing panchayats within a reasonable time in local areas with populations not exceeding 30,000, subject to specified exclusions.
The challenged area had a population of 12,249 and was declared a nagar after the prescribed inquiry.
members.legal_principle: An essential legislative function is the determination of legislative policy and its formulation as a binding rule; after laying down that policy, the legislature may leave administrative agencies discretion to execute it and work out details. The court applied In re Delhi Laws Act and Raj Narain Singh v. Chairman, Patna Administration Committee. It held that the Act's policy of establishing panchayats in eligible local areas guided and controlled the discretion under section 9(1); the possibility of abuse in administration did not make the provision unconstitutional.
members.conclusion: Section 9(1) did not suffer from excessive delegation, and the declaration was lawful.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_declaration_power and legislative_policy_guides_local_units and population_criteria_set and inquiry_confines_administrative_details

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_declaration_: A party challenged the legislature's delegation of authority to designate local self-government areas.
predicates.legislative_policy_guides_local_units: The law states a policy of establishing local self-government units in eligible areas.
predicates.population_criteria_set: The law specifies population criteria for the categories of local self-government units.
predicates.inquiry_confines_administrative_details: The required inquiry concerns factual and administrative matters needed to implement the statutory scheme.

members.legal_issue: The power to reorganize gram and nagar areas under section 9(2) is not an excessive delegation of legislative power.
material_facts: Section 9(2) authorized alteration of the limits of grams and nagars, inclusion or exclusion of local areas, and termination of a gram or nagar designation after consultation with specified panchayats.
The Act provided for establishment or reconstitution of panchayats and for amalgamation or division of areas following such changes.
No action under section 9(2) had been taken against the appellants.
members.legal_principle: The legislature may leave administrative discretion over details needed to implement its policy. The court held that reorganization into new local self-government units could require inclusion, exclusion, alteration, amalgamation, division, or termination, and that not every contingency could be anticipated. The statutory consultation requirement and related provisions governing consequential changes supported the delegation.
members.conclusion: Section 9(2) was not unconstitutional for excessive delegation.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_reorganizati: A party challenged a government's power to alter the boundaries or status of local self-government areas.
predicates.law_requires_consultation: The law requires consultation with relevant local bodies before the government exercises the reorganization power.
predicates.consequential_reorganization_provisions_: The law provides for consequences such as reconstitution, amalgamation, or division of local bodies after boundary or status changes.
predicates.reorganization_serves_local_self_governm: The reorganization power is directed to forming or arranging units of local self-government.

members.legal_issue: Notifications and acquisition proceedings dependent on an improvement scheme whose originating notification was unauthorized are invalid.
material_facts: The later notifications and the Land Acquisition Officer's order related to the scheme initiated by the first notification.
The first notification was not authorized because the scheme did not fall within the statutory purposes for which an improvement scheme could be made.
members.legal_principle: The later notifications were invalid because they referred to a scheme whose origin was not justified by the Act; acquisition proceedings could not be valid when their underlying notifications were invalid. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The subsequent notifications and the Land Acquisition Officer's order were invalid, and the acquisition proceedings could not stand.

predicates.acquisition_proceeding_challenge: The proceeding challenges notifications and an acquisition order relating to a municipal improvement scheme.
predicates.originating_scheme_notice_unauthorized: The initial notice for the scheme was issued even though the scheme did not fall within the authorized purposes for making such a scheme.
predicates.later_notices_and_order_depend_on_scheme: The later notifications and acquisition order related to the scheme initiated by the initial notice.

members.legal_issue: A defective initial acquisition notification invalidates the subsequent declaration and vesting that depend on it.
material_facts: The initial acquisition notification did not comply with the statutory description requirement and was held invalid.
The later declaration and purported vesting followed from the initial notification and the intervening acquisition steps.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 3D(1) and 3D(2) of the National Highways Act, 1956, declaration and vesting follow the preceding acquisition process. When the foundational notification is invalid, the consequential steps founded on it fall with it; purported vesting cannot validate the defective acquisition.
members.conclusion: The later steps, including the purported vesting of the land, were invalid because the initial notification was invalid.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.initial_notice_invalid: The initial acquisition notification was held not to comply with a governing statutory requirement.
predicates.later_vesting_depends_on_notice: The later declaration and purported transfer of ownership resulted from steps taken under the initial notification.

members.legal_issue: Measures granting permanent rights to agricultural-land hut occupants and settling them on small holdings in panchayat areas can form part of agrarian reform.
material_facts: The challenged provisions protected kudikidappukars from eviction and enabled them to obtain rights in their homesteads and adjoining land.
The State’s evidence described kudikidappukars as people who had historically lived on land in return for services, often including agricultural labour.
The provisions concerned lands in panchayat areas.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the problem of kudikidappukars was intimately connected with agricultural land and that improving their circumstances and granting permanent rights could fall within agrarian reform under Article 31A. It referred to Armugha Konar v. Sanku Muthammal, Saimva Umma v. Kunhammad, and Mariam v. Ouseph Xavier, as well as the history of protective legislation described by the State. The Court confined this holding to panchayat areas and did not decide the corresponding problem in municipal areas.
members.conclusion: The settlement of kudikidappukars and tenants of kudiyiruppus on small holdings in panchayat areas was covered by agrarian reform or purposes ancillary to it.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A litigant brought a constitutional challenge to a measure reallocating rights in land.
predicates.occupants_live_on_agricultural_land_in_p: The occupants whose rights are affected live on agricultural land in a panchayat area.
predicates.occupants_have_historical_or_work_relate: The occupants have a historical or work-related connection to the land, including residence there in connection with agricultural labour.

members.legal_issue: Benefits allowing hut occupants to acquire land can be protected as agrarian reform where the land is agricultural and the beneficiaries and transfer are connected with agriculture, even if the beneficiary definition is not limited to agricultural labourers.
material_facts: The cases concerned agricultural lands constituting estates and occupants of huts on those lands who were connected with agriculture.
The law allowed eligible occupants to acquire the hut site and a limited surrounding area of land.
The land transferred was intended primarily for agricultural purposes, with part of it available for a homestead, and the general agricultural purpose was not displaced by that use.
No case before the Court involved a beneficiary unconnected with agriculture occupying non-agricultural land.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-A(1)(a), read with Article 31-A(2)(a)(iii), protects laws relating to agrarian reform affecting rights in estates. Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab supports a liberal construction covering ancillary measures needed to give effect to an agrarian-reform scheme, and Inder Singh v. State of Punjab was cited in support. The Court also relied on the principles in the decisions reported at AIR 1959 SC 459 and AIR 1959 SC 519 that a transfer of a landlord’s right to a tenant may constitute an extinguishment or modification of the landlord’s rights. The Court expressed no opinion on cases involving non-agricultural land or beneficiaries not substantially connected with agriculture.
members.conclusion: The objection that the definition was not limited to agricultural labourers did not invalidate the benefits in the cases before the Court; those benefits were protected as measures of agrarian reform.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: A party challenges statutory benefits granted to occupants of huts on land as outside the constitutional protection for agrarian reform.
predicates.land_is_agricultural_estate: The land concerned is held for agricultural purposes or purposes ancillary to agriculture and constitutes an estate.
predicates.hut_occupants_are_connected_with_agricul: The beneficiaries occupying huts on the land are connected with agriculture.
predicates.transfer_is_ancillary_to_agricultural_us: The transfer of land to the occupants is primarily for agricultural use, with any homestead use remaining ancillary to that purpose.

members.legal_issue: A jungle or forest is not an estate merely by being included in a holding, but it may fall within an estate when held as part of land used for agriculture or an ancillary purpose.
material_facts: Some petitioners held forest and jungle land.
The Court distinguished land held independently as jungle from forest land included in an estate consisting of land held for agricultural purposes or purposes ancillary to agriculture.
Private forests were specially exempted from acquisition under the Act.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 31A(2)(a) and (iii) and relied on U.P. State v. Raja Anand, which held that forest or waste land is not an estate under the relevant category unless held or let for agricultural purposes or purposes ancillary to them. The Court also noted the Act’s special exemption for private forests.
members.conclusion: A holding consisting only of jungle could not be acquired as an estate on that basis; forest or jungle land included within an agricultural estate could fall within the estate, subject to the statutory exemption for private forests.

rule.if: land_reform_acquisition_case and land_is_forest_or_jungle and (holding_contains_only_forest_or_jungle or not land_is_part_of_agricultural_estate)

predicates.land_reform_acquisition_case: The dispute concerns acquisition under a land-reform law.
predicates.land_is_forest_or_jungle: The land is forest or jungle land.
predicates.holding_contains_only_forest_or_jungle: The holding or tenure consists only of forest or jungle.
predicates.land_is_part_of_agricultural_estate: The forest or jungle land is held as part of an estate used for agriculture or an ancillary purpose.

members.legal_issue: Forest or waste land falls within the constitutional category of land held or let for agriculture or purposes ancillary to agriculture only when it is held or let for such purposes.
material_facts: The area included cultivated land as well as forest, hills, and waste land.
The cultivated portion was accepted as falling within the constitutional category, but the forest and waste land were not shown to be held or let for agricultural or ancillary purposes.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(2)(a)(iii) treats waste land and forest land as included within land held or let for agriculture or purposes ancillary thereto; it does not list them as independent categories. The Court reasoned that this reading accords with the agrarian-reform purpose of Article 31A.
members.conclusion: Forest or waste land does not fall within that category merely because it is forest or waste land; it must be held or let for agricultural or ancillary purposes.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: A party challenged the constitutional validity of a land acquisition.
predicates.forest_land: The land at issue was forest land.
predicates.waste_land: The land at issue was waste land.
predicates.held_or_let_for_agricultural_or_ancillar: The land was held or let for agriculture or for a purpose ancillary to agriculture.
predicates.land_does_not_qualify_under_the_agricult: The land does not qualify under the category of land held or let for agriculture or ancillary purposes.

members.legal_issue: When a secured-asset sale is set aside after the purchaser has paid the purchase price and property-related liabilities, restoration of the property and repayment to the purchaser may be made conditional on reimbursement.
material_facts: The purchaser paid the sale consideration and amounts relating to registration, stamp duty, and liabilities encumbering the property.
The purchaser also paid later municipal liabilities and had used the property in the meantime.

The Court set aside the sale and directed that the borrower could recover the property by paying the bank’s dues and reimbursing the purchaser’s specified expenses and the liabilities paid on the borrower’s behalf.

The Court directed that if the borrower did not make the required payments, the bank could proceed with a fresh sale under the law and the purchaser was to be refunded the amounts spent, without interest because the purchaser had used the property.
members.legal_principle: In setting aside the sale, the Court fashioned conditional restitution to account for the purchaser’s payments, the borrower’s liabilities discharged by the purchaser, and the purchaser’s use of the property. The Court directed reimbursement of the purchaser and denied interest in light of that use.
members.conclusion: The property would revert to the borrower if the borrower made the directed payments within the specified time; otherwise the bank could sell it again in accordance with law, and the purchaser was entitled to a refund without interest.

rule.if: secured_asset_sale_appeal and sale_set_aside and purchaser_paid_sale_and_property_costs and purchaser_used_property

predicates.secured_asset_sale_appeal: A court reviewed an appeal concerning a creditor’s sale of secured property.
predicates.sale_set_aside: The court set aside the completed sale of the secured property.
predicates.purchaser_paid_sale_and_property_costs: The purchaser paid the purchase price and expenses or liabilities relating to the property.
predicates.purchaser_used_property: The purchaser used the property after the sale.

members.legal_issue: After an invalid secured-asset sale, restoration of possession to the borrowers may be conditioned on reimbursing the purchasers and returning the sale proceeds held by the lender.
material_facts: The purchasers paid the full sale consideration, paid stamp duty, and received possession of the property.
The sale consideration was deposited with the bank in a fixed deposit, which accrued interest.
The borrowers agreed to repay the purchasers' sale-price and stamp-duty amounts with interest.

The Court directed the bank to return the fixed-deposit proceeds with accrued interest and directed that possession be delivered to the borrowers upon the purchasers receiving the full amount due to them.
members.legal_principle: The Court moulded relief in light of the invalid sale, the purchasers' payment and possession, the borrowers' agreement to reimburse them, and the sale proceeds held by the bank. It directed restitution to the purchasers and made return of possession conditional on their receiving the full amount due.
members.conclusion: The sale was set aside; the bank had to return the fixed-deposit proceeds with accrued interest, and the purchasers had to deliver possession to the borrowers once the borrowers had paid the purchasers the full amount directed.

rule.if: appeal_concerning_relief_after_invalid_sale and purchasers_paid_sale_consideration_and_transaction_costs and purchasers_received_possession and borrowers_agree_to_reimburse_purchasers and lender_holds_sale_proceeds

predicates.appeal_concerning_relief_after_invalid_s: An appeal concerns the appropriate relief after a secured-asset sale has been held invalid.
predicates.purchasers_paid_sale_consideration_and_t: The purchasers paid the sale price and transaction costs associated with the sale.
predicates.purchasers_received_possession: The purchasers received possession of the property under the sale.
predicates.borrowers_agree_to_reimburse_purchasers: The borrowers agreed to repay the purchasers the amounts due to them.
predicates.lender_holds_sale_proceeds: The lender holds the sale proceeds, including any interest accrued on them.

members.legal_issue: A court exercising discretionary public-law writ jurisdiction must independently assess the relevant facts and procedural considerations before granting relief.
material_facts: The writ petition alleged that public authorities had used privately owned land without acquisition or compensation, and sought directions for acquisition or alternative relief.
The claim was brought more than 35 years after the alleged loss of possession, and the authority pleaded delay and laches.
Ownership, the nature of the land, the petitioner’s authority to litigate for the trust, and the effect of conveyance documents were unresolved and disputed.
The High Court granted relief without findings on those matters or on whether they could be satisfactorily resolved in writ proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, writ relief, including mandamus, is discretionary and cannot be claimed as of right. The court must consider, among other matters, whether disputed facts can be satisfactorily resolved, whether material facts have been disclosed, whether an effective alternative remedy exists, whether there is unexplained delay or a limitation bar, and whether relief would conflict with public policy or law. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s orders were set aside and the matter was remitted for fresh consideration because the court had not assessed the relevant facts and discretionary factors; the Supreme Court expressed no view on the merits.

rule.if: public_law_writ and (material_facts_unresolved or material_facts_omitted or unexplained_delay_raised) and relief_granted_without_assessing_relevant_factors

predicates.public_law_writ: A person brought a public-law proceeding seeking discretionary relief from a court.
predicates.material_facts_unresolved: The parties’ claims depended on material factual matters that had not been resolved.
predicates.material_facts_omitted: The record or pleadings indicated that material facts may not have been disclosed.
predicates.unexplained_delay_raised: A party raised the other party’s unexplained delay in seeking relief.
predicates.relief_granted_without_assessing_relevan: The court granted relief without assessing the relevant facts and discretionary considerations.
predicates.writ_relief_set_aside_and_matter_remitte: The relief is set aside and the matter is returned for fresh consideration.

members.legal_issue: In writ proceedings, the High Court must independently determine a preliminary fact on which an administrative authority's jurisdiction depends.
material_facts: The claimant sought relief under Article 226 after revenue authorities rejected the claim concerning the tanks and wells.
Whether the properties were on occupied land and within the statutory exclusion determined whether the State could take possession of them.
The High Court quashed the revenue authorities' orders on the ground that the matter should be decided under the compensation inquiry procedure, without deciding the disputed jurisdictional fact.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226, when an administrative authority's jurisdiction depends on a preliminary finding of fact, the High Court may determine independently whether that fact is established and must not allow an inferior tribunal to determine the limits of its own jurisdiction conclusively. The Court applied Rex v. Shoreditch Assessment Committee and White & Collins v. Minister of Health.
members.conclusion: The High Court was required to decide independently whether the claim that the tanks and wells belonged to the jagirdar within the meaning of the exemption was substantiated; if it was, the High Court could direct the State to hand over possession. The cases of Rex v. Shoreditch Assessment Committee and White & Collins v. Minister of Health were applied.

predicates.writ_proceeding_challenging_administrati: A claimant brought a writ proceeding challenging an administrative authority's action or decision.
predicates.authority_jurisdiction_depends_on_prelim: The authority's power to act depends on whether a preliminary fact is true.

members.legal_issue: A zamindar in a merged territory is an intermediary only when the relevant record or instrument establishes that the person holds an interest between the cultivators and the superior holder.
material_facts: The proprietors of the two properties claimed that their ancestors had been independent chiefs before becoming subordinate to a regional ruler, but their status in relation to that ruler had never been settled.
There was no evidence that their ancestors had received or accepted a grant or sanad from the ruler.
They and their predecessors paid an annual amount described variously as takoli, tribute, or rent, but the record did not establish that they held their properties as intermediaries.
The State issued notifications purporting to vest the properties under the estates-abolition legislation.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(h) and 2(g) of the Orissa Estates Abolition Act, 1951, a zamindar in merged territory must be a zamindar within the meaning of a wajib-ul-arz or a sanad, deed, or other instrument, and an estate must be held by an intermediary. The title of zamindar and payments to a superior ruler, without evidence establishing the required intermediate status, do not suffice. Section 3 authorizes a vesting notification only for property meeting the statutory definition of an estate. No earlier case was relied on for this holding.
members.conclusion: The proprietors were not intermediaries within the statutory definition, their properties were not estates under that definition, and the State lacked authority to issue vesting notifications for them.

predicates.challenge_to_vesting_notification: A person challenges a government notification that purports to vest property under an estates-abolition scheme.
predicates.merged_territory_zamindari: The property is in a merged territory and its holder is described as a zamindar.
predicates.status_not_established_by_relevant_recor: The relevant records or instruments do not establish that the holder possesses an interest between the cultivators and a superior holder.

members.legal_issue: A non-sovereign holder of an interest in land between cultivators and the state is an intermediary, and that interest may be acquired when it falls within the statutory definition of an estate.
material_facts: After the merger, the former rulers were not sovereigns and held interests in land between the cultivators and the state.
They were not cultivators and had paid takoli to the ruler of the larger state and later to the successor state; the Court treated those payments as land revenue.
The amended definitions covered holders or owners of interests in land between the cultivator and the state and included qualifying lands and interests held by an intermediary.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(h) and 2(g) of the Orissa Estates Abolition Act, 1952, as amended by the Orissa Estates Abolition (Amendment) Act, 1954, define an intermediary to include other holders or owners of interests in land between the raiyat and the state, and define an estate to include qualifying land held by or vested in an intermediary. Explanations I and III to section 2(g) address land revenue and estates in merged territories. The Court also noted its earlier decision in Biswambhar Singh v. State of Orissa, [1954] S.C.R. 842, which had held that these proprietors were not intermediaries under the earlier definition.
members.conclusion: The former rulers were intermediaries, their lands were estates under the amended definitions, and their interests in those lands could be acquired under the Act.

rule.if: land_acquisition_appeal and holders_lacked_sovereignty and holders_not_cultivators and land_interest_between_cultivators_and_state and land_payments_made_to_ruler

predicates.land_acquisition_appeal: An appeal challenged the state’s acquisition of land held by former local rulers.
predicates.holders_lacked_sovereignty: The holders had no sovereign authority when the relevant territories became part of the successor state.
predicates.holders_not_cultivators: The holders did not occupy the land as cultivators.
predicates.land_interest_between_cultivators_and_st: The holders owned or held an interest in land between the cultivators and the state.
predicates.land_payments_made_to_ruler: The holders made payments relating to the land to the superior ruler or the successor state.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to the suitability of land selected for acquisition fails absent a sufficient basis to interfere with the acquisition authority’s assessment, particularly when alleged alternatives are not properly identified.
material_facts: The land was proposed for acquisition to house families displaced by floods.
The challenger alleged that other land and open spaces were more suitable but did not provide proper particulars of those alternatives.
The acquisition authority’s assessment of the proposed land’s suitability was primarily for that authority to make, and no sufficient reason to interfere with its assessment was shown.
members.legal_principle: The assessment of the suitability of land proposed for acquisition is primarily for the Land Acquisition Officer. Interference is not warranted without a good reason, and a challenger who does not provide proper particulars of allegedly more suitable alternative land cannot establish a grievance that those alternatives were not considered.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the acquisition authority’s assessment of the proposed land’s suitability, and the challenge based on alternative land failed.

rule.if: land_suitability_challenge and acquisition_officer_assessed_suitability and claimant_lacked_specific_alternative_land_details and no_basis_to_interfere

predicates.land_suitability_challenge: The proceeding challenges the suitability of land selected for acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_officer_assessed_suitability: The acquisition officer assessed the proposed land’s suitability for the stated public purpose.
predicates.claimant_lacked_specific_alternative_lan: The challenger did not properly identify the allegedly more suitable alternative land.
predicates.no_basis_to_interfere: No sufficient reason was shown to displace the acquisition officer’s assessment.

members.legal_issue: A claim that no acquisition steps have been taken fails when the authority has advanced a proposed acquisition, and alternative-site allotment does not arise before the land is acquired.
material_facts: The society sought to prevent acquisition and obtained an interim stay of dispossession that remained in force during the proceedings.
The authority submitted an acquisition proposal to the collector, obtained the collector’s agreement, sent a draft notification for publication, and provided an advance toward compensation.
The land had not yet been acquired.
members.legal_principle: The court assessed the concrete steps taken under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and held that the proposal, official processing, preparation of a notification, and advance toward compensation showed that acquisition steps had been taken. It held that alternative-site allotment did not arise because the land had not yet been acquired. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: It was incorrect to contend that no acquisition steps had been taken, and the question of allotting alternative sites did not arise before acquisition.

rule.if: acquisition_steps_challenge and acquisition_proceeding_is_contested and authority_has_advanced_acquisition_process and land_has_not_yet_been_acquired

predicates.acquisition_steps_challenge: The proceeding alleges that the acquiring authority has taken no steps to acquire the land.
predicates.acquisition_proceeding_is_contested: The landowner is contesting the proposed acquisition.
predicates.authority_has_advanced_acquisition_proce: The authority has submitted the proposal for official processing and taken concrete steps toward notification and compensation.
predicates.land_has_not_yet_been_acquired: The acquisition has not been completed.

members.legal_issue: A decomposed recovered body may be identified through witness testimony and distinctive physical features, and the condition of the body does not by itself defeat proof of the victim’s death and identity.
material_facts: The recovered body was decomposed, with some soft tissue eaten away, but the scalp hair remained intact.
A village watchman who had known the deceased since childhood identified the body by its facial features, thick moustache, grey hair patch, and a coin tied at the waist.
The informant and another witness also identified the body as that of the deceased.
The medical and investigative evidence did not establish that identifying features were wholly absent.
members.legal_principle: Proof of the corpus delicti is not an indispensable legal requirement where strong evidence establishes death and the accused’s responsibility; discovery of a body is a rule of caution, not law. Identification and proof depend on the evidence and circumstances of the case. The Court relied on Rama Nand v. State of Himachal Pradesh, Ram Gulam Chaudhary v. State of Bihar, and Lakshmi v. State of U.P.; the charge considered was under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The courts below were entitled to find that the recovered body was that of the deceased; the challenge based on the body’s condition failed.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed a criminal conviction.
predicates.decomposed_body_recovered: A body was recovered in a decomposed condition.
predicates.distinctive_features_remained: The recovered body retained physical features capable of assisting identification.
predicates.witnesses_familiar_with_victim_identifie: Witnesses who knew the victim identified the recovered body as the victim.

members.legal_issue: The identity of a deceased person’s body may be established by a discovery made at an accused’s instance together with independent evidence identifying the remains.
material_facts: The remains were discovered at the instance of an accused.
Witnesses, including independent witnesses, proved the discovery.
The remains and associated clothing were identified through evidence including clothing recovered near the body and a receipt found in a pocket.
members.legal_principle: A fact discovered at the instance of an accused is admissible under section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act. The court relied on the discovery evidence and independent identification evidence to establish the identity of the remains.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the discovery evidence was admissible and, together with the corroborating evidence, established that the remains were those of the deceased.

predicates.identity_of_remains_in_dispute: The identity of recovered human remains is disputed in the proceeding.
predicates.discovery_at_accused_instance: The remains are discovered at the instance of an accused.
predicates.independent_evidence_identifies_remains: Independent evidence, such as identifying features or associated personal effects, supports the identity of the remains.

members.legal_issue: A tenant cannot deduct or adjust repair expenses against rent when the tenant's claim to recover those expenses is barred by limitation.
material_facts: A tenant claimed that amounts spent on repairs to rented premises should be adjusted against rent arrears.
The claim to recover some of the repair expenses had become barred by limitation.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rents Act, 1957, as explained in Maganlal v. Chandrakant, deduction is a mode of recovery; when recovery by suit is barred, recovery by deduction is barred as well. The same principle applies to adjustment of repair expenses against rent, since it would be anomalous for one mode of recovery to remain available after the other is barred.
members.conclusion: Repair expenses that the tenant can no longer recover because of limitation cannot be adjusted against rent due.

predicates.landlord_tenant_rent_arrears_case: A landlord brought a proceeding to recover rent arrears from a tenant.
predicates.tenant_repair_cost_claim_time_barred: A tenant sought to recover repair expenses, but the claim for those expenses was barred by limitation.
predicates.time_barred_repair_cost_cannot_be_set_of: A tenant cannot apply repair expenses that are no longer recoverable against rent due.

members.legal_issue: An overpayment of rent cannot be deducted from later rent after the right to recover that overpayment has become time-barred.
material_facts: The tenant paid rent in excess of the standard rent up to August 4, 1954.
The tenant did not deduct the overpayments from rent within six months of payment and instead later sued to recover them.
The tenant did not pay rent falling due after August 4, 1954.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rents Control Act, 1947 gives a tenant six months from payment to recover overpaid rent, including by deduction from rent payable. Deduction is a mode of recovery and is subject to the same limitation as recovery by suit. The Court approved Sohrab Tavaria v. Jafferali, 58 Bom. L.R. 680, 687–88, and Karamsey Kanji v. Velji Virji, 56 Bom. L.R. 619, 626, and referred to Bayley v. Walker, [1925] 1 K.B. 447.
members.conclusion: The overpayments could not be deducted from or adjusted against rent falling due after August 4, 1954, and the rent was in arrears.

rule.if: tenant_rent_arrears_dispute and excess_rent_paid and overpayment_not_deducted_within_recovery_period and recovery_right_time_barred

predicates.tenant_rent_arrears_dispute: The case concerns a tenant’s alleged arrears of rent.
predicates.excess_rent_paid: The tenant paid more than the rent legally due.
predicates.overpayment_not_deducted_within_recovery: The tenant did not deduct the overpayment from rent while it remained recoverable.
predicates.recovery_right_time_barred: The tenant’s right to recover the overpayment had become time-barred.

members.legal_issue: A compromise award made by a Lok Adalat cannot serve as the court award required for redetermination of compensation for another landholder.
material_facts: The landholders seeking redetermination had not sought enhancement through a reference of their own under the land acquisition law.
A different landholder's compensation reference was referred to a Lok Adalat, where the parties agreed to a settlement fixing enhanced compensation.
The Lok Adalat recorded the compromise as its award; the reference court did not independently adjudicate the compensation claim or make an award under Part III of the land acquisition law.
members.legal_principle: Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires an award under Part III resulting from adjudication by the Court defined in that Act. Sections 18, 23 and 26 reflect the reference, assessment and reasoned award contemplated by that scheme. Under Sections 19 and 20 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, a Lok Adalat facilitates compromise or settlement and has no adjudicatory role: State of Punjab v. Jalour Singh and Union of India v. Ananto. The Court approved Umadevi Rajkumar Jeure and the relevant view in Vasudave. The beneficial purpose of Section 28A does not permit extending its text beyond the award it specifies; Union of India v. Hansoli Devi explains the interpretation of that provision.
members.conclusion: An application for redetermination of compensation cannot be maintained on the basis of an award passed by a Lok Adalat under the Legal Services Authorities Act.

predicates.compensation_redetermination_claim: A person seeks redetermination of compensation by relying on another person's compensation award.
predicates.lok_adalat_award_is_compromise_based: The award relied on was made by a Lok Adalat after the parties agreed to a compromise or settlement.
predicates.award_not_independently_adjudicated_by_c: The court with authority to adjudicate the compensation claim did not independently determine it and issue its own award.

members.legal_issue: The statutory treatment of a Lok Adalat award as a decree does not convert it into an adjudicated court award for a third party's compensation redetermination claim.
material_facts: The award relied on was the Lok Adalat's own award recording a compromise, rather than an award independently made by the referring court.
A person who was not a party to that compromise sought to use the award to support redetermination of compensation.
members.legal_principle: Section 21 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 deems a Lok Adalat award to be a decree of a civil court or, as the case may be, an order of another court. The fiction must be given effect for its statutory purpose but cannot be extended beyond that purpose or enlarged by importing another fiction. The Court relied on K.N. Govindan Kutty Menon v. C.D. Shaji for the award's enforceability, and on the principles of statutory fiction discussed in State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu, including State of W.B. v. Sadan K. Bormal. Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act requires an adjudicated award under Part III, not merely an enforceable Lok Adalat award.
members.conclusion: The decree fiction attached to a Lok Adalat award serves to make the award enforceable and does not make it an award of a court under Part III of the land acquisition law for purposes of third-party redetermination.

predicates.third_party_redetermination_claim: A person seeks a compensation benefit based on an award made in a dispute to which that person was not a party.
predicates.lok_adalat_award_is_compromise_based: The award relied on was made by a Lok Adalat after the disputing parties agreed to a compromise or settlement.
predicates.claimant_not_party_to_award: The person seeking the benefit was not a party to the compromise recorded in the award.

members.legal_issue: A fixed asset belonging to the owner of a mine and assigned as a staff vehicle for the mine falls within the statutory definition of a mine and vests in the Central Government upon nationalisation.
material_facts: The vehicle belonged to the company that owned the mine.
The vehicle was a fixed asset and had been placed at the disposal of the mine’s Technical Advisor as his staff car.
The mine was nationalised, and the dispute concerned whether the vehicle vested with it.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(h)(xii) and 3(1) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 provide for vesting of fixed assets, movable or immovable, belonging to the owner of a mine, wherever situated. Whether an asset falls within the definition depends on whether it answers that description. The Court noted that fixed assets are assets held for conducting a business, as discussed in Words & Phrases, Permanent Edition, Volume 17, page 161, Black’s Law Dictionary, 5th edition, page 573, and Stroud’s Judicial Dictionary, 4th edition, Volume 1, page 201.
members.conclusion: The staff car was a fixed asset belonging to the mine owner and fell within the definition of a mine under Section 2(h)(xii) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973. It therefore vested in the Central Government under Section 3(1).

rule.if: mine_nationalisation_vesting_case and asset_is_fixed and asset_belongs_to_mine_owner and asset_assigned_as_mine_staff_vehicle

predicates.mine_nationalisation_vesting_case: The proceeding concerns whether an asset connected with a mine vested in the government following nationalisation.
predicates.asset_is_fixed: The asset was held for conducting a business rather than for conversion into cash.
predicates.asset_belongs_to_mine_owner: The asset was owned by the person or entity that owned the mine.
predicates.asset_assigned_as_mine_staff_vehicle: The asset was assigned for use as a staff vehicle by an officer serving the mine.

members.legal_issue: A contractor engaged to work a nationalised mine is treated as an owner for vesting purposes, so assets installed or brought into the mine for its operation vest with the mine.
material_facts: The contractors had agreements to work the collieries, including a long-term agreement giving them substantial control over one colliery.
The contractors were entitled to, and in fact had, actual possession and enjoyment of the collieries.
They installed machinery, plants and equipment and brought other assets into the mines for their operation.
The mines were taken over and nationalised, and the contractors claimed that their assets had not vested because they were not owners.
members.legal_principle: The Nationalisation Act, s. 3(n), incorporates the definition of owner in the Mines Act, 1952, s. 2(1). That definition includes an occupier and treats a contractor for working a mine as if the contractor were an owner. The legal fiction must be given its full effect and carried to its logical consequences, as stated in East End Dwelling Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council. The Court distinguished The Chief Inspector of Mines v. Lala Karamchand Thapar because the contractors here possessed and controlled the mines in their own right. The separate definition of managing contractor in s. 3(i) of the Nationalisation Act serves the compensation-apportionment provision in s. 26(2) and does not narrow the meaning of owner for vesting under s. 4(1).
members.conclusion: The contractors fell within the statutory meaning of owner, and the assets used in the mines vested in the Central Government.

rule.if: nationalisation_vesting_proceeding and mine_working_contractor and (contractor_actual_occupier or contractor_substantially_controlled_mine) and assets_used_in_mine

predicates.nationalisation_vesting_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether interests in a mine and assets used in it pass to the state under a nationalisation measure.
predicates.mine_working_contractor: A contractor was engaged to work the mine or a part of it.
predicates.contractor_actual_occupier: The contractor was in actual possession and occupation of the mine.
predicates.contractor_substantially_controlled_mine: The contractor exercised substantial control over the mine's operations.
predicates.assets_used_in_mine: The disputed assets were installed or brought into the mine for use in its operation.

members.legal_issue: A claim that acquisition proceedings concerning part of the land lapsed for want of possession and an award fails when the record shows that possession covered the whole land and an award covered the acquisition.
material_facts: A challenger asserted that the authorities had not taken possession of a portion of the acquired land and that no award related to that portion.
The Court found that possession of the entire land had been delivered to the authority and that the proceeding of 31 July 1984 was an award in substance.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(1), 11 and 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, taking possession under the urgency procedure vests the land, and the Court found that the award proceeding covered the acquisition. The Court also relied on the prior decision in Ajodhya Bhagat v. State of Bihar, AIR 1974 SC 1886, in concluding that the contention about possession was against the record.
members.conclusion: The contention that proceedings relating to a portion of the land had lapsed was rejected as contrary to the record.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and party_claims_partial_nonpossession and record_shows_entire_land_delivered and award_covers_acquisition

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns proceedings to acquire land.
predicates.party_claims_partial_nonpossession: A party asserts that possession was not taken of part of the land covered by the acquisition.
predicates.record_shows_entire_land_delivered: The record establishes that possession of the whole acquired land was delivered to the acquiring authority.
predicates.award_covers_acquisition: An award in substance relates to the acquisition at issue.

members.legal_issue: A claim that part of acquired land was left unacquired cannot succeed where the whole extent was notified and a final prior judgment has determined that the whole extent was acquired.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications covered the entire survey extent, including the portion claimed by the appellants to have been left out.
The records showed that the disputed eight-gunta portion was kharab-B land, while compensation had been awarded for the revenue-paying portion.
A prior civil suit raising the same contention was dismissed, and the dismissal was confirmed on appeal; the appellate finding that the entire extent had been acquired had become final.
The appellants later raised the same contention in their writ proceedings.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the acquisition notifications and records showing that the whole extent was included and that the disputed portion was kharab-B land, for which compensation was not payable. It also applied the finality of the prior appellate judgment. The earlier appeal had treated the suit as impliedly barred under Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure because the acquisition had become final and conclusive. The Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Section 18, was part of the compensation-reference history but was not the basis for reopening the acquisition issue.
members.conclusion: The entire extent, including the disputed kharab-B land, had been acquired; no compensation was payable for that kharab-B portion. The final prior appellate finding was binding, and the writ court could not sit in appeal over it.

predicates.acquisition_dispute_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a claim that land was not included in an acquisition.
predicates.land_extent_included_in_acquisition_noti: The acquisition notifications covered the whole land extent, including the portion later claimed to have been left out.
predicates.disputed_portion_is_kharab_land: The records identify the disputed portion as kharab land for which compensation was not payable.
predicates.prior_final_judgment_determined_entire_e: A final judgment in earlier litigation determined that the acquisition covered the entire extent.

members.legal_issue: Accepting compensation under protest preserves the ability to seek a reference on award matters but does not, by itself, show that the claimant preserved a challenge to the acquisition.
material_facts: The claimant accepted the Collector’s compensation under protest and applied for enhancement before the competent court.
The claimant’s writ petition challenging the acquisition was filed after the award and approximately five years after the notification.
The Court found that the protest was made to preserve the right to seek a reference on matters covered by the award, not to safeguard a challenge to the acquisition.
members.legal_principle: Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, allows an interested person to seek a reference only if that person has not accepted the award. Acceptance of compensation under protest indicates non-acceptance for that purpose, because acceptance without protest may result in loss of the right to a reference on matters covered by Section 18.
members.conclusion: The claimant’s acceptance of compensation under protest protected the remedy of reference concerning award matters; it did not establish that he had preserved a challenge to the acquisition itself.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_dispute: The proceeding concerns compensation awarded for acquired land.
predicates.compensation_accepted_under_protest: The claimant accepted the awarded compensation while expressly maintaining a protest.
predicates.claimant_seeks_reference_on_award_matter: The claimant seeks a reference for determination of matters relating to the award.

members.legal_issue: Accepting compensation under protest and without prejudice does not make the compensation determination final or estop a recipient from challenging it.
material_facts: The recipients did not file objections to the compensation assessed and accepted the compensation paid under protest and without prejudice.
Government circulars directed compensation officers to await the outcome of references and appeals against the agricultural tax assessments before finalising compensation.
The State argued that the lack of objections and acceptance of payment made the compensation final and barred a challenge.
members.legal_principle: A payment accepted under protest and without prejudice is not an unconditional acceptance that bars a challenge. Where government circulars direct officers to await related tax proceedings, the compensation is not final while those proceedings remain unresolved.
members.conclusion: The compensation had not become final, and its acceptance under protest and without prejudice did not estop the recipients from challenging it.

predicates.compensation_assessment_case: A compensation assessment is being made while a related agricultural tax assessment may affect the amount.
predicates.government_directed_wait_for_tax_appeals: The government directed compensation officers to wait for the outcome of related tax references or appeals before finalising compensation.
predicates.compensation_accepted_under_protest: The recipient accepted the compensation payment expressly under protest and without prejudice.

members.legal_issue: A court hearing a statutory reference may not decide legal questions that were not referred to it by the tribunal.
material_facts: The tribunal referred a question about whether income from property transferred to the assessee’s wife for consideration could be assessed as the assessee’s income.
The referred question proceeded on the basis that the transfer was valid.
The High Court reframed the matter to address whether an oral transfer in satisfaction of dower debt was legally possible, as well as whether the income was assessable.
The High Court did not call for a fresh statement of the case from the tribunal.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, the High Court’s role in a reference is limited to giving its opinion on questions of law referred by the tribunal. If the question referred does not bring out the real issue, the High Court may call for a fresh statement of the case rather than decide unreferenced questions.
members.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by raising and deciding questions that did not flow from the question referred. If the referred question did not identify the real issue, the High Court could have called for a fresh statement of the case.

predicates.statutory_reference_proceeding: A tribunal has referred a question of law to a court for an opinion under a statutory reference procedure.
predicates.court_decides_unreferred_question: The court decides a legal question that the tribunal did not refer.
predicates.court_reframes_question_beyond_referred_: The court reframes the referred question to address an issue that does not flow from it.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court reviewing a decision made in a statutory reference has no wider authority to consider issues than the reference court.
material_facts: The department argued before the Supreme Court that the transfer was invalid and that the account of the transaction was unbelievable.
The validity and evidentiary support of the transfer were not questions referred to the High Court.
The appeal arose from the High Court’s decision in a statutory reference.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal from a High Court’s decision on a reference under Section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, the Supreme Court’s advisory jurisdiction is no more extensive than the High Court’s; it cannot consider questions outside the reference.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court could not consider the department’s arguments about the transfer’s invalidity or credibility because its jurisdiction was subject to the same limits as the High Court’s jurisdiction in the reference.

predicates.appeal_from_statutory_reference: An appeal arises from a court’s decision on a question referred under a statutory reference procedure.
predicates.disputed_issue_outside_referred_question: A party asks the appellate court to decide an issue that was not included in the question referred.

members.legal_issue: A scheme-making procedure for a religious institution that provides for judicial inquiry and an appeal to a court does not impose an unreasonable restriction on the head of the institution’s property rights.
material_facts: The challenged law required an initial inquiry by an Assistant Commissioner holding judicial office, followed by an inquiry by a Commissioner who was a judicial officer of at least the rank of a Subordinate Judge.
The Commissioner’s inquiry was, so far as applicable, to follow the Code of Civil Procedure rules for the trial of suits.
The law provided an appeal to the High Court in broad terms, permitting challenges on facts and law.
The earlier procedure had been invalidated because an executive officer could settle a scheme without judicial intervention or a right of appeal.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) protects the property interest of a head of a Math, although reasonable restrictions may be imposed in the public interest. A scheme-making process is not an unreasonable restriction merely because the initial decision is made by a Commissioner rather than through a separate civil suit, if the affected person can present the case in a judicial inquiry and has a regular appeal to a court. The Court applied Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Math ([1954] S.C.R. 1005) and distinguished Mahant Sri Jagannath Ramanuj Das v. The State of Orissa ([1954] S.C.R. 1046).
members.conclusion: The scheme-making provisions were not unconstitutional as unreasonable restrictions on the heads’ property rights.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_scheme_procedure and judicial_officers_conduct_the_inquiries and inquiry_follows_civil_trial_procedure and broad_court_appeal_is_available

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_scheme_proce: A person challenges the constitutionality of a process for settling a scheme for a religious institution.
predicates.judicial_officers_conduct_the_inquiries: The preliminary and principal inquiries are conducted by officers holding judicial office.
predicates.inquiry_follows_civil_trial_procedure: The principal inquiry follows, so far as applicable, the procedures used in a civil trial.
predicates.broad_court_appeal_is_available: An affected person can appeal to a court on factual and legal grounds.

members.legal_issue: A statutory process for removing a religious institution’s head, including suspension during an inquiry, does not violate equality or the right to hold and enjoy property when it is based on misconduct or unfitness and includes procedural safeguards.
material_facts: The officeholder faced charges concerning alleged misappropriation and defalcation of trust funds, as well as leading an immoral life.
He was suspended while the charges were investigated.
The inquiry was quasi-judicial, and an order of removal could be challenged in court, with a further appeal to the High Court.
The suspension was intended to prevent interference with evidence or other conduct that could defeat the inquiry.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 14 and 19(1)(f), restrictions must be reasonable and in the interest of the general public. A head of a math holds property subject to duties as a trustee and may be removed for relevant misconduct or incapacity. The Court relied on The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Shirur Mutt, [1954] S.C.R. 1005, and H. H. Sudhundra Thirtha Swamiar v.
