Commissioner for Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Mysore, [1963] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 302. It held that changing the removal procedure to a quasi-judicial inquiry, subject to court review and appeal, was not unconstitutional, and that suspension during the inquiry was a necessary and reasonable safeguard.
members.conclusion: The challenged removal and suspension provisions imposed reasonable restrictions in the interest of the general public and did not violate Articles 14 or 19(1)(f) of the Constitution.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and charges_concern_unfitness_or_trust_misconduct and officeholder_suspended_during_inquiry and inquiry_has_review_safeguards

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A person challenged the constitutionality of a process for removing or suspending the head of a religious institution.
predicates.charges_concern_unfitness_or_trust_misco: The officeholder faced charges concerning incapacity, failure to perform duties, breach of trust, misuse of institutional property, or other relevant misconduct.
predicates.officeholder_suspended_during_inquiry: The authority suspended the officeholder while an inquiry into the charges was pending.
predicates.inquiry_has_review_safeguards: The authority conducted a quasi-judicial inquiry, and the resulting removal decision could be challenged in court with a further appeal available.

members.legal_issue: The legislature may deem previously framed schemes to have been settled under a later law, while providing a new appeal, without impermissibly overriding a judicial determination of unconstitutionality or impairing access to constitutional remedies.
material_facts: Schemes had been framed under an earlier law during a period when the procedure lacked the judicial appeal later required by the Court’s ruling.
The legislature provided that the schemes would be treated as settled under the later law and gave affected persons an appeal to the High Court.
The provision did not deem the schemes valid under the earlier law as it then stood; it treated them as schemes under the later law.
The affected persons remained able to seek relief under Article 32, and the petitions were considered on their merits.
members.legal_principle: A legislature cannot override unconstitutionality by declaring a measure valid under the law that existed when it was made. It may, however, enact a competent new law that adopts prior acts by deeming them to have been taken under that new law, subject to the new law’s procedures and remedies. Such legislation does not take away the Article 32 remedy merely because the legal basis for an earlier constitutional challenge has been changed. The Court applied Article 32 and distinguished the invalidity ruling in Mahant Sri Jagannath Ramanuj Das v. The State of Orissa ([1954] S.C.R. 1046).
members.conclusion: The provision deeming the earlier schemes to have been settled under the later law was within legislative competence and did not improperly interfere with the Court’s jurisdiction or the right to seek relief under Article 32.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_legislative_adoption_of_prior_schemes and prior_schemes_were_given_new_legal_basis and appeal_under_new_law_is_available and constitutional_remedy_remains_available

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_legislative_: A person challenges a law that adopts previously framed schemes by deeming them to have been made under a later legal regime.
predicates.prior_schemes_were_given_new_legal_basis: The law treats the earlier schemes as having been settled under the new regime rather than as valid under the former regime when they were made.
predicates.appeal_under_new_law_is_available: The law provides an appeal against an adopted scheme under the new regime.
predicates.constitutional_remedy_remains_available: A person remains able to seek a constitutional remedy against the adopted scheme.

members.legal_issue: Deeming previously framed schemes to have been settled under a later law does not impose an unreasonable property restriction when the affected persons retain an appeal and the earlier proceedings provided substantially equivalent safeguards.
material_facts: The later law provided a right of appeal against the schemes and allowed a period to bring that appeal.
Although the earlier procedure did not include a preliminary inquiry by an Assistant Commissioner, the schemes had in fact been settled by a judicial officer.
The procedure actually followed under the earlier rules was consistent with the civil-trial procedure used under the later law.
The earlier schemes had been framed jointly by the Commissioner and one or more government officers, providing a safeguard absent from the later procedure.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) requires consideration of whether the procedure, taken as a whole, unreasonably restricts the protected property interest. A deeming provision is not unreasonable merely because it does not reproduce every procedural step of the later law where a court appeal is provided and the actual earlier proceedings had substantially equivalent safeguards. The Court applied the principles in Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Math ([1954] S.C.R. 1005) and Mahant Sri Jagannath Ramanuj Das v. The State of Orissa ([1954] S.C.R. 1046).
members.conclusion: The deeming provision did not place the affected persons at a substantial procedural disadvantage and was not an unreasonable restriction on their property rights.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_deemed_schem: A person challenges a law that treats schemes framed under an earlier regime as having been settled under a later regime.
predicates.appeal_is_available: An affected person can appeal against the scheme to a court.
predicates.earlier_inquiry_was_conducted_by_judicia: The officer who conducted the earlier scheme inquiry held judicial office.
predicates.earlier_procedure_followed_civil_trial_p: The procedure actually used in the earlier inquiry was consistent with civil-trial practice.
predicates.earlier_process_had_additional_participa: The earlier scheme process included participation by one or more additional officials alongside the decision-maker.

members.legal_issue: A compensation officer’s authority to determine proprietary rights in property vested in the State does not extend to deciding competing private claims to the compensation based on rival titles.
material_facts: Property vested in the State under the land-abolition legislation, and a compensation officer made a summary order concerning compensation for it.
The rival claimants asserted competing private titles to the property and the resulting compensation.
No timely civil suit was brought to set aside the compensation officer’s order.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3, 14 and 35(7) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1951, distinguish the State’s liability to pay compensation from private disputes over entitlement to compensation. Section 14 permits summary determination of proprietary rights in the property as against the State; it does not confer jurisdiction to determine competing private claims founded on rival titles. Section 35(7) preserves the ability of another person to enforce rights against the person paid by due process of law.
members.conclusion: The compensation officer’s order did not finally determine the competing private claims to compensation, and the civil court could decide which claimant was entitled to it.

rule.if: abolition_compensation_proceeding and compensation_officer_made_summary_order and competing_private_title_claims and claim_to_compensation_is_against_recipient

predicates.abolition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute arises in a proceeding to determine compensation after proprietary rights in property have vested in the State under an abolition scheme.
predicates.compensation_officer_made_summary_order: A compensation officer made a summary order concerning proprietary rights or compensation for the vested property.
predicates.competing_private_title_claims: Two or more private claimants assert competing titles to the property or the compensation derived from it.
predicates.claim_to_compensation_is_against_recipie: A claimant seeks to enforce an entitlement to compensation against the person who received or is to receive it.

members.legal_issue: An administrative officer cannot adjudicate disputed private title claims in order to determine that property has escheated to the government.
material_facts: The government claimed that property registered in the name of an individual had escheated because that individual had died without an heir.
A trust claimed an interest in the property based on its account of the acquisition, a will, a declaration by the registered owner, and its long management and occupation of the property.

The competing claims raised disputed questions about the source of the purchase funds, the validity and effect of documents, the identity and death of the registered owner, and the existence of heirs.
The Collector resolved those factual disputes and ordered that possession be taken, although the governing escheat provision supplied no procedure for adjudicating disputed questions of title.
members.legal_principle: Section 29 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, provides for government devolution when an intestate leaves no qualified heir, and the government takes subject to the obligations and liabilities to which an heir would have been subject. Escheat requires a total absence of heirs, and the burden of establishing that absence rests heavily on the party asserting escheat; the Court relied on State of Punjab v Balwant Singh and State of Bihar v Radha Krishna Singh, which also emphasizes public notice before entertaining an escheat claim. A state authority cannot exercise adjudicatory powers over private civil disputes unless the law confers them; such title disputes fall within ordinary civil jurisdiction under Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, unless excluded by law. The Administrators-General Act, 1963, including Sections 7 and 9–12, 14 and 20, provides for estate protection and administration through applications to, and adjudication by, the High Court; it does not confer judicial power on the Collector. The Court also relied on Rambir Das v Kalyan Das and Mahant Sital Das v Sant Ram concerning the devolution and regulation of religious endowments.
members.conclusion: The Collector acted in excess of jurisdiction by adjudicating the competing claims. The Collector’s order was set aside, without the Court determining whether the trust had valid title; disputed title matters must be pursued in a competent civil court.

rule.if: administrative_escheat_proceeding and administrative_officer_decides_property_claim and competing_private_title_claims and disputed_facts_require_title_adjudication

predicates.administrative_escheat_proceeding: An administrative proceeding is used to determine whether property should pass to the government because an owner allegedly died without an heir.
predicates.administrative_officer_decides_property_: An administrative officer resolves who owns or is entitled to property.
predicates.competing_private_title_claims: A private person or entity asserts an interest in property contrary to the government’s claim.
predicates.disputed_facts_require_title_adjudicatio: The competing claims depend on contested facts that require adjudication of title or entitlement.

members.legal_issue: A recurring allowance granted in consideration of relinquishing rights in land and land revenue, but not itself constituting an interest in land or land revenue, is not extinguished merely because the land estates vest in the State.
material_facts: The allowance arose from a compromise of a civil dispute over the resumption of rights in land and was granted in consideration of relinquishing those rights.

The allowance relating to the settled villages was calculated as a share of net revenue, but the Government collected the entire land revenue and the recipients had no interest or obligation in its collection.
The allowance was described as a pension and was paid annually; its amount was measured by reference to revenue rather than being a right to that revenue.

The recipient's right to the allowance was not an estate or an assignment of land revenue recorded in the relevant revenue records, and the statutory compensation scheme did not provide compensation for that allowance.
The dispute concerned the effect of statutory vesting of land estates on a pre-existing allowance.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 6(b) of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, vesting extinguishes estates and rights or privileges directly connected with land in an estate or its land revenue. An allowance granted as consideration for extinguishing a former right to land or land revenue is distinct from such a right, even when its amount is measured by reference to revenue. Sections 37–45 provide for compensation to specified intermediaries; section 45 is a machinery provision and does not enlarge the rights extinguished under section 6. A person receiving this kind of allowance is not, by that fact alone, an assignee of land revenue for purposes of section 32(a)–(d) of the U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The allowance granted in consideration for relinquishing rights in the settled villages was not extinguished by the vesting of the estates, and the order requiring its continued payment was confirmed.

predicates.statutory_estate_vesting_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a statutory vesting of land estates extinguished a pre-existing right.
predicates.allowance_granted_for_relinquishing_land: The government granted an allowance in consideration for the recipient or a predecessor relinquishing rights in land or its revenue.
predicates.allowance_recipient_has_no_interest_in_u: The recipient had no interest in the land or in collecting or receiving the land revenue used as a reference for the allowance.
predicates.allowance_amount_only_measures_underlyin: The allowance amount was calculated by reference to land revenue, but that calculation served only as a measure of the allowance.
predicates.allowance_not_recorded_as_land_revenue_a: The recipient's allowance was not recorded as an assignment of land revenue in the relevant revenue records.

members.legal_issue: A permanent allowance paid in lieu of former proprietary rights does not cease merely because the estates in which the recipient formerly held proprietary interests vest in the State.
material_facts: The recipient had long received a permanent allowance in lieu of proprietary rights in land formerly held by him.
The estates in which he held proprietary interests vested in the State after a vesting notification.
The State stopped paying the allowance on the ground that it had vested along with the estates.
Cess had been deducted from the allowance, but the Court held that this did not establish that the allowance was an interest in the estates.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 3 and 4(a) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, vesting transferred the estate and the interests in it, but did not extinguish a separate permanent monetary allowance granted in lieu of former proprietary rights. The Court relied on State of Uttar Pradesh v. Kunwar Sri Trivikram Narain Singh, which held that an allowance paid for abandonment of rights in estates was not itself an interest in land. It also considered the historical character of permanent malikana as a compensatory, pensionary grant.
members.conclusion: The allowance was not an interest in the estates that vested and did not cease on their vesting; the State remained obliged to pay it.

predicates.appeal_from_order_enforcing_allowance_pa: The matter is an appeal from an order requiring payment of an allowance.
predicates.estates_vested_in_state: The estates in which the recipient held proprietary interests passed to the State under a vesting process.
predicates.permanent_allowance_paid_for_former_prop: The recipient received a permanent allowance in consideration of proprietary rights in land that had been lost.
predicates.allowance_is_separate_from_vested_estate: The allowance was not an interest in, income from, or charge on the estates that vested.

members.legal_issue: A party’s ability to develop acquired land and realize its potential is not a relevant factor in determining compensation by reference to a hypothetical sale.
material_facts: Land was acquired and compensation was determined by reference to comparable land sales.

The High Court declined to rely on an earlier compensation determination based on sales of developed plots, reasoning that the other landowner could develop the land and realize its potential better than the claimants.
The claimants relied on that compensation determination for their acquired land.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, compensation is assessed on the basis of a hypothetical sale at or about the notification date between a willing seller and a willing buyer, absent other factors that would depress or augment the price. The particular parties’ ability or inability to develop the land and realize its potential is not relevant. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred by treating a particular landowner’s ability to develop the land and realize its potential as relevant to its value for compensation.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.development_capacity_used_to_raise_value: The valuation treated a party’s ability to develop the land and realize its potential as a reason to increase its value.
predicates.development_capacity_used_to_lower_value: The valuation treated a party’s inability to develop the land and realize its potential as a reason to decrease its value.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land must be assessed without treating a particular owner’s ability to develop the land and realise its potential as a relevant factor.
material_facts: The acquired land was valued by reference to a sale of comparable land shortly before the acquisition notification, with an adjustment for the passage of time and rise in land values.
The claimants relied on compensation awarded for similar nearby land, which had been assessed using sales of developed plots and a deduction for development costs.
The High Court discounted that comparison largely because the other landowner was better able to develop the land and realise its potential.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, compensation is assessed by reference to a hypothetical sale of similar land, at or about the time of the notification, between a willing seller and a willing buyer. Factors that would depress or augment the price, such as an urgent need for money or a special-purpose need for the land, may be considered, but a particular party’s ability or inability to develop the land and realise its potential is not relevant. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred by relying on a particular landowner’s ability to develop the land and realise its potential when determining compensation.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by the government.
predicates.high_court_relied_on_individual_developm: The High Court relied on a particular landowner’s ability to develop the land and realise its potential when assessing compensation.
predicates.individual_development_ability_is_not_re: A particular landowner’s ability to develop the land and realise its potential is not treated as relevant to compensation.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may set aside confirmation of a winding-up sale where the confirming judge failed to consider that bidders left after the liquidators delayed the resumed auction, and the remaining bidding produced a substantially lower price.
material_facts: At the first auction, a bidder offered the highest price but did not immediately make the required deposit.
The liquidators allowed that bidder time to return with the deposit, and several other bidders left before the auction resumed.
At the resumed auction, the successful bidder offered substantially less than the earlier highest bid.
The company judge confirmed the resumed-auction sale without considering that bidders had left; the Division Bench set the confirmation aside and ordered a resale.
members.legal_principle: A court considering confirmation of a liquidator’s sale must consider material circumstances bearing on whether the sale was fair and whether the interests of those sharing in the proceeds were protected. An appellate court was justified in interfering where the confirming judge overlooked that the delayed resumption caused bidders to leave and the resulting sale price was substantially lower. The Court applied the court-approved sale conditions and the supervision of winding-up sales under section 179(c) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913; it relied on no earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The Division Bench was justified in setting aside confirmation of the sale and directing a resale.

rule.if: appeal_from_sale_confirmation and bidders_left_before_resumed_auction and resumed_sale_price_substantially_lower and confirming_judge_ignored_departed_bidders

predicates.appeal_from_sale_confirmation: A party appeals from a court order confirming a liquidator’s sale in a winding-up proceeding.
predicates.bidders_left_before_resumed_auction: Bidders left after the liquidators delayed resuming the auction while an accepted bidder was given time to pay.
predicates.resumed_sale_price_substantially_lower: The resumed auction produced a sale price substantially below the earlier highest bid.
predicates.confirming_judge_ignored_departed_bidder: The judge confirming the sale did not consider that bidders had left before the resumed auction.

members.legal_issue: Liquidators cannot rely on a sale condition allowing them to put property up for sale again after a failed deposit when their delay in resuming the auction has led bidders to leave under the impression that no further auction will occur.
material_facts: The sale condition required the accepted bidder to make the specified deposit immediately and allowed the liquidators to put the property up for sale again in default.
After the highest bidder failed to pay immediately, the liquidators gave him time to return with the money.
Several bidders left while the liquidators waited, believing the accepted sale would proceed.
The liquidators then resumed the auction without a fresh advertisement.
members.legal_principle: The court-approved condition required immediate payment and permitted the property to be put up for sale again in default. Read in context, that authority did not permit the liquidators to grant an appreciable interval that caused bidders to leave and then resume the auction without fresh advertisement. The Court applied condition 5 of the sale conditions and section 179(c) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913; it relied on no earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: On these facts, the liquidators were not entitled to continue the sale without a fresh advertisement after the interval they allowed for payment.

rule.if: liquidator_sale and accepted_bidder_fails_immediate_deposit and liquidator_allows_payment_interval and bidders_leave_in_reliance_on_expected_sale

predicates.liquidator_sale: A liquidator conducts a sale of company property in a winding-up proceeding.
predicates.accepted_bidder_fails_immediate_deposit: The accepted bidder does not make the required deposit immediately.
predicates.liquidator_allows_payment_interval: The liquidator gives the accepted bidder an appreciable interval to return and pay.
predicates.bidders_leave_in_reliance_on_expected_sa: Other bidders leave because they believe the accepted sale will proceed and there will be no further auction.

members.legal_issue: Factual findings in one tax assessment proceeding do not necessarily prevent their reconsideration in a later assessment proceeding.
material_facts: The Court did not examine whether the tribunal’s factual findings were correct; it accepted them because their validity was not in issue in the reference.
The dispute concerned tax assessment years, and the Court noted that the facts could still be considered in a future assessment.
members.legal_principle: The general rule is that res judicata does not apply to taxation proceedings. Because the Court had not reviewed the correctness of the tribunal’s findings, their correctness could remain open for consideration in a future assessment.
members.conclusion: The Court’s decision did not foreclose reconsideration of the factual findings in a future assessment; generally, res judicata does not apply to taxation proceedings.

predicates.tax_assessment_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the assessment of tax for an assessment period.
predicates.current_court_did_not_review_factual_cor: The court accepted the fact finder's findings without deciding whether they were factually correct.

members.legal_issue: A method used in earlier assessment years does not prevent the tax authority from using the correct method in a later assessment year.
material_facts: The taxpayer said that it had maintained regular accounts and used the original acquisition costs in its business balance sheets in earlier years.
The taxpayer said that the tax department had not allowed a loss based on scaling down the properties’ values in earlier years.
For the assessment year under appeal, the tax officer used the conversion schedule to determine the acquisition costs in Malayan currency.
The Court held that the use of another method in previous years did not prevent the officer from ascertaining and using the correct method for the year under assessment.
members.legal_principle: The correct method may be applied to the assessment year in question notwithstanding a different method used in previous years. The Court relied on its conclusion that a common currency standard was necessary to determine the real profit or loss and approved the reasoning in S. L. N. Sathappa Chettiar v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras, (1959) 35 I.T.R. 641. The dispute arose through the reference procedure under sections 66(1) and 66(2) of the Income-tax Act, but those provisions did not supply the substantive conversion rule.
members.conclusion: The tax officer was not prevented from using the correct method for the assessment year merely because a different method had been used in earlier years.

predicates.income_tax_profit_assessment: A tax assessment requires the profit or loss for the relevant assessment year to be determined.
predicates.prior_year_method_differed: A method different from the one used for the relevant assessment year was used in earlier years.
predicates.current_year_method_is_correct: The method used for the relevant assessment year correctly determines profit or loss on the facts of the transaction.

members.legal_issue: Income received under a managing-agency arrangement formed for the benefit of a joint family belongs to the family while the arrangement continues.
material_facts: Two family members joined a partnership on behalf of and for the benefit of the joint family.
The partnership obtained the company's managing agency, and the family members received commissions and other remuneration under that arrangement.
The receipts were treated as joint-family income, entered in the family accounts, and reported as such before a family dispute arose.
One family member later claimed the income personally and sought to retain part of it for services rendered.
members.legal_principle: The partnership and managing-agency interests were held on behalf of the family, so income earned under those arrangements remained family property while the arrangements continued. Joint-family property cannot be converted into personal property by unilateral declaration. The distinction between a return on family investment and compensation for an individual's services, explained in Raj Kumar Singh Hukum Chandji v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Madhya Pradesh, [1971] 1 SCR 748, informs the characterization of remuneration; the Court also considered the managing-agency agreement's termination under section 87A(2) of the Companies Act.
members.conclusion: Commissions, directors' fees, and managing-agent remuneration received under the arrangement while it continued belonged to the joint family; the member could not retain part as personal income merely because he performed services or declared his intention to treat the income as personal.

rule.if: joint_family_partition_proceeding and family_members_joined_partnership_for_family_benefit and partnership_held_managing_agency and income_received_under_continuing_agency and income_treated_as_family_income

predicates.joint_family_partition_proceeding: The dispute concerns the division or accounting of property claimed to belong to a joint family.
predicates.family_members_joined_partnership_for_fa: Family members joined the partnership as representatives of the family and for its benefit.
predicates.partnership_held_managing_agency: The partnership, rather than an individual family member, held the company's managing-agency arrangement.
predicates.income_received_under_continuing_agency: The disputed income was received under that arrangement while it remained in force.
predicates.income_treated_as_family_income: The family treated the receipts as family income, including in its accounts or tax reporting.

members.legal_issue: Income from family property allotted to members for their enjoyment remains income of the family when the arrangement provides only for maintenance and the income is applied to discharge the family’s maintenance obligation.
material_facts: A Hindu undivided family entered into a family arrangement under which properties were placed in the possession of certain male members for their enjoyment and maintenance.

The arrangement did not disrupt the family’s joint status, give the members absolute rights in the properties, or provide for devolution of those properties; the properties remained family property and could return to the family’s management.
The arrangement could be revised if the family’s circumstances substantially changed.
The family remained responsible for maintaining its members and for other family obligations, and the members used the income from the allotted properties for their maintenance.
The arrangement relieved the family of the expense of maintaining those members, and the members received and applied the income on behalf of the family.
members.legal_principle: Under section 9(1) of the Kerala Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950, agricultural income arising to another person from assets that remain the settlor’s or disponer’s property is deemed to be the settlor’s or disponer’s income. The provision is similar to section 16(1)(c) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922. Applying the test in Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay City v. Sitaldas Tirathdas, income applied after receipt to discharge the assessee’s obligation remains assessable, whereas income diverted by an overriding charge before it reaches the assessee is not. Raja Bejoy Singh Dudhuria v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bengal was explained as a case of diversion by an overriding charge; P. C. Mullick v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bengal was applied to distinguish application of received income. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay v. Makanji Lalji and Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay City v. Ratilal Nathalal were also referred to.
members.conclusion: The income from the allotted properties was deemed to be the family’s agricultural income and was includible in its taxable income.

rule.if: family_income_tax_assessment and assets_remain_family_property and arrangement_provides_only_maintenance and arrangement_is_revisable_on_substantial_change and allotted_income_is_applied_to_family_maintenance and family_is_relieved_of_maintenance_expense

predicates.family_income_tax_assessment: A tax assessment concerns income claimed to belong to a family.
predicates.assets_remain_family_property: The property producing the income remains owned by the family despite being placed in members’ possession.
predicates.arrangement_provides_only_maintenance: The family arrangement gives members enjoyment of property for maintenance without giving them absolute rights in it.
predicates.arrangement_is_revisable_on_substantial_: The arrangement can be changed if the family’s circumstances substantially change.
predicates.allotted_income_is_applied_to_family_mai: Members use income from the allotted property to maintain themselves under the family arrangement.
predicates.family_is_relieved_of_maintenance_expens: The arrangement relieves the family of an obligation to maintain the members receiving the income.

members.legal_issue: A decree concerning immovable property requires registration when it creates a new present right rather than merely declaring a pre-existing right.
material_facts: The decree purported to make the claimant owner in possession of the property after the defendant’s death, although the claimant had no pre-existing right declared by the decree.
The property was the subject matter of the earlier suit, and the decree was not registered.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 17(1) and 17(2)(vi) of the Registration Act, 1908, the exception for a court decree, including a compromise decree, covers a decree declaring a pre-existing right, but not one creating a new present right in immovable property. The court must examine whether the decree records an unqualified present disposition of rights. This accords with Tek Bahadur v. Debi Singh and Maturi Pullaiah v. Maturi Narasimham, which distinguish a document recording an arrangement from one creating rights, and Ratan Lal Sharma v. Purshottam Harit, which requires registration where a decree creates rights in immovable property.
members.conclusion: The exception for court decrees does not exempt a decree that creates a new present right in immovable property from compulsory registration; a decree that merely declares a pre-existing right is treated differently.

predicates.proceeding_tests_registration_of_court_d: A party asks a court to determine whether a decree concerning property must be registered.
predicates.decree_creates_new_present_right: The decree itself gives a party a present right that the party did not already hold.
predicates.immovable_property_meets_registration_th: The decree concerns immovable property of a kind and value for which registration is compulsory.

members.legal_issue: A gift that creates an interest in immovable property for the first time requires compulsory registration even when a court decree is also made concerning the property.
material_facts: The landowner testified that part of the disputed land had been purchased by him and was his self-acquired property.
The Court found that he had gifted this portion to the claimant of his own free will, thereby creating the claimant’s interest in that portion for the first time.
The value of the immovable property exceeded the registration threshold.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(a) of the Registration Act, 1908 requires registration of an instrument that effects a gift of immovable property of the relevant value. Applying Bhoop Singh v. Ram Singh Major, (1995) 5 SCC 709, the Court held that a decree does not remove the registration requirement where the transfer creates a right, title or interest in the property for the first time. This differs from the treatment of the portion recognized under the family settlement under Section 17(2)(vi).
members.conclusion: The gift of the self-acquired portion required compulsory registration.

rule.if: property_transfer_dispute and transfer_is_gift and gift_creates_first_time_interest and immovable_property_exceeds_registration_threshold

predicates.property_transfer_dispute: The proceeding concerns the transfer of rights in immovable property.
predicates.transfer_is_gift: The owner gave the property to another person as a gift.
predicates.gift_creates_first_time_interest: The gift created the recipient’s right in the property for the first time.
predicates.immovable_property_exceeds_registration_: The value of the immovable property is above the threshold at which registration is required.

members.legal_issue: An entry recording possession without payment of rent does not, by itself, establish a historic rent-free grant for purposes of presuming a lost grant.
material_facts: The record of rights described the lands as “Bhog Dakhal Sutre Niskar.”

The applicable settlement instruction directed that land occupied by a person who was not actually paying rent be recorded as Niskar and that the words “Bhog Dakhal Sutre” be added if no rent-free title deed was produced.
The defendants stated that they had been unable to produce a revenue-free grant and that the settlement officers recorded their right in a general way.
members.legal_principle: Under Rule 37 of the Technical Rules and Instructions issued by the Settlement Department, the described entry could record possession without actual payment of rent where no sanad or title deed was produced. In that context, the entry did not establish a grant, and its evidentiary weight could not overcome the finding that the land was part of the assessed estate.
members.conclusion: The record-of-rights entry showed that rent was not actually being paid; it did not prove a rent-free grant and could not support the presumption of a lost pre-settlement grant.

rule.if: lost_grant_dispute and possession_recorded_as_rent_free and no_title_deed_produced and entry_made_to_record_nonpayment

predicates.lost_grant_dispute: The proceeding involves a claim that a grant should be presumed from long possession.
predicates.possession_recorded_as_rent_free: An official land record describes the occupant’s possession as rent-free or uses equivalent wording.
predicates.no_title_deed_produced: The occupant produced no title deed establishing a rent-free grant.
predicates.entry_made_to_record_nonpayment: The entry was made under a recordkeeping practice that described possession without actual rent payment.

members.legal_issue: An entry showing a tenancy at a fixed rent does not, by itself, establish that the tenancy existed from the time of the Permanent Settlement.
material_facts: A record of rights described certain tenancies as being at a fixed rate of rent.
The claimants argued that the entry, read with section 50(2) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885, showed that their ancestors held the plots from the time of the Permanent Settlement.
The circumstances in which the entries were made and whether they concerned the relevant frontier plots had not been investigated.
The point was not raised in the courts below and was raised for the first time at the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: Section 50(2) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885, provides a presumption, in a suit or proceeding under that Act, that a raiyat has held at the same rate of rent since the Permanent Settlement if the rate has not changed during the preceding twenty years. Fixity of rent may also result from an express grant, so an entry recording a fixed rate does not necessarily establish the historical commencement of the tenancy. A new point dependent on uninvestigated circumstances should not be allowed to be raised for the first time at the final appellate stage.
members.conclusion: The fixed-rent entries did not establish that the tenancies dated from the Permanent Settlement, and the Court declined to allow the newly raised point to be argued without the relevant circumstances having been investigated.

rule.if: civil_property_title_appeal and record_shows_fixed_rent and historical_duration_unproved and entry_circumstances_uninvestigated and argument_first_raised_on_final_appeal

predicates.civil_property_title_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a dispute over title to property.
predicates.record_shows_fixed_rent: A land record describes a tenancy as having a fixed rate of rent.
predicates.historical_duration_unproved: The evidence does not establish how long the tenancy or fixed rate had existed.
predicates.entry_circumstances_uninvestigated: The circumstances behind the record entry, or whether it concerns the relevant land, have not been investigated.
predicates.argument_first_raised_on_final_appeal: A party raises the argument for the first time in the final appeal.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking an injunction is not unmaintainable merely because the plaint does not separately seek a declaration of title when the plaint, read as a whole, seeks to establish title as the basis for the injunction.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought a perpetual injunction and expressly pleaded that the land had been transferred to their predecessor and that they were owners in possession.
The plaint relied on the asserted title as the basis for restraining interference, although it did not separately request a declaration of title.
members.legal_principle: To determine the nature of a suit, the entire plaint must be read rather than only its relief portion. Where the plaint as a whole seeks to establish title as the basis for an injunction, the absence of a separately worded prayer for declaration does not make the suit unmaintainable. Court fees are to be assessed in accordance with the suit's nature. No earlier cases or specific provisions were cited.
members.conclusion: The objection that the suit was not maintainable because it did not specifically seek a declaration of title was rejected. The plaint had to be read as a whole, and court fees had to be assessed accordingly.

predicates.injunction_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking an injunction against interference with possession.
predicates.plaint_asserts_title: The plaintiff pleaded title in the plaint as the basis for the requested injunction.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking a declaration of rights together with an injunction is not a suit for a declaration simpliciter merely because the claimed injunction is consequential on the declaration.
material_facts: The claimants sought a declaration of their rights to participate in the endowment’s income and ceremonies and an injunction restraining interference with those rights.
The endowment was managed by trustees, and the claimants sought relief against persons said to obstruct their exercise of the claimed rights.
members.legal_principle: Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act does not require dismissal of a suit seeking a declaration and an injunction; an injunction is further relief. The Court relied on Kunj Behari Prasadji Purshottam Prasadji v. Keshavlal Hiralal, which held that such a suit may be maintainable, while adequacy of the further relief depends on the circumstances of the case.
members.conclusion: The suit was maintainable because it sought an injunction as further relief and was not a suit for a declaration simpliciter.

predicates.declaratory_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking a declaration of a right.
predicates.consequential_injunction_sought: The claimant also sought an injunction to prevent interference with the exercise of that right.

members.legal_issue: Buildings erected bona fide on another’s land with the landowner’s permission do not vest in the landowner merely because they are attached to the soil.
material_facts: The land belonged to the State.
With the State’s permission, a family member used joint-family funds to construct and manage a dharmasala, temple and shops on the land.
The buildings were not shown to have been transferred to the State.
members.legal_principle: The maxim that what is attached to the soil goes with the soil is not an absolute rule of law in India. A person who bona fide constructs buildings on another’s land with permission is not thereby a trespasser, and the buildings do not automatically vest in the landowner. The Court relied on Thakoor Chunder Parmanick v. Ramdhone Bhuttacharjee, Lala Beni Ram v. Kundan Lall, and Narayan Das Khettry v. Jatindranath.
members.conclusion: The State did not acquire ownership of the buildings merely because they stood on State-owned land.

predicates.construction_on_another_persons_land: The construction was erected on land belonging to someone other than the person who arranged or funded it.
predicates.bona_fide_construction: The construction was made bona fide rather than as a trespass.

members.legal_issue: Permission to construct a building does not, by itself, make the occupant’s possession of the land permissive or prevent acquisition of title by adverse possession.
material_facts: The claimant obtained a court’s permission to construct a building while another person’s title suit was pending.
The claimant undertook to vacate the building without compensation if the plaintiff in that suit succeeded.
The State relied on that undertaking to characterize the claimant’s possession as permissive.
members.legal_principle: A permission limited to constructing a building does not establish permission to possess the underlying land. The nature of possession must be assessed independently, and the construction permission does not itself prevent adverse possession if the required possession and hostile intention are otherwise proved.
members.conclusion: The permission to construct the building did not make the claimant’s possession of the land permissive; it did not defeat an adverse-possession claim if its other requirements were satisfied.

predicates.possession_dispute: A proceeding disputes whether an occupant’s possession of land is permissive or adverse.
predicates.court_permission_limited_to_construction: A court permitted the occupant to construct a building, without granting permission to possess the underlying land.

members.legal_issue: A lump-sum payment to perfect title to an income-producing asset is capital expenditure in full when claims to profits are merely ancillary to the claim to the asset.
material_facts: The taxpayer paid a lump sum to the vendor's sons to obtain a release of any claims they had to the mill.
The compromise considered both the sons' possible interest in the mill and their claim to profits from it.
The court found that the payment was made to perfect the taxpayer's title to the mill, a capital asset, and that the profit claim was ancillary to the claim to the asset.
members.legal_principle: Expenditure to acquire or perfect title to a capital asset or an enduring source of income is capital, rather than revenue, expenditure. The Court relied on Atherton v. British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd. and Commissioner of Taxes v. Nchanga Consolidated Copper Mines Ltd., and held that considering a related profit claim when fixing the settlement did not make any part of the lump sum revenue expenditure.
members.conclusion: The entire payment was capital expenditure, no part could be apportioned as a revenue payment, and no portion could be set off against the income being assessed.

rule.if: income_tax_deduction_dispute and lump_sum_release_payment and payment_perfects_title_to_income_producing_asset and profit_claim_is_ancillary

predicates.income_tax_deduction_dispute: A dispute in an income-tax assessment concerns whether a payment may be deducted or set off against assessed income.
predicates.lump_sum_release_payment: The taxpayer made one lump-sum payment to obtain a release of claims relating to an asset.
predicates.payment_perfects_title_to_income_produci: The payment was made to perfect title to an asset that produces income.
predicates.profit_claim_is_ancillary: Any claim to profits was incidental to the claim to the asset rather than a separate basis for the payment.

members.legal_issue: A lump-sum payment made to obtain release of claims to an income-producing asset and perfect title is capital expenditure, even if the claims also included profits, when the profit claim is ancillary and no share of profits is granted.
material_facts: The taxpayer paid a lump sum under a court-approved compromise to the vendor’s sons to obtain release of their claims to the mill and its profits.
The payment was made while litigation challenged the vendor’s title and the taxpayer’s ownership of the mill.
The compromise gave the taxpayer release of the sons’ claims; it did not give them a share in the taxpayer’s profits.
The Court found that the payment was made to perfect title to the mill and that the claim relating to profits was ancillary to the claim to the asset.
members.legal_principle: Under section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, expenditure to acquire or perfect title to a capital asset, remove a defect in title, or end a threat of litigation is capital rather than revenue expenditure. Expenditure to acquire a source of income is capital; a payment does not become partly revenue expenditure merely because income was considered in assessing the fairness of the settlement when the payment acquired the asset and the profit claim was ancillary. The Court applied the enduring-benefit reasoning in Atherton v. British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd. and the distinction between acquiring the income-producing structure and earning income in Commissioner of Taxes v. Nchanga Consolidated Copper Mines Ltd.
members.conclusion: The entire lump-sum payment was capital expenditure, and no part of it could be deducted or set off against the mill income as business expenditure.

rule.if: business_expense_deduction_claim and lump_sum_paid_to_release_asset_claims and payment_perfected_title_to_income_producing_asset and profit_claim_was_ancillary

predicates.business_expense_deduction_claim: The taxpayer claimed a payment as a deductible business expense against income from an asset.
predicates.lump_sum_paid_to_release_asset_claims: The taxpayer paid a lump sum to claimants in return for release of their claims to an asset.
predicates.payment_perfected_title_to_income_produc: The payment was made to perfect the taxpayer’s title to an asset that generated income.
predicates.profit_claim_was_ancillary: The claim relating to profits was ancillary to the claim to the asset, and the settlement did not grant the claimants a share in the taxpayer’s profits.

members.legal_issue: A claim that a decree was procured by fraud cannot be accepted when fraud was neither pleaded nor proved.
material_facts: The respondent alleged in later proceedings that the eviction decree had been obtained by fraud.
The alleged fraud had not been pleaded or proved in the proceedings leading to the decree.
The respondent repeated the fraud allegation in challenging execution of the decree.
members.legal_principle: Fraud must necessarily be pleaded and proved before a court can act on it. The Court considered S.P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath and United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Rajendra Singh, while holding that the general proposition that fraud unravels judicial acts did not assist the respondent without a factual basis.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the fraud allegation because it had no pleaded or proved basis.

rule.if: decree_enforcement_challenge and fraud_alleged and not fraud_pleaded_and_proved

predicates.decree_enforcement_challenge: A party challenged or sought to impede enforcement of a judicial decree.
predicates.fraud_alleged: A party asserted that the decree had been obtained through fraud.
predicates.fraud_pleaded_and_proved: The alleged fraud was properly raised and established with evidence.
predicates.fraud_claim_not_accepted: The court does not accept the fraud claim as a basis for relief.

members.legal_issue: Fraud allegations that do not materially address the security underlying a recovery decree and are unsupported by specific factual particulars do not prevent rejection of a vexatious plaint.
material_facts: The plaintiffs alleged that fraud had been used to create the security and obtain the recovery decree, but the pleaded fraud concerned a partnership deed rather than the guarantor’s guarantee or mortgage.
The criminal proceedings and conviction relied upon concerned the partnership deed; they did not address the guarantee or mortgage, and the bank was not a party to those proceedings.

The plaintiffs claimed through sale deeds executed by the guarantor as an attorney for the original owners, although the property had already been mortgaged; the guarantor did not disclose the alleged sales when later seeking relief from the tribunal decree.
On a meaningful reading of the plaints, the court found the fraud allegations illusory and the suits vexatious and an abuse of process.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the plaint must be read as a whole and meaningfully, and a plaint may be rejected where it discloses no genuine right to sue or is manifestly vexatious. Fraud must be pleaded with specific material particulars; merely using the word “fraud” does not suffice. The Court applied T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal, (1977) 4 SCC 467; Church of Christ Charitable Trust v. Ponniamman Educational Trust, (2012) 8 SCC 706; A.B.C. Laminart Pvt. Ltd. v. A.P. Agencies, (1989) 2 SCC 163; Sopan Sukhdeo Sable v. Assistant Charity Commissioner, (2004) 3 SCC 137; Madanuri Sri Rama Chandra Murthy v. Syed Jalal, (2017) 13 SCC 174; and the Madras High Court decision in M/s Cambridge Solutions Ltd. v. Global Software Ltd., 2016-5-L.W. 45.
members.conclusion: The fraud allegations did not save the suits from rejection; the plaints were vexatious and liable to be rejected.

predicates.civil_suit_seeking_to_avoid_recovery_dec: The plaintiff brought a civil suit seeking to defeat or avoid a decree made in a recovery proceeding.
predicates.fraud_allegations_unconnected_to_securit: The pleaded fraud concerned matters other than the creation or execution of the security relied upon for the recovery decree.
predicates.specific_material_particulars_supporting: The plaintiff pleaded concrete factual particulars and supporting material connecting the alleged fraud to the challenged security or decree.

members.legal_issue: Semi-digested food in a deceased person’s stomach does not, by itself, discredit eyewitness testimony about the time of an attack when stomach contents cannot reliably establish the time of death or eating.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses said that the family had eaten shortly before the attack.
The post-mortem examination found semi-digested food in the deceased’s stomach.
The Court noted that stomach contents cannot be determined with precision at the time of death.
members.legal_principle: Medical evidence about stomach contents cannot precisely establish the time of death or eating, and an uncertain medical observation should not displace otherwise reliable eyewitness testimony. The Court cited no provision or earlier case for this evidentiary principle.
members.conclusion: The medical observation did not contradict the eyewitness account strongly enough to discredit it.

rule.if: appeal_after_reversal_of_acquittal and eyewitnesses_describe_recent_meal and stomach_contents_are_semi_digested and stomach_contents_cannot_fix_timing

predicates.appeal_after_reversal_of_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal following a conviction entered after an earlier acquittal was reversed.
predicates.eyewitnesses_describe_recent_meal: Eyewitnesses said that the deceased and others ate shortly before the attack.
predicates.stomach_contents_are_semi_digested: A medical examination found semi-digested food in the deceased’s stomach.
predicates.stomach_contents_cannot_fix_timing: The medical evidence does not allow the time of eating or death to be determined precisely.

members.legal_issue: Semi-digested food in a deceased person’s stomach does not discredit otherwise reliable eyewitness testimony about the approximate time of a meal and a fatal occurrence when the medical timing evidence is inconclusive.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses testified that the deceased ate a meal at about 10:30 a.m. and that the shooting occurred around noon.
The doctor found semi-solid, undigested food in the stomach and stated that digestion begins after about one to one and a half hours.
The doctor did not specify the extent of the undigested food.
The witnesses’ stated times were approximate, and the evidence did not establish the type or amount of food eaten.
The eyewitnesses’ testimony was otherwise reliable.
members.legal_principle: Medical evidence about digestion is opinion evidence and is not decisive where digestion varies with the individual and with the type and amount of food, and the medical evidence does not specify the extent of digestion. Approximate timing based on such evidence is not enough to discredit otherwise reliable eyewitness testimony.
members.conclusion: The medical evidence did not contradict or discredit the eyewitnesses’ account of the meal and the time of the occurrence.

rule.if: criminal_homicide_case and approximate_meal_time and digestion_varies and medical_timing_unspecific and eyewitnesses_otherwise_reliable

predicates.criminal_homicide_case: The proceeding concerned a prosecution for a fatal assault.
predicates.approximate_meal_time: The witnesses gave an approximate rather than precisely measured time for the deceased’s meal.
predicates.digestion_varies: The evidence showed that digestion differs among people and depends on the type and amount of food.
predicates.medical_timing_unspecific: The doctor did not specify the extent of undigested food or provide a conclusive time for the meal.
predicates.eyewitnesses_otherwise_reliable: The witnesses’ account was otherwise consistent and reliable.

members.legal_issue: Earlier dispositions and partitions remain unaffected by the amendment, and a statutory notional partition arising before commencement does not become subject to the amendment's formal-partition rule.
material_facts: The father died before the amendment commenced, causing succession shares to crystallize under the prior law through a notional partition.
The daughter sought to have those shares redefined under the amendment.
The Court considered the effect of the amendment's provisions concerning dispositions and partitions before the statutory cutoff and the definition of partition.
members.legal_principle: Section 6(1)'s proviso and Section 6(5), including its Explanation, preserve the specified earlier transactions and define partition for the amendment's purposes. The provisions must be read harmoniously with the substantive right and cannot be used to reopen transactions valid under the prior law or to treat a statutory notional partition as a formal partition. The Court relied on the interpretive principles discussed in S. Sundaram Pillai v. R. Pattabiraman and Keshavji Ravji & Co. v. CIT, and on the principle that statutory deeming provisions are given full effect as discussed in Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum.
members.conclusion: Dispositions, alienations and partitions made before the statutory cutoff remain unaffected. A notional partition arising by operation of the prior law is not subject to the amendment's registered-deed-or-court-decree definition. A partition effected after the cutoff is governed by that definition.

predicates.partition_or_succession_claim: A party seeks a share in property affected by a partition or succession.
predicates.pre_cutoff_transaction: A disposition, alienation or partition was made before the cutoff specified for preserving earlier transactions.
predicates.notional_partition_under_prior_law: A partition was deemed to occur by operation of the prior law when succession opened, rather than being effected by a partition deed or court decree.

members.legal_issue: The 2005 amendment to the law governing devolution of coparcenary interests does not affect a partition completed by court decree before the amendment’s protected cutoff.
material_facts: The partition suit was filed in 1998 and a decree was made in 2000.
The 2005 amendment commenced after the decree, and its saving provision protected partitions completed by court decree before the specified cutoff.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 6 as amended in 2005 preserves dispositions, alienations, partitions and testamentary dispositions completed before 20 December 2004; the explanation recognizes a partition effected by a court decree. The amendment commenced on 9 September 2005. Because the decree here preceded the protected cutoff, it was not affected by the amendment.
members.conclusion: The 2005 amendment did not affect the decree in this case and did not govern the parties’ rights.

predicates.appeal_concerning_partition_rights: A party appealed in a proceeding concerning rights to partition property.
predicates.partition_completed_by_court_decree_befo: A court completed the partition by decree before the applicable preservation cutoff.

members.legal_issue: Dumpers and rockers suitable for use on public roads are motor vehicles liable to taxation when used or kept for use within the state.
material_facts: The appellants used dumpers and rockers in their mining operations within their leasehold areas.
The machines had rubber tyres, and materials before the Court showed that dumpers could be permitted to run on public roads, subject to speed limits.
The machines were not shown to be specially adapted for use only in factories or other enclosed premises.

The appellants challenged the tax demands on the ground that the machines were not adapted for use on roads; they did not challenge the validity or retrospectivity of the amending legislation in these appeals.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(b) and 3(1) of the Orissa Motor Vehicles Taxation Act, 1975, a motor vehicle adapted for use on roads is taxable when used or kept for use within the state. Following Bolani Ores Ltd. v. State of Orissa, the word “adapted” means “suitable.” Rubber tyres and the ability to operate on public roads supported the conclusion that the machines were suitable for road use; their weight, limited permitted speeds, or use in mining areas did not make them unsuitable. The exclusion for a vehicle specially adapted for use only in a factory or other enclosed premises did not apply.
members.conclusion: The dumpers and rockers were adapted or suitable for use on roads and were liable to taxation when used or kept for use on public roads; the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: motor_vehicle_tax_appeal and vehicle_has_rubber_tyres and vehicle_can_be_permitted_on_public_roads and not vehicle_adapted_only_for_enclosed_use and vehicle_used_or_kept_for_use_in_state

predicates.motor_vehicle_tax_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a demand for motor vehicle tax on a vehicle.
predicates.vehicle_has_rubber_tyres: The vehicle runs on rubber tyres rather than chain plates.
predicates.vehicle_can_be_permitted_on_public_roads: The vehicle is capable of being permitted to operate on public roads, even if subject to restrictions.
predicates.vehicle_adapted_only_for_enclosed_use: The vehicle is specially adapted for use only in a factory or another enclosed premises.
predicates.vehicle_used_or_kept_for_use_in_state: The vehicle is used or kept for use within the state imposing the tax.
predicates.vehicle_is_liable_to_motor_vehicle_tax: The vehicle is liable to motor vehicle taxation.

members.legal_issue: A state vehicle tax imposed on vehicles used or kept for use within the state applies only to vehicles used or kept for use on the state's public roads.
material_facts: The vehicles were mechanically propelled and suitable for use on roads.
The company claimed that the vehicles were used or kept for use only on roads within its private estates, not on public roads.
The tax provision described its scope by reference to vehicles used or kept for use in the state.
The statutory scheme provided procedures for establishing non-use and obtaining exemption or refund.
members.legal_principle: Entry 57 of List II authorises taxation of vehicles suitable for use on roads, but, applying Bolani Ores Ltd. v. State of Orissa, the taxing power has a nexus with vehicles using public roads. The Court distinguished Bolani Ores on the separate question of how the meaning of “motor vehicle” was incorporated into the Kerala Act.
members.conclusion: The tax was contemplated only for vehicles used or kept for use on public roads; use or keeping for use solely on private estate roads did not, by itself, attract the tax.

predicates.state_vehicle_tax_case: The proceeding concerns a tax imposed by a state on motor vehicles.
predicates.vehicles_suitable_for_roads: The vehicles are suitable for use on roads.
predicates.charging_rule_uses_in_state_language: The charging rule describes taxable vehicles by whether they are used or kept for use within the state.
predicates.taxable_use_is_limited_to_public_roads: The tax applies only where vehicles are used or kept for use on public roads.

members.legal_issue: A widow landlady may seek recovery of premises for her own residence regardless of whether she became a widow before or after the premises were let.
material_facts: The premises had been let by the landlady or her husband.
The landlady was a widow and sought possession for her own residence.
The tenant argued that the special recovery right applied only if the landlady became a widow after the letting.
members.legal_principle: Section 14-D of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, does not distinguish between a landlady who became a widow before letting and one who became a widow afterwards. Its language covers premises let by her or by her husband, and permits recovery when she requires them for her own residence. The Court overruled the contrary Delhi High Court decision in Dr. P.P. Kapur v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The special recovery right is available whether the landlady became a widow before or after the premises were let.

rule.if: widow_specific_recovery_proceeding and widow_landlady and premises_let_by_landlady_or_husband and own_residence_need

predicates.widow_specific_recovery_proceeding: A landlord seeks recovery under a special procedure for a widow landlady.
predicates.premises_let_by_landlady_or_husband: The premises were let by the landlady or by her husband.
predicates.own_residence_need: The landlady requires the premises for her own residence.

members.legal_issue: A widow-landlady’s request to recover premises for her own residence is bona fide when it is genuine rather than a pretext, and her present residence with family elsewhere does not by itself defeat the claim.
material_facts: The widow had no other premises of her own in the city where the rented premises were situated.
She wished to live separately there rather than continue living with her son and his family in another city.
The tenant produced no positive material showing that the stated need was not genuine or was merely an excuse to evict him.
The landlord had sought possession for residence, and the record described family strain and his health-related treatment as circumstances behind the wish to shift.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14-D of the Delhi Rent Control Act, the relevant matters are that the landlady is a widow, requires the premises for her own residence, and makes a bona fide request rather than using the provision as a pretext to get rid of the tenant. V. Rajaswari v. Bombay Tyres International Ltd. held that living with a daughter or another person does not by itself show that premises are not required for the widow’s residence. Under Section 14(1)(e), the requirement must be bona fide and the move to seek eviction genuine. The landlady’s choice must not be whimsical or fanciful, but courts should not impose their own view of how she should arrange her affairs based only on the tenant’s hardship.
members.conclusion: The widow’s need was bona fide, and eviction was ordered.

rule.if: widow_eviction_claim and widow_seeks_own_residence and no_other_owned_premises_nearby and separate_residence_desired and not tenant_produced_evidence_of_pretext

predicates.widow_eviction_claim: A landlady brings an eviction claim under a special ground available to widow-landlords.
predicates.widow_seeks_own_residence: The widow states that she requires the premises as her own residence.
predicates.no_other_owned_premises_nearby: The widow has no other premises of her own in the relevant area.
predicates.separate_residence_desired: The widow wishes to live separately from family members with whom she is presently residing elsewhere.
predicates.tenant_produced_evidence_of_pretext: The tenant produces positive material showing that the asserted need is not genuine and is only an excuse to evict the tenant.

members.legal_issue: The absence of an appeal against some decisions made by an officer under a statute does not, by itself, make the statutory procedure discriminatory or arbitrary.
material_facts: The statute provided appeals to a board for some categories of decisions by the town planning officer but not for the compensation determination at issue.
The town planning officer exercised defined functions as part of implementing the scheme.
A person aggrieved by an order could seek relief under Article 226 of the Constitution.
members.legal_principle: There is no general rule that every decision of every statutory officer must be appealable. A lack of appeal warrants constitutional condemnation only where it is likely to make the procedure oppressive and arbitrary. The Court relied on M/s Babubhai & Co. v. State of Gujarat and noted the availability of relief under Article 226.
members.conclusion: The lack of an appeal against the compensation determination did not make the statutory procedure unconstitutional or confer uncanalised and arbitrary power on the officer.

rule.if: statutory_officer_decision_challenge and appeal_exists_for_some_decisions_but_not_this_one and officer_has_defined_functions and judicial_review_remains_available

predicates.statutory_officer_decision_challenge: The proceeding challenges a statutory process because a decision by an officer cannot be appealed.
predicates.appeal_exists_for_some_decisions_but_not: The statute allows appeals against some decisions by the officer but not against the decision at issue.
predicates.officer_has_defined_functions: The officer performs functions defined by the statutory scheme rather than exercising unbounded authority.
predicates.judicial_review_remains_available: An aggrieved person may seek judicial review of the officer's decision.

members.legal_issue: The absence of an appellate or revisional remedy does not, by itself, make a statutory power of summary eviction arbitrary or invalid.
material_facts: A final town-planning scheme allotted the occupants’ lands for roads and other public purposes, and the lands vested in the local authority.
The local authority issued notices seeking possession from occupants who were no longer entitled to occupy the lands under the scheme.
The power was exercised at the scheme-execution stage by a responsible local authority and required an objective determination by reference to the final scheme.
The occupants were entitled to a hearing and a reasoned order, and an adverse order remained subject to judicial review.
There was no appeal or revision to a superior authority against an eviction order.
members.legal_principle: Whether the absence of corrective machinery makes a power arbitrary or invalid depends on the cumulative effect of relevant factors, including who exercises the power, whether it is exercised objectively, whether natural justice and a speaking order are required, the availability of judicial review, and the enactment’s scheme and purpose. The Court applied Article 14 and the safeguards associated with the quasi-judicial power under section 54 read with Rule 27. It relied on Organo Chemical Industries v. Union of India, where a quasi-judicial power requiring a hearing and reasons was upheld despite the absence of appellate review; it also considered C.R.H. Readymoney Ltd., Chandrakant Krishnarao, Lala Hari Chand Sarda, and Excel Wear, noting that the cumulative circumstances in the cases striking down provisions mattered.
members.conclusion: The absence of an appeal or revision did not, by itself, render the summary-eviction power invalid; the appeals were dismissed and the provision’s validity was upheld.

rule.if: summary_eviction_proceeding and no_internal_appeal and power_given_to_responsible_body and decision_based_on_objective_facts and hearing_required and reasoned_order_required and judicial_review_available

predicates.summary_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns summary eviction of occupants from land they are no longer entitled to occupy.
predicates.no_internal_appeal: The governing arrangement provides no appeal or revision to a superior authority against the eviction decision.
predicates.power_given_to_responsible_body: The power is exercised by a responsible public body rather than a minor or petty officer.
predicates.decision_based_on_objective_facts: The decision depends on objectively determining the occupants’ entitlement by reference to the applicable scheme.
predicates.hearing_required: The occupants must be given an opportunity to be heard before eviction is ordered.
predicates.reasoned_order_required: The decision-maker must issue a speaking order that gives reasons.
predicates.judicial_review_available: The decision remains open to judicial review for such defects as reliance on irrelevant considerations, bad faith, or perversity.

members.legal_issue: A subsequent factual allegation that is admitted or left undisputed need not be proved, although the court may require independent proof in appropriate circumstances.
material_facts: The landlord relied on subsequent changes in family and health circumstances in the revision petition.
The tenant’s engaged counsel did not appear at the revisional hearings and did not challenge those allegations.
The High Court treated the allegations as proved, apparently because they were not challenged.
members.legal_principle: The distinction between pleading and proof does not make proof necessary for facts admitted or deemed admitted. The court may nevertheless require independent proof depending on the nature of the circumstances. For proof of subsequent events in an appeal or revision, the Court also referred to affidavits under Order 19 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: If subsequent factual allegations are admitted, including by non-traverse, they need not be proved; however, the court may require independent proof having regard to the nature of the circumstances.

predicates.appellate_or_revisional_proceeding: The matter is being considered in an appeal or revision.
predicates.subsequent_fact_allegation: A party alleges a factual event that occurred after the proceeding began.
predicates.allegation_admitted_or_undisputed: The opposing party admits the alleged fact or does not traverse it.

members.legal_issue: A material factual allegation in a civil pleading that is not specifically denied may be treated as admitted and need not be proved.
material_facts: The plaintiffs alleged that the required settlement payment had not been made.
That allegation was not denied or disputed in the opposing pleading.
The trial court also found that the payment had not been made, and the High Court affirmed that finding.
members.legal_principle: Order VIII Rules 3 and 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure require specific treatment of factual allegations and provide that an allegation not specifically denied, denied by necessary implication, or stated not to be admitted may be taken as admitted. The court may require an admitted fact to be proved otherwise. Under Section 58 of the Evidence Act, a fact admitted need not be proved.
members.conclusion: The undenied allegation could be treated as admitted; independently, the courts’ finding that the payment had not been made supported the conclusion that the settlement had not taken full effect.

predicates.civil_pleading_proceeding: The dispute is being decided in a civil proceeding in which the parties have filed pleadings.
predicates.material_fact_alleged: A party alleged a fact material to the dispute in its pleading.
predicates.opposing_pleading_lacks_specific_denial: The opposing party did not specifically deny the alleged fact, deny it by necessary implication, or state that it was not admitted.

members.legal_issue: Expenditure wholly and exclusively incurred for business that is not capital in nature may qualify for deduction as business expenditure even if repairs are not current repairs.
material_facts: The assessee claimed a deduction for expenditure on renovating buildings, reconditioning machinery and clearing accumulated debris so that mining operations could resume.
The expenditure was incurred wholly and exclusively for the business.
The Revenue argued that the expenditure could not be considered under the residuary business-expenditure provision because the work was not current repairs.
members.legal_principle: Section 10(2)(v) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922, concerns current repairs; it does not declare or necessarily imply that other repairs cannot qualify under section 10(2)(xv). The latter provision should be construed liberally, consistently with the commercial principle that business expenditure wholly and exclusively incurred for business and not capital in nature is deducted in computing profits. The Court relied on C.I.T. v. Chitnis, Motipur Sugar Factory Ltd. v. C.I.T., Devi Films Ltd. v. C.I.T., Badridas Daga v. C.I.T., Calcutta Co. Ltd. v. C.I.T., and The Law Shipping Co. Ltd. v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue.
members.conclusion: Even if the expenditure did not constitute current repairs, it could be considered for deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922.

rule.if: business_income_deduction_claim and expenditure_wholly_for_business and expenditure_not_capital and (repairs_are_current or repairs_are_not_current)

predicates.business_income_deduction_claim: A taxpayer claims a deduction for expenditure in computing income from a business.
predicates.expenditure_wholly_for_business: The taxpayer incurred the expenditure wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business.
predicates.expenditure_not_capital: The expenditure is not capital in nature.
predicates.repairs_are_current: The claimed expenditure is for repairs that qualify as current repairs.
predicates.repairs_are_not_current: The claimed expenditure is for repairs that do not qualify as current repairs.

members.legal_issue: Expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for an indivisible business is deductible in full even when part of the business income is not taxable.
material_facts: The assessee’s cultivation of sugar cane and manufacture of sugar were found to constitute one single and indivisible business.
The assessee paid its managing agents commission for managing the business and claimed the commission as a business expense.
