The commission was incurred wholly and exclusively for the business, although income arising from the cultivation activity was not taxable.
members.legal_principle: Under section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, expenditure laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business is deductible. The court must apply the statutory language, not equitable considerations, and need not trace otherwise deductible business expenditure to taxable income. The court followed C.I.T., Bombay v. Parakh and (India) Ltd. and C.I.T., Madras v. Indian Bank Ltd.; it also referred to S.A.S.S. Chellappa Chettiar v. C.I.T., Madras and Salt & Industries Agencies Ltd. v. C.I.T., Bombay City.
members.conclusion: The entire managing agency commission was deductible; the fact that part of the income from the business was not taxable was irrelevant.

rule.if: business_tax_deduction_assessment and indivisible_business and expense_wholly_for_business and part_business_income_not_taxable

predicates.business_tax_deduction_assessment: The case concerns a claim to deduct a business expense in a tax assessment.
predicates.indivisible_business: The business activities giving rise to taxable and non-taxable income form one single and indivisible business.
predicates.expense_wholly_for_business: The taxpayer incurred the claimed expense wholly and exclusively for the purpose of that business.
predicates.part_business_income_not_taxable: Some income arising from the business is not taxable.

members.legal_issue: A tax on circumstances and property is distinct from a tax on income even when income is used to assess the levy.
material_facts: The levy was imposed on persons according to their circumstances and property, and its assessment could use income or turnover from a trade, calling, or property as a measure.

The levy could apply by reference to a person's financial position and status, including the pursuit of a beneficial calling or an interest in property, without requiring taxable income in the sense used for income tax.
members.legal_principle: The nature of a tax is determined by its real character and substance, not its name or the measure used to calculate it. A tax on circumstances may relate to a person's overall financial position or status and need not depend on the existence of income taxable under income-tax law. The Court relied on District Board of Farrukhabad v. Prag Dutt, Zila Parishad, Muzaffarnagar v. Jugal Kishore Ram Swarup, and Pandit Ram Narain v. State of U.P.; it also referred to Re a Reference under the Government of Ireland Act and Governor-General in Council v. Province of Madras.
members.conclusion: The tax on circumstances and property is not a tax on income; using income as a measure does not determine the tax's nature.

predicates.tax_nature_challenge: A person challenges the legal character of a local levy imposed on them.
predicates.levy_assessed_by_status_or_property_or_c: The levy is assessed by reference to a person's overall financial position, property interest, or pursuit of a trade or calling.

members.legal_issue: A tax on aggregate net wealth that includes land is distinct from a tax imposed directly on lands and buildings as separate units.
material_facts: The challenged central law imposed tax on an assessee’s net wealth, calculated by aggregating assets and deducting debts.
The amendment brought agricultural land into the assets included in that calculation.
The value of land was included as one component of the assessee’s aggregate wealth, rather than being taxed directly as a separate unit of property.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 246 and Entry 49 of List II, a tax on lands and buildings is directly imposed on those properties as units and is not concerned with the owner’s total assets or debts. A tax on aggregate net wealth is a personal tax on the assessee and is conceptually distinct. The Court relied on Sudhir Chandra Nawn v. Wealth Tax Officer, Assistant Commissioner of Urban Land Tax v. Buckingham & Carnatic Co. Ltd., and Gift Tax Officer v. Nazareth. It also cautioned, relying on Attorney-General for Canada v. Attorney-General for Ontario and Attorney-General for Alberta v. Attorney-General for Canada, that legislation is invalid if its true effect is to invade the State field.
members.conclusion: The amended wealth tax was not a tax on lands and buildings within the State legislative field.

predicates.wealth_tax_competence_challenge: A taxpayer challenges a central wealth-tax law on the ground that the legislature lacked competence to enact it.
predicates.tax_on_aggregate_net_wealth: The law calculates tax by aggregating an assessee’s assets and deducting debts.
predicates.land_not_taxed_as_a_separate_unit: The law includes land only as a component of aggregate wealth and does not impose tax directly on each parcel as a separate unit.

members.legal_issue: The permission for a defendant to contest the adequacy of court fees in a civil suit does not itself authorize the defendant to seek revision of the court’s decision on that issue.
material_facts: The plaintiff filed a suit and paid court fees on the plaint.
The defendant objected to the valuation and adequacy of the court fees, and the trial court decided the issue after considering the valuation evidence.
The defendant sought revision of the court-fee determination.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(2) of the Madras Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955 enables a defendant to plead that the suit is improperly valued or that the fee paid is insufficient, so that the court can decide the issue before evidence on the merits is recorded. It does not authorize a revision application by the defendant. Section 19 permits the court to conduct an inquiry, including by commission, into valuation and fee sufficiency; it does not give the defendant a revisional right. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The defendant could raise the court-fee issue before the trial court and assist it in deciding the issue, but the relevant provision did not confer a right to seek revision of that decision.

predicates.civil_suit_involving_plaint_court_fee: A plaintiff brought a civil suit in which the court had to determine the fee payable on the plaint.
predicates.defendant_raised_fee_objection: The defendant objected to the valuation of the suit or the sufficiency of the fee paid.
predicates.defendant_sought_revision_of_fee_decisio: The defendant asked a superior court to revise the court’s decision on the fee payable.

members.legal_issue: A defendant may not invoke revisional jurisdiction to challenge a court-fee determination when the challenge does not involve a ground within the revisional court’s jurisdiction.
material_facts: The defendant sought revision of the trial court’s determination of the court fees payable on the plaint.
The revision concerned the adequacy of the fee, and no question of jurisdiction was involved.
members.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure confines revisional jurisdiction to the grounds set out in clauses (a) to (c), including a subordinate court’s refusal to exercise jurisdiction vested in it, assumption of jurisdiction it does not possess, or illegal or materially irregular exercise of its jurisdiction. A defendant who disputes the fee paid on a plaint has no right to seek revision merely on that basis. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in entertaining the defendant’s revision application because no question of jurisdiction was involved.

predicates.civil_suit_involving_plaint_court_fee: A plaintiff brought a civil suit in which the court had to determine the fee payable on the plaint.
predicates.defendant_sought_revision_of_fee_decisio: The defendant asked a superior court to revise the court’s decision on the fee payable.
predicates.no_revisionable_jurisdiction_issue_was_i: The defendant’s challenge to the fee decision did not involve a qualifying issue about the subordinate court’s jurisdiction or its exercise of jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: Immediate delivery of possession should not be ordered while a related declaratory suit concerning the occupant’s claimed rights remains pending.
material_facts: An eviction decree had been granted and affirmed, including on the ground of unlawful subletting, but it had not been executed.
The occupant obstructed delivery of possession and claimed rights as a tenant through a party to the eviction proceedings.
The occupant had filed a declaratory suit concerning those claimed rights, and that suit remained pending.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered it inappropriate to order possession at that stage while the occupant’s declaratory suit was pending. The judgment cites no earlier cases or specific statutory provision as the basis for that decision; it recounts that an execution application had been made under Order XXI Rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to direct immediate delivery of possession while the declaratory suit remained pending and did not express an opinion on the merits of the parties’ contentions in that suit.

predicates.eviction_decree_unexecuted: A party obtained an eviction decree, but delivery of possession under it has not occurred.
predicates.occupant_claims_rights: The person in possession obstructed enforcement and asserted a right to remain in the property.
predicates.related_declaratory_suit_pending: The person in possession filed a suit seeking a declaration of the asserted rights, and that suit remains pending.

members.legal_issue: A related pending declaratory suit should be disposed of expeditiously when its pendency delays resolution of a property-possession dispute arising from an unexecuted eviction decree.
material_facts: An eviction decree had not been executed, and the occupant’s claim to rights in the property was being pursued in a declaratory suit.
The declaratory suit remained pending while the parties disputed possession and compensation.
members.legal_principle: The Court issued a case-management direction for expeditious disposal in view of the prolonged proceedings and the pending suit concerning the occupant’s asserted rights. It cited no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this direction.
members.conclusion: The Court directed that the declaratory suit be disposed of as expeditiously as possible, preferably within one year.

predicates.eviction_decree_unexecuted: A party obtained an eviction decree, but delivery of possession under it has not occurred.
predicates.related_declaratory_suit_pending: The person in possession filed a suit seeking a declaration of the asserted rights, and that suit remains pending.
predicates.possession_dispute_continues: The decree-holder and the person in possession continue to dispute who is entitled to possession of the property.

members.legal_issue: An arbitral award is not properly set aside for misconduct based on an unsupported, belated allegation about attendance or the return of documents not shown to have been evidence.
material_facts: The allegation that the arbitrator falsely recorded a party’s attendance was first raised after the arbitrator’s death and was not included in the timely original objections.
The allegation was unsupported by corroborating contemporaneous evidence; the party had not raised it before the arbitrator, and the other parties had signed records recording the attendance.
Some municipal assessment statements were taken away for typing and were not produced again, and the record did not show that they had been accepted as evidence or relied on.
The nature of other returned documents was not established, and there was no evidence that they formed part of the evidence produced before the arbitrator.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 30(a) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, an award may be set aside for misconduct of the arbitrator or proceedings, but a serious allegation must be supported by reliable evidence. The Court found an uncorroborated assertion, raised belatedly and not tested in cross-examination, insufficient in the circumstances; returning documents was not misconduct where they were not shown to be evidence produced before the arbitrator.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in finding misconduct on either basis or in setting aside the award on that ground.

rule.if: arbitration_award_challenge and ((attendance_misconduct_allegation_is_late and attendance_misconduct_allegation_is_uncorroborated) or (documents_were_returned and documents_not_shown_to_be_evidence))

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: A party challenged an arbitral award on the ground of misconduct.
predicates.attendance_misconduct_allegation_is_late: The allegation that the arbitrator falsely recorded attendance was raised only after the arbitrator had died.
predicates.attendance_misconduct_allegation_is_unco: No corroborating contemporaneous evidence supported the allegation, and it had not been raised before the arbitrator.
predicates.documents_were_returned: The arbitrator returned documents to a party after they had been submitted during the proceedings.
predicates.documents_not_shown_to_be_evidence: The record did not establish that the returned documents formed part of the evidence produced before the arbitrator.

members.legal_issue: An award is not set aside for failing to discuss documents unless the challenge establishes that material documents necessary to resolve the dispute were not considered or otherwise establishes legal misconduct.
material_facts: The challenging party asserted that important documents had not been referred to or discussed in the award.
The party did not identify a particular document shown to be essential to resolving the dispute or demonstrate that such a document had not been considered.
The challenge was framed as an error of law on the face of the award, not as legal misconduct by the arbitrator.
members.legal_principle: K. P. Poulose v. State of Kerala and Another recognizes that failure to consider material documents necessary for a just and fair resolution may amount to legal misconduct. That principle did not assist the challengers because they did not identify or establish the omission of any essential document, and their objection was not based on misconduct.
members.conclusion: The contention that documents had been omitted was unsupported and did not provide a basis for setting aside the award.

rule.if: arbitration_award_challenge and appellant_alleges_documents_were_omitted and not essential_omitted_document_demonstrated and not legal_misconduct_established

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: A party seeks to set aside or correct an arbitrator’s award.
predicates.appellant_alleges_documents_were_omitted: The challenging party alleges that the arbitrator failed to consider or discuss documents.
predicates.essential_omitted_document_demonstrated: The challenging party identifies and demonstrates that an omitted document was essential to resolving the dispute.
predicates.legal_misconduct_established: The challenging party establishes that the arbitrator’s conduct amounted to legal misconduct.

members.legal_issue: Frustration of a contract does not invalidate a completed transfer of property created by a lease.
material_facts: The parties had entered into a lease, the lessee had obtained possession, and the rights under the lease had vested.
The lessee relied on events arising after the lease to claim that the lease should no longer bind him.
There was no claim that the lease itself was void or voidable, or that it had been determined in a manner recognized by law.
members.legal_principle: Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act applies to contracts and does not invalidate a completed transfer of property. Section 4 of the Transfer of Property Act does not incorporate the Contract Act into the Transfer of Property Act. The court distinguished an executory contract from a completed conveyance: events that discharge a contract do not invalidate a concluded transfer. A covenant under a lease may be affected by section 56, but that does not void the transfer resulting from the lease.
members.conclusion: Section 56 does not apply to invalidate a completed transfer created by a lease, although a lease covenant to perform an act may become void if that act later becomes impossible or unlawful.

predicates.completed_lease_dispute: A dispute concerns rights created by a lease of immovable property that has been granted and acted upon.
predicates.lease_transfer_completed: The lease has transferred the right to enjoy the property to the lessee.
predicates.supervening_event_impairs_use: An event occurring after the lease makes the lessee's use of the property difficult or impossible.

members.legal_issue: The doctrine of frustration does not discharge a completed transfer of property.
material_facts: The conveyance was executed and registered, and possession of the property was delivered to the purchasers.
The change in the permitted floor-area ratio occurred after the auction and before the conveyance, and the purchasers proceeded with the conveyance despite knowing of the change.
The purchasers entered into possession and constructed a multi-storeyed building.
members.legal_principle: Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act addresses impossibility and frustration of contracts. Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur and Co. explains that impossibility may include impracticability where an event destroys the foundation of the bargain; Alopi Parshad and Sons Ltd. v. Union of India holds that mere onerousness does not discharge a contract. The doctrine applies to executory contracts, not completed transfers: the Court relied on H.V. Rajan v. C.N. Gopal and Raja Dhruv Dev Chand v. Harmohinder Singh for the distinction between a completed conveyance and an executory contract.
members.conclusion: The purchasers could not rely on frustration to undo the completed conveyance or obtain a refund.

predicates.frustration_claim: A party seeks to undo a transaction on the ground that a later event made performance impossible or fundamentally altered the bargain.
predicates.completed_property_transfer: The transfer of property was completed before the party sought to undo it.

members.legal_issue: A tribunal hearing a statutory appeal must decide it on its merits and record its decision even when the appellant does not appear.
material_facts: The appellants brought statutory appeals against compensation awards.
The tribunal dismissed the appeals because the appellants’ advocate did not appear, without deciding the merits.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 17(1) and 20 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953, the tribunal must decide an appeal and record its decision, and that decision is final and conclusive. Dismissal for want of prosecution is not a decision of the appeal within section 17(1). The court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The tribunal had no power to dismiss the appeals for non-prosecution; it was required to decide them on their merits and record its decision despite the appellants’ default.

rule.if: statutory_appeal and merits_decision_required and appeal_decision_final and appellant_absent

predicates.statutory_appeal: A party has brought an appeal to a tribunal under a statutory compensation scheme.
predicates.merits_decision_required: The governing law requires the tribunal to decide the appeal and record its decision.
predicates.appeal_decision_final: The governing law makes the tribunal’s decision on appeal final and conclusive.
predicates.appellant_absent: The appellant does not appear when the appeal is called for hearing.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court cannot decide an appeal on its merits when the appellant does not appear for the hearing.
material_facts: The matter before the High Court was a second appeal.
When the appeal was called for hearing, counsel for the appellants was absent and no request was made on their behalf.
The High Court proceeded to decide the appeal on its merits and dismissed it.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 17(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, read with its Explanation, permits dismissal for default when the appellant does not appear but does not empower the appellate court to dismiss the appeal on its merits. The Explanation was added by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1976, to clarify that rule. Abdur Rahman v. Athifa Begum and Ghanshyam Dass Gupta v. Makhan Lal confirm that an appellate court cannot decide the merits in the appellant’s absence; doing so deprives the appellant of an opportunity to show sufficient cause for non-appearance.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in deciding the appeal on its merits in the appellants’ absence. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s judgment and decree and remitted the matter for fresh disposal in accordance with law.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the court was a second appeal.
predicates.appellant_absent_when_called: The appellant or the appellant’s counsel did not appear when the appeal was called for hearing.
predicates.court_decided_appeal_on_merits: The court proceeded to decide the appeal on its merits despite the appellant’s absence.
predicates.merits_decision_must_be_set_aside_and_ca: The merits decision must be set aside and the case sent back for fresh disposal.

members.legal_issue: The filing of a charge sheet during the pendency of a petition to quash criminal proceedings does not prevent the court from considering whether those proceedings should be quashed.
material_facts: The accused had sought quashing of an FIR under the High Court’s inherent jurisdiction.
A charge sheet was filed while the challenge to the FIR was pending, and the accused also sought to quash the charge sheet.
members.legal_principle: Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure preserves the High Court’s inherent power to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice, and its text does not confine that power to the FIR stage. In Joseph Salvaraj A. v. State of Gujarat, the Court held that a court may examine whether alleged offences are prima facie made out even when a charge sheet has been filed during the pendency of a quashing petition. The Court also referred to G. Sagar Suri v. State of U.P. and Umesh Kumar v. State of Andhra Pradesh for the settled principle that the power may be exercised even when a discharge application is pending before the trial court.
members.conclusion: The charge sheet did not make the challenge to the FIR untenable; the court could consider quashing both the FIR and the charge sheet.

predicates.criminal_proceeding_challenged_under_inh: A person asks a court to use its inherent power to stop a criminal proceeding.
predicates.quashing_petition_pending: The request to quash the criminal proceeding remains pending before the court.
predicates.charge_sheet_filed_during_petition: A charge sheet is filed while the request to quash the proceeding is pending.

members.legal_issue: Filing a chargesheet and taking cognizance while a challenge to the refusal to quash an FIR is pending does not make that challenge infructuous, and a related writ challenging the resulting proceedings may be entertained in the same procedural circumstances.
material_facts: The challenge to the refusal to quash the FIRs was pending when the investigation was completed and chargesheets were filed.
A related writ petition challenging the chargesheets was filed while the appeals concerning the refusal to quash the FIRs were pending.
The Court considered the challenges together and held that the appeals had not become infructuous; it entertained the writ petition in view of those particular circumstances.
members.legal_principle: The Court dealt with the issue on the particular procedural facts: the challenge to the refusal to quash was already pending when the chargesheets and cognizance order followed, and the related writ was brought in that setting. It entertained the writ in those circumstances and stated that quashing the FIRs vitiated the cognizance order. No earlier case was identified by the Court as the basis for this procedural ruling.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the argument that the appeals had become infructuous and entertained the related writ petition; after quashing the FIRs, it held that the cognizance order stood vitiated.

predicates.pending_challenge_to_refusal_to_quash: A challenge to a court’s refusal to quash criminal proceedings remains pending.
predicates.chargesheet_and_cognizance_followed_duri: A chargesheet was filed and a court took cognizance while that challenge was pending.
predicates.related_writ_challenged_resulting_procee: A related writ petition challenged the proceedings that followed the investigation.

members.legal_issue: A tenant who has already obtained protection from eviction for a premises and then defaults again for three consecutive months cannot obtain that protection a second time.
material_facts: In an earlier eviction proceeding concerning the premises, the tenant deposited the arrears as directed and the proceeding was disposed of.
The tenant thereby obtained the benefit of protection from eviction in that proceeding.
The tenant later defaulted in payment of rent for three consecutive months and made no payment required in the new proceeding.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, prevents an eviction order on the rent-default ground when the tenant makes the payment or deposit required by section 15, but its proviso states that a tenant who has obtained the benefit once for the premises and then defaults again for three consecutive months is not entitled to that benefit again. The Court held that the proviso was not directory; in any event, the tenant had made no payment required in the current proceeding and the refusal of repeat relief was justified.
members.conclusion: The tenant was not entitled to the benefit of protection from eviction again.

rule.if: rent_arrears_eviction_proceeding and prior_eviction_protection_obtained_for_premises and subsequent_consecutive_rent_default and required_current_payment_not_made

predicates.rent_arrears_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant for default in payment of rent.
predicates.prior_eviction_protection_obtained_for_p: The tenant previously obtained protection from eviction in a proceeding concerning the same premises.
predicates.subsequent_consecutive_rent_default: After obtaining that protection, the tenant again defaulted in rent for three consecutive months.
predicates.required_current_payment_not_made: The tenant did not make the payment or deposit required in the current proceeding.

members.legal_issue: The bar on repeat protection against eviction applies only when a tenant who previously received that protection in an earlier eviction proceeding later defaults for three consecutive months.
material_facts: The landlord argued that the tenant’s consecutive late deposits in the proceeding at issue triggered the statutory bar on receiving protection against eviction again.
The Court construed the bar as requiring the tenant to have obtained protection in a previously instituted eviction proceeding before making a later three-month consecutive default.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 14(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, on its plain construction, denies the benefit of that subsection only to a tenant who has obtained the benefit once in respect of the premises and thereafter defaults in rent for three consecutive months. The earlier benefit must have been obtained in a previously instituted eviction proceeding.
members.conclusion: Consecutive defaults in the current proceeding do not trigger the bar; it applies only if the tenant previously obtained the protection in an earlier eviction proceeding and subsequently defaulted for three consecutive months.

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks a tenant’s eviction on the ground that rent was not paid or tendered.
predicates.earlier_eviction_protection_granted: The tenant previously received protection against eviction in an earlier eviction proceeding concerning the premises.
predicates.later_three_consecutive_month_default: After receiving that protection, the tenant defaults in paying rent for three consecutive months.
predicates.tenant_barred_from_repeat_eviction_prote: The tenant is not entitled to receive the statutory protection against eviction again.

members.legal_issue: Cultivating rights in sir and khudkasht land that became a proprietor’s home-farm after abolition of proprietary rights cannot be sold in execution of a decree for a pre-vesting debt unless those rights were validly mortgaged or charged.
material_facts: A money decree for a debt incurred before vesting was being executed against the judgment-debtor’s proprietary share and the attached sir and khudkasht lands.
The attachment occurred before the abolition enactment took effect in the area, but the sale took place after proprietary rights had vested in the State.
The lands were the judgment-debtor’s sir and khudkasht home-farm, and no mortgage or charge had been created over the cultivating rights.
The decree-holder had only a money decree; the prior attachment did not create a charge securing the debt.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 4(2), 2(g)(i) and 38 of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, the former proprietor retained possession of qualifying home-farm land and became a malik makbuza of it. Section 43 protects land recorded as sir, and the cultivating rights in it, from attachment or sale in execution for a debt incurred before vesting, except where the rights were validly secured by mortgage or charge. An attachment alone does not create such a charge. Section 49 of the Central Provinces Tenancy Act, 1920, provided relevant background concerning the former proprietor’s rights in sir land. Govind Prasad v. Pawan Kumar was distinguished because it concerned whether a pre-enactment attachment continued against the home-farm, not whether a post-enactment sale could proceed under section 43.
members.conclusion: The sale of the cultivating rights in the sir lands was without jurisdiction and illegal, and was set aside.

rule.if: execution_of_debt_decree and debt_incurred_before_vesting and land_is_protected_home_farm and sale_occurs_after_vesting and not cultivating_rights_validly_mortgaged_or_charged

predicates.execution_of_debt_decree: A creditor seeks to recover a debt by selling land through execution of a decree.
predicates.debt_incurred_before_vesting: The debt being enforced was incurred before the relevant land vested in the State.
predicates.land_is_protected_home_farm: The land was recorded as sir or khudkasht and became the former proprietor’s home-farm, with cultivating rights retained by that person.
predicates.sale_occurs_after_vesting: The execution sale takes place after the land has vested in the State.
predicates.cultivating_rights_validly_mortgaged_or_: The cultivating rights were validly made security for the debt by mortgage or charge.
predicates.post_vesting_sale_is_without_jurisdictio: The sale of the protected cultivating rights after vesting is without jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: Agricultural land belonging to an agriculturist cannot be attached before judgment or sold in execution of a decree for a debt unless the land was specifically mortgaged for that debt.
material_facts: The decree was obtained on a promissory note, not on the basis of a mortgage of the land.
The properties belonged to an agriculturist family and were sold in execution after an attachment made before judgment.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1) of the Mysore Agriculturists’ Relief Act, 1928, agricultural land belonging to an agriculturist could not be attached or sold in execution of a decree unless specifically mortgaged for the debt to which the decree related. Section 14(2) permitted attachment only in execution of a decree; Section 14(3), which applied the procedure for attachment before judgment under Order XXXVIII of the Code of Civil Procedure, did not authorize a pre-judgment attachment of the land.
members.conclusion: The attachment before judgment was invalid, and the execution sale made in pursuance of it was void.

predicates.execution_sale_of_protected_agricultural: A creditor sought to sell agricultural land belonging to an agriculturist in execution of a decree.
predicates.land_not_mortgaged_for_the_debt: The land had not been specifically mortgaged to secure the debt underlying the decree.
predicates.attachment_made_before_judgment: The creditor attached the land before the court entered judgment on the debt.

members.legal_issue: Residents with a sufficient interest in protecting their locality’s environment and public facilities may challenge unlawful administrative action by writ petition without proving individual personal injury.
material_facts: The challengers were residents of the locality affected by the conversion of its reserved park into a site for a private hospital.
They sought to protect the public open space, local environment, and facilities intended for the enjoyment and health of the public.
The challenge raised whether the authorities had acted contrary to the law and the sanctioned scheme.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the broadened public-interest standing principle that sufficient interest, rather than narrowly defined personal injury, may support a writ challenge to public administrative action. Residents seeking protection of their locality’s environment and public facilities are not mere interlopers. The Court relied on S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, Akhil Bhartiya Soshit Karamchari Sangh v. Union of India, and Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The residents had locus standi to bring the writ petition.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_public_administrative_: A writ petition was brought to challenge administrative action affecting a public interest.
predicates.challengers_are_local_residents: The challengers live in the locality affected by the administrative action.
predicates.action_threatens_local_public_environmen: The challenged action threatens the locality’s environment or public facilities.

members.legal_issue: A resident personally affected by alleged unlawful activity that harms a wider group may maintain a public-interest writ proceeding.
material_facts: The appellant lived in the building where the diagnostic centre operated and was personally affected by its operation.
Residents made repeated complaints about nuisance, hardship, traffic and parking problems caused by the centre.
The challenge alleged violations of land-use requirements and harm to local residents, rather than only a private dispute.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226, standing is not confined to a person asserting an individual proprietary right where a legal wrong affects a determinate group. Public-interest standing is to be applied liberally to facilitate access to justice. The Court relied on S. P. Gupta v. President of India, State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal, Gadde Venkateswara Rao v. State of A.P., and the standing principles discussed in Calcutta Gas Company (Proprietary) Ltd. v. State of West Bengal.
members.conclusion: The proceeding raised matters of public interest, and the appellant had standing to pursue it; the High Court’s contrary finding was set aside.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_proceeding and group_harm_alleged and multiple_residents_complained and petitioner_personally_affected

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: A person brought a constitutional writ proceeding challenging alleged unlawful activity.
predicates.group_harm_alleged: The proceeding alleged that the activity caused legal harm or nuisance to a group of residents, rather than only a private injury.
predicates.multiple_residents_complained: More than one resident complained to public authorities about the activity.
predicates.petitioner_personally_affected: The person bringing the proceeding was also personally affected by the activity.

members.legal_issue: A High Court cannot issue a writ where the effective final order was made by an authority outside its territorial jurisdiction.
material_facts: A state government rejected an application for a mining lease.
The applicant sought review by the central government, which rejected the review and thereby effectively rejected the application.
The central government was located outside the territorial jurisdiction of the High Court.
A writ against the state government would not have displaced the central government's operative order.
members.legal_principle: Article 226 imposes a two-fold territorial limitation: the writ must operate within the High Court's territorial jurisdiction, and the person or authority to whom it is directed must be within that jurisdiction. The Court applied Election Commission of India v. Saka Venkata Subba Rao and Lt. Col. Khajoor Singh v. Union of India, and relied on A. Thangal Kunju Musaliar v. M. Venkitachalam Potti for the point that a writ against an inferior local authority would be ineffectual if an operative order of a superior authority outside the territory remained. State of Uttar Pradesh v. Mohammad Nooh was distinguished because it concerned the retrospective application of Article 226 to an earlier dismissal, not the territorial jurisdiction issue here.
members.conclusion: The High Court lacked jurisdiction to issue the requested writ, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: The proceeding is an application for a constitutional writ.
predicates.state_decision_reviewed_by_central_autho: A central authority reviewed a state authority's decision and disposed of the review.
predicates.central_authority_outside_high_court_ter: The central authority that made the operative order is outside the High Court's territorial jurisdiction.
predicates.central_order_remains_effective: The central authority's order remains operative, so a writ against the state authority alone would not afford relief.

members.legal_issue: A High Court cannot quash a Union Government order over which it lacks territorial jurisdiction.
material_facts: The petition sought a writ quashing the Union Government’s order concerning the disputed mining area.
The High Court lacked territorial jurisdiction over the Union Government.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court could not issue certiorari to quash an order of an authority over which it did not exercise territorial jurisdiction. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not quash the Union Government’s order.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenges_union_ord: A party brings a constitutional writ petition seeking to quash an order made by the Union Government.
predicates.union_order_maker_outside_high_court_ter: The authority that made the challenged order is outside the territorial jurisdiction of the High Court.

members.legal_issue: The absence of bloodstains on witnesses does not by itself disprove their account of an attack with bloodstained weapons.
material_facts: The witnesses said they had caught the assailants or taken weapons from them.
The weapons were bloodstained, but there was no proof that the witnesses' hands or clothes were bloodstained.
The court found no adequate basis to conclude that blood must have stained the witnesses during the incident.
members.legal_principle: Whether witnesses or their clothing would have been stained depended on the circumstances; the absence of proof of bloodstains did not disprove the prosecution account. No provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The eyewitness testimony could not be rejected because the witnesses had no proven bloodstains on their hands or clothing.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and witnesses_handle_or_seize_weapons and weapons_are_bloodstained and not witness_bloodstains_proved

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal against an acquittal.
predicates.witnesses_handle_or_seize_weapons: Witnesses say they held an assailant or handled or seized a weapon during or after the incident.
predicates.weapons_are_bloodstained: The weapons connected to the incident are found to bear blood.
predicates.witness_bloodstains_proved: The witnesses' hands or clothing are shown to bear bloodstains.

members.legal_issue: Eyewitness presence is not made doubtful solely because witnesses did not attempt a rescue or could not accurately identify the location of each injury during a violent attack.
material_facts: Two witnesses were near the victim when the attack occurred, and one of them had accompanied the victim to hospital and lodged the initial report.
The assailants were armed with dangerous weapons, which could have deterred the witnesses from intervening.
The attack involved several assailants and multiple blows, and one witness did not accurately describe the location of the injuries.
members.legal_principle: A witness’s reaction to a dangerous event cannot be judged by a universal standard; armed assailants may deter a bystander from intervening. In a fast-moving attack, a witness need not be expected to describe the nature and location of every injury with photographic accuracy. No earlier case is relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The witnesses’ presence at the scene was not reasonably doubted on the grounds that they did not intervene or that one witness inaccurately described injury locations.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_eyewitness_c: The proceeding is a criminal appeal in which the credibility or presence of eyewitnesses is challenged.
predicates.witnesses_naturally_present: The witnesses had an ordinary reason to be at or near the scene when the incident occurred.
predicates.armed_attack_could_deter_intervention: The assailants’ weapons or conduct could reasonably have deterred a witness from trying to rescue the victim.
predicates.attack_was_fast_moving: The victim was subjected to a rapid, multiple-person attack in which movement and confusion could make precise injury-location recall difficult.

members.legal_issue: Medical opinion about shock and speech does not conclusively exclude a dying declaration when other evidence supports the declarant's ability to speak at the time.
material_facts: Witnesses said the injured person named assailants shortly after the attack.

One doctor described the injured person as affected in speech and under shock when examined, while the doctor who conducted the post-mortem considered that he may have remained conscious and able to speak for some time.
The court found that the medical evidence did not rule out the possibility of speech immediately after the occurrence.
members.legal_principle: Medical opinion about later examination and the likely onset of shock is not conclusive about whether the injured person could speak immediately after being injured; the circumstances observed by witnesses are relevant to that assessment. No provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The possibility that the injured person made the reported dying declaration could not be ruled out, and the High Court was right to accept it.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal against an acquittal.
predicates.witnesses_report_declaration_soon_after_: Witnesses say the injured person made a statement shortly after sustaining the injuries.
predicates.medical_opinion_does_not_exclude_speech: Medical evidence does not conclusively establish that the injured person could not speak at the time of the reported statement.

members.legal_issue: A dying declaration is not unsafe merely because the declarant was described as being in shock when the evidence shows that the declarant retained the capacity to make a coherent statement.
material_facts: The doctor who recorded the declaration said the deceased was in shock from a serious abdominal injury.
The doctor was not cross-examined on whether the deceased retained his mental faculties despite the shock.
The declaration was coherent and consistent, and the doctor recorded that the patient became semi-conscious toward its end.
members.legal_principle: A medical condition such as shock must be assessed in light of evidence about the declarant’s actual mental state. A medical-jurisprudence view relied on by a party must be put to the doctor in cross-examination so its application to the particular facts can be assessed.
members.conclusion: The evidence did not establish that the deceased lacked his mental faculties when he began making the declaration, and the shock ground did not make the declaration unsafe to rely on.

rule.if: dying_declaration_case and declarant_described_as_in_shock and coherent_statement_before_later_decline and doctor_not_questioned_on_retained_faculties

predicates.dying_declaration_case: The proceeding concerns the evidentiary reliability of a dying declaration.
predicates.declarant_described_as_in_shock: A medical witness describes the declarant as being in shock.
predicates.coherent_statement_before_later_decline: The declarant makes a coherent statement before becoming semi-conscious or otherwise declining.
predicates.doctor_not_questioned_on_retained_facult: The medical witness is not questioned about whether the declarant retained mental faculties despite the shock.

members.legal_issue: An arbitral award that purports to determine all referred disputes is not incomplete merely because it is silent on a claim for accounts and profits following a declaration that a lease is invalid.
material_facts: The arbitration reference covered disputes concerning a company, its management and the parties’ acts in relation to it.
A claimant sought accounts and a share of profits concerning a company lease.
The award declared the lease invalid and not binding on the company or its shareholders but gave no express direction on the accounting claim.
The award stated that it determined all disputes referred to the arbitrator.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 30 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, an award may be challenged on the statutory grounds for setting it aside. A court should support an award if reasonably possible; unless the reference specifically requires separate decisions on every claim, an arbitrator may make a consolidated award. Where an award purports to determine all matters referred, the presumption is that it is final and complete, and silence generally amounts to rejection of a claim unless its nature requires specific adjudication. The Court relied on Salby v. Whitbread and Co., Re Brown and the Croydon Canal Co., Jewell v. Christie, and Harrison v. Creswick. An accounting claim did not necessarily follow from invalidating the lease, and an amount due might already have been adjusted in other parts of the award.
members.conclusion: The award’s silence on the accounting claim was to be treated as rejection of that relief, not as an omission making the award incomplete.

rule.if: arbitration_award_challenge and award_professes_to_determine_all_referred_disputes and award_silent_on_accounting_claim and (accounting_not_necessarily_implicit_in_lease_invalidation or accounting_may_have_been_adjusted_elsewhere)

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: A party challenged an arbitral award on the ground that it did not resolve all referred disputes.
predicates.award_professes_to_determine_all_referre: The award stated that it determined all disputes referred to the arbitrator.
predicates.award_silent_on_accounting_claim: The award did not expressly grant or reject a claim for accounts and profits connected with a lease it invalidated.
predicates.accounting_not_necessarily_implicit_in_l: Invalidating the lease did not necessarily establish that an accounting or payment of profits was due.
predicates.accounting_may_have_been_adjusted_elsewh: The amount potentially due on an accounting might have been taken into account in other provisions of the award.

members.legal_issue: An arbitral award that purports to determine all referred disputes is not incomplete merely because it does not expressly address a claim for relief based on alleged misappropriation.
material_facts: A claimant alleged that company money had been misappropriated and sought relief requiring the money to be restored for division among the parties.
Evidence concerning the allegation was presented to the arbitrator.
The award purported to determine all referred disputes but included no specific provision granting relief on the misappropriation claim.
members.legal_principle: Where an award professes to determine all matters referred, the presumption is that it disposes finally of them; silence on a claim may therefore signify its rejection. An arbitrator need not separately state a decision on each matter unless the reference specifically requires it. The Court relied on Harrison v. Creswick and the general principles stated in Salby v. Whitbread and Co., Re Brown and the Croydon Canal Co., and Jewell v. Christie.
members.conclusion: The award’s silence on the misappropriation claim meant that the arbitrator had rejected it, so the award was not incomplete on that account.

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: A party challenged an arbitral award on the ground that it did not resolve all referred disputes.
predicates.award_professes_to_determine_all_referre: The award stated that it determined all disputes referred to the arbitrator.
predicates.award_silent_on_misappropriation_claim: The award contained no express provision granting relief on a claim that company money had been misappropriated.

members.legal_issue: The transitional provision prescribing a deadline for awards does not validate or excuse unreasonable delay that occurred before it took effect.
material_facts: The declarations had been published before the 1984 amendment took effect.
The awards in these proceedings had been made before that amendment took effect.
The authorities relied on the amendment’s transitional deadline to argue that the earlier delay was permissible.
members.legal_principle: Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act imposes a deadline for making an award and provides for lapse if the deadline is not met. Its proviso gives a deadline for awards following declarations published before the amendment commenced; it does not retrospectively validate prior delay or condone inaction that had already occurred. A proviso carves out an exception within the provision rather than supplying retrospective validation.
members.conclusion: The transitional provision did not validate or justify the authorities’ earlier inaction, and it did not apply to proceedings in which awards had already been made before the amendment came into force.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerned the compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.pre_amendment_declaration: The declaration that the land was required for acquisition was published before the new award-deadline rule took effect.
predicates.award_made_before_deadline_provision_too: The compensation award was made before the new award-deadline rule took effect.
predicates.authority_claims_prior_delay_was_validat: The acquiring authority argued that the new deadline rule excused or validated its earlier delay.

members.legal_issue: A later statutory deadline for making acquisition awards does not validate earlier unreasonable inaction or apply to awards already made before that deadline took effect.
material_facts: The acquisition declarations predated the 1984 amendment that introduced a deadline for making awards.
The awards in the proceedings at issue had been made before the amendment came into force.
The authority argued that the amendment's transitional deadline validated the earlier delay.
members.legal_principle: Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act introduced a deadline for making awards. Its proviso set a transitional deadline for declarations published before the amendment, but the proviso did not retrospectively validate earlier inaction and did not apply where the awards had already been made before commencement of the amendment.
members.conclusion: The transitional deadline did not validate or justify the earlier delay, and it did not apply to proceedings in which awards had already been made before the amendment came into force.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The case concerns compulsory acquisition of land and the completion of the acquisition process.
predicates.delay_occurred_before_later_award_deadli: The authority's delay in making the award occurred before a later statutory deadline for awards took effect.
predicates.award_made_before_later_deadline_took_ef: The authority made the award before the later statutory deadline took effect.

members.legal_issue: A person whose possession derives from a decree-holder must restore possession when the decree under which the decree-holder obtained possession is set aside, even if that person claims to be a bona fide tenant.
material_facts: An ex parte eviction order enabled the landlord to obtain possession of the premises from the tenant.
After the eviction order was set aside and the eviction proceeding revived, the tenant sought restoration of possession.
Before restoration was carried out, another person objected, stating that the landlord had inducted him as a tenant and that he had acted bona fide without knowledge of the earlier proceeding.
The later occupant obtained possession from the landlord, rather than through an independent auction purchase.
members.legal_principle: Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires restitution when a decree or order is varied or reversed, including restoration of benefits obtained under it. A tenant inducted into possession by a decree-holder derives possession from that decree-holder and cannot claim the independent position of a stranger who purchases at an execution sale and was not a party to the decree. The Court applied Binayak Swain v. Ramesh Chandra Panigrahi, which approved the distinction stated in Zain-ul-Abdin Khan v. Muhammad Asghar Ali Khan between a decree-holder purchasing under a decree later reversed and a bona fide stranger purchasing at a valid execution sale.
members.conclusion: The later occupant was required to restore possession because his possession derived from the landlord, who had obtained possession under the eviction order that was set aside. The tenant was entitled to restoration, subject to the result of the revived eviction proceeding.

predicates.restitution_after_reversal: A party seeks restoration of possession after the order under which possession was obtained has been set aside or reversed.
predicates.occupant_possession_derived_from_decree_: The current occupant obtained possession from the person who obtained it under the order that was set aside or reversed.
predicates.derivative_occupant_must_restore_possess: An occupant whose possession derives from the decree-holder must restore possession.

members.legal_issue: A tenant who has been evicted is entitled to restoration of possession after the eviction order is set aside, even if the landlord has inducted another tenant.
material_facts: The court allowed the tenant’s appeal and set aside the eviction order.
The tenant had already been evicted.
The landlord had inducted another tenant into the premises.
members.legal_principle: Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for restitution following reversal or variation of a decree or order; the court directed restoration of possession despite the subsequent induction of another tenant.
members.conclusion: The court directed the trial court to restore the former tenant to possession under Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure, notwithstanding the induction of another tenant.

rule.if: appeal_against_eviction_order and eviction_order_set_aside and tenant_already_evicted and another_tenant_inducted

predicates.appeal_against_eviction_order: The tenant brought an appeal challenging an order for eviction.
predicates.eviction_order_set_aside: The appellate court set aside the eviction order.
predicates.tenant_already_evicted: The tenant had been removed from possession before the appeal was decided.
predicates.another_tenant_inducted: The landlord placed another tenant in the premises after the former tenant was evicted.

members.legal_issue: A court may permit a party to deal with property during a pending property suit free from the ordinary effect of lis pendens, subject to appropriate security.
material_facts: The pending specific-performance suit concerned immovable property and restricted the owner's ability to deal with it or obtain its fair market value.
The plaintiff described the proposed collaboration as a commercial venture and stated the intended investment and expected benefit.
The Court considered security sufficient to protect the opposing party while allowing the owners to deal with the property.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 allows the court in which the suit is pending to exempt the property from the operation of lis pendens on conditions it considers appropriate. The Court applied that power and found reasonable security an appropriate condition in the circumstances.
members.conclusion: The defendants were permitted to deal with or dispose of the property despite the pending suit, provided they furnished security to the satisfaction of the court.

predicates.pending_civil_suit_directly_concerns_imm: A civil suit is pending in which rights to immovable property are directly in issue.
predicates.suit_pendency_restricts_owner_dealing: The pending suit materially restricts the owner's ability to deal with the property or obtain its fair market value.
predicates.court_finds_exemption_appropriate: The court determines that the circumstances justify allowing the owner to deal with the property despite the pending suit.
predicates.reasonable_security_can_protect_opposing: Security can reasonably protect the opposing party's interests while the property is dealt with.

members.legal_issue: A court hearing a pending suit may permit a sale of property otherwise subject to an interim restraint if sufficient sale proceeds are secured to protect the buyer’s claim.
material_facts: The sellers submitted that a complete freeze on sale could prevent development of the property and asked to be allowed to sell with the trial court’s permission and safeguards.
The Supreme Court left the parties at liberty to apply to the court hearing the suit for permission to sell.

The Court directed that the court hearing the suit could consider permission after hearing the buyers and requiring enough of the sale consideration to be deposited in court to protect their claims pending the suit’s outcome.
members.legal_principle: The Court preserved the interim protection of the buyer’s claim while allowing the court hearing the suit to consider a request to sell. Any permission is subject to hearing the buyer and securing in court the portion of the sale consideration necessary to meet the buyer’s claim pending the final decision.
members.conclusion: The parties may seek permission from the court hearing the suit to sell the property, and that court may permit the sale if sufficient sale proceeds are deposited to safeguard the buyers’ claims.

predicates.property_sale_is_restrained_pending_suit: An interim order restrains the seller from dealing with the property while the suit is pending.
predicates.seller_seeks_permission_to_sell: The seller asks the court hearing the suit for permission to sell the property.
predicates.sale_proceeds_can_be_secured_for_buyer_c: Sufficient sale proceeds can be deposited or otherwise secured to protect the buyer’s claim pending the suit.

members.legal_issue: A partition of family property that disadvantages minor coparceners may be reopened despite the adults’ consent or the passage of time.
material_facts: The movable-property schedules showed an apparent disparity of about Rs. 10,000 between the brothers’ allotments.
Evidence established that a further Rs. 55,000, intended to be divided between the brothers, had been omitted from the partition deed; the minors’ father did not insist on its division.
The plaintiffs were minor coparceners when the partition occurred, and the omitted and unequal allotments deprived them of part of their shares.
The plaintiffs did not press their allegations of fraud and undue influence before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: A consensual partition ordinarily cannot be reopened without proof of fraud, coercion, misrepresentation, or undue influence, for which strict proof is required. But where a partition involving minors is shown to be unjust, unfair, and detrimental to their interests, it may be reopened regardless of the time elapsed; the court must protect the minors, and the party supporting the partition bears the burden of showing it was just and fair. The Court relied on Bishundeo Narain v. Seogeni Rai, Devarajan v. Janaki Ammal, Lal Bahadur Singh v. Sispal Singh, Chanvira 'Pa' v. Da 'Na' 'Va', and Maruti v. Rama.
members.conclusion: The movable-property partition was unfair and detrimental to the minors and could be reopened; the Court determined their share and modified the decree to award them Rs. 46,500, with future interest at six per cent per annum until payment.

predicates.partition_challenge_involving_minor_copa: A party challenges a family partition made while minor coparceners were members of the family.
predicates.partition_proved_unjust_or_unfair: The evidence establishes that the partition was unjust or unfair to the minors.
predicates.minors_interests_detrimentally_affected: The partition deprived the minors of property or value to which their interests entitled them.

members.legal_issue: A minor coparcener may seek to reopen a partition that is unfair or prejudicial to the minor's interest even when the minor's branch was represented by a parent and the partition involved no fraud or misrepresentation.
material_facts: The business was found to be ancestral, giving the sons of the two brothers an interest by birth.
The plaintiff was a minor when the partition was made, and his branch was represented in it by his father.
The High Court found no fraud or undue influence but found that the division of shares in the business was unfair and prejudicial to the interests of the minor sons in the plaintiff's branch.
members.legal_principle: Applying Ratnam Chettiar v. S. M. Kuppuswami Chettiar, the Court held that unfairness or prejudice to a minor coparcener's interest can justify reopening a partition even without fraud, misrepresentation, or undue influence, and even if the minor's branch was represented by the father.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the partition could be reopened on the ground that it was unfair or prejudicial to the minor's interest, despite the absence of fraud or misrepresentation and the parent's representation of the minor's branch.

rule.if: joint_family_partition and minor_coparcener_affected and minor_branch_represented_by_parent and partition_unfair_or_prejudicial

predicates.joint_family_partition: Members of a joint family divided joint family property by partition.
predicates.minor_coparcener_affected: A coparcener was a minor when the partition affected that coparcener's interest.
predicates.minor_branch_represented_by_parent: The minor coparcener's branch was represented in the partition by a parent.
predicates.partition_unfair_or_prejudicial: The partition allocated property or interests unfairly or prejudicially to the minor coparcener.

members.legal_issue: When the movable and immovable property divisions are distinct or separable, a court may preserve the fair division and reopen only the unfair division.
material_facts: The immovable properties were divided under a separate deed from the movable properties, and the movable-property division had occurred at a different time.
The courts found the immovable-property division fair but found an unfair disparity in the movable-property division.
members.legal_principle: Where divisions of movable and immovable property are distinct and separable, or occur at different times, a court may maintain the transaction that is fair and reopen only the transaction that is unjust or unfair. The Court applied this proposition alongside the principles governing partitions involving minors, relying on Bishundeo Narain v. Seogeni Rai and the other authorities discussed in its judgment.
members.conclusion: The Court left the fair division of immovable properties undisturbed while reopening the unfair division of movable properties.

rule.if: family_partition_challenge_involving_minors and property_divisions_are_separable and one_division_is_fair and another_division_is_unfair

predicates.family_partition_challenge_involving_min: A party challenges a family partition made while minor coparceners were members of the family.
predicates.property_divisions_are_separable: The divisions of different categories of family property are distinct, separable, or occurred at different times.
predicates.one_division_is_fair: The evidence establishes that one property division was fair.
predicates.another_division_is_unfair: The evidence establishes that a separate property division was unjust or unfair to the minors.

members.legal_issue: Reopening a partition may be confined to a distinct and separable part of the partition scheme that was unfair or prejudicial.
material_facts: The unfairness found by the High Court concerned the division of shares in the business, a distinct part of the partition scheme.
The Court relied on the principle that the whole partition need not be reopened when the unfair part is distinct and separable.
members.legal_principle: Under Ratnam Chettiar v. S. M. Kuppuswami Chettiar, the entire partition need not be reopened when unfairness relates to a distinct and separable part of the partition scheme; the reopening may be circumscribed accordingly.
members.conclusion: The Court held that reopening may be suitably confined to the distinct and separable part of the partition that was unfair or prejudicial.

predicates.partition_reopening_warranted: The facts provide a basis for reopening a partition.
predicates.unfair_part_distinct_and_separable: The unfair or prejudicial part of the partition scheme is distinct and separable from the rest.

members.legal_issue: Land allotments made contrary to mandatory statutory disposal rules are invalid even when they are made for a beneficial or public-minded purpose.
material_facts: Land was allotted to a newspaper proprietor for a printing and publishing enterprise and to a charitable organization.
The allotments relied on State policies or directions rather than being processed by the development authority in accordance with the statutory rules.
The rules distinguished State land from authority land and specified the procedures and conditions for disposing of authority land.
members.legal_principle: The State and the development authority, as statutory bodies, must act within the governing legislation and rules. Under Sections 58 and 85 of the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, and Rules 3–5 and 19–20 of the 1975 Rules, disposal must follow the prescribed process. A beneficial purpose cannot validate an allotment that contravenes mandatory statutory requirements. The Court also relied on Punjab State Electricity Board Ltd. v. Zora Singh and Union of India v. V. Ramakrishna for the principle that an order made for an unauthorized purpose is vitiated by malice in law.
members.conclusion: The allotments were contrary to the governing Act and rules and were void and of no effect; their stated purposes did not cure the illegality.

predicates.public_interest_land_allotment_challenge: A public-interest proceeding challenges an allotment made under a statutory land-disposal scheme.
predicates.statutory_land_disposal: The disputed land is subject to statutory rules governing its disposal.
predicates.mandatory_disposal_rules_bypassed: The allotment was made without following mandatory procedures or conditions imposed by the governing rules.

members.legal_issue: An allotment made under an asserted government policy is invalid when it uses public power to confer private benefits contrary to the governing law and declared public purpose.
material_facts: The asserted policy relied on an acquisition award that had purported to allot land to former owners and their sub-awardees or nominees.
A minister acting as chair of the development authority directed allotments to that selected group, and officials acted on those directions.
The allotments were not made under the established rules for disposal of urban land, and no evidence showed that the general public could apply for them.
The land had been acquired for a declared public development scheme.
members.legal_principle: Public power must be exercised to advance the declared public purpose and within the limits of law and applicable rules. An asserted policy cannot camouflage the diversion of public property for private benefit. The Court relied on the principle in Radhey Shyam that the land acquisition officer lacked power to make the original allotments, and considered the applicable statutory and urban-land-disposal rules. It also explained that public officials are accountable for the exercise of public office and that public action must serve public welfare rather than private gain.
members.conclusion: The asserted policy was not a genuine public policy; the allotments were ultra vires, contrary to the statute and rules, and could not confer a right on the respondents.

predicates.public_land_allotment_case: The proceeding concerns an allotment of publicly owned or acquired land by a public authority.
predicates.allotment_relies_on_void_award: The allotment rests on an award or prior decision that was made without legal authority.
predicates.allotment_favours_selected_private_group: The allotment benefits a selected private group without a generally available eligibility process.
predicates.allotment_conflicts_with_public_purpose_: The allotment diverts land from its declared public purpose or is inconsistent with the rules governing its disposal.

members.legal_issue: A co-owner may use jointly owned land and a common channel for irrigation from an exclusive well unless that use prejudicially affects or detrimentally burdens another co-owner.
material_facts: The parties admitted their co-ownership of the land and channel in which the common well was situated.
One side used a small channel across the common land to carry water from its exclusive well to its own fields.
The opposing co-owners objected but did not plead or prove damage, injury, hardship, or other prejudice from that use.
The lower courts found the use advantageous to the users and modified the decree to address possible prejudice.
members.legal_principle: A co-owner's rights comprise a bundle of rights that includes use of the common property, subject to the limitation that the use must not prejudicially affect or put another co-owner to a detriment. Findings must be made with reference to the specific pleadings. The Court approved the reasoning in Subbiah Goundan v. Ramaswamy Goundan, AIR 1973 Mad. 42, and distinguished Sivarama Pillai v. Marichami Pillai, AIR 1971 Mad. 230, which concerned agreed terms governing use of a common well.
members.conclusion: The users were entitled to use the common land and channel to carry water from their exclusive well, and the opposing co-owners could not prevent that use in the absence of pleaded or proved prejudice or detriment.

rule.if: co_ownership_use_dispute and shared_land_or_channel and exclusive_source_used_for_irrigation and not prejudice_pleaded_or_proved

predicates.co_ownership_use_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over one co-owner's use of jointly owned property.
predicates.shared_land_or_channel: The property used to convey water is held in common by the disputing co-owners.
predicates.exclusive_source_used_for_irrigation: A co-owner conveys water from a source under that co-owner's exclusive control across the common property to irrigate land.
predicates.prejudice_pleaded_or_proved: Another co-owner specifically alleges or establishes that the use prejudicially affects or detrimentally burdens that co-owner.

members.legal_issue: An agreed arrangement governing the use of common irrigation property controls, but an unstipulated limitation cannot be inferred merely because a co-owner uses an exclusive water source or irrigates additional land.
material_facts: The common well and channel had been kept for the parties' common enjoyment at partition.
There was no stipulation governing the manner or mode of enjoyment of the common well or channel.

The water was taken from a well on land exclusively belonging to the users, and the opposing co-owners argued that use of the channel would impose an additional burden and that newly acquired land could not be irrigated through it.
The decision relied on in support of that argument concerned a partition arrangement that expressly fixed the manner and duration of use.
members.legal_principle: The terms of an agreement governing common property control the parties' use of it. Sivarama Pillai v. Marichami Pillai, AIR 1971 Mad. 230, was distinguishable because the parties there had agreed on a mode and duration of use at partition; no comparable term existed here.
members.conclusion: Any contract governing use would control, but there was no such stipulation here; neither law nor expediency justified preventing irrigation through the common channel from the exclusive well.

rule.if: common_property_use_proceeding and partition_created_shared_irrigation_property and no_agreed_mode_of_use and exclusive_source_used_for_irrigation

predicates.common_property_use_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the use of jointly held property for irrigation.
predicates.partition_created_shared_irrigation_prop: A partition left an irrigation source or conveyance property in common for the parties' enjoyment.
predicates.no_agreed_mode_of_use: The parties did not stipulate how or when the common irrigation property could be used.
predicates.exclusive_source_used_for_irrigation: A co-owner conveys water from a source under that co-owner's exclusive control through the common property for irrigation.

members.legal_issue: An arbitration clause contained in an insufficiently stamped instrument cannot be acted upon to appoint an arbitrator unless the required stamp duty and penalty are paid.
material_facts: The arbitration clause was contained in a lease deed that was chargeable with stamp duty but was insufficiently stamped.
The High Court Registrar (Judicial) determined the deficit stamp duty and penalty and directed payment.
The parties seeking arbitration did not pay the determined deficit duty and penalty.
The High Court nevertheless relied on the lease deed to appoint an arbitrator on their application.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 33 and 34 of the Karnataka Stamp Act, 1957, a court must examine a chargeable instrument produced before it and, if it is not duly stamped, impound it; the instrument cannot be admitted in evidence or acted upon unless the applicable duty and penalty are paid. Applying SMS Tea Estates Private Limited v. Chandmari Tea Company Private Limited, (2011) 14 SCC 66, the Court held that this bar also prevents a court from acting on an arbitration clause contained in the instrument. The analogous provisions considered in SMS Tea Estates were Sections 33 and 35 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899; the instrument may be acted upon after the duty and penalty are paid in the manner provided by the applicable stamp law.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not rely on the lease deed or its arbitration clause while the instrument remained insufficiently stamped and the required duty and penalty remained unpaid. The appointment order was set aside and the arbitration application was rejected.

rule.if: arbitration_appointment_application and arbitration_clause_in_chargeable_instrument and instrument_insufficiently_stamped and stamp_deficit_unpaid

predicates.arbitration_appointment_application: A party applied for appointment of an arbitrator to resolve a dispute.
predicates.arbitration_clause_in_chargeable_instrum: The arbitration clause was contained in an instrument chargeable with stamp duty.
predicates.instrument_insufficiently_stamped: The instrument did not bear the stamp duty required for it.
predicates.stamp_deficit_unpaid: The party relying on the instrument had not paid the required deficit duty and penalty.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot act on an arbitration clause in an instrument chargeable with stamp duty until the instrument is duly stamped or the stamp defect is cured.
material_facts: The arbitration clause was contained in a lease deed that was alleged to be insufficiently stamped.
The court had to consider the deed in deciding the application for appointment of an arbitrator.
The stamp-duty issue had not yet been determined, so the Supreme Court remitted the matter for that determination and directed appointment of an arbitrator if the deed was duly stamped.
members.legal_principle: Indian Stamp Act, 1899, section 33 requires examination and impounding of an instrument that appears insufficiently stamped. Section 35 bars an insufficiently stamped instrument from being admitted in evidence or acted upon, including its arbitration clause, until the duty and applicable penalty are paid. Sections 38 and 40 provide for the subsequent procedure. Unlike Registration Act, 1908, section 49, section 35 has no collateral-transaction exception.
members.conclusion: The court must examine whether the instrument is duly stamped and, if it is not, impound it and follow the applicable procedure; it cannot act on the instrument or its arbitration clause until the defect is cured. The matter was remitted for the stamp-duty issue to be decided first and for an arbitrator to be appointed if the instrument was duly stamped.

rule.if: application_for_arbitrator_appointment and instrument_is_chargeable_with_stamp_duty and instrument_is_not_duly_stamped and stamp_defect_is_not_cured

predicates.application_for_arbitrator_appointment: A party has applied for the appointment of an arbitrator under an agreement contained in an instrument.
predicates.instrument_is_chargeable_with_stamp_duty: The instrument is of a kind on which stamp duty is payable.
predicates.instrument_is_not_duly_stamped: The instrument does not bear the stamp duty required for it.
predicates.stamp_defect_is_not_cured: The required duty and applicable penalty have not been paid.

members.legal_issue: A suit whose plaint is returned because the original court lacked jurisdiction is instituted in the proper court only when the plaint is presented there.
material_facts: The suit sought specific performance concerning immovable property and recovery of possession, but was instituted in a court that lacked jurisdiction over the property.
