predicates.appeal_challenges_private_sale_permissio: A party appealed from a decision upholding governmental permission for a private sale of institutional property.
predicates.property_belongs_to_religious_or_charita: The property proposed for sale belonged to a religious or charitable institution or endowment.
predicates.public_auction_is_the_normal_sale_mode: The applicable sale framework makes public auction the ordinary method for selling the property.
predicates.private_sale_permission_is_unsupported: The permission to sell privately lacks the required institutional-interest finding or recorded reasons.
predicates.a_competing_offer_exceeds_the_private_sa: A prospective purchaser made a firm offer higher than the price proposed for the private sale.

members.legal_issue: A sale of public charitable trust property by private negotiation without public visibility and for less than market value should be set aside absent special reasons, and the property should be sold through a publicly advertised auction.
material_facts: Trustees obtained court permission to sell two trust properties through private negotiations.
The sales were conducted without newspaper publication or notice on the court notice board inviting the public to make offers.
The applicants alleged that the negotiated prices were about one-fifth of market value, and the Court was satisfied that the trust had not received market value.
Offers substantially above the prices paid had been made to the Court, supported by deposits.
members.legal_principle: Under Chenchu Ram Reddy v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, property of religious and charitable endowments must be jealously protected because the community has a beneficial interest in it. A private sale lacking public visibility, and liable to create public suspicion, should not be permitted unless special reasons justify it. The reserve price should be fixed after ascertaining market value to safeguard the endowment's interests.
members.conclusion: The orders permitting the sales and the resulting sales were set aside. The properties were directed to be sold by public auction with wide publicity. The purchasers were entitled to repayment of the price with interest and compensation for superstructures and improvements, to be assessed by the subordinate court.

rule.if: public_charitable_trust_property_sale and sale_by_private_negotiation and no_public_visibility and below_market_price and no_special_reason

predicates.public_charitable_trust_property_sale: The proceeding concerns the sale of property held by a public charitable or religious trust.
predicates.sale_by_private_negotiation: The trustees arranged the property sale through private negotiations rather than an open auction.
predicates.no_public_visibility: The sale process did not give the public meaningful notice or opportunity to compete.
predicates.below_market_price: The trust received a price below the property's market value.
predicates.no_special_reason: No special reason justified selling the property through private negotiations.

members.legal_issue: A decree made before rent-control legislation was extended to a cantonment is saved when it was made by applying that legislation as if it were already in force.
material_facts: A landlord obtained a compromise decree under state rent-control legislation for possession of premises in a cantonment before that legislation had been formally extended to the cantonment.
The legislation was subsequently extended to the cantonment, and the tenant challenged whether the later amendment saved the earlier decree.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(4) of the Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957, as amended by the Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Amendment Act, 1972, saves qualifying decrees and orders made before the extension of state rent-control legislation to a cantonment. Its application is not confined to extensions made retrospectively under section 3(2). The statutory scheme addressed the effect of the rule in Indu Bhushan Bose v. Rama Sundari Devi, which held that Parliament had exclusive competence over regulation of house accommodation in cantonments.
members.conclusion: The decree was saved by the amended law, whether or not the extension of the rent-control legislation was retrospective.

predicates.pre_extension_rent_control_decree: A court made a decree regulating or ordering eviction from housing before rent-control legislation was extended to the area.
predicates.decree_applied_state_rent_law_as_if_in_f: The court made the decree by applying state rent-control legislation as though it were already in force in that area.
predicates.later_extension_to_cantonment: The state rent-control legislation was later extended to the cantonment.

members.legal_issue: An order made under the state rent-control law in force at the time may be preserved as an order under the later-extended amended law, even if the amendment had not yet been expressly extended to the cantonment when the order was made.
material_facts: The notification extending the new state enactment to cantonments limited the extension to that enactment as it stood on the notification date.
The state later amended the enactment, including provisions governing the prescribed authority, and the amendments were extended to cantonments by a later notification.
Before that later notification, a rent-control application was transferred to and decided by an authority appointed under the state law as then in force.
The later extension took effect before the appellate proceedings were concluded.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(4) of the Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957, as amended, deems qualifying orders made under the state law in force before extension to have been made under the corresponding provisions of the extended rent-control law. The Court applied Jai Singh Jairam Tyagi v. Mamanchand Ratilal Agarwal, which held that this saving provision applies independently of whether the extension is retrospective, and S. P. Jain v. Krishna Mohan Gupta, which applied the saving rule to proceedings under the amended state rent law. The Court separately held that the earlier notification’s express limitation to the law as it stood on its date could not be ignored.
members.conclusion: Although the earlier notification did not itself extend later amendments, the order was preserved and deemed to have been made under the corresponding provisions of the amended rent-control law extended to the cantonment.

rule.if: cantonment_rent_control_proceeding and prior_order_made_under_state_law and authority_valid_under_state_law and later_extension_covers_corresponding_law

predicates.cantonment_rent_control_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a rent-control order relating to premises in a cantonment.
predicates.prior_order_made_under_state_law: An order was made under the rent-control law then in force in the state before that law or its relevant amendment was extended to the cantonment.
predicates.authority_valid_under_state_law: The authority that made the order was appointed and empowered under the state law then in force.
predicates.later_extension_covers_corresponding_law: A later extension brings the corresponding state rent-control law or amendment within the law applicable to the cantonment.

members.legal_issue: A charitable arrangement creates a trust only when the donor intends to extinguish private title through complete dedication; otherwise, the property remains private and is subject to a charge for the charity.
material_facts: A prior registered deed had dedicated property to public charities and required the whole income to be used only for those purposes.
A later compromise decree partitioned the property between the donor and his son and allotted some property to the donor.
The decree described the donor as sole trustee during his lifetime, allowed him to enjoy the property, and required income to be used for the charities according to their needs.

The decree directed that the property pass after the donor’s death to his grandson subject to the charities, and allowed the grandson to enjoy the property and conduct the charities without a restriction on his dealing with it.
The parties agreed that the property in the appellants’ hands remained burdened by the obligation to perform the charities.
members.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, whether a charitable dedication is complete depends on the donor’s intention, gathered from a fair construction of the document as a whole. Complete dedication creates a trust; partial dedication leaves the property’s private character intact and creates a charge. Use of the words “trust” or “trustee” is not conclusive; the central test is whether private title was intended to be extinguished. The Court relied on Maharani Hemanta Kumari Debi v. Gauri Shankar Tewari, Jadu Nath Singh v. Thakur Sita Ramji, Pande Har Narayan v. Surja Kunwari, Sonatun Bysack v. Sreemutti Juggutsoondyee Dossee, Gopal Lal Sett v. Purna Chandra Basak, and Chairman of the Howrah Municipality v. Khetra Krishna Mitra. The suit was brought under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The compromise decree did not create a public charitable trust in the allotted property; the property remained private and was subject to a charge for the charities. The suit for a scheme was therefore dismissed.

predicates.charity_scheme_suit: The proceeding seeks a scheme for administering property alleged to be held in trust for public charity.
predicates.charitable_obligation_attaches_to_proper: The governing arrangement requires the property or its income to support specified charitable purposes.
predicates.private_enjoyment_or_succession_is_retai: The arrangement allows a private individual to enjoy the property or provides for it to pass by private succession.
predicates.charitable_income_is_limited_to_need: The arrangement requires only such income as the charities need to be used for them, rather than dedicating all income exclusively to charity.

members.legal_issue: A charitable dedication is complete only when the property is shown to have been devoted to the charity rather than retained as private property subject to a charitable charge.
material_facts: A settlement deed set properties apart for specified charities but also provided that any surplus after conducting the charities could be used for family expenses by the manager and heirs.
The plaintiffs claimed that the properties had been completely dedicated and that a trust for the charity had been created.
The plaintiffs did not provide acceptable evidence of the properties’ income, leaving no adequate basis to determine whether a substantial surplus remained after charitable expenses.
The evidence did not establish that the income was substantially intended for the charity or that only an insignificant portion could be used for the manager’s or worshipper’s maintenance.
members.legal_principle: A dedication to religious or charitable purposes may be complete or partial. Complete dedication creates a trust in favor of the charity; partial dedication creates a charge in favor of the charity while the property retains its private and secular character. Whether dedication is complete is a question of fact determined, where there is a document, by its fair and reasonable construction and the intention shown by it. If income is substantially intended for charity and only an insignificant portion is available for the manager’s or worshipper’s maintenance, complete dedication may be found; if only a minor portion is required for charity and a substantial surplus is available for private purposes, complete dedication is difficult to find. The party asserting complete dedication must establish it. The Court relied on Menakuru Dasaratharami Reddi v. Duddukuru Subba Rao and referred to Kalipada Chakraborti v. Palani Bala Devi.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs failed to establish a complete dedication. The dedication was treated as partial, the properties retained their private character subject to the charitable purpose, and the widows had a beneficial interest in them.

predicates.complete_charitable_dedication_claim: A claimant asserts that property was completely dedicated to charitable purposes.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_establish_income_and_: The claimant did not establish the property income or show that the income was substantially intended for charity rather than leaving a substantial surplus for private use.

members.legal_issue: A railway administration is liable for a consolidated municipal tax assessed as a rate on lands and buildings when a government notification makes it liable for tax on lands and buildings and the consolidated tax replaces multiple municipal levies.
material_facts: The railway owned lands and buildings within the municipality and was initially made liable for house tax by a government notification.
The municipality later replaced separate taxes with a consolidated tax assessed as a rate on buildings and lands.
After the railway objected that the earlier notification covered only house tax, the government issued a further notification making the railway liable for tax on lands and buildings.

Government correspondence leading to the further notification showed that the municipality sought to make the railway liable for the consolidated tax, which replaced the house tax and a proposed general water rate.
Later municipal rules removed the exemption for government property, and the applicable municipal legislation retained materially identical language authorising the consolidated tax.
The railway’s successor sued to recover the consolidated tax collected from the railway; the High Court dismissed the suit, and the successor appealed.
members.legal_principle: Under section 135(1) of the Indian Railways Act, 1890, the government could make a railway administration liable for specified local taxes. Section 59(1) and its second proviso, clause (c), of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901, and the materially equivalent section 73(1) and second proviso, clause (c), of the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925, allowed a municipality to impose one consolidated tax, assessed as a rate on buildings or lands, in lieu of two or more specified taxes. Although all taxes are not rates, all rates are taxes; a consolidated tax assessed as a rate on buildings and lands is therefore a tax on buildings and lands. The Court read the notification’s wording in light of the statutory scheme, the Rules, and the circumstances of its issuance, including the prior notification and the government correspondence requesting liability for the consolidated tax. Borough Municipality, Ahmedabad v. Ahmedabad Manufacturing and Calico Printing Co. Ltd. supported treating a tax in the form of a rate assessed on buildings and lands as within language concerning a rate on buildings or lands; Raza Buland Sugar Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Board, Rampur supported treating a water rate as a tax on buildings and lands rather than a service tax. Municipal Council, Cuddappah v. M. & S.M. Ry. Co. Ltd. was distinguished because it turned on different statutory and notification wording. Patel Gordhandas Hargovindas v. Municipal Commissioner, Ahmedabad provided little assistance.
members.conclusion: The notification making the railway liable for tax on lands and buildings covered the consolidated tax, so the railway was liable for that tax and the suit for its refund was properly dismissed.

rule.if: a_railway_tax_refund_dispute and railway_property_in_municipal_area and municipality_replaced_multiple_levies_with_consolidated_tax and consolidated_tax_assessed_as_rate_on_land_and_buildings and government_notice_covers_tax_on_land_and_buildings and government_correspondence_sought_railway_liability_for_consolidated_tax and government_property_not_exempted_under_applicable_rules and later_municipal_law_retains_equivalent_consolidated_tax_authority

predicates.a_railway_tax_refund_dispute: A railway administration or its successor brought a dispute seeking recovery of municipal taxes collected from the railway.
predicates.railway_property_in_municipal_area: The railway owned lands or buildings situated within a municipality.
predicates.municipality_replaced_multiple_levies_wi: The municipality replaced separate municipal levies with a single consolidated tax.
predicates.consolidated_tax_assessed_as_rate_on_lan: The municipality assessed the consolidated tax as a rate on lands or buildings.
predicates.government_notice_covers_tax_on_land_and: The government issued a notice making the railway administration liable for tax on lands and buildings.
predicates.government_correspondence_sought_railway: Government correspondence preceding the notice requested that the railway be made liable for the consolidated tax.
predicates.government_property_not_exempted_under_a: The applicable municipal rules did not exempt government-owned property from the tax.
predicates.later_municipal_law_retains_equivalent_c: A later applicable municipal law retained materially equivalent authority to impose the consolidated tax.

members.legal_issue: A notification making a railway administration liable for tax on buildings and lands encompasses a consolidated tax assessed as a rate on buildings and lands when that consolidated tax replaces multiple municipal taxes.
material_facts: The municipality replaced the separate house tax and water rate with a consolidated tax assessed as a rate on buildings and lands.
A government notification made the railway administration liable for tax on buildings and lands within the municipality.
The notification followed correspondence in which the provincial government asked that the railway be made liable for the consolidated tax imposed in place of the house tax.
The railway paid the consolidated tax, and the Union brought a suit seeking its refund; the Union appealed after the High Court dismissed the suit.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 135(1) of the Indian Railways Act, 1890, the government could make a railway administration liable for specified local taxes. Sections 59(1) and its second proviso clause (c) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901, and Section 73(1) and its second proviso clause (c) of the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925, permitted a consolidated tax assessed as a rate on buildings or lands in lieu of specified separate taxes. A consolidated tax assessed in that way is a tax on buildings and lands for purposes of a notification describing the liability in those terms. The Court relied on Borough Municipality, Ahmedabad v. Ahmedabad Manufacturing and Calico Printing Co. Ltd. for the analogous principle that a tax imposed in the form of a rate assessed on buildings and lands is not distinct from a rate on buildings or lands, and referred to Raza Buland Sugar Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Board, Rampur concerning the character of a water rate. It distinguished Municipal Council, Cuddappah v. M. and S. M. Ry. Co. Ltd. as turning on different statutory language and noted that Patel Gordhandas Hargovindas v. Municipal Commissioner, Ahmedabad provided little assistance.
members.conclusion: The notification covered the consolidated tax, so the railway was liable to pay it and the municipality had collected it lawfully. The appeal was dismissed.

predicates.appeal_from_refund_suit: The railway's owner appealed after a court dismissed its suit seeking return of municipal taxes paid by the railway.
predicates.consolidated_tax_replaced_separate_munic: The municipality substituted one consolidated tax for multiple separate municipal taxes.
predicates.consolidated_tax_assessed_on_buildings_o: The municipality assessed the consolidated tax as a rate on buildings or lands.
predicates.notification_made_railway_liable_for_bui: The government issued a notification making the railway administration liable for tax on buildings or lands within the municipality.
predicates.notification_followed_request_to_cover_c: The notification followed a government request that the railway administration be made liable for the consolidated tax.
predicates.railway_liable_for_consolidated_tax: The railway administration is liable to pay the consolidated tax.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff is not entitled to exclude the time spent prosecuting an earlier proceeding when the plaintiff fails to establish that the proceeding was pursued with due care and attention and with due diligence.
material_facts: The plaintiff filed a possession suit in a court that lacked pecuniary jurisdiction, and the suit was later returned and re-presented to the proper court after the limitation period had expired.

The plaintiff knew the value of the properties exceeded the original court’s jurisdictional limit but omitted their value from the plaint; he had drafted the plaint himself, while his plaint in a similar suit stated the property’s value.
The plaintiff sought return of the plaint after a similar suit had been dismissed on the merits, although the relevant facts had been known from the outset.
The plaintiff produced no order-sheet or equivalent evidence showing that he had prosecuted the earlier suit with due diligence during its lengthy pendency.
The parties accepted that the earlier proceeding involved the same cause of action and that the earlier court could not entertain it for want of jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Limitation Act requires the plaintiff affirmatively to establish that the earlier civil proceeding was pursued with due diligence, was founded on the same cause of action, was prosecuted in good faith, and was in a court unable to entertain it because of a jurisdictional defect or a similar cause. Under section 2(7) of that Act, good faith requires due care and attention; mere honesty is insufficient. The burden initially rests on the plaintiff, and it does not shift to the defendant until the plaintiff satisfies that burden. The Court applied these statutory provisions and cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff did not establish the requirements for excluding the time spent in the earlier proceeding under section 14, so the suit was barred by limitation. The Court did not decide the separate argument about limitation under Article 142.

rule.if: civil_suit_seeks_time_exclusion and same_cause_prior_proceeding and prior_court_unable_to_entertain and (prior_prosecution_lacked_due_care or prior_diligence_not_proved)

predicates.civil_suit_seeks_time_exclusion: A plaintiff in a civil suit seeks to exclude time spent pursuing an earlier civil proceeding when calculating limitation.
predicates.same_cause_prior_proceeding: The earlier civil proceeding was founded on the same cause of action as the later suit.
predicates.prior_court_unable_to_entertain: The court handling the earlier proceeding could not entertain it because of a jurisdictional defect or a similar cause.
predicates.prior_prosecution_lacked_due_care: The plaintiff pursued the earlier proceeding without the due care and attention required for good faith, such as by omitting information the plaintiff knew was needed to establish the proper court’s jurisdiction.
predicates.prior_diligence_not_proved: The plaintiff did not provide evidence establishing diligent prosecution of the earlier proceeding.
predicates.time_exclusion_for_prior_proceeding_deni: The time spent pursuing the earlier proceeding is not excluded from the limitation calculation.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff cannot exclude the time spent prosecuting an earlier proceeding from the limitation period when the plaintiff deliberately proceeds despite an early objection that a necessary party is absent and chooses to bear the risk of that omission.
material_facts: The later suit was filed more than twelve years after the relevant revenue sales, so it depended on excluding the time spent in the earlier suit and appeal to be within limitation.
The earlier suit concerned the same cause of action but was ultimately dismissed because the Government was a necessary party and had not been impleaded.
The defendants objected to the omission of the Government at an early stage.
The plaintiff resisted the objection and, during revision proceedings, expressly chose to proceed without adding the Government, accepting the risk of that choice.
members.legal_principle: Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1908 permits exclusion of time spent prosecuting another civil proceeding, with due diligence and in good faith, against the defendant, on the same cause of action, in a court unable to entertain it because of a defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature. Under Section 2(7), an act is not done in good faith unless it is done with due care and attention. The deliberate choice to continue despite an early objection to non-joinder, rather than correct the defect, was not a case of ignorance of law or a bona fide mistake on a doubtful point. Bishambhur Haldar v. Bonomali Haldar, ILR 26 Calcutta 414, was distinguished as involving a mistake of law on a doubtful point.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff did not prosecute the earlier proceeding in good faith, so its duration could not be excluded from the limitation period; the later suit was barred by limitation and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: civil_suit_with_limitation_claim and earlier_same_cause_proceeding and necessary_party_omitted and objection_raised_early and plaintiff_refused_to_add_party and plaintiff_chose_to_proceed_at_risk and later_suit_filed_after_limitation_period

predicates.civil_suit_with_limitation_claim: A party brought a civil suit whose timeliness depended on whether time spent in an earlier proceeding could be excluded.
predicates.earlier_same_cause_proceeding: The party previously prosecuted a civil proceeding against the opposing party on the same cause of action.
predicates.necessary_party_omitted: A party necessary to the earlier suit was not joined in that proceeding.
predicates.objection_raised_early: The opposing party objected to the missing necessary party at an early stage of the earlier proceeding.
predicates.plaintiff_refused_to_add_party: The plaintiff resisted the objection and did not add the necessary party to the earlier proceeding.
predicates.plaintiff_chose_to_proceed_at_risk: The plaintiff expressly chose to continue the earlier proceeding while accepting the risk of proceeding without the necessary party.
predicates.later_suit_filed_after_limitation_period: The later suit was filed after the applicable limitation period measured without excluding time spent in the earlier proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A court-ordered stay or status quo order does not suspend or extend the five-year period relevant to lapse of land-acquisition proceedings.
material_facts: Interim status quo orders protected the landowner's possession during the proceedings.
The acquiring authorities did not take possession while those orders were in force.
The award was more than five years old when the new regime commenced.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act does not exclude periods during which acquisition proceedings were stayed or affected by an injunction. The Court applied Sree Balaji Nagar Residential Association v. State of Tamil Nadu and relied on the provision's unambiguous wording and the literal-interpretation principle discussed in C.I.T., Mysore v. The Indo Mercantile Bank Ltd. and Madras & Southern Mahratta Railway Co. v. Bezwada Municipality.
members.conclusion: The period during which the court orders operated was not excluded from the five-year period, and the orders did not prevent the acquisition proceedings from lapsing.

predicates.legacy_land_acquisition: The government initiated land-acquisition proceedings under the former land-acquisition regime.
predicates.court_order_prevented_possession: A court order kept the acquiring authorities from taking possession while the proceedings were pending.
predicates.award_at_least_five_years_old: The acquiring authority made an award at least five years before the new regime commenced.

members.legal_issue: A court-ordered stay or status quo order does not extend the five-year period used to determine lapse under the new land acquisition law.
material_facts: The owner's possession was protected by status quo orders during the acquisition proceedings.
The owner relied on the rule that the period was not extended because of the court orders, and the Court applied the prior decision stating that such periods are not excluded.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) contains no exclusion of time during which proceedings were delayed by a stay, injunction, or status quo order. The Court relied on Sree Balaji Nagar Residential Association v. State of Tamil Nadu, which held that the legislature had not extended the five-year period for such delays.
members.conclusion: The period during which the proceedings were affected by a stay, injunction, or status quo order is not excluded from the five-year period.

predicates.former_law_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding was for acquisition under the former land acquisition law.
predicates.judicial_order_delayed_proceedings: A stay, injunction, or status quo order of a court delayed or affected the acquisition proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A power-of-attorney holder may testify about acts performed by the holder but may not testify in place of the principal about the principal’s personal acts or matters within the principal’s personal knowledge.
material_facts: The seller did not testify in person.
A power-of-attorney holder gave evidence concerning matters including whether the purchaser had said he could not raise the balance of the purchase price.
The purchaser denied making that statement, and the seller’s allegation was not established by evidence.
members.legal_principle: Order III Rules 1 and 2 CPC permit a power-of-attorney holder to act for the principal, but the term “acts” does not authorize the holder to testify in place of the principal about the principal’s personal acts or knowledge. The court relied on Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao, Janki Vashdeo Bhojwani v. Indusind Bank Ltd., M/S Shankar Finance and Investment v. State of A.P., and Man Kaur v. Hartar Singh Sangha.
members.conclusion: The power-of-attorney holder could not depose for the seller about acts performed by the seller or matters within the seller’s personal knowledge.

predicates.civil_case: The matter is a civil proceeding in which a party’s evidence is relevant.
predicates.witness_is_power_of_attorney_holder: The witness is authorized to act for a principal under a power of attorney.
predicates.matter_concerns_principal_personal_acts: The evidence concerns acts done by the principal, or matters within the principal’s personal knowledge, rather than acts done by the witness under the power of attorney.

members.legal_issue: A power-of-attorney holder may not testify in place of a principal about matters within the principal’s personal knowledge or acts done by the principal.
material_facts: The claimants were required to prove that they had an ownership share by showing their independent income and contribution to the property’s purchase.
The claimants did not testify themselves; the tribunal instead permitted one claimant’s husband, who held a power of attorney, to testify on their behalf.
The power-of-attorney holder did not have personal knowledge of the claimants’ relevant financial matters.
members.legal_principle: Order III Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure permit a power-of-attorney holder to act for a principal but do not authorize the holder to depose in place of the principal about the principal’s personal acts or knowledge. The Court approved Shambhu Dutt Shastri v. State of Rajasthan and Ram Prasad v. Hari Narain, and rejected the contrary view in Humberto Luis v. Floriano Armando Luis. It also referred to Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao, under which a party’s failure to testify and submit to cross-examination may support a presumption that the party’s case is not correct.
members.conclusion: The power-of-attorney holder could not testify in place of the claimants about matters within their personal knowledge or acts done by them. He could testify about acts he himself performed under the power of attorney and matters within his own personal knowledge.

predicates.civil_proceeding: The dispute is being decided in a civil proceeding.
predicates.agent_offered_as_principal_witness: A party presents an agent to give evidence in place of that party.
predicates.testimony_concerns_principal_personal_kn: The proposed evidence concerns matters personally known to the principal or acts of the principal, rather than acts performed or matters personally known by the agent.
predicates.agent_cannot_testify_for_principal_on_pe: The agent does not give evidence in place of the principal about matters personally known to the principal or acts done by the principal.

members.legal_issue: A claim that a party lacks standing because the relevant premises have been derequisitioned cannot be accepted on the record when the asserted derequisition order is not produced.
material_facts: The respondent argued that the premises had been derequisitioned and that the appellant therefore lacked standing to prosecute the appeal.
Despite repeated opportunities, the respondent did not produce the asserted derequisition order.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to accept the factual contention without production of the order said to establish derequisition, while leaving the respondent at liberty to raise the matter before the High Court.
members.conclusion: The Court did not accept the standing objection on the available record, but gave the respondent liberty to satisfy the High Court that the premises had been derequisitioned.

predicates.appeal_involving_standing_objection: The proceeding includes an objection that a party lacks standing because the relevant property has been derequisitioned.
predicates.derequisition_order_not_produced: The party asserting derequisition does not produce the order said to establish it.

members.legal_issue: A claim based on urban land ceiling proceedings cannot be determined when the relevant orders and necessary supporting material are absent from the record.
material_facts: The respondents relied on proceedings under urban land ceiling legislation and asserted that the land had not been shown as belonging to the deceased owner’s heirs.
The orders from those proceedings were not placed before the Supreme Court.
The respondents stated that the proceedings had lapsed following repeal of the legislation.
members.legal_principle: The court did not determine the substantive effect of the ceiling proceedings because their orders were not in the record and the relevant factual basis was not established.
members.conclusion: The court declined to examine the urban land ceiling issue and left it open for the State Government to examine.

predicates.urban_land_ceiling_issue_raised: A party relied on prior proceedings concerning a statutory limit on landholding.
predicates.relevant_orders_not_in_record: The orders needed to determine the effect of those proceedings were not submitted to the court.

members.legal_issue: The statutory protection for communications between spouses does not prevent testimony about a confession when the witness was not the accused’s legally wedded spouse.
material_facts: A witness testified that an accused had told her about the killings.
The witness was living as the accused’s mistress and was not his legally wedded wife; his marriage to another woman remained subsisting.
The courts below found that the witness’s relationship with the accused did not constitute a marriage attracting the claimed protection.
members.legal_principle: Section 122 of the Evidence Act did not apply on these facts because the witness was the accused’s mistress rather than his legally wedded wife. The Court upheld the factual finding that the provision was not attracted.
members.conclusion: The witness’s testimony was not excluded by Section 122 of the Evidence Act because she was not the accused’s legally wedded spouse.

predicates.criminal_appeal_review: The court is reviewing a criminal appeal in which testimony is challenged as protected marital communication.
predicates.witness_testifies_to_spousal_communicati: A witness testified about a communication made by the accused in their relationship.
predicates.witness_not_legally_wedded_spouse: The witness was not legally married to the accused.

members.legal_issue: The marital-communications privilege does not bar testimony by a person who was living as a partner but was not legally married to the accused.
material_facts: A witness testified about statements and events involving the accused.
The witness was living with the accused as his mistress, while his existing marriage remained in force.
The court found that the witness was not legally married to the accused.
members.legal_principle: Section 122 of the Evidence Act does not apply to communications between persons who were not legally married to each other; the court therefore treated the witness as a mistress rather than a spouse for this purpose.
members.conclusion: The privilege for communications between spouses did not prevent the witness’s testimony from being used against the accused.

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The evidence is being considered in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.witness_not_legally_married_to_accused: The witness and the accused were not legally married to each other.

members.legal_issue: A sentencing hearing requirement is met when the trial court questions each convicted accused about sentence and considers the answers before choosing the punishment.
material_facts: After recording convictions, the trial judge specifically questioned each accused about sentence and recorded the answers.
The trial judge considered those answers, reviewed the relevant sentencing decisions, and considered the role of each accused and aggravating and mitigating circumstances before imposing sentence.
members.legal_principle: Section 235(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires the court, after conviction, to hear the accused on sentence. On the facts, the individual questioning and consideration of the answers satisfied that requirement.
members.conclusion: The trial court complied with Section 235(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the challenge alleging non-compliance was rejected.

predicates.criminal_appeal_review: The court is reviewing a criminal conviction and sentence on appeal.
predicates.each_convicted_accused_questioned_on_sen: After conviction, the trial court asked each accused about the sentence to be imposed.
predicates.answers_considered_before_sentence: The trial court considered the accused’s answers before selecting the sentences.

members.legal_issue: A required sentencing hearing is satisfied when the court questions each convicted accused about sentence and considers the answers before choosing the punishment.
material_facts: After recording convictions, the trial court specifically questioned each accused about sentence and recorded the answers.
The trial court considered those answers along with the aggravating and mitigating circumstances before imposing sentence.
members.legal_principle: Section 235(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires an opportunity to be heard on sentence after conviction. The court found the requirement met because the trial court questioned each accused and considered the responses in its sentencing decision.
members.conclusion: The court found no failure to comply with the sentencing-hearing requirement.

predicates.criminal_appeal: The case is an appeal in a criminal prosecution.
predicates.each_convicted_accused_heard_on_sentence: After conviction, the court asked each convicted accused to address the sentence.
predicates.sentencing_responses_considered: The court considered the accused persons’ responses when deciding the sentences.

members.legal_issue: Court deposits made toward a debt bearing interest are applied first to interest and costs unless the creditor was informed of, and accepted, the condition that the deposits be applied to principal.
material_facts: The mortgagors deposited payments in court under the mortgage decree, and some applications recited that payments were toward principal.
The mortgagees were not shown to have been informed that the deposits were conditional on application to principal or to have accepted that condition.
The mortgagees' account applied the deposits first to interest and costs and then to principal.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XXI Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the ordinary rule for unappropriated payments on a debt carrying interest is that they are applied first to interest and then to principal. A debtor relying on a condition attached to a court deposit must plead and prove that the creditor was informed of and accepted it. The Court relied on Venkatadri Appa Row v. Parthasarathi Appa Row, which quoted the same principle from Parr's Barking Co. v. Yates.
members.conclusion: The deposits were properly applied first to interest and costs, with the remaining amounts credited to principal.

rule.if: mortgage_payment_accounting_proceeding and court_deposits_made and (not creditor_informed_of_principal_condition or not creditor_accepted_principal_condition)

predicates.mortgage_payment_accounting_proceeding: The court was deciding how payments should be credited in an accounting under a mortgage decree.
predicates.court_deposits_made: The debtors deposited payments in court toward a debt bearing interest.
predicates.creditor_informed_of_principal_condition: The creditor was informed that the debtors required the deposits to be applied to principal rather than interest and costs.
predicates.creditor_accepted_principal_condition: The creditor accepted the deposits on the condition that they be applied to principal rather than interest and costs.

members.legal_issue: Payments made toward a decretal debt carrying interest and costs must be allocated according to the decree or a proven agreement, and otherwise to interest and costs before principal.
material_facts: The decree imposed liability for principal, costs, and current and future interest, and prescribed instalments but did not prescribe how payments were to be allocated.
The parties had no agreement about allocation of the payments.

The executing court found that the decree-holder had allocated the payments to costs and interest before principal, and the judgment debtors had not established an agreement requiring a different allocation.
members.legal_principle: The ordinary rule is that a payment on a debt carrying interest is applied first to interest and then to principal: Venkatadri Appa Row v. Parthasarathi Appa Row and Meghraj v. Mst. Bayabai. The rule applies to decretal payments subject to the decree and any agreement between the parties. Order 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs payment under decrees; the party asserting a different agreed allocation bears the burden of proving it.
members.conclusion: The general rule is that payments toward a decretal amount must first follow any allocation directed by the decree; absent such a direction, they are applied to interest and costs before principal, unless the parties have agreed on another allocation. The party relying on such an agreement must prove it.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and payment_toward_decretal_debt and not proven_agreement_for_different_allocation

predicates.execution_proceeding: A court is executing a decree for payment.
predicates.payment_toward_decretal_debt: The judgment debtor has made a payment toward the amount due under the decree.
predicates.proven_agreement_for_different_allocatio: The parties have established an agreement allocating payments differently from the decree or the ordinary order of allocation.

members.legal_issue: The restriction on a landlord’s successive applications for possession does not bar a later application where the tenant moved to another part of the same building under a settlement rather than vacating the building pursuant to an eviction order, or where a genuine new requirement has arisen.
material_facts: In an earlier eviction proceeding, the parties settled while the tenant’s appeal was pending; the tenant moved from the first floor to a room, kitchen, and passage on the ground floor of the same building.
The tenant’s move was not made under an eviction order, and the landlords did not obtain possession of the building through the settlement.
The landlords later sought possession for the first appellant’s family after its residential needs increased.
members.legal_principle: The third proviso to Section 14(3) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987 applies where the landlord obtains possession of a building pursuant to an eviction order under the specified clauses; a tenant’s move to another part of the same building by settlement is not the tenant vacating the building or the landlord obtaining its possession. The proviso prevents a landlord from repeatedly relying on the same or similar circumstances after obtaining possession, but does not bar relief when the requirement has changed or a new, unrelated requirement has arisen. Molar Mal (dead) through L.Rs. v. M/s. Kay Iron Works (Pvt.) Ltd. was distinguished as not deciding this situation; the Court relied on the pragmatic approach to statutory interpretation in Rakesh Wadhawan v. Jagdamba Industrial Corporation and on the reasoning in Jagir Singh v. Jagdish Pal Sagar and Brij Lal Puri v. Smt. Muni Tandon.
members.conclusion: The third proviso did not bar the later eviction application; the tenant had not vacated the building and the landlords had not obtained possession under an eviction order. The restriction also does not prevent a later application based on a changed or new genuine requirement.

rule.if: residential_own_occupation_eviction_case and (no_eviction_order_led_to_possession or tenant_did_not_leave_building or genuine_requirement_changed)

predicates.residential_own_occupation_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks possession of a residential premises for the landlord’s own occupation.
predicates.no_eviction_order_led_to_possession: The landlord did not obtain possession of the premises pursuant to an eviction order.
predicates.tenant_did_not_leave_building: The tenant moved to another part of the same building rather than leaving the building.
predicates.genuine_requirement_changed: The landlord’s genuine need materially changed or a new, unrelated genuine need arose.

members.legal_issue: A restriction on repeated eviction for a landlord’s own use applies at the stage of deciding whether to order actual eviction, including when possession of other premises is obtained after the eviction application was filed, and is not limited to separate buildings or premises.
material_facts: While the eviction application was pending, the landlord obtained possession of three other rented premises through eviction proceedings.

The landlord maintained that possession obtained after filing the current application could not bar the current eviction and relied on High Court decisions distinguishing parts of the same premises from independent buildings.
The Supreme Court concluded that limiting the restriction to the filing stage would allow a landlord to evade it by filing multiple applications simultaneously.
The Court rejected the distinction between premises occupied by different tenants in the same building and premises in separate buildings.
members.legal_principle: Sections 13(1) and 13(3)(i)(b) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973 restrict the grounds and circumstances in which a tenant may be evicted. Reading the statute as a whole and in light of its purpose, the words concerning applying again cannot be confined to the filing of an application where that would defeat the restriction. The Court rejected the interpretation in Shri Brij Lal Puri v. Smt. Muni Tandon alias Urmala (1979) 1 Rent Law Reporter 58 and Jagir Singh v. Jagdish Pal Sagar (1980) 1 RLR 494.
members.conclusion: The restriction extends through the stage at which actual eviction is considered, and the distinction drawn by the cited High Court decisions was not correct law; whether the other premises were of the same class remained to be determined on evidence.

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant for the landlord’s own use.
predicates.landlord_obtained_other_premises_under_s: The landlord obtained possession of other rented premises through proceedings on the same eviction ground, whether before or after filing the current application.
predicates.other_premises_are_of_same_class: The other premises belong to the same class as the premises for which eviction is sought.

members.legal_issue: A maintenance holding forming part of a Saranjam does not pass to an adopted heir against a valid government resumption and fresh grant.
material_facts: The lands had been assigned to a junior family member as a maintenance holding within a Saranjam estate.
After the holder died, the government directed that the holding be continued to his undivided brother, effective from the holder’s death.
The deceased holder’s widow adopted a son without obtaining the government’s sanction.
The adopted son claimed the lands against the brother on the basis of his adoption.
members.legal_principle: The Saranjam Rules, particularly Rules 1, 2, 5, 7 and 8, govern a maintenance holding that forms part of a Saranjam. A Saranjam is held subject to the sovereign’s power to resume it and make a fresh grant; private rights cannot fetter that power. The Court relied on Daulatrao Malojirao v. Province of Bombay (1946) 49 Bom. L.R. 270, which discussed Shekh Sultan Sani v. Shekh Ajmodin (1892) L.R. 20 I.A. 50 and Raghojirao v. Laxmanrao (1912) 14 Bom. L.R. 1226.
members.conclusion: The government could resume the maintenance holding and make a fresh grant to the brother; the adoption without government sanction did not displace that grant, and the adopted son was not entitled to the lands under the Saranjam Rules.

rule.if: claim_to_saranjam_maintenance_lands and grant_part_of_saranjam and government_resumed_and_regranted_after_holder_death and adoption_without_government_sanction

predicates.claim_to_saranjam_maintenance_lands: A person in a claim concerning a maintenance holding within a Saranjam asserts entitlement through succession or adoption.
predicates.grant_part_of_saranjam: The holding was treated as part of the Saranjam and subject to its incidents.
predicates.government_resumed_and_regranted_after_h: After the holder died, the government resumed the holding and made a fresh grant to another family member.
predicates.adoption_without_government_sanction: A widow adopted an heir without obtaining the government’s sanction.

members.legal_issue: A maintenance holding forming part of a Saranjam may be resumed and freshly granted by the government, and an adoption made without government sanction does not divest the resulting grant.
material_facts: The properties were maintenance holdings within a Saranjam and were treated by the government and the family as part of that Saranjam.
After the holder died, the government directed that the holdings be continued to his undivided brother, with effect from the holder’s death.
The widow adopted a son before the government issued that direction, but had not obtained government sanction for the adoption.
members.legal_principle: Under Rules 1, 2 and 5 of the Saranjam Rules, a Saranjam is held as a life estate, is ordinarily resumed on the holder’s death, and may then be freshly granted by the government. The sovereign power may grant or withhold a Saranjam, and private rights cannot fetter that power. The Court relied on Daulatrao Malojirao v. Province of Bombay, which discussed Shekh Sultan Sani v. Shekh Ajmodin and Raghojirao v. Laxmanrao.
members.conclusion: The government’s direction amounted to a valid resumption and fresh grant to the brother. The later government order was not invalidated by the adoption, and the adopted son could not claim the properties under the Saranjam Rules.

rule.if: saranjam_property_appeal and maintenance_holding_part_of_saranjam and government_freshly_granted_holding_to_another_person and adoption_lacked_government_sanction

predicates.saranjam_property_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a claim to property held as part of a Saranjam.
predicates.maintenance_holding_part_of_saranjam: The claimed property was assigned as a maintenance holding within a Saranjam.
predicates.government_freshly_granted_holding_to_an: After the prior holder died, the government resumed the holding and granted it to another person.
predicates.adoption_lacked_government_sanction: The claimant’s adoption was made without the government’s sanction.

members.legal_issue: Alleged political motives do not invalidate legislation when the enacting legislature has competence over its subject matter.
material_facts: The petitioners alleged that the legislation and the preceding ordinances were politically motivated.
The petitioners provided no particulars of the alleged political malice.
The Court examined Parliament's competence to enact the legislation.
members.legal_principle: Under K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa and Board of Trustees, Ayurvedic and Unani Tibia College v. State of Delhi, the doctrine of colourable legislation concerns legislative competence, not legislative bona fides or motives. If the legislature is competent, its motives are irrelevant; if it is not competent, motive is immaterial.
members.conclusion: The allegation of political malice did not provide a basis for invalidating the Act; the controlling question was legislative competence.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of legislation.
predicates.legislative_motive_alleged: A challenger alleges that the legislature acted from an improper or political motive.
predicates.legislature_has_subject_matter_competenc: The legislature has constitutional competence over the subject matter of the legislation.

members.legal_issue: A claim that legislation is colourable does not succeed where the legislature acted within its constitutional limits, because legislative motive is immaterial to that inquiry.
material_facts: The challenge alleged that the legislature acted mala fide in enacting the law.
The Court had determined that the State legislature did not transgress the limits of its legislative competence.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of colourable legislation concerns legislative competence, not the legislature’s good faith or motive. If the legislature is competent to enact the law, its motives are irrelevant; the doctrine applies to a disguised or indirect transgression of constitutional limits. The Court relied on K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the colourable-legislation and mala-fides challenge.

predicates.colourable_legislation_challenge: A party alleges that a legislature used a law to disguise an act beyond its constitutional powers.
predicates.legislature_within_constitutional_limits: The legislature acted within the constitutional limits of its law-making authority.

members.legal_issue: A sentence enhancement cannot be sustained on a distinction between accused persons when the stated basis for the distinction applies equally to others convicted of comparable conduct.
material_facts: The trial court imposed life imprisonment on the accused convicted of the relevant killings, treating their drunkenness as an extenuating circumstance.
The High Court enhanced the sentences of two accused to death because the prosecution had directly connected them with the deaths of more than one person.

The Supreme Court observed that other accused must also have been responsible for causing the deaths of some of the deceased, so the stated reason did not distinguish the two enhanced sentences from the others.
The High Court did not enhance the sentences of those other accused on the same stated basis.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the stated ground for enhancement was unsound where it applied equally to accused whose sentences were not enhanced. It also rejected drunkenness, on the facts described, as a sound reason for imposing a lesser sentence. No earlier case or specific statutory provision was cited for the sentencing conclusion.
members.conclusion: The Court set aside the High Court's enhancement and restored the sentences imposed by the trial court; it also considered the trial court's reliance on drunkenness as an extenuating circumstance unsound.

predicates.appeal_from_sentence_enhancement: The proceeding challenges an appellate court's decision to enhance a criminal sentence.
predicates.enhancement_based_on_multiple_deaths: The sentence was enhanced because the accused were connected with the deaths of more than one person.
predicates.same_basis_applies_to_unenhanced_coaccus: The stated reason for enhancement applies equally to co-accused whose sentences were not enhanced.

members.legal_issue: A conviction cannot be maintained where it would produce inconsistent and unequal treatment of similarly situated members after comparable acquittals have become final.
material_facts: The High Court treated some accused as members of the unlawful assembly but did not convict certain similarly situated members of the related group-liability offence.
The acquittals of those members were not challenged by the State and had become final.
The Supreme Court considered that maintaining the remaining convictions would be inconsistent and would treat similarly situated accused unequally.
members.legal_principle: The finality of unchallenged acquittals prevents the court from convicting those acquitted persons in the accused’s appeal; where maintaining convictions against similarly situated members would be self-contradictory and unequal, those convictions must also be set aside. The Court considered liability under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code and the procedural finality of the unchallenged acquittals.
members.conclusion: The convictions of the remaining similarly situated accused for the group-liability offence were set aside.

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal by an accused against a conviction.
predicates.comparable_acquittals_became_final: Acquittals of similarly situated persons for the comparable offence were not challenged and became final.
predicates.conviction_would_create_inconsistent_une: Maintaining the appellant’s conviction would produce inconsistent findings or unequal treatment of similarly situated persons.

members.legal_issue: Whether a profit from a single, isolated land transaction outside the taxpayer’s ordinary business is taxable as profit from an adventure in the nature of trade.
material_facts: The taxpayer was an engineer engaged in several business activities, but had no dealings in land apart from this transaction.
He agreed to buy a residential plot from a land-development society and paid an advance toward its price.
The land remained requisitioned, and the taxpayer’s construction business began to decline; he later assigned his rights under the purchase agreement to another buyer for more than he had paid.

The taxpayer said he had intended to build a residence and a workshop on the plot. The Court considered that use plausible and found that the Department had not established that his dominant intention at the time of purchase was to embark on a trading venture.
The Tribunal treated the profit as taxable trade income, relying in part on the taxpayer’s finances and ability to complete the purchase and build on the land.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(4) and 10 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, a single transaction can be an adventure in the nature of trade, but an isolated transaction outside the taxpayer’s ordinary business is not trade merely because it yields a profit or was undertaken in the hope of resale at a gain. The Department bears the burden of establishing that the transaction had the character of a trading venture. No universal test decides the question; the court considers the total impression created by all the facts and circumstances. Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Reinhold was applied. G. Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. Commissioner of Income-tax was distinguished on its facts; Jones v. Leeming and Leeming v. Jones were also relied on in considering the distinction between an accretion to capital and trading profit.
members.conclusion: The Department did not prove that the taxpayer’s dominant intention at the time of the agreement was to embark on an adventure in the nature of trade. The appeal was allowed, and the Tribunal’s orders assessing the profit as trade income were set aside.

rule.if: tax_assessment_appeal and single_isolated_transaction and transaction_outside_ordinary_business and department_failed_to_prove_dominant_trading_intention

predicates.tax_assessment_appeal: A taxpayer appeals an assessment that treats profit from a transaction as income from a trading venture.
predicates.single_isolated_transaction: The taxpayer undertook only one transaction of this kind.
predicates.transaction_outside_ordinary_business: The transaction was not in the line of business the taxpayer ordinarily carried on.
predicates.department_failed_to_prove_dominant_trad: The taxing authority did not establish that the taxpayer’s dominant intention when entering the transaction was to undertake a trading venture.

members.legal_issue: Whether profit from an isolated purchase and resale of property is taxable as business income when the transaction is not connected with the assessee’s existing business.
material_facts: The assessee carried on a business dealing in iron scrap and hardware, but had never carried on a jute-pressing business.

The assessee purchased a jute press and appurtenant property subject to pending litigation, repaired the factory and kept it in working condition, but did not organize or begin a jute-pressing business.
The assessee agreed to resell the property after receiving an offer soon after the purchase and made a substantial profit.

The property was capable of being let out and had previously been let out; apart from the expectation of profit and its realization, there was no evidence establishing that the purchase was intended as a trading venture.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 10 and 2(4) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, business income includes profits from an adventure in the nature of trade. The revenue must establish that the profit falls within the taxing provision. Whether a transaction is such an adventure is a mixed question of law and fact, determined from the collective effect of the circumstances; no single fact is decisive. A transaction related to the assessee’s usual business, or dealings such as subdividing, altering, treating, or converting an acquired commodity before resale, may support an inference of trade. But profit motive or an expectation of resale at a profit alone does not turn an accretion to capital into taxable income, and a purchase of property cannot, without more, be assumed to be a trading venture. The Court relied on G. Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. Commissioner of Income-tax and Saroj Kumar Mazumdar v. Commissioner of Income-tax, West Bengal, and considered the illustrative authorities Martin v. Lowry, Rutledge v. Commissioner of Inland Revenue, Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Fraser, Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Reinhold, and Leeming v. Jones.
members.conclusion: The transaction was not shown to be an adventure in the nature of trade, so the profit was not taxable as business income. The question was answered in the negative and the appeal was allowed.

rule.if: income_tax_profit_assessment and isolated_asset_transaction and unrelated_to_existing_business and property_not_ordinary_trading_commodity and no_business_operations_on_asset and resale_expectation_only

predicates.income_tax_profit_assessment: The proceeding determines whether profit from the sale of an acquired asset is taxable as income from business.
predicates.isolated_asset_transaction: The assessee made a single purchase and resale rather than conducting a recurring business in the asset.
predicates.unrelated_to_existing_business: The acquired asset and its intended use were unrelated to the business the assessee ordinarily carried on.
predicates.property_not_ordinary_trading_commodity: The acquired asset was property that could not, from its nature alone, be treated as an ordinary trading commodity.
predicates.no_business_operations_on_asset: The assessee did not organize or carry on the business associated with the acquired asset before reselling it.
predicates.resale_expectation_only: The established circumstances showed an expectation of resale for profit, but did not establish an additional trading purpose for the purchase.

members.legal_issue: Uncultivated banjar land that is not occupied or let for agricultural purposes is excluded when calculating whether a landowner is a small landowner and whether the holding is surplus.
material_facts: The landowners’ holdings were assessed as of the date the Act came into force.
After uncultivated banjar land was excluded, each landowner’s holding was below the permissible area.
The tenants sought to purchase surplus land, but the authorities found no surplus area.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(2) and 2(8) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, read with section 4(1) of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887, land for this purpose must be occupied or let for agricultural or related purposes. Banjar Kadim and Banjar Jadid do not fall within that definition. The relevant holdings are assessed as of the commencement of the 1953 Act. The Court relied on Bhagwan Das v. State of Punjab and Munshi Ram v. Financial Commissioner, Haryana.
members.conclusion: Uncultivated banjar land could not be included in calculating the landowners’ holdings, and the tenants’ purchase applications were rightly dismissed because no surplus area remained.

predicates.tenant_surplus_purchase_proceeding: A tenant sought to purchase land alleged to be surplus to a landowner’s permissible holding.
predicates.holding_assessed_at_commencement: The landowner’s holding was assessed as it stood when the relevant land-ceiling scheme began.
predicates.uncultivated_banjar_not_used_for_agricul: The land in question was uncultivated banjar land and was not occupied or let for agricultural or related purposes.

members.legal_issue: Uncultivated Banjar and Gair Mumkin areas that are not occupied or let for agricultural or agriculture-subservient purposes are excluded when computing permissible or surplus area.
material_facts: Uncultivated Banjar Qadim, Banjar Jadid and Gair Mumkin areas had been included in calculating the allottees’ holdings.
The extent of those areas was disputed, so the Court directed that it be ascertained and the permissible area recomputed after their exclusion.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(8) of the Punjab Security of Lands Tenure Act, 1953, and 2(c) of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887, define land by reference to occupation or letting for agricultural purposes, purposes subservient to agriculture, or pasture. The Court approved Nemi Chand Jain v. Financial Commissioner, Punjab, AIR 1964 Punj. 373, which held that Banjar Qadim and Banjar Jadid not occupied or let for those purposes fall outside the definition of land.
members.conclusion: Banjar Qadim and Banjar Jadid areas that do not meet the statutory definition of land cannot be counted. The extent of the Banjar and Gair Mumkin areas was to be determined and the permissible area recomputed after excluding them.

predicates.is_land_tenure_area_computation: The proceeding requires land area to be computed for a land-tenure determination.
predicates.parcels_are_uncultivated_banjar_or_gair_: The parcels being assessed are uncultivated Banjar or Gair Mumkin areas.
predicates.parcels_are_not_occupied_or_let_for_agri: The parcels are not occupied or let for agriculture, purposes subservient to agriculture, or pasture.
predicates.such_parcels_are_excluded_from_area_comp: The parcels are left out when the relevant permissible or surplus area is computed.

members.legal_issue: A land-reform statute applies to government-owned land unless the government is expressly or by necessary implication exempted from its operation.
material_facts: A tenant applied to acquire proprietary rights in land that he cultivated and held under the Union, paying rent and land revenue.
The land was assessed to land revenue, and the revenue record identified the applicant as an occupancy tenant.
The Union challenged the application on the ground that the statute did not bind the government or apply to government-owned land.
The lower authorities found the applicant to be the Union’s tenant and allowed the application under the statute.
members.legal_principle: Under Superintendent and Legal Remembrancer, West Bengal v. Corporation of Calcutta, the ordinary rule is that legislation applies to the State as it does to citizens unless the State is expressly or by necessary implication exempted. That decision rejected the contrary approach in Director of Rationing v. Corporation of Calcutta, which had relied on the rule associated with Province of Bombay v. Municipal Corporation of Bombay. Sections 2(3), 2(5), 2(6), 2(13), 2(17), 2(19), 3, 8 and 11–27 of the Act defined the relevant land, landlord, tenant and tenancy and provided for transfer of landowner rights to tenants; they did not expressly or by necessary implication exclude government land. The Act’s purpose of abolishing landlordism and improving tenants’ conditions also did not support treating government tenants differently from other tenants.
members.conclusion: The statute bound the Union and applied to the land; the tenant’s application was competent, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: land_reform_proceeding and government_is_landlord and land_meets_general_coverage_terms and not express_government_exemption and not necessary_government_exemption

predicates.land_reform_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a tenant’s claim under a land-reform scheme to acquire rights in the land held by the tenant.
predicates.government_is_landlord: The government owns or holds the land and is the landlord under whom the tenant holds it.
predicates.land_meets_general_coverage_terms: The land and the parties’ relationship fall within the law’s general descriptions of covered land, landlord and tenant.
predicates.express_government_exemption: The law expressly exempts the government or government-owned land from its operation.
predicates.necessary_government_exemption: The law’s scheme or purpose necessarily implies that the government or government-owned land is excluded.

members.legal_issue: Land-reform legislation applies to government-owned land unless the legislation expressly or by necessary implication exempts the government.
material_facts: The tenant was recorded and treated throughout the proceedings as an occupancy tenant of the land, and the government was accepted as its landlord and landowner.
The tenant applied to acquire proprietary rights in the land under the legislation.
The legislation contained no express exemption for the government, and its scheme and object did not imply such an exemption.
members.legal_principle: A statute applies to the State as it does to a citizen unless the State is expressly or by necessary implication exempted. The Court followed Superintendent and Legal Remembrancer v. Corporation of Calcutta, [1967] 2 S.C.R. 170, and rejected the contrary majority rule in Director of Rationing v. Corporation of Calcutta, [1961] 1 S.C.R. 158. The Court considered sections 11 to 27 of the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, including the scheme for transferring landowners’ rights to tenants, to the State, or through the State to tenants. It found no provision or feature of that scheme implying an exemption for government land; such an exemption would also frustrate the Act’s object of alleviating occupancy tenants’ conditions and eliminating landlordism without discrimination between government and citizen landlords.
members.conclusion: The legislation applied to the government-owned land, and the tenant’s application to acquire proprietary rights was competent. The appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: statutory_land_tenancy_application and occupancy_tenant and government_landowner and law_has_no_state_exemption

predicates.statutory_land_tenancy_application: A tenant applies under a land-tenancy reform law to acquire proprietary rights in land.
predicates.occupancy_tenant: The applicant holds the land as an occupancy tenant.
predicates.government_landowner: The government owns the land and is the tenant’s landlord.
predicates.law_has_no_state_exemption: The law neither expressly exempts the government nor, in its scheme and object, implies such an exemption.

members.legal_issue: A municipal building valuation is not procedurally defective where the owner had an ample opportunity to be heard and relevant circumstances were considered.
material_facts: The lower appellate court’s judgment recorded that the owners’ counsel had been given ample opportunity to present their case to the municipal commissioner.
That judgment also recorded that the assessment officer had considered the relevant circumstances bearing on the building’s reasonable letting value.
The owners’ counsel did not argue before the Supreme Court that a hearing had been denied or that relevant factors had been overlooked.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the record of the lower appellate court, which showed that the owners had an ample opportunity to present their case and that relevant circumstances had been considered; the owners did not contest those matters before the Supreme Court.
members.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to find that the owners had not received a full hearing or that the valuation was based on no principle.

predicates.municipal_building_value_assessment: A municipal authority is assessing a building’s annual value for property taxation.
predicates.owner_given_ample_opportunity: The owner was given an ample opportunity to present the owner’s case to the assessing authority.
predicates.relevant_factors_considered: The assessing authority considered the relevant circumstances bearing on the valuation.

members.legal_issue: A building’s annual-value assessment is not shown to be procedurally defective for lack of a hearing or an principled basis when the owner had an adequate opportunity to present the case and relevant circumstances were considered.
material_facts: The owner was given ample opportunity by the municipal commissioner to present the objection to the assessment.
The assessment officer considered the relevant circumstances bearing on the building’s reasonable letting value.
The appellate judge found that the hearing was adequate and relevant factors had been considered; the owner did not pursue those objections before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The record showed an adequate opportunity to make representations and consideration of the relevant circumstances. On those facts, the High Court’s contrary procedural findings were not supported by the record.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in finding that the owner had not received a full hearing or that the valuation was based on no principle.

predicates.property_tax_assessment_challenge: An owner challenges the procedure or basis used to determine a building’s annual value for property-tax assessment.
predicates.owner_given_adequate_opportunity: The owner was given an adequate opportunity to present the case to the assessing authority.
predicates.relevant_circumstances_considered: The assessing authority considered the circumstances relevant to determining reasonable letting value.
predicates.assessment_not_invalid_for_lack_of_heari: The assessment is not invalid on the grounds that the owner lacked a hearing or that the valuation lacked a principled basis.

members.legal_issue: The State may recover the full price of minerals raised without lawful authority under Section 21(5), including minerals unlawfully extracted within a lease area, and that recovery is compensatory rather than criminal punishment.
material_facts: Minerals were allegedly extracted without required clearances or beyond permitted limits, including within leased areas.

Some minerals had been disposed of, and the parties disputed whether Section 21(5) applied only to extraction outside a lease and whether recovery could be limited to a fraction of the mineral’s value.
The Committee recommended partial recovery, while the Union and petitioners argued for full recovery.
members.legal_principle: Section 21(5) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 applies to minerals raised without lawful authority from any land and permits recovery of the mineral or its price. The Court relied on Karnataka Rare Earth v. Senior Geologist, Department of Mines & Geology, which characterized recovery of the price as compensatory, and held that Khemka & Co. (Agencies) Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra was inapposite. Section 21(1) separately provides for prosecution for contravention of Section 4(1). The Mineral Concession Rules do not restrict the scope of the Act.
members.conclusion: Section 21(5) applies to unlawful extraction inside or outside a lease area, and the State is entitled to recover the mineral or, if it has been disposed of, its full price; only one set of compensation is recoverable for overlapping violations.

predicates.mining_case: A court is considering recovery arising from mineral extraction.
predicates.mineral_extracted_without_lawful_authori: A person extracted minerals in breach of a legal requirement governing the extraction, whether inside or outside a lease area.
predicates.mineral_disposed: The extracted mineral was sold, transferred, or otherwise disposed of rather than remaining available for recovery.

members.legal_issue: Recovery of the price of minerals removed without lawful authority is compensatory rather than penal.
material_facts: The State demanded the price of granite blocks extracted and exported under interim court orders that ceased to operate when the lessees' appeals were dismissed.
The demand was for the price of the minerals, and rent, royalty or tax had already been recovered.
No penal or criminal proceedings had been initiated, and the lessees did not claim that the demanded price exceeded what they had realised or was arbitrary or unreasonable.
members.legal_principle: Section 21(5) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 provides for recovery of the mineral or, if disposed of, its price, and for recovery of rent, royalty or tax. The Court held that recovery of the mineral's price compensates the State for loss of its mineral and prevents a person acting without lawful authority from being better placed than one acting with authority. It distinguished Hindustan Steel Ltd. v. State of Orissa, which concerned a statutory penalty, and Consolidated Coffee Ltd. v.
