members.legal_issue: Requiring payment of the tax claimed before entertaining a tax appeal does not violate equality or nullify the right of appeal when the appellate judge may waive the payment for undue hardship.
material_facts: The ratepayers appealed assessments but did not deposit the amounts claimed, and the appeals were not entertained.
The law permitted the appellate judge to dispense with all or part of the deposit if it would cause undue hardship.
The challenge concerned the deposit condition and related appeal and recovery provisions.
members.legal_principle: Under section 406(2)(e) of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, as amended, the claimed amount must be deposited before the relevant appeal is entertained, subject to the judge's discretion to waive all or part of the deposit for undue hardship. A statutory right of appeal may be subject to conditions that regulate its exercise, and a disadvantage resulting from a person's own default does not create an Article 14 classification. The validity of section 411(bb) and rule 42 depended on that of section 406(2)(e). The Court relied on Hannah Cohen v Beneficial Loan Corporation and referred to the condition for appeal under section 30 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
members.conclusion: The deposit condition was constitutionally valid and did not nullify the right of appeal or create an invidious distinction; the related appeal and recovery provisions were also valid.

rule.if: challenge_to_tax_appeal_deposit_condition and tax_appeal_required_deposit and appellant_did_not_deposit_claimed_amount and judge_could_waive_deposit_for_undue_hardship and appellant_did_not_show_undue_hardship

predicates.challenge_to_tax_appeal_deposit_conditio: A party challenged a legal condition governing whether an appeal against a tax assessment could be entertained.
predicates.tax_appeal_required_deposit: The appeal process required the appellant to deposit the amount claimed before the appeal could be entertained.
predicates.appellant_did_not_deposit_claimed_amount: The appellant failed to deposit the amount claimed.
predicates.judge_could_waive_deposit_for_undue_hard: The appellate judge had discretion to dispense with all or part of the deposit if it would cause undue hardship.
predicates.appellant_did_not_show_undue_hardship: The appellant did not establish that making the deposit would cause undue hardship.

members.legal_issue: A requirement to deposit disputed tax before a statutory appeal is entertained, with hardship relief limited to part of the deposit, does not violate equality or make the right of appeal illusory.
material_facts: Property owners challenged revised property-tax assessments through statutory appeals and sought interim relief from payment while those appeals were pending.
The law required the disputed tax, or the tax calculated on the disputed rateable value, to be deposited before an appeal could be entertained.
A judge could relieve an appellant from part of the deposit on grounds of undue hardship, but the relief was capped at a portion of the deposit.
The property owners challenged the deposit requirement and the cap on hardship relief as unconstitutional.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not prohibit a legislature from attaching conditions to a statutory right of appeal. A pre-deposit requirement regulates the exercise of that right and balances the appellant’s right to challenge tax with the public authority’s interest in recovering it. A disadvantage resulting from an appellant’s own default does not create unconstitutional discrimination where the condition applies equally and hardship relief is available. The Court relied on Section 406(2)(e) and its proviso of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, and noted the complaint procedure under Section 406(2)(c) and the arbitration procedure under Section 408. It applied The Anant Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Gujarat, Smt. Ganga Bai v. Vijay Kumar, Shyam Kishore v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi, and Vijay Prakash D. Mehta v. Collector of Customs (Preventive), Bombay.
members.conclusion: The deposit requirement, including the limit on hardship relief, is constitutionally valid and does not violate Article 14 or nullify the statutory right of appeal.

rule.if: tax_appeal_predeposit_challenge and statutory_appeal_right and deposit_required_before_appeal and hardship_relief_available and relief_limited_to_part_of_deposit and condition_applies_equally and nonpayment_without_undue_hardship_bars_appeal

predicates.tax_appeal_predeposit_challenge: A party in a tax proceeding challenged the constitutionality of a requirement to deposit money before an appeal could be entertained.
predicates.statutory_appeal_right: The legislature created a right for an aggrieved person to appeal a tax determination.
predicates.deposit_required_before_appeal: The law required an appellant to deposit the disputed tax, or tax calculated on the disputed valuation, before the appeal could be entertained.
predicates.hardship_relief_available: A judge could reduce or dispense with the deposit when it would cause undue hardship to the appellant.
predicates.relief_limited_to_part_of_deposit: The law limited how much of the required deposit the judge could waive or dispense with.
predicates.condition_applies_equally: The deposit condition applied to all persons seeking the relevant statutory appeal.
predicates.nonpayment_without_undue_hardship_bars_a: An appellant who did not deposit the required amount and could not establish undue hardship could not have the appeal entertained.

members.legal_issue: A court may give directions for the ordinary administration of a public trust under an existing management scheme without requiring a separate suit.
material_facts: A decree settling a management scheme appointed two joint managers and allowed either manager to apply to the court for directions when an occasion arose to carry out the scheme.
One manager applied for directions concerning the trust’s cattle and the cultivation of its lands; the managers were unable to agree.
The requested directions concerned the management and use of trust property.
members.legal_principle: A suit under Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, section 92, to settle a scheme is analogous to an administration suit. A scheme may provide for its modification when necessary, and modifications for administration may be made on an application under the scheme without a separate section 92 suit. The Court followed Raje Anandrao v. Shamrao, [1961] 3 S.C.R. 930.
members.conclusion: The scheme authorized the court to give directions for ordinary administration on an application by a manager, without a separate suit.

predicates.manager_applies_for_directions_under_exi: A manager of a trust applies to a court for directions under an existing management scheme.
predicates.scheme_authorizes_court_directions: The management scheme provides that a manager may seek court directions when needed to carry it out.
predicates.direction_concerns_ordinary_trust_admini: The requested direction concerns the ordinary administration of the trust.

members.legal_issue: A scheme settled in a public-trust suit may reserve power to amend the scheme by application, without requiring a separate suit, when the amendment is for the administration of the trust.
material_facts: A scheme for the administration of a public religious trust was settled in a suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The scheme and the judgment settling it reserved the ability to modify the scheme as circumstances required.
The District Judge revised the scheme after an investigation into the temple’s management.
members.legal_principle: Section 92(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers the court to settle a scheme, and Section 92(2) does not bar an application made under a modification provision contained in that scheme. A suit to settle a scheme is analogous to an administration suit, and the decree may provide for a future change in the manner of administration without losing its finality. The court approved Chandraprasad Ramprasad v. Jinabharathi Narayanabharathi, Sri Swami Rangacharya v. Gangaram, Umeshananda Dutta Jha v. Sir Ravaneswar Prasad Singh, Manadananda Jha v. Tarakananda Jha Panda, Srijib Nyayatirtha v. Sreemant Dandy Swami Jagannath Ashram, Mahomed Waheb Hussain v. Syed Abbas Hussain, and Gangaram Govind Pashankar v. Sardar K. R. Vinchurkar; it disapproved Veeraraghavachariar v. The Advocate-General of Madras. The Privy Council schemes in Prayaga Doss Jee Varu v. Tirumala Anandam Pillai Purisa Sriranga Charylu Varu and Sevak Kirpashanker Daji v. Gopal Rao Manohar Tambekar were also referred to.
members.conclusion: The court may amend the scheme by an application under its reserved modification clause when the change concerns administration; a separate suit under Section 92 is not required.

predicates.public_trust_scheme_proceeding: A proceeding is brought to settle a scheme for administering a public charitable or religious trust.
predicates.scheme_reserves_modification: The settled scheme provides that it may be modified when circumstances require.
predicates.change_concerns_administration: The proposed change concerns the administration of the trust.

members.legal_issue: Interim compensation during a stay of an eviction decree may be fixed tentatively using available evidence of prevailing rental value and the area occupied.
material_facts: The premises were in a prime commercial locality, and the parties provided material about rents paid for other premises in the locality and building.
The parties disputed the area occupied, and the court used the area stated by the occupants.
The landlords sought monthly compensation during the appeal, and the court treated its assessment as tentative and subject to determination by a competent forum.
members.legal_principle: Applying Atma Ram Properties (P) Ltd. v. Federal Motors (P) Ltd., the court assessed reasonable interim compensation by considering the available evidence of rents in the locality rather than the former contractual rent. The assessment was tentative and did not determine the amount recoverable in properly constituted proceedings.
members.conclusion: The occupants were directed to pay or deposit interim compensation calculated by reference to the area they acknowledged occupying and the rental evidence, subject to final determination of the amount.

predicates.eviction_appeal_stay: An appeal against an eviction decree is pending and execution of the decree has been stayed.
predicates.prevailing_rent_evidence_available: The parties provide evidence of rents paid for comparable premises in the locality or building.
predicates.occupied_area_is_disputed: The parties disagree about the area occupied, and the occupant states the area it acknowledges possessing.

members.legal_issue: The amount of mesne profits during a stay may be fixed by assessing the premises’ current letting value in light of their location, character, and rental evidence.
material_facts: The premises were in a commercial area on a main road in the heart of a city.
The High Court considered the location and the documentary record when assessing the area and value of the premises.
The standard rent had been fixed years earlier, and the eviction decree had also been in place for several years.
The Supreme Court found the factual findings supported by the record and the monthly amount fixed by the High Court just and proper.
members.legal_principle: Marshall Sons & Co. (I) Ltd. v. Sahi Oretrans (P) Ltd. and Another, (1999) 2 SCC 325, and Atma Ram Properties (P) Ltd. v. Federal Motors (P) Ltd., (2005) 1 SCC 705, support mesne profits or compensation based on the rent obtainable in the present market. State of Maharashtra v. Super Max International Pvt. Ltd. and others, (2009) 9 SCC 772, reaffirmed the principle. The amount depends on the circumstances of each case, including whether the property is in a village, city, or metropolitan area, its location, whether it is commercial or residential, and the prevailing rental rates for comparable letting. A factual assessment supported by the record and not shown to be perverse or illegal does not warrant appellate interference.
members.conclusion: The amount fixed by the High Court was reasonable and warranted no interference.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_mesne_profit_amount and premises_are_held_after_eviction_decree and market_rent_assessment_considers_location_and_property_character and amount_finding_is_supported_by_record

predicates.appeal_challenges_mesne_profit_amount: A party appeals the amount of mesne profits fixed for premises held after an eviction decree.
predicates.premises_are_held_after_eviction_decree: The occupant continues to hold the premises after an eviction decree.
predicates.market_rent_assessment_considers_locatio: The assessment considers the premises’ location, whether they are commercial or residential, and the rent they could presently obtain.
predicates.amount_finding_is_supported_by_record: The amount is based on material in the record and is not shown to be perverse or illegal.

members.legal_issue: A party seeking specific performance of an oral sale agreement must prove that the parties reached agreement on its vital and fundamental terms.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought specific performance based on an alleged oral agreement to sell immovable property.
The seller's acceptance of the proposed price was conveyed through an intermediary, and no direct discussion with the seller about other terms took place at that time.
The amount and timing of the advance, the timing of the sale deed and its registration, and who would obtain the required clearance were not settled at that time.
A further meeting was arranged to discuss the transaction, but negotiations failed when the parties did not agree on the seller obtaining the clearance.
The intermediary was not authorised as the seller's general power of attorney to negotiate or settle terms for the property.
members.legal_principle: An agreement to sell immovable property need not be in writing. However, a plaintiff seeking specific performance on the basis of an oral agreement bears a heavy burden to prove consensus ad idem on the vital and fundamental terms, and to show that any later writing would merely formalise terms already agreed. Whether a concluded contract exists is a question of fact. The Court distinguished Kollipara Sriramulu v. T. Aswathanarayana, [1968] 3 SCR 387, where the vital terms had been fixed and part of the agreement performed; it did not adopt a different rule from Nathulal v. Phoolchand, [1970] 2 SCR 854.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs did not prove a concluded oral contract, so they were not entitled to specific performance; the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: oral_specific_performance_suit and price_only_accepted and essential_terms_unsettled and future_meeting_required and negotiations_failed

predicates.oral_specific_performance_suit: The claimant sought specific performance of an immovable-property sale said to have been made orally.
predicates.price_only_accepted: The seller's acceptance of the offered price was conveyed, but agreement on the other terms was not established.
predicates.essential_terms_unsettled: The parties had not settled material terms such as the advance, payment or completion arrangements, or responsibility for obtaining a required clearance.
predicates.future_meeting_required: The parties arranged a later meeting to discuss or settle terms of the transaction.
predicates.negotiations_failed: The parties failed to agree on a condition during their later negotiations.

members.legal_issue: An alleged oral agreement to reconvey property must be proved by convincing evidence before specific performance can be granted.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought specific performance of an alleged oral agreement to reconvey property sold under a written deed.
The deed recorded an outright transfer and contained only a restriction on mortgaging or assigning the property during the vendor’s lifetime; it did not record an agreement to reconvey.
The plaintiff gave no satisfactory explanation for not recording the alleged reconveyance agreement in writing.
The principal supporting witnesses were interested or unreliable, and a document relied on to support the agreement was found suspicious.
The trial court itself observed that there was no clear-cut evidence proving the terms of the alleged oral contract.
members.legal_principle: The burden of proving the alleged contract rested on the plaintiff. A specific-performance contract must be specific and established by convincing evidence; a decree is rarely granted where the agreement rests solely on oral evidence. The judgment concerns specific performance under section 12 of the Specific Relief Act 1877.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff failed to prove the alleged agreement, and the claim for specific performance on that basis could not succeed.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and alleged_reconveyance_was_oral and sale_document_recorded_an_outright_transfer and no_satisfactory_explanation_for_omitting_reconveyance_from_writing and supporting_evidence_was_unconvincing

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.alleged_reconveyance_was_oral: The claimant alleged that the agreement to reconvey the property was made orally.
predicates.sale_document_recorded_an_outright_trans: The written transfer document recorded an outright conveyance and did not record the alleged agreement to reconvey.
predicates.no_satisfactory_explanation_for_omitting: The claimant did not satisfactorily explain why the alleged reconveyance agreement was not recorded in writing.
predicates.supporting_evidence_was_unconvincing: The evidence supporting the alleged agreement was interested, unreliable, suspicious, or otherwise insufficiently convincing.

members.legal_issue: A personal-law preference for a child’s maternal relatives may be considered in interim custody without displacing the paramount consideration of the child’s welfare.
material_facts: The dispute concerned interim custody of children whose mother had died.
The maternal relatives sought custody, and the father remained the natural guardian.
The Court found a prima facie preference for the maternal relatives under the children’s personal law and found no conflict between that course and the children’s welfare.
members.legal_principle: Section 19 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 concerns appointment of a guardian and does not bar the court from placing custody with a relative. Section 12 permits temporary-custody orders, while Section 17 makes welfare central to decisions concerning a minor. The Court relied on Rafiq v. Bashiran for the distinction between appointment of a guardian and custody, and on Mt. Siddiqunnisa Bibi v. Nizamuddin Khan concerning custody rights under Mohammedan law. It also considered the preference described in Section 353 of Mohammedan Law and the welfare principle in Hassan Bhatt v. Ghulam Mohamad Bhat.
members.conclusion: The personal-law preference for maternal relatives, particularly the maternal aunt, could be applied to interim custody, subject to the children’s welfare.

predicates.interim_custody_proceeding: The court is deciding temporary custody while a guardianship or custody proceeding remains pending.
predicates.personal_law_prefers_maternal_relative: The personal law applicable to the child gives a maternal relative a preference for custody.
predicates.personal_law_course_is_consistent_with_c: The arrangement favored by the personal-law preference is consistent with the child’s welfare on the facts before the court.

members.legal_issue: A sufficiently mature child’s stated custody preference may be given weight in an interim-custody decision without being treated as conclusive.
material_facts: The older child expressed reluctance to live with her father and a preference to remain with the maternal relatives.
The younger child was too young to form an intelligent opinion about who should care for him.
The court was deciding interim custody rather than final guardianship.
members.legal_principle: The paramount consideration in custody is the child’s welfare. The Court distinguished the assessment of a child’s preference in interim custody from the final guardianship determination and considered Bal Krishna Pandey v. Sanjeev Bajpayee in relation to the limited conclusiveness of a child’s preference at a tender age.
members.conclusion: The older child’s preference should not be overlooked and may be given weight, but it is not conclusive; the younger child’s preference could not be treated as an intelligent choice.

predicates.interim_custody_proceeding: The court is deciding temporary custody while a guardianship or custody proceeding remains pending.
predicates.older_child_expresses_preference: An older child has stated which caregiver the child wishes to live with.
predicates.older_child_can_form_intelligent_prefere: The older child is capable of expressing a considered preference about care and residence.

members.legal_issue: The central revisional authority may grant a mining-lease application through a direction to the state authority to issue the lease.
material_facts: The applicant sought a mining lease, and the state authority did not decide the application despite a direction to do so.
On a later revision, the central authority directed the state authority to grant the lease over a compact block selected by the applicant.
members.legal_principle: Rule 54 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 makes the Central Government a revisional tribunal against orders of the State Government and gives it the same powers as the State Government. The Court relied on State of Assam v. Om Prakash Mehta, which recognised that the revisional authority may pass an order it considers just and proper, including an order granting an application.
members.conclusion: The central authority’s direction left the state authority no discretion to reject the application and was, in substance, an order granting the applicant’s request.

predicates.mining_lease_revision_case: A proceeding concerns review of a state authority’s decision or failure to decide an application for a mining lease.
predicates.revisional_authority_has_power_to_grant: The revisional authority has power to make an order granting the application under review.
predicates.central_authority_directed_state_to_gran: The central revisional authority directed the state authority to grant the application.

members.legal_issue: A State Government’s decision to grant a mining lease is subject to the Union Government’s order on review, and the State Government implements that order.
material_facts: The State Government had power under the applicable rules to grant the mining lease.
The Union Government directed the State Government to grant the disputed area to the third party, provided that party was otherwise eligible.
The State Government acted in accordance with that direction.
members.legal_principle: Under the Mineral Concession Rules, including Rule 57, the State Government’s lease decision was subject to the Union Government’s order on review. The State Government was required to carry out that order, which remained final. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The State Government’s grant was subject to the Union Government’s review order, which remained the final order; the State Government merely effectuated it.

predicates.reviewable_mining_concession_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a mining concession governed by a scheme that permits review by the Union Government.
predicates.state_lease_decision_subject_to_union_re: The State Government’s power to decide whether to grant a mining lease is subject to the Union Government’s order on review.
predicates.union_government_directed_lease_grant: The Union Government directed the State Government to grant the lease, subject to the proposed recipient being otherwise eligible.

members.legal_issue: A state authority must comply with an unvaried direction of a superior revisional authority and cannot reject the application on its own grounds.
material_facts: The central authority directed the state authority to grant the mining lease over a compact block selected by the applicant.
The state authority later rejected the application, first relying on a policy concerning cement factories and then on pending litigation.
The central authority had not revised or vacated its earlier direction.
members.legal_principle: A subordinate authority must carry out the orders of the superior revisional tribunal; permitting it to disregard those orders would undermine judicial discipline. If the state authority cannot implement a direction, or a later ground warrants reconsideration, it must refer the matter to the central authority rather than reject the application itself.
members.conclusion: The state authority was bound to implement the earlier direction and could not refuse to do so unless the central authority itself revised that direction.

rule.if: mining_lease_revision_case and prior_central_grant_direction and state_rejected_application_despite_direction and not central_revised_prior_direction

predicates.mining_lease_revision_case: A proceeding concerns review of a state authority’s decision or failure to decide an application for a mining lease.
predicates.prior_central_grant_direction: The central revisional authority previously directed the state authority to grant the application.
predicates.state_rejected_application_despite_direc: The state authority rejected the application despite the central authority’s direction.
predicates.central_revised_prior_direction: The central authority revised or vacated its earlier direction.

members.legal_issue: A revisional authority cannot uphold a state authority’s rejection contrary to its earlier unvaried order unless a fresh ground arose after that order.
material_facts: The state authority rejected the application despite the central authority’s earlier direction to grant the lease.
The central authority upheld the rejection in a later revision, relying on litigation concerning the area that had already been pending when it made its earlier direction.
The earlier direction had not been varied or vacated.
members.legal_principle: Even assuming the central authority could revise its earlier order, it could do so only if a fresh ground arose warranting reconsideration. A ground already known when the earlier order was made does not justify going back on that unvaried and unvacated order.
members.conclusion: The central authority had no legal justification to go back on its earlier order because the cited litigation was not a fresh ground arising after that order; it should have set aside the state authority’s rejection and directed implementation of the grant.

rule.if: mining_lease_revision_case and prior_central_order_unvaried and later_review_reconsidered_prior_order and not fresh_ground_arose_after_prior_order

predicates.mining_lease_revision_case: A proceeding concerns review of a state authority’s decision or failure to decide an application for a mining lease.
predicates.prior_central_order_unvaried: The central authority’s earlier order remained unvaried and unvacated.
predicates.later_review_reconsidered_prior_order: In a later review, the central authority reconsidered the matter decided by its earlier order.
predicates.fresh_ground_arose_after_prior_order: A material ground warranting reconsideration arose after the earlier order was made.

members.legal_issue: A court imposing sentence must assess the appropriate sentence rather than reduce it to time already served without considering the relevant circumstances.
material_facts: The High Court retained a conviction for a lesser homicide offence but reduced the sentence to the period already undergone.
The High Court did not state how long the respondent had already been imprisoned or why a sentence shorter than the available maximum was appropriate.
members.legal_principle: Every conviction must be followed by an appropriate sentence within the limits prescribed by law. Sentencing discretion is controlled by law and by judicial discretion applied to the facts; it is not absolute or whimsical. The Court cited no earlier case for this proposition.
members.conclusion: The Court deprecated reducing a sentence to time already undergone without applying the court’s mind to the appropriate sentence, the reason for imposing a lesser sentence, or the period already served.

rule.if: sentencing_proceeding and sentence_reduced_to_time_already_served and (time_served_not_assessed or reasons_for_reduction_not_assessed)

predicates.sentencing_proceeding: The proceeding involves a court determining or reviewing a sentence following conviction.
predicates.sentence_reduced_to_time_already_served: The court reduced the sentence to the period the convicted person had already served.
predicates.time_served_not_assessed: The court did not determine or take account of the period the person had actually served.
predicates.reasons_for_reduction_not_assessed: The court did not assess or explain why the sentence should be reduced in light of the case’s circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A sentencing court may not reduce a sentence to time already served without assessing the gravity and manner of the offence and other relevant circumstances.
material_facts: The accused was convicted of offences arising from inflicting injuries on the complainant with a gandasa while a dispute between them was pending.
The Sessions Court upheld the conviction under the offence relating to simple hurt and imposed a sentence of imprisonment.
In revision, the High Court reduced the sentence to the period already undergone, referring to the time that had passed since the incident and the period of imprisonment already served.
The High Court did not properly consider the evidence or the gravity and manner of the offence.
members.legal_principle: A court must impose a just and proportionate sentence after considering the nature and gravity of the offence, the manner of its commission, relevant aggravating and mitigating circumstances, the offender's conduct, and the rights of the victim and society. Undue sympathy or a meagre sentence based only on the lapse of time undermines public confidence and may harm the interests of society. The Court relied on Sevaka Perumal v. State of Tamil Nadu, Dhananjoy Chatterjee v. State of West Bengal, Mahesh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Hazara Singh v. Raj Kumar, Shailesh Jasvantbhai v. State of Gujarat, Ahmed Hussein Vali Mohammed Saiyed v. State of Gujarat, State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bablu, and State of Madhya Pradesh v. Surendra Singh. No statutory provision was relied on for this principle.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's sentencing order and remanded the revision for a fresh decision after hearing the parties and applying the principles governing appropriate sentencing.

rule.if: criminal_revision_sentence_reduction and accused_inflicted_injuries_with_weapon and dispute_was_pending and sentence_reduced_due_to_elapsed_time and gravity_and_manner_not_considered

predicates.criminal_revision_sentence_reduction: A criminal revision challenged a sentence, and the revisional court reduced it to the time already served.
predicates.accused_inflicted_injuries_with_weapon: The accused inflicted injuries on the complainant using a weapon.
predicates.dispute_was_pending: A dispute between the accused and the complainant was already pending.
predicates.sentence_reduced_due_to_elapsed_time: The revisional court reduced the sentence by relying on the time that had passed and the imprisonment already served.
predicates.gravity_and_manner_not_considered: The revisional court reduced the sentence without properly considering the gravity and manner of the offence.

members.legal_issue: The rule permitting the State Government to settle fisheries otherwise than by sale is within the rule-making authority and is not inconsistent with the governing law on fishery rights.
material_facts: The governing law provided that fishery rights could be acquired as provided by rules and authorized the State Government to make rules concerning licences and the farming of fishery rights.
The rule provided that a fishery could not be settled otherwise than by sale except by the State Government.
The High Court had held the rule invalid, relying on an earlier decision that the Supreme Court found inapplicable.
members.legal_principle: The fishery-rights provision stated no principles or policy governing how rules for acquiring fishery rights must be framed, leaving that matter to the State Government’s discretion. The rule-making power authorized rules concerning licences and the farming of fishery rights, subject to consistency with the Regulation. The rule was therefore neither ultra vires nor repugnant to section 16 of the Assam Land and Revenue Regulation, 1886. State of Assam v. Keshab Prasad Singh, (1953) S.C.R. 865, did not address this controversy; Nuruddin Ahmed v. State of Assam, A.I.R. 1956 Assam 48, was wrongly decided.
members.conclusion: The rule is valid and does not conflict with the governing law. The earlier High Court decision holding it invalid was wrong and was overruled.

predicates.challenge_to_fishery_settlement_rule: A challenge was brought to a government rule governing settlement of fishery rights.
predicates.rulemaking_power_covers_fishery_rights: The governing law authorized the government to make rules concerning licences or the farming of fishery rights.
predicates.parent_law_states_no_guiding_policy: The governing law gave no principles or policy directing how those fishery-rights rules had to be framed.

members.legal_issue: The State Government may settle fishery rights individually and otherwise than by sale under the rule, and a settlement made that way is authorized.
material_facts: The State Government had settled a fishery with the first leaseholder for a fixed term.
After the Deputy Commissioner cancelled that settlement for alleged breaches, the State Government settled the fishery with the appellant without using an auction sale.
The High Court set aside both settlements on the ground that the rule authorizing a non-sale settlement was invalid.
members.legal_principle: Read in context, the rule followed provisions prescribing sale as the ordinary procedure and created an exception for the State Government. That exception imposed no limitation on the State Government’s power to settle otherwise than by sale. The State Government could use the tender system or make an individual settlement where circumstances warranted; the rules providing a procedure for tender settlements did not narrow that authority. This interpretation is consistent with sections 16 and 155(f) of the Assam Land and Revenue Regulation, 1886.
members.conclusion: The rule specifically empowered the State Government to settle fishery rights otherwise than by sale, including through individual settlements. The settlement with the appellant was valid and operative.

predicates.appeal_against_set_aside_fishery_settlem: An appeal concerns a government fishery settlement that a lower court set aside.
predicates.government_made_non_sale_settlement: The government settled fishery rights without using a sale.
predicates.settlement_rule_exempts_government_from_: The applicable settlement rule bars non-sale settlements generally but makes an exception for the government.

members.legal_issue: A licensor may obtain an order for surrender of possession through a suit framed as a mandatory injunction after revoking a licence, where the suit is brought without considerable delay.
material_facts: The respondent occupied the shed under a one-year licence granted by the appellant.
The appellant revoked the licence before filing suit and sought an order directing the respondent to vacate.
The court found no considerable delay that would disentitle the appellant to discretionary relief.
members.legal_principle: Under section 55 of the Specific Relief Act, a licensee who fails to surrender possession after termination of the licence may be compelled to do so by mandatory injunction. Milka Singh v. Diana was relied on for the principle that a licensee remains a licensee after termination and must surrender possession. Although considerable delay may lead a court to refuse discretionary injunctive relief and require a separate possession suit, no such delay was shown here; avoiding multiplicity of suits also supported granting relief.
members.conclusion: The suit was effectively one for possession and should not fail merely because it was framed as a suit for mandatory injunction; the appellant was entitled to relief.

predicates.licensor_sues_after_license_revocation: The licensor filed a suit seeking the licensee's surrender of possession after revoking the licence.
predicates.licensee_has_not_surrendered_possession: The licensee continued to hold the property rather than surrendering it to the licensor.
predicates.no_considerable_delay: The licensor brought the suit without considerable delay after the licence was revoked.

members.legal_issue: A suit for mandatory injunction against an occupant whose licence has ended is maintainable when the licensor acts within a reasonable time, assessed in light of the circumstances.
material_facts: The property owners had permitted an occupant to construct and operate a cinema theatre under a licence, which was renewed for a further term.

The licence required the property to be returned with the structures removed at the end of the term, and the occupant died before the term ended; the lower courts found that the licence ended on his death.
The owners explained that they allowed time for the occupant’s family to wind up the business and filed suit when the agreed licence term expired.
The High Court treated the interval after the occupant’s death as unexplained delay, but did not find the owners’ explanation unacceptable.
The Supreme Court considered the explanation plausible and held that the High Court’s conclusion on delay could not stand.
members.legal_principle: A licensee’s occupation does not become hostile or trespassory immediately upon termination of the licence; the licensor may retain control or possession through the licensee, who may need time to wind up a business. Whether the licensor acted within a reasonable time depends on the circumstances. If the licensor fails to act promptly and the former licensee is treated as a trespasser, recovery of possession may be required. The Court applied the approach to reasonable time in Veerayee Ammal v. Seeni Ammal and the treatment of a mandatory-injunction suit as effectively one for possession in Sant Lal Jain v. Avtar Singh.
members.conclusion: The suit for mandatory injunction was maintainable in the circumstances, and the High Court’s ruling that the owners had to seek recovery of possession was set aside.

predicates.injunction_suit_after_licence_terminatio: The claimant brings an injunction suit against an occupant after the occupant’s licence has ended.
predicates.occupant_entered_with_permission: The occupant originally entered or remained on the property with the claimant’s permission.
predicates.licensor_acted_within_reasonable_time: The claimant acted within a reasonable time after termination, considering the circumstances of the case.

members.legal_issue: A custodian authority empowered to administer evacuee property has jurisdiction to cancel an allotment of that property.
material_facts: The allottees received quasi-permanent allotments of evacuee land.
Their allotments were cancelled after it was found that their claims concerned lower-grade land than the land allotted to them.
The cancellation was made by the Deputy Custodian.
members.legal_principle: The definition of “allotment” in section 2(a), the custodian’s cancellation power under section 12(1), and the rule-making power under section 56(2)(h) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, corresponded in substance to the relevant provisions of the East Punjab Evacuees’ (Administration of Property) Act, 1947. Those provisions conferred authority to cancel allotments. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The Deputy Custodian had jurisdiction to cancel the allotments under both the applicable state legislation and its successor central legislation.

predicates.evacuee_property_allotment_cancellation_: The proceeding challenges the cancellation of an allotment of evacuee property.
predicates.cancellation_made_by_empowered_custodian: An officer empowered to administer the evacuee property made the cancellation.

members.legal_issue: A custodian may cancel a lease over evacuee property that the custodian granted, and the power to cancel is not limited to cases where cancellation is needed to override a conflicting law rather than the lease contract.
material_facts: The properties had been declared evacuee property and vested in the custodian.
The custodian granted the appellants a lease of the properties under a composite agreement that also included other transactions.
The custodian issued a notice alleging breaches of the lease and calling on the appellants to show cause why it should not be cancelled.
A retrospective amendment provided that the relevant statutory reference to a lease included a lease granted by the custodian.
The appellants argued that the statutory power could override a legal bar but could not be used to cancel a lease contract.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(1) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, as amended by section 5 of the 1954 Amendment Act, included leases granted by the custodian, with the amendment deemed always to have been in force. The operative part of section 12(1) gave an unqualified power to cancel or vary a lease; the non-obstante clause was included ex abundanti cautela to meet the argument that the section did not impliedly repeal statutes conferring rights on lessees, and did not limit the power as against a contract. The Court relied on its observations concerning non-obstante clauses in Aswini Kumar Ghose v. Arabinda Bose and Dominion of India v. Shrinbai A. Irani.
members.conclusion: The custodian had authority to issue the notice proposing cancellation of the lease. The operative power to cancel or vary a lease was unqualified and could not be restricted by the non-obstante clause to cases involving a conflict with another law.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_custodian_notice and property_vested_in_custodian_as_evacuee_property and custodian_granted_lease and unqualified_lease_cancellation_power

predicates.appeal_challenges_custodian_notice: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a custodian's notice proposing cancellation of a lease.
predicates.property_vested_in_custodian_as_evacuee_: The property was treated as evacuee property and vested in the custodian.
predicates.custodian_granted_lease: The custodian granted the lease over the property.
predicates.unqualified_lease_cancellation_power: The governing legal rule states an unqualified power to cancel or vary the lease.
predicates.custodian_authorized_to_cancel_lease: The custodian is authorized to cancel the lease.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to a requisition is not barred merely because it is brought long after the order was made when it also asserts that the requisition cannot continue indefinitely.
material_facts: The owner challenged the requisition in a writ petition about thirty years after the order was made.
The challenge included the claim that the requisition could not survive for such a long period and that the State was bound to end it.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished a challenge resting only on the absence of a public purpose, which might face an objection based on delay, from the independent ground that requisition cannot continue for an unreasonable period. On that latter ground, the challenge was maintainable.
members.conclusion: The writ petition was maintainable despite the lapse of about thirty years because it raised the independent ground that the requisition could not continue indefinitely.

predicates.writ_challenges_old_requisition: A writ petition challenges an order requisitioning property long after the order was made.
predicates.challenge_includes_unreasonable_continua: The writ petition asserts that the requisition has continued for an unreasonably long time and cannot continue indefinitely.
predicates.challenge_is_maintainable_despite_delay: The challenge may be heard despite the time that passed before it was brought.

members.legal_issue: A statutory revision power that is not limited by time is not barred merely because the revision notice was issued years after the challenged order.
material_facts: The order proposed to be revised was made in 1956.
The revision notice was issued several years later, in 1964.
The Court held that the applicable revision power was not curtailed by any limitation of time.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that Section 27 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, imposed no limitation of time on the revision power. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The revision proceeding was not barred by limitation.

predicates.statutory_revision_proceeding: An authority initiated a revision proceeding under a statutory power.
predicates.governing_enactment_sets_no_time_limit: The governing enactment sets no time limit for exercising the revision power.
predicates.revision_not_barred_by_lapse_of_time: The revision proceeding is not barred merely because time has passed.

members.legal_issue: A previously adjudicated determination that a temple is a Jain temple cannot be reopened in later proceedings between the relevant parties.
material_facts: In an earlier round of litigation, the Supreme Court had determined that the temple was a Jain temple, not a Hindu temple.
In the present proceedings, the State and other respondents again sought to contend that it was a Hindu temple.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied res judicata to the issue decided in the earlier litigation and treated the prior Supreme Court judgment, State of Rajasthan v. Shri Sajjanlal Panjawat, as binding. The Court stated that the issue could not be reopened in the present proceedings.
members.conclusion: The prior determination that the temple was a Jain temple was binding, and the State and respondents could not reopen the issue by asserting that it was a Hindu temple.

predicates.public_trust_temple_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the character or management of a public temple trust.
predicates.same_issue_decided_in_prior_judgment: A prior judgment in litigation involving the relevant parties determined the same issue.
predicates.current_party_seeks_to_reopen_issue: A party in the later proceeding seeks a determination inconsistent with the prior decision on that issue.

members.legal_issue: A final determination between the parties that a religious group is entitled to administer a temple cannot be reopened in later litigation between them merely by relying on subsequent interpretations of law or disputing the group’s qualification to administer the temple.
material_facts: An earlier judgment between the temple administrators and the State had recognized the administrators as a religious denomination or section and recognized their right to participate in administering the temple.
The State’s appeal from that judgment was dismissed after the State withdrew the notification that had prompted the dispute, and the determination became final.

In the later proceedings, the administrators again challenged State action affecting their administration of the temple, and the High Court reconsidered whether the earlier determination bound the parties.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of res judicata applies to writ proceedings and makes a final determination between the same parties conclusive in later litigation, even if the earlier decision is alleged to be erroneous or a later interpretation of law might differ. A final judgment must be given effect unless reversed or modified by an appellate authority. Article 26 protects the rights of religious denominations, and Section 107 of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959 preserves those rights. The Court relied on Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Deorajin Debi, Amalgamated Coalfields Ltd. v. Janapada Sabha Chhindwara, Hope Plantations Ltd. v. Taluk Land Board, Union of India v. Nanak Singh, and other authorities on finality and res judicata.
members.conclusion: The earlier determination was binding between the parties, and the High Court could not sit in appeal over it or re-examine the administrators’ status and right to administer the temple. State authorities could not deny those previously determined rights through later orders.

predicates.later_proceeding_between_same_parties: A later court proceeding takes place between the same parties, or their relevant successors, as an earlier proceeding.
predicates.prior_final_judgment_decided_same_issue: An earlier final judgment between those parties decided the issue raised again in the later proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A vested remainder does not lapse merely because its beneficiary dies before the life tenant, and the beneficiary’s heirs take the remainder rather than the property falling into residue or a resulting trust.
material_facts: The will gave the widow a life interest and then gave the remainder to the testator’s cousin, with a further gift to the cousin’s sons after the cousin’s death.
The cousin died before the widow.
The will did not make the cousin’s legacy conditional on payment or provide that it would lapse if he died before the widow.
members.legal_principle: A remainder may vest before the prior life interest ends, with possession postponed until that interest expires. A vested interest devolves on the beneficiary’s heirs upon the beneficiary’s death unless the gift is conditional or lapses under the instrument. Section 81 of the Indian Trusts Act did not support a trust for the testator’s heirs because the testator’s intention, assessed when the will was executed, was to make a testamentary disposition of the beneficial remainder. The succession to the testator’s property was governed by the Indian Succession Act, but no specific provision of that Act was applied to this issue.
members.conclusion: The cousin’s vested remainder passed to his heirs, who were entitled to the estate under the will; there was no lapse, resulting trust, or intestacy as to the remainder.

predicates.testamentary_remainder_dispute: A party disputed entitlement to property left as a remainder under a will.
predicates.remainder_possession_deferred: The will gave another person a prior life interest and postponed possession of the remainder until that interest ended.
predicates.remainder_beneficiary_predeceased_life_t: The named remainder beneficiary died before the life tenant.
predicates.will_made_no_applicable_condition_or_lap: The will did not make the remainder conditional on a separate obligation or provide that it would lapse upon the beneficiary’s death before the life tenant.

members.legal_issue: A beneficiary's vested interest in property is not defeated by the beneficiary's death before the right to possession becomes exercisable.
material_facts: The settlement deed gave the later beneficiary an interest in the property while postponing enjoyment until the life beneficiary's death.
The later beneficiary died before the life beneficiary and before obtaining possession.
The later beneficiary's widow was his sole heir.
members.legal_principle: A vested interest acquired under a disposition is not defeated merely because the beneficiary dies before obtaining possession; the interest passes to the beneficiary's heir. The Court relied on the deed's construction and the principle of construction discussed in Ramachandra Shenoy & Anr. v. Mrs. Hilda Brite & Ors., [1964] 2 S.C.R. 722.
members.conclusion: The later beneficiary's vested right was not defeated by his death before possession, and his sole heir was entitled to the property when the life estate ended.

rule.if: property_inheritance_dispute and document_grants_a_later_property_interest_after_a_life_estate and possession_is_postponed_until_the_life_estate_ends and later_beneficiary_dies_before_possession and later_beneficiary_has_a_sole_heir

predicates.property_inheritance_dispute: The proceeding concerns entitlement to property following the death of a beneficiary.
predicates.document_grants_a_later_property_interes: A property document directs an interest to a beneficiary after another person's life estate.
predicates.possession_is_postponed_until_the_life_e: The beneficiary's enjoyment or possession is deferred until the life estate ends.
predicates.later_beneficiary_dies_before_possession: The beneficiary dies before obtaining possession of the property.
predicates.later_beneficiary_has_a_sole_heir: The beneficiary leaves one person who is the sole heir.

members.legal_issue: Whether construction materially alters an accommodation requires consideration of whether it is permanent or temporary and removable.
material_facts: The partition was temporary, lacked a foundation, did not reach the ceiling, and could be removed without damage.
The tin shed was temporary, stood on open land, and could be removed without damage.
The High Court treated the temporary nature and removability of the disputed work as irrelevant to material alteration.
members.legal_principle: The nature of construction, including whether it is permanent or temporary, is relevant to deciding whether an alteration is material. Permanent construction tends to change the accommodation on a lasting basis; temporary construction that can readily be removed without damage ordinarily does not affect the building’s form or structure. The Court rejected the contrary observation in the Full Bench decision in Sita Ram Sharan v. Johri Mal and explained that Babu Manmohan Das Shah v. Bishun Das did not make permanence irrelevant.
members.conclusion: The permanent or temporary nature of construction is a relevant consideration; temporary work that can be removed without damage ordinarily does not affect the building’s form or structure in the same way as permanent construction.

predicates.material_alteration_assessment: The court is deciding whether construction materially altered an accommodation.
predicates.construction_is_temporary_and_removable: The construction is temporary and can be removed without damage to the building.

members.legal_issue: Whether a tenant’s alterations to leased premises constitute permanent structures that support eviction depends on the circumstances of the case.
material_facts: The tenant constructed cabins and lofts after taking the premises, with pillars and stanchions sunk into the flooring and structures attached to the building.
The structures were substantial, durable, and not easily removable; the lower courts considered their nature, construction, and effect on the premises and found them permanent.
The lower courts found that the structures had been erected without the landlords’ consent.
The trial court and appellate court both ordered eviction on the ground of permanent construction.
members.legal_principle: Under section 108(p) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lessee may not erect a permanent structure without the lessor’s consent, except for agricultural purposes; section 13(1)(b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1974 also provides a ground for eviction for permanent construction. No hard-and-fast test determines whether a structure is permanent. The court considers the structure’s nature and purpose, how it affects enjoyment of the premises, its durability, and other relevant circumstances. Surya Properties Private Ltd. v. Bimalendu Nath Sarkar, A.I.R. 1964 Calcutta 1 and A.I.R. 1965 Calcutta 408 were approved; Khureshi Ibrahim Ahmed v. Ahmed Haji Khanmahomad, A.I.R. 1965 Gujarat 152, and Ramji Virji v. Kadarbhai Esufali, A.I.R. 1973 Gujarat 110, were referred to.
members.conclusion: The structures were permanent, and their erection without the landlords’ consent supported eviction under the applicable tenancy law.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_proceeding and tenant_constructed_structure_after_lease and without_landlord_consent and (substantial_structure or durable_structure or structure_affixed_to_premises)

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant from leased premises.
predicates.tenant_constructed_structure_after_lease: The tenant erected the disputed structure after taking the premises on lease.
predicates.without_landlord_consent: The tenant erected the structure without the landlord’s consent.
predicates.substantial_structure: The structure was substantial in its construction or scale.
predicates.durable_structure: The structure was intended or suited to last for a substantial period.
predicates.structure_affixed_to_premises: The structure was attached to or incorporated into the premises.

members.legal_issue: Whether construction materially alters an accommodation is a mixed question of fact and law, and a second appellate court must apply the correct legal principles when reviewing that determination.
material_facts: The first appellate court found that the partition and tin shed did not materially alter the accommodation.
The High Court reversed that determination in second appeal, treating the temporary construction as material despite its removability and the absence of substantial structural change.
The Supreme Court found no evidence supporting the High Court’s finding of substantial permanent walls and concluded that the High Court applied an incorrect approach.
members.legal_principle: Findings about what construction was made are findings of fact, but whether those constructions materially alter the accommodation is a mixed question of fact and law that must be decided using the correct principles. The Court applied the material-alteration test in Babu Manmohan Das Shah v. Bishun Das and rejected the High Court’s reliance on the contrary observation in Sita Ram Sharan v. Johri Mal.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in interfering with the first appellate court’s determination; its order was set aside and the first appellate court’s judgment and decree were restored.

predicates.second_appeal_in_eviction_case: The matter is a second appeal in an eviction case.
predicates.material_alteration_is_mixed_question_of: The disputed determination concerns whether established construction materially altered the accommodation, a mixed question of fact and law.
predicates.first_appellate_court_found_no_material_: The first appellate court found that the construction did not materially alter the accommodation.
predicates.second_appellate_court_applied_incorrect: The second appellate court reversed that finding using an incorrect legal approach to material alteration.

members.legal_issue: Whether a finding of material impairment by a tenant’s construction is a pure question of fact or a mixed question of fact and law determines whether a reviewing court must apply the correct legal test.
material_facts: The lower authorities found that the parchhati materially impaired the building without a sufficient evidentiary basis, despite the tenant’s expert evidence that it was temporary and did not affect the building’s soundness or utility.
The High Court affirmed the concurrent findings without applying the correct legal test for material impairment.
The tenant appealed from the High Court’s dismissal of the revision against the eviction orders.
members.legal_principle: The physical nature of a construction may be a question of fact, but whether it materially impairs the premises is a mixed question of fact and law that must be determined using the correct legal test. The Court relied particularly on Om Prakash v. Amar Singh, [1987] 1 SCC 458, and applied the material-impairment standard under section 13(2)(iii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949; the appeal arose after revision under section 15(5) of that Act.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in affirming the findings without applying the correct legal principles; the Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s order and the eviction orders, and dismissed the eviction petition.

predicates.appeal_from_revisional_eviction_order: A party appealed from a reviewing court’s decision affirming eviction orders after a revision proceeding.
predicates.lower_findings_lack_evidentiary_basis: The authorities that first decided the eviction claim found material impairment without an adequate evidentiary basis.
predicates.reviewing_court_did_not_apply_correct_te: The reviewing court affirmed the findings without applying the legal test governing material impairment.

members.legal_issue: Vesting of property in the state under an abolition law does not necessarily extinguish a former holder’s interest in establishing ownership at vesting and obtaining statutory compensation.
material_facts: The suit properties vested in the State under the Jagir Abolition Act while the suit was pending.
The claimant asserted that he owned the properties when the Act came into force.
It was conceded that, if the claimant’s ownership at that time were proved, he would be entitled to compensation under the Act.
The State had not been joined, and the courts had not finally determined the rights of all interested parties.
members.legal_principle: The Jagir Abolition Act vested the properties in the State but provided compensation to a person proved to have owned them when the Act came into force. Applying Himatrao v. Jaikishandas and Others, [1963] 3 S.C.R. 815, the Court held that the claimant’s possible compensation interest warranted determination of the parties’ rights after the State was impleaded.
members.conclusion: The claimant had not necessarily lost all rights in the properties, because proof of ownership when the Act came into force could entitle him to compensation. The State should be joined and the rights of all parties determined.

predicates.property_vested_in_state_under_abolition: Property held by a claimant vested in the State under a law abolishing the claimant’s former property-holding arrangement.
predicates.claimant_asserted_ownership_at_vesting: The claimant asserted that they owned the property when the vesting took effect.
predicates.compensation_available_if_ownership_prov: The applicable law provided compensation if the claimant’s ownership at vesting were proved.
predicates.state_not_joined_for_final_determination: The State had not been joined before the rights concerning the vested property were finally determined.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who may have owned property when it vested in the State retains an interest in establishing that ownership if it affects entitlement to compensation, and the State should be joined so the parties’ rights can be determined.
material_facts: The suit properties vested in the State under an abolition law while the suit was pending.
The claimant asserted that he was the full owner of the properties when the law came into force.
It was conceded that a person proved to have been the owner at that time would be entitled to compensation under the law.
The State was not a party to the appeal, and the High Court held that the claimant had lost his rights in the properties.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the rule in Himatrao v. Jaikishandas and Others, [1963] 3 S.C.R. 815. Where property has vested in the State but a claimant’s ownership at vesting may determine entitlement to compensation, that claimant remains interested in establishing ownership; the State should be joined so the parties’ rights can be finally determined.
members.conclusion: The claimant’s possible entitlement to compensation meant that he remained interested in establishing his ownership at the time of vesting. The High Court’s decree was set aside, and the case was remanded with a direction to join the State and determine the rights of all parties.

rule.if: appeal_concerns_property_vested_in_state and claimant_ownership_at_vesting_disputed and ownership_affects_compensation and state_not_party

predicates.appeal_concerns_property_vested_in_state: The appeal concerns property that vested in the State.
predicates.claimant_ownership_at_vesting_disputed: A claimant asserts ownership of the property when it vested, and that ownership is disputed.
predicates.ownership_affects_compensation: The claimant’s ownership at vesting affects whether the claimant is entitled to compensation.
predicates.state_not_party: The State in which the property vested is not a party to the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: Once the required facts for the statutory presumption are established, the accused may rebut the presumption with reliable direct or circumstantial evidence.
material_facts: The prosecution proved demand and acceptance, and the marked money was recovered from the public servant’s desk drawer.
The defence suggested that the trap was arranged to implicate the public servant and that the complainant might have touched the marked money while taking out the registration fee.
The defence did not produce direct or circumstantial evidence sufficient to support those suggestions or otherwise explain the money as something other than gratification.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 requires the Court to raise the statutory presumption when its factual basis is established, while permitting the accused to rebut it through cross-examination or reliable evidence. The Court relied on C.M. Girish Babu v. CBI, Cochin, and held that the suggested explanations, unsupported by direct or circumstantial evidence, did not rebut the presumption.
members.conclusion: The presumption under Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act applied and was not rebutted.

predicates.corruption_prosecution: The proceeding is a prosecution alleging corruption by a public servant.
predicates.demand_and_acceptance_are_proved: The prosecution proves that the public servant demanded and accepted the money.
predicates.accused_produces_no_reliable_evidence_re: The accused does not produce reliable direct or circumstantial evidence showing that the money was not gratification.

members.legal_issue: The statutory presumption of acceptance of illegal gratification is rebuttable, and an accused who possesses the bribe money must provide a satisfactory explanation to rebut it.
material_facts: The marked money was recovered from one accused.
The accused did not offer an explanation to rebut the presumption arising from possession of the money.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 raises a rebuttable presumption for an offence under Section 7. The accused may rebut it through cross-examination or reliable evidence, and the burden is one of preponderance of probabilities, not the prosecution’s burden beyond reasonable doubt. The Court relied on C.M. Girish Babu v. C.B.I., Cochin (2009) 3 SCC 779.
members.conclusion: The presumption of acceptance was not rebutted and supported the finding that the accused had accepted the bribe.

predicates.prosecution_for_accepting_illegal_gratif: The proceeding alleges that an accused accepted illegal gratification.
predicates.accused_possessed_bribe_money: The accused was found possessing money established to be the bribe money.
predicates.no_satisfactory_explanation_for_possessi: The accused did not provide a satisfactory explanation for possessing the money.

members.legal_issue: A previous unsuccessful or inconsistent eviction history does not automatically defeat a later eviction claim based on a currently proved bona fide requirement.
material_facts: A previous tenant had been evicted on a ground relating to rebuilding, but the landlord did not rebuild the premises and later let them to another tenant.
The rebuilding ground was not accepted in the present proceeding.
The present claim relied on the requirement for an existing pawn-broking business, and the Court held that the claim had to be assessed on the evidence in the present proceeding.
members.legal_principle: A cause for eviction based on bona fide requirement is recurring. A prior finding that a cause was not established, or a prior failure to rebuild after obtaining possession, does not foreclose a later claim founded on a subsequent cause or changed circumstances. Section 10(3)(a)(iii) governs the current business-requirement claim; rejection of a rebuilding claim under Section 14(1)(b) does not by itself bar a distinct, proved ground. The Court did not rely on an earlier case for this holding.
members.conclusion: The earlier conduct and the rejection of the rebuilding ground did not require the later eviction claim to be dismissed if the current bona fide requirement was established by cogent evidence.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_case and later_eviction_claim and prior_eviction_history_or_inconsistent_conduct and current_bona_fide_ground_proved

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: A landlord seeks recovery of rented premises in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.later_eviction_claim: The landlord brings a later claim to recover premises from a tenant.
predicates.prior_eviction_history_or_inconsistent_c: The landlord previously pursued an eviction ground unsuccessfully or acted inconsistently with an earlier asserted ground.
predicates.current_bona_fide_ground_proved: The landlord establishes by cogent evidence a bona fide ground for eviction in the later proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A predecessor's unsuccessful eviction proceeding does not by itself establish that a successor landlord's claim for eviction is mala fide.
material_facts: The former owner had earlier brought an unsuccessful eviction suit against the tenant.
The present landlords acquired the property as legatees and later sought eviction for additional accommodation.
members.legal_principle: The court held that the motives of successor landlords cannot be treated as mala fide merely because their predecessor in title had previously brought an unsuccessful eviction suit.
members.conclusion: The former owner's unsuccessful eviction suit did not make the legatee landlords' claim mala fide.

predicates.successor_landlord_seeks_eviction: A person who succeeded to ownership seeks eviction of a tenant.
predicates.predecessor_brought_unsuccessful_evictio: A former owner previously brought an eviction suit against the same tenant and did not succeed.

members.legal_issue: A suit concerning a public religious trust falls outside the special public-trust procedure when its dominant purpose is to vindicate an individual’s right, or another person’s individual right, to hold an office.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought a declaration that a particular person was the duly installed head of the trust and asked the court to appoint him, or alternatively another person, to that office.
The plaint challenged the incumbent’s entitlement to the office but did not challenge the validity of the claimed appointee’s installation or allege mismanagement by him.
The plaintiffs did not implead or refer to other persons nominated to succeed the former head, despite relying on the custom of nomination.
The courts below found that the suit’s primary purpose was to establish the claimed appointee’s right to the office, and the Supreme Court found no reason to disturb that finding.
members.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides a special procedure for suits concerning public religious or charitable trusts. The court must consider the suit’s dominant purpose, the capacity in which the plaintiffs sue, and the plaint’s allegations, rather than relying only on the reliefs claimed or the plaintiffs’ number or sanction. A suit primarily seeking to remedy an infringement of an individual right, including another person’s individual right to an office, does not fall within Section 92. The Court followed Sugra Bibi v. Hazi Kummu Mia, (1969) 3 SCR 83, and approved Shamukhan v. Govinda, AIR 1937 Madras 92, and Tirumalai Devasthanams v. Krishnayya, AIR 1943 Madras 466.
members.conclusion: The suit’s dominant purpose was to vindicate an individual claim to the headship, not a public right of the trust’s beneficiaries, and it was therefore outside the scope of Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.public_religious_trust_suit: The proceeding is brought by interested persons concerning the administration of a public religious or charitable trust.
predicates.individual_office_claim_is_dominant_purp: The suit’s dominant purpose is to establish or vindicate an individual’s claim, or another person’s individual claim, to hold an office.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking the removal and replacement of a trustee of a public charitable or religious trust is subject to the requirement of written consent when it is brought representatively for the trust’s beneficiaries rather than to vindicate a plaintiff’s private right.
material_facts: The suit concerned a trust created substantially for public charitable or religious purposes.
The plaintiff sought a declaration that the trustee was unfit, his removal, the appointment of a replacement trustee, and the appointment of a receiver until the proposed replacement came of age.
The reliefs sought were for the administration of the trust and were not to enforce a private right of the plaintiff.
The suit was treated as brought in a representative capacity on behalf of all the trust’s beneficiaries.
The plaintiff had not obtained the written consent of the Advocate-General.
members.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies where a suit concerns a public charitable or religious trust, alleges a breach of trust or seeks directions for its administration, and claims reliefs specified in the section. Even where those conditions are met, the suit must be representative and brought in the public interest, not merely to vindicate an individual or personal right. The Court relied on Budreedas v. Choonilal, Appanna v. Narasinga, and The Tirumalai-Tirupati Devasthanams Committee v. Udiavar Krishnayya Shanbhaga.
members.conclusion: The suit fell within section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure and was not maintainable without the Advocate-General’s written consent.

rule.if: suit_concerning_public_charitable_or_religious_trust and administration_or_breach_issue and trustee_removal_or_replacement_sought and representative_beneficiary_interest and not written_consent_obtained

predicates.suit_concerning_public_charitable_or_rel: The plaintiff brought a suit concerning a trust created substantially for public charitable or religious purposes.
predicates.administration_or_breach_issue: The suit alleged a breach of trust or sought directions for administering the trust.
predicates.trustee_removal_or_replacement_sought: The plaintiff sought removal of a trustee or appointment of a replacement trustee.
predicates.representative_beneficiary_interest: The plaintiff brought the suit on behalf of the trust’s beneficiaries to protect their common interest, rather than solely to enforce a personal right.
predicates.written_consent_obtained: The plaintiff obtained the Advocate-General’s written consent before bringing the suit.

members.legal_issue: The special revisional authority may revise a verified claim that became final under the earlier claims regime, including a claim finalized on revision.
material_facts: A claim had been verified and valued under the earlier claims regime.
The Claims Commissioner had increased the valuation on revision, making the claim final under that regime.
The Settlement Commissioner, exercising the special revisional authority, initiated revision on his own motion.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(1)(b) of the Displaced Persons (Claims) Supplementary Act, 1954 authorizes the Chief Settlement Commissioner, subject to applicable rules, to revise any verified claim and make such order as he thinks fit. Section 2(f) defines a verified claim by reference to a claim for which a final order has been passed under the principal Act. The provision's unambiguous language is not restricted by the preamble, and the statutory scheme does not exclude claims finalized on revision.
members.conclusion: The special revisional power extends to verified claims that became final under the earlier regime, including claims finalized by an order on revision.

predicates.special_revision_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the exercise of a special power to revise a verified claim.
predicates.claim_finalized_under_prior_scheme: A claim was finally determined under an earlier claims regime, including through a revisional order.
predicates.officer_initiated_revision: The revisional officer initiated the revision on the officer's own motion.

members.legal_issue: The special power to revise a verified claim extends to the valuation of the claim as well as verification of title.
material_facts: The claim concerned ownership of immovable property left behind by a displaced person.
The original decision and the order on revision both addressed the amount at which the claim was valued.
The special revisional authority sought to alter that valuation.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(f) of the Displaced Persons (Claims) Supplementary Act, 1954 defines a verified claim by reference to the final order under the principal Act. Under the principal Act, the Claims Officer determines both title and value, so the final order embraces both. Section 5(1)(b) therefore permits revision of valuation as part of revision of a verified claim.
members.conclusion: The special revisional power covers valuation as well as verification of title.

predicates.special_revision_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the exercise of a special power to revise a verified claim.
predicates.final_claim_order_includes_valuation: The final determination of the claim addressed both the claimant's asserted interest and the value of the property.
predicates.valuation_revision_sought: The revisional officer sought to alter the value assigned to the claim.

members.legal_issue: A government auction of public property conducted through collusion, material procedural irregularities, and disregard of the public authority’s duty to obtain a fair market price cannot stand.
material_facts: The disputed plots belonged to a public industrial development corporation, but it was not notified of their attachment or sale.
A bank’s claim that it held a mortgage over one plot was disregarded.
The sale proclamations did not adequately describe the property rights being sold, and the auction was not widely advertised.
The reserve prices were omitted from the sale records, although reserve prices had been fixed; bids far below those prices were accepted.
A court’s stay of recovery proceedings concerning one plot was ignored when the sale was confirmed.

The auction records falsely stated that the required initial deposits had been made immediately after the auction; the deposits were made the following day, and the remaining purchase price for one plot was never paid.
