The evidence supported the conclusion that the purported auctions were collusive and that the public land was being acquired through manipulation of the process.
members.legal_principle: The disposal of public property is in the nature of a trust, requiring public authorities to make all reasonable efforts to obtain the best available market price through a fair and transparent process. A government authority may not dispose of public property below the reserve price. The Court relied on Ram and Shyam Co. v. State of Haryana, (1985) 3 SCC 267; V. Purushotham Rao v. Union of India, (2001) 10 SCC 305; Aggarwal and Modi Enterprises (P.) Ltd. v. New Delhi Municipal Council, (2007) 8 SCC 75; Meerut Development Authority v. Association of Management Studies, (2009) 6 SCC 171; and Anil Kumar Srivastava v. State of U.P., (2004) 8 SCC 671. The recovery and sale process was governed by sections 279, 284, 286 and 341 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, and rules 273, 273-A, 282 and 285-A to 285-N of the 1952 Rules.
members.conclusion: The auction sales were illegal, fraudulent, collusive, and mala fide, and the appeal challenging their setting aside was dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_challenging_public_property_auction and public_property_sold_for_recovery and owner_not_notified and (secured_claim_ignored or judicial_stay_ignored) and no_wide_auction_publicity and accepted_bid_below_reserve and (auction_record_misstated_deposit or purchase_balance_unpaid)

predicates.appeal_challenging_public_property_aucti: A party appealed a decision setting aside an auction of public property.
predicates.public_property_sold_for_recovery: A public asset was put up for auction to recover money owed to the government.
predicates.owner_not_notified: The authority conducting the sale did not notify the public body that owned the property about the attachment or sale.
predicates.secured_claim_ignored: The sale authority proceeded despite a creditor’s claim that it held security over the property.
predicates.judicial_stay_ignored: The sale authority proceeded with or confirmed a sale despite being informed of a court order staying the recovery proceedings.
predicates.no_wide_auction_publicity: The proposed auction was not publicized through means likely to give the public wide notice.
predicates.accepted_bid_below_reserve: The sale authority accepted a bid below a reserve price fixed for the property.
predicates.auction_record_misstated_deposit: The auction record stated that the required initial deposit was made immediately after the auction when it was actually made later.
predicates.purchase_balance_unpaid: The purchaser did not pay the full purchase price for the property.

members.legal_issue: A public authority cannot revive a rejected request and grant public property through an irregular process that fails statutory disposal requirements and disregards the property's current value.
material_facts: The municipal authority and the chair of its standing committee had rejected the request to enter the applicant's name in the lease register.

The applicant made no fresh application and supplied no new material before the matter was again placed before the standing committee, despite the absence of authority to review the earlier decisions.
The proposal was not on the meeting agenda, and the purported resolution followed a direction from a state minister and was considered in undue haste.
The later order proceeded on an unsupported assertion that possession had been delivered, although no record documented delivery of possession.

The authority directed a lease without properly meeting the statutory requirements for disposal of municipal property, including the requirement that the consideration for a transfer not be below current market value.
members.legal_principle: Section 79 of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, governed disposal of the Corporation's property, required the prescribed sanction for a qualifying lease, and prohibited consideration below current market value. A file noting or unsupported assertion does not itself confer a right, as explained in Bachhittar Singh v. State of Punjab. A statutory decision made at the behest of someone without a statutory role is ultra vires under Commissioner of Police, Bombay v. Gordhandas Bhanji and Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner. The Court also relied on Dr. S.P. Kapoor v. State of Himachal Pradesh regarding haste as evidence from which mala fides may be presumed, and Bangalore Medical Trust v. B.S. Muddappa regarding fair, rational and non-arbitrary exercise of discretion over public property.
members.conclusion: The purported resolution and the order granting the lease were illegal and were rightly quashed.

rule.if: public_property_disposal_case and prior_request_rejected and (no_review_authority or (no_fresh_application and no_new_material)) and (required_disposal_approval_missing or consideration_below_current_market_value) and (decision_taken_off_agenda or decision_made_at_external_direction)

predicates.public_property_disposal_case: The proceeding concerns a public authority's decision to dispose of property held for public purposes.
predicates.prior_request_rejected: The public authority had already rejected the request to obtain an interest in the property.
predicates.no_review_authority: The official or body that reconsidered the rejected request had no authority to review the earlier decision.
predicates.no_fresh_application: The applicant did not submit a fresh application before the later decision.
predicates.no_new_material: The applicant supplied no new material supporting reconsideration of the rejected request.
predicates.required_disposal_approval_missing: The decision did not obtain the approval required for the public authority's disposal of the property.
predicates.consideration_below_current_market_value: The proposed transfer did not provide consideration at least equal to the property's current market value.
predicates.decision_taken_off_agenda: The proposal was considered despite not appearing on the meeting's agenda.
predicates.decision_made_at_external_direction: The decision was made following a direction from a person who had no statutory role in deciding the matter.

members.legal_issue: A successful bidder at a recovery auction must make the required initial deposit immediately after the auction and pay the balance within the prescribed time.
material_facts: The auction conditions required the highest bidder to deposit one fourth of the bid immediately after the auction and the remainder within fifteen days.
The auction records stated that the initial deposits had been made immediately after the auctions, but the government register showed that they were made the next day.
The register showed that the remaining three fourths of the bid for one plot was never deposited, although a sale certificate was issued.
members.legal_principle: Rule 285-D of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1952 requires the declared purchaser to deposit twenty-five per cent of the bid immediately, failing which the land must be put up for sale again. Rule 285-E requires payment of the full purchase price by the fifteenth day after the sale and provides for forfeiture and resale in case of default.
members.conclusion: The required initial deposits were not made immediately after the auctions, and the full purchase price for one plot was not paid; the auction payment requirements were therefore breached.

predicates.recovery_auction_payment_challenge: The dispute concerns payment obligations in an auction conducted to recover public dues.
predicates.initial_deposit_made_later_than_immediat: The successful bidder did not pay the required initial portion of the bid immediately after the auction.
predicates.purchase_balance_not_paid_within_require: The purchaser did not pay the remaining purchase price within the required time.

members.legal_issue: A successful execution-auction bidder satisfies the required initial and balance payments when the initial portion is paid with reasonable speed in the circumstances and the balance is paid within the prescribed period.
material_facts: The successful bidder provided drafts for the required initial portion on the day the auction was completed, and the court auctioneer recorded receipt of them.
The bidder deposited the remaining portion within the prescribed period.
The initial payment was made by drafts rather than cash at the fall of the hammer.
members.legal_principle: Order 21 Rules 84 and 85 of the Code of Civil Procedure require payment of the initial portion immediately and the balance within the prescribed period. In Rosali V. v. Talco Bank, AIR 2007 SC 998, the Court held that “immediately” means with all reasonable speed in light of the circumstances, not necessarily instantaneously. Applying that construction, payment by drafts on the auction day was sufficient in this case.
members.conclusion: The bidder complied with the payment requirements, and the auction sale was properly confirmed.

predicates.execution_auction: The property was sold through an auction conducted to execute a court decree.
predicates.bidder_paid_initial_share_with_reasonabl: The successful bidder paid the required initial portion with reasonable speed in the circumstances of the auction.
predicates.bidder_paid_balance_within_required_peri: The successful bidder paid the remaining portion within the period required for payment.

members.legal_issue: The absence of an executed and registered lease deed does not by itself prevent a person who acted on an agreement of lease and took possession from relying on the protection of that possession.
material_facts: The village body approved a proposal to lease the land, and the competent authority approved the proposed grant and the successful auction bid.
The claimants were put in possession after the bid was accepted and continued in possession while cultivating the land.
No lease deed was executed and registered.
members.legal_principle: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 can protect a person in possession who has acted on a contract even though the contemplated instrument was not executed and registered. The Court relied on Maneklal Mansukhbhai v. Hormusji Jamshedji Ginwalla & Sons for an agreement of lease and Hamzabi v. Syed Karimuddin for the protection of possession under a contract. It held that Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor and C.M. Beena v. P.N. Ramachandra Rao did not assist the challenge on these facts.
members.conclusion: The claimants could rely on Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 to protect their possession despite the absence of an executed and registered lease deed.

rule.if: dispute_involves_unregistered_lease and competent_authority_approved_lease_grant and land_granted_after_auction and claimant_took_possession_under_agreement

predicates.dispute_involves_unregistered_lease: A dispute concerns rights asserted under an agreement to lease for which no lease deed was executed and registered.
predicates.competent_authority_approved_lease_grant: The proposed lease grant received approval from the authority competent to approve it.
predicates.land_granted_after_auction: The land was granted to the successful bidder after an auction.
predicates.claimant_took_possession_under_agreement: The claimant took possession of the land pursuant to the agreed grant.

members.legal_issue: A person claiming through a lessee may resist ejectment under the doctrine of part performance when a signed written agreement to lease has sufficiently ascertainable terms and possession and performance satisfy the statutory requirements, even though no formal registered lease was executed.
material_facts: The predecessor of the person resisting ejectment applied in writing for a lease for consideration, and the settlement officer accepted the offer in writing subject to government sanction; the sanction was granted.
Government records summarised the correspondence and the sanction, and the court treated those records as reliable secondary evidence of the written agreement and its terms.
The agreement’s terms, including the permanent character of the lease and the rent, could be ascertained with reasonable certainty.

The lessee took possession in furtherance of the agreement, built and operated a factory and related structures, and tendered the agreed rent, which successive managers and the plaintiffs accepted for years.

The person resisting ejectment claimed through the original lessee and had performed, or was willing to perform, the obligations under the agreement; execution and registration of a formal lease remained outstanding.
The plaintiffs sued to eject the occupant on the ground that no registered lease existed.
members.legal_principle: Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, provides a statutory defence to a transferee in possession under a written contract signed by the transferor, where the terms necessary to constitute the transfer are ascertainable with reasonable certainty, possession was taken or continued in part performance, an act in furtherance of the contract was done, and the transferee performed or was willing to perform their part. The provision is a partial statutory importation of the English doctrine of part performance. A formal registered lease is not necessary to invoke the defence. Under section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, an agreement creating a present demise may be admissible as evidence of part performance; the court accepted reliable secondary evidence of the agreement where the primary documents were in the possession or power of the opposing side and were not produced despite notice. Section 27-A of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, concerned an active equity for certain lease contracts made after 1 April 1930 and did not apply to this contract, but that did not prevent reliance on section 53-A as a defence. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The requirements for the statutory defence of part performance were satisfied. The plaintiffs could not eject the defendant on the ground that no registered lease existed. The appeal was allowed, the Assistant Judge’s dismissal of the suit was restored, and the High Court’s decision was reversed.

rule.if: ejectment_suit and written_signed_agreement_with_ascertainable_terms and possession_in_part_performance and act_furthering_agreement and (obligations_performed or willing_to_perform) and claimant_derives_through_transferee

predicates.ejectment_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking to eject a person from property.
predicates.written_signed_agreement_with_ascertaina: The transferor and the other contracting party made a written agreement signed by or on behalf of the transferor, and its necessary terms can be ascertained with reasonable certainty.
predicates.possession_in_part_performance: The person claiming under the agreement took or continued in possession of the property in part performance of it.
predicates.act_furthering_agreement: The person claiming under the agreement did an act in furtherance of it, such as building on the property or tendering agreed rent.
predicates.obligations_performed: The person claiming under the agreement performed their part of it.
predicates.willing_to_perform: The person claiming under the agreement was willing to perform their part of it.
predicates.claimant_derives_through_transferee: The person resisting ejectment claims through the person who took the transfer under the agreement.

members.legal_issue: Succession to a sovereign and impartible estate is governed by primogeniture, and the rule does not cease merely because the ruler later loses sovereignty.
material_facts: Primogeniture governed succession to the chiefship in the ruling family.
The ruler was deposed, and his son was installed as the next ruler.
The merger covenant guaranteed succession according to law and custom, and no later repeal of the applicable succession rule was established.
members.legal_principle: A sovereign ruler held the estate by virtue of sovereignty, rather than by ordinary coparcenary law; primogeniture was presumed for a sovereign ruler and applied to an impartible estate. The Court relied on Baboo Gunesh Dutt Singh v. Maharaja Moheshur Singh, D.S. Meramwala Bhayavala v. Ba Shri Amarba Jethsurbhai, Mirza Raja Shri Pushavathi Viziaram Gajapathi Raj Manne Sultan Bahadur v. Shri Pushvathi Visweswar Gajapathi Raj, Thakore Shri Vinaysinhji v. Kumar Shri Natwarsinhji, Article XIV of the merger covenant, Article 372 of the Constitution, and Section 5(ii) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
members.conclusion: Primogeniture governed succession to the ruling estate and continued to apply to an impartible estate after the ruler ceased to be sovereign.

predicates.succession_dispute_concerns_sovereign_im: The proceeding concerns succession to an estate held as a sovereign or impartible estate.
predicates.customary_primogeniture_applied: The ruling family followed primogeniture in succession to its chiefship or estate.
predicates.covenant_guarantees_customary_succession: An agreement made on integration guarantees succession according to the applicable law and custom.
predicates.succession_rule_remains_unrepealed: No later law or agreement shown in the proceeding repeals the applicable succession rule.

members.legal_issue: Succession to an impartible estate of a sovereign ruler follows primogeniture, and that rule continues after the ruler ceases to exercise sovereignty unless it is repealed.
material_facts: The ruling house followed primogeniture for succession to the Gaddi, with the eldest son succeeding as ruler.
The dispute concerned property said to form part of the estate of a former ruler, and the applicable succession rule was relevant to the competing claims of his heirs.
The court treated the rule of succession for an impartible ruler’s estate as continuing after the loss of sovereignty.
members.legal_principle: The court relied on Baboo Gunesh Dutt Singh v. Maharaja Moheshur Singh, the Digest of Customary Law in the Punjab, Jai Kaur v. Sher Singh, Salig Rain v. Maya Devi, Gopal Singh v. Ujagar Singh, the Privy Purses case, D.S. Meramwala Bhayavala v. Ba Shri Atarba Jethsurbhai, Thakore Shri Vinayasinghji v. Kumar Shri Natwarsinhji, and Rajkumar Narsingh Pratap Singh Deo v. State of Orissa. It held that primogeniture and impartibility are presumed for a sovereign ruler’s estate, and that the existing succession law continues under Article 372 of the Constitution. It also considered Section 5 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, which excludes certain estates descending to a single heir under a covenant or agreement.
members.conclusion: The rule of primogeniture applies to succession to the Gaddi of a sovereign ruler and continues to govern an impartible estate after the ruler ceases to be sovereign, unless repealed.

rule.if: succession_to_former_ruler_estate_case and primogeniture_custom_applies and (estate_is_impartible or estate_is_held_as_sovereign_estate) and succession_rule_not_repealed

predicates.succession_to_former_ruler_estate_case: The proceeding concerns succession to the estate of a former ruler.
predicates.primogeniture_custom_applies: The ruling house followed a custom under which the eldest son succeeded to the rulership.
predicates.estate_is_impartible: The estate descends as a single estate rather than being divided among heirs.
predicates.estate_is_held_as_sovereign_estate: The estate was held by its ruler as part of the ruler’s sovereign estate.
predicates.succession_rule_not_repealed: No later law or other change had repealed the applicable succession rule.

members.legal_issue: A ruler's property inventory accepted by the other sovereign parties to an integration covenant can establish the ruler's private title to the listed property as an act of State, even where the property had previously been treated as State property.
material_facts: The property had been acquired and managed as State property before integration.
The ruler included the property in the inventory of properties he sought to retain as private property under the integration covenant.
The covenant authorities accepted the inventory and formally declared the property to be the ruler's private property.
The ruler later sued for possession against family members claiming through the former ruler's estate.
members.legal_principle: Article VI of the covenant dealt with State assets, while Article XII addressed a ruler's private property and provided for inventories and resolution of disputes about classification. The Court held that recognition by the sovereign parties to the covenant that the property was the ruler's private property amounted to an act of State. The Court also referred to Article XIV in addressing the covenant's treatment of rulership and succession.
members.conclusion: The accepted recognition of the property as the successor ruler's private property amounted to an act of State; the successor ruler's title prevailed, and his possession suit was allowed.

predicates.civil_possession_suit_claims_title_under: The proceeding is a civil suit for possession in which a ruler relies on title recognized during integration of the State.
predicates.property_was_treated_as_state_property_b: Before integration, State records and conduct treated the property as belonging to the State.
predicates.ruler_included_property_in_private_inven: The ruler listed the property as private property he sought to retain when the State was integrated.
predicates.covenant_authorities_accepted_private_cl: The authorities acting for the parties to the integration covenant accepted and formally recognized the property's private classification.

members.legal_issue: A property treated and administered as State property may be recognized as the ruler’s private property upon merger when the ruler includes it in the inventory and the covenanting authorities accept that classification.
material_facts: The property was bought in another person’s name and was treated for years as belonging to the State, including through State management, payment of expenses, leasing, and a formal release to the State.
After succeeding to the rulership, the ruler included the property in the inventory of properties he sought to retain as private property upon the State’s merger.
The authorities accepted the inventory and later records identified the property as the ruler’s private property.

The competing family claim that the property had remained the personal property of the former ruler was inconsistent with the contemporary records and with the claimant’s earlier assertion that the property had been given to her by the ruler.
members.legal_principle: Article VI of the covenant dealt with State assets, while Article XII entitled a ruler to retain private property belonging to him when administration was transferred and required an inventory of that property. The court held that the accepted recognition of the property as the ruler’s private property by the covenanting authorities amounted to an act of State. It rejected the contention that the ruler’s inclusion of the property could be disregarded in light of the State’s prior records and conduct, and relied on the rule against acquiring immovable property in British territory by a ruling chief, which explained the use of a benamidar.
members.conclusion: The property was recognized as the ruler’s private property upon merger, and he was entitled to recover possession of it.

predicates.possession_recovery_case: The proceeding seeks recovery of possession of property from persons occupying or claiming it.
predicates.property_was_acquired_and_administered_a: The property was acquired in another person’s name but was managed, maintained, leased, or recorded as belonging to the State.
predicates.ruler_included_property_in_private_inven: The ruler included the property in an inventory of property he sought to retain as private property when the State’s administration was transferred.
predicates.covenanting_authorities_accepted_invento: The authorities responsible for the merger accepted the inventory and recognized the property as the ruler’s private property.

members.legal_issue: The value of mineral output supplied from an owned mine to the owner’s manufacturing facilities may be included when determining the mine’s profits for a cess assessment, even when the output is not sold separately.
material_facts: The company owned both a colliery and iron and steel factories and workshops.
Most of the coal raised from the colliery was supplied to and used in the company’s factories and workshops; some coal was sold to outsiders.
The company claimed that no profit from the colliery could be assessed on coal used in its own factories because that coal was not sold.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 6 and 72 of the Bengal Cess Act, 1880, cess could be assessed on the annual net profits of a mine. Following Tata Iron and Steel Co. Ltd. v. State of Bihar, [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 199, where mining and manufacturing are parts of an integrated undertaking and the mine’s profit is embedded in the proceeds from the ultimate product, the profit attributable to the mine may be identified and assessed. The fact that the mined material is consumed in manufacturing rather than incorporated into the final product does not alter that principle; the comparable education-cess provisions were treated similarly.
members.conclusion: The assessing authority could take into consideration the value of the coal supplied to the company’s factories and workshops when computing the colliery’s profits.

predicates.mine_profit_cess_assessment: An authority is assessing cess by reference to the profits of a mine.
predicates.integrated_mining_and_manufacturing: The mine and the owner’s manufacturing operations form parts of an integrated undertaking whose ultimate products are sold.
predicates.mine_output_used_in_owner_facilities: The owner supplies output from the mine to its own manufacturing facilities for use there.

members.legal_issue: A mine owner may derive taxable annual net profits from mining when extracted ore is used to manufacture products that are sold, even if the ore itself is not sold.
material_facts: The companies held mines and extracted ore from them.
They used the extracted ore in their own manufacturing operations rather than selling it as ore.
They sold the finished products made using the ore.
The assessment treated the companies as having earned profits from their mining operations.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 5, 6 and 72 of the Bengal Cess Act, 1880, as amended in Bihar, where a mine owner uses ore in further activities and sells the resulting product, the profit from mining may be embedded in the final realisation and apportioned. Kikabhai Premchand v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay was distinguished because the stock there was withdrawn without a sale or other commercial realisation; Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay v. Ahmedbhai Umarbhai & Co. and Anglo-French Textile Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras were relied on for the possibility of apportionment. Commissioner of Income-tax v. Dewan Bahadur S. L. Mathias and Commissioner of Income-tax v. Bai Shirinbai K. Kooka were considered.
members.conclusion: The profits attributable to the mining operation may be separated from the profits of the integrated manufacturing and selling activities and assessed as annual net profits from the mines.

rule.if: cess_assessment_appeal and mine_owner and extracted_ore_used_in_manufacturing and manufactured_product_sold

predicates.cess_assessment_appeal: The proceeding challenges an assessment of a local cess imposed by reference to profits from a mine.
predicates.mine_owner: The assessee held or owned the mine from which the material was extracted.
predicates.extracted_ore_used_in_manufacturing: The mine owner used the extracted ore in further manufacturing instead of selling it as ore.
predicates.manufactured_product_sold: The mine owner sold the product made using the extracted ore.

members.legal_issue: For a possession claim governed by the adverse-possession limitation rule, a defendant cannot add the possession of an independent trespasser to the possession of the defendant or those through whom the defendant claims.
material_facts: The Raja took possession in 1938, and the transferee and then the appellants obtained possession through transfers or a decree connected to the Raja's title.
The adverse possession of the Raja and those claiming through him was less than the limitation period when the suit was filed.

The adopted son and the person who had received part of the property from him had possessed it before the Raja, but they were independent trespassers in relation to the Raja and those claiming through him.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 144 of the Limitation Act, 1908, limitation begins when the defendant's possession becomes adverse to the plaintiff, and the defendant bears the burden of establishing adverse possession for the required period. Under section 2(4), a defendant may rely on possession of a person from or through whom the defendant derives liability, but not on the possession of an independent trespasser, because no jural relationship connects independent trespassers. Ramayya v. Kotamma was explained as a case governed by Article 142 and therefore distinguishable; the court also relied on Agency Co. v. Short and referred to Rajagopala Naidu v. Ramasubramania Ayyar and Willis v. Earl Howe.
members.conclusion: Article 144 applied, but the suit was not barred by limitation because the defendants' chain of adverse possession was shorter than the limitation period and could not be extended by adding the independent trespassers' possession.

rule.if: possession_suit and defendants_claim_through_later_possessors and defendants_chain_below_limitation_period and earlier_possession_by_independent_trespasser

predicates.possession_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit to recover possession of property.
predicates.defendants_claim_through_later_possessor: The defendants claimed through later possessors whose adverse possession was connected to the defendants' chain of title or claim.
predicates.defendants_chain_below_limitation_period: The adverse possession of the defendants and persons through whom they claimed was shorter than the applicable limitation period.
predicates.earlier_possession_by_independent_trespa: An earlier possessor held the property as a trespasser independent of the defendants' chain of claim.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff’s prior possession gives a claim against a defendant who is a mere trespasser, and another plaintiff’s withdrawal or compromise cannot by itself defeat that independent claim.
material_facts: The trial court found that the appellant had possessed the properties and that the respondent had dispossessed her through criminal proceedings.
The trial court found that the respondent was a mere trespasser and had no title under the alleged gift deed.
The other plaintiff withdrew her claim and entered into a compromise with the respondent; the appellant was not a party to that compromise.
The High Court treated the compromise as giving the respondent the rights of the other plaintiff and dismissed the appellant’s suit.
members.legal_principle: Relying on Ismail Ariff v. Mohamed Ghouse, the court held that possession is sufficient evidence of title against a defendant who has no title and is a mere wrongdoer; the possessor may seek a declaration and consequential relief. The court also referred to section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, concerning recovery after dispossession otherwise than in due course of law. A co-plaintiff’s withdrawal or compromise did not transfer away the appellant’s independent rights merely because the co-plaintiff ceased prosecuting the suit.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in allowing the other plaintiff’s compromise to justify dismissal of the appellant’s claim. If the trial court’s findings were correct, the appellant’s possessory claim against the trespasser remained available, and the case required further decision on the issues remanded by the District Judge.

rule.if: civil_property_suit_appeal and plaintiff_was_in_possession and defendant_is_mere_trespasser and other_co_plaintiff_settled_or_withdrew and plaintiff_was_not_party_to_settlement

predicates.civil_property_suit_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal in a civil suit concerning rights in property.
predicates.plaintiff_was_in_possession: A plaintiff possessed the property before being dispossessed.
predicates.defendant_is_mere_trespasser: The defendant had no title or other right to the property and was a mere trespasser.
predicates.other_co_plaintiff_settled_or_withdrew: Another plaintiff withdrew from the suit or compromised with the defendant.
predicates.plaintiff_was_not_party_to_settlement: The plaintiff whose possession was challenged did not join in the other plaintiff’s withdrawal or compromise.

members.legal_issue: An agreement directing that a particular fund be applied to a debt can create an equitable assignment of the fund to the extent of the debt, even without a legal transfer of the underlying right.
material_facts: The debtor’s power of attorney authorised the bank to realise amounts payable under a decree and to credit the proceeds against the debt owed to it.
The decree proceeds were specifically earmarked as a fund for discharging the debt, although the document contained no words transferring the decree and left the debtor as its owner.
members.legal_principle: An engagement to pay a creditor out of a specified fund constitutes an equitable assignment of so much of that fund as is needed to discharge the debt. The Court applied Watson v. The Duke of Wellington, [1830] 39 E.R. 231, and Burn v. Carvalho, [1839] 41 E.R. 265, and approved Jagabhai Lallubhai v. Rustamji Nasarwanji, [1885] I.L.R. IX Bom. 311, and Prahlad Pd. Modi v. Tikaitni Faldani Kumari, A.I.R. 1956 Patna 233.
members.conclusion: The arrangement constituted an equitable assignment to the bank of the amount due under the decree, to the extent necessary to discharge the debt owed to it.

predicates.debt_owed_to_creditor: The debtor owed a debt to the creditor.
predicates.particular_fund_identified: The debtor identified a particular fund from which payment could be made.
predicates.fund_committed_to_debt: The debtor directed that the identified fund be applied to the debt.

members.legal_issue: A direction to realise a specifically designated fund and apply it toward a debt can create an equitable assignment of that fund even without a legal transfer of the underlying decree.
material_facts: The power of attorney directed that amounts recovered under the decree be credited to the debtor’s account with the bank.
The decree proceeds were specifically earmarked to discharge the debt owed to the bank, and the bank was authorised to realise those proceeds and set them off against the debt.
The document contained no words transferring the decree, and it described the bank as acting on the debtor’s behalf.
members.legal_principle: A direction or engagement to pay a creditor out of a particular fund can amount in equity to an assignment of so much of the fund as is needed to discharge the debt. The Court relied on Watson v. Duke of Wellington, (1830) 39 E.R. 231; Burn v. Carvalho, (1839) 41 E.R. 265; Jaga bhai Lallubhai v. Rustamji Nasarwanji, (1885) I.L.R. 9 Bom. 311; and Prahlad Pd. Modi v. Tikaiini Faldani Kumari. Because the document contained no words of transfer and left ownership of the decree proceeds with the debtor, there was no legal assignment.
members.conclusion: The document did not legally transfer the decree, but it effected an equitable assignment of the decree proceeds to the extent necessary to discharge the debt owed to the bank.

predicates.debt_owed_to_agent: The person entitled to the fund owes a debt to the person authorised to receive or apply it.
predicates.particular_fund_identified_for_debt_paym: A particular fund is designated for payment of the debt.
predicates.agent_authorized_to_realize_fund_and_app: The creditor or its agent is authorised to realise the designated fund and apply the proceeds to the debt.

members.legal_issue: Proceedings to declare a person an evacuee and that person's property evacuee property lapse if the person dies before the declaration, and cannot be continued against the heirs to make that declaration.
material_facts: Proceedings had begun to determine whether a person and his property should be declared evacuee and evacuee property.
The person died while an appeal concerning that determination was pending and before a declaration that he was an evacuee had been made.
His property devolved on his heirs under Mohammedan law upon his death.
The authority later continued the proceedings and declared the deceased to be an evacuee and his property to be evacuee property.
The Act provided no procedure for substituting the heirs and continuing the proceedings against them after the person's death.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(d) and 2(f) define an evacuee and evacuee property by reference to a person's status and rights or interests in property. Under section 7, notice and inquiry precede a declaration, and section 8 provides for vesting following that declaration; the statutory doctrine of relation-back cannot displace devolution to heirs where the person dies before declaration. Section 43 addresses death after vesting and supports the conclusion that vesting must occur during the alleged evacuee's lifetime. The Code of Civil Procedure's substitution procedure did not apply because the Custodian was not a court; section 45 applied the Code only to specified matters, and the Act contained no provision for continuing the proceedings against heirs. The court distinguished insolvency provisions, including section 93 of the Presidency Towns Insolvency Act and section 17 of the Provincial Insolvency Act, which expressly provide for continuation after death. No earlier case was relied on for the substantive conclusion.
members.conclusion: The proceedings lapsed on the person's death; the authority lacked jurisdiction to declare him an evacuee after his death or to declare the property that had devolved on his heirs evacuee property, and its order was set aside.

rule.if: evacuee_status_and_property_declaration_proceeding and person_died_before_declaration and property_devolved_to_heirs_by_succession and no_statutory_continuation_mechanism

predicates.evacuee_status_and_property_declaration_: An administrative proceeding was pending to determine whether a person was an evacuee and whether the person's property was evacuee property.
predicates.person_died_before_declaration: The person whose status was being determined died before the authority made the declaration.
predicates.property_devolved_to_heirs_by_succession: The person's property passed to heirs by succession upon the person's death.
predicates.no_statutory_continuation_mechanism: The governing legal scheme provided no procedure for continuing the proceeding against heirs after the person's death.

members.legal_issue: Proceedings to determine whether a person and their property are evacuee property cannot continue to a posthumous declaration when the person dies before the declaration and the property has devolved to heirs by succession.
material_facts: Proceedings to determine the person’s status and the status of their property began while the person was alive.
An appeal seeking a declaration that the person and their property were evacuee was pending when the person died, before the appellate authority made that declaration.
The property devolved on the heirs in specific shares by succession under Mohammedan law, rather than by transfer from the deceased.
The governing scheme contained no provision for substituting the heirs or continuing the proceedings against them after the person’s death.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(d) and 2(f), the definitions of evacuee and evacuee property concern a person with a right or interest in the property; section 7 requires notice and an inquiry before property may be declared evacuee property, and section 8 provides for vesting following that declaration. Read together with rule 6 and its notice form, these provisions contemplate proceedings against a living person. A declaration cannot operate retrospectively to displace property that has already devolved on heirs by operation of law. Succession is not a transfer within section 2(f)(1), and the restriction on transfers in section 40 does not alter devolution by death. Section 43 addresses death after vesting and does not authorize a declaration after death. Section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply to the Custodian, and section 45 applies the Code only for specified purposes, not substitution; unlike section 93 of the Presidency Towns Insolvency Act and section 17 of the Provincial Insolvency Act, the governing scheme has no provision for continuation after death. The earlier decision in Ebrahim Aboobaker v. Custodian General of Evacuee Property decided only that the informant could appeal and left this jurisdictional question open.
members.conclusion: The proceedings lapsed on the person’s death. The appellate authority had no jurisdiction to declare the deceased an evacuee or the property that had devolved on the heirs to be evacuee property, and its declaration was set aside.

rule.if: evacuee_property_status_appeal and person_died_before_declaration and property_devolved_to_heirs_by_succession and no_post_death_continuation_procedure

predicates.evacuee_property_status_appeal: An appeal is pending to determine whether a person and their property have the relevant evacuee status.
predicates.person_died_before_declaration: The person whose status is being determined dies before the authority declares that person or the property to have that status.
predicates.property_devolved_to_heirs_by_succession: The property passes to the person’s heirs by succession upon death, rather than by a transfer from the deceased.
predicates.no_post_death_continuation_procedure: The governing scheme provides no procedure to substitute heirs or continue the status proceedings after the person dies.

members.legal_issue: A grant of land carries the underlying mineral and subsoil rights unless those rights were expressly or impliedly reserved.
material_facts: The historical grants conveyed the estate and everything appertaining to it, without reserving mineral rights to the government.
The estate was permanently settled, and the relevant settlement recognized proprietors as proprietors of the soil.
The grantee’s use of the land was not restricted to agriculture, and evidence of dealings and conduct supported the grantee’s ownership of mineral rights.
The limestone was quarried from the acquired land.
members.legal_principle: A transfer of the surface ordinarily conveys the minerals beneath it unless the grant contains an express or implied reservation. The court relied on the terms of the grants, the Benares Regulation 1 of 1795 and the permanent-settlement regulations for Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, and the principle discussed in Halsbury’s Laws of England and Mitchell v. Mosley. It also relied on Ranjit Singh v. Kali Dasi Debi, Hari Narayan Singh v. Sriram Chakravarti, Durga Prasad Singh v. Braja Nath Bose, and Sashi Bhushan Misra v. Jyoti Prasad Singh Deo concerning proprietary rights in the soil and minerals.
members.conclusion: The appellant owned the minerals and subsoil rights, including the limestone, and was entitled to compensation for them.

predicates.land_grant_conveys_estate_and_appurtenan: A grant conveys the land together with the estate or property appertaining to it.
predicates.no_mineral_reservation: The grant contains no express or implied reservation of the underlying mineral rights.

members.legal_issue: A grant of land that includes the estate and everything appertaining to it carries the underlying mineral rights unless those rights were expressly or impliedly reserved.
material_facts: Historical grants gave the holder the estate and described everything appertaining to it as belonging to him, without reserving mineral rights to the government.
The permanent settlement recognized estate holders as proprietors of the soil.
Historical records and subordinate leases were consistent with the holder exercising mineral rights, and the government had not asserted a reservation of those rights.
members.legal_principle: A grant of the land or its surface ordinarily includes minerals beneath it unless the grant contains an express or implied reservation. The Court relied on Regulation VIII of 1793, Regulations I and II of 1793, Benares Regulation I of 1795, Ranjit Singh v. Kali Dasi Debi, Hari Narayan Singh v. Sriram Chakravarti, Durga Prasad Singh v. Braja Nath Bose, Sashi Bhushan Misra v. Jyoti Prasad Singh Deo, and Mitchell v. Mosley. It also held that the Mirzapur Stone Mahal Act did not remove the proprietor’s rights to sub-soil minerals.
members.conclusion: The appellant owned the minerals and sub-soil rights in the area, and the High Court’s contrary conclusion was overruled.

predicates.mineral_title_dispute: A dispute arose over whether a holder of a land grant owned the minerals beneath the land.
predicates.land_grant_includes_estate_and_appurtena: The grant conveyed the land or estate together with what appertained to it.
predicates.no_mineral_reservation: The grant contained no express or implied reservation of mineral rights to the grantor.

members.legal_issue: A pre-emptor’s qualification is assessed through the decree of the court of first instance, and a subsequent loss of qualification or prospective change in law during an appeal does not defeat the decree.
material_facts: The plaintiffs claimed a preferential right to purchase as co-sharers and obtained a decree for pre-emption from the trial court.
After the decree, they deposited the purchase money as required by Order XX Rule 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The decree was affirmed by the appellate courts, and a statutory amendment removing a co-sharer’s right of pre-emption came into force while a further appeal was pending.
members.legal_principle: The rule in Hans Nath v. Ragho Prasad Singh, Bhagwan Das v. Chet Ram, Rikhi Ram v. Ram Kumar and Didar Singh v. Ishar Singh is that the pre-emptor must retain the qualification through the trial court’s decree, not thereafter. Under Order XX Rule 14 CPC, deposit of the purchase money following a decree transfers title to the pre-emptor. The appellate court considers whether the trial court’s decree was correct on the rights then existing; subsequent events cannot displace a vested right unless a retrospective law requires that result. The Court approved Didar Singh and held that Ramjilal v. Ghisa Ram did not state the correct law.
members.conclusion: The appellate court had to decide the appeal by reference to the parties’ substantive rights when the pre-emption suit was adjudicated; the later amendment did not affect the decree or the plaintiffs’ claim. A pre-emptor must possess the right on the date of sale, the date of filing suit, and the date of the trial court’s decree, but a loss of that right after the decree does not defeat the claim.

rule.if: preemption_suit and appeal_from_preemption_decree and preemptor_qualified_through_trial_decree and trial_court_decreed_preemption and purchase_money_deposited and post_decree_qualification_loss_or_prospective_law_change

predicates.preemption_suit: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking to purchase property in preference to a buyer.
predicates.appeal_from_preemption_decree: A party appealed from a trial court’s decree in the pre-emption proceeding.
predicates.preemptor_qualified_through_trial_decree: The claimant possessed the required preferential qualification on the sale date, when suit was filed, and when the trial court adjudicated the suit.
predicates.trial_court_decreed_preemption: The trial court granted the claimant a decree for pre-emption.
predicates.purchase_money_deposited: The claimant deposited the purchase money following the decree.
predicates.post_decree_qualification_loss_or_prospe: After the trial court’s decree, the claimant lost the qualification or a prospective change in law removed the claimed right while an appeal was pending.

members.legal_issue: A pre-emption claimant’s post-decree loss of qualification does not defeat a decree where the claimant possessed the right at the legally relevant stages and the right became vested.
material_facts: The claimant asserted a co-sharer’s pre-emption right arising from a sale.
The trial court granted the pre-emption decree, and the claimant deposited the purchase money.
The claimant’s asserted loss of qualification arose after the trial court decree, during the appeal; the subsequent statutory change was not retrospective.
members.legal_principle: Under the pre-emption authorities, including Hans Nath v. Ragho Prasad Singh, Bhagwan Das v. Chet Ram, Rikhi Ram v. Ram Kumar and Didar Singh v. Ishar Singh, qualification must subsist through the trial court’s decree, but a later loss ordinarily does not affect the claim. Under Order 20 Rule 14 CPC, after the decree-holder deposits the purchase money, title vests in the claimant. The appellate court reviews the correctness of the trial court’s decision on the rights existing at the time of adjudication; later events cannot be used to impair that vested right unless a retrospective law requires it.
members.conclusion: The claimant had to establish the pre-emption right on the date of sale, the date of suit and the date of the trial court decree. A subsequent loss of qualification or change in law that is not retrospective did not defeat the decree on appeal.

rule.if: preemption_suit_appeal and claimant_qualified_at_relevant_stages and first_instance_decree_for_claimant and purchase_money_deposited and later_change_is_nonretroactive

predicates.preemption_suit_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a suit seeking pre-emption of a sale.
predicates.claimant_qualified_at_relevant_stages: The claimant possessed the pre-emption qualification on the sale date, the suit date and the date of the trial court decree.
predicates.first_instance_decree_for_claimant: The court of first instance granted the claimant a decree for pre-emption.
predicates.purchase_money_deposited: The claimant deposited the purchase money after the decree.
predicates.later_change_is_nonretroactive: The claimant’s loss of qualification or the change in law occurred after the decree and does not apply retrospectively.

members.legal_issue: Testimony given under oath before a committing court and admitted at trial as substantive evidence ordinarily requires extrinsic support when the witness gives a contradictory sworn account at trial, unless the factfinder is independently satisfied that the earlier account is true.
material_facts: A witness gave an account identifying the accused as participants in the killings before the committing court.
At the later trial, the witness gave a contradictory sworn account and said she had not seen the occurrence.
The earlier account was admitted as substantive evidence, but the record did not provide adequate extrinsic support for the witness's account of the occurrence and the accused's participation.
The court found unresolved difficulties in the earlier account, including uncertainty about the witness's opportunity to observe and unexplained aspects of the events.
members.legal_principle: Section 288 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 made the committing-court testimony substantive evidence at trial, but did not make corroboration an absolute legal requirement. The Court relied on Bhuboni Sahu v. The King, A.I.R. 1949 P.C. 257, for the principle that it is unsafe to rely implicitly on a witness who has given two different stories on oath. Ordinarily, extrinsic evidence should reasonably support both the occurrence and the particular accused's participation; if the factfinder is independently satisfied of the truth of one statement despite the inconsistency, it may rely on it without such support.
members.conclusion: The earlier testimony was substantive evidence and corroboration was not an absolute legal prerequisite. But in the ordinary case, it was unsafe to rely on it implicitly after the witness had made contradictory statements on oath; extrinsic support concerning both the occurrence and the particular accused's participation was ordinarily needed, unless the factfinder was independently satisfied of the truth of one account. On these facts, the testimony could not safely sustain the convictions without adequate corroboration.

rule.if: criminal_case and testimony_admitted_as_substantive_evidence and witness_gave_contradictory_sworn_accounts and not adequate_extrinsic_support and not factfinder_independently_satisfied

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the evidence is considered as a basis for conviction.
predicates.testimony_admitted_as_substantive_eviden: A witness's earlier testimony is admitted as substantive evidence in the later trial.
predicates.witness_gave_contradictory_sworn_account: The witness gave materially contradictory accounts under oath in different proceedings.
predicates.adequate_extrinsic_support: Evidence apart from the witness's disputed testimony reasonably supports both the occurrence and the particular accused's participation.
predicates.factfinder_independently_satisfied: The factfinder is independently satisfied, despite the contradictory sworn accounts, that one account is true.

members.legal_issue: Prior testimony admitted after a witness gives inconsistent evidence at trial may be relied on when extrinsic evidence supports its truth, including its implication of the particular accused, or when the judge is otherwise satisfied it is reliable.
material_facts: Two witnesses gave trial evidence inconsistent with their statements before the committing court.
Their earlier statements were admitted as evidence at trial.
The confession and other circumstances supported important parts of the earlier statements, including the accused persons’ presence at a hotel.
One witness affirmed that the earlier account was true, while the explanations offered for resiling from the earlier statements were found unconvincing.
members.legal_principle: Under section 288 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, when a witness gives inconsistent statements on oath, it is unsafe to rely implicitly on the evidence without assessing its reliability. Extrinsic support should ordinarily give reasonable assurance that the account of the occurrence and the accusation against the particular accused are true; however, a judge who is otherwise satisfied that the evidence is reliable may rely on it even without such support. Shranappa Mutyappa Halke v. State of Maharashtra was followed, and Har Prasad v. State of Madhya Pradesh was applied.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the Sessions Court was entitled to rely on the earlier statements and that the High Court erred in rejecting them without assessing the supporting circumstances.

predicates.trial_uses_prior_committing_court_testim: The trial uses testimony previously given by the witness before a committing court.
predicates.witness_gives_inconsistent_trial_account: The witness gives an account at trial that is inconsistent with the earlier testimony.
predicates.extrinsic_evidence_supports_prior_accoun: Evidence outside the inconsistent testimony supports the earlier account and its implication of the accused.
predicates.judge_independently_satisfied_of_reliabi: The judge is satisfied, after considering the inconsistency and the evidence, that the earlier account is true and safe to rely on.

members.legal_issue: The amount of a tax is generally a legislative matter and is not invalid merely because it is heavy unless the levy is confiscatory, extortionate, or a device for confiscating property.
material_facts: The challenged levy was a non-recurring tax on buildings calculated using a uniform multiplier.
The challengers argued that the resulting tax could exceed the construction cost of a building and could be disproportionate to competing investment returns.
The Court considered rental income, the non-recurring nature of the levy, and the potential appreciation in the building’s value.
The Court found no basis to characterize the levy as confiscatory or extortionate.
members.legal_principle: The quantum and conditions of a tax are within legislative competence; courts do not question the reasonableness of the amount unless the tax is confiscatory or extortionate. A taxing statute is not colourable merely because the levy is high; the legislature must be using taxation as a device or cloak for confiscation. The Court relied on Rai Ramkrishna v. State of Bihar, Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, Assistant Commissioner of Urban Land Tax v. The Buckingham and Carnatic Co. Ltd., Raja Jagannath Baksh Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and S. Kodar v. State of Kerala.
members.conclusion: The tax’s amount and multiplier were not shown to be confiscatory, extortionate, or otherwise invalid.

predicates.tax_amount_challenge: The proceeding challenged the amount or rate of the tax as unreasonable.
predicates.tax_is_nonrecurring: The tax was payable as a non-recurring charge on a building.
predicates.levy_not_shown_confiscatory_or_extortion: The challengers did not establish that the levy confiscated property or was extortionate.

members.legal_issue: A taxing enactment is not colourable merely because its tax is alleged to be excessive; the challenge requires evidence supporting an inference that taxation is a device to confiscate property.
material_facts: The petitioner alleged that cultivation costs left little net income and that the tax was confiscatory.
The respondents disputed those calculations and supplied figures indicating that the petitioner’s net income substantially exceeded the tax assessed.
The petitioner did not provide information about the rent used to determine annual value, an important basis for assessing the burden.
The Court found that the statutory scheme did not disclose a constitutional infirmity in its charging or assessment provisions.
members.legal_principle: Excessiveness of a tax alone does not establish colourable legislation; relevant circumstances must justify an inference of fraud on legislative power. The Court considered K. T. Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, [1961] 3 SCR 77, but explained that it involved discriminatory and unreasonable provisions as well as a confiscatory effect, and did not authorize courts to strike down a tax simply because its rate was high.
members.conclusion: The petitioner did not establish that the enactment was confiscatory or a colourable exercise of legislative power, and the challenge failed.

predicates.colourable_legislation_challenge_to_tax: A party alleges that a tax law is a pretence for an exercise of legislative power aimed at confiscating property.
predicates.tax_burden_alone_is_not_supported_by_rel: The claim that the tax consumes the taxpayer’s property or income is not established by reliable evidence.
predicates.no_other_circumstances_show_a_confiscato: The evidence does not otherwise indicate a design to use taxation as a device for confiscating property.

members.legal_issue: The new rule on the time limit for acquisition declarations does not reopen completed matters in which awards were made and compensation was paid.
material_facts: The Court adopted a rule rejecting a fresh limitation period after an acquisition declaration is quashed.
The State argued that applying the rule could unsettle completed acquisitions.
The Court directed that matters in which awards had been made and compensation paid would not be reopened under its ruling.
members.legal_principle: The Court limited the prospective operation of its ruling to preserve completed matters where an award had been made and compensation paid. It did not identify a statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this limitation.
members.conclusion: The judgment operates prospectively to the extent that matters in which awards have been made and compensation has been paid are not reopened by applying its rule.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land.
predicates.award_made: An award determining compensation for the acquisition was made.
predicates.compensation_paid: Compensation under the award was paid.

members.legal_issue: The new ruling on the deadline does not reopen acquisitions for which awards have been made and compensation has been paid.
material_facts: The Court accepted that applying its ruling could affect acquisitions that had already become final.
It limited the prospective operation of its judgment for cases in which awards had been made and compensation had been paid.
members.legal_principle: The Court directed that its judgment operate prospectively to the extent that acquisitions for which awards had been made and compensation paid would not be reopened under the judgment’s ratio.
members.conclusion: Cases in which an award had been made and compensation paid were not to be reopened by applying the ruling.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns a proceeding to acquire land for a public purpose or a company.
predicates.award_made: An award determining compensation for the acquired land was made.
predicates.compensation_paid: Compensation for the acquired land was paid.

members.legal_issue: Excluding pre-arrest bail for offences arising from the practice of untouchability does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
material_facts: The challenged provision excluded pre-arrest bail in cases involving accusations of offences against members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
The offences at issue were connected to the practice of untouchability and formed a distinct category from ordinary offences.

The legislative background described members of these communities as vulnerable to intimidation when they asserted their rights, and the Court considered that accused persons released on pre-arrest bail could intimidate victims or obstruct prosecution.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the offences as a distinct class because they arise from the practice of untouchability and the social conditions that give rise to them differ from those associated with ordinary offences. It relied on Article 17 of the Constitution, the purpose and legislative background of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, and Jai Singh v. Union of India, AIR 1993 Rajasthan 117.
members.conclusion: The exclusion of pre-arrest bail for the covered offences does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality because those offences form a distinct class and can be treated differently from other offences.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_prearrest_ba: A person challenges the exclusion of pre-arrest bail for a defined category of offences on equality grounds.
predicates.covered_offences_arise_from_untouchabili: The offences covered by the exclusion arise from the practice of untouchability.
predicates.victims_are_vulnerable_to_intimidation: Members of the targeted community are vulnerable to intimidation that may deter them from pursuing complaints or prosecution.
predicates.covered_offences_are_distinct_from_ordin: The covered offences and the social conditions giving rise to them form a distinct class from ordinary offences.

members.legal_issue: Excluding pre-arrest bail for a special category of offences does not violate the constitutional protection of life and personal liberty because pre-arrest bail is not an essential ingredient of that protection.
material_facts: The challenged provision made pre-arrest bail unavailable in cases involving accusations of offences under the special legislation.
Pre-arrest bail was first introduced by the 1973 Code of Criminal Procedure; it did not exist in the earlier Code.
The power to grant pre-arrest bail was conferred on the High Court and Court of Session and was discretionary rather than an automatic right.
The Court considered the risk that accused persons released on pre-arrest bail could intimidate victims or obstruct proper investigation.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that pre-arrest bail is a statutory right introduced after the Constitution came into force, is discretionary, and is not an essential ingredient of the right to life and personal liberty. It relied on Article 21 of the Constitution, the 41st Report of the Law Commission, and Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, JT 1994 (2) SC 423, which upheld a comparable exclusion of pre-arrest bail.
members.conclusion: The exclusion of pre-arrest bail for the covered offences does not violate the constitutional protection of life and personal liberty.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_prearrest_ba: A person challenges the exclusion of pre-arrest bail for a defined category of offences on personal-liberty grounds.
predicates.prearrest_bail_is_a_later_statutory_disc: Pre-arrest bail was created by legislation after the Constitution came into force and is granted through a court's discretion rather than as an automatic entitlement.
predicates.covered_offences_carry_risk_of_victim_in: The circumstances surrounding the covered offences create a risk that an accused person at liberty before arrest could intimidate victims or obstruct investigation.

members.legal_issue: The conservation legislation governs conversion of land included in the relevant data bank as paddy land or wetland and qualifying as such under the statutory definition.
material_facts: The dispute concerned land whose recorded classification was Nilam, or wetland.
The Court held that land included in the data bank or draft data bank as paddy land or wetland, and qualifying under the statutory definition, is governed by the conservation legislation.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(xii) and 2(xviii) of the Kerala Conservation of Paddy Land and Wetland Act, 2008 define paddy land and wetlands. Section 3 prohibits conversion or reclamation except in accordance with the Act, and Section 13 empowers the District Collector to order reconversion where conversion or reclamation occurred after the Act commenced. Sections 5, 7, 8 and 9 provide for monitoring, reporting and committee functions, including consideration of specified applications. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: Where land is included in the data bank or draft data bank as paddy land or wetland and falls within the statutory definition, conversion is governed by the conservation legislation and its procedures.

predicates.land_conversion_proceeding: A proceeding concerns proposed or completed conversion of land to another use.
predicates.land_listed_as_paddy_or_wetland: The land is included in the relevant data bank or draft data bank as paddy land or wetland.
predicates.land_meets_statutory_land_definition: The land has the characteristics of paddy land or wetland under the applicable statutory definition.

members.legal_issue: The land-utilization regime governs conversion of land not included in the relevant data bank and not qualifying as paddy land or wetland under the statutory definition.
material_facts: The Court distinguished land included in the data bank as paddy land or wetland from land not so included.

The Court held that land not included in the data bank and not qualifying as paddy land or wetland under the statutory definition remains governed by the land-utilization regime, even if revenue records describe it as Nilam.
members.legal_principle: The Kerala Land Utilization Order, 1967 governs land outside the scope of the Kerala Conservation of Paddy Land and Wetland Act, 2008. Under Clause 2(a) of the Order, the Collector considers requests for residential use on their merits; the Court also referred to the restrictions and directions in the Government notification of 5 February 2002. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: Land not included in the data bank and not qualifying as paddy land or wetland under the statutory definition is governed by the Kerala Land Utilization Order, 1967, under which the competent Collector considers a request for other use on its merits.

rule.if: land_conversion_proceeding and not land_listed_as_paddy_or_wetland and not land_meets_statutory_land_definition

predicates.land_conversion_proceeding: A proceeding concerns proposed or completed conversion of land to another use.
predicates.land_listed_as_paddy_or_wetland: The land is included in the relevant data bank or draft data bank as paddy land or wetland.
predicates.land_meets_statutory_land_definition: The land has the characteristics of paddy land or wetland under the applicable statutory definition.

members.legal_issue: A declaration that a tax levy is unconstitutional does not automatically entitle the payer to a refund of all amounts collected before the declaration.
material_facts: The Court held the challenged cess levies unconstitutional, and the assessees sought refunds of sums collected before the relevant judgments declaring the levies invalid.
The levies had been collected over time, and the States relied on the prior legal position and the consequences that repayment of all earlier collections would have for State interests and finances.

The Court directed refunds only for collections made on or after the relevant judgment declaring the levy unconstitutional, with interest; where an intermediary had collected the cess, it was to pass the refund to its customers.
members.legal_principle: The declaration that a levy is invalid and the relief granted as a consequence are distinct; a court has discretion to grant, withhold, or restrict relief to advance justice. In writ proceedings, delay, laches, third-party rights, unjust enrichment, and vital State interests may be relevant, and invalidity does not compel repayment of every earlier collection. The Court followed India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu and relied on State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhailal Bhai, Tilok Chand Motichand v. Munshi, D. Cawasji & Co. v. State of Mysore, Salonah Tea Co. Ltd. v. Superintendent of Taxes, and other authorities on discretionary relief and delay.
members.conclusion: Refund was not automatic: no refund was directed for collections before the relevant declaration of invalidity, while post-declaration collections were to be refunded with interest.

predicates.constitutional_levy_refund_claim: A party seeks repayment in a constitutional challenge to a state levy.
predicates.levy_is_declared_invalid: A court declares the challenged levy unconstitutional.
predicates.state_collected_cess_before_the_declarat: The state collected the cess before the court declared the levy unconstitutional.

members.legal_issue: A levy previously collected in reliance on an earlier decision upholding it may be declared invalid prospectively without requiring repayment of amounts already collected.
material_facts: A prior decision of the Supreme Court had upheld a similar levy calculated on royalty.
The state had collected the cess in reliance on that decision.
The Court held the levy invalid but limited the effect of its declaration to the future.
members.legal_principle: The Court limited retrospective relief because amounts had been collected on the basis of H.R.S. Murthy v. Collector of Chittoor, which it was overruling. It therefore declared the levy ultra vires prospectively and denied refunds of amounts already paid or collected.
members.conclusion: The levy was invalid only prospectively, and the state was not required to refund cess already paid or collected.

predicates.challenge_to_levy: A party challenged a levy that had already been collected.
predicates.earlier_high_court_decision_upheld_simil: The highest court had previously upheld a similar levy.
predicates.collections_made_in_reliance: The government collected the levy in reliance on the earlier decision.

members.legal_issue: The absence of a legally appointed manager does not suspend limitation against a math when possession of its property becomes adverse.
material_facts: After the lease ended, the occupants possessed the lands on their own behalf and adversely to the math.
The math had no legally appointed manager when the possession became adverse.
The adverse possession continued for the period required for limitation to run.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 144 read with section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908, limitation for recovery of property runs from when the defendant’s possession becomes adverse, and completion of the period extinguishes the owner’s title. A math is a juristic person capable of owning property and suing; it may act through a de facto manager, and, where necessary, beneficiaries may take steps to protect its rights. The Court followed the majority view in Venkateswara v. Venkatesa, and relied on Mahadeo Prasad Singh v. Karia Bharti and Vithalbowa v. Narayan Daji Thite. It distinguished Jagadindra Nath Roy v. Hemanta Kumari Debi, where a shebait existed at the start of limitation and claimed the benefit of a disability provision.
members.conclusion: Limitation ran against the math despite the absence of a legally appointed manager, and the math’s title was extinguished when the limitation period was completed.

rule.if: suit_seeks_recovery_of_math_property and possession_became_adverse_to_math and no_appointed_manager_when_adversity_began and limitation_period_completed

predicates.suit_seeks_recovery_of_math_property: A party brought a suit seeking recovery of property belonging to a math.
predicates.possession_became_adverse_to_math: A person possessed the math’s property on their own behalf in a manner adverse to the math.
predicates.no_appointed_manager_when_adversity_bega: The math had no legally appointed manager when the possession became adverse.
predicates.limitation_period_completed: The possession continued for the period required for limitation to run.

members.legal_issue: Appointment of a new manager does not create a fresh right to recover property whose title the math had already lost by adverse possession.
material_facts: Limitation began running against the math while it had no legally appointed manager.
The limitation period was completed and the math’s title was extinguished before a new manager was elected.
The new manager later sought recovery of the property on behalf of the math.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 144 read with section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908, once adverse possession extinguishes the math’s title, the rights of its beneficiaries in the property are also extinguished. A later manager acquires no right to recover property that no longer belongs to the math. The Court relied on the principles concerning the math’s ownership and capacity to sue discussed in Vidya Varuthi Thirtha v. Balusami Ayyar and The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Srirur Mutt.
members.conclusion: The new manager’s appointment did not give the math or the manager a new right to recover the property or a fresh starting point for limitation.

predicates.suit_seeks_recovery_of_math_property: A party brought a suit seeking recovery of property belonging to a math.
predicates.limitation_period_completed_before_new_m: The period required for limitation to run was completed before a new manager was appointed.

members.legal_issue: An initial police report and a further-investigation report are both considered in deciding whether to take cognizance, even when they reach different conclusions.
material_facts: The police initially filed a report alleging that the accused had committed offences.
After further investigation, the police filed a report recommending that proceedings against the accused be dropped.
The Magistrate had not yet decided whether to take cognizance on the reports.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 173(2) and 173(8) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an initial report and a further report are forwarded to the Magistrate. Under Section 190(1)(b), the Magistrate decides whether to take cognizance on a police report. Abhinandan Jha v. Dinesh Mishra and Rupan Deol Bajaj v. Kanwar Pal Singh Gill establish that the Magistrate may take cognizance despite a police recommendation to the contrary and must exercise judicial discretion.
members.conclusion: Both the initial report and the further report are police reports to be considered by the Magistrate, who must decide whether to take cognizance after applying judicial mind to them.

predicates.criminal_case_with_initial_and_further_r: The matter is a criminal proceeding in which the police have submitted an initial report and a report after further investigation.
predicates.reports_reach_conflicting_conclusions: The initial report alleges that a person committed an offence, while the further report concludes that the person did not commit it.

members.legal_issue: Separate first information reports and investigations may proceed for the same incident when they present different versions of events.
material_facts: Two reports concerned the same dacoity and killing but gave materially different accounts of who committed the offences.
The complainant in one report was himself facing trial in connection with the incident described in the other report.
members.legal_principle: The sameness test applies to multiple reports concerning one incident; separate reports are permissible where they set out different versions, allowing cross-cases or counter-cases. The Court relied on Ram Lal Narang v. State (Delhi Admn.), Sudhir v. State of M.P., T.T. Antony v. State of Kerala, Upkar Singh v. Ved Prakash, and Babubhai v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The complainant’s pending trial and the fact that both reports concerned the same incident did not bar proceedings based on the other report, because the reports presented different versions.

predicates.multiple_report_proceeding: The matter concerns multiple reports and investigations arising from one incident.
predicates.same_incident: The reports concern the same incident.
predicates.different_versions: The reports give materially different accounts of the events or the persons responsible.

members.legal_issue: A Hindu male, his wife, and his unmarried daughter can constitute a Hindu undivided family for income-tax purposes despite the absence of an antecedent history of jointness.
material_facts: The assessee's family consisted of himself, his wife, and an unmarried daughter, with no son.
The Department argued that the absence of an earlier joint family or of more than one male prevented the family from being a Hindu undivided family.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(9), 3, and 55 of the Income-tax Act, 1922 treat a Hindu undivided family, rather than a coparcenary, as a taxable unit. The undefined statutory expression is understood according to Hindu law. A joint Hindu family may include a single male, his wife, and his unmarried daughter; the presumption is that a Hindu family is joint unless division is proved. The Court relied on Gowli Buddanna v. Commissioner of Income-tax and N. V. Narendranath v. Commissioner of Wealth-tax.
