members.conclusion: The assessee, his wife, and his unmarried daughter constituted a Hindu undivided family; neither a prior history of jointness nor a second male member was necessary.

predicates.income_tax_assessment: The proceeding concerns the classification of income for income-tax assessment.
predicates.single_hindu_male_with_wife_and_unmarrie: A Hindu male's family consists of him, his wife, and his unmarried daughter, without another male member.
predicates.no_antecedent_jointness: The family has no established history of jointness before the relevant dispute.

members.legal_issue: A Hindu family consisting of one male member, his wife, and his daughters may qualify as a Hindu Undivided Family for wealth-tax assessment.
material_facts: At the relevant time, the assessee’s family consisted of him, his wife, and two minor daughters, with no other male member.
He filed wealth-tax returns claiming assessment as a Hindu Undivided Family.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Wealth Tax Act treats a Hindu Undivided Family, rather than only a Hindu coparcenary, as an assessable entity. The expression is understood in the sense of a Hindu joint family under Hindu personal law. A joint family includes its members’ wives and unmarried daughters and may consist of a single male member with those female family members. Kalyanji Vithaldas v. Commissioner of Income Tax supports treating the statutory expression as wider than a coparcenary.
members.conclusion: The family could be assessed as a Hindu Undivided Family even though it had only one male member.

predicates.wealth_tax_assessment: The proceeding determines the status in which property is assessed to wealth tax.
predicates.family_has_one_male_member: The family has one male member and no other male member.
predicates.family_includes_wife_or_unmarried_daught: The family includes the male member’s wife or unmarried daughters.

members.legal_issue: A landlord cannot recover a residential tenancy on the ground of non-residence when a member of the tenant’s family continues to reside in the premises during the relevant period.
material_facts: The premises had been let for residential use.
The tenant moved abroad and did not return, but his mother, brother and sister continued to reside in the premises, including throughout the six months before the eviction application.
The relatives had lived in the premises with the tenant, and the Rent Controller found that they continued residing there when the eviction action was brought.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1)(d) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 requires proof that the premises were let for residential use, that the tenant ceased to reside there, and that no member of the tenant’s family resided there for six months immediately before the application. The provision focuses on whether the family actually resides in the premises, not solely on the tenant’s physical presence; it permits recovery only when the premises have been completely vacated by the tenant and family. The court also relied on the broad construction of family, supported by section 2(1)(i)(iii), as amended by Act 18 of 1976, and Price v. Gould, G.V. Shukla v. Shri Prabhu Ram Sukhram Dass Ojha, Govind Dass v. Kuldip Singh, and Hira Lal v. Banarsi Dass.
members.conclusion: The landlord failed to establish the requirements for eviction on the non-residence ground. The appeal was allowed, the eviction order was set aside, and the eviction action was dismissed.

rule.if: nonresidence_eviction_proceeding and residential_premises and tenant_ceased_to_reside and family_member_resided_throughout_relevant_period

predicates.nonresidence_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking recovery of a residence on the ground that the tenant and the tenant’s family had ceased to reside there.
predicates.residential_premises: The premises were let for use as a residence.
predicates.tenant_ceased_to_reside: The tenant stopped residing in the premises.
predicates.family_member_resided_throughout_relevan: At least one member of the tenant’s family continued to reside in the premises throughout the period immediately preceding the eviction application.

members.legal_issue: A tenant is not deemed to have vacated a rented building merely because other people reside there alongside the tenant or the tenant’s family; the relevant occupation must be by a non-family member in that person’s own right.
material_facts: The inspection report recorded that the original tenant’s son and family, the tenant’s brother’s family, and other relatives were residing in the premises.
The report did not establish that a person outside the tenant’s family had been given possession to occupy the premises in that person’s own right.
The vacancy finding treated the presence of the other occupants as sufficient to establish deemed vacancy.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(1)(b) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 applies where the tenant has allowed a person who is not a member of the tenant’s family to occupy the building in that person’s own right. In Harish Tandon v. Addl. District Magistrate, Allahabad, the Court held that mere residence by another person alongside the tenant or the tenant’s family does not satisfy that requirement; the significant words are “allowed” and “occupy.”
members.conclusion: The premises were not deemed vacant on the facts recorded in the inspection report, and the vacancy finding was contrary to the governing interpretation of the Act.

predicates.rent_control_vacancy_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a rented building is vacant because of the occupants’ use of it.
predicates.tenant_or_tenant_family_resides_in_premi: The tenant or members of the tenant’s family reside in the premises.
predicates.other_occupants_reside_alongside_tenant_: Other people reside in the premises alongside the tenant or the tenant’s family.
predicates.no_nonfamily_occupies_in_own_right: No person outside the tenant’s family has been given possession to occupy the premises in that person’s own right.
predicates.premises_not_deemed_vacant: The presence of the other occupants does not make the premises deemed vacant.

members.legal_issue: A judge should recuse from a pending appeal when disclosed facts give rise to a reasonable, non-fanciful apprehension that the hearing may not be fair, even without proof that the judge’s decision would actually be influenced.
material_facts: A party sought the recusal of the judge hearing its appeal after presenting documents indicating that the judge had purchased a flat in which a respondent had resided.
The judge had been informed of the alleged connection and the supporting documents.

The Supreme Court found that the disclosed circumstances could give rise to a reasonable apprehension that the trial might not be fair, without finding that the judge’s decision would actually have been influenced.
members.legal_principle: Judges must decide impartially, free from personal bias or prejudice, and justice must not only be done but be seen to be done. A judge should recuse where established facts create a reasonable, rather than fanciful, apprehension that the hearing may not be fair; proof of actual influence on the outcome is not required.
members.conclusion: The recusal request was not unjustified, and the judge should have declined to hear the appeal in keeping with the highest traditions of the judiciary.

predicates.appeal_pending_before_judge: An appeal was pending for hearing before the judge.
predicates.party_requests_recusal: A party asked the judge to withdraw from hearing the appeal.
predicates.judge_owned_property_occupied_by_litigan: The judge owned property in which a person involved in the case had resided.

members.legal_issue: A request for a judge to recuse, supported by material giving rise to a reasonable apprehension of unfairness, does not by itself warrant contempt proceedings.
material_facts: The appellant requested recusal and supported the request with documents concerning the judge’s purchase of property in which a respondent had resided.
The single judge suggested that contempt proceedings be initiated against the appellant and some of its lawyers.
The Supreme Court found no cause to initiate contempt proceedings for making the recusal request.
members.legal_principle: Contempt jurisdiction is special and must be exercised cautiously, sparingly, and with restraint. It is to protect the administration of justice, not to punish fair comment or trivial reflections; the cited authorities include Jaswant Singh v. Virender Singh, Queen v. Grey, and the authority reported at 1974 (1) SCC 374. The Court described substantial and mala fide interference with fearless judicial action as the relevant concern.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to initiate contempt proceedings against the appellant or its lawyers on the basis of the recusal request.

predicates.contempt_reference_based_on_recusal_requ: A judge referred a party or its lawyers for contempt because they requested the judge’s recusal.
predicates.recusal_request_supported_by_material: The party supported its recusal request with material concerning circumstances relevant to the judge’s impartiality.
predicates.no_substantial_malicious_interference: The conduct did not amount to substantial and malicious interference with the administration of justice.

members.legal_issue: An eyewitness account is not rendered artificial or unreliable solely because it recounts the incident and the assailants’ individual acts with precision.
material_facts: The appellants challenged the eyewitnesses’ detailed accounts, including their descriptions of individual assailants’ acts, because the incident occurred at night.
The incident occurred on a moonlit night, and the trial court had heard the witnesses’ accounts and believed them.
The witnesses described the sequence and details of an exceptional violent incident, and their answers were elicited through questions in examination-in-chief.
members.legal_principle: Witness testimony must be assessed pragmatically and from broad angles, not by rigid or exacting standards. An account may be detailed if the incident made a strong impression on the witness, and precision alone does not establish tutoring or artificiality. The court also considered the trial court’s opportunity to hear the witnesses and the possibility that the order of detail reflected the examiner’s questions. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this principle.
members.conclusion: The eyewitness testimony should not be rejected as artificial merely because it was precise; the trial and appellate courts were justified in accepting it.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused brought a criminal appeal challenging their conviction.
predicates.eyewitness_account_was_precise: An eyewitness gave a detailed account of the incident and the individual acts of the assailants.
predicates.trial_court_had_credited_account: The trial court heard the eyewitness account and accepted it.

members.legal_issue: A detailed account of an assault is not inherently unreliable when the witnesses had a clear opportunity to observe it and the event could leave a strong impression on their memory.
material_facts: The witnesses observed the assault from close range while an electric bulb was burning.
The assault was gruesome and involved repeated blows with weapons.
The accused were known to the informant, who named them in the report.
members.legal_principle: The evidentiary value of a detailed account depends on the witness’s opportunity to observe and the circumstances affecting recollection; a graphic description is not by itself evidence of tutoring or fabrication. The Court considered the observations in Shival Sahabrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra distinguishable on the facts.
members.conclusion: The witnesses’ detailed description of the injuries and the parts of the bodies struck did not make their evidence suspect.

predicates.eyewitness_account_is_detailed: An eyewitness gives a detailed description of the event, including the injuries or manner of assault.
predicates.clear_observation_conditions: The witness had a clear opportunity to observe, such as close proximity, adequate light, or familiarity with the persons involved.
predicates.event_striking_to_memory: The event was sufficiently striking or serious to leave a strong impression on the witness.

members.legal_issue: Income received by an administrator while a testamentary estate is still being administered is not received on behalf of residuary beneficiaries merely because they are entitled to the eventual residue.
material_facts: The will directed that specified legacies be paid from savings from the estate’s income and that the residue go to the testator’s five sons.
The administrator was appointed while administration of the estate remained incomplete.
During administration, the administrator could apply income to different legacies or estate expenses; the sons were entitled to the residue only after it was ascertained.
The administrator claimed that the income was specifically receivable on behalf of the sons, whose shares were fixed.
members.legal_principle: Section 41 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 applies only when a covered person receives income on behalf of another person; being expressly named in the section does not dispense with that condition. Until the residue is ascertained, estate income remains available as a mixed fund for administration, and residuary beneficiaries do not have an interest in that income as their own. The Court relied on V. M. Raghavalu Naidu v. Commissioner of Income-tax and Excess Profits Tax, R. v. Income-tax Special Commissioners (Dr. Barnardo’s Homes), Lord Sudeley v. Attorney-General, Maria Celeste Samaritan Society of the London Hospital v. Commissioner of Inland Revenue, and Corbett v. Commissioner of Inland Revenue; it distinguished In re Cunliffe-Owen Mountain v. Inland Revenue Commissioners. The Court noted that, where section 41 did not apply, the administrator was assessable under sections 3 and 4 of the Act.
members.conclusion: The administrator received the income on behalf of the estate in the course of administration, not on behalf of the sons. Section 41 therefore did not apply, and assessment of the administrator as an individual rather than separately on behalf of the beneficiaries was in accordance with law.

rule.if: estate_income_tax_assessment and estate_administration_incomplete and administrator_controls_income_for_estate_purposes and beneficiaries_entitled_only_to_residue

predicates.estate_income_tax_assessment: An income-tax assessment concerns income received by a person administering a deceased person’s estate.
predicates.estate_administration_incomplete: The administration of the estate has not been completed and the residue has not yet been ascertained.
predicates.administrator_controls_income_for_estate: The administrator may apply estate income to legacies or expenses in carrying out the administration.
predicates.beneficiaries_entitled_only_to_residue: The beneficiaries are entitled to the estate’s residue after administration rather than to the income as it is received.

members.legal_issue: Income from a deceased person's estate remains assessable in the hands of the person administering it until the estate has been distributed to the beneficiaries according to their interests.
material_facts: The will left the deceased's property to two beneficiaries and named no executor; the deceased's son took charge of and administered the estate.
The estate was not distributed to the beneficiaries during the assessment years in dispute, and the Tribunal found that nothing was distributed until a later date.
The estate included movable and immovable property requiring division and a share in a firm whose devolution to the beneficiaries had not been shown.
The income from the estate had previously been assessed in the hands of the person administering it.
members.legal_principle: Under section 168(1) and (3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, the estate's income is assessed in the hands of the executor, and that assessment continues for the period up to distribution to the beneficiaries according to their interests; section 168's explanation includes an administrator or other person administering the estate. Section 168(3) reflects the pre-existing law described in Raghavalu Naidu & Sons v. C.I.T.: executors must administer the estate, satisfy its obligations, ascertain the residue, and hand it over; a residuary beneficiary's interest in the residue does not become absolute until it is ascertained and distribution or appropriation occurs. The Court also referred to Lord Sudeley v. Attorney-General, Barnardo's Homes v. Special Income Tax Commissioners, Attenborough v. Solomon, C.I.T. v. Bakshi Sampuran Singh, and C.I.T. v. Ghosh.
members.conclusion: The administration had not been completed during the relevant years, so the income was assessable in the hands of the person administering the estate, not as the beneficiaries' income. The appeals were allowed and the question was answered in favour of the assessee.

predicates.income_tax_estate_income_proceeding: The proceeding concerned income-tax assessment of income arising from a deceased person's estate.
predicates.administrator_administered_estate: A person took charge of and administered the deceased person's estate.
predicates.estate_not_distributed: The estate had not been distributed to the beneficiaries according to their interests during the period at issue.
predicates.estate_income_assessed_to_administrator: The income from the estate is assessed to the person administering it.

members.legal_issue: The national legislature may authorize the central government to declare a proposed route through undeveloped land as a national highway.
material_facts: The challenged declarations designated proposed highway stretches that included land without an existing road or highway.
The declarations were made under a statute empowering the central government to declare a highway as a national highway, and the proposed land acquisition was for building the highway.
members.legal_principle: Article 246 and Entry 23 of List I empower Parliament to legislate on national highways and matters connected with them. Entries must be construed broadly, and incidental overlap with a State List subject does not invalidate a law whose substance falls within a Union List entry. Article 248 also supports Parliament’s power over matters not enumerated in the State or Concurrent Lists. Sections 2(2) and 3A of the National Highways Act, 1956 permit declaration of a highway and acquisition of “any land” for its construction, including undeveloped land. The Court relied on K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka on legislative competence and the doctrine of pith and substance, and Synthetics and Chemicals Ltd. v. State of U.P. on construing federal constitutional provisions broadly.
members.conclusion: The declarations were within the legislative authority of Parliament and the statutory power of the central government; the power was not limited to existing roads or highways.

predicates.challenge_to_national_highway_declaratio: A proceeding challenges a declaration designating a proposed route as a national highway.
predicates.parliament_has_authority_over_national_h: The national legislature has authority to make laws concerning national highways and matters connected with them.
predicates.proposed_route_crosses_land_without_an_e: The proposed highway route crosses land on which no road or highway previously existed.

members.legal_issue: The central government has executive authority to declare and construct a national highway over a route that is not an existing road.
material_facts: The challenged declarations were issued by the central government for proposed highway stretches that included undeveloped land.
The statutory provision authorizing the central government to declare highways as national highways had not itself been challenged as unconstitutional.
members.legal_principle: Article 257 concerns Union-State administrative relations and does not restrict the Union’s exercise of executive power to carry out a valid law on national highways. The proviso to Article 257(2) confirms that the provision does not restrict Parliament’s power to declare highways to be national highways or the Union’s power concerning them. Sections 2(2) and 5 of the National Highways Act, 1956 support the central government’s authority to declare and develop national highways. The Court’s conclusion followed its construction of Entry 23 of List I and Article 246.
members.conclusion: The challenge based on the asserted absence of Union executive power failed; the central government could declare and construct a new national highway, including over undeveloped land.

predicates.challenge_to_union_executive_authority: A proceeding challenges the central government's executive authority to act concerning a proposed national highway.
predicates.valid_law_authorizes_central_highway_act: A valid law authorizes the central government to declare and develop national highways.
predicates.proposed_highway_is_not_an_existing_road: The proposed national highway would be built on a route that was not already a road or highway.

members.legal_issue: A suit may proceed without the legal representatives of a deceased joint lessee where they are not necessary to determine the relief sought.
material_facts: One person sued as a representative of a joint lessee had died before the suit began, and that person’s legal representatives were not added to the record.
The claim for accounts of rents was directed only against the defendant who effectively controlled the building and received its rents.
The omitted person and representatives had not taken an active role concerning the building, and the requested declaration could be granted in their absence.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the necessary-party principle by considering the nature of the relief and whether it could be granted in the absence of the omitted representatives. It noted the concession made at trial that the suit could not be dismissed merely for this non-joinder and concluded that the omitted representatives were not necessary parties. No earlier case or specific statutory provision was relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The suit could not be dismissed for non-joinder because the absent legal representatives were not necessary parties to the relief sought.

predicates.civil_suit_proceeding: The matter is a civil suit seeking relief concerning property or its income.
predicates.deceased_joint_lessee_representatives_om: The legal representatives of a deceased joint lessee have not been joined to the suit.
predicates.omitted_representatives_not_controlling_: The omitted representatives do not effectively control the property or the dispute about the relief sought.
predicates.relief_determinable_without_them: The court can determine and grant the requested relief without the omitted representatives.
predicates.suit_not_dismissed_for_nonjoinder: The suit is not dismissed solely because those representatives were not joined.

members.legal_issue: A notice to one joint tenant is sufficient to terminate a joint tenancy, and a suit against the surviving joint tenant is not defective for failing to join the deceased joint tenant’s legal representatives.
material_facts: The lease rights were assigned to two assignees expressly as joint tenants, and the lessor accepted the assignment.
One joint tenant died before the ejectment suit was filed.
The lessor gave notice to the surviving joint tenant, and the suit proceeded against that tenant.
members.legal_principle: Where a tenancy is joint, notice to one joint tenant is sufficient; on that basis, the suit against the surviving joint tenant was properly framed. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The notice to one joint tenant was sufficient, and the suit was not bad for non-joinder of the deceased tenant’s legal representatives.

rule.if: ejectment_suit and joint_tenancy and notice_served_on_one_joint_tenant and other_joint_tenant_deceased

predicates.ejectment_suit: The lessor brought a suit to recover possession from a tenant.
predicates.joint_tenancy: The tenancy rights were held jointly by the tenants.
predicates.notice_served_on_one_joint_tenant: The lessor gave termination notice to one of the joint tenants.
predicates.other_joint_tenant_deceased: The other joint tenant had died before the suit was filed.

members.legal_issue: Misconduct in a disciplinary enquiry is assessed on the balance of probabilities, with the degree of probability depending on the subject matter, rather than by the criminal standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The disciplinary enquiry concerned allegations that the employee was involved in a murder and related service misconduct.
The disciplinary record included evidence of prior hostility and a threat, the employee’s presence near the scene, and the presence of his tractor nearby.
The criminal court acquitted the employee, but the disciplinary enquiry applied a different standard of proof.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on Suresh Pathrella v. Oriental Bank of Commerce and Samar Bahadur Singh v. State of U.P. for the distinction between criminal and disciplinary standards of proof. It relied on M. Siddiq v. Suresh Das, including its discussion of Miller v. Minister of Pensions and Bater v. Bater, for the principle that probabilities may have different degrees depending on the subject matter.
members.conclusion: The disciplinary enquiry was not required to establish the allegations beyond reasonable doubt; the relevant standard was a preponderance of probabilities, whose degree depends on the subject matter.

predicates.disciplinary_proceeding: An employer conducted a disciplinary enquiry into an employee’s alleged misconduct.
predicates.misconduct_alleged: The employer alleged conduct that could constitute a breach of the employee’s service obligations.

members.legal_issue: Misconduct in a disciplinary inquiry is determined on the balance of probabilities using logically probative material, rather than the criminal standard of proof or strict criminal-trial evidence rules.
material_facts: The complainant did not support the charge in the disciplinary inquiry but acknowledged his signatures on the complaint and the pre-trap and trap records.
A shadow witness described the alleged demand and acceptance of money, its recovery, and related trap procedures; the investigating officer corroborated aspects of that account.
The employee maintained that the recovered money was repayment of a loan made to the complainant's brother-in-law, who testified in support of that explanation.
The inquiry officer considered the evidence and rejected the loan explanation, finding the misconduct proved.
members.legal_principle: A disciplinary charge is proved on a preponderance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt. Strict rules of evidence do not apply; logically probative material, including hearsay with reasonable nexus and credibility, may be considered. The inquiry must nevertheless be fair and objective, and its finding must rest on relevant material rather than conjecture or suspicion. The Court relied on State of Haryana v. Rattan Singh and explained that the ratio in Union of India v. Gyan Chand Chattar concerns relevant material and compliance with natural justice, not a requirement to prove corruption beyond reasonable doubt.
members.conclusion: The misconduct finding was sustainable on the disciplinary inquiry evidence, which the inquiry officer assessed on the applicable standard of proof.

predicates.disciplinary_inquiry: An employer held an inquiry to decide whether an employee committed misconduct.
predicates.relevant_evidence_supports_misconduct_on: The inquiry record contains material with a reasonable connection to the charge that makes misconduct more likely than not.
predicates.inquiry_is_fair: The inquiry was conducted objectively with observance of natural justice.

members.legal_issue: An acquittal in a criminal trial, including one based on benefit of doubt or witnesses turning hostile, does not by itself bar disciplinary proceedings or require reinstatement.
material_facts: The employee was acquitted of murder after the criminal court found the sole alleged eyewitness unreliable and several prosecution witnesses had turned hostile.
The disciplinary enquiry proceeded on a different evidentiary standard and addressed service-rule violations and the effect of the employee’s conduct on the police force.
The disciplinary authority relied on the criminal acquittal as an acquittal on benefit of doubt, not as a determination that eliminated the disciplinary case.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on Southern Railway Officers Association v. Union of India and Inspector General of Police v. S. Samuthiram. In discussing the expression “honourable acquittal,” it referred to RBI v. Bhopal Singh Panchal, R.P. Kapur v. Union of India, State of Assam v. Raghava Rajgopalachari and Robert Stuart Wauchope v. Emperor. It reiterated that criminal and disciplinary proceedings have different standards of proof and that the expression “honourable acquittal” is not found in the penal statutes or procedural code.
members.conclusion: The criminal acquittal did not conclude the disciplinary enquiry or require reinstatement; the two proceedings could reach different outcomes because they apply different standards and address different matters.

rule.if: disciplinary_proceeding and criminal_acquittal and (acquittal_based_on_benefit_of_doubt or prosecution_witnesses_turned_hostile)

predicates.disciplinary_proceeding: An employer conducted a disciplinary enquiry into the employee’s conduct.
predicates.criminal_acquittal: A criminal court acquitted the employee of the alleged offence.
predicates.acquittal_based_on_benefit_of_doubt: The criminal court acquitted the employee because the prosecution did not establish guilt to the required criminal standard.
predicates.prosecution_witnesses_turned_hostile: One or more prosecution witnesses withdrew or resiled from their earlier statements during the criminal trial.

members.legal_issue: An acquittal in a criminal trial does not prevent an employer from deciding a related charge of employee misconduct in a disciplinary proceeding.
material_facts: The employee was acquitted in a criminal prosecution arising from an alleged bribe transaction because the prosecution had not proved the charge beyond reasonable doubt.
A separate disciplinary inquiry considered the alleged transaction and found misconduct proved on the inquiry evidence.
The disciplinary authority imposed compulsory retirement, and the administrative tribunal upheld that penalty.
members.legal_principle: Criminal and disciplinary proceedings have different purposes, standards of proof, and rules of procedure. An acquittal does not preclude disciplinary action, and the disciplinary authority is not bound by the criminal court's decision. The Court relied on Karnataka Power Transmission Corporation Ltd. v. C. Nagaraju, State of Haryana v. Rattan Singh, and the principles reiterated in Commissioner of Police, Delhi v. Narender Singh.
members.conclusion: The criminal acquittal did not bar the disciplinary proceeding or invalidate its finding of misconduct.

predicates.disciplinary_misconduct_proceeding: An employer conducted a proceeding to determine whether an employee's conduct breached employment rules.
predicates.related_criminal_acquittal: A criminal court acquitted the employee of charges arising from the same or related alleged conduct.

members.legal_issue: Compensation calculated by capitalizing the yield from trees should use an appropriate multiplier that accounts for the income, duration, and risks of that yield.
material_facts: The claimants sought compensation for damage caused by cutting trees while the land remained with them.
The High Court calculated compensation using the yield from the trees and applied an 18-year multiplier.
members.legal_principle: Capitalization converts expected net income into present value and must take account of the income’s duration, the life span and risks of the trees, and the return available from safe investments. Where compensation is based on tree or plantation yield, the land must not be valued separately in a way that counts its value twice, and the appropriate multiplier is 8 years. The Court relied on State of Haryana v. Gurcharan Singh, Union of India v. Shanti Devi, and Special Land Acquisition Officer, Davangere v. P. Veerabhadarappa.
members.conclusion: The 18-year multiplier was erroneous; when compensation is calculated from the yield of trees or plantations, an 8-year multiplier is appropriate.

predicates.tree_cutting_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation for damage caused by cutting trees.
predicates.compensation_based_on_tree_yield: The compensation is calculated by capitalizing the income produced by the trees.
predicates.land_remains_with_owner: The land remains with its owner rather than being acquired.

members.legal_issue: The appropriate method for valuing an orchard is to capitalize its net income using a multiplier suited to the nature and expected yielding life of its trees and the other circumstances.
material_facts: Compensation was assessed for land containing coconut and orange topes acquired for a public project.
The valuation officer capitalized the topes’ net income using a 20-year purchase multiplier, after finding that the fruit-bearing trees would yield for more than 20 years.
The reference court increased the estimated yield and produce prices but retained the multiplier; the High Court considered the method fair.
The State challenged the multiplier, relying on an earlier decision that had used a 10-year purchase multiplier for a coconut garden.
members.legal_principle: The approved method for valuing orchards is to capitalize net income at a number of years’ purchase fixed with reference to the nature of the trees and other circumstances. The Court relied on Kompalli Nageshwara Rao v. Special Deputy Collector, Land Acquisition, which applied that approach, and Elias M. Cohen v. Secretary of State, which capitalized orchard income at 15 years’ purchase. It distinguished Shunmuga Velayuda Mudaliar v. Collector of Tanjore because that decision gave no reasoned principle for selecting 10 years’ purchase. The Court also noted that Rajammal v. Head Quarters Deputy Collector, Vellore had used 20 years’ annual rental for long-lived, productive mango trees.
members.conclusion: The Court held that capitalizing the net income at 20 years’ purchase was a fair and reasonable method in the circumstances, and dismissed the appeals.

predicates.land_acquisition_valuation_appeal: The matter was an appeal concerning compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.orchard_valued_by_net_income_capitalizat: The valuation officer assessed an orchard by capitalizing its net income.
predicates.trees_expected_to_yield_for_period_suppo: The valuation officer found that the trees were expected to yield for a period supporting the multiplier selected.

members.legal_issue: A written record of a Muslim gift of immovable property is not invalid merely because it is unregistered when the essential requirements of a valid gift are met.
material_facts: A donor’s written deed purported to gift immovable properties to his son.
The donee signed the deed, and the trial court found that the donor declared the gift, the donee accepted it, and possession was delivered to him.
The High Court set aside the trial court’s decree on the ground that the unregistered deed could not convey title.
The Supreme Court found that the deed recorded the donor’s declaration and that the three requirements of a valid gift were satisfied.
members.legal_principle: Under Muslim law, a valid gift requires a declaration by the donor, acceptance by or on behalf of the donee, and delivery of possession. Section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 preserves Muslim law and excludes the application of Section 123 to such gifts. A writing does not become a formal instrument of gift merely because the gift is recorded in writing; whether registration is required depends on the facts, and the distinction between a contemporaneous writing and a later record is not determinative. The Court approved Nasib Ali v. Wajed Ali and Md. Hesabuddin v. Md. Hesaruddin, and disapproved the contrary view in Inspector General of Registration and Stamps v. Tayyaba Begum. It also relied on Mohammad Abdul Ghani v. Fakhr Jahan Begam and Mahboob Sahab v. Syed Ismail. Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 therefore did not make this evidentiary writing ineffective.
members.conclusion: The unregistered writing did not invalidate the gift. The gift was complete and irrevocable, so the appeal was allowed and the trial court’s judgment and decree were restored.

rule.if: muslim_gift_validity_proceeding and written_gift_record and donor_declared_gift and donee_accepted_gift and possession_delivered

predicates.muslim_gift_validity_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the validity or effect of an inter vivos gift made under Muslim law.
predicates.written_gift_record: The donor’s declaration of the gift was recorded in writing.
predicates.donor_declared_gift: The donor declared an intention to give the property to the donee.
predicates.donee_accepted_gift: The donee expressly or impliedly accepted the gift.
predicates.possession_delivered: The donor delivered possession of the gifted property to the donee, actually or constructively.
predicates.unregistered_written_muslim_gift_effecti: The written gift remains effective despite being unregistered.

members.legal_issue: A written instrument recording a gift under Muhammadan law does not invariably require registration merely because it is written or contemporaneous with the gift.
material_facts: The dispute concerned an instrument executed in connection with an alleged gift of immovable property under Muhammadan law.

The lower courts treated the instrument as evidence of an earlier oral gift, while the High Court treated it as an instrument transferring the property in the present and therefore requiring registration.

The Supreme Court held that the nature and registration requirement of a written instrument depend on the circumstances, but did not need to determine registration in this case because the alleged gift was incomplete for want of possession.
members.legal_principle: Sections 123 and 129 of the Transfer of Property Act distinguish the general registration requirement for gifts of immovable property from the saving of Muhammadan law. Section 17 of the Registration Act does not apply categorically to every written Muhammadan gift. Applying Hafeeza Bibi v. Shaikh Farid, Nasib Ali v. Wajid Ali, and Mahboob Sahab v. Syed Ismail, the Court held that the character and registration requirement of the writing depend on the facts; the essential requirements of a valid Muhammadan gift must still be fulfilled.
members.conclusion: A written instrument relating to a Muhammadan gift is not invariably required to be registered; writing alone does not determine whether registration is required. The question of registration did not arise on these facts because the gift was incomplete for want of possession.

predicates.muhammadan_gift_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a gift made under Muhammadan law is valid.
predicates.gift_is_recorded_in_writing: The alleged gift is recorded in a written instrument.

members.legal_issue: An alienation by a widow is not justified by legal necessity when the transaction is made to implement a settlement and its consideration is not shown to meet legal necessity.
material_facts: The widow had obtained letters of administration subject to a restriction on dealing with the property without the required sanction.
The transfer document purported to implement the earlier settlement and did not purport to be founded on legal necessity.

Of the stated consideration, only a portion represented debts of the deceased; other identified items included document-execution expenses and funeral expenses, and the remaining items did not purport to meet legal necessity.
members.legal_principle: A widow’s alienation must be supported by legal necessity to bind the reversioner; amounts paid for purposes that do not constitute legal necessity do not establish that justification. The Court also considered the restriction attached to the letters of administration and the terms of the transfer document.
members.conclusion: The transfer was not justified by legal necessity and was not binding on the reversioner.

predicates.reversioner_suit_to_avoid_widow_alienati: A person claiming as reversioner sued to avoid an alienation made by a widow of the deceased holder’s property.
predicates.alienation_implemented_settlement: The transfer was made to carry out an earlier settlement between the widow and another person.
predicates.consideration_not_shown_to_meet_legal_ne: The stated payments were not shown to be for purposes that legally justified the widow’s alienation.

members.legal_issue: A sale of a widow’s share cannot be upheld on the asserted basis of legal necessity when the purchaser fails to prove that necessity.
material_facts: The widow executed a sale of her share in the house to the appellants.
The trial court found that the appellants had not proved that the sale was for legal necessity.
The High Court affirmed that finding, and the Supreme Court agreed with the concurrent findings.
members.legal_principle: The purchaser relying on a sale made by a widow had to establish that it was supported by legal necessity; the concurrent finding that this had not been proved was accepted. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The finding that the sale was not supported by legal necessity was affirmed.

predicates.appeal_from_partition_decree: The matter is an appeal from a decree in a suit seeking partition.
predicates.widow_sold_share: A widow transferred her share in the property by sale.
predicates.purchaser_failed_to_prove_legal_necessit: The purchaser did not prove that the sale was made for legal necessity.

members.legal_issue: A statutory proceeding to frame a scheme for the management of a temple is an exhaustive inquiry rather than a summary proceeding.
material_facts: The Board framed a scheme for the temple under the statutory provision governing temple schemes.
The statutory scheme made the Board’s order final subject to a suit to modify or set it aside, and the court proceeding was to be tried in the manner of an ordinary civil suit.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 57(1) and 57(3) of the Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1927, the Board could settle a scheme, and an interested person could bring a suit to modify or set aside its order. The court proceeding was to be tried as an ordinary suit under the Civil Procedure Code. The Court relied on (Sri Mahant) Sitaram Dass Bavaji v. Madras Religious Endowment Board, Madras, and Arikapudi Balakotayya v. Yadlapalli Nagayya.
members.conclusion: The Board’s power to frame a scheme was not summary; the statutory process provided for an exhaustive inquiry by the Board and, if challenged, by the court.

predicates.temple_scheme_proceeding: An authority considers framing a scheme for the management of a temple.
predicates.board_conducts_inquiry: The authority examines matters relevant to framing the temple-management scheme.
predicates.court_challenge_available: An affected person can challenge the authority’s scheme order in court, where the matter is tried as an ordinary suit.

members.legal_issue: A proceeding determining disputed institutional status or hereditary trusteeship must provide a judicial and sufficiently elaborate inquiry rather than a summary inquiry.
material_facts: The respondents contested the institution's public character and claimed hereditary trusteeship.

The appointment authority conducted only a summary inquiry, in which the affected persons did not receive a full opportunity to present their case and evidence was not recorded in the manner required for an elaborate adjudication.
The statutory scheme provided a separate proceeding for determining the disputed status and an appeal from its determination.
members.legal_principle: Section 41 provides for adjudication of disputes about whether an institution is public and whether a trustee is hereditary. Under section 44, decisions in that proceeding are appealable. Section 74 and Rule 43 require the civil-procedure and evidence rules to be followed as far as practicable in proceedings of the relevant adjudicative character. By contrast, an inquiry connected with section 27 is summary and does not provide the same opportunity to present the entire case. The Court relied on Ramakrishna Padhy v. Ramesh Chandra Das.
members.conclusion: A summary inquiry associated with trustee appointment is not a substitute for the judicial and elaborate inquiry required to determine the disputed status.

predicates.status_determination_proceeding: An authority is conducting a proceeding to determine the public character of an institution or the existence of hereditary trustees.
predicates.affected_persons_contest_relevant_status: People affected by the determination dispute the institution's character or the trustees' status.

members.legal_issue: A party commits contempt by completing a restrained transfer of property after a court order forbids further allotments, even when an agreement of sale was made before the order.
material_facts: The Court had ordered that no further allotments of flats be made while the proceedings were pending.
The respondent claimed that an agreement of sale for the flats had been entered into before the order; the Court assumed the agreement was genuine without deciding that question.
After the order, the respondent delivered possession of the flats to third parties and registered sale deeds in their favour.
The respondent did not seek clarification of the order before proceeding with delivery of possession and registration.
members.legal_principle: An order must be interpreted reasonably and in its context. Here, the term “allotment” covered the effective transfer of the flats by delivery of possession and registration of sale deeds; a party could not adopt a restrictive interpretation that rendered the order nugatory, and should have sought clarification if genuinely in doubt. The Court held the respondent guilty of contempt and imposed punishment under Section 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The respondent violated the order and was guilty of contempt. In context, the prohibition on further allotments covered making over the flats, including delivery of possession and registration of sale deeds; it was not confined to entering into agreements of sale.

rule.if: contempt_proceeding and order_barred_further_transfers and possession_delivered_after_order and sale_deeds_registered_after_order

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The proceeding asked the court to determine whether a party had disobeyed a court order.
predicates.order_barred_further_transfers: The court had ordered a party not to make further transfers of the relevant property.
predicates.possession_delivered_after_order: The party delivered possession of the property to third parties after the order was made.
predicates.sale_deeds_registered_after_order: The party registered sale deeds transferring the property to third parties after the order was made.

members.legal_issue: A company and responsible directors or agents commit contempt when, with knowledge of a restraint on disposal, they deliberately complete a property transfer in defiance of that restraint.
material_facts: The company appeared in the proceedings and knew of the order restraining disposal of its capital assets without permission.
The transfer was completed by registration after the order.
The purported authority for the sale predated the asserted change in the company’s status and was not shown to have been renewed through a proper later decision.

The person who registered the conveyance had resigned as a director, but the company and its responsible directors or agents did not take steps to prevent registration or inform the Court of the earlier document.
The Court found the conduct to be a deliberate device to complete the transfer despite the restraint.
members.legal_principle: A party with knowledge of a court order must obey it; deliberate disobedience of the restraint may be punished as contempt. The Court found that the company and the identified directors or agents knowingly participated in completing the transfer after the order.
members.conclusion: The company and the responsible directors or agents were found guilty of violating the order and were fined.

predicates.contempt_proceeding_for_disobeying_asset: The proceeding alleges disobedience of a court order restraining disposal of a company’s assets.
predicates.company_knew_of_restraint: The company was a party to the relevant proceedings or otherwise had knowledge of the restraint.
predicates.transfer_registered_after_restraint: The property transfer was completed by registration after the restraint was made.
predicates.responsible_company_actors_deliberately_: Directors or agents responsible for the company’s conduct enabled the post-restraint registration and did not take steps to prevent it despite the company’s knowledge.

members.legal_issue: A later amendment removing a publication requirement does not retrospectively validate earlier notifications that failed to comply with that requirement when the amendment does not operate retrospectively.
material_facts: A later amendment removed the requirement to publish notifications in newspaper issues.
The amendment made certain changes to another subsection retrospectively but did not make the change removing the newspaper-publication requirement retrospective.
The notification at issue had not been shown to satisfy the newspaper-publication requirement applicable when it was issued.
members.legal_principle: The Bihar Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1954 amended section 3(2) to remove the newspaper-publication requirement but did not make that amendment retrospective, although it expressly made specified amendments to section 3(3) retrospective. The Court inferred that the earlier publication requirement remained material to notifications issued before the amendment and that earlier failures to comply were not retrospectively cured.
members.conclusion: The amendment did not retrospectively make the noncompliant notification effective.

rule.if: estate_vesting_proceeding and earlier_notification_noncompliant and later_amendment_removed_publication_requirement and amendment_not_made_retroactive

predicates.estate_vesting_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a notification caused an estate to vest in the State.
predicates.earlier_notification_noncompliant: The notification did not satisfy a publication requirement that applied when it was issued.
predicates.later_amendment_removed_publication_requ: A later amendment removed the publication requirement that had applied to the notification.
predicates.amendment_not_made_retroactive: The amendment did not state that the removal of the publication requirement applied retrospectively.
predicates.earlier_notification_remains_ineffective: The earlier notification is not made effective by the later amendment.

members.legal_issue: An amendment that adds notifications to a statutory saving clause does not save notifications issued under a repealed enactment for the period before the amendment came into force when the amendment has no retrospective effect.
material_facts: The municipal enactment was repealed and replaced before the amendment was enacted.
The original saving clause did not expressly list notifications among the saved matters.
A later amendment added notifications to the saving clause and came into force after publication in the official gazette.
The amendment did not receive retrospective operation.
members.legal_principle: The court held that the 1958 amending Act came into force upon publication and was not given retrospective operation. Its addition of notifications to the saving clause therefore could not itself save notifications for the earlier period. The court relied on no earlier cases for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The amendment did not retrospectively save the earlier notification; its continued force was instead supported by the general saving rule in the Assam General Clauses Act.

rule.if: earlier_notification_under_repealed_law and original_saving_clause_omitted_notifications and later_amendment_added_notifications and amendment_not_retrospective

predicates.earlier_notification_under_repealed_law: The government had issued a notification under an enactment before that enactment was repealed.
predicates.original_saving_clause_omitted_notificat: The original saving clause did not expressly include notifications among the matters preserved on repeal.
predicates.later_amendment_added_notifications: A later amendment added notifications to the saving clause.
predicates.amendment_not_retrospective: The amendment was not given effect for a period before it came into force.

members.legal_issue: A territorial superior court has supervisory jurisdiction over tribunals exercising authority within its territory.
material_facts: The Rent Controller and District Judge exercised jurisdiction under the rent law within the territories covered by the Court of the Judicial Commissioner.
The appeal challenged that court’s authority to supervise those bodies.
members.legal_principle: Article 227(1), read with Article 241, confers supervisory power over courts and tribunals functioning within the relevant territory. The words “in relation to which” qualify “territories,” not “courts and tribunals.”
members.conclusion: The Rent Controller and District Judge were tribunals within the meaning of Article 227, and Article 227(1), read with Article 241, conferred supervisory jurisdiction over them because they exercised authority within the court’s territory.

predicates.supervision_scope_dispute: The proceeding disputed whether a territorial superior court could supervise a tribunal.
predicates.local_tribunal_exercised_authority: A tribunal exercised adjudicative authority within the territory in question.
predicates.supervisory_court_covers_territory: The superior court’s jurisdiction extended throughout the territory where the tribunal exercised authority.

members.legal_issue: A subordinate tribunal must comply with directions issued by a superior court exercising supervisory jurisdiction.
material_facts: The High Court had set aside the tribunal’s earlier decision and remitted the matter with directions for fresh consideration.
The tribunal treated the directions as observations and reaffirmed its earlier result without complying with them.
The Supreme Court held that the tribunal was subject to the High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction and was bound to obey its directions.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution, judgments and orders of a High Court bind inferior courts and tribunals subject to its supervisory jurisdiction. The Court relied on Bhopal Sugar Industries Limited v. Income-tax Officer, Bhopal, which held that refusal to carry out a superior adjudicatory body’s clear directions amounts to a denial of justice and undermines the hierarchy of courts. The Court also compared this duty to the obedience owed to Supreme Court orders under Article 142.
members.conclusion: The tribunal was bound to comply with the High Court’s directions, and its refusal to do so was improper.

predicates.subordinate_tribunal: The decision-maker is a tribunal subject to a superior court’s supervisory jurisdiction.
predicates.superior_court_issued_case_directions: A superior court issued directions governing the further determination of the same matter.
predicates.tribunal_refused_to_comply: The tribunal declined to follow those directions when reconsidering the matter.

members.legal_issue: State rulemaking authority over minor minerals does not extend to prohibiting the interstate movement of minerals that have already been lawfully excavated.
material_facts: The challenged rules prohibited sand from being transported beyond the State’s borders, including sand excavated under valid leases and accompanied by authorized transport documents.
The rules applied after excavation and restricted the movement or sale of the excavated sand outside the State.
The appeals challenged the High Court’s decision striking down the rules.
members.legal_principle: Sections 15(1) and 15(1A) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 authorize rules concerning the grant and regulation of mineral concessions, but do not authorize control over minor minerals after excavation, including their sale or movement outside the State. Section 23-C authorizes rules to prevent illegal mining, transportation and storage; read in light of its object, it does not authorize restrictions on transporting legally excavated minerals. M.P.P. Kavery Chetty v. State of Tamil Nadu, (1995) 2 SCC 402, and K.T. Varghese v. State of Kerala, (2008) 3 SCC 735, establish the limits on control over minerals after excavation. D.K. Trivedi & Sons v. State of Gujarat, 1986 Supp SCC 20, and State of Tamil Nadu v. Hind Stone, (1981) 2 SCC 205, concern measures connected to the grant or refusal of leases; Hind Stone permits prohibition as regulation where it has a direct nexus with mineral conservation and exploitation, unlike a ban on movement after lawful excavation.
members.conclusion: The rules exceeded the State’s delegated rulemaking powers and were ultra vires the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957.

predicates.appeal_challenges_mineral_transport_rule: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a rule governing the transport of minerals.
predicates.mineral_was_lawfully_excavated: A leaseholder excavated the mineral under valid authorization.
predicates.rule_bars_post_excavation_interstate_mov: The rule prohibits the mineral from being transported across a state border after excavation.

members.legal_issue: A state rulemaking power confined to regulating grants of minor-mineral concessions does not authorize control of sales or prices after minerals have been extracted.
material_facts: The challenged rules authorized the State, its officers, or a state-owned company or corporation to regulate sales of quarried granite and similar decorative or ornamental rock.
The rules also authorized those bodies to fix minimum sale prices.
The State directed a state-owned company to regulate those sales, relying on conservation of granite resources as the purpose.
The rules applied to minerals after quarrying and therefore concerned their subsequent sale and sale price.
members.legal_principle: Sections 15(1) and 15(1A) authorize State rules regulating the grant of quarry leases, mining leases, and other mineral concessions for minor minerals, and matters connected with those grants. Section 15(1A)(o), concerning other prescribed matters, remains confined to that subject and does not authorize regulation of the sale of minerals already mined or their sale price. Section 18 places a conservation duty on the Central Government but does not confer on the State the power to control post-extraction sales or prices. Such control cannot be justified as a means of conserving the mineral resource after excavation.
members.conclusion: The rules regulating sales and fixing minimum prices after extraction were beyond the State’s rulemaking power and were invalid. The related government orders were invalid to the extent that they prescribed or implemented those rules.

rule.if: state_mineral_rule_challenge and minor_mineral_regulation and minerals_extracted and (sale_control or minimum_price_control)

predicates.state_mineral_rule_challenge: A party challenges a state rule made in relation to minor minerals.
predicates.minor_mineral_regulation: The rule purports to regulate minor minerals under the State’s delegated rulemaking authority.
predicates.minerals_extracted: The minerals covered by the rule have already been quarried or otherwise extracted.
predicates.sale_control: The rule authorizes a state body to control the sale of the extracted minerals.
predicates.minimum_price_control: The rule authorizes a state body to fix a minimum price for the extracted minerals.

members.legal_issue: Property bought in execution by the decree-holder and transferred through a fictitious transaction to a person who did not bona fide acquire rights may be restored to the judgment-debtor.
material_facts: The decree-holders purchased two groups of properties at execution sales, with the sale proceeds set off against the decretal dues.
The decree-holders later executed a conveyance of those properties to another person, and the courts found that conveyance fictitious.
The judgment-debtors sought restoration of the properties in the proceedings to reopen the decrees.
members.legal_principle: Under section 36(2)(c) of the Bengal Money-Lenders Act, property sold in execution may be restored where the decree-holder purchased it and the statutory conditions apply. A person who did not bona fide acquire rights through a subsequent fictitious transfer does not obtain the protection contemplated by section 36(2)(b).
members.conclusion: The orders restoring those properties to the judgment-debtors were upheld because the decree-holders were the purchasers and the purported transferee had not bona fide acquired rights.

predicates.statutory_borrower_relief_reopening: The proceeding seeks statutory borrower relief by reopening an existing decree.
predicates.decreeholder_bought_property_at_executio: The decree-holder purchased the property at the execution sale.
predicates.subsequent_transferee_did_not_bona_fide_: A later transferee did not genuinely and bona fide acquire rights in the property.

members.legal_issue: A property bought at an execution sale by someone other than the decree-holder is not restored merely because the purchase money came from another person, where the decree-holder neither bought nor possessed the property.
material_facts: A property was purchased at the execution sale by a person other than the decree-holders.
The purchase money may have come from that purchaser’s husband, but the decree-holders did not buy the property.
There was no proof that the decree-holders possessed the property either directly or through the purchaser.
members.legal_principle: Under section 36(2)(c) of the Bengal Money-Lenders Act, restoration on the basis that the decree-holder purchased property in execution does not apply when the decree-holder did not purchase it. The source of funds used by the person who purchased it does not alter that result where the decree-holder is not shown to have possessed the property directly or through that person.
members.conclusion: The property was not subject to restoration, and its possession remained with the execution-sale purchaser; the source of the purchase money was immaterial.

predicates.statutory_borrower_relief_reopening: The proceeding seeks statutory borrower relief by reopening an existing decree.
predicates.another_person_bought_property_at_execut: A person other than the decree-holder purchased the property at the execution sale.
predicates.decreeholder_did_not_buy_property: The decree-holder was not the purchaser of the property at the execution sale.
predicates.decreeholder_not_shown_to_possess_proper: There is no proof that the decree-holder possessed the property directly or through the execution-sale purchaser.

members.legal_issue: Permission to raise an additional ground in revision does not permit a party to make a new case that is outside the existing pleadings without amending them.
material_facts: The landlord’s original eviction claim included a ground of personal requirement under one statutory clause, which had been rejected.
In revision, the landlord sought permission to raise a different ground for additional accommodation under another clause.
The landlord obtained permission to raise the additional ground but did not apply to amend the eviction pleadings.
members.legal_principle: A party may raise an additional ground based on pleadings and material already on record without amending the pleadings. A new plea not borne out by the pleadings requires an amendment; the opposing party must then have a reasonable opportunity to plead further and present relevant evidence. A court or rent authority may permit such steps when the circumstances justify them, including where a plea rests on subsequent events.
members.conclusion: The High Court could allow the landlord to raise additional grounds, but that permission had no effect where the proposed ground constituted a new case and the pleadings had not been amended. The landlord could not obtain eviction on that basis.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_revision: A party seeks to rely on an eviction ground in revision of a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.proposed_ground_is_new_case: The proposed ground depends on a case not supported by the existing pleadings and material on record.
predicates.pleadings_not_amended: The party did not amend the eviction pleadings to include the proposed new case.

members.legal_issue: Permission to amend pleadings on remand to address res judicata does not authorize unrelated new pleas or reopen findings on matters the remand court did not address.
material_facts: The High Court remanded the case to reconsider res judicata and allowed amendments setting out the particulars of that plea.
The High Court also permitted the trial court to consider other amendments, but the Supreme Court construed these as amendments consequential to the res judicata plea.
The High Court’s order set aside the lower courts’ findings on the points it had considered, not findings on other issues that had not been before it.
members.legal_principle: An order must be read in the context of the issues it addresses: permission to amend a particular plea and make consequential amendments does not permit the introduction of unrelated new pleas, and setting aside findings on considered points does not set aside unconsidered findings. The Court relied on its construction of the High Court’s remand order and cited no earlier case or statutory provision for this point.
members.conclusion: The remand did not permit unrelated amendments alleging fraud or backdating, and it did not set aside findings on issues the High Court had not considered.

predicates.civil_case_remanded_to_reconsider_res_ju: The case was remanded for reconsideration of a res judicata plea.
predicates.amendment_permission_is_for_res_judicata: The permission to amend concerns particulars of the res judicata plea and amendments consequential to it.
predicates.other_findings_were_not_considered_on_ap: The appellate court did not consider the other findings made below.

members.legal_issue: A court assessing a Will must determine whether it was genuinely executed by a testator of sound disposing mind, rather than reject the bequest because it appears unreasonable or disinherits expected heirs.
material_facts: The Will clearly gave the testator's entire property to his wife, who had lived with and cared for him.
The Will recited that his daughters were married and that he had spent substantial amounts on their marriages and related ceremonies.
Evidence accepted by the trial court and first appellate court supported that the testator executed the Will and was of sound disposing mind.
The High Court set aside those findings principally because it considered that a prudent person would not disinherit his daughters.
members.legal_principle: The court's role in examining a Will is limited to determining whether the instrument is the testator's Will and whether it was the product of a free and sound disposing mind. The court must read the Will's language in the context of the testator's circumstances, and must not substitute its own view of the testator's intentions or assess the bequest by the rules of intestate succession. Where a Will appears on its face to have been duly executed and attested as required by law, a presumption of due execution and attestation applies. No earlier case was cited for these Will-specific principles in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The High Court wrongly substituted its view of what a prudent testator would do for the testator's expressed intention. The Will's validity was to be assessed by its authenticity and the testator's free and sound disposing mind; the concurrent findings upholding the Will could not be displaced on the ground that the bequest disinherited the daughters.

rule.if: will_validity_dispute and evidence_supports_execution_and_capacity and will_expresses_clear_intention and challenge_rests_on_expected_inheritance

predicates.will_validity_dispute: A party disputes whether an instrument is the deceased person's valid Will.
predicates.evidence_supports_execution_and_capacity: Witness or other evidence supports that the testator executed the instrument while of sound disposing mind.
predicates.will_expresses_clear_intention: The instrument clearly states how the testator intended to dispose of the property.
predicates.challenge_rests_on_expected_inheritance: The challenge to the instrument rests on the view that the testator would ordinarily have left property to heirs who were disinherited.

members.legal_issue: A probate court determines whether the document was duly executed and attested by a testator of sound disposing mind, rather than whether a particular bequest in it is valid.
material_facts: The probate application was rejected in part because the disposition dedicating property to a deity was considered void for uncertainty and therefore not a will.
The will also made provision for the testator’s daughter.
The Supreme Court considered the validity of the bequest to be outside the probate court’s inquiry.
members.legal_principle: The probate court’s inquiry is confined to whether the document is the deceased person’s will, duly executed and attested in accordance with law, and whether the testator had a sound disposing mind at execution. Section 2(h) of the Indian Succession Act defines a will, but does not make the validity of each bequest part of the probate inquiry. The Court rejected the lower courts’ reliance on Phundan Lal v. Arya Prithi Nidhi Sabha, 33 All 793, to treat uncertainty in a disposition as a reason to deny probate.
members.conclusion: The uncertainty or invalidity of a particular bequest is not a proper ground for refusing probate; the probate court must decide due execution and attestation and the testator’s sound disposing mind.

predicates.probate_proceeding: A party is asking a court to grant probate of a document asserted to be a deceased person’s will.
predicates.objection_concerns_validity_of_bequest: An objection to probate alleges that a gift or other disposition in the will is invalid or uncertain.

members.legal_issue: In a proceeding to release requisitioned property, possession is ordinarily to be returned to the person from whom it was taken, and the release inquiry does not determine claims based on facts preceding requisition.
material_facts: The requisition orders were addressed to the appellants as the persons in possession, and possession was taken from them.
Before requisition, their allotments had been provisional and cancellation had been communicated, but the department had not recovered possession.
No subsequent event creating a competing claim to possession was identified; the release orders instead specified the Director of Industries as the recipient.
members.legal_principle: Sections 29(2) and 35(1) of the Defence of India Act, 1962, provide for requisition by an order addressed to the owner or person in possession and for specifying the recipient of possession on release. Section 35(1) permits an inquiry when necessary, including a summary and prima facie inquiry where post-requisition events create a dispute. It does not enlarge the government's authority to adjudicate competing claims based on facts anterior to requisition. Under section 35(2), delivery does not prejudice another person's rights enforceable through due process of law. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The release inquiry under section 35(1) is required only when facts or events arising after requisition make it necessary. Otherwise, possession should be released to the person from whom it was taken; the government is not to investigate antecedent title in that inquiry.

predicates.requisition_release_proceeding: The matter concerns release of property that had been requisitioned.
predicates.possession_taken_from_person: The government took possession of the property from a person in possession when it requisitioned the property.
predicates.claim_based_only_on_pre_requisition_fact: The competing claim to possession rests on facts that existed before requisition, with no later event necessitating an inquiry into who should receive possession.
predicates.possession_returned_to_person_from_whom_: Possession is released to the person from whom it was taken at requisition.

members.legal_issue: On release of requisitioned property, possession is ordinarily to be given to the person from whom it was taken, without determining that person’s antecedent title.
material_facts: The property was requisitioned by a written order addressed to the person then in possession, and possession was taken from that person.
Before release from requisition, the government had not formally or symbolically taken possession of the property from that person.
The release order specified a government department as the recipient of possession.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 29(2) of the Defence of India Act, 1962, requisition may be effected by an order served on the person deemed to be the owner or person in possession. Section 35(1) provides for specifying the person to whom possession is to be given on release, as far as practicable the person appearing entitled to possession at that time. The inquiry under Section 35(1) is summary and is concerned with relevant events after requisition, not adjudication of antecedent title. Section 35(2) makes delivery a discharge of the government’s liabilities without prejudicing rights enforceable by due process of law. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The release inquiry under Section 35(1) concerns events after requisition that may affect who should receive possession; ordinarily, possession should be returned to the person from whom it was taken. The inquiry does not extend to determining competing antecedent title, and delivery under Section 35(2) does not prejudice rights enforceable through due process of law.

predicates.requisition_release_proceeding: The matter concerns who should receive possession when requisitioned property is released.
predicates.possession_taken_from_person: The authorities took possession of the property from a person when it was requisitioned.
predicates.no_post_requisition_event_changes_entitl: No event after requisition occurred that changes who should receive possession on release.

members.legal_issue: A person whose provisional allotment had not become final could receive a conditional order for return of possession where the government had not recovered possession before requisition and no third party had subsequently been allotted the property.
material_facts: The appellant had been given possession under a provisional allotment that was subject to final government approval, and the allotment was later cancelled.
The department had not recovered possession before requisition, and the requisitioning authority took possession from the appellant.
After release from requisition, possession was specified to be given to the department, but the plot had not been allotted to a third party.
The Supreme Court considered that the special-leave appeal warranted a qualified rather than an unconditional order.
members.legal_principle: Applying sections 29 and 35 of the Defence of India Act, 1962, the Court held that possession should technically have been released to the person from whom it had been taken. In exercising its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, it made relief conditional in light of the provisional nature of the allotment and the fact that the government had not recovered possession before requisition. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed in part: possession was directed to be delivered to the appellant unless the government took adequate and lawful steps to recover formal possession within the specified period. The government remained able to recover possession later, and an aggrieved party could pursue the statutory process for adjudication of rights.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal_from_derequisition_order and possession_taken_from_appellant and provisional_allotment_only and government_had_not_recovered_possession_before_requisition and not third_party_allotment_after_release

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_derequisition_: The proceeding is a special-leave appeal challenging an order specifying who should receive possession when requisitioned property was released.
predicates.possession_taken_from_appellant: The requisitioning authority took possession of the property from the appellant.
predicates.provisional_allotment_only: The appellant had received possession under an allotment that remained provisional and subject to final approval.
predicates.government_had_not_recovered_possession_: The government had not taken back possession from the appellant before the property was requisitioned.
predicates.third_party_allotment_after_release: After release from requisition, the property was allotted to a third party.
predicates.conditional_possession_return_order: The court conditionally directs return of possession to the appellant while leaving the government able to recover possession by lawful steps.

members.legal_issue: A person whose possession was taken on requisition may receive conditional relief on appeal even though the person’s allotment was provisional, where the government had not retaken possession before requisition.
material_facts: The appellant was put in possession under a provisional allotment that required final government approval, which was never given.
The allotment had been cancelled, but the government had not recovered possession before the property was requisitioned from the appellant.
The appeal challenged the refusal to direct delivery of possession to the appellant after release from requisition.
members.legal_principle: Applying Sections 29 and 35 of the Defence of India Act, 1962, the Court treated the person from whom possession had been taken as the proper recipient on release, while recognizing that the provisional allotment did not establish a final entitlement to the property.
