Deorajin Debi, subject to the exceptions in Sections 97 and 105(2) of that Code.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in holding that the revision was not maintainable on the ground that the vacancy order could not be challenged along with the final order.

rule.if: rent_control_allotment_proceeding and vacancy_order_is_preliminary and final_allotment_order_made and revision_challenges_final_order and not statutory_bar_to_later_challenge

predicates.rent_control_allotment_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the control of a rented building and its allotment after a vacancy determination.
predicates.vacancy_order_is_preliminary: The vacancy determination is a step in the process leading to a final allotment or release order.
predicates.final_allotment_order_made: The authority has made the final order that follows the vacancy determination.
predicates.revision_challenges_final_order: An aggrieved person seeks statutory revision of the final order and also challenges the preliminary vacancy determination.
predicates.statutory_bar_to_later_challenge: A law expressly precludes a later challenge to the preliminary order or gives that order final effect.
predicates.vacancy_order_challenge_permissible: The preliminary vacancy determination may be challenged in the statutory revision against the final order.

members.legal_issue: A court should not extend the time for payment under a specific-performance decree as a matter of course when the decree-holder has substantially delayed compliance without explanation or fault by the opposing party.
material_facts: The decrees required the purchasers to deposit the balance consideration by a specified date, but one purchaser deposited it much later and the other did not deposit it.
The purchasers sought extensions years after the decrees and after the appeals had been dismissed; they had not sought an extension in the trial court within the time fixed by the decrees.
No explanation was given for the failure to pay on time, and the purchasers did not claim that any act of the vendors prevented payment.
The High Court directed the executing court to consider the extension applications and suggested that the purchasers might have waited until the appeals ended or until execution was sought.
members.legal_principle: Section 28 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, gives the court discretion to extend time, not an obligation to do so automatically. Section 16(c) requires a specific-performance plaintiff to aver and prove performance or continuing readiness and willingness to perform essential contractual terms. Specific performance is equitable and discretionary: the court must assess the party's conduct, the circumstances of delay, and whether compliance was prevented by the other party. K. Kalpana Saraswathi v. P.S.S. Somasundaram Chettiar recognizes the power to extend time while emphasizing equitable terms; K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan, Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, and N.P. Thirugnanam v. R. Jagan Mohan Rao address reasonable performance, conduct, and readiness and willingness; Ramankutty Guptan v. Avara addresses the court's continuing jurisdiction under Section 28.
members.conclusion: The extension applications should be refused; the High Court's judgment was set aside and the executing court's dismissal of the execution applications was confirmed.

rule.if: specific_performance_execution and payment_deadline_missed and extension_sought_after_substantial_delay and no_explanation_for_default and no_opposing_party_caused_obstacle

predicates.specific_performance_execution: The proceeding concerns execution of a decree requiring performance of a contract for the sale or lease of immovable property.
predicates.payment_deadline_missed: The decree-holder did not pay the required amount within the time fixed by the decree.
predicates.extension_sought_after_substantial_delay: The decree-holder sought more time only after a substantial period had passed since the payment deadline.
predicates.no_explanation_for_default: The decree-holder gave no explanation for failing to make payment within the time fixed by the decree.
predicates.no_opposing_party_caused_obstacle: The decree-holder did not show that the opposing party caused an obstacle that prevented timely payment.

members.legal_issue: A court should not grant a grossly delayed extension of a payment deadline in a compromise decree where the circumstances show that doing so would be unjust.
material_facts: A compromise recorded in an appellate proceeding allowed a party to acquire part of the other parties’ share by paying in instalments by fixed dates.
The first instalment was paid, but the remaining amount was not paid by the deadline.
The party applied for an extension more than a year and a half after the missed deadline.
The court had previously permitted the other parties to refund the first instalment after the default, and the defaulting party had obtained extensions but failed to comply with directions.
The agreed price was substantially below the market value of the property, and the court found that justice favored the parties seeking to enforce the deadline.
members.legal_principle: Even where a court has power to extend time under a compromise, it should not do so liberally: under Smt. Periyakkal v. Smt. Dakshyani, time is not ordinarily extended or extended merely on request, but may be extended in rare cases to prevent manifest injustice. The court found that the circumstances favored enforcing the deadline and that the term was not a forfeiture clause. It did not decide the abstract question of the court’s general power to alter a consent order.
members.conclusion: The extension was unjustified; the order granting it was set aside and the application for more time was rejected.

rule.if: extension_request_in_consent_decree_case and payment_was_grossly_delayed and prior_noncompliance_was_recorded and (special_bargain_was_below_market_value or justice_favored_enforcing_deadline)

predicates.extension_request_in_consent_decree_case: A party in a proceeding concerning a court-recorded compromise asks the court to extend a payment deadline in that compromise.
predicates.payment_was_grossly_delayed: The party sought more time only after a substantial delay beyond the agreed payment deadline.
predicates.prior_noncompliance_was_recorded: The court record showed that the party had previously failed to comply with payment or court directions.
predicates.special_bargain_was_below_market_value: The agreement gave the party an opportunity to acquire a property interest for less than its market value.
predicates.justice_favored_enforcing_deadline: The circumstances showed that enforcing the agreed deadline favored the party entitled to receive payment.

members.legal_issue: A short-term lessee whose lease has expired or is about to expire is entitled only to compensation for the limited leasehold interest, while the reversionary owner is entitled to the remaining compensation.
material_facts: The acquired property was government land held under a lease, not land owned outright by the claimant.
The Court found that the lease had expired before possession was taken and that no renewal had been proved.
Even on the claimant’s account, possession was taken shortly before the asserted expiry of the lease.
The High Court apportioned the compensation equally between the claimant and the State.
members.legal_principle: A lessee’s limited interest is distinct from ownership and does not entitle the lessee to the entire compensation. Under Sections 105, 108, and 111(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, a lease transfers a right to enjoy property for a term and ordinarily determines by efflux of time. Compensation must reflect the interests acquired. The Court relied on Radha Charan v. Secretary of State, AIR 1943 Allahabad 238; Inder Parshad v. Union of India, 1994 (5) SCC 239; and Ratan Kumar Tandon v. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1996 SC 2710, distinguishing the circumstances of a perpetual lease and the earlier acquisition made well before expiry.
members.conclusion: The claimant was entitled to 20 per cent of the compensation for the land and the State was entitled to the remaining 80 per cent.

rule.if: compulsory_acquisition_proceeding and claimant_holds_limited_leasehold_interest and lease_expired_or_near_expiry_at_possession and renewal_not_established

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation for property acquired compulsorily.
predicates.claimant_holds_limited_leasehold_interes: The claimant holds a leasehold interest rather than ownership of the land.
predicates.lease_expired_or_near_expiry_at_possessi: The lease had expired or was due to expire shortly when possession was taken.
predicates.renewal_not_established: The claimant has not established that the lease was renewed.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for wrongful premature termination of a lease may be limited to a period shorter than the full unexpired term of the lease.
material_facts: The leases were terminated before their stated expiry dates.
The lease holder sought compensation for the wrongful termination.
The leases had specified original expiry dates, and the mines had been operated by the successor lessee for several years.
members.legal_principle: The Court exercised its remedial discretion, having regard to the circumstances of the case, to restrict the period for which compensation or damages could be claimed rather than allow recovery for the entire unexpired lease term. No earlier case was relied on for this limitation.
members.conclusion: The Court limited compensation to a period shorter than the full unexpired term of the leases, applying the earlier applicable endpoint stated in its order.

rule.if: proceeding_challenges_premature_lease_termination and termination_order_invalid and compensation_claimed_for_termination and leases_had_original_expiry_dates

predicates.proceeding_challenges_premature_lease_te: A proceeding challenges a government decision to end a lease before its ordinary expiry.
predicates.termination_order_invalid: The order ending the lease early is invalid.
predicates.compensation_claimed_for_termination: The lease holder seeks compensation for the early termination.
predicates.leases_had_original_expiry_dates: The leases specified dates on which they would ordinarily expire.

members.legal_issue: A landlord may seek a lawful rent revision after improvements or reconstruction but may not make payment of an increased rent a condition of the tenant’s return.
material_facts: The landlord substantially reconstructed and altered the premises at the landlord’s expense.
The landlord offered the rebuilt premises at a rent substantially higher than the rent previously paid.
The landlord’s offer made the increased rent a condition of the tenants’ return.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(1) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, permits an increase in fair rent where an addition, improvement or alteration is carried out at the landlord’s expense, subject to the statutory limits and the Controller’s jurisdiction to decide disputes. Read with Sections 4, 6 and 12, reconstruction may constitute an addition, improvement or alteration for this purpose. The right to seek revision does not make revision a precondition to the tenant’s re-entry.
members.conclusion: The landlord could not insist on the increased rent as a condition of re-entry. The landlord could seek fair-rent revision as permitted by law, and until a lawful revision was made the tenants remained liable at the previous rent.

predicates.rent_control_reconstruction_case: The proceeding concerns a tenant’s return after possession was delivered for repairs or reconstruction under a rent-control process.
predicates.landlord_made_improvements_at_own_expens: The landlord carried out improvements, additions, alterations or reconstruction at the landlord’s expense.
predicates.landlord_conditioned_tenant_return_on_hi: The landlord required the tenant to accept a higher rent as a condition of returning to the premises.

members.legal_issue: A landlord may recover premises to adapt or reconstruct them to meet the landlord’s requirements, provided the landlord complies with the restrictions governing use and transfer after recovery.
material_facts: A landlord sought recovery in order to use the premises for a business and later reconstruct the building according to the landlord’s needs.
The tenant argued that reconstruction was not an available ground for recovery.
The court found no prohibition on reconstruction so long as the landlord did not breach the applicable post-recovery conditions.
members.legal_principle: Section 13-B of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 requires the landlord to establish a genuine need for the premises but does not prohibit adapting or reconstructing them to meet that need. The landlord remains subject to the restrictions in Section 13-B(3) and the consequences under Section 19(2-B).
members.conclusion: Reconstruction according to the landlord’s needs is not prohibited, provided the landlord complies with the applicable restrictions after recovery.

predicates.special_nri_eviction_proceeding: The case is a proceeding seeking expedited recovery of rented premises by a landlord in the specially classified returning-resident category.
predicates.landlord_requires_premises_for_personal_: The landlord genuinely requires the premises for the landlord’s own use or a dependent’s use.
predicates.landlord_plans_adaptation_or_reconstruct: The landlord intends to alter or reconstruct the premises to suit the intended use.
predicates.post_recovery_restrictions_are_observed: The landlord complies with the restrictions on use, transfer, and letting after recovering possession.

members.legal_issue: A landholder who accepted a grant condition prohibiting eviction cannot obtain a statutory personal-cultivation allotment that would enable eviction in breach of the condition.
material_facts: The landholder accepted the government’s confirmation of his grant subject to a condition that he would not evict the tenants.
He applied for an allotment of land for personal cultivation, which would enable him to evict tenants from the allotted land.
The tenants did not have chav or buta hak, but their right not to be evicted arose from the grant condition.
The revenue tribunal dismissed the application, and the High Court declined to interfere.
members.legal_principle: Sections 18, 19 and 20 of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, 1951 do not permit a personal-cultivation allotment that would abridge a tenant’s preserved rights. Section 20(2) provides for an allotment order, and section 20(4) makes that order the basis on which a Girasdar may obtain possession; those provisions do not override section 18. The appellant accepted the grant subject to its conditions and was bound by them. The Court also referred to State of Saurashtra v. Jamadar Mohammad Abdulla for the proposition that annulment of a grant by the government would be an act of State not open to challenge before municipal tribunals.
members.conclusion: The application for allotment was incompetent because an allotment order could not limit or abridge the tenants’ rights under the grant condition. The appeal was dismissed.

predicates.statutory_personal_cultivation_allotment: A landholder applies under a statutory scheme for an allotment of land for personal cultivation.
predicates.accepted_grant_forbids_eviction: The landholder accepted a grant subject to a condition that the tenants must not be evicted.
predicates.allotment_would_enable_eviction: The requested allotment would enable the landholder to obtain possession by evicting tenants.
predicates.tenants_have_grant_based_non_eviction_ri: The tenants have a right not to be evicted that arises from the grant condition.

members.legal_issue: A grantee cannot obtain an allotment for personal cultivation when the allotment would enable eviction in breach of a grant condition protecting tenants from eviction.
material_facts: The grantee applied for allotment of land for personal cultivation under the legislation.
An allotment order would enable the grantee to evict tenants from the allotted land.
The grant was subject to a condition that the grantee would not evict the tenants, and that condition gave them a protected privilege.
The tribunals found that the tenants did not hold the special land rights that would exclude the land from the allotment provisions.
members.legal_principle: Sections 19 and 20 of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, 1951, provide for applications and orders allotting land to a Girasdar for personal cultivation, with an allotment order enabling possession from a tenant. Section 18 prevents Chapter IV from limiting or abridging tenants’ rights or privileges arising from a grant. Section 27 excludes land where a tenant has acquired specified special rights; those rights were not found here. Accordingly, the Mamlatdar could not make an order enabling the grantee to evict the tenants in breach of the grant condition.
members.conclusion: The application for allotment was incompetent because an order granting it would enable eviction in breach of the tenants’ protected privilege.

rule.if: personal_cultivation_allotment_application and allotment_would_enable_eviction and grant_condition_bars_eviction and tenant_privilege_from_grant and special_tenant_land_rights_absent

predicates.personal_cultivation_allotment_applicati: A grantee applied for an allotment of land for personal cultivation.
predicates.allotment_would_enable_eviction: The requested allotment would enable the grantee to evict tenants from the allotted land.
predicates.grant_condition_bars_eviction: The grant was subject to a condition that the grantee would not evict the tenants.
predicates.tenant_privilege_from_grant: The tenants’ protection against eviction arose from a condition attached to the grant.
predicates.special_tenant_land_rights_absent: The tenants were found not to hold special land rights that would independently exclude the land from the allotment process.
predicates.allotment_application_is_incompetent: The application for allotment cannot be maintained.

members.legal_issue: A Hindu deity is an individual within the meaning of the income-tax law’s category of taxable units.
material_facts: The tax authority assessed the deities as individuals on income from property dedicated to them.
The deities were treated in law as juristic entities capable of holding property.
The applicable tax law imposed tax on the income of specified taxable units, and its definition of individual did not expressly exclude artificial juridical persons.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 includes artificial juridical persons within individual; sections 2(9) and 3 were considered alongside section 2(31) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The Court relied on Commissioner of Income-tax v. Sodra Devi for the breadth of individual and on Cape Brandy Syndicate v. I.R.C. and Attorney General v. Clarkson for using later legislation to clarify an earlier ambiguous enactment. The Court also relied on the authorities establishing the juristic status of Hindu idols, including Manohar Ganesh v. Lakshmiram and Pramatha Nath Mullick v. Pradyumna Kumar Mullick.
members.conclusion: A Hindu deity falls within the meaning of individual and may be treated as a unit of assessment.

predicates.income_tax_assessment_proceeding: The matter concerns an assessment of income for tax purposes.
predicates.assessed_entity_is_artificial_juridical_: The entity assessed is recognized in law as an artificial juridical person.
predicates.tax_law_charges_income_of_taxable_units: The applicable tax law imposes tax on income of entities within its taxable-unit categories.

members.legal_issue: A Hindu deity falls within the meaning of “individual” for assessment under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
material_facts: Property had been dedicated to a Hindu deity and the dedication was held to be valid.
The deity was capable of holding the dedicated property and receiving income from it, and of suing and being sued.
The income of the debutter estate was assessed through the Official Trustee, who possessed and managed the property.
members.legal_principle: Under section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, “individual” includes a Hindu deity that is a juristic person capable of holding property and receiving income. The Court followed Jogendra Nath Naskar v. Commissioner of Income-tax (1969) 74 ITR 33 and relied on Commissioner of Income-tax v. Sodra Devi (32 ITR 615) for the breadth of “individual,” alongside the established authorities recognizing a Hindu deity as a juristic person, including Pramatha Nath Mullick v. Pradyumna Kumar Mullick (1925) LR 52 IA 245. The statutory language can encompass the deity without being strained, and assessment is made through the shebaits in possession and management of its property.
members.conclusion: A Hindu deity is an “individual” within section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, and can be treated as a unit of assessment; its income is assessed through the shebaits managing its property.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment_dispute and hindu_deity_is_juristic_person and deity_can_hold_property and deity_can_receive_income and deity_can_sue_or_be_sued

predicates.income_tax_assessment_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether income associated with a Hindu religious endowment is assessable as income-tax.
predicates.hindu_deity_is_juristic_person: The religious endowment is dedicated to a Hindu deity recognized as a juristic person.
predicates.deity_can_hold_property: The deity is capable of holding the property associated with the endowment.
predicates.deity_can_receive_income: The deity is capable of receiving income from its property.
predicates.deity_can_sue_or_be_sued: The deity has the capacity to sue and be sued in court.

members.legal_issue: Courts do not re-examine the merits of a considered policy decision to undertake an infrastructure project unless the decision-making process is unlawful, arbitrary, irrational, or transgresses fundamental rights.
material_facts: The project had been considered at several stages by the Government and expert bodies, and the Government had adopted a system for its execution.
The challenge sought, among other things, to halt a project that was already at an advanced stage.
members.legal_principle: Applying Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India, (2000) 10 SCC 664, and drawing an analogy with BALCO Employees’ Union (Regd.) v. Union of India, (2002) 2 SCC 333, the Court treated the conception and decision to undertake an infrastructure project as policy matters. Judicial review remains available for illegality, infringement of fundamental rights, arbitrariness, irrationality, or failure to consider relevant material.
members.conclusion: The Court would not revisit the policy choice to construct the dam or substitute its assessment for the Government’s, while retaining the duty to ensure that the law is followed and fundamental rights are not impermissibly infringed.

rule.if: infrastructure_policy_case and considered_policy_decision and (expert_review_completed or implementation_system_put_in_place) and not (arbitrary_decision or irrational_decision or legal_violation or impermissible_fundamental_rights_infringement)

predicates.infrastructure_policy_case: The proceeding challenges a governmental decision to undertake or execute an infrastructure project.
predicates.considered_policy_decision: The government made the project decision after considering the relevant policy choices.
predicates.expert_review_completed: One or more expert bodies examined the project or its relevant effects.
predicates.implementation_system_put_in_place: The government established a system for carrying out the project decision.
predicates.legal_violation: The challenged decision or its implementation violated the law.
predicates.impermissible_fundamental_rights_infring: The project decision impermissibly transgressed a fundamental right.

members.legal_issue: Courts should not substitute their judgment for a considered government policy decision to undertake a major infrastructure project unless the decision involves illegality, bad faith, or a violation of fundamental rights.
material_facts: The project had been considered over an extended period by the Union Government and multiple States, and an inter-State tribunal had determined the dispute and the project parameters.
The project had received government and Planning Commission consideration, and construction had commenced.
The government had considered competing public benefits and displacement concerns, and the Court found no material establishing bad faith or a basis to fault the project decision.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the constitutional division between executive policy-making and judicial review. Courts may ensure that government action does not violate law or impermissibly transgress fundamental rights, but should not act as an approval authority or sit in appeal over a considered policy decision among competing options. The Court also applied the principles concerning laches in public-interest litigation described above.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to review the project decision as a policy choice and held that the project should proceed unless a blatant illegality in its undertaking or execution was shown.

rule.if: judicial_review_of_infrastructure_policy and considered_government_decision and project_execution_started and no_blantant_illegality_or_bad_faith_shown

predicates.judicial_review_of_infrastructure_policy: A proceeding asks a court to reconsider the government’s choice to undertake or execute major infrastructure.
predicates.considered_government_decision: The responsible government considered the project and competing interests before deciding to proceed.
predicates.project_execution_started: The project had moved from policy decision to execution before the court was asked to intervene.
predicates.no_blantant_illegality_or_bad_faith_show: The proceeding does not establish blatant illegality or bad faith in the project’s undertaking or execution.

members.legal_issue: An arbitrator cannot decide whether a will was duly executed or is genuine when that question falls within probate jurisdiction.
material_facts: A will appointed an executrix, and probate proceedings concerning that will were pending before a High Court.
An arbitrator appointed to settle disputes concerning representation of the deceased’s estate framed issues about the execution and genuineness of the will.
members.legal_principle: Under the Indian Succession Act, 1925, including sections 213, 217, 222, 223, 276, 295 and 299, probate is determined through the statutory probate process, and the probate court must decide due execution and genuineness. The court relied on Inswardeo Narain Singh v. Smt. Kanta Devi, Sheoparsan Singh v. Ramnandan Prasad Singh, Narbheram Jivram v. Jayvallabh Harjivan, Chellan Bhai v. Nandu Bhai, Gopi Rai v. B.N. Rai and Manmohini Guha v. Banga Chandra Das.
members.conclusion: The probate court alone had jurisdiction to determine the will’s execution and validity; the arbitrator could not decide those issues.

predicates.probate_proceeding: A proceeding is brought to obtain or contest probate of a will.
predicates.will_execution_or_validity_in_dispute: A party asks for a determination of whether a will was duly executed or is genuine and valid.

members.legal_issue: Consent to arbitration cannot confer authority on an arbitrator to decide a matter reserved to the probate court.
material_facts: The parties had consented to referring disputes, including the will dispute, to arbitration.
The will dispute concerned matters assigned to the probate court by the statutory scheme.
Other legatees named in the will were not parties to the arbitration.
members.legal_principle: Jurisdiction derives from law and cannot be conferred by consent or waiver where a tribunal lacks inherent authority. A decision made without jurisdiction is a nullity. The court relied on A.R. Antulay v. R.S. Naik, Bahadur Singh v. Muni Subrat Dass, Kaushalya Devi v. K.L. Bansal, Ferozi Lal Jain v. Man Mal and Sushil Kumar Mehta v. Gobind Ram Bohra, as well as the statutory probate scheme under the Indian Succession Act, 1925.
members.conclusion: Even if the parties consented to arbitration, that consent did not give the arbitrator jurisdiction to decide the will’s execution or validity.

predicates.arbitration_proceeding: A dispute is referred to an arbitrator for decision.
predicates.parties_consented_to_arbitration: The parties agreed to refer the disputed matter to arbitration.
predicates.issue_reserved_to_probate_court: The disputed matter is one that the law assigns exclusively to a probate court.

members.legal_issue: A competent probate grant conclusively establishes a will’s due execution and validity against all persons unless the grant is revoked through the prescribed process.
material_facts: The dispute concerned the execution and validity of a will that was the subject of probate proceedings.
The Court considered the legal effect of a probate grant, which would bind persons beyond those who appeared in the probate proceeding.
members.legal_principle: The Indian Succession Act, 1925 provides for grants of probate and their legal effect, including under sections 227 and 273, and provides for appeal and revocation through the statutory process. The Court approved Sheoparsan Singh v. Ramnandan Prasad Singh and Narbheram Jivram v. Jayvallabh Harjivan.
members.conclusion: A probate grant is a judgment in rem and remains conclusive as to the will’s due execution and validity unless revoked according to law.

predicates.competent_probate_grant: A court with probate jurisdiction has granted probate of a will.
predicates.grant_not_revoked: The probate grant has not been revoked through the legally prescribed process.

members.legal_issue: A probate grant that remains in force is conclusive as to the validity of the will and cannot be challenged collaterally by a person who was cited but did not contest the probate proceeding.
material_facts: The probate court granted probate of the will.
The appellants were cited in the probate proceeding but did not appear or contest the grant.
The appellants later challenged the will’s validity in execution proceedings and in a separate civil suit; the grant had not been revoked.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 41 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, a final judgment or order of a competent court exercising probate jurisdiction is conclusive proof of what it decides, including the genuineness of the will. A probate grant operates as a judgment in rem and can be impeached only in proceedings to revoke it. In Surinder Kumar v. Gian Chand, 1958 SCR 548, the Court held that admission of a will to probate operates as a judgment in rem and removes an asserted infirmity concerning attestation under Section 63(1)(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925.
members.conclusion: The grant was conclusive as to the will’s execution and validity while it remained in force. The appellants could not contest the will’s validity in other proceedings unless the grant was revoked.

rule.if: probate_grant_exists and granting_court_is_competent and probate_grant_remains_in_force and citation_served_on_challenger and challenger_did_not_contest_probate and collateral_proceeding_challenges_will_validity

predicates.probate_grant_exists: A court exercising probate jurisdiction granted probate of the will.
predicates.granting_court_is_competent: The court that granted probate was competent to exercise probate jurisdiction.
predicates.probate_grant_remains_in_force: The probate grant has not been revoked.
predicates.citation_served_on_challenger: The person later challenging the will was cited in the probate proceeding.
predicates.challenger_did_not_contest_probate: The cited person did not appear or contest the probate proceeding.
predicates.collateral_proceeding_challenges_will_va: The person seeks to challenge the will’s validity in a proceeding other than one to revoke the probate grant.

members.legal_issue: A court hearing an appeal from a rioting conviction must make a definite finding on possession when the charged common object includes dispossessing a person and possession is material to determining the assembly's object, the aggressor, or the availability of private defence.
material_facts: The charge alleged that the assembly's common object included dispossessing the complainant from disputed land, as well as assaulting and murdering others.
The trial court found that possession of the land was disputed but made no determination of who possessed it at the time of the occurrence.

The High Court treated possession as immaterial and upheld the rioting conviction, although the possession issue could affect whether the accused's party was dispossessing the complainant and whether private defence was available.
The Supreme Court considered the absence of a definite finding on possession a serious defect and remanded the appeal for rehearing.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 141 and 147 of the Indian Penal Code, the alleged common object is material to whether an assembly is unlawful and whether its members committed rioting. Where the prosecution frames dispossession as a central common object, possession cannot be dismissed as immaterial if it bears on that object, on who was the aggressor, or on private defence. Failure to determine that vital issue may cause serious and substantial injustice warranting appellate intervention.
members.conclusion: The conviction and sentence were set aside, and the appeal was remanded to the High Court for rehearing and a definite finding on possession.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_rioting_conviction and charged_common_object_includes_dispossession and possession_is_disputed and possession_material_to_object_or_defence and appellate_court_makes_no_definite_possession_finding

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_rioting_convicti: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction for rioting.
predicates.charged_common_object_includes_disposses: The charge alleges that the assembly's common object included dispossessing a person from land.
predicates.possession_is_disputed: The parties dispute who possessed the land at the time of the occurrence.
predicates.possession_material_to_object_or_defence: Possession could affect whether the assembly was dispossessing the person, who was the aggressor, or whether private defence was available.
predicates.appellate_court_makes_no_definite_posses: The court hearing the appeal does not make a definite finding about possession.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court considering collective-liability convictions must determine whether an unlawful assembly existed, what acts its members committed in furtherance of its common object, and whether the appellants participated before deciding their liability.
material_facts: The High Court was not satisfied with the trial court’s treatment of the case but assumed that an unlawful assembly existed.
It did not fully examine the evidence to decide whether at least five persons other than the acquitted persons formed an unlawful assembly.
It did not determine the particular acts committed in furtherance of the common object or whether any appellant participated in the incident.
members.legal_principle: An appellate court must examine the evidence and make definite findings on whether an unlawful assembly existed, the acts committed by its members in furtherance of the common object, and the participation of the appellants before deciding whether collective liability applies. Section 423(1)(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was discussed in connection with appellate powers, but the Court expressed no opinion on whether the interpretation in Sunder Singh was consistent with R. v. Plummer. The Court also relied on the principles stated in Mohan Singh v. State of Punjab and the other authorities concerning unlawful assembly and collective liability.
members.conclusion: The High Court failed to determine essential questions. The Supreme Court set aside its judgment and remanded the case for a fresh decision.

predicates.collective_liability_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal involving convictions based on alleged membership in an unlawful assembly.
predicates.appellate_court_has_not_determined_assem: The appellate court has not examined the evidence and reached a definite conclusion about whether an unlawful assembly existed.
predicates.appellate_court_has_not_determined_membe: The appellate court has not determined what acts members committed in furtherance of the common object and whether the appellants participated.

members.legal_issue: For general municipal taxation, a building separately owned in parts, flats or rooms is assessed as a whole, with the several owners jointly and severally liable, except where the statute treats a portion as a separate property.
material_facts: The municipal legislation generally levied tax on land and buildings as a whole rather than on each independently owned part.
The statute provided joint and several liability for owners of buildings separately owned in parts, flats or rooms.
The statute also treated certain portions as separate properties when they were subject to a higher tax rate or an applicable exemption.
members.legal_principle: Sections 114 and 115 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, provide for taxation of land and buildings as a whole and specify circumstances in which a portion is treated as a separate property. Section 120(3) makes the liability of several owners of a building separately owned in parts, flats or rooms joint and several.
members.conclusion: The building is assessed as a whole and its several owners are jointly and severally liable for the tax, except for portions that the statute expressly treats as separate properties.

predicates.municipal_general_property_tax_assessmen: A municipal authority assesses a building to general property tax.
predicates.building_is_separately_owned_in_parts: Different owners separately own parts, flats or rooms within one building.
predicates.no_portion_is_statutorily_separate: No portion qualifies for statutory treatment as a separate property.

members.legal_issue: When a building includes a distinct portion used for trade or business or from which rent is derived, that portion is treated separately for municipal taxation, and the charitable use of another portion does not itself exempt it.
material_facts: A charitable trust owned a building containing portions occupied by a press and other portions used for the trust’s activities.
The press occupied identified areas of the building, and rent was derived from property use.
The dispute included whether the press-occupied areas could be exempt along with the other portions.
members.legal_principle: Sections 115(5) and 115(6) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 provide that land or buildings, or portions of them, are not treated as exclusively occupied and used for charitable purposes where trade or business is carried on or rent is derived, and that an exempt portion is treated as a separate property for municipal taxation. The Court also explained that a trade or business may serve as a means to a charitable end where its profits are applied to charity and no part is distributed to members; the portions are assessed separately.
members.conclusion: The trade or rental portion is separately subject to tax; the remaining portion may be considered separately for exemption if it independently satisfies the statutory conditions.

predicates.property_tax_exemption_claim: A society or body claims property-tax exemption for a building or part of a building.
predicates.identifiable_trade_or_rental_portion: An identifiable portion of the property is used for trade or business or produces rental income.

members.legal_issue: An order dismissing an application for temporary injunction as outside the scope of the injunction rule is an order under that rule and is appealable.
material_facts: The applicants sought a temporary injunction in an application invoking the procedural rules governing temporary injunctions and the court’s inherent powers.
The trial court rejected the application on the ground that the threatened execution of an eviction order was not an injury covered by the injunction rule.
The appellate court declined to hear an appeal, reasoning that the trial court had acted under its inherent powers rather than under the injunction rule.
members.legal_principle: Under section 104 and Order XLIII rule 1(r) of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal lies from an order under Order XXXIX rule 2. Where a court considers an application under that rule and rejects it because the asserted harm does not fall within the rule, it is deciding the application under the rule, not exercising inherent powers. An appellant may challenge the court’s interpretation of the rule, including its understanding of injury. The court referred to Hemant Kumar v. Ayodhya Prasad, AIR 1957 MB 95, and Abdul Hamid Khan v. Tridip Kumar Chanda, AIR 1953 Assam 104, as authorities followed by the trial court on the underlying sub-tenancy issue.
members.conclusion: The trial court’s order was made under the temporary-injunction rule and was appealable; the lower courts erred in holding otherwise.

predicates.temporary_injunction_application: A party filed an application seeking a temporary injunction under the procedural rules governing such injunctions.
predicates.rejection_based_on_scope_of_injunction_r: The court rejected the application because it considered the alleged harm outside the scope of the injunction rule.

members.legal_issue: An order disposing of an application for temporary injunctive relief is appealable when the trial court rejects the application on the ground that the injunction rule does not apply, even if the application also invokes inherent jurisdiction.
material_facts: The applicants sought a temporary injunction under the procedural rules for injunctions and also invoked the court’s inherent powers.
The trial court rejected the application on the ground that the complained-of harm did not fall within the injunction rule.
The appellate court declined to hear an appeal, reasoning that the trial court had acted under its inherent powers rather than under the injunction rules.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 104 and Order XLIII Rule 1(r) of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal lies from an order under Order XXXIX Rules 1, 2, 4 or 10. When a court deciding an application for temporary injunction determines that the relief sought does not fall within Order XXXIX Rule 2, it is deciding the application under that rule, and the order is appealable. The inclusion of a request under Section 151 does not make the decision an exercise of inherent powers where the court has decided the scope of Order XXXIX Rule 2.
members.conclusion: The order was appealable because the trial court had decided whether the application was competent under the injunction rule; the appellate court and the High Court erred in holding that no appeal lay.

predicates.appeal_from_temporary_injunction_order: The applicant appealed from an order disposing of a request for temporary injunctive relief.
predicates.application_invoked_injunction_procedure: The applicant asked the trial court for temporary injunctive relief under the procedural rules governing injunctions.
predicates.trial_court_decided_injunction_rule_scop: The trial court rejected the request by deciding that the complained-of harm did not fall within the injunction rule.

members.legal_issue: A prior lower-court view that has been disapproved by a later larger bench and remains under review does not establish that an acquisition is invalid.
material_facts: The owners relied on an earlier division-bench decision that had quashed acquisition notifications on the basis that acquisition required a sanctioned scheme.
Special leave petitions against that decision were pending before the Supreme Court.
A later full bench of the same High Court disagreed with the earlier decision’s reading of Supreme Court authority.
members.legal_principle: The Court noted that the earlier decision was under challenge and had not been approved by the later full bench. On the merits, it held that the earlier decision misread Gandhi Grah Nirman Sahkari Samiti Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan (1993) 2 SCC 662, whose combined reasoning supported acquisition without a scheme where the State Government acted for a purpose authorized by the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act.
members.conclusion: The earlier division-bench decision did not affect the acquisitions and did not state the correct law; the later full-bench view was correct.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns a government proceeding to acquire land.
predicates.prior_division_bench_view_challenged: A party relied on an earlier division-bench decision that was itself under challenge before a higher court.
predicates.later_full_bench_disapproved_that_view: A later full bench of the same court disagreed with the earlier decision's reasoning.

members.legal_issue: A prior ruling that an acquisition scheme was vague cannot support quashing the acquisition when the controversy has since been considered by a larger bench of the Supreme Court.
material_facts: The High Court’s Division Bench quashed the acquisition on the ground that the scheme was vague, following an earlier Supreme Court decision.
A three-judge bench of the Supreme Court had subsequently considered the controversy concerning vagueness and failure to make the scheme.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on State of Tamil Nadu v. L. Krishnan, decided by a three-judge bench, which had considered the controversy concerning vagueness and failure to make the scheme; the earlier reliance on State of Tamil Nadu v. A. Mohammed Yusuf did not sustain the High Court’s ruling after that consideration.
members.conclusion: The Division Bench’s decision quashing the acquisition on that basis could not be sustained.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: An owner challenges an acquisition proceeding.
predicates.acquisition_quashed_for_scheme_vagueness: A court quashed the acquisition on the ground that the scheme was vague or had not been made.
predicates.larger_bench_has_considered_that_controv: A larger bench of the Supreme Court has already considered the controversy concerning the scheme’s vagueness or failure to make the scheme.
predicates.acquisition_not_quashed_on_that_vaguenes: The acquisition cannot be quashed on that vagueness ground.

members.legal_issue: Rejecting eyewitness testimony because it conflicts with a dying declaration does not by itself make the dying declaration unreliable.
material_facts: The trial court rejected the eyewitnesses as unreliable and treated their conflict with the dying declaration as a reason to reject the declaration as well.
The Supreme Court found the declaration coherent, consistent, and reliable, and agreed that it could sustain the conviction despite the rejection of the eyewitness testimony.
members.legal_principle: The reliability of a dying declaration must be assessed on its own merits. A conflict between it and eyewitness testimony does not necessarily make the declaration unreliable. Section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act gives qualifying statements about the cause or circumstances of death relevance; Khushal Rao v. State of Bombay was relied on for the special evidentiary status of such declarations.
members.conclusion: The trial court erred in treating the rejection of the conflicting eyewitness testimony as a reason to reject the dying declaration; the declaration could be assessed independently.

predicates.criminal_case_based_on_dying_declaration: The proceeding is a criminal case in which a dying declaration is relied on as evidence.
predicates.eyewitness_testimony_rejected_as_inconsi: The court rejects eyewitness testimony because it conflicts with the dying declaration.
predicates.declaration_independently_coherent: The dying declaration is coherent when assessed independently.

members.legal_issue: The fact that a dying declaration names additional persons who are not prosecuted does not by itself establish that the declaration is false.
material_facts: The deceased named persons in addition to the appellants as participants in the assault.
Those additional persons were not charge-sheeted.
The Court considered that their omission from the prosecution could have resulted from ulterior motives and did not by itself undermine the declaration.
members.legal_principle: A dying declaration must be assessed on its evidentiary merits; the omission from prosecution of persons named in it does not alone establish falsity. Section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act recognizes relevant statements about the cause or circumstances of death.
members.conclusion: The non-prosecution of additional persons named in the declaration did not, by itself, prove that the declaration was false.

predicates.dying_declaration_case: The proceeding concerns the truth or reliability of a dying declaration.
predicates.declaration_names_additional_persons: The dying declaration names persons in addition to those prosecuted.
predicates.additional_persons_not_prosecuted: The additional persons named in the declaration are not prosecuted.

members.legal_issue: A creditor enforcing a composite decree that makes a guarantor personally liable and secures part of the debt by mortgage must proceed against the mortgaged property before executing against the guarantor.
material_facts: The bank obtained a composite decree against the principal debtor and guarantors, making them personally liable and declaring part of the debt recoverable under a mortgage.
The bank sought execution against the guarantor, and the execution court and High Court required the bank to proceed first against the mortgaged property and the principal debtor.
The bank relied on the guarantor’s independent undertaking and on an earlier decision concerning execution against a surety.
members.legal_principle: In Bank of Bihar Ltd. v. Damodar Prasad, the Court held that, absent special equity, a surety ordinarily cannot restrain execution against the surety until remedies against the principal debtor have been exhausted. That general rule did not displace the requirement applied here: where a composite decree secures part of the debt by mortgage, the decree-holder must first proceed against the mortgaged property before proceeding against the guarantor.
members.conclusion: The Court held that, because part of the decreed amount was covered by the mortgage, the bank had to proceed against the mortgaged property before executing against the guarantor. The High Court was not shown that these steps had been taken, so its direction was not shown to be erroneous on the record before it.

predicates.execution_of_composite_decree: A creditor seeks to enforce a decree that imposes personal liability and also grants relief against property securing the debt.
predicates.debt_partly_secured_by_mortgage: Part of the debt covered by the decree is secured by mortgaged property.
predicates.mortgaged_property_must_be_pursued_befor: The creditor must proceed against the mortgaged property before seeking execution against the guarantor.

members.legal_issue: Execution against a guarantor is maintainable after the decree-holder has proceeded against both the mortgaged property and the principal debtor, if those steps were in fact taken.
material_facts: In its statement of facts in the special leave petition, the bank said it had applied for sale of the mortgaged property but received no purchase offer, and had also filed an execution application against the principal debtor.
The Court had not been told in the High Court that these steps had been taken.
The guarantor was given liberty to dispute whether the bank’s statement was correct.
members.legal_principle: Applying the requirement that a decree-holder first proceed against the mortgaged property in a composite decree, the Court stated that execution against the guarantor would be maintainable if the decree-holder had proceeded against both the mortgaged property and the principal debtor. It relied on Bank of Bihar Ltd. v. Damodar Prasad for the general rule that a surety ordinarily cannot require the creditor to exhaust remedies against the principal debtor first, but resolved this case in light of the mortgage component and the disputed claim that prior steps had been taken.
members.conclusion: If the bank’s statement that it had proceeded against the mortgaged property and the principal debtor was correct, execution against the guarantor was maintainable. The Court remanded the matter to the High Court so the bank could advance that case and the guarantor could dispute it.

rule.if: execution_of_composite_decree and debt_partly_secured_by_mortgage and mortgaged_property_pursued and principal_debtor_pursued

predicates.execution_of_composite_decree: A creditor seeks to enforce a decree that imposes personal liability and also grants relief against property securing the debt.
predicates.debt_partly_secured_by_mortgage: Part of the debt covered by the decree is secured by mortgaged property.
predicates.mortgaged_property_pursued: The creditor has taken steps to proceed against the mortgaged property.
predicates.principal_debtor_pursued: The creditor has taken steps to proceed against the principal debtor.
predicates.execution_against_guarantor_is_maintaina: The creditor may execute the decree against the guarantor.

members.legal_issue: Co-owners receiving fixed individual shares of estate income are not assessed as an association of individuals unless they join in a common enterprise to produce income.
material_facts: Four heirs each became entitled to a fixed one-quarter share of an estate and its income.
The heirs did not join in a common enterprise to produce income, profits, or gains.
The assessee returned only his share of the estate income, but the tax officer assessed him on the income of all four co-sharers as an association of individuals.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(k) and 3 of the Hyderabad Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950, permit assessment of an individual or an association of individuals. An association requires two or more persons to join in a common purpose or common action directed at producing income, profits, or gains; co-ownership alone does not suffice. The Court applied the test stated in its earlier decisions, including Mohamed Noorullah v. Commissioner of Income-tax.
members.conclusion: The assessee was assessable on his individual share of the estate income, not on the total income of all four co-sharers as an association of individuals.

rule.if: agricultural_income_tax_assessment and co_ownership_with_fixed_shares and not joint_income_producing_enterprise

predicates.agricultural_income_tax_assessment: An assessee's agricultural income is being assessed for tax.
predicates.co_ownership_with_fixed_shares: Two or more persons hold an estate as co-owners, each entitled to a fixed individual share of its income.
predicates.joint_income_producing_enterprise: The co-owners have joined in a common enterprise directed at producing income, profits, or gains.

members.legal_issue: Joint heirs who merely receive income from inherited assets do not constitute an association of persons for income-tax assessment unless they join in a common purpose or action to produce income.
material_facts: Three widows inherited an estate as joint tenants, each entitled to an equal share of its income.
The shares were registered separately in the names of the widows, and there was no finding that they jointly managed them.
The widows jointly received dividends and interest but did no act that helped produce that income.
members.legal_principle: Under section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, an association of persons requires two or more persons to join in a common purpose or common action, with the object of producing income, profits or gains. It must be a combination formed to promote a joint enterprise for producing income. Mere joint receipt of income is insufficient. The Court approved the tests in In re B. N. Elias, Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay v. Laxmidas Devidas, and In re Dwarakanath Harishchandra Pitale; whether an association exists depends on the facts and circumstances of each case.
members.conclusion: The widows were not an association of persons in respect of the income at issue, and the assessment of that income on that basis was not valid.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment_proceeding and joint_heirs and jointly_received_income and not joint_income_producing_action

predicates.income_tax_assessment_proceeding: The matter concerns the assessment of income for income-tax purposes.
predicates.joint_heirs: Two or more people inherited property together and were entitled to share its income.
predicates.joint_income_producing_action: The co-heirs acted together in a way that helped produce income.

members.legal_issue: A husband cannot gift ancestral immovable property belonging to a joint family to his wife merely out of affection.
material_facts: The husband executed a gift of immovable joint family property in favour of his second wife.
The gift deed referred to affection, and the donee argued that the gift covered only a reasonable portion of the property.
The property was ancestral immovable property.
members.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, a Hindu father or other managing member may make a gift of ancestral immovable property within reasonable limits for pious purposes, but affection does not make a gift of such property to a wife permissible. The court relied on Kamala Devi v. Bachu Lal Gupta, [1957] S.C.R. 452, and Guramma Bharatar Chanbassappa Deshmukh v. Malappa, [1964] 4 S.C.R. 497, for the limited scope of gifts for pious purposes and declined to extend that scope to gifts to a wife.
members.conclusion: The gift to the wife was invalid; affection did not make a gift of ancestral immovable property permissible.

predicates.husband_gifted_to_wife: A husband made the gift to his wife.

members.legal_issue: A manager cannot give joint family property to an outsider merely out of affection or gratitude.
material_facts: The manager gave immovable joint family property to a relative outside the coparcenary.
The deed described the transfer as a token of love and appreciation for services rendered.
The transfer was not established as a permitted small gift for a pious purpose.
members.legal_principle: A manager has no absolute power of disposal over joint family property. Hindu law permits only limited gifts of a small extent of property to strangers for pious purposes; affection, gratitude, or a broad charitable characterization does not authorize the gift at issue. The Court referred to Mitakshara, Chapter I, section 1, verse 28, and Partha Sarathi Pillai v. Tiruvengada (1907) I.L.R. 30 Mad. 340.
members.conclusion: The gift to the outsider was void.

rule.if: joint_family_gift_dispute and donor_was_family_manager and recipient_was_outside_coparcenary and not gift_within_permitted_pious_gift_limit

predicates.joint_family_gift_dispute: A proceeding disputes a gift of joint family property.
predicates.donor_was_family_manager: The donor managed the joint family property but was not its sole owner with absolute disposal power.
predicates.recipient_was_outside_coparcenary: The recipient was a stranger to the coparcenary.
predicates.gift_within_permitted_pious_gift_limit: The gift fell within the limited category of small gifts to outsiders permitted for pious purposes.

members.legal_issue: The executive authority deciding whether to consent to a suit against a ruler of a former state must not adjudicate the merits and should normally consent where the proposed claim raises justiciable and triable issues.
material_facts: The petitioner sought consent to bring a partition suit against a ruler of a former state.
The government refused consent for some properties on the ground that they belonged to the ruler and were not partible.
The government also rejected the petitioner's interpretation of a communication concerning the rights of third parties, thereby deciding disputed questions relevant to the proposed suit.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 87B of the Code of Civil Procedure, the consent power is intended substantially to protect former rulers from frivolous suits, not to transfer the civil court's function of deciding the merits to the executive. The Court relied on its guidance in Narottam Kishore Deb Verma v. Union of India that consent should not be refused casually and may legitimately be refused where the proposed claim appears prima facie frivolous. It also compared the possible dispute-avoidance function of Section 87B with the notice procedure under Section 80.
members.conclusion: The government impermissibly adjudicated the merits; the consent authority should normally allow a suit raising justiciable and triable issues and should refuse consent only where the claim appears prima facie frivolous.

predicates.consent_application_for_suit_against_for: A litigant asks the executive for consent to sue a ruler of a former state.
predicates.proposed_claim_raises_triable_issues: The proposed claim presents justiciable issues that can be tried by a competent civil court.
predicates.executive_decides_disputed_merits: The executive resolves disputed questions about the merits of the proposed claim when deciding whether to consent.

members.legal_issue: The authority deciding whether to permit a suit against a former ruler should ordinarily allow a genuine dispute that appears prima facie triable to be heard by a court.
material_facts: The petitioners sought consent to sue a former ruler over a claimed maintenance entitlement based on family custom.
The Central Government refused consent.
The Court considered that the petitioners appeared prima facie to have a genuine grievance and that the dispute appeared triable by a court.
members.legal_principle: Under section 87B of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Court stated that the consent power should not be used to stifle claims. Consent should ordinarily, if not as a matter of course, be granted where a genuine dispute prima facie appears triable by a court; refusal may be justified where the claim is frivolous or clearly far-fetched.
members.conclusion: The authority should ordinarily grant consent for a genuine dispute that prima facie appears triable; refusal may be justified for frivolous claims. The Court left the petitioners’ particular grievance for the Central Government to consider and dismissed the writ petition without ordering that consent be granted.

predicates.sanction_application_for_suit_against_fo: A litigant sought prior consent to bring a civil suit against a former ruler.
predicates.genuine_dispute: The litigant presented a genuine dispute rather than a frivolous claim.
predicates.prima_facie_triable: The dispute appeared on its face to be one that a court could try.

members.legal_issue: A tenant cannot waive by agreement the statutory protection against an eviction suit brought without prior permission when that protection is founded on public policy.
material_facts: The lease stated that neither party would claim the benefit of the rent-control legislation and that its provisions would not apply to the lease.
The owners brought an eviction suit without first obtaining the District Magistrate’s permission.
The statutory protection was intended to protect tenants as a weaker class and to require an authority to consider the landlord’s claim and the tenant’s needs.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 is prohibitive and protects tenants from eviction suits without permission. Although a person may waive a statutory benefit enacted solely for private benefit when no public policy is involved, this protection rests on public policy because it protects a weaker class and serves the community interest. Under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement whose object defeats a provision of law is void. Lachoo Mal v. Radhey Shyam recognizes waiver only where public policy does not prevent it; the Court also refers to Gherulal Parakh v. Mahadeodas Maiya in discussing public policy.
members.conclusion: The tenant was not barred by the lease from relying on the statutory protection; the agreement could not waive that protection, and the suit was not maintainable without permission.

rule.if: eviction_suit_under_tenant_protection_regime and agreement_disclaims_tenant_protection and suit_filed_without_required_permission and protection_serves_public_policy

predicates.eviction_suit_under_tenant_protection_re: A landlord brought a suit to evict a tenant in a regime that restricts eviction suits.
predicates.agreement_disclaims_tenant_protection: The landlord and tenant agreed that the tenant would not claim the statutory protection against eviction.
predicates.suit_filed_without_required_permission: The landlord filed the suit without first obtaining the required administrative permission.
predicates.protection_serves_public_policy: The protection is intended to safeguard a weaker class and serves a public interest beyond the parties’ private interests.

members.legal_issue: A tenant cannot waive by contract a statutory restriction on eviction suits that is founded on public policy.
material_facts: The lease stated that neither party would claim the benefit of the rent-control legislation and that its provisions would not apply to the lease.
The landlord brought an eviction suit without obtaining the permission required by the legislation.
The Court found that the restriction protected tenants, a weaker section, and served the wider community by limiting eviction suits without reasonable grounds.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, is prohibitive and embodies public policy by protecting tenants and limiting eviction suits without reasonable grounds. Under section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement whose object defeats a legal provision is void. The Court considered Lachoo Mal v. Radhey Shyam, [1971] 3 S.C.R. 693, and Gherulal Parakh v. Mahadeodas Maiya Das, [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 406, and held that the tenant could not waive this protection.
members.conclusion: The tenant could not waive the protection, and the lease clause did not make the suit maintainable.

rule.if: civil_eviction_suit and statutory_permission_required and permission_not_obtained and contract_purports_to_waive_tenant_protection and protection_serves_public_policy

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: A landlord brings a civil proceeding to evict an occupant from accommodation.
predicates.statutory_permission_required: The governing law requires the landlord to obtain permission from a responsible authority before bringing the eviction suit.
predicates.permission_not_obtained: The landlord brings the eviction suit without obtaining that required permission.
predicates.contract_purports_to_waive_tenant_protec: The lease states that the tenant will not claim the statutory protection against eviction.
predicates.protection_serves_public_policy: The protection is intended to shield a weaker class from unjustified eviction proceedings and serves the interests of the community.

members.legal_issue: Whether compensation for compulsory acquisition and statutory interest on that compensation are capital gains must be determined by distinguishing their nature on the facts of each case.
material_facts: The company received compensation for compulsory acquisition of land and distributed amounts attributable to that compensation to its shareholder.
The High Court proceeded on the assumption that the entire compensation was capital gain.
The Court noted that compensation for land forming part of a company’s fixed assets is prima facie capital in nature, while statutory interest payable on compensation is income, not capital gain.
members.legal_principle: The character of compulsory-acquisition compensation must be assessed on the facts; compensation for land forming part of fixed assets is prima facie capital in nature under Senairam Doongarmall v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Assam. Statutory interest on compensation is income and not capital gain under Dr. Shamlal Narula v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Patiala. The question arose in a reference under section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
members.conclusion: The High Court had to determine on the facts whether any part of the compensation was capital gain; it could not assume that the entire amount was capital gain, and statutory interest was income rather than capital gain.

predicates.statutory_tax_reference: A tribunal referred a tax question to a High Court for decision in a statutory reference.
predicates.compensation_for_compulsory_acquisition_: A company distributed to a shareholder an amount attributable to compensation it received for compulsory acquisition of land.

members.legal_issue: Whether salami received for granting long-term leases is capital gain must be determined on the facts of each case.
material_facts: The company received salami for granting long-term leases and distributed amounts attributable to those receipts to its shareholder.
The Tribunal referred to the High Court whether the shareholder’s receipt was taxable as income from other sources and whether it was dividend.
The High Court answered the questions by following earlier judgments without deciding on the facts whether any salami was capital gain.
members.legal_principle: In a reference under section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, the High Court must determine the character of salami on the facts of the particular case; the Court cited no earlier authority for this point.
members.conclusion: The High Court had to decide on the facts of this case whether any amount of salami was capital gain.

predicates.statutory_tax_reference: A tribunal referred a tax question to a High Court for decision in a statutory reference.
predicates.salami_received_for_long_term_lease_dist: A company distributed to a shareholder an amount attributable to salami it received for granting a long-term lease.

members.legal_issue: A claim for an injunction protecting alleged possession cannot be dismissed as time-barred merely because the related claim for specific performance is found time-barred.
material_facts: The suit sought both specific performance and a perpetual injunction against interference with the plaintiffs’ alleged possession.
The plaintiffs alleged that their predecessor had been put in possession under a subsequent agreement or receipt.

The courts below dismissed the suit as a whole based on their finding that the specific-performance claim was time-barred, without determining the limitation period applicable to the injunction claim.
members.legal_principle: A claim for injunction is governed by Article 113 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and its limitation period depends on when the right to sue accrued. Whether an injunction is independent of, or merely consequential to, a claim for specific performance and whether the plaintiff proves possession are matters for determination on the pleadings and evidence. Section 27 of the Limitation Act concerns extinguishment of a right to property at the end of the period for a suit for possession; the Court noted that the suit was not, as such, a suit for possession.
members.conclusion: The injunction claim could not be held barred at the preliminary stage on the basis of the limitation finding concerning specific performance. Its limitation and whether it was independent or consequential required determination on the pleadings and evidence.

predicates.suit_includes_possession_protection_inju: The plaintiff sought an injunction to protect alleged possession of the property.
predicates.specific_performance_claim_dismissed_as_: The court dismissed the specific-performance claim as time-barred.
predicates.injunction_limitation_not_separately_det: The court did not separately determine when the right to sue for the injunction accrued.

members.legal_issue: A prayer for injunction based on a disputed title is consequential, and when the declaratory claim is time-barred, the dependent injunction claim is also time-barred.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought cancellation of a registered sale deed and a declaration that it was not binding, along with an injunction concerning the land.

The registered sale deed stated that the purchaser had received possession, and the purchaser’s name was recorded as owner and cultivator from the year after the sale until the suit was filed approximately 22 years later.

The plaintiff claimed possession and cultivation of part of the land, but the court held that she would have had knowledge of the registered deed and the continuing revenue entries through due diligence.
The declaratory and cancellation claims were rejected, and that rejection became final; the injunction was sought to protect possession in the context of those claims.
members.legal_principle: Under Dilboo v. Dhanraji (2000) 7 SCC 702, registration gives deemed knowledge of a document, and a plaintiff disputing limitation must aver and prove that the claim is within time; knowledge may also be attributed where due diligence would have disclosed the relevant facts. Although an injunction is ordinarily a substantive relief whose limitation period may run from interference with possession, that approach does not apply where the injunction is consequential to a declaration that is itself time-barred.
members.conclusion: The injunction was consequential to the declaratory and cancellation claims, so the limitation bar applying to those substantive claims also barred the injunction claim.

rule.if: suit_seeks_declaration_and_dependent_injunction and title_document_was_registered and public_records_consistently_showed_another_person_as_owner_or_cultivator and claimant_asserted_possession_or_cultivation and declaratory_claim_is_time_barred

predicates.suit_seeks_declaration_and_dependent_inj: The claimant brought a suit seeking a declaration about title together with an injunction that depends on that title claim.
predicates.title_document_was_registered: A document recording the competing title was registered.
predicates.public_records_consistently_showed_anoth: Public land records continuously identified another person as owner or cultivator of the land.
predicates.claimant_asserted_possession_or_cultivat: The claimant asserted possession of, or cultivation on, the land, making the recorded entries discoverable through due diligence.
predicates.declaratory_claim_is_time_barred: The claim for a declaration concerning title is outside the applicable limitation period.

members.legal_issue: A marginal heading cannot control the meaning of clear statutory text.
material_facts: The lessees relied on the marginal heading of the statutory section, which referred to penalties, to argue that recovery of the mineral price was penal.
The Court considered the text and structure of the section and concluded that the price-recovery provision compensated the State rather than imposed punishment.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle of statutory interpretation that a marginal note cannot restrict or control clear language in the body of a section. It relied on Director of Public Prosecutions v. Schildkamp and the discussion of marginal notes in G.P. Singh's Principles of Statutory Interpretation.
members.conclusion: The marginal heading could not give the price-recovery provision a penal meaning contrary to its clear text.

predicates.case_involves_interpretation_of_a_sectio: The proceeding requires the court to interpret the text of a statutory section.
predicates.operative_text_has_clear_meaning: The operative words of the section clearly state the meaning relevant to the dispute.
predicates.marginal_heading_suggests_a_different_me: The section's marginal heading appears to suggest a meaning different from the operative words.

members.legal_issue: A marginal heading cannot override the clear and unambiguous language of a statutory section.
material_facts: The section’s marginal heading described a duty to pay compensation.
The section’s operative language distinguished compensation, determined by specified principles and due on resumption, from interest payable until payment.
The assessee relied on the heading to argue that the interest formed part of the compensation.
members.legal_principle: A marginal heading cannot control the words of a statutory section when those words are clear and unambiguous. The Court applied this principle in interpreting section 8 of the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagir Act, 1951.
members.conclusion: The marginal heading could not control the interpretation of the section’s clear and unambiguous operative language.

predicates.statutory_text_interpretation_case: The proceeding requires interpretation of statutory text.
predicates.marginal_heading_suggests_a_broader_mean: The marginal heading suggests a meaning broader than the operative text supports.
predicates.operative_text_is_clear_and_unambiguous: The operative text expresses its meaning clearly and unambiguously.

members.legal_issue: A decree cannot be treated as fraudulent merely because relevant facts were concealed or fraud was alleged; fraud must be specifically established with intent to deceive.
material_facts: A decree in favour of the property owner followed a full trial and was upheld on appeal, and the dismissal of the opposing party’s specific-performance suit became final.
In a later suit seeking to invalidate that decree, the opposing party did not specifically plead that the decree had been obtained by fraud.
The opposing party relied on a certified copy of an alleged power of attorney that the courts found insufficient to establish the alleged fraud.
members.legal_principle: Fraud has a definite legal meaning and must be proved, not merely alleged or inferred. Where fraud is alleged through concealment or non-disclosure, it must be inquired into, but a conclusion of fraud requires evidence together with intent to deceive; mere concealment, non-disclosure without that intent, or a bald allegation without proof is insufficient. The Court relied on A.V. Papayya Sastry v. Government of A.P.; Union of India v. Ramesh Gandhi; Meghmala v. G. Narasimha Reddy; Bhaurao Dagdu Paralkar v. State of Maharashtra; and State of Orissa v. Harapriya Bisoi.
members.conclusion: The decree was not shown to have been obtained by fraud, so the allegation did not justify setting it aside.

predicates.collateral_challenge_to_decree: A party brought a later proceeding seeking to invalidate a decree obtained in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.fraud_not_specifically_pleaded: The party seeking to invalidate the decree did not specifically allege in its pleading that the decree had been obtained by fraud.
predicates.fraud_not_proved_with_intent_to_deceive: The evidence did not establish fraud accompanied by intent to deceive.
