The society was short of space, and the record showed that the proposed quarters, students’ home, publication department, guest house and panthasala would facilitate its activities.
The government’s satisfaction and consent were supported by the acquisition inquiry and the agreement with the society.
The agreement restricted the land to the identified purposes and required completion and equipping of the facilities within a specified time, with a right of re-entry in case of non-compliance.
members.legal_principle: Section 40(1)(aa), Section 41(4-A), and Section 7 of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1962, permit and retrospectively validate acquisition for a building or work for a company engaged in an industry or work for a public purpose when the building or work subserves that public-purpose activity and the agreement addresses construction conditions. The Court applied the second R. L. Arora v. State of U.P., 1964 AIR SC 1230. It distinguished State of West Bengal v. P. N. Talukdar, 1965 AIR SC 646, because the evidence there did not establish the necessary connection between the buildings and the public-purpose work. The Court also treated public purpose broadly, consistent with Babu Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay, 1961 (1) SCR 128; AIR 1960 SC 1203, while noting that the earlier company-acquisition provisions required direct public use under the first Arora case.
members.conclusion: The retrospective amendment applied, the acquisition satisfied its requirements, and the acquisition was valid.

rule.if: company_land_acquisition and acquisition_preceded_retroactive_change and entity_pursued_public_purpose_work and proposed_buildings_subserved_that_work and government_satisfaction_and_consent_evidenced and agreement_specified_construction_conditions

predicates.company_land_acquisition: The land was acquired for an entity treated as a company for land-acquisition purposes.
predicates.acquisition_preceded_retroactive_change: The acquisition was made before a later legal change that applied retrospectively to such acquisitions.
predicates.entity_pursued_public_purpose_work: The acquiring entity was engaged in work serving a public purpose.
predicates.proposed_buildings_subserved_that_work: The proposed buildings or works facilitated the entity’s public-purpose activities.
predicates.government_satisfaction_and_consent_evid: The record, including inquiry materials or the agreement, showed that the government was satisfied about and consented to the qualifying purpose.
predicates.agreement_specified_construction_conditi: The agreement set out conditions governing the construction or execution of the proposed buildings or works.

members.legal_issue: A pre-amendment land acquisition for a company may be retrospectively validated where the acquisition was completed, the land vested in the government, and the acquisition met the requirements for a company engaged in an industry or work serving a public purpose.
material_facts: The acquisition proceedings began before the amendment took effect, and the required acquisition notification was published before then.
An award was made, the land vested in the government, and possession was delivered to the company before the amendment took effect.
The land was acquired for construction or work connected with a company engaged in manufacturing goods that benefited the public and reduced reliance on imports.
members.legal_principle: Section 7 of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1962 validated qualifying acquisitions made before July 20, 1962, notwithstanding court orders, if the acquisition was complete and the land had vested absolutely in the government under section 16 or section 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and the acquisition fell within section 40(1)(aa) as amended. The Court applied the interpretation in R. L. Arora v. State of U.P. (the second Arora case) and followed Himalayan Tiles and Marbles v. Francis Victor Coutinho.
members.conclusion: The acquisition satisfied the conditions for retrospective validation and the challenge to its validity failed.

rule.if: appeal_challenging_land_acquisition and acquisition_before_amendment and land_vested_in_government and company_industry_served_public_purpose and acquired_work_served_company_public_purpose

predicates.appeal_challenging_land_acquisition: The proceeding was an appeal challenging the validity of a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_before_amendment: The acquisition was made before the relevant amendment took effect.
predicates.land_vested_in_government: The acquisition was completed and the land vested absolutely in the government.
predicates.company_industry_served_public_purpose: The company was engaged, or was taking steps to engage, in an industry or work that served a public purpose.
predicates.acquired_work_served_company_public_purp: The building or work for which the land was acquired served the public purpose of the company's industry or work.

members.legal_issue: Children born from a marriage void because it was contracted while an earlier spouse was living are legitimate and may be treated as successors to their parent’s property for the purposes of an eviction proceeding.
material_facts: The deceased owner contracted a second marriage while his first marriage was subsisting.
Two daughters were born from the second marriage.
The daughters were joined in the pending revision concerning an eviction proceeding over property owned by their father.
The court held that their inheritance rights did not require final adjudication in the eviction proceeding.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 bars a marriage when either party has a living spouse, and section 11 makes a marriage in contravention of that condition void. Under section 16(1), a child of a marriage void under section 11 is legitimate and may succeed to a parent’s property. The court relied on these provisions while clarifying that the eviction proceeding did not finally determine title.
members.conclusion: The daughters were entitled to be treated as successors to their father’s property for the purposes of the eviction proceeding, although their ultimate rights of inheritance and title were not finally determined.

predicates.tenancy_eviction_proceeding: A proceeding was brought to evict a tenant from property under tenancy law.
predicates.deceased_parent_owned_disputed_property: The parent of the child owned the property in dispute and had died.
predicates.child_born_from_marriage_during_prior_ma: The child was born from a marriage contracted while an earlier marriage of that parent was still subsisting.

members.legal_issue: Children of a void marriage are treated as legitimate for inheritance from their parents even when the marriage and the children's birth preceded the amendment that extended that protection.
material_facts: The children were born of a marriage contracted while a regional law prohibited and voided a second marriage during the lifetime of a prior spouse.
The children were born before the amendment to the legitimacy provision.
They claimed shares in property left by their father.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, as amended by the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976, applies notwithstanding that a marriage is void and whether the child was born before or after the amendment, or a decree of nullity was granted. Section 16(3) limits the resulting property rights to the parents' property. The Court applied the principles governing statutory legal fictions in J.K. Cotton Spinning and Weaving Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, American Home Products Corporation v. Mac Laboratories, East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council, and M. Venugopal v. Divisional Manager, LIC.
members.conclusion: The children were to be treated as legitimate and were entitled to inherit their father's property; the statutory status did not give them rights in property of persons other than their parents.

rule.if: parental_inheritance_proceeding and child_born_of_void_marriage and child_claims_property_of_parent and legitimacy_protection_covers_children_regardless_of_birth_timing

predicates.parental_inheritance_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a child's claim to inherit from a parent.
predicates.child_born_of_void_marriage: A child was born of a marriage that was void under the law governing it.
predicates.child_claims_property_of_parent: The child claims property belonging to one of the child's parents.
predicates.legitimacy_protection_covers_children_re: The applicable legitimacy rule extends protection to children without distinguishing by when they were born.
predicates.child_is_legitimate_for_inheritance_from: The child is treated as legitimate for inheritance from a parent.

members.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel does not prevent a statutory assessment where the law imposes the assessment, and an assurance limited to government-run units does not exempt a separate incorporated company.
material_facts: A central government letter stated that no separate exemption notification was required while the units were run by the Government of India in the public sector.
The company relied on that correspondence to claim that the State Government was estopped from levying assessment.
The company was a separate legal entity that ran its own industry, and the applicable amended law imposed assessment liability on qualifying lessees.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the rule that there can be no estoppel against a statute. It also construed the State Government’s letter according to its terms: it concerned units run by the Government of India in the public sector, whereas the company was a distinct legal entity running its own industry. The assessment liability arose under Sections 2(j), 3 and 12 of the Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, as amended.
members.conclusion: The State Government was not estopped from levying the assessment. There can be no estoppel against a statute, and the correspondence did not promise an exemption to a separate company merely because its shares were government-owned.

predicates.state_non_agricultural_assessment_procee: A state authority seeks non-agricultural assessment in a proceeding concerning land.
predicates.statutory_assessment_duty_applies: The applicable law imposes assessment liability on the claimant in the circumstances.
predicates.claimant_invokes_government_assurance: The claimant relies on a government assurance as a reason to resist the assessment.

members.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel does not prevent assessment contrary to a statute, and a statement that no separate exemption notification is required for government-run public-sector units does not promise exemption to a separate company.
material_facts: A government letter stated that no separate notification was required to exempt the land from assessment so long as the units were run by the Union in the public sector.
The appellant was a company with a legal identity separate from the Union and ran its own industry.
The company claimed that it had acted on the letter and that the State was estopped from assessing it.
members.legal_principle: There can be no estoppel against a statute. In addition, the letter, read according to its terms, did not promise exemption to a company that was a separate legal entity and ran its own industry. The Court applied the separate-entity principle recognized in Western Coalfields Limited v. Special Area Development Authority, Korba, Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, and Heavy Engineering Mazdoor Union v. State of Bihar.
members.conclusion: The State was not estopped from assessing the company: estoppel could not operate against the statute, and the letter did not promise an exemption to a separate company.

predicates.promissory_estoppel_claim_in_assessment_: A company claims that a government promise prevents an assessment imposed on it.
predicates.statute_imposes_assessment_liability: The applicable statute imposes assessment liability on the company in the circumstances.
predicates.communication_does_not_promise_company_e: The government communication does not promise an exemption to the company itself.
predicates.company_is_separate_from_government: The company has a legal identity distinct from the government.

members.legal_issue: Government land in a scheduled area cannot be leased or otherwise transferred to a non-tribal person for mining, subject to the exception for a State instrumentality or a cooperative society composed solely of Scheduled Tribes.
material_facts: Mining leases for land in a notified scheduled area were granted by the State to non-tribal individuals and companies.
Some individual lessees transferred their mining interests to companies.
The lands included reserved forest and other land in the scheduled area.
members.legal_principle: Article 244 and paragraph 5(2)(b) of the Fifth Schedule empower regulation of land allotment in scheduled areas for peace and good government; paragraph 5(2)(a) concerns restrictions on land transfers. Section 3(1)(a) of the Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Area Land Transfer Regulation, as amended in 1970, prohibits transfers of immovable property in the scheduled area except to a Scheduled Tribe or a cooperative society composed solely of Scheduled Tribes. Article 298 is subject to the Constitution, including the Fifth Schedule. A lease is a transfer of an interest in land under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act. The Court relied on P. Rami Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Manchegowda v. State of Karnataka, Lingappa Pochanna Appelwar v. State of Maharashtra, and M/s. Victoria Granites (P) Ltd. v. P. Rama Rao.
members.conclusion: The State is a person for purposes of the land-transfer restriction, and a lease transfers an interest in land. Government leases and transfers to non-tribals are void, except transfers to a State instrumentality or a cooperative society composed solely of Scheduled Tribes.

predicates.challenge_to_land_transfer_in_scheduled_: A proceeding challenged a land transfer or mining lease involving land in a scheduled area.
predicates.government_granted_mining_interest_to_no: The government granted or transferred a mining interest in the land to a person who was not a Scheduled Tribe member.
predicates.recipient_is_permitted_public_or_tribal_: The recipient was a State instrumentality or a cooperative society composed solely of Scheduled Tribes.

members.legal_issue: Land cultivated and occupied by Scheduled Tribes within the identified enclosures is their patta land and cannot be leased by the government for mining.
material_facts: Scheduled Tribe families cultivated and occupied land within five identified enclosures.
A joint survey identified the enclosures as outside the reserved forest area.
The respondents conceded that the government had no power to grant mining leases over those lands.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the protections for Scheduled Tribe land in the Fifth Schedule and the Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Area Land Transfer Regulation, together with the factual finding that the enclosures had been excluded from the reserved forest area and were occupied and cultivated by the tribes. The judgment does not identify a separate earlier case as the basis for this specific determination.
members.conclusion: The enclosure lands occupied and cultivated by the Scheduled Tribes are their patta lands, the concerned officers must grant the pattas, and the government cannot grant mining leases over them.

predicates.challenge_to_mining_lease_over_tribal_en: A proceeding challenged a government mining lease over land in an enclosure occupied by Scheduled Tribes.
predicates.scheduled_tribes_occupy_and_cultivate_th: Scheduled Tribe families occupied and cultivated the land.
predicates.enclosure_is_outside_reserved_forest: The identified enclosure was outside the reserved forest area.

members.legal_issue: A government’s control over a licensing authority does not authorize the government to take over the authority’s initial consideration and determination of licence applications.
material_facts: The statute designated a local licensing authority to consider and determine applications for cinema licences in the first instance, with the government exercising control and hearing appeals from refusals.

While an application to construct a permanent cinema was pending, the government directed that all such applications be referred to it for orders, and required specified information to accompany them.
The local licensing authority forwarded the application, and the government rejected it in the first instance; the government also rejected the applicant’s appeal.
The High Court held that the government lacked authority to require referral of all applications and decide them in the first instance.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 5(1)–(3) of the Punjab Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1952, the designated licensing authority decides applications in the first instance, while the government exercises control and hears appeals against refusals. The broad control in section 5(2) permits legitimate and reasonable general directions and may include revisional correction of erroneous grants, but does not permit the government to usurp the licensing authority’s function. Sections 8 and 9 are consistent with the statutory scheme assigning functions to both authorities; executive directions or rules cannot alter the licensing authority’s initial jurisdiction. Karnati Rangaiah v. A. Sultan Mohiddin, M/s. Vishnu Talkies v. The State, and Bharat Bhushan v. Cinema and City Magistrate were overruled to the extent they supported government determination of applications in the first instance. The Allahabad High Court’s view that the government may revise an order granting a licence was approved.
members.conclusion: The government had no authority to require all licence applications to be forwarded to it and determine them in the first instance. The licensing authority must decide applications initially; the government may issue legitimate and reasonable general directions, review erroneous grants, and hear appeals from refusals.

predicates.licensing_application_proceeding: A proceeding concerns an application for a licence to conduct a regulated activity.
predicates.initial_decision_assigned_to_local_autho: The governing scheme assigns a designated local authority the task of deciding licence applications in the first instance.
predicates.government_required_direct_referral: The government directed that applications be referred to it before the designated authority decided them.
predicates.government_decided_application_first_ins: The government itself determined an application before the designated authority had made an initial decision.

members.legal_issue: Executive control over a designated licensing authority does not permit the executive to take over that authority's statutory licensing function.
material_facts: The statutory scheme vested licensing authority in the District Magistrate, subject to control by the State Government.
The State Government directed the outcome of the application through the Licensing Authority and relied on its own role in considering whether a certificate should issue.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 5 of the Bombay Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1953, licensing authority was vested in the designated Licensing Authority, subject to State Government control. Control is not power to supplant that authority. Rule 5(2) did not allow the State Government to assume the Licensing Authority's statutory jurisdiction. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The State Government could not use its control over the Licensing Authority to assume the Licensing Authority's jurisdiction to issue a licence.

predicates.cinema_licensing_proceeding: A decision is being made about permission to use premises as a cinema.
predicates.licensing_power_vested_in_designated_aut: The governing arrangement assigns the licensing function to a designated authority.
predicates.executive_control_over_licensing_authori: The executive has a power to control the designated licensing authority.
predicates.executive_directed_licensing_outcome: The executive directed the outcome of the licensing decision.

members.legal_issue: A transferee may rely on a transferor's erroneous representation of authority to transfer property when the transferor subsequently acquires the interest represented, provided the transferee acted on the representation and did not know it was false.
material_facts: The transferor executed a sale deed for consideration on the same day he deposited the amount required to acquire higher rights in the land.
At the time of the sale, the transferor had not yet received the certificate granting those rights; he received it afterward.
The circumstances showed that the transferor represented that he was authorized to transfer the property and that the vendee acted on that representation.
The challengers did not claim to be transferees in good faith, and the Court found no basis to conclude that the vendee knew the transferor lacked the represented title.
members.legal_principle: Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act embodies an estoppel: a transferor who fraudulently or erroneously represents authority to transfer property cannot deny that representation against a transferee who acted on it, once the transferor subsequently acquires the represented interest. The transferor's good or bad faith is immaterial; the transferee's reliance is material, and section 43 does not assist a transferee who knew the transferor lacked the represented title. Section 6(a) addresses a different subject and does not displace section 43. The Court relied on Jumma Masjid v. Kodimaniandra Deviah, AIR 1962 SC 847, and approved the reasoning in Ram Swarup v. Deputy Director, Consolidation, ILR 1971 (1) All. 698; it also discussed Official Assignee, Madras v. Sanpath Naidu, 65 Mad LJ 588.
members.conclusion: Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act applied, so the transferor's subsequently acquired title enured to the vendee and the challenge to the sale failed.

rule.if: property_transfer_dispute and transferor_represented_authority_to_transfer and transfer_made_for_consideration and transferor_later_acquired_represented_interest and transferee_acted_on_representation and not transferee_knew_representation_was_false

predicates.transferor_represented_authority_to_tran: The transferor represented that they had authority to transfer the property.
predicates.transfer_made_for_consideration: The transferor purported to transfer the property for consideration.
predicates.transferor_later_acquired_represented_in: The transferor subsequently acquired the interest they had represented themselves as having.
predicates.transferee_acted_on_representation: The transferee relied on the transferor's representation when taking the transfer.
predicates.transferee_knew_representation_was_false: The transferee knew, when taking the transfer, that the transferor lacked the represented interest or authority.

members.legal_issue: A transferee for consideration may elect to claim an interest that the transferor later acquires when the transfer was made on a representation of authority, the contract remains subsisting, and the transfer was not invalid under law; the requirements of good faith and reasonable care applicable to an ostensible-owner transfer do not govern that claim.
material_facts: The transferor sold the land for consideration while litigation over the land was pending.
The transfer was not held void or contrary to law merely because it occurred during the litigation.
The transferor later became entitled, through succession, to an interest in the land.
There was no finding that the purchaser knew the transferor lacked title; knowledge of pending litigation was not treated as equivalent to such knowledge.
The purchaser's claim was supported under the rule concerning a transferor who later acquires the interest purportedly transferred.
members.legal_principle: Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 embodies the rule of feeding the estoppel: where a competent contracting transferor fraudulently or erroneously represents authority and transfers property for consideration, the transferee may, at their option, claim an interest the transferor later acquires if the contract is then subsisting. The transfer must not be invalid under law or contrary to public policy under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and a later good-faith transferee for value without notice is protected. Unlike Section 41, Section 43 does not require the transferee to establish good faith and reasonable care. Jumma Masjid, Mercara v. Kodimaniandra Deviah, AIR 1962 SC 847, explains the breadth of Section 43 and the rule of feeding the estoppel. Kartar Singh v. Harbans Kaur, (1994) 4 SCC 730, concerned an alienation that was void as to a minor's share and a contract that could not subsist; N. Srinivasa Rao v. Special Court under the A.P. Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, (2006) 4 SCC 214, concerned an invalid transfer. Neither controlled a transaction that was not invalid under law.
members.conclusion: Section 43 applied to the transfer, allowing the purchaser to claim the interest the transferor later acquired. The purchaser did not have to satisfy the good-faith and reasonable-care requirements of Section 41 merely because those requirements apply to a transfer by an ostensible owner.

members.legal_issue: A written lease term referring future disputes arising from the lease to the lessor for a final decision constitutes an arbitration agreement.
material_facts: The lease was a contract between the lessee and the State.

The lease term provided that future doubts, differences, or disputes concerning the lease, the leased land, its working, or rent or royalty payable under it would be decided by the lessor, whose decision would be final.
The lessee invoked that term to refer a royalty dispute to the State Government for decision.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 2(a) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, a written agreement to submit present or future differences to arbitration is an arbitration agreement. No particular form is required: the question is whether the parties agreed to refer disputes concerning the contract to a decision-maker for decision. The Court relied on Russel on Arbitration, 19th edition, page 59, and Chief Conservator of Forests v. Rattan Singh, which treated an identical contractual clause as an arbitration agreement.
members.conclusion: The lease term constituted an arbitration agreement referring future disputes to the Governor as lessor.

predicates.contractual_lease_dispute: The parties disputed a matter arising from the performance or terms of a lease contract.
predicates.written_term_refers_future_disputes_to_l: The written lease term referred future disputes concerning the lease to the lessor for decision.
predicates.lessor_decision_is_final: The written lease term stated that the lessor’s decision on the referred dispute would be final.

members.legal_issue: A dispute covered by a lease arbitration clause may be referred to arbitration under Section 8 when photocopies of the lease agreements are produced to establish the clause.
material_facts: A landlord sued a corporate tenant for eviction and recovery of rent under leases that contained an arbitration clause.
The tenant applied under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and produced photocopies of the lease agreements; the parties disputed whether the landlord held the originals.
The trial court rejected the application, but the High Court directed referral of the dispute to arbitration.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, photocopies of agreements may be taken on record to ascertain the existence of an arbitration clause. A dispute within the scope of that clause is arbitrable. The Court relied on no earlier cases for this holding.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right to accept the photocopies for the limited purpose of ascertaining whether an arbitration clause existed and to direct the parties to arbitration.

predicates.civil_suit_with_section_eight_applicatio: A party to a civil suit applied for referral of the dispute to arbitration.
predicates.lease_copy_shows_arbitration_clause: A copy of the lease produced in the proceeding showed an arbitration clause.

members.legal_issue: A parliamentary deeming provision incorporating earlier State levy provisions can itself create those levies retrospectively.
material_facts: The validation law deemed provisions in scheduled State enactments relating to mineral cesses and taxes to have been enacted by Parliament.
The earlier State provisions contained the terms creating the levies.
The validation law deemed those provisions to have remained in force for a specified past period.
members.legal_principle: A validating law is not required to follow a fixed verbal formula if its language achieves its purpose. The Court relied on Krishnachandra Gangopadhyaya v. Union of India, which upheld materially similar deeming language, and considered the approach in Joara Sugar Mills v. State of Madhya Pradesh and the Sugarcane Cess (Validation) Act, 1961.
members.conclusion: The deeming provision was sufficient to create the levies retrospectively; Parliament was not required to enact a separate provision expressly imposing each levy before giving it retrospective effect.

predicates.validation_statute_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law enacted to validate a levy previously held invalid by a court.
predicates.parliament_adopted_existing_levy_terms: Parliament incorporated provisions that set out the terms of the previously imposed levy.
predicates.deeming_language_makes_them_parliamentar: The law deems the incorporated provisions to have been enacted by Parliament for the relevant past period.

members.legal_issue: A parliamentary law may itself impose a cess retrospectively by adopting provisions of an invalid state law, rather than validating that state law as such.
material_facts: After the state levy had been held invalid, Parliament enacted a law concerning the cess.
The parliamentary law adopted the relevant state-law provisions, notifications, orders, and rules and provided for retrospective operation.
The demand for cess concerned a period before the parliamentary law commenced.
members.legal_principle: Under section 3 of the Sugarcane Cess (Validation) Act, 1961, the relevant state-law provisions and instruments were adopted as part of the parliamentary enactment, which operated retrospectively. The Court relied on Jaora Sugar Mills (P) Ltd. v. State of M.P. for the principle that the resulting command to pay was Parliament’s own law, not a validation of the invalid state statutes.
members.conclusion: The parliamentary law did not validate the invalid state law; it made a parliamentary law concerning the cess and gave that law retrospective operation.

predicates.challenge_to_retrospective_cess_law: The proceeding challenges a parliamentary measure that applies retrospectively to a cess.
predicates.parliament_enacted_cess_measure: Parliament enacted a law concerning the cess.
predicates.parliamentary_law_adopted_prior_levy_pro: The parliamentary law incorporated the relevant provisions and instruments previously used to impose or collect the cess.
predicates.parliamentary_law_operates_retrospective: The parliamentary law provides that its operation extends to an earlier period.

members.legal_issue: A person cannot enforce a covered covenant in a pre-Constitution agreement with a former ruler in a municipal court.
material_facts: A government letter accompanying a merger arrangement guaranteed that certain earlier orders and actions of the former ruler would not be questioned, subject to stated qualifications.
The claimants were not parties to the merger arrangement or the letter, but relied on the letter to argue that the successor government had relinquished its ability to reject the forest grant.
members.legal_principle: Article 363 of the Constitution bars municipal courts from adjudicating disputes arising from covered agreements with former rulers. Under Maharaj Umeg Singh v. State of Bombay, a person who is not a party to such an agreement cannot enforce its covenants; a party is barred by Article 363. The agreement cannot independently establish recognition or waiver where the covenant itself is not enforceable in court.
members.conclusion: The claimants could not enforce the covenant in the municipal courts; if they had been parties to the agreement, the constitutional bar would have prevented that claim as well.

predicates.municipal_claim_seeks_enforcement_of_cov: A claimant brought a municipal-court proceeding seeking to enforce a covenant in a pre-Constitution agreement with a former ruler.

members.legal_issue: A court lacks jurisdiction over a dispute whose substance is enforcement of a pre-constitutional merger agreement or guarantee made between a ruler and the Dominion government.
material_facts: The petitions challenged legislation abolishing jagirs and relied on guarantees in letters connected with merger agreements made before the Constitution commenced.
The petitioners claimed that the legislation deprived them of ownership said to be guaranteed by those instruments.
The Court found that the petitions’ substance was a claim to enforce rights under the guarantees.
members.legal_principle: Article 363(1) bars courts from exercising jurisdiction over disputes arising out of specified pre-constitutional instruments made by rulers and the Dominion government. The Court applied State of Seraikella v. Union of India, which treated a claim as arising out of an instrument where the claim’s substance was enforcement of rights under it. The Court did not decide whether the petitioners were entitled to enforce the guarantees, referring to Vajesingji Joravarsingji v. Secretary of State and Secretary of State v. Sardar Rustam Khan in discussing that unresolved question.
members.conclusion: The dispute arose out of the merger agreements and guarantees, so the Court had no jurisdiction to decide it. The Court also stated that persons who were not parties to the instruments could not enforce the obligations; it left that question unresolved because either way the petitions could not proceed.

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: A claimant brings a constitutional writ proceeding to obtain judicial relief.
predicates.dispute_arises_from_preconstitutional_in: The claim’s substance is that government action violates rights or obligations said to arise from an instrument made before the Constitution commenced between a ruler and the Dominion government.

members.legal_issue: A demonstrated threat to take control of property without lawful authority warrants constitutional relief against interference with that property.
material_facts: The managing committee held the school land and building as trustees for the school’s purposes.
Government officers formed an ad hoc committee and demanded that the existing committee hand over charge of the school.
An official communication directed officers to obtain help from local executive authorities if necessary to implement the takeover.
The respondents had no legal authority, apart from the administrative provision, to deprive the committee of its rights in the property.
members.legal_principle: Article 32 provides a remedy where a fundamental right is actually infringed or threatened with infringement. Read with Article 31(1), property cannot be taken without authority of law. The official communication authorizing recourse to local executive assistance showed that the apprehended dispossession was not merely imaginary. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The Court allowed the petition and prohibited the respondents from interfering with the petitioners’ property except by authority of law.

rule.if: constitutional_property_proceeding and property_held_as_trustee and threatened_forced_takeover and no_lawful_authority_for_takeover

predicates.constitutional_property_proceeding: A claimant brings a constitutional proceeding seeking protection of a property right.
predicates.property_held_as_trustee: A managing body holds an institution’s property as trustee for the institution’s purposes.
predicates.threatened_forced_takeover: Officials demand transfer of control and are authorized to seek executive assistance to carry it out.
predicates.no_lawful_authority_for_takeover: The officials have no legal authority for the proposed takeover.

members.legal_issue: A serious and inevitable threat of deprivation of property caused by an unlawful state order can support constitutional relief before the deprivation occurs.
material_facts: The challenged state order restored a repartition that allotted the disputed plots to another landholder.
If the order stood, the other landholder could seek possession and the State would give effect to that allotment, leaving the petitioner unable to resist the transfer.
Possession had not yet been delivered, but the resulting loss of the petitioner’s property was considered inevitable if the order remained in force.
members.legal_principle: Article 32 permits relief where an unlawful state order presents a sufficiently serious threat to a fundamental right. The Court treated the inevitable loss of property upon implementation of the order as a sufficient threat, even though possession had not yet changed hands.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the threatened property deprivation was sufficient to affect the petitioner’s fundamental rights and permit relief under Article 32 without requiring the petitioner to wait for the deprivation to occur.

predicates.constitutional_rights_petition: A person applied to the Supreme Court for relief against an alleged infringement of a fundamental right.
predicates.state_order_would_transfer_property_to_a: A state order, if implemented, would entitle another person to take possession of property claimed by the applicant.
predicates.resulting_property_loss_is_inevitable: The applicant would be unable to prevent the loss of the property if the state order were implemented.

members.legal_issue: A separately owned coke plant that does not extract coal is not a coal mine, and its operator is not an employer under the provident fund scheme, merely because the plant is adjacent to or situated on land associated with a coal mine.
material_facts: The operator owned a coke plant that had been transferred to him separately from the collieries and coal mine.
The operator leased the land on which the plant stood from the company that owned the coal mine; the plant was adjacent to the mine and situated on surface land forming part of the coalfield.
The operator did not excavate coal or carry on operations to obtain coal; the plant manufactured hard coke and other by-products.
The operator was prosecuted for failing to pay employer and employee provident fund contributions and submit returns under the scheme.
members.legal_principle: Under section 2(e) of the Coal Mines Provident Fund and Bonus Schemes Act, 1948, an employer is the owner of a coal mine. By section 8 of the General Clauses Act, the reference to the definition of owner in the repealed Indian Mines Act, 1923, is read with the corresponding definition in section 2(l) of the Mines Act, 1952; see State of Uttar Pradesh v. M.P. Singh. Section 2(b) of the 1952 Act defines a coal mine by reference to excavation for obtaining coal and includes associated works, machinery, tramways and sidings. The word “or” before “belonging to a coal mine” is read as “and,” so those subsidiary things are included only when they appertain to and belong to the mine, in the sense of being under the same ownership. Mere adjacency or location on coalfield land does not suffice.
members.conclusion: The operator was not the owner of a coal mine and was not liable as an employer under the scheme on these facts. The appeal was dismissed and the acquittal upheld.

predicates.scheme_employer_prosecution: The proceeding alleges that a person failed to meet scheme obligations on the ground that the person was an employer of a coal mine.
