members.legal_issue: A distinct coke oven plant used to manufacture hard coke does not vest with a nationalised coal mine merely because it is located in or associated with the mine.
material_facts: The coal mine and coke oven had been transferred and leased separately.
The mine was nationalised, but no action was taken to nationalise the coke oven plant.
The coke oven was a significant facility for manufacturing hard coke, not merely minor equipment subsidiary to the mining operation.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3(b) and 3(j), including clauses 3(j)(vi) and 3(j)(x), establish a statutory distinction between a coke oven plant and a mine. A facility for manufacturing hard coke with an independent existence is not treated as part of a mine merely because it is associated with mining; minor equipment used for washing coal or manufacturing coke may fall within the definition of a mine. The court rejected the argument based on section 8 of the Transfer of Property Act. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The coke oven plant was distinct from the mine and did not vest in the Central Government by virtue of the mine’s nationalisation.

predicates.appeal_from_lower_court_judgment: A party appealed from a lower court’s judgment concerning the treatment of a coke oven associated with a coal mine.
predicates.coal_mine_nationalised: The coal mine was taken over through nationalisation.
predicates.coke_oven_plant_not_separately_nationali: No separate step was taken to nationalise the coke oven plant.
predicates.hard_coke_facility_has_independent_exist: The facility was a significant, independently existing operation for manufacturing hard coke rather than minor equipment subsidiary to mining.

members.legal_issue: An indivisible scheme that is partly invalid cannot be upheld in part and must stand or fall as a whole.
material_facts: The scheme combined development and housing purposes and covered land both within and outside municipal limits.
The Court found that the scheme was one and indivisible, rather than separable into independently valid and invalid parts.
members.legal_principle: Where a statutory scheme is one and indivisible, it cannot be treated as partly valid and partly invalid; it must stand or fall as a whole.
members.conclusion: The scheme could not be upheld in part and had to be set aside as a whole.

predicates.statutory_improvement_scheme_challenge: A proceeding challenges the validity of a statutory improvement scheme.
predicates.scheme_is_indivisible: The scheme cannot be separated into distinct portions that can operate independently.
predicates.part_of_scheme_is_invalid: At least one part of the scheme is invalid.

members.legal_issue: An award containing an invalid component must be set aside in its entirety when that component cannot be separated from the rest of the award.
material_facts: The arbitrator included unauthorized depreciation and appreciation in a lump-sum valuation.
The award did not permit the value of those unauthorized adjustments to be separated from the valuation as a whole.
members.legal_principle: Section 30 of the Indian Arbitration Act, 1940, permits an award to be set aside when it is otherwise invalid. An award invalid for an excess of jurisdiction may fail only to the extent of the excess if that part can be separated; where the unauthorized amount cannot be severed from the valuation, the entire award must be set aside.
members.conclusion: Because the unauthorized component could not be severed, the award failed in its entirety.

predicates.award_challenge_proceeding: A party asks a court to set aside an arbitration award.
predicates.award_contains_invalid_component: The award includes a component that is invalid because the arbitrator exceeded the authority conferred by the reference.
predicates.invalid_component_cannot_be_severed: The invalid component cannot be separated from the rest of the award.

members.legal_issue: The delegated rule-making power to regulate grants of minor-mineral concessions is constitutionally valid because the governing statute supplies sufficient guidance.
material_facts: The State made rules governing quarry and mining leases for minor minerals under a statutory delegation.
The lessees challenged the delegation as excessive and unguided.
members.legal_principle: Section 15(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 must be read with the statute's public-interest object, the meaning and scope of regulating the grant of concessions and connected matters, the illustrative matters in section 13(2), and the restrictions in sections 4 to 12. Parliament's authority derives from Entry 54 of the Union List, to which Entry 23 of the State List is subject. Legislative history and practice are relevant to interpretation and validity: State of Bombay v. Narothamdas Jethabai and State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley. The illustrative character of particular rule-making topics is supported by King Emperor v. Sibnath Banerjee, Om Prakash v. Union of India, and Shiv Kirpal Singh v. V.V. Giri.
members.conclusion: The delegation is constitutional and does not amount to excessive delegation of legislative power.

rule.if: minor_mineral_rulemaking_case and statute_states_public_purpose and statute_supplies_subject_matter_guidance and statute_sets_related_constraints

predicates.minor_mineral_rulemaking_case: The proceeding challenges a delegation to make rules regulating grants of concessions for minor minerals.
predicates.statute_states_public_purpose: The governing statute identifies a public-interest purpose for regulating mines and developing minerals.
predicates.statute_supplies_subject_matter_guidance: The statute confines rulemaking to regulating mineral concessions and purposes connected with their grant.
predicates.statute_sets_related_constraints: The statute contains related restrictions and identifies illustrative matters that guide the exercise of the delegated power.

members.legal_issue: Delegated authority to regulate royalties for minor minerals is sufficiently guided and is not an unbridled delegation of legislative power.
material_facts: The State fixed and enhanced royalties for minor minerals under authority delegated by Parliament.

The governing framework stated the purpose of regulating and developing mines and minerals and included provisions addressing mineral conservation, environmental protection, lease termination, and prevention of illegal mining.
The framework also required State rules and notifications to be placed before the State Legislature.
members.legal_principle: Section 15(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, read with Section 15(1-A), confers rule-making power concerning minor minerals. The guidance is found in the Act’s purpose and scheme, the illustrative matters for rulemaking, relevant provisions including Sections 4-A, 17, 18 and 23-C, and the requirement in Section 28(3) to place State rules and notifications before the State Legislature. D.K. Trivedi & Sons v. State of Gujarat held that the power under Section 15 is guided and includes power to alter royalty and dead rent. The Court also relied on the principles concerning guided delegation and statutory purpose in Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Birla Cotton, Spinning and Weaving Mills, Corporation of Calcutta v. Liberty Cinema, Bhatnagar & Co. v. Union of India, and State of Tamil Nadu v. Hind Stone; it applied the purposive approach in Heydon’s Case and authorities following it.
members.conclusion: The delegation to the State is not excessive or unbridled; statutory purposes, provisions, and legislative scrutiny provide sufficient guidance and checks.

rule.if: minor_mineral_royalty_rulemaking_case and state_received_delegated_rulemaking_power and statutory_policy_guides_mineral_regulation and related_rules_and_controls_exist and legislative_scrutiny_is_provided

predicates.minor_mineral_royalty_rulemaking_case: The proceeding concerns rules or notifications governing royalty for minor minerals.
predicates.state_received_delegated_rulemaking_powe: The State exercised rule-making authority delegated to it by the legislature.
predicates.statutory_policy_guides_mineral_regulati: The governing framework states a policy of regulating and developing mineral resources.
predicates.related_rules_and_controls_exist: The governing framework contains related provisions addressing matters such as conservation, environmental protection, and mining operations.
predicates.legislative_scrutiny_is_provided: The governing framework requires State rules or notifications to be placed before the State Legislature.

members.legal_issue: A substantial increase in dead rent is not an unreasonable restriction when assessed together with a corresponding substantial reduction in royalty.
material_facts: An amendment substantially increased dead rent and drastically reduced royalty.
The affected concession holders argued that the increased dead rent unreasonably restricted their ability to carry on business.
The two charges operated together under the concession rules.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution protects the right to carry on trade or business, subject to reasonable restrictions. The rates of dead rent cannot be assessed in isolation where the same amendment drastically reduces royalty. Section 15(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 authorizes the State to amend the rules, subject to applicable limitations.
members.conclusion: The dead-rent increase was valid and did not impose an unreasonable restriction when considered together with the reduced royalty.

rule.if: minor_mineral_lease_rule_amendment_case and dead_rent_is_increased and royalty_is_substantially_reduced_in_same_scheme and combined_burden_is_not_unreasonable

predicates.minor_mineral_lease_rule_amendment_case: The proceeding challenges a State rule amendment affecting financial terms of minor-mineral concessions.
predicates.dead_rent_is_increased: The amended rules increase the fixed charge based on the leased area.
predicates.royalty_is_substantially_reduced_in_same: The same regulatory scheme substantially reduces the charge based on minerals extracted.
predicates.combined_burden_is_not_unreasonable: The overall financial terms, considered together, do not impose an unreasonable burden on concession holders.

members.legal_issue: The later amendment permitting royalty without dead rent is valid and does not impose an unreasonable restriction when the royalty rates are assessed in the context of the former combined charges.
material_facts: A later amendment deleted dead rent and prescribed royalty rates that were higher than the immediately preceding reduced rates.
The lessees challenged the royalty increase as excessive and unreasonable.
The preceding scheme had imposed dead rent as well as royalty, and the Court compared the new rates with the earlier scheme that included both charges.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution permits reasonable restrictions. The rates must be considered in the context of the whole payment scheme, including the fact that dead rent ceased to be payable, rather than compared only with a temporary, substantially reduced royalty rate. Section 15(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 authorized amendments to the State rules. The Court also applied the four-year frequency restriction and found the royalty increase to be the first increase in the relevant block.
members.conclusion: The later amendment was valid and constitutional and did not violate the right to carry on business; the royalty rates were not unreasonable when considered in the context of the earlier combined charges and the elimination of dead rent.

predicates.minor_mineral_rule_amendment_case: The proceeding challenges a State amendment changing charges for minor-mineral concessions.
predicates.dead_rent_ceases_to_be_payable: The amended scheme no longer requires payment of dead rent.
predicates.royalty_increase_is_first_in_rule_anchor: The royalty rate has not previously been increased during the applicable four-year block measured from commencement of the rules.
predicates.total_charge_is_not_unreasonable_in_comp: The overall burden under the amended scheme is not unreasonable when compared with the earlier scheme that charged both royalty and dead rent.

members.legal_issue: An ordinary writ petition is not maintainable by a petitioner whose asserted personal right is not affected by the challenged action, absent an applicable exceptional basis for standing.
material_facts: The petitioner challenged a mining lease granted to another party, alleging that the leased area included the area for which he had applied.
The petitioner’s application was not for any part of the area covered by the other party’s lease, so he had no interest in the subject matter of that lease.
The petitioner relied on an alleged direct infringement of his own right and was neither a party to nor a person aggrieved or affected by the grant.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226, the existence of a right affected by the challenged action ordinarily grounds the court’s jurisdiction; the relevant right is ordinarily the petitioner’s personal or individual right. A proprietary interest is not essential if another personal interest is affected, and exceptional cases may permit a prejudicially affected person without a proprietary or fiduciary interest to seek relief. The rule may be relaxed for writs such as habeas corpus or quo warranto. For a stranger, intervention may depend on the nature and extent of the asserted interest and whether the public interest calls for intervention, and ultimately rests in the court’s discretion. The Court relied on Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India, State of Orissa v. Madan Gopal Rungta, Calcutta Gas Company v. State of West Bengal, Godde Venkateswara Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, and R. v. Thames Magistrates’ Court, ex parte Greenbaum.
members.conclusion: The petitioner had no locus standi, and the writ petition was not maintainable.

rule.if: ordinary_writ_proceeding and petitioner_asserts_personal_right and asserted_right_not_affected and petitioner_not_party_or_affected and no_exceptional_basis_for_stranger_standing

predicates.ordinary_writ_proceeding: The proceeding is an ordinary application for a constitutional writ, rather than a proceeding such as habeas corpus or quo warranto.
predicates.petitioner_asserts_personal_right: The petitioner seeks relief on the basis that the challenged action directly infringed the petitioner’s own right.
predicates.asserted_right_not_affected: The facts show that the challenged action did not affect the right the petitioner asserted.
predicates.petitioner_not_party_or_affected: The petitioner was neither a party to the relevant subject matter nor a person aggrieved or otherwise affected by the challenged action.
predicates.no_exceptional_basis_for_stranger_standi: The circumstances do not provide an exceptional basis, such as a public-interest reason for intervention, to permit a stranger to seek relief.

members.legal_issue: A writ petition challenging an acquisition is not maintainable where the petitioners had no right or interest in the land when they filed it and cannot alter that position on appeal.
material_facts: In a set of acquisition proceedings, the High Court recorded that the petitioners had no right or interest in the relevant land when they filed their writ petitions.
Their counsel admitted that position before the High Court.
The petitioners could not establish a basis for taking a different position before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the rule that an appellant cannot depart from the position on which the case proceeded below where that position was admitted, and upheld the conclusion that a petitioner without a right or interest in the land at filing could not maintain the writ petition.
members.conclusion: The writ petitions were not maintainable, and the High Court was justified in dismissing them on that basis.

rule.if: land_acquisition_appeal and petitioner_lacked_land_right_or_interest_when_filing and lack_of_interest_admitted_below and no_basis_for_changing_position_on_appeal

predicates.land_acquisition_appeal: An appeal concerns a writ petition challenging a land acquisition.
predicates.petitioner_lacked_land_right_or_interest: The petitioner had no right or interest in the land when the writ petition was filed.
predicates.lack_of_interest_admitted_below: The petitioner or counsel admitted the lack of a right or interest before the lower court.
predicates.no_basis_for_changing_position_on_appeal: The petitioner has no sufficient basis to take a different position on appeal.

members.legal_issue: A court need not accept claimant testimony in a land-acquisition compensation proceeding merely because it was not effectively challenged in cross-examination or rebutted by contrary evidence.
material_facts: The claimant relied on oral testimony in support of a higher compensation claim.
The Supreme Court considered whether testimony must be accepted when the opposing party did not effectively cross-examine the witnesses or adduce rebuttal evidence.
The Court held that a court may test the testimony against probabilities and its experience and reject it if it is untrustworthy.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the evidentiary principle stated in Chaturbhuj Pande v. Collector, Raigarh, AIR 1969 SC 255: a court is not bound to accept testimony merely because it was not effectively cross-examined or rebutted, and may test it against probabilities and experience.
members.conclusion: A court may reject unchallenged or inadequately challenged testimony if, on assessment of probabilities and experience, it finds the testimony untrustworthy.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding determines compensation for land acquired by compulsory acquisition.
predicates.claimant_testimony_not_effectively_chall: The claimant's witness testimony was not effectively tested in cross-examination or by contrary evidence.
predicates.testimony_found_untrustworthy_on_probabi: The court assessed the testimony against probabilities and experience and found it untrustworthy.

members.legal_issue: A fact-finder assessing compensation is not bound to accept oral evidence merely because it was not effectively challenged or contradicted by rebuttal evidence.
material_facts: The appellants relied on oral testimony to support their claimed value for the orchard.
The appellants produced no documentary evidence supporting that claim.
The witnesses were not effectively cross-examined, and the Collector adduced no evidence in rebuttal.
The High Court found the oral evidence unacceptable after assessing it in light of probabilities and experience.
members.legal_principle: In assessing the value of oral evidence, judges may use their experience of life and test the evidence against probabilities; they are not bound to accept testimony simply because it was not effectively cross-examined or contradicted by rebuttal evidence. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The court was not bound to accept the appellants’ oral evidence and could reject it as unacceptable.

rule.if: compensation_assessment_appeal and claim_supported_by_oral_testimony and no_documentary_support and fact_finder_assesses_evidence_on_probabilities

predicates.compensation_assessment_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in which compensation is being assessed.
predicates.claim_supported_by_oral_testimony: The claimant relied on oral testimony to support the claimed compensation.
predicates.no_documentary_support: The claimant supplied no documentary evidence supporting the claim.
predicates.fact_finder_assesses_evidence_on_probabi: The fact-finder assessed the testimony against probabilities and its experience of life.

members.legal_issue: A criminal case should be transferred when the presiding judge’s strongly expressed earlier views create a continuing reasonable apprehension that the judge may not approach the matter fairly, even though the earlier order was set aside and a higher court directed a fresh decision uninfluenced by those views.
material_facts: The complainant sought transfer of a pending criminal sessions case after the trial judge had discharged the accused on the relevant charges.
The discharge order contained strongly worded observations about alleged misuse of the relevant law and concluded that there was no real basis to frame charges under it.
The High Court set aside the discharge order and directed the trial judge to reconsider the matter afresh without being influenced by the earlier observations.
The complainant continued to apprehend that the trial judge’s earlier views would affect the fresh decision.
members.legal_principle: The majority applied the principle that justice must not only be done but must also appear to be done. Although setting aside an order ordinarily obliterates its findings, and a direction to disregard earlier observations ordinarily safeguards a fresh decision, transfer may still be warranted where the nature and force of those observations create a reasonable apprehension that the judge has committed to an approach and may not take a fair, non-partisan view. The inquiry concerns the reasonableness of the apprehension, not whether the judge is actually biased or incapable of reconsidering the matter. The majority cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion. In dissent, Justice Banumathi considered good and sufficient grounds necessary, treated mere presumptions or casual observations as insufficient, and relied on Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and K.P. Tiwari v. State of M.P.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed and the criminal case was directed to be transferred to another competent court because the complainant’s apprehension was reasonable despite the safeguards in the remand order.

rule.if: criminal_case_transfer_request and strong_prior_judicial_commitment and remand_neutrality_direction and continuing_reasonable_apprehension

predicates.criminal_case_transfer_request: A party sought transfer of a pending criminal case from the court hearing it.
predicates.strong_prior_judicial_commitment: The presiding judge previously expressed strongly worded views on the matter that must be reconsidered.
predicates.remand_neutrality_direction: A higher court set aside the earlier decision and directed the presiding judge to reconsider the matter without being influenced by the earlier views.
predicates.continuing_reasonable_apprehension: The party continued to have a reasonable apprehension that the earlier views could prevent a fair and non-partisan reconsideration.

members.legal_issue: A criminal case should be transferred when the trial magistrate's partisan opposition to an accused person's transfer application jeopardizes the fairness of the trial.
material_facts: An accused person applied to transfer a criminal case pending before the magistrate.
The magistrate filed an affidavit opposing transfer on behalf of the administration and advanced a position on an issue relevant to the accused person's defence.
The court concluded that the magistrate had entered the arena and that the essential attributes of a fair and impartial trial were in jeopardy.
members.legal_principle: A transfer is expedient in the interests of justice where the conduct of the magistrate presiding over a criminal trial puts the fairness and impartiality of that trial in jeopardy. The judgment relies on the elementary principle that judges must not enter the arena and must remain impartial; it cites no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The case should be transferred to a court of competent jurisdiction in the interests of justice, without deciding the merits of the accused person's other contentions.

rule.if: criminal_case_transfer_petition and accused_sought_transfer and trial_magistrate_filed_opposition_affidavit and affidavit_put_fair_trial_in_jeopardy

predicates.criminal_case_transfer_petition: A petition sought transfer of a pending criminal case.
predicates.accused_sought_transfer: An accused person asked for the criminal case to be transferred.
predicates.trial_magistrate_filed_opposition_affida: The magistrate trying the case filed an affidavit opposing the transfer request.
predicates.affidavit_put_fair_trial_in_jeopardy: The magistrate's affidavit took a partisan position that placed the fairness and impartiality of the trial in jeopardy.

members.legal_issue: A local customary record does not displace the general custom on collateral inheritance when it addresses only direct inheritance from the natural father and no contrary local custom is proved.
material_facts: The local customary record addressed whether an adopted son could inherit from his natural father and stated that he could not inherit directly, while recognizing an entitlement to property that would come to the adoptive father as a collateral.
The record did not address inheritance from collaterals in the natural family.

The cited instances of exclusion concerned inheritance in the presence of natural brothers or an uncontested transfer following a daughter’s remarriage, and did not establish a contrary custom governing collateral inheritance.
The party asserting a local custom that excluded the claimants did not establish that custom.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Punjab Laws Act, 1872 makes an applicable, established custom the rule of decision and otherwise applies personal law; the party asserting custom must prove both its applicability and content, as stated in Daya Ram v. Sohel Singh and affirmed in Abdul Hussain Khan v. Bibi Sona Dero. A local Riwaj-i-am ordinarily has an initial presumption of correctness and prevails over conflicting general custom, but the court found no relevant conflict here; it relied on Jai Kapur v. Sher Singh. Article 48 of Rattigan’s Digest records the general custom preserving an appointed heir’s right against collaterals in the natural family.
members.conclusion: The local customary record and cited instances did not establish a special custom excluding the claimants from collateral inheritance, so the general custom applied.

predicates.customary_inheritance_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim to inheritance governed by customary law.
predicates.local_customary_record_addresses_direct_: The local customary record concerns whether an appointed heir may inherit directly from the natural father.
predicates.no_proven_local_rule_on_collateral_inher: The evidence does not establish a local customary rule excluding an appointed heir or descendants from inheritance from collaterals in the natural family.

members.legal_issue: A record of local custom does not displace the general rule preferring a daughter if it is unreliable and untrustworthy as evidence of the custom it purports to record.
material_facts: The collateral relied on a district record of custom whose answers stated that daughters were excluded by male kindred and that no distinction was made between ancestral and self-acquired property.
The record's compiler acknowledged that people had sometimes stated what the custom should be rather than what it actually was.
The record contained collected instances of daughters inheriting, and its answers on daughters' succession had been contradicted and discredited in judicial proceedings.
The disputed entries adversely affected women's rights, although women had no opportunity to appear before the revenue authorities.
members.legal_principle: Riwaj-i-am entries receive an initial presumption of correctness, but the evidence needed to rebut that presumption depends on the circumstances. The presumption is weaker when the recorded custom conflicts with the general custom or adversely affects women who had no opportunity to participate. Under Qamar-ud-Din v. Mt. Fateh Bano, a record can support a special custom if it is reliable and trustworthy, carefully prepared, free of internal contradictions, and not merely a record of what respondents wished the custom to be; an unreliable record has no presumptive value. The Court also relied on the principles in Beg v. Allah Ditta, Mt. Vaishno Ditti v. Mt. Rameshri, Khan Beg v. Mt. Fateh Khatun, Jagat Singh v. Mst. Jiwan, Mst. Subhani v. Nawab, and Mohammad Khalil v. Mohammad Bakhsh.
members.conclusion: The district records were not reliable or trustworthy on daughters' succession to self-acquired property, had no presumptive value on that question, and did not shift the initial burden from the collateral to the daughter.

rule.if: succession_dispute and record_claims_custom_excluding_daughter and (record_conflicts_with_general_custom or record_adversely_affects_unrepresented_women) and compiler_doubted_actual_custom and record_contains_contrary_instances and record_was_discredited_in_judicial_proceedings

predicates.succession_dispute: A proceeding concerns competing claims to succession to a deceased person's property.
predicates.record_claims_custom_excluding_daughter: A record of custom states that male kindred exclude a daughter from succession.
predicates.record_conflicts_with_general_custom: The custom stated in the record conflicts with the generally prevailing custom on the succession in dispute.
predicates.record_adversely_affects_unrepresented_w: The recorded custom adversely affects women who had no opportunity to participate in its recording.
predicates.compiler_doubted_actual_custom: The compiler stated that respondents sometimes described what the custom should be rather than what it actually was.
predicates.record_contains_contrary_instances: The record includes instances inconsistent with the custom stated in its answers.
predicates.record_was_discredited_in_judicial_proce: Courts had previously rejected the record's statements on the relevant custom as incorrect.

members.legal_issue: Requisitioning premises to provide living accommodation for an employee of a public utility corporation may serve a public purpose when the accommodation is a statutory activity essential to the efficient performance of the corporation’s public services.
material_facts: The government requisitioned premises to house an officer of a road transport corporation that was a public utility concern.
The requisition did not name a particular individual, and the premises were available to the corporation to house an officer to be named later.
The officer was required to perform duties in the relevant city, and the corporation appointed officers it considered necessary for the efficient performance of its functions.
The corporation had statutory power to provide living accommodation for employees.

The court found that accommodation for the corporation’s employees was essential to the efficient operation of the road transport system, with which the community’s general interest was directly and vitally concerned.
members.legal_principle: Under section 5(1) of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948, requisition must be for a public purpose. Sections 14, 18, 19(1)(c), and 19(2)(a) and (b) of the Road Transport Corporations Act, 1950, read together, establish the corporation’s functions and its power to provide employee accommodation as part of its statutory activities. A purpose is public when the community’s general interest, rather than merely an individual’s particular interest, is directly and vitally concerned. Applying Hamabai Framjee Petit v. Secretary of State for India in Council, State of Bombay v. Bhanji Munji, and State of Bombay v. Ali Gulshan, the Court held that accommodation essential to the efficient functioning of a public utility corporation can serve that public interest.
members.conclusion: The requisition was for a public purpose and was validly made.

rule.if: land_requisition_for_employee_housing and public_utility_employer and statutory_employee_housing_function and employee_needed_for_efficient_service and accommodation_essential_to_public_service

predicates.land_requisition_for_employee_housing: The proceeding concerns land requisitioned to provide living accommodation for an employee.
predicates.public_utility_employer: The employee’s employer provides a public utility service whose activities directly and vitally concern the community’s general interest.
predicates.statutory_employee_housing_function: The employer has statutory authority to provide living accommodation for its employees as part of its activities.
predicates.employee_needed_for_efficient_service: The employer requires the employee to perform duties necessary for the efficient performance of its functions.
predicates.accommodation_essential_to_public_servic: Providing accommodation for employees is essential to the efficient operation of the public service.

members.legal_issue: Providing residential accommodation to a public institution’s employees can constitute use of premises for the furtherance of the institution’s activities.
material_facts: The landlord was a university that had received the building under a will and obtained probate of the will.
The university sought eviction so that the building could be used to provide residential accommodation for its employees.
The lower courts concurrently found that the university’s need for the premises was bona fide and that the building was residential in nature, although some portions had been used commercially.
members.legal_principle: Section 22 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 permits a public institution to seek eviction notwithstanding Section 14 or any other law when the requirements in the section are met. Under Section 22(d), premises bona fide required by a public institution for the furtherance of its activities may be recovered; the Explanation includes educational institutions within ‘public institution.’ Providing residential accommodation for employees can directly further an institution’s activities because adequate housing helps employees remain contented and enables the institution to function properly. The Court stated that it was unnecessary to deal with the earlier decisions cited at the hearing.
members.conclusion: The employee-housing use furthered the university’s activities, so the eviction applications fell within Section 22(d) and the eviction orders were correct. The appeals and special leave petitions were dismissed.

predicates.institutional_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding is an eviction case brought by an institution against occupants of premises it owns or controls.
predicates.landlord_is_public_institution: The landlord is a public institution, including an educational institution.
predicates.premises_bona_fide_needed_for_employee_h: The institution genuinely requires the premises to provide residential accommodation for its employees.
predicates.employee_housing_supports_institutional_: Providing accommodation for the employees helps the institution operate effectively.

members.legal_issue: A prior will cannot be given effect after a valid later will expressly revokes it.
material_facts: The testator had made an earlier will in favour of the challengers.
In a later valid will, the testator expressly revoked or cancelled the earlier will and made a different disposition of the property.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the effect of the testator’s express revocation of the earlier will in the later will, which it found validly executed under the requirements of Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, with proof of attestation under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The earlier will stood revoked and could not be given effect.

predicates.competing_wills_proceeding: The proceeding concerns competing wills made by the same testator.
predicates.later_will_is_valid: The later will is proved to have been validly executed.
predicates.later_will_expressly_revokes_earlier_wil: The later will expressly cancels the earlier will.

members.legal_issue: A duly proved later will that expresses the testator’s last wishes makes an inconsistent earlier will redundant without a separate express revocation.
material_facts: An earlier will distributed the testator’s share among his sons.
The later will bequeathed the testator’s share to one son and included a general statement cancelling any prior will.
The Court found the later will duly executed and proved.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that a later duly proved will represents the testator’s last wish and makes an inconsistent earlier will redundant; a separate categorical recital specifically identifying and cancelling the earlier will is not necessary for that result.
members.conclusion: Once the later will was duly proved, the earlier will became redundant because the later will represented the testator’s last wishes.

predicates.will_validity_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the effect or validity of competing wills.
predicates.earlier_will_exists: The testator made an earlier will dealing with the relevant property.
predicates.inconsistent_later_will_proved: The testator made a later will that was proved and made a different disposition of the relevant property.

members.legal_issue: A statutory board’s authority to partition family property is not unbridled when its rights-affecting function carries quasi-judicial duties and its conduct remains reviewable in writ proceedings.
material_facts: The amendment entrusted the existing statutory Board with partitioning the estate and made the resulting partition valid.
The Board was a longstanding body whose members included senior representatives of the family’s branches.
The Board’s partition decisions would affect members’ rights, and its actions remained subject to constitutional writ review.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 14 and held that a statutory body determining rights must act quasi-judicially. It relied on the availability of review under Article 226 and on the principles of natural justice discussed in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, M. S. Gill v. Union of India, and Organo Chemical Industries v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The Board’s power was not unbridled or unconstitutional because the statute implied quasi-judicial responsibilities and its deviations could be reviewed under Article 226.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_partition_am: A party challenges the constitutionality of legislation changing how a family estate is partitioned.
predicates.statutory_board_determines_member_rights: A board created or continued by statute is assigned to decide matters that affect members’ rights.
predicates.writ_review_available: The board’s departures from legal requirements or arbitrary or bad-faith conduct can be challenged through constitutional writ proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A statutory board partitioning property while determining members’ rights must provide the fairness and procedural opportunities required of a quasi-judicial body.
material_facts: The Board was assigned to partition property and thereby determine the rights of family members.
The petitioner argued that the statute did not expressly require a hearing and could permit a secret or unfair process.
The Court directed that affected parties receive natural justice, reasons for conclusions, opportunities to address valuations and reports, and other reasonable procedural facilities.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated quasi-judicial duties and natural justice as implied in the Board’s statutory function. It relied on Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India and M. S. Gill v. Union of India on natural justice, and Organo Chemical Industries v. Union of India on reasons and procedural fairness in quasi-judicial proceedings.
members.conclusion: The Board must act quasi-judicially and provide the procedural fairness and opportunities appropriate to determining members’ rights; its decisions remain reviewable for non-compliance.

predicates.statutory_board_partition_proceeding: A statutory board is conducting a proceeding to divide and allot family property.
predicates.board_determines_member_rights: The board’s decisions in the proceeding affect the rights or interests of persons entitled to shares.

members.legal_issue: A notification under a former forest law directed to protecting specified tree species constitutes a protected forest, not a reserved forest, under the extended forest law.
material_facts: The prosecutions concerned conduct in forest areas whose boundaries had been notified under the former state's forest law.
That law principally protected specified classes of trees, and its notifications designated areas for that protection.
The former law's notification process did not extinguish or acquire private rights in the areas as the reserved-forest scheme of the extended law did.
The accused were prosecuted for conduct that was an offence under the extended law only if it occurred in a reserved forest.
members.legal_principle: Under the Indian Forest Act, 1927, Chapter II, including sections 3–21, a reserved forest is constituted through a process that includes notification, proclamation, inquiry into claims, and a final notification; the scheme reserves the forest area as a whole and addresses private rights. Chapter IV, including sections 30–33, protects particular trees and designated areas. The Court held that the former Tripura Forest Act's purpose and provisions corresponded to Chapter IV, not Chapter II. Because section 26 offences required conduct in a reserved forest, those offences were not established on these notifications.
members.conclusion: The notifications corresponded to the protected-forest provisions, not the reserved-forest provisions; the areas were not established as reserved forests, so the convictions could not stand and the acquittals were upheld.

predicates.criminal_prosecution_for_reserved_forest: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution for conduct punishable only if committed in a reserved forest.
predicates.former_notification_protected_specified_: The former law and its notification designated an area principally to protect specified kinds of trees.
predicates.former_notification_did_not_reserve_enti: The former law's notification did not reserve the forest area as a whole through a process addressing claims to private rights.

members.legal_issue: A notification under a law directed to protecting specified tree species does not establish that the notified area is a reserved forest under a replacement law whose reserved-forest provisions govern the forest area as a whole.
material_facts: The former state law principally protected specified classes of trees, and its notifications fixed the boundaries of three forest areas.
The notifications permitted certain existing settled uses and forest-product activities within the areas.

The replacement law distinguished between provisions for reserved forests, which concerned the forest area as a whole, and provisions for protected forests, which protected particular trees or classes of trees.

The prosecutions were for acts that constituted offences only if committed in a reserved forest; the areas had not been declared reserved forests through the replacement law’s reserved-forest procedure.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11 and 20 of Chapter II of the Indian Forest Act, 1927, provide for constitution of a reserved forest after the prescribed process, including the determination or extinction of private rights, and section 26 penalizes specified acts in a reserved forest. Sections 30 to 33 in Chapter IV concern protected forests and the protection of particular trees or classes of trees. The Tripura Forest Act, particularly sections 4, 5, 16 and 19, was directed principally to protecting specified trees, so its notifications corresponded to Chapter IV rather than Chapter II. Sections 3 and 4 of the Part C States (Laws) Act, 1950, including the saving proviso to section 4, preserved the notifications only as actions under the corresponding provisions. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The notifications corresponded to the replacement law’s protected-forest provisions, not its reserved-forest provisions. The areas therefore were not established as reserved forests for the offences charged, and the acquittals were upheld.

rule.if: prosecution_for_reserved_forest_offense and area_notified_under_tree_protection_law and former_law_targets_specified_tree_species and replacement_law_distinguishes_area_reservation_from_tree_protection

predicates.prosecution_for_reserved_forest_offense: A person was prosecuted for conduct that is an offence only if committed in a reserved forest.
predicates.area_notified_under_tree_protection_law: An area was notified under a former law directed to forest protection.
predicates.former_law_targets_specified_tree_specie: The former law principally protected specified tree species rather than reserving the forest area as a whole.
predicates.replacement_law_distinguishes_area_reser: The replacement law has distinct regimes for reserving an entire forest area and protecting particular trees or classes of trees.

members.legal_issue: A person claiming an interest in the property, or an underlying owner, need not be joined in a landlord-tenant eviction appeal when their presence is unnecessary to decide the dispute between the parties.
material_facts: A person claiming a share in the property and the municipal owner separately sought to be joined in the appeals.
The share and title claims were the subject of other proceedings or matters outside the landlord-tenant dispute before the Court.
The relationship and mutual rights between the municipal owner and the landlords were not necessary to determine the eviction issues.
Neither applicant’s presence was necessary for an effective and complete decision of the issues in the appeals.
members.legal_principle: A person is not a necessary or proper party to a landlord-tenant proceeding merely because that person claims an interest in the property. Joinder is unwarranted when the person’s presence is unnecessary to decide the questions in the proceeding and would introduce controversies beyond its scope. The Court stated that any independent title claims could be pursued before a competent forum.
members.conclusion: The applications to join the claimants and the municipal owner were dismissed; they remained free to pursue their claims in independent proceedings.

predicates.landlord_tenant_eviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning eviction in a landlord-tenant dispute.
predicates.proposed_party_claims_separate_property_: A proposed party asserts an ownership, share, or other property interest that is separate from the eviction dispute.
predicates.proposed_party_presence_unnecessary_to_d: The court can decide the eviction issues completely and effectively without the proposed party.

members.legal_issue: A person claiming co-ownership of rented premises is not entitled to join an eviction suit when the dispute can be decided without that person’s presence.
material_facts: The plaintiffs brought an eviction suit against tenants on grounds including non-payment of rent, subletting, and personal need.
A person claiming to be a family member and co-owner of the premises applied to join the suit as a co-plaintiff.

The eviction suit concerned whether a landlord-tenant relationship existed and whether the pleaded grounds for eviction were established; it could be decided without resolving the applicant’s claimed ownership or share.
members.legal_principle: In an eviction suit under a rent law, the landlord and tenant are the necessary parties, and the questions are whether the landlord-tenant relationship exists and whether a ground for eviction is established; title is not germane to those questions. A plaintiff, as dominus litis, cannot be compelled to add a party unless that person is necessary or proper. A necessary party is one without whom no effective order can be made; a proper party is one whose presence is needed for a complete and final decision. Any co-owner or co-landlord may bring an eviction suit without joining all the others. The Court relied on Order 1 Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and Dr. Ranbir Singh v. Asharfi Lal, Ruma Chakraborty v. Sudha Rani Banerjee, Udit Narain Singh Malpaharia v. Additional Member Board of Revenue, and Kasthuri Radhakrishnan v. M. Chinniyan.
members.conclusion: The applicant was neither a necessary nor a proper party to the eviction suit, and the application to join was dismissed.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and applicant_claimed_coownership and eviction_turns_on_tenancy_and_eviction_grounds and title_claim_cannot_be_resolved_in_proceeding and proceeding_decidable_without_applicant

predicates.eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought an action seeking eviction of tenants from rented premises.
predicates.applicant_claimed_coownership: A person who was not already a party claimed to co-own the premises and sought to join the action.
predicates.eviction_turns_on_tenancy_and_eviction_g: The action’s decision depended on whether a landlord-tenant relationship existed and whether the asserted grounds for eviction were established.
predicates.title_claim_cannot_be_resolved_in_procee: The asserted ownership rights or shares between the applicant and the plaintiff were outside the questions to be decided in the eviction action.
predicates.proceeding_decidable_without_applicant: The action could be decided effectively without the applicant’s presence.

members.legal_issue: A dispute seeking enforcement of rights under an accession or merger agreement is outside the courts’ jurisdiction when it arises from that agreement.
material_facts: The former ruler relied on the Instrument of Accession and Merger Agreement to argue that the land-acquisition law could not affect his rights.
The dispute concerned the effect of those agreements on his rights after the state had been ceded and integrated.
members.legal_principle: Article 363(1) of the Constitution bars judicial inquiry into disputes arising out of specified agreements and covenants relating to the integration of Indian States. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The courts could not inquire into the dispute arising from the agreements.

predicates.constitutional_property_challenge: A person brings a constitutional challenge concerning the effect of a land measure on claimed property rights.
predicates.claim_based_on_state_integration_agreeme: The person bases the claimed property protection on an agreement made in connection with the integration of a former state.

members.legal_issue: Courts lack jurisdiction to decide disputes arising out of a covenant or agreement of merger.
material_facts: The petitioners’ challenge to acquisition of property depended on the terms and effect of a covenant of merger.
The Court considered the constitutional bar on judicial determination of disputes arising out of such covenants.
members.legal_principle: Article 363 of the Constitution bars the jurisdiction of courts over disputes arising out of specified treaties, agreements, covenants, engagements and similar instruments. The judgment states that the bar independently foreclosed judicial determination of the covenant dispute.
members.conclusion: The jurisdiction of the Court to decide disputes arising out of the covenant of merger was barred.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_proceeding: A party brings a constitutional challenge involving property recognized under a merger arrangement.
predicates.claim_depends_on_merger_covenant: The party’s claim depends on the terms or effect of a covenant of merger.
predicates.dispute_arises_from_covenant: The dispute arises out of the covenant or agreement itself.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional petition asserting ownership over property not recognized as the claimant’s private property by the government is not maintainable on that basis.
material_facts: The appellant asserted ownership over villages that had not been recognized by the Government of India as his private property.
The claimed ownership depended on the Merger Agreement’s provisions concerning recognition of private property.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the relevant provisions of the Merger Agreement concerning recognition of private property and held that Article 363(1) barred judicial inquiry into disputes arising from that agreement. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The petition was not maintainable as to those villages because they had not been recognized as the appellant’s private property.

predicates.constitutional_property_petition: A person brings a constitutional petition asserting ownership of particular property.
predicates.ownership_claim_depends_on_government_re: The asserted ownership depends on the government having recognized the property as the claimant’s private property.
predicates.property_not_recognized_as_claimant_priv: The government has not recognized the property as the claimant’s private property.

members.legal_issue: A petition asserting a fundamental right to hold and dispose of property cannot be maintained when the petitioner has not acquired the property claimed.
material_facts: The petitioners sought relief under Article 32, claiming that the State was preventing them from holding and disposing of timber, charcoal, kattha, and other forest produce.
The Court concluded that no legal transfer of ownership of the trees or the resulting products to the petitioners had occurred.
The claimed fundamental right depended on the forest produce being the petitioners’ property.
members.legal_principle: A petition under Article 32 is not maintainable unless the petitioner establishes a fundamental right. The asserted right to hold and dispose of property could not support these petitions because ownership of the claimed forest produce had not passed to the petitioners.
members.conclusion: The petitioners could not maintain the petitions on the asserted fundamental-rights ground, and the petitions were dismissed.

predicates.article_32_fundamental_rights_petition: The claimant brought a constitutional petition seeking enforcement of a fundamental right.
predicates.property_right_claimed: The claimant asserted a fundamental right to hold and dispose of particular property.
predicates.no_legal_title_to_claimed_property: The claimant had not legally acquired ownership of the property on which the asserted right depended.

members.legal_issue: A failure to decide a layout-plan application within the prescribed period does not, by itself, amount to approval of the plan.
material_facts: The owner applied for sanction of a revised layout plan.
The municipal Standing Committee did not decide the application within the prescribed period.
The owner claimed that the revised plan should therefore be treated as sanctioned.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 313(3) and 313(5) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, the Standing Committee is expected to deal with an application within the prescribed period, but those provisions do not state that failure to do so results in deemed sanction. The Court distinguished the more tightly time-bound scheme for building or work approvals under Sections 336 and 337, which expressly permits commencement in specified circumstances. It disapproved and overruled the contrary view in Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Smt. Kamala Bhandari.
members.conclusion: The Committee’s failure to consider the application within the prescribed period did not entitle the owner to treat the layout plan as sanctioned.

predicates.case_is_layout_sanction_delay_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal involving a claim that delay in deciding a layout-plan application amounted to approval.
predicates.committee_missed_decision_deadline: The municipal decision-making body did not decide the layout-plan application within the prescribed period.
predicates.deadline_rule_does_not_make_silence_appr: The governing scheme sets a decision deadline but does not state that silence or delay amounts to approval.

members.legal_issue: Expiry of the time allowed for deciding a building-sanction application does not itself create deemed sanction or a right to build.
material_facts: An application for permission to construct additional floors remained undecided beyond the periods set out in the applicable rules and court orders.
The governing enactment and rules required express sanction and did not provide that failure to decide within the specified period would amount to deemed sanction or deemed refusal.
members.legal_principle: Sections 173 to 175 of the Howrah Municipal Corporation Act and Rule 3 of the Building Rules require sanction before construction, and neither the Act nor the rules creates deemed sanction or deemed refusal on expiry of the decision period. Applying Chet Ram Vashist v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi, failure to decide within a prescribed period does not by itself create a right to claim sanction.
members.conclusion: The applicant acquired no sanction merely because the application remained undecided after the relevant periods; construction required express approval.

predicates.building_sanction_proceeding: A person sought permission from a public authority to construct or alter a building.
predicates.application_undecided_past_deadline: The authority did not decide the building-sanction application within the period allowed for its decision.
predicates.no_automatic_approval_rule: The governing rules did not make an undecided application automatically approved or rejected after the decision period.

members.legal_issue: Leaving the amount and timing of compensation instalments to rules did not make the acquisition law unenforceable or amount to an improper delegation of essential legislative power.
material_facts: The law authorized compensation to be paid in one or more modes, including instalments or bonds.
The statute left details of instalment payments to rules made under it.
The statute also required an interim payment if full compensation was not paid within the specified period.
The statute fixed the compensation framework rather than leaving the essential legislative choice to the executive.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on its reasoning in the Bihar case and on the statutory provisions empowering rule-making and requiring interim compensation. It distinguished implementation details from essential legislative functions.
members.conclusion: The delegation objection was rejected, and the absence of instalment details in the statute did not make it unenforceable; rules could prescribe those details, subject to challenge if their application abused the delegated power.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_law and statute_sets_compensation_framework and payment_details_are_left_to_rules and statute_provides_interim_payment

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A person challenged a law that provides for acquisition of property.
predicates.statute_sets_compensation_framework: The statute itself establishes the framework for determining compensation.
predicates.payment_details_are_left_to_rules: The statute leaves the detailed method or schedule of payment to rules.
predicates.statute_provides_interim_payment: The statute requires an interim payment if full compensation is not made within the prescribed time.

members.legal_issue: A provision requiring compensation for acquired property to be paid in instalments is within the legislature’s power to prescribe the form and manner of compensation and is not colourable legislation merely because payment is deferred.
material_facts: The acquisition law required compensation, with interest, to be paid in annual instalments.
The law allowed the State to make full payment earlier.
The challengers argued that the instalment provision was colourable legislation.
members.legal_principle: List III, entry 42 includes legislative authority to prescribe the principles for determining compensation and the form and manner in which it is given. A provision governing the payment of compensation in instalments is within that subject and is not legislation about a non-existent or factually unrelated matter. The Court distinguished the provisions invalidated in State of Bihar v. Maharajah Kameshwar Singh.
members.conclusion: The instalment provision was valid; it prescribed the form and manner of giving compensation and was not colourable legislation.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compensation: A party challenges the constitutionality of a provision governing how compensation for acquired property is paid.
predicates.law_prescribes_how_compensation_is_paid: The law specifies a method or schedule for paying compensation.

members.legal_issue: Interest should not also be awarded when delayed possession is provided at the original price and the allottee thereby benefits from the land's price escalation.
material_facts: The District Forum ensured that possession would be provided at the original price.
The allottees thereby received the benefit of the escalation in the price of the land.
The District Forum had also awarded interest on the compensation amount.
members.legal_principle: Compensation must address loss or injury and should not duplicate a benefit already received. The judgment relies on Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Balbir Singh for the requirement that compensation be based on and correlated with loss or injury.
members.conclusion: Interest should not also be awarded where possession is given at the original price, because the allottee has received the benefit of land-price escalation.

predicates.consumer_plot_allotment_dispute: The proceeding concerns a consumer dispute arising from the allotment of a plot.
predicates.possession_provided_at_original_price: The authority provided possession of the plot at the original price.
predicates.allottee_benefits_from_land_price_escala: The allottee received the benefit of the increase in the land's value while retaining the original price.

members.legal_issue: An allottee who accepts delayed delivery of a house at the agreed price and receives the benefit of the property's appreciation is not entitled to interest on the amount paid for the period before delivery.
material_facts: The allottee's payment for the houses was adjusted from money refundable for other units, and the price of the houses was treated as paid on the date of that adjustment.
The houses were delivered years later at the agreed prices, and the allottee accepted delivery.
The Commission awarded interest at a uniform rate without a proper basis for its commencement date.
The value of the houses had increased substantially by the time they were delivered.
members.legal_principle: Under the principles in Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta, Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Balbir Singh, Haryana Development Authority v. Darsh Kumar, and Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Union of India, relief for delayed delivery depends on the circumstances and cannot be based on an automatic, uniform interest rate. Where delayed performance is accepted at the agreed price and the allottee benefits from appreciation in value, interest on the price paid until delivery does not arise.
members.conclusion: The interest award was unsustainable. Because the houses were delivered and accepted at the agreed prices, the allottee was not entitled to interest on the price paid for the period before delivery.

predicates.consumer_complaint_for_delayed_housing_a: An allottee brought a consumer complaint alleging delay in delivery of an allotted house.
predicates.delayed_houses_were_delivered_and_accept: The housing authority delivered the delayed houses and the allottee accepted them at the agreed prices.
predicates.allottee_benefited_from_property_appreci: The value of the houses had increased by the time the allottee received them.

members.legal_issue: The provision on wrongful withholding of company property applies to former officers and employees who retain property obtained during their employment after that employment ends.
material_facts: The company obtained the flat under a leave-and-licence agreement and allowed the employee to occupy it as an employee.
The employee resigned but remained in possession of the flat and refused to deliver it to the company.
members.legal_principle: Section 630 of the Companies Act, 1956 covers both existing and past officers or employees. It applies where an officer or employee wrongfully obtains company property, or obtains it during employment and wrongfully withholds it after employment ends. The Court relied on Sh. Baldev Krishna Sahi v. Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. and Amrit Lal Chum v. Devo Prasad Dutta Roy.
members.conclusion: The employee’s status as a former employee did not take the case outside the provision; retaining the company’s property after employment ended could attract its application.

rule.if: company_property_wrongful_withholding_case and possession_obtained_during_employment and employment_ended and property_retained_after_employment

predicates.company_property_wrongful_withholding_ca: The proceeding alleges that an officer or employee wrongfully obtained or withheld property belonging to a company.
predicates.possession_obtained_during_employment: The employee received possession of the company’s property while employed by the company.
predicates.employment_ended: The employee’s service with the company ended.
predicates.property_retained_after_employment: The former employee continued to hold the company’s property after the employment ended.

members.legal_issue: The terms covering a company’s officers and employees include former officers and employees who wrongfully retain company property after their employment ends.
material_facts: The respondents had been allotted company quarters for use during their employment.
After retiring, the respondents did not vacate or return the quarters despite being required to do so.
members.legal_principle: Section 630(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1956 applies to wrongful withholding of company property after employment ends. In Baldev Krishna Sahi v. Shipping Corporation of India Ltd., the Court held that the terms “officer or employee” are not restricted to current officers or employees; Amrit Lal Chum v. Devoprasad Dutta Roy likewise recognized that wrongful retention of company property after termination of employment is an offence under the section. The provision should be construed broadly and liberally to advance its purpose of enabling the company to retrieve its property.
members.conclusion: A former officer or employee can fall within the scope of the provision dealing with wrongful withholding of company property.

predicates.company_property_was_provided_during_emp: The company provided its property to a worker for use during the worker’s employment.
predicates.former_worker_wrongfully_retained_it_aft: After the employment ended, the former worker wrongfully kept the company’s property instead of returning it.
predicates.criminal_proceeding_concerns_company_pro: A criminal proceeding concerns the worker’s alleged wrongful obtaining or withholding of company property.

members.legal_issue: An order made without the hearing required by the governing procedure may be treated as non-est and ignored, rather than as a reviewable order.
material_facts: An applicant’s challenge to a consolidation scheme was dismissed when he did not attend the hearing.
The applicant soon sought restoration and submitted an affidavit attributing his absence to illness.
The authority accepted that illness had prevented his attendance and exercised its statutory power to address his grievance.
The Supreme Court treated the applicant’s lack of an opportunity to be heard as meaning that the earlier order was not duly made under the statutory procedure.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to section 42 of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948 makes notice to interested parties and an opportunity to be heard conditions precedent to varying or reversing an order, scheme, or repartition, except where proceedings have been vitiated by unlawful consideration. Although section 42 does not confer a power of review, an order that is non-est may be ignored at any stage. Harbhajan Singh v. Karam Singh does not bar that treatment of a non-est order.
members.conclusion: Because the earlier order was not duly passed in accordance with the required opportunity to be heard, it could be ignored as non-est; the rule against reviewing a previous order did not prevent that result.

predicates.statutory_proceeding_requires_hearing: The proceeding was governed by a procedure that required an affected person to receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the order was made.
predicates.affected_person_lacked_hearing_opportuni: The person whose interests were affected did not have an opportunity to be heard before the earlier order was made.
predicates.absence_prevented_participation: The authority accepted that illness or another circumstance beyond the person’s control prevented attendance and participation.
predicates.defective_order_may_be_ignored_as_non_es: An order made without the required hearing may be treated as non-est and ignored.

members.legal_issue: An administrative authority may disregard an earlier order that was not duly made because an interested party was denied the required opportunity to be heard, even though the authority has no general power of review.
material_facts: A consolidation petition was dismissed when the petitioner was absent.
The petitioner promptly sought restoration, supported by an affidavit explaining that illness had prevented attendance.
The Additional Director accepted that explanation and, after examining the records, acted under the authority’s statutory powers.
The Supreme Court treated the lack of an opportunity to be heard as preventing the earlier order from being a duly passed order.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 42 of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948 makes notice to interested parties and an opportunity to be heard conditions precedent to varying an order, scheme, or repartition. Although Section 42 confers no general power of review, Harbhajan Singh v. Karan Singh does not govern an order that was not duly passed because the required hearing was unavailable; such an order may be ignored.
members.conclusion: The earlier order could be treated as invalid and disregarded; the absence of a general review power did not prevent the authority from acting in these circumstances.

predicates.consolidation_revision_proceeding: An authority was considering a matter concerning the consolidation of holdings.
predicates.interested_party_denied_hearing: An interested party was not given an opportunity to be heard before the earlier order was made.
predicates.absence_caused_by_illness: The interested party’s absence that led to the earlier order was caused by illness.

members.legal_issue: A written statement made by a mortgagor in context may acknowledge a mortgagee’s subsisting right and renew the limitation period when it admits their jural relationship.
material_facts: The mortgagor had granted mortgage security to the mortgagee, and their only subsisting relationship when the letter was written was that of mortgagor and mortgagee.
After the mortgagor had earlier asked the mortgagee to prevent a sale by a prior mortgagee, and the mortgagee had paid money to avert that sale, the property was again advertised for sale.
The mortgagor wrote and signed a letter referring to the mortgagee as interested, inviting him to take up the whole, and stating that a payment would stop the sale.
Read in that context, the letter referred to the mortgagee’s interest as a puisne mortgagee and acknowledged the mortgage relationship before the relevant limitation period expired.
members.legal_principle: Under section 19 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, a written and signed acknowledgment made before expiry of limitation in respect of the right claimed starts a fresh limitation period. It must relate to a subsisting liability and the words, read in their context and with surrounding circumstances, must indicate and be intended expressly or impliedly to admit the parties’ jural relationship. The precise nature of the right need not be specified, and no promise to pay is necessary; the acknowledgment does not create a new cause of action. The Court relied on Green v. Humphreys (1884) 26 Ch. D. 474; Beti Maharani v. Collector of Etawah (1894) L.R. 22 I.A. 31; Sukhamoni Chowdhrani v. Ishan Chunder Roy (1897) L.R. 25 I.A. 95; Munshi Lal v. Hira Lal, I.L.R. [1947] All. 11; and Swaminatha Odayar v. Subbarama Ayyar (1927) I.L.R. 50 Mad. 548. It distinguished Dharma Vithal v. Govind Sadvalkar (1881) I.L.R. 8 Bom. 99, where the writing did not itself admit the relevant jural relationship.
members.conclusion: The letter was a valid acknowledgment of the mortgagee’s right under section 19 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, and a fresh limitation period ran from the acknowledgment; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: limitation_suit and written_signed_statement and statement_before_limitation_expiry and relates_to_subsisting_liability and admits_jural_relationship and maker_intended_admission

predicates.limitation_suit: A claimant brings a suit seeking to enforce a right for which the applicable limitation period matters.
predicates.written_signed_statement: The person against whom the right is claimed makes a written statement and signs it.
predicates.statement_before_limitation_expiry: The person makes the statement before the limitation period for the claim has expired.
predicates.relates_to_subsisting_liability: The statement concerns a liability that still exists when the person makes it.
predicates.admits_jural_relationship: The statement, read in context, indicates the existing legal relationship between the person making it and the person claiming the right.
predicates.maker_intended_admission: The words and circumstances show that the person making the statement intended expressly or impliedly to admit that relationship.

members.legal_issue: A statement referring to a mortgage relationship restarts limitation only if it is intended to acknowledge the subsisting right to redeem and the corresponding liability to be redeemed.
material_facts: The claimants brought a suit seeking redemption and possession of their share of mortgaged property after the applicable sixty-year limitation period had expired.

They relied on earlier deeds and pleadings that referred to the mortgage relationship. The deeds and plaint referred to the mortgage rights to describe interests being mortgaged, sold, or asserted; the written statement denied the claimants’ right to redeem.
The Court found that none of the statements was intended to acknowledge a subsisting liability to permit redemption.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1908, an acknowledgment must be in writing, signed by the party against whom the right is claimed or a person through whom that party derives title or liability, and made before expiry of the limitation period. Explanation 1 means the acknowledgment need not specify the exact nature of the right, but it must relate to a subsisting liability. Applying Shapur Fredoom Mazda v. Durga Prosad, the Court held that the words and circumstances must show an intention to admit the subsisting jural relationship; that intention may be inferred, but cannot be imposed by strained reasoning. A reference to mortgage status made merely to describe rights in a transaction, or in a pleading that denies redemption, does not by itself establish the required acknowledgment. The Court also referred to Green v. Humphreys on the need for an admission that the writer owed the liability.
members.conclusion: The statements were not acknowledgments capable of saving the suit from limitation. The suit was barred, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: redemption_proceeding and limitation_period_expired and writings_referred_to_mortgage_status and writings_were_descriptive_or_denied_redemption and no_intent_to_admit_subsisting_liability

predicates.redemption_proceeding: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking redemption of mortgaged property.
predicates.limitation_period_expired: The applicable limitation period had elapsed before the claimant filed the proceeding.
predicates.writings_referred_to_mortgage_status: Earlier writings attributable to the opposing side or its predecessors referred to a mortgage relationship.
predicates.writings_were_descriptive_or_denied_rede: The writings used the mortgage references to describe interests being dealt with or asserted, or denied the claimant’s right to redeem.
predicates.no_intent_to_admit_subsisting_liability: The writers did not intend to admit that a current liability to permit redemption subsisted.

members.legal_issue: A statutory framework for charging a betterment fee does not involve excessive delegation when the selection of scheme areas is guided, affected owners have opportunities to object, and disputed assessments are independently reviewable.
material_facts: The framework limited schemes to public improvement purposes, including creating or improving streets and traffic facilities.
A scheme required approval by the State Government, which could modify or refuse it.
Affected owners could object to the proposed recovery of a fee and be heard, and the scheme could be modified to exclude land.
The fee depended on an increase in land value attributable to the scheme, which the assessing body had to determine objectively.
An owner who disputed the assessment could have the matter determined by independent arbitrators.
members.legal_principle: Sections 39 and 78A to 78G of the Calcutta Improvement Act, 1911 supplied the purposes and framework for schemes and betterment fees. The Court considered the statutory guidance, government sanction, opportunities to object, objective assessment of increased land value, and review by independent arbitrators sufficient to prevent arbitrary or uncontrolled exercise of delegated power. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The provisions governing betterment fees were not invalid for excessive delegation of legislative power.
