members.legal_issue: The statutory betterment-fee framework does not violate equal protection when its operation is guided and includes safeguards against arbitrary assessments.
material_facts: The framework confined schemes to stated public improvement purposes and required State Government sanction.
Affected owners could object to the proposed fee and be heard.
The fee was tied to an objectively determined increase in land value attributable to the scheme.
Owners could refer disputed assessments to independent arbitrators.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 of the Constitution was considered in connection with sections 78A to 78G of the Calcutta Improvement Act, 1911. The Court treated the equality challenge as another facet of the excessive-delegation challenge and relied on the framework's guidance and safeguards against arbitrary decisions. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The challenge under Article 14 failed because it was another facet of the unsuccessful excessive-delegation challenge.

members.legal_issue: The electoral-roll preparation requirement that elector names be arranged by house numbers does not permit occupants of illegal, unnumbered buildings to be included in the roll.
material_facts: The electoral roll included people living in illegal buildings that had no house numbers.
The applicable rule required elector names in each part of the roll to be arranged according to house numbers.
The court found that the roll-preparation rule was consistent with the statutory elector qualifications.
members.legal_principle: Rule 10(3) of the Cantonment Electoral Rules, 2007 requires elector names to be arranged according to house numbers. Read with Section 28 of the Cantonment Act, 2006, it does not conflict with the statutory qualifications and does not authorize inclusion of occupants of illegal, unnumbered buildings.
members.conclusion: Occupants of illegally constructed buildings without house numbers are not entitled to inclusion in the electoral roll prepared under the applicable rule.

predicates.cantonment_electoral_roll_preparation_ca: The proceeding concerns preparation of an electoral roll for a cantonment board election.
predicates.illegal_buildings_lack_house_numbers: People included in the proposed roll live in illegal buildings that have no house numbers.
predicates.omit_occupants_of_illegal_buildings_from: The occupants of those illegal buildings are omitted from the electoral roll.

members.legal_issue: A final direction to prepare an electoral roll in accordance with the applicable rules does not authorize inclusion of occupants of illegal buildings when a later review removes language that had directed their inclusion.
material_facts: An earlier judgment, which became final, directed preparation of electoral rolls in accordance with the applicable rule.
An appellate judgment initially included language directing that encroachers be mentioned in the roll, but that language was deleted on review.
The board later included occupants of illegal buildings in the electoral roll and contended that the modified judgment permitted it to do so.
members.legal_principle: The binding directions must be read in light of the review that deleted the language directing inclusion of encroachers. The remaining directions required compliance with the electoral-roll rule and did not authorize their inclusion.
members.conclusion: The earlier final directions did not authorize the board to include occupants of illegal buildings in the electoral roll.

predicates.board_included_illegal_building_occupant: The board included occupants of illegal buildings in the electoral roll.

members.legal_issue: A defendant’s allegation of a landlord–tenant relationship does not by itself oust the ordinary civil court’s jurisdiction where the suit as framed denies that relationship and seeks relief not arising under rent-control law.
material_facts: The plaintiff was in possession of the premises as a tenant of their owner and alleged that the defendants had been allowed to enter only to conduct commission-agency business under an agreement.
The plaintiff alleged that the defendants’ permission had ended, denied that they were tenants, and sought a declaration concerning possession, an injunction against entry, and unpaid commission.
The defendants alleged that the agreement was a sham and that the premises had in substance been sublet to them as tenants.
Deciding the suit as framed required deciding whether the defendants were licensees; the court concluded that no claim or question arising under the Act needed to be decided.
members.legal_principle: Section 28(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 gives the specified court exclusive jurisdiction over suits between landlord and tenant relating to rent or possession of premises covered by Part II, applications under the Act, and claims or questions arising out of the Act. That jurisdiction does not extend to deciding title or other collateral questions where the plaint denies a landlord–tenant relationship and the relief claimed does not arise under the Act; a defendant cannot compel a different forum merely by pleading tenancy. Section 29 does not alter that result, and Section 29-A confirms that the Act does not confer exclusive jurisdiction over questions of title. The general principle that jurisdiction is assessed from the suit as framed is supported by Ananti v. Chhannu and Govindram Salamatrai v. Dharampal; Govindram and Jaswantlal v. Western Company, India were approved, and Babulal Bhuramal v. Nandram Shivram was explained as concerning a suit whose substance and relief brought it within the Act. The separate opinion also reasoned that creating a tenancy is not a question arising under the Act, which regulates relations in a tenancy otherwise created. Whether Section 51 applied to a particular proceeding was not argued or decided.
members.conclusion: The City Civil Court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit. The defendants’ plea that they were tenants did not make the suit one within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Court of Small Causes.

rule.if: civil_suit_concerning_premises and plaintiff_denies_landlord_tenant_relationship and relief_not_based_on_rent_control_rights and defendant_alleges_tenancy

predicates.civil_suit_concerning_premises: The plaintiff brought a civil suit seeking relief concerning possession or use of premises.
predicates.plaintiff_denies_landlord_tenant_relatio: The plaintiff’s pleading denied that the parties had a landlord–tenant relationship.
predicates.relief_not_based_on_rent_control_rights: The relief sought by the plaintiff was based on rights alleged independently of rent-control protections.
predicates.defendant_alleges_tenancy: The defendant alleged that the parties’ relationship was one of landlord and tenant.

members.legal_issue: A party's plea that it is a tenant does not itself give the rent-control forum exclusive jurisdiction when the party seeking relief does not claim that a landlord-and-tenant relationship exists.
material_facts: The society sought possession on the basis of the member's persistent default and the society's right to terminate the agreement, rather than on the basis of a landlord-and-tenant relationship.
The member contended that the rent-control forum alone could decide the possession claim because the member was a tenant.
The society's claim before the arbitrators did not allege that the member was its tenant.
members.legal_principle: Section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, gives the designated court exclusive jurisdiction over proceedings between landlord and tenant relating to recovery of rent or possession of covered premises, and related claims or questions. The claim invoking jurisdiction must allege the landlord-and-tenant relationship; a defendant or respondent cannot displace ordinary jurisdiction merely by pleading that relationship. Babulal Bhuramal v. Nandram Shivram concerned a suit in which the plaintiffs themselves claimed to be tenants, and did not establish that an opposing party's plea alone suffices.
members.conclusion: The member's tenancy plea did not displace the arbitrators' jurisdiction. Exclusive jurisdiction under section 28 depended on the proceeding being brought on a claim of a landlord-and-tenant relationship and seeking relief within that section.

predicates.cooperative_arbitration_proceeding: The dispute was before an arbitrator appointed through a cooperative-society process.
predicates.claimant_sought_possession_on_non_tenanc: The party seeking possession relied on a basis other than a claimed landlord-and-tenant relationship.
predicates.opposing_party_alone_pleaded_tenancy: The party resisting possession, rather than the party seeking it, asserted that a landlord-and-tenant relationship existed.

members.legal_issue: The Hindu Succession Act does not enlarge a male’s life interest arising on severance of an Aliyasantana family into an absolute interest or make that limited interest transferable by will.
material_facts: The partition claim had severed joint status before the deceased’s death, so he did not die with an undivided interest in a kutumba or kavaru.
The deceased’s branch was nissanthathi and, because the sister’s branch was santhathi, his interest was limited to his lifetime.
The deceased had executed a will purporting to benefit his wife and children.
members.legal_principle: Sections 7(2) and its Explanation of the Hindu Succession Act apply to an undivided interest in a kutumba or kavaru; they do not convert an interest held after severance into an absolute estate. Section 30 permits testamentary disposition of an interest in kutumba or kavaru property but does not make a post-severance life interest disposable. Section 14 enlarges certain limited interests of female Hindus, but the Act contains no corresponding provision enlarging the male life interest at issue. Section 4(1) displaces prior law only to the extent provided for or inconsistent with the Act, and section 17 concerns specified intestate succession provisions. Dundara Adapa v. Girija, Padmaraja v. Dhanavanthi, and the reasoning quoted from that decision are relied on.
members.conclusion: The deceased’s life interest was not enlarged into an absolute interest and could not be bequeathed; it ended with his lifetime, so the will did not give his heirs the claimed share.

rule.if: aliyasantana_succession_or_will_case and joint_status_severed_before_death and male_interest_is_life_limited and no_statutory_enlargement_applies

predicates.aliyasantana_succession_or_will_case: The proceeding concerns succession to, or a will disposing of, an interest arising in an Aliyasantana family.
predicates.joint_status_severed_before_death: The family’s joint status was severed before the male member died.
predicates.male_interest_is_life_limited: The male member held only a life interest after severance.
predicates.no_statutory_enlargement_applies: No applicable statutory provision enlarges that male life interest into an absolute interest.

members.legal_issue: A limited life interest held under the Aliyasantana law does not cause property to revert to the kutumba or a santhathi kavaru on the holder’s death when the Hindu Succession Act governs succession.
material_facts: The defendants belonged to a nissanthathi kavaru and were entitled to a life interest in the property allotted to it at partition under the Aliyasantana Act.
The parties disputed whether the property or the deceased members’ interests should pass to their heirs or revert under the Aliyasantana rule.
The Court held that the Hindu Succession Act governed the devolution after the deaths.
members.legal_principle: Section 36(5) of the Madras Aliyasantana Act provides for devolution of property allotted to a nissanthathi kavaru upon the kutumba or, in specified circumstances, a santhathi kavaru. Section 4 of the Hindu Succession Act overrides inconsistent prior law. For an undivided interest, section 7(2) governs; for separate property, section 17 applies specified succession provisions, including section 8, with modifications. The Court held that the customary mode of reversion under section 36(5) could not displace the applicable succession provisions of the Hindu Succession Act.
members.conclusion: The customary rule that the property would devolve to the kutumba or nearest santhathi kavaru gave way to the Hindu Succession Act; the property devolved to the deceased holder’s heirs under that Act.

rule.if: intestate_succession_dispute and life_interest_under_customary_law and death_of_interest_holder and succession_reform_in_force

predicates.intestate_succession_dispute: Heirs disputed devolution of property after a person died without a will.

members.legal_issue: A child of the husband from whom a female seller inherited property is entitled to pre-emption when she sells that property, even if the child is not her own offspring.
material_facts: The female seller had inherited the land through her husband and later sold it.
The claimant was the daughter of that husband by another wife.
members.legal_principle: Section 15(2)(b) of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, gives the first right of pre-emption to the son or daughter of the husband through whom the female seller inherited the property; this includes that husband's child by another wife. The scheme of section 15(2) confines the right to the lineal descendants of the last male holder. The Court relied on Mota Singh v. Prem Parkash Kaur for the principle that the property should not pass outside the line of the last male holder.
members.conclusion: The claimant had a right of pre-emption under the first paragraph of clause (b) of section 15(2), even before the 1964 amendment.

predicates.preemption_proceeding: The dispute concerns a claim to obtain property by exercising a right of pre-emption.
predicates.female_sold_property_inherited_through_h: A female seller sold property that she had inherited through her husband.
predicates.claimant_is_child_of_inheriting_husband: The person claiming pre-emption was a child of the husband through whom the seller inherited the property, whether or not the child was born to the seller.
predicates.claimant_has_preemption_right: The claimant is entitled to exercise the right of pre-emption over the property.

members.legal_issue: A child of the husband from whom a female vendor inherited property is within the class entitled to pre-empt a sale of that property, even if the child was born to another wife.
material_facts: The female vendor inherited the property through her husband and later sold it.
The claimant was a daughter of that husband, but not of the female vendor.
The claimant sought possession by pre-emption of the property sold.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 15(2)(b) of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, the right is confined to the lineal descendants of the last male holder from whom the property came by inheritance. The reference to the female vendor’s son or daughter means the child of the husband through whom she inherited the property, including that husband’s child by another wife. This construction accords with the scheme described in Mote Singh v. Prem Parkash Kaur and the reasoning in Moti Ram v. Bakhwant Singh.
members.conclusion: The claimant was entitled to exercise the right of pre-emption as a child of the husband from whom the vendor had inherited the property.

predicates.is_preemption_claim: A claimant seeks to exercise a right of pre-emption against a sale of property.
predicates.vendor_inherited_property_through_husban: The female vendor inherited the property through her husband before selling it.
predicates.claimant_is_child_of_that_husband: The claimant is a child of the husband through whom the vendor inherited the property, whether or not the claimant is also the vendor’s child.

members.legal_issue: Undue influence is not established, and the burden does not shift to the beneficiary, unless the claimant first proves that the beneficiary could dominate the claimant’s will and that the transaction was unconscionable.
material_facts: The first appellate court found that the transferee was not in a position to dominate the transferor’s will and had not exercised undue influence.
The transferor was old but was physically fit, and there was no evidence that age or another cause impaired his mental capacity to understand the deed.

The deed writer testified that the deed was prepared on the transferor’s instructions, read to him, accepted by him as correct, and then thumbmarked by him; an attesting witness corroborated that account.

The first appellate court found the deed writer and attesting witness independent and credible, and found that the transferor executed the deed voluntarily after understanding its contents and effect.
members.legal_principle: Section 16 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, requires the court to consider in sequence whether the beneficiary could dominate the donor’s will, whether that position was used to obtain an unfair advantage, and, if the transaction is unconscionable, whether the burden shifts to the beneficiary to show that the transaction was not induced by undue influence. The burden shifts only when the claimant proves both dominance and an unconscionable transaction. The Court relied on Subhas Chandra v. Gana Prasad, which approved the stages stated in Raghunath Prasad v. Sarju Prasad, and on Poosathurai v. Kappanna Chettiar for the requirement that more than mere influence must be shown to establish undue influence.
members.conclusion: The claimant failed to prove the beneficiary’s ability to dominate the claimant’s will, so undue influence was not established and the burden did not shift to the beneficiary.

predicates.undue_influence_claim: A claimant seeks to set aside a transaction on the ground that the beneficiary exercised undue influence.
predicates.beneficiary_dominance_not_proved: The evidence does not establish that the beneficiary was in a position to dominate the other party’s will.

members.legal_issue: The burden of disproving undue influence in a gift shifts to its beneficiary only after the donor-beneficiary relationship and the unconscionable nature of the transaction are established.
material_facts: The suit challenged an inter vivos gift made by an elderly donor to his grandson.

The High Court presumed influence from the family relationship and the donor’s age, without finding that the donee was in a position to dominate the donor’s will or that the transaction was unconscionable.
members.legal_principle: Under section 16(1) of the Indian Contract Act, undue influence requires a relationship enabling one party to dominate the other’s will and use of that position to obtain an unfair advantage. Section 16(2) illustrates circumstances in which a person may be in such a position, including real or apparent authority, a fiduciary relationship, or impaired mental capacity. Under section 16(3), where the beneficiary is in a position to dominate the donor’s will and the transaction appears unconscionable, the burden shifts to the beneficiary to prove that the transaction was not induced by undue influence. The same law applies to gifts inter vivos as to contracts. The court applied Raghunath Prasad v. Sarju Prasad, Poosathurai v. Kannappa Chettiar, and Ladli Prasad Jaiswal v. Karnal Distillery Co. Ltd.
members.conclusion: The High Court applied the burden of proof in the wrong order. A court must first consider whether the donee was in a position to dominate the donor’s will and whether the transaction was unconscionable; only when both are established does the beneficiary bear the burden of proving that the gift was not induced by undue influence.

predicates.gift_challenged_for_undue_influence: A party to a proceeding challenges a gift on the ground that it was induced by undue influence.
predicates.donee_in_position_to_dominate_donor: The circumstances place the donee in a position to dominate the donor’s will.
predicates.transaction_unconscionable: The transaction appears unconscionable from its terms or the evidence.

members.legal_issue: The evidence did not establish a concluded sale agreement from the initial negotiations.
material_facts: The parties met to discuss a possible sale, but the seller said he still had to consult his brothers.
The later correspondence showed that the sale consideration had not been finalised and that further agreement was contemplated.
The plaintiff’s own notice acknowledged that consultation with the seller’s brothers was still required.
members.legal_principle: In a suit for specific performance, the agreement and its terms must be proved with absolute clarity and certainty. The Court relied on the principles governing the discretionary remedy under section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and on Madamsetty Satyanarayana v. G. Yellogi Rao and Sardar Singh v. Smt. Krishna Devi.
members.conclusion: No concluded agreement was made at the initial meeting, so specific performance could not be granted on the basis of that alleged agreement.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of an alleged sale agreement.
predicates.seller_reserved_consultation: The seller said that he still needed to consult other owners before finalising the proposed sale.
predicates.later_correspondence_left_terms_unsettle: Correspondence after the meeting showed that material sale terms remained open for further discussion.

members.legal_issue: The evidence did not establish a separate sale agreement at the later meeting.
material_facts: The plaintiff’s witness testified that no agreement was received at the later meeting.

The plaintiff testified that the seller asked him to return later, keep the consideration ready, and expected to execute a sale deed, but the evidence did not show that the parties negotiated and concluded a fresh agreement at that meeting.
The plaintiff’s evidence continued to assert that the agreement had been concluded at the initial meeting.
members.legal_principle: A specific-performance decree requires clear and certain proof of the agreement and its terms. The Court applied section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and the principles on certainty and variance described in Gonesh Ram v. Ganpat Rai, Md. Ziaul Haque v. Calcutta Vyapar Pratisthan, and Hawkins v. Maltby.
members.conclusion: No fresh agreement was proved at the later meeting, and the evidence did not support specific performance on that basis.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of an alleged agreement.
predicates.later_meeting_evidence_shows_only_future: Evidence of the later meeting showed requests to prepare for a future transaction rather than negotiations of a concluded sale.
predicates.no_fresh_terms_concluded: The evidence did not show that the parties settled and accepted the terms of a new agreement at the later meeting.

members.legal_issue: The government's relinquishment of property previously taken under an act of state constituted a fresh inam grant, making the property an estate under the applicable land-tenure law.
material_facts: After the ruler died without a male heir, the East India Company took possession of all his properties, including his private property.
In 1862, the Government of India sanctioned relinquishment of the landed property in favour of the ruler's heirs.
The disputed lands were part of the property derived from that relinquishment.
members.legal_principle: Where an act of state extinguishes existing rights in property, its later relinquishment by the government in favour of former claimants is a fresh grant rather than a revival of those rights. The Court applied section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act and relied on Jijoyiamba Bayi Saiba v. Kamakshi Bayi Saiba, Sundaram Ayyar v. Ramachandra Ayyar, Maharaja of Kolhapur v. Sundaram Iyer, Sundaram v. Deva Sankara, and T. R. Bhavani Shankar Joshi v. Somasundra Moopanar.
members.conclusion: The 1862 relinquishment was a fresh grant, not a restoration of antecedent rights, and the property qualified as an estate under section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act.

predicates.inam_estate_classification_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether land belongs to an estate formed by an inam grant.
predicates.government_relinquished_property_after_a: After the government had taken property under an act of state, it relinquished that property in favour of former claimants.

members.legal_issue: The government’s later return of property seized in an act of state constitutes a fresh grant when the seizure extinguished all prior rights, rather than restoring antecedent title.
material_facts: The government seized the ruler’s private and public properties in an exercise of sovereign power.
The Privy Council had held that the seizure covered both private and public properties and that the municipal courts had no jurisdiction to question it.
The government later issued an order relinquishing and restoring the private properties to the ruler’s widows.
The property in dispute derived from the Tanjore Palace Estate, and the character of the government’s order was contested in an appeal concerning rights in that property.
members.legal_principle: Under The Secretary of State in Council of India v. Kamachee Boye Sahaba (1859), a sovereign seizure of both private and public property is an act of state that municipal courts cannot question and leaves no prior title outstanding. The subsequent order therefore operates as a fresh grant, not as a revival of antecedent rights. The Court relied on Jijoyamba Bayi Saiba v. Kamakshi Bayi Saiba (1868), Srimant Chota Raja Saheb Mohitai v. Sundaram Ayyar (1936), and Chidambaram Chettiar v. Ramaswamy Odayar (1957), among other decisions treating the order as a grant.
members.conclusion: The act of state extinguished the prior rights in the properties, and the later government order was a fresh grant; the grantees’ title had its root in that order.

rule.if: estate_property_appeal and sovereign_seizure_included_private_property and no_prior_rights_survived_seizure and later_order_returned_property

predicates.estate_property_appeal: The dispute arose in an appeal concerning rights in property whose status affected an estate-law claim.
predicates.sovereign_seizure_included_private_prope: The government, acting as a sovereign power, seized the ruler’s private property as well as public property.
predicates.no_prior_rights_survived_seizure: The seizure extinguished the prior claimants’ rights in the seized property.
predicates.later_order_returned_property: The government later issued an order returning the property to the former ruler’s family.

members.legal_issue: A Hindu widow who is not a coparcener cannot act as the karta of a Hindu undivided family, but may manage its affairs as guardian of its sole surviving minor male coparcener.
material_facts: After the father’s death, his son was the sole surviving male coparcener and was a minor.
The son’s stepmother actively and dominantly managed the family’s affairs, while the son’s natural mother played a submissive role and did not oppose that management.
The stepmother’s role was consistent with acting as guardian of the minor coparcener rather than as karta in her own right.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished the role of a manager from that of a karta: a Hindu widow is not a coparcener and cannot act as karta, but the mother of a minor male coparcener may act as his legal guardian and manage the family’s affairs in that capacity. The Court relied on Sushila Devi Rampuria v. Income Tax Officer and Dhujram v. Chandan Singh, and distinguished Commissioner of Income Tax v. Seth Govindram Sugar Mills Ltd. and Controller of Estate Duty, Madras v. Alladi Kuppuswamy. The Court noted that the position remained unchanged after the 2005 amendment to the Hindu Succession Act.
members.conclusion: The widow could manage the family’s affairs as guardian of the sole surviving minor male coparcener, although she could not assume the position of karta.

predicates.hindu_family_management_dispute: The proceeding concerned management of a Hindu family and its property.
predicates.sole_surviving_male_coparcener_was_a_min: The only surviving male coparcener was a minor when the family needed management.
predicates.widow_managed_family_affairs_as_his_guar: A widow managed the family’s affairs in a role attributable to guardianship of the minor coparcener.

members.legal_issue: A widow who is a member of a joint Hindu family but is not a coparcener cannot become the manager of that family.
material_facts: The deceased partner’s branch of the family included widows and minor sons.
The possibility that a widow could represent that branch as its manager was raised in considering whether a partnership existed after the partner’s death.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that coparcenership is a necessary qualification for managership of a joint Hindu family and that a widow is not a coparcener. It followed V.M.N. Radha Ammal v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras, and Budhi Jena v. Dhobai Naik, and overruled Commissioner of Income-tax, C.P. & Berar v. Seth Lakshmi Narayan Raghunathdas and Pandurang Dahke v. Pandurang Gorle.
members.conclusion: A widow, though a member of a joint Hindu family, cannot become its manager.

predicates.joint_family_management_dispute: The dispute concerns who may manage a joint Hindu family.
predicates.woman_is_family_member: A woman is a member of the joint Hindu family whose management is in issue.
predicates.woman_is_not_coparcener: The woman is not a coparcener of that family.

members.legal_issue: A valid tax law does not violate the constitutional protection against deprivation of property merely because the tax is burdensome; a tax is not an acquisition or requisition of property.
material_facts: The challenged enactment imposed a tax and did not purport to acquire or requisition the petitioner’s property.
The petitioner invoked Article 31 against the tax.
The Court found no violation of other fundamental rights that would make the law invalid.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(1) requires deprivation of property to be authorized by a valid law. Article 31(2) concerns acquisition or requisition and does not apply to a taxing statute, even if an excessive tax might ultimately cause loss of property. The Court also relied on Articles 31(2A) and 31(5)(b)(i), which support that distinction.
members.conclusion: The challenge under Article 31 failed: Article 31(2) did not apply to the tax, and a tax imposed under an otherwise valid law satisfied Article 31(1).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_tax_law: A party challenges a tax law under constitutional property protections.
predicates.levy_is_a_tax_not_an_acquisition_or_requ: The law requires payment of a tax and does not purport to acquire or requisition property.
predicates.law_is_otherwise_valid: The tax law does not otherwise infringe a fundamental right or exceed legislative competence.

members.legal_issue: A law authorising an assessment or tax does not constitute deprivation, acquisition, or requisition of property merely because it imposes a payment obligation.
material_facts: The law imposed rent assessment on agricultural lands that had previously been exempt from assessment.
It authorised a levy and did not purport to take, acquire, or requisition the lands.
The challenge was to the validity of the levy under the constitutional protection concerning property.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(1) concerns deprivation of property otherwise than by authority of law, and Article 31(2) concerns compulsory acquisition or requisition; neither applies merely because a law imposes a tax. Article 31(5)(b)(i) provides that Article 31(2) does not affect laws imposing or levying a tax or penalty. The Court agreed with the decision upholding the Act in Pratap Kesari Deo v. State of Orissa, A.I.R. 1961 Orissa 131.
members.conclusion: The law was outside the purview of Article 31 because it authorised a tax levy without depriving the owners of property or acquiring or requisitioning it.

rule.if: property_rights_challenge and levy_only_imposes_assessment and not property_taken_or_acquired

predicates.property_rights_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law on the ground that it infringes constitutional protection of property.
predicates.levy_only_imposes_assessment: The law imposes an assessment or tax payment obligation on property.
predicates.property_taken_or_acquired: The law deprives the owner of the property or provides for its compulsory acquisition or requisition.

members.legal_issue: A contractual delay-compensation claim reserved for determination by a designated departmental official is excluded from arbitration where the arbitration clause excludes matters otherwise provided for in the contract.
material_facts: The contract required the contractor to follow a specified work schedule and provided compensation for delay, with the amount to be determined by a departmental official who could reduce or waive it after considering the circumstances.
The contract stated that the official’s written decision was final and that the arbitration clause did not cover matters otherwise provided for in the contract.
The department sought delay compensation before the arbitrator, who awarded it compensation under the contractual delay provision.
members.legal_principle: Reading the contractual delay-compensation and arbitration clauses together, the Court held that the compensation determination was reserved to the designated departmental official and excluded from arbitration. The Court treated the case as arising under the Arbitration Act, 1940, but did not rely on a particular statutory section or any earlier case in reaching this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The contractual delay-compensation claim was outside the arbitrator’s jurisdiction, and the compensation awarded to the department was deleted.

rule.if: arbitral_award_challenge and delay_compensation_claim and contract_reserves_assessment_to_department_official and official_can_consider_excuses_and_reduce_compensation and arbitration_clause_excludes_matters_provided_for_elsewhere

predicates.arbitral_award_challenge: A party challenges an arbitral award in a proceeding concerning the award.
predicates.delay_compensation_claim: A party seeks compensation under the contract for delay in performing the work.
predicates.contract_reserves_assessment_to_departme: The contract assigns determination of the delay compensation to a designated departmental official.
predicates.official_can_consider_excuses_and_reduce: The designated official can consider the contractor’s circumstances and reduce or waive the compensation.
predicates.arbitration_clause_excludes_matters_prov: The contract’s arbitration clause excludes matters for which the contract makes other provision.

members.legal_issue: A contractual provision reserving specified decisions to an official does not exclude arbitration of claims that do not fall within those specified matters.
material_facts: The contract provided for arbitration of disputes arising out of or relating to the contract, except where the contract provided otherwise.
A separate clause made an official's decision final on specified matters, including disputes about rates, completion time, and the proportion of additional work to original work.
The arbitrator decided claims for alleged additional work, and the Court found that the claims decided were not among the matters reserved by the separate clause.
members.legal_principle: The contract's reservation of final decision-making authority must be read together with its arbitration clause. Only disputes falling within the specific matters reserved by the contract are excluded from arbitration. The Court referred to State of Orissa v. Gokulchandra Kanungo and distinguished Bombay Housing Board v. Karbhase Naik & Co., Chief Administrator, Dandakaranya Project v. Prabartak Commercial Corporation, and Food Corporation of India v. P.L. Juneja on the wording of their contracts and the nature of the disputes involved.
members.conclusion: The reserved-matters clause did not apply to the claims decided by the arbitrator, and the claims were not excluded from arbitration on that basis.

predicates.contractual_arbitration_scope_dispute: A party challenges whether a dispute arising under a contract may be decided by arbitration.
predicates.contract_reserves_final_decisions_on_def: The contract assigns final decision-making authority to a specified person for particular categories of disputes.
predicates.claim_is_outside_reserved_matters: The claim decided by the arbitrator does not fall within the categories assigned to that person.

members.legal_issue: Land held by earlier tenants does not automatically fall outside a landowner’s surplus area when those tenants give up possession, and a new tenant must meet the statutory conditions to purchase it.
material_facts: At the commencement of the Act, one disputed parcel was in the landowner’s own cultivation and two parcels were occupied by tenants.
The earlier tenants later gave up possession, and the land came into the landowner’s actual possession; the new applicants were not transferees from those earlier tenants.
There was no evidence establishing that the disputed parcels formed part of the earlier tenants’ permissible area.
The new applicants’ occupation began after the Act commenced and, on the surplus-area authority’s findings, had not lasted for the required continuous period when they applied to purchase.
The landowner had made a gift of the parcels before the claimed leases to the applicants.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(3) and 2(5-a) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, a tenant’s permissible area is excluded from the surplus area, but land is not excluded merely because it was once held by a tenant: it must be shown to have been within that tenant’s permissible area. Where the earlier tenancy ends and possession reverts to the landowner, a new tenant cannot claim the earlier tenant’s status merely by occupying the land later. Section 18(1) gives a purchase right to an eligible tenant, including a tenant with the required continuous occupation; Sahib Ram v. Financial Commissioner, Punjab was cited concerning the categories and qualification of tenants entitled to purchase. Sections 10A(a) and 10A(b) protect the State’s ability to use surplus land for resettlement.
members.conclusion: The parcels were properly included in the landowner’s surplus area; the claimed new leases diminished that area and the applicants did not qualify to purchase the land under section 18.

rule.if: surplus_area_determination_proceeding and earlier_tenants_relinquished_possession and not_proven_within_earlier_tenants_permissible_area and new_tenant_inducted_after_reversion and not_qualified_continuous_occupation

predicates.surplus_area_determination_proceeding: An authority is determining whether land belongs in the statutory surplus pool.
predicates.earlier_tenants_relinquished_possession: The tenants occupying the land at the relevant starting point later gave up possession and the land returned to the landowner.
predicates.proven_within_earlier_tenants_permissibl: Evidence establishes that the land fell within the earlier tenants’ permissible holdings.
predicates.new_tenant_inducted_after_reversion: A different tenant began occupying the land after the earlier tenancy ended and possession returned to the landowner.
predicates.qualified_continuous_occupation: The applicant had the continuous occupation required by law when applying to purchase the tenancy.

members.legal_issue: A tenant seeking to purchase land need not have been a tenant of that land when the governing enactment commenced.
material_facts: The landlords disputed purchase claims on the ground that the claimants had to be tenants when the Act commenced.
The Court considered the statutory scheme, which contemplated tenancies beginning after the Act commenced.
The purchase claims were made by tenants applying to purchase land from their landlords.
members.legal_principle: Section 18(1)(i) does not state that a claimant must have been a tenant when the Act commenced. The Court also relied on the scheme’s recognition that a tenancy could begin after commencement, including the indication in the second proviso to section 9-A. It therefore declined to read a commencement-date tenancy requirement into section 18(1)(i).
members.conclusion: It is not necessary for a tenant claiming under section 18(1)(i) to have been a tenant of the land when the Act commenced, provided the other applicable conditions are satisfied.

predicates.tenant_purchase_application_case: A tenant sought, through a purchase application, to acquire land held under the tenancy from the landlord.
predicates.post_commencement_tenancy_recognized: The governing scheme contemplated a tenancy coming into existence after the enactment commenced.
predicates.other_purchase_conditions_satisfied: The tenant met the other conditions applicable to the claimed purchase right.

members.legal_issue: A court-appointed receiver may seek the winding up of a debtor company as a means of realizing a debt forming part of the estate under the receiver’s administration.
material_facts: A court appointed a receiver to administer the joint family’s properties, including the unpaid purchase price owed by the company.
The receiver had powers under the court’s order to realize the estate’s assets and debts.
The court later authorized the receiver to file a winding-up petition against the company.
members.legal_principle: Order XL Rule 1(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a court to confer on a receiver powers necessary to realize and manage the estate. Even assuming a winding-up petition is not a suit, the powers relating to realization of property and debts are broad enough to permit such a petition as a form of equitable execution. The court may also confer powers appropriate to the receiver’s administration of the estate. The Court relied on Bowes v. Hope Life Insurance and Guarantee Co., Re General Company for Promotion of Land Credit, and Re National Permanent Building Society.
members.conclusion: The receiver had power to file the winding-up petition to realize the debt due to the estate.

predicates.receiver_seeks_winding_up_of_debtor_comp: A receiver seeks to have a company wound up as a means of pursuing an estate’s claim against it.
predicates.court_appointed_receiver_administers_est: A court appoints a receiver to administer property belonging to an estate.
predicates.debt_forms_part_of_estate: The debt sought from the company is an asset of the estate administered by the receiver.
predicates.winding_up_can_realize_estate_debt: Winding up the debtor company can serve as a means of realizing the estate’s debt.

members.legal_issue: A court-appointed receiver authorized to sue to recover an estate debt is a creditor entitled to present a winding-up petition in respect of that debt.
material_facts: The receiver was appointed to administer the joint family’s properties and was authorized to sue to realize its assets, including the debt owed by the company.
The receiver could demand payment of the debt and, under the court’s authority, could bring an action to recover it in the receiver’s own name.
The receiver presented the winding-up petition based on the company’s unpaid debt.
members.legal_principle: Sections 434 and 439(1) of the Companies Act allow a creditor to initiate winding-up proceedings. A creditor includes a person to whom a debt is payable, including a receiver empowered by the court to sue for that debt. The Court relied on K. V. Mallayya v. T. Ramaswami & Co. and considered In re Sacker and In re Macoun, explaining that a receiver able to maintain an action to recover a debt can be a petitioning creditor.
members.conclusion: The receiver was a creditor within the meaning of section 439(1) of the Companies Act and was competent to maintain the winding-up petition.

predicates.receiver_presents_winding_up_petition: A receiver presents a petition seeking the winding up of a company.
predicates.receiver_is_authorized_to_sue_for_estate: The receiver has authority to bring an action in the receiver’s own name to recover a debt belonging to the administered estate.
predicates.company_owes_that_debt: The company owes the estate the debt that the receiver is authorized to recover.

members.legal_issue: A reversioner may maintain a representative suit seeking a declaration that an alienation by a limited owner is not binding on the reversioners, notwithstanding the subsequent change in the limited owner’s estate.
material_facts: A widow holding inherited property under limited ownership made settlements of land before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.

Persons claiming to be reversioners sued in a representative capacity to challenge the settlements as invalid and not binding on the reversioners; they did not seek possession while the widow was alive.
The courts below found that the settlements were not bona fide and were not supported by legal necessity or benefit to the estate.
members.legal_principle: A presumptive or contingent reversioner may sue in a representative capacity to protect the estate from waste or danger and to obtain a declaration that an alienation by a limited owner is not binding on the body of reversioners. That remedy cannot be taken away without specific legislation, and the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 contains no such bar for an alienation made before it came into force. The Court relied on Venkatanarayana Pillai v. Subbamal and Radha Rani Bhargava v. Hanuman Prasad Bhargava.
members.conclusion: The reversioners were entitled to maintain the suit. The Hindu Succession Act did not take away their right to seek a declaration concerning the earlier alienations.

rule.if: reversioner_representative_suit and limited_owner_alienation_challenged and suit_seeks_estate_preservation and alienation_lacks_legal_necessity

predicates.reversioner_representative_suit: A person claiming a future inheritance brought suit in a representative capacity for the body of reversioners.
predicates.limited_owner_alienation_challenged: A limited owner transferred property and the reversioners challenged that transfer.
predicates.suit_seeks_estate_preservation: The suit sought a declaration that the transfer would not bind the reversioners, rather than possession during the limited owner's lifetime.
predicates.alienation_lacks_legal_necessity: The transfer was found not to be bona fide or supported by legal necessity or benefit to the estate.

members.legal_issue: A reversioner may maintain a declaratory suit challenging a Hindu female limited owner's pre-existing alienation despite the subsequent commencement of the Hindu Succession Act.
material_facts: A widow had alienated her husband's estate before the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
A daughter sued representatively for the reversioners, seeking a declaration that the alienation was not binding on them.
The Act came into force while the alienees' appeal was pending, and the High Court dismissed the suit on the ground that reversionary rights no longer existed.
members.legal_principle: Sections 14, 15 and 16 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 do not abolish reversionary rights in property already alienated by a Hindu female before the Act came into force. A reversioner may sue for a declaration that such an alienation was made without legal necessity and is not binding on the reversioners. The Court followed Gummalapura Taggina Matada Kotturuswami v. Sera Veerayya and Brahmadeo Singh v. Deomani Missir.
members.conclusion: The suit remained maintainable. The High Court's contrary decree was set aside, and the appeal was allowed for the High Court to hear the remaining merits.

predicates.representative_reversioner_declaratory_s: A reversioner brought a declaratory suit in a representative capacity on behalf of the reversioners.
predicates.pre_act_limited_owner_alienation: A Hindu female limited owner alienated property before the relevant succession-law change came into force.
predicates.alienation_challenged_as_without_legal_n: The suit challenged the alienation as made without legal necessity and as not binding on the reversioners.

members.legal_issue: When a court agrees to treat an application to sue without paying court fees as a plaint and extends time to pay the fee, a later order rejecting only the request to sue without fees does not itself reject the plaint, and accepted fee payment may take effect from the application's original presentation.
material_facts: Before the question of the plaintiff's eligibility to sue without paying court fees was decided, the plaintiff offered to pay the fee and asked the court to treat the application as a plaint.
The court agreed to treat the application as a plaint and extended time for payment.
The plaintiff did not pay by the extended deadline, and the court subsequently ordered that the application to sue without paying court fees be dismissed.
The plaintiff later paid the fee and the defendants' costs, and the court restored the proceeding after setting aside the dismissal order.
The court had not rejected the plaint; it had rejected only the request to sue without paying court fees.
The application had originally been presented within the limitation period.
members.legal_principle: Order 33 Rule 8 treats an allowed application to sue as a pauper as the plaint. Where, before formal disposal of the application, the applicant offers to pay the fee and the court agrees to treat the application as a plaint and enlarges time, the application is regarded as a plaint instituted on its presentation. Section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits enlargement of time for payment of court fees, and accepted payment has the same force and effect as payment in the first instance. If the plaint is not rejected under Order 7 Rule 11(c), an order rejecting only the withdrawn request to sue as a pauper does not end the suit. The court relied on Stuart Skinner v. William Orde and Devender Kumar Bharti v. Mahanta Raghuraj Bharti in approving the relation-back principle.
members.conclusion: The dismissal of the request to sue without paying court fees did not terminate the suit because the plaint had not been rejected. Under Section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the accepted fee payment had the same effect as payment on the date of original presentation, so the suit was within limitation.

rule.if: pauper_suit and original_application_was_timely and pauper_request_withdrawn_before_decision and court_agreed_to_treat_application_as_plaint and court_extended_fee_time and proceeding_restored and fee_paid_and_accepted and plaint_not_rejected

predicates.pauper_suit: The proceeding is a suit initiated by a person seeking permission to sue without paying court fees.
predicates.original_application_was_timely: The applicant presented the original application within the applicable limitation period.
predicates.pauper_request_withdrawn_before_decision: The applicant withdrew the request to proceed without paying court fees before the court decided that request.
predicates.court_agreed_to_treat_application_as_pla: The court agreed to proceed on the basis that the application would serve as the plaint.
predicates.court_extended_fee_time: The court allowed additional time for payment of the court fee.
predicates.proceeding_restored: After the proceeding was dismissed, the court set aside that dismissal and restored the proceeding.
predicates.fee_paid_and_accepted: The applicant later paid the court fee and the court accepted it.
predicates.plaint_not_rejected: The court did not reject the plaint itself.

members.legal_issue: A court may permit a deficient court fee to be paid after the limitation period, and payment cures the deficiency from the date the plaint was first presented if the plaint was originally presented within limitation.
material_facts: The plaint was first presented within the applicable limitation period but with a deficient court fee.
The plaintiffs later paid the deficit court fee after the limitation period had expired.
members.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits the court, in its discretion and at any stage, to allow payment of a deficient fee and gives the document the same force and effect as if the fee had been paid initially. It mitigates the operation of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code and Section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955. In Mannan Lal v. Mst. Chhotka Bibi, this Court held that making good the deficiency cures the defect from the date of initial presentation; Mannan Lal approved the relevant Madras Full Bench approach in Gavaranga Sahu v. Batakrishna Patro and considered Faizullah v. Mauladad.
members.conclusion: A plaint originally presented within limitation is not necessarily invalid because the court fee was deficient; if the court permits the deficit to be paid, the plaint is treated as having the same force and effect as if the fee had been paid at the outset.

predicates.civil_suit_plaint_presented_within_limit: A plaint in a civil suit was first presented within the limitation period applicable to the suit.
predicates.deficit_court_fee_later_paid: The plaintiff later paid the court fee that was deficient when the plaint was first presented.

members.legal_issue: An expired compensation agreement may be considered as evidence of the parties’ assessment of market value, but it does not bind the court determining compensation on reference.
material_facts: The Collector’s agreed-compensation award was made after the time limit for making an award under the agreement had expired.
A reference to the civil court for determination of market value was pending.
The agreement recorded the parties’ assessment of the land’s value by reference to the acquisition notification.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 16 and 18 of the Kerala Land Acquisition Act, 1961, expiry of the period for making an agreed award does not preclude the agreement from being considered as evidence in a reference. Its evidentiary value is for the court determining market value, and it is not binding on that court.
members.conclusion: The civil court may consider the agreement as evidence of the parties’ assessment of market value, and must decide its evidentiary value; the agreement does not bind the court in determining compensation.

predicates.civil_reference_to_determine_market_valu: A compensation dispute has been referred to a civil court for determination of market value.
predicates.compensation_agreement_exists: The landowner and the acquiring authority’s collector made an agreement fixing compensation for the land.
predicates.agreement_records_assessment_of_market_v: The agreement records the parties’ assessment of the land’s market value by reference to the relevant acquisition date.

members.legal_issue: A prior compensation award is evidence but does not conclusively establish market value or justify applying a fixed annual escalation rate.
material_facts: The claimants relied on an earlier valuation of land acquired in another year and proposed applying a fixed annual increase to derive the value of the land in this case.
The court found no justifiable basis to determine value solely by that escalation calculation.
members.legal_principle: The court held that a judgment or award fixing compensation is not conclusive and that there is no fixed criterion for increasing land value at a constant rate. It also referred to Union of India v. Ram Phool, which rejected reliance on an isolated sale showing a very high price, and to Union of India v. Pramod Gupta for other relevant valuation factors.
members.conclusion: A prior award is only a piece of evidence, and market value cannot be determined by applying a fixed rate of increase without a case-specific basis.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.prior_award_used_as_basis_for_fixed_esca: A party relies on an earlier compensation award and applies a fixed rate of increase to calculate the current market value.

members.legal_issue: Property taken into custody as evacuee property under a repealed law could become validly vested evacuee property under the replacement law without a fresh declaration.
material_facts: The properties had been taken into the Custodian’s possession as evacuee properties under the local law before the central ordinance came into force.
They remained in the Custodian’s possession when the central ordinance and then the Act came into force.
The Act’s retrospective provision deemed property that purported to have vested under a repealed law to have validly vested and deemed it evacuee property under the Act.
members.legal_principle: Sections 8(2) and 8(2A) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 deemed property vested under a repealed law to be evacuee property vested under the Act; subsection (2A), given retrospective effect, validated the vesting and related actions even where the earlier law or procedure was defective. The Court relied on The Dominion of India v. Shrinbai A. Irani, Azimunissa v. Deputy Custodian Evacuee Properties, and Haji Ismail Noor Mohammad and Co. v. Competent Officer, which recognized the validating and deeming effect of these provisions and the absence of a need for a fresh declaration.
members.conclusion: The properties were evacuee property validly vested in the Custodian under the Act, and no fresh declaration under the later law was required.

predicates.property_claim_under_successor_evacuee_p: A claim concerns property dealt with under a successor law governing evacuee property.
predicates.property_taken_as_evacuee_property_under: A custodian had taken the property as evacuee property under a law that was later repealed.
predicates.property_remained_with_custodian_at_succ: The property was still in the custodian’s possession when the successor law came into force.

members.legal_issue: Property that has automatically vested in a custodian under provincial evacuee-property law and is carried forward under successor central legislation does not require a fresh declaration under the central legislation.
material_facts: A partner left for Pakistan amid disturbed conditions and was held to be an evacuee under provincial law.
The evacuee’s interest in the partnership business, including its property in the province, vested automatically in the Custodian under that law.
The successor central ordinance and Act provided that property already vested would be deemed to continue vested.
The firm contended that a fresh notice and declaration under the central law were necessary.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(c), 2(d) and 5 of the U.P. Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949, an evacuee’s property interest in the province vested automatically in the Custodian. Sections 8(2) and 55(3) of the Central Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949, and sections 8(2) and 58(3) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, continued that vesting by deeming provisions and savings clauses. Section 7 applied to property not already vested automatically; it did not require a further declaration for property whose vesting had already continued under the successor legislation. The Court also referred to the retrospective validation considered in Azimunnissa v. The Deputy Custodian, Evacuee Properties, District Deoria, [1961] 2 S.C.R. 91.
members.conclusion: No fresh notice or declaration under section 7 was necessary because the interest had already vested automatically and continued to vest under the successor legislation.

predicates.successor_regime_proceeding: The dispute concerns property under a successor regime that carries forward property previously vested under an earlier evacuee-property regime.
predicates.property_previously_vested: The property interest had already vested automatically in a custodian under the earlier regime.
predicates.departure_triggered_evacuee_status: A person left the relevant territory for another country because of disturbed conditions and was treated as an evacuee under the applicable law.

members.legal_issue: Possession that has not continued for the required limitation period before a timely suit for recovery does not ripen into title by adverse possession.
material_facts: The appellants' possession became illegal and adverse after the transferor died.
The transferor's sons brought a suit for recovery of possession within six years of that possession becoming adverse.
The suit was decreed, and the later proceedings arose after further proceedings in the appeals were stayed during consolidation operations.
members.legal_principle: Adverse possession does not mature into title before the applicable twelve-year period has elapsed. The court found that the owners sued for recovery within six years of the possession becoming adverse, before the required period could run.
members.conclusion: The appellants did not acquire title to the disputed land by adverse possession.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim: The matter includes a claim that possession has matured into title by adverse possession.
predicates.possession_adverse_to_owner: The claimant's possession was adverse to the person entitled to the land.
predicates.recovery_suit_filed_before_limitation_pe: The person entitled to the land filed a recovery suit before the applicable limitation period elapsed.
predicates.no_title_by_adverse_possession: The claimant did not acquire title by adverse possession.

members.legal_issue: A possessor does not acquire title by adverse possession when the period of possession is shorter than the required limitation period and an earlier period said to be capable of tacking is not proved.
material_facts: The appellants had possession of the disputed lands from 1934 until the debt-adjustment application was filed in 1945, a period shorter than twelve years.
The appellants contended that an earlier period should be added because the first respondent had occupied the lands as their tenant before they took possession.
The courts below found that the appellants had not proved that the first respondent occupied the lands as their tenant during that earlier period.
members.legal_principle: The possession relied on for adverse possession had not continued for twelve years by the time the adjustment application was filed. The claimed earlier period could not be added because the alleged tenancy and possession during that period were not proved. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this issue in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The appellants had not acquired title to the lands by adverse possession.

rule.if: agricultural_debt_adjustment_proceeding and adverse_possession_title_claim and possession_period_below_limitation and not prior_tacking_period_proven

predicates.agricultural_debt_adjustment_proceeding: The matter was a proceeding seeking adjustment of an agricultural debtor’s debt.
predicates.adverse_possession_title_claim: A party claimed ownership of the disputed property based on adverse possession.
predicates.possession_period_below_limitation: The party’s proved possession had not lasted for the full period required to acquire title by adverse possession.
predicates.prior_tacking_period_proven: The party proved an earlier period of possession that could be added to its own period of possession.

members.legal_issue: A reviewing court may set aside a quasi-judicial cancellation of an allotment when the required finding of fraud is unsupported by evidence and rests on an incomplete consideration of the relevant material.
material_facts: The Chief Settlement Commissioner cancelled an allotment after concluding that the extracts supporting its grant were not genuine.

The original land records were unavailable, and the Commissioner relied on records from earlier years without addressing reports from revenue officials concerning the poor condition of the land and the risk of river erosion.
The Commissioner’s order identified no evidence supporting the conclusion that the extracts were not genuine.
The High Court found no evidence supporting the fraud finding and set aside the cancellation order.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 empowers the Chief Settlement Commissioner to cancel an allotment obtained by fraud, false representation, or concealment of a material fact. The Commissioner’s satisfaction on that matter is a jurisdictional fact, not a conclusive determination. Because the power is judicial in character, a superior authority or a High Court exercising writ jurisdiction may examine whether the satisfaction was based on material and whether the order was arbitrary, capricious, or perverse. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to set aside the cancellation order because the Chief Settlement Commissioner’s finding of fraud was unsupported by evidence; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: writ_review_of_allotment_cancellation and original_records_unavailable and relevant_reports_ignored and fraud_finding_unsupported

predicates.writ_review_of_allotment_cancellation: A party sought review in writ proceedings of an authority’s order cancelling an allotment.
predicates.original_records_unavailable: The decision-maker did not have the original records relevant to the alleged fraud.
predicates.relevant_reports_ignored: The decision-maker did not consider reports relevant to whether the allotment had been obtained by fraud.
predicates.fraud_finding_unsupported: The decision-maker’s finding of fraud had no evidentiary support in the material considered.

members.legal_issue: A reviewing court may decline to interfere with cancellation of an allotment when the authorities’ finding that the claimant lacked the qualifying interest is supported by relevant material and amounts to a finding that the allotment was obtained through false representation, even without an express finding using those words.
material_facts: The allotment was made on the basis of a claimed occupancy interest in abandoned property.
The authorities relied on land records showing that the claimants were ordinary tenants at will rather than occupancy tenants, and found that the supporting affidavits could not be relied on.
The claimants did not challenge the accuracy of the land records when responding to the cancellation notice.
The High Court dismissed the constitutional challenge to the cancellation, and the claimants appealed by special leave.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 24(2) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, the Chief Settlement Commissioner could cancel the allotment; Section 33 provided for revision. An express finding of fraud or false representation was not essential where the authorities’ findings, based on relevant material, necessarily supported the inference that the allotment had been obtained by false representation. The High Court was justified in declining relief under Articles 226 and 227 where no jurisdictional error or error of law apparent on the face of the record was shown. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The authorities’ findings and the inference of false representation were supported by relevant material; the High Court was justified in declining to exercise its constitutional review jurisdiction, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_writ_dismissal: The claimant brought a special-leave appeal after a court dismissed a constitutional challenge to an administrative decision.
predicates.official_records_negated_qualifying_inte: The authorities relied on official records that showed the claimant did not hold the interest required to qualify for the benefit.
predicates.claimant_did_not_challenge_underlying_re: The claimant did not contest the accuracy of the official records when given an opportunity to respond to the proposed cancellation.
predicates.authorities_inferred_false_representatio: The authorities’ findings about the claimant’s lack of a qualifying interest supported an inference that the benefit had been obtained through a false representation.

members.legal_issue: The absence of a right for a displaced tenant to return after demolition and reconstruction, when a right to return after repairs is provided, does not create an unreasonable classification.
material_facts: The challenged scheme allowed a tenant displaced for repairs to return after the repairs were completed, but did not provide a corresponding right after demolition and reconstruction.
Repairs could generally be completed within a few months, whereas reconstruction could take years, during which a displaced tenant would be expected to find other suitable accommodation.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a classification is valid if it has a rational basis; the absence of a right to return after reconstruction does not by itself make a rent-control scheme unfair or unconstitutional. The Court relied on sections 14(1)(a), 14(1)(b), 14(2)(a), 14(2)(b), and 15 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, and applied the principles in State of Madhya Pradesh v. G.C. Mandawar and the decisions concerning the scheme of those provisions, including Shah Bhojraj Kuverji Oil Mills and Ginning Factory v. Subbash Chandra Yograj Sinha.
members.conclusion: The different treatment of tenants displaced for repairs and those displaced for demolition and reconstruction is rational and does not violate the guarantee of equality.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_rent_law: A party challenged the constitutionality of a rent-control law in court.
predicates.repairs_allow_return: The law allows a tenant displaced for repairs to return to the premises after the repairs are completed.
predicates.reconstruction_takes_substantially_longe: Reconstruction is expected to take substantially longer than repairs, so the displaced tenant is expected to find other accommodation.

members.legal_issue: A limited exemption from rent-control protections for a building reconstructed after eviction for demolition and rebuilding is not unconstitutional merely because the displaced tenant cannot return to it.
material_facts: The law exempted a new building erected after the original building was demolished from rent-control provisions for a limited period.
The exemption was intended to encourage landlords to replace dilapidated, uneconomic buildings with new accommodation.
members.legal_principle: A legislature may provide a limited exemption from rent control to encourage construction and increase available accommodation, provided the measure is not otherwise unreasonable or arbitrary. The Court relied on section 16(2) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, and the principles in Punjab Tin Supply Co. v. Central Government, Mohinder Kumar v. State of Haryana, and Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The limited exemption for a reconstructed building is not discriminatory or unreasonable and does not violate Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_rent_law: A party challenged the constitutionality of a rent-control law in court.
predicates.reconstructed_building_is_exempt_for_lim: The law exempts a building reconstructed after demolition from rent-control restrictions for a limited period.
predicates.exemption_encourages_additional_housing: The exemption is intended to encourage construction that adds accommodation.

members.legal_issue: The detaining government must independently consider a detainee’s representation against a preventive detention order regardless of whether the representation is addressed to the government or to the advisory body.
material_facts: The detainee made a representation against the detention order and addressed it to the advisory body while its reference was pending.
The advisory body considered the representation and the detention reference.
The government confirmed the detention order after receiving the advisory body’s opinion but never independently considered the representation.
The government argued that it had no duty to consider the representation because it was addressed to the advisory body.
members.legal_principle: Article 22(5), read with Article 22(4), requires the detaining government to consider a representation against detention independently of the advisory body’s consideration. The advisory body’s consideration is an additional safeguard, not a substitute. The duty applies regardless of whether the representation is addressed to the government, the advisory body, or both; the mode of address is a matter of form. The Court relied on K.M. Abdulla Kunhi and B.L. Abdul Khader v. Union of India, which discussed Sk. Abdul Karim v. State of West Bengal, Pankaj Kumar Chakrabarty v. State of West Bengal, Shayamal Chakraborty v. Commissioner of Police, B. Sundar Rao v. State of Orissa, John Martin v. State of West Bengal, S.K. Sekawat v. State of West Bengal, and Haradhan Saha v. State of West Bengal.
members.conclusion: The government breached its constitutional duty by failing to consider the representation independently. The detention order and its confirmation were quashed; this did not affect prosecution for the alleged offence or direct release if the detainee remained in custody because bail had been refused.

predicates.preventive_detention_challenge: A person challenges an order made to detain someone preventively.
predicates.representation_made: The detainee makes a representation against the detention order.
predicates.government_failed_independent_review: The government does not independently consider and decide the detainee’s representation.
predicates.detention_order_and_confirmation_invalid: The preventive detention order and its confirmation are invalid.

members.legal_issue: The State Government must consider a detainee’s representation independently and expeditiously, rather than wait for the Advisory Board’s opinion.
material_facts: The State Government received the appellants’ representations on February 20, 1993.
It kept the representations pending while awaiting the Advisory Board’s opinion, received the Board’s report on March 23, 1993, and rejected the representations that day.
The State Government did not provide a satisfactory explanation for postponing consideration until the Board’s opinion.
members.legal_principle: Article 22(5) requires the Government to consider a representation independently of the Advisory Board’s consideration and to do so with reasonable speed and a sense of urgency. Any delay must be satisfactorily explained. The Court relied on Jayanarayan Sukul v. State of West Bengal, Haradhan Saha v. State of West Bengal, K.M. Abdulla Kunhi v. Union of India, and Moosa Husein Sanghar v. State of Gujarat; Article 21 protects the liberty affected by detention.
members.conclusion: Keeping the representations pending until the Advisory Board reported and considering them only afterward was unlawful and breached the constitutional requirement of expeditious consideration.

rule.if: preventive_detention_proceeding and representation_received_by_government and government_waited_for_advisory_board and not satisfactory_delay_explanation

predicates.preventive_detention_proceeding: The case concerns a person held under a preventive-detention order.
predicates.representation_received_by_government: The Government received the detainee’s representation against detention.
predicates.government_waited_for_advisory_board: The Government postponed its consideration of the representation until it received the Advisory Board’s opinion.
predicates.satisfactory_delay_explanation: The Government gave a satisfactory explanation for any delay in considering the representation.

members.legal_issue: A successor sovereign is not bound by a liability incurred by a former sovereign before territorial merger unless the successor expressly or impliedly accepts the claim, even when the liability concerns public property retained by the successor.
material_facts: Builders constructed public court and secretariat buildings for the former state, and its ruler admitted the amount claimed and executed a promissory note for it.
After the former state merged into the successor state, the successor took possession of and retained the buildings as public property.
The successor state had not expressly or impliedly undertaken to pay the claim.
members.legal_principle: An Act of State is an exercise of sovereign power over territory not previously subject to that sovereign. Following acquisition or merger, inhabitants may enforce only rights the new sovereign has recognized, and the defence ends only upon express or implied acceptance of the claim. The principle applies even to liabilities concerning public property of the former state that the successor takes over and retains. The Court relied on Raja Rajender Chand v. Sukhi, State of Saurashtra v. Memon Haji Ismail, and Vaje Singh Ji Joravar Singh v. Secretary of State for India in Council.
members.conclusion: The claim could not be enforced against the successor state because it had not accepted the liability; the Act of State defence was available, including in respect of liability concerning public property retained by the successor.

rule.if: successor_state_claim and territory_newly_acquired and former_state_liability and public_property_retained and not successor_acceptance

predicates.successor_state_claim: A claimant seeks to enforce against a successor sovereign a liability associated with a former sovereign.
predicates.territory_newly_acquired: The territory in which the liability arose came under the successor sovereign's authority for the first time.
predicates.former_state_liability: The liability was incurred by or on behalf of the former sovereign before the territorial change.
predicates.public_property_retained: The successor sovereign took over and retained as public property property connected with the liability.
predicates.successor_acceptance: The successor sovereign expressly or impliedly accepted the claim or undertook to honour the liability.
predicates.successor_state_not_bound: The successor sovereign is not bound to pay the unaccepted former-state liability.

members.legal_issue: A successor sovereign state is bound by a predecessor state's contractual liability only to the extent that the successor recognizes that liability.
material_facts: A predecessor state had allegedly promised a customs-duty reduction as part of a plot-sale contract.
The successor state and the governments preceding it continued to allow the reduction, but the concession was available under customs legislation governing the relevant territory.
The successor state later revoked the concession, and the claimant sought recovery on the basis of the alleged contractual promise.
members.legal_principle: A change of sovereignty is an act of State, and rights under a predecessor state's contracts are enforceable in the successor's municipal courts only if the successor recognizes them, expressly or by implication.
