The Court relied on The Secretary of State in Council of India v. Kamachee Boye Saheba, Vajesingji Joravarsingji v. Secretary of State for India in Council, Secretary of State v. Sardar Rustom Khan, M/s. Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, State of Saurashtra v. Jamadar Mohamat Abdulla, Maharaja Shree Umaid Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, and State of Gujarat v. Vora Fiddali Badruddin Mithibarwala.
members.conclusion: The alleged contractual right was not enforceable against the successor state because the successor had not recognized the contractual liability; the continued concession was attributable to customs law and did not establish implied recognition.

predicates.civil_recovery_claim_against_successor: A claimant brought a civil recovery claim against a successor state based on an alleged obligation of its predecessor state.
predicates.predecessor_state_contract_claimed: The claimant asserted that the predecessor state had undertaken a contractual obligation.
predicates.successor_state_did_not_recognize_contra: The successor state did not expressly or impliedly recognize the alleged contractual obligation.

members.legal_issue: A registration authority may register a unilateral cancellation deed when no applicable rule requires the consent or participation of the parties to the earlier conveyance.
material_facts: A society had executed a deed purporting to extinguish an earlier registered sale deed and presented it for registration without the participation of the earlier purchaser or the purchaser’s successors.
The dispute arose in a state where no rule comparable to the rule discussed in the judgment required the parties to the earlier conveyance to execute or consent to a cancellation deed.
The appellant asked registration authorities to cancel the registration, and the dispute reached the Court in an appeal from the dismissal of a writ petition.
members.legal_principle: The Registration Act, 1908, including Sections 17, 20, 21, 32, 34 and 69, gives registration officers administrative functions and does not confer general authority to adjudicate title or disputed questions. Section 69 empowers the Inspector-General to make rules consistent with the Act. Justice Dipak Misra distinguished the Andhra Pradesh rule considered in Thota Ganga Laxmi v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, (2010) 15 SCC 207, and discussed Yanala Malleshwari v. Anantula Sayamma, AIR 2007 AP 57, E.R. Kalaivan v. Inspector General of Registration, AIR 2010 Madras 18, and M. Ramakrishna Reddy v. Sub Registrar, AIR 2000 Karnataka 46.
members.conclusion: Justice Dipak Misra expressed the view that, absent a specific rule requiring the earlier parties’ participation, the registration authority could not refuse to register a cancellation deed solely because those parties were absent or had not consented. He considered the general observations in Thota Ganga Laxmi to require consideration by a larger Bench. The judges disagreed, and the matter was referred to the Chief Justice for constitution of a larger Bench; this proposition was therefore not resolved by a majority holding in this judgment.

rule.if: registration_challenge_proceeding and cancellation_deed_presented and no_applicable_rule_requires_prior_party_consent and registration_requirements_met

predicates.registration_challenge_proceeding: A party challenges a registration authority’s handling of a document in a proceeding concerning registration.
predicates.cancellation_deed_presented: A document purporting to cancel or extinguish an earlier registered conveyance is presented for registration.
predicates.no_applicable_rule_requires_prior_party_: No applicable rule requires the parties to the earlier conveyance to execute or consent to the cancellation document.
predicates.registration_requirements_met: The presented document satisfies the applicable requirements for registration.

members.legal_issue: In the absence of an applicable rule requiring the other party’s participation, unilateral presentation of an extinguishment document by a housing society does not, by itself, make its registration invalid.
material_facts: A housing society presented an extinguishment deed for registration to record its decision to cancel a member’s plot allotment after an alleged failure to build on the plot.
The original allottee or her representative was not present when the society presented the deed.
The deed was registered, and no applicable Madhya Pradesh provision or rule requiring both parties’ signatures or presence was identified.
The deed concerned the society’s decision about an allotment and membership, rather than cancellation of a sale deed between private parties.
members.legal_principle: Sections 32, 34 and 35 of the Registration Act, 1908 do not require both parties to be present when a document is presented for registration, and the registering officer’s inquiry is not a quasi-judicial determination of title or the document’s substantive legality. A procedural irregularity does not by itself establish fraud or nullity; Section 87 protects acts done in good faith from invalidity merely for procedural defects. A registered document may be challenged before a competent court. Thota Ganga Laxmi v. Government of Andhra Pradesh applied an express requirement in Rule 26(k)(i) of the Andhra Pradesh Registration Rules and did not establish a universal rule. The Court also relied on Yanala Malleshwari v. Ananthula Sayamma and Park View Enterprises v. State of Tamil Nadu.
members.conclusion: The unilateral presentation and registration of the extinguishment deed could not be treated as fraudulent or void solely because the other party was not present. The rule in Thota Ganga Laxmi did not apply generally because it concerned an express Andhra Pradesh rule; the validity of the society’s underlying cancellation decision remained for the competent forum to decide.

predicates.is_unilateral_extinguishment_document_pr: A party presented an extinguishment or cancellation document for registration without the other party joining in its presentation.
predicates.no_applicable_rule_requires_both_parties: No applicable law or rule requires the other party to sign the document or be present for its registration.
predicates.registration_requirements_are_followed: The document was presented and processed in accordance with the applicable registration procedure.

members.legal_issue: Rent deposited in the lower courts while the parties dispute entitlement to it should be held for disbursement after the title dispute is resolved or settled.
material_facts: The tenants had deposited rent in one or more of the courts below during the rent and eviction proceedings.
The parties’ dispute over who was entitled to receive the rent was to be determined by the court competent to decide title, or could be resolved by agreement.
members.legal_principle: The Court directed that the deposited rent be retained and disbursed according to the eventual decision on title or an amicable settlement. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this direction.
members.conclusion: The deposited rent was not to be refunded to the tenants and was to be disbursed in accordance with the decision of the appropriate civil court or an amicable settlement of the title dispute.

predicates.appeal_from_tenant_rent_or_eviction_suit: An appeal concerns a landlord’s rent or eviction suit against a tenant.
predicates.rent_deposited_in_lower_court: The tenant has deposited rent in a court below during the proceedings.
predicates.entitlement_to_deposited_rent_unresolved: The parties’ dispute over who is entitled to the rent remains unresolved.

members.legal_issue: Tenants should continue depositing rent while the dispute over title and entitlement to rent remains unresolved.
material_facts: The tenants remained in the rented premises while the title dispute was pending determination or settlement.
The Court directed the tenants to deposit rent regularly during that period.
members.legal_principle: The Court directed continuing rent deposits pending resolution of title, applying sub-section (2) of Section 30 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1977. No earlier case was cited.
members.conclusion: The tenant-appellants were directed to continue depositing rent regularly until the title dispute was decided or settled, as contemplated by the applicable rent law.

predicates.appeal_from_tenant_rent_or_eviction_suit: An appeal concerns a landlord’s rent or eviction suit against tenants.
predicates.tenants_remain_in_rented_property: The tenants continue to occupy the rented property while the dispute is pending.
predicates.title_dispute_unresolved: The dispute about title or entitlement to rent has not yet been decided or settled.

members.legal_issue: The passage of time since an offence, by itself, does not justify reducing a sentence that is not harsh.
material_facts: The appellants sought reduced sentences, relying on the time elapsed since the occurrence and the time already served.
One appellant had already served the sentence imposed on him.
The Court found that the sentences imposed were not harsh.
members.legal_principle: The passage of time since the occurrence is not, by itself, a sufficient reason to reduce a sentence; the Court found the sentences in this case not harsh.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to reduce the sentences and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_sentence: The accused appealed against the sentence imposed in a criminal case.
predicates.sentence_not_harsh: The court found that the sentence imposed was not harsh.
predicates.elapsed_time_is_reduction_ground: The accused relied on the time elapsed since the occurrence as a reason to reduce the sentence.

members.legal_issue: The passage of time during a trial or appeal, by itself, does not justify reducing a sentence for a serious offence to the period already served.
material_facts: The accused had undergone different periods of imprisonment, and the proceedings had continued for many years.
The High Court relied on the accused having faced a long trial and appeal when reducing their sentences.
The convictions were for attempted murder, and the record included serious injuries, including injuries dangerous to life.
members.legal_principle: A sentence reduction must rest on recognised judicial principles and relevant circumstances, not merely on the length of the proceedings. The Court relied on Sadha Singh v. State of Punjab, which rejected similar grounds for reducing a sentence, and State of U.P. v. Nankau Prasad Misra, in which a sentence reduction without adequate reasons was set aside.
members.conclusion: The long pendency of the proceedings did not justify the reduction; the trial court's sentences were restored.

predicates.appeal_challenging_sentence_reduction: A complainant or other appellant challenges an appellate court's reduction of a criminal sentence.
predicates.serious_offence_conviction: The accused were convicted of a serious criminal offence.
predicates.sentence_reduced_solely_for_proceeding_d: The appellate court relied on the length of the trial or appeal as the sole basis for reducing the sentence.

members.legal_issue: A court may enter judgment on admissions drawn from pleadings and other material in the same suit when the admissions leave no genuine controversy over the facts establishing entitlement to relief.
material_facts: The lessor sought possession after terminating a lease for non-payment of rent.
The lessee admitted in its written statement that it had withheld rent and acknowledged the termination notice.
In a separate application in the lessor’s suit seeking relief against forfeiture, the lessee stated that it had no objection to paying rent under the lease and undertook to pay future rent.
The lessee did not specifically deny several material assertions in the lessor’s application for judgment on admissions.
members.legal_principle: Order 12 Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure is broader than Order 12 Rule 1: admissions may be in pleadings or otherwise, orally or in writing, and may be inferred from the facts and circumstances. It is an enabling and discretionary provision intended to allow speedy judgment where there is no real controversy. The Court relied on Thorp v. Holdsworth, Charanjit Lal Mehra v. Kamal Saroj Mahajan, Uttam Singh Duggal & Co. Ltd. v. United Bank of India, and Shikharchand v. Mst. Bari Bai. The Court rejected the contention that the first proviso to Order 8 Rule 5 necessarily required independent proof in these circumstances.
members.conclusion: The admissions in the pleadings and in the lessee’s application in the same suit could be considered under Order 12 Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the possession judgment could stand.

rule.if: civil_suit_for_possession and clear_admission_of_landlord_tenant_relationship and clear_admission_of_rent_nonpayment and admission_of_termination_notice

predicates.civil_suit_for_possession: A claimant brought a civil suit seeking possession of property from an occupant.
predicates.clear_admission_of_landlord_tenant_relat: The occupant clearly admitted that the claimant had let the property to the occupant.
predicates.clear_admission_of_rent_nonpayment: The occupant clearly admitted that it had not paid rent due under the lease.
predicates.admission_of_termination_notice: The occupant admitted receiving notice terminating the lease.

members.legal_issue: A court may decide a suit on preliminary issues when admitted facts make those issues decisive of the suit.
material_facts: The parties did not dispute the earlier allotment-cancellation and mutation proceedings or their adjudication by revenue authorities.
The High Court had the suit record and admitted documents before it.
The issues of res judicata and maintainability could be determined on the admitted facts.
members.legal_principle: Order XIV Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a civil court to dispose of a suit on preliminary issues. Where facts are admitted, issues of res judicata, constructive res judicata, and maintainability can ordinarily be decided as preliminary issues. The High Court also referred to its inherent powers under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: No particular procedure was required before the High Court disposed of the suit on the decisive preliminary issues.

rule.if: civil_suit_proceeding and suit_withdrawn_to_high_court and material_facts_admitted and threshold_issue_decisive

predicates.civil_suit_proceeding: The proceeding is a civil suit.
predicates.suit_withdrawn_to_high_court: The suit was withdrawn from a subordinate court to the High Court for decision.
predicates.material_facts_admitted: The parties admitted the material facts and the existence and adjudication of earlier proceedings.
predicates.threshold_issue_decisive: A preliminary issue concerning matters such as res judicata or maintainability could decide the suit.

members.legal_issue: A trust deed creates a public charitable trust when its operative objects benefit a defined public class in need and do not require the trustees to confine benefits to the settlor’s employees.
material_facts: The deed as rectified provided for charitable and public-utility objects, including assistance with housing for workmen in the area who were poor and in need.
It also provided for schools, libraries, hospitals, recreation facilities, and other public-utility works.
The deed did not require the trustees to give benefits only to the settlor’s employees; evidence showed that workers outside the settlor’s group benefited as well.
For later assessment periods, the tribunal had allowed exemption under the applicable provisions, subject to the statutory limit and conditions for the years governed by the later Act.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the charitable-purpose provisions in section 4(3)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 and sections 2(15) and 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. A defined section of the public may be a charitable class, and a discretionary ability to benefit the settlor’s employees does not defeat public character where the deed does not oblige the trustees to prefer them. The Court relied on Trustees of the Charity Fund v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, Commissioner of Income-Tax v. Andhra Chamber of Commerce, Ahmedabad Rana Caste Association v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, Abdul Sathar Haji Moosa Sait Dharmastapanam v. Commissioner of Agricultural Income-Tax, Sole Trustee, Loka Sikshana Trust v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, and Yogiraj Charity Trust v. Commissioner of Income-Tax. It also applied the distinction in Commissioner of Income-Tax v. Walchand Diamond Jubilee Trust between discretionary preference and a binding priority for a private group.
members.conclusion: The deed as rectified created a public charitable trust. The trust’s income qualified for exemption for the relevant later assessment periods, subject to the conditions applicable under the governing tax provisions.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment and charitable_public_objects and defined_public_class_in_need and no_mandatory_employee_priority

predicates.income_tax_assessment: A tax authority was determining a trust’s entitlement to exemption for its income.
predicates.charitable_public_objects: The trust instrument provided objects directed to charitable purposes or public utility.
predicates.defined_public_class_in_need: The instrument identified a section of the public in need as beneficiaries.
predicates.no_mandatory_employee_priority: The instrument did not require the trustees to confine benefits or give binding priority to the settlor’s employees.

members.legal_issue: A deed creating a charitable endowment that permits benefits without religious, caste, or creed restrictions creates a secular public charitable trust rather than a wakf.
material_facts: The deed authorized the trust property and income to be used for relief of the poor, religious institutions, education, medical relief, and other objects of general public utility.
The deed stated that the charitable benefits were not to be restricted to any particular religion and contemplated purposes without distinction of religion, caste, or creed.
The deed transferred legal title to the trustees and gave them discretion to select and fund the specified charitable purposes.
The deed appointed trustees including non-Muslims and provided for management not restricted by Muslim-law rules.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(1) of the Wakf Act, 1954, covers a permanent dedication for purposes recognized by Muslim law as pious, religious, or charitable. The Court distinguished a wakf, in which ownership is transferred to God, from a trust in which legal title is vested in trustees, relying on Vidya Varuthi Thirtha v. Balusami Ayyar, (1921) L.R. 48 I.A. 302. In construing an instrument, where two constructions are reasonably possible, the construction that gives effect to all its clauses is preferred to one that defeats some clauses.
members.conclusion: The deed created a secular, comprehensive public charitable trust, not a wakf.

rule.if: charitable_endowment_classification_case and unrestricted_public_charitable_purposes and legal_title_vested_in_trustees and broad_trustee_discretion

predicates.charitable_endowment_classification_case: The proceeding requires classification of an instrument that creates a charitable endowment.
predicates.unrestricted_public_charitable_purposes: The instrument permits charitable benefits without restriction to a particular religion, caste, or creed.
predicates.legal_title_vested_in_trustees: The instrument transfers legal title to the endowment property to trustees.
predicates.broad_trustee_discretion: The instrument gives trustees broad discretion to select and fund its charitable purposes.

members.legal_issue: A re-grant of an abolished impartible service estate to the eldest son as representative of the family group does not make the estate his personal property and leaves the other heirs entitled to their shares under their applicable law of inheritance.
material_facts: The agricultural properties had been impartible Inams that devolved on the eldest son by primogeniture because services to the ruler were rendered through him.
After abolition of the Inams, the properties were re-granted to the eldest son as Watandar.
The other children claimed their inheritance shares, and the eldest son argued that the re-granted properties were his personal property.

The court found no basis to distinguish the principles applied in Nagesh Bisto Desai and Annasaheb Bapusaheb Patil merely because the heirs were Muslim; it held that the heirs could claim shares under Shariat law.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the principle in Nagesh Bisto Desai and Annasaheb Bapusaheb Patil that when an impartible service estate is abolished and re-granted to its holder, the former impartibility ends and the family group may claim shares. It found no reason to exclude Muslim heirs from that principle and held that their shares were determined under Shariat law. The abolition and re-grant occurred under the Bombay Merged Territories Miscellaneous Alienations Abolition Act, 1955.
members.conclusion: The re-grant did not make the properties the eldest son's personal estate; the other heirs were entitled to their respective shares under Shariat law.

rule.if: abolition_regrant_dispute and impartible_service_estate and estate_held_for_family_group and regrant_to_family_representative and regrant_ended_impartibility

predicates.abolition_regrant_dispute: The dispute concerns an estate that was abolished as a tenure and subsequently re-granted.
predicates.impartible_service_estate: The estate was impartible and services associated with it were rendered through the eldest family member.
predicates.estate_held_for_family_group: The eldest holder represented a group of family members in holding the estate.
predicates.regrant_to_family_representative: The estate was re-granted to the family member who had represented the group.
predicates.regrant_ended_impartibility: The re-grant ended the estate's former impartible character.

members.legal_issue: A statutory abolition of an impartible hereditary service estate followed by regrant to its former holder does not make ancestral estate the holder’s separate property, and the regranted property is partible among the joint family members.
material_facts: The lands were attached to a hereditary office and had been impartible under the rule of primogeniture.
The senior male family member succeeded to the watan under the pre-existing law and received a regrant after abolition of the watan.
The other family members claimed partition of the lands; there was no finding that they had renounced their rights of succession.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 5 of the Maharashtra Revenue Patels (Abolition of Office) Act, 1962 extinguish the watan and its incidents, including the service obligation and the rule of primogeniture; the land is regranted to the watandar as an occupant. The regrant does not convert ancestral watan land into the watandar’s separate property. An impartible ancestral estate may remain joint family property, and the senior member’s right to take by survivorship persists unless the junior members expressly or impliedly renounce succession. The Court relied on Nagesh Bisto Desai v. Khando Tirmal Desai, Dattatraya v. Krishna Rao and Anant Kibe v. Purushottam Rao; it also noted that Kalgonda Babgonda was reversed and that Shiddappa Satappa Murugude was decided without notice of the controlling three-Judge decisions.
members.conclusion: The regrant enured to the benefit of the joint Hindu family, and the lands became partible joint family property. The claimant was entitled to a share, and the decree granting partition was restored.

rule.if: partition_claim_concerning_hereditary_service_land and ancestral_joint_family_estate and estate_was_impartible_under_primogeniture and land_was_regranted_after_abolition

predicates.partition_claim_concerning_hereditary_se: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking partition of land attached to a hereditary service estate.
predicates.ancestral_joint_family_estate: The land was ancestral property of a joint family.
predicates.estate_was_impartible_under_primogenitur: The estate was impartible under a rule giving succession preference to the senior family member.
predicates.land_was_regranted_after_abolition: After the hereditary office and its incidents were abolished, the land was regranted to the former holder.

members.legal_issue: A partnership consisting of two partners is dissolved by the death of either partner even if the partnership agreement provides that death will not dissolve the firm, where the remaining partner cannot continue the same partnership without the other partner’s agreement.
material_facts: The firm had only two partners.
The deed stated that the firm would continue for a fixed term and that a partner’s death would not dissolve it.
One partner died, and that partner’s legal representatives were not willing to continue the firm or enter into a new partnership.
members.legal_principle: Section 42(c) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, makes dissolution on a partner’s death subject to the partners’ contract, but a two-partner firm cannot continue as the same partnership after one partner dies. Under Section 4, partnership is a contractual relationship, not a heritable status; the deceased partner’s legal representatives cannot be compelled to form a new partnership. The Court relied on Smt. S. Parvathammal v. CIT.
members.conclusion: The firm stood dissolved on the death of one of its two partners notwithstanding the deed’s contrary clause.

rule.if: partnership_dissolution_proceeding and two_partner_firm and partner_died and surviving_partner_cannot_continue_without_new_agreement

predicates.partnership_dissolution_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a partnership firm has been dissolved.
predicates.two_partner_firm: The firm consisted of two partners.
predicates.partner_died: One of the partners died while the firm was in existence.
predicates.surviving_partner_cannot_continue_withou: Continuing the partnership after the death would require the other partner or the deceased partner’s representatives to enter into a new agreement, and they did not agree to do so.

members.legal_issue: A partnership consisting of two partners is dissolved when one partner dies, despite a term purporting to continue the firm with the deceased partner’s heir or nominee.
material_facts: The partnership was formed by two individuals, each acting as karta for a joint Hindu family.
The partnership deed provided that a partner’s death would not dissolve the partnership and that the deceased partner’s heir or nominee would take the deceased partner’s place.
One of the two partners died.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 5 of the Partnership Act, 1932, partnership arises from contract, not status. Section 42(c) can preserve a partnership with more than two partners when one dies, but a two-person partnership ends on the death of either partner, leaving no subsisting firm into which another person can be introduced under section 31. The Court followed Mt. Sughra v. Babu and Narayanan v. Umayal, and rejected the contrary view in Hansraj Manot v. Messrs. Gorak Nath Pandey.
members.conclusion: The two-person partnership came to an end on the partner’s death; the deed could not automatically make the heir or nominee a partner in its place.

rule.if: partnership_dissolution_dispute and partnership_had_two_partners and one_partner_died and agreement_named_successor

predicates.partnership_dissolution_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a partnership continued after a partner died.
predicates.partnership_had_two_partners: The partnership had only two partners before the death.
predicates.agreement_named_successor: The partners had agreed that an heir or nominee would take the place of a partner who died.

members.legal_issue: A civil suit to establish title is not barred after consolidation unless the statute expressly bars that suit or the claim is one that could be made under the statute’s procedures.
material_facts: After consolidation, the plaintiff sued for joint possession of her claimed share in two plots.
The High Court held that the suit was barred after completion of consolidation proceedings.
The plaintiff sought to establish her title, and the Court found no applicable express bar to that title-based suit.
members.legal_principle: Courts do not readily infer a bar to a suit to establish title without an express statutory provision. The Court relied on Subha Singh v. Mahendra Singh, A.I.R. 1974 S.C. 1657, which held that a claim not capable of being brought under the relevant statute’s procedures did not attract the statutory bar to civil-court jurisdiction over title.
members.conclusion: The suit was not barred, and the High Court erred in holding otherwise.

rule.if: title_based_civil_suit and post_consolidation_dispute and not express_suit_bar

predicates.title_based_civil_suit: A party brings a civil suit seeking to establish title to land.
predicates.post_consolidation_dispute: The suit is brought after land-consolidation proceedings have concluded.
predicates.express_suit_bar: The statute expressly bars the civil suit seeking to establish title.

members.legal_issue: A civil court’s jurisdiction to decide an inheritance-based title claim is not barred when the claim arises after the consolidation scheme has been finalized and implemented and the claim cannot be brought under the consolidation statute.
material_facts: The plaintiff brought a civil suit for partition, claiming a share as the son of a person who had predeceased the property owner.
The consolidation scheme concerning the property had been finalized and published while the property owner was alive, and the scheme had been implemented so that possession was delivered.
The property owner died after those consolidation operations, giving rise to the inheritance claim.
The consolidation statute provided no procedure for deciding a title dispute arising after confirmation of the scheme; subsequent revenue records were governed by land-revenue law.
members.legal_principle: An exclusion of civil-court jurisdiction must be strictly construed. The first limb of Section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 applies to matters directly connected with and arising out of consolidation proceedings, not matters merely arising during them. Its second limb applies only to matters for which a suit or application could be filed under that Act. Where an inheritance claim arises after the scheme has been finalized and implemented and the Act supplies no procedure for that later claim, neither limb bars a civil suit. Sections 23 and 27(1), (3) of the Act, read with Sections 33 and 48 of the U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901, support that distinction. The Court approved the reasoning in Shrimati Natho v. Board of Revenue, U.P. and Smt. Bhuri v. Sunder, insofar as consistent with its analysis.
members.conclusion: The civil court’s jurisdiction was not barred, and it could investigate and adjudicate the disputed title and sonship. The appeal was dismissed.

predicates.civil_partition_or_title_suit: A person brought a civil suit seeking partition or determination of title to property.
predicates.inheritance_claim_arose_after_scheme_fin: The event giving rise to the inheritance claim occurred after the consolidation scheme had been finalized.
predicates.consolidation_substantially_completed_fo: The scheme had been implemented for the property, including the allotment or delivery of possession, before the later claim arose.
predicates.later_claim_outside_consolidation_remedi: The consolidation statute provided no procedure for bringing or deciding the claim that arose after the scheme was finalized.

members.legal_issue: An objection that concerns only the mode of proving an otherwise admissible document must be raised when the document is tendered, or it is waived.
material_facts: Photocopies of a public order and a rent agreement were admitted in evidence and marked as exhibits without objection.
The opposing parties challenged the photocopies in the second appeal because the originals had not been produced and, as to the rent agreement, because the copy was said to be unreadable.
The tenant admitted signing the rent agreement, and the plaintiff explained why the certified copy of the public order was not available in the proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Order 13 Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for the court's endorsement when a document is admitted in evidence. An objection that a document is itself inadmissible may still be raised later, but an objection only to an irregular or insufficient mode of proof must be made when the document is tendered. If a timely objection could have allowed the party tendering the document to cure the defect, failure to object waives the need for formal proof. This distinction is supported by Padman v. Hanwanta, P.C. Purushothama Reddiar v. S. Perumal, and the rule discussed in The Roman Catholic Mission v. The State of Madras.
members.conclusion: The later objections concerned the mode of proof and could not be raised after the documents had been admitted without timely objection. The second appellate court erred in excluding the documents.

rule.if: civil_evidence_proceeding and document_itself_admissible and objection_only_to_proof_method and no_timely_objection

predicates.civil_evidence_proceeding: The dispute involves documents tendered as evidence in a civil proceeding.
predicates.document_itself_admissible: The document is of a kind that is admissible in evidence, rather than being barred from evidence altogether.
predicates.objection_only_to_proof_method: The objection concerns how the document was proved, such as the use of a copy, rather than the document's inherent admissibility.
predicates.no_timely_objection: The opposing party did not object when the document was tendered and admitted.

members.legal_issue: Failure to object promptly to the mode of proving an otherwise admissible document waives a later challenge to that mode of proof.
material_facts: The plaintiff tendered a certified copy of a registered sale deed as evidence, and it was marked and admitted without objection.
The defendant’s later objection concerned the mode of proving the deed, rather than whether the deed was itself admissible in evidence.
The original deed was available in collateral proceedings and could have been produced if an objection had been made at trial.
The defendant first challenged the sufficiency of the mode of proof in the lower appellate court.
members.legal_principle: An objection that an otherwise admissible document was proved by an irregular or insufficient mode must be raised when the document is tendered and before it is marked as an exhibit. If a timely objection could have allowed the party tendering the document to cure the defect, failure to object waives the objection. The Court applied Order XIII Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and relied on R.V.E. Venkatachala Gounder v. Arulmigu Viswesaraswami & V.P. Temple, Gopal Das & Anr. v. Sri Thakurji & Ors., and the statement in Sarkar on Evidence. The asserted need to lay a foundation for secondary evidence under Section 65(a) and (f) of the Evidence Act did not preserve a belated objection to the mode of proof; the Court did not decide the appeal by independently resolving the applicability of Section 90 of that Act.
members.conclusion: The defendant could not raise the mode-of-proof objection for the first time in the lower appellate court; the civil appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: civil_evidence_dispute and document_is_otherwise_admissible and objection_concerns_mode_of_proof and document_marked_without_timely_objection and objection_first_raised_on_appeal and timely_objection_could_enable_cure

predicates.civil_evidence_dispute: The dispute is a civil proceeding in which a party relies on documentary evidence.
predicates.document_is_otherwise_admissible: The document is not challenged as inherently inadmissible in evidence.
predicates.objection_concerns_mode_of_proof: The opposing party disputes the method used to prove the document, rather than its inherent admissibility.
predicates.document_marked_without_timely_objection: The document is admitted and marked as an exhibit without an objection when it is tendered.
predicates.objection_first_raised_on_appeal: The opposing party first raises the mode-of-proof objection at an appellate stage.
predicates.timely_objection_could_enable_cure: An objection made when the document was tendered could have allowed the party relying on it to use a proper method of proof.

members.legal_issue: Whether a civil suit seeking decisions about the administration, possession or succession of property belonging to a registered public religious trust is barred when those matters are assigned to the statutory trust authorities.
material_facts: The religious body whose property was in dispute had been registered as a public trust.
The suit sought declarations about the body's dissolution and its successor, and injunctions affecting church property and its administration and possession.
The claimant had obtained registration as a public trust, but its change report concerning the trust records had not been decided.
The suit did not allege that the statutory authorities had failed to comply with the governing law or fundamental principles of judicial procedure.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 19–22, 31, 50, 51, 79 and 80 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, the trust authorities inquire into trust status and trust property, record and amend trust entries, and decide matters assigned to them; suits seeking specified reliefs concerning public trusts are subject to the Act's requirements, including consent where applicable. Section 26 applies only to questions a competent civil court may decide because they are not expressly or impliedly barred. The court applies Dhulabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh on statutory finality and exclusion of civil jurisdiction, and relies on Virupakshayya Shankarayya v. Neelakanta Shivacharya Pattadadevaru and Shree Gollaleshwar Dev v. Gangawwa Kom Shantayya Math concerning statutory procedures for claims involving trust property. The statutory scheme provides a remedy and appeal process, and the suit's substance concerned trust administration, property and succession rather than a matter outside that scheme.
members.conclusion: The suit was not maintainable because the matters its requested reliefs required the court to decide fell within the jurisdiction of the statutory trust authorities.

predicates.civil_suit_concerning_public_trust: A civil suit concerns property or affairs of a public trust.
predicates.claim_requires_decision_about_trust_admi: The relief sought depends on deciding how the trust is administered, who succeeds to it, or who may possess or manage its property.
predicates.statutory_authority_has_power_to_decide_: A statutory authority is empowered to decide the trust-related matter and the governing scheme provides a means to challenge its decision.

members.legal_issue: Whether a civil court may determine the foundational question of whether a trust exists or property is trust property when that question falls outside the statutory authority's jurisdiction.
material_facts: The claim concerned the successor to a religious body registered as a public trust and rights over property treated in the plaint as belonging to that trust.
The court found no case in the plaint that the trust was legally invalid or that the property had never validly vested in it.
members.legal_principle: Section 80 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act excludes civil jurisdiction only over questions that the Act assigns to its officers or authorities. The court held that a question whether property ever validly vested in a trust, or whether the trust itself is valid in law, may remain for the civil court because it is a jurisdictional question outside the statutory authorities' power.
members.conclusion: Civil-court jurisdiction is not barred for a foundational question where the property is not trust property in law or the trust itself is invalid in law, because the statutory authorities would then lack jurisdiction to decide it.

predicates.civil_suit_concerning_trust_status_or_pr: A civil suit raises a foundational dispute about whether a trust exists or whether property belongs to it.
predicates.property_is_not_trust_property_in_law_or: The property did not validly vest in a trust, or the trust itself is legally invalid.

members.legal_issue: The intent to annoy required for criminal trespass is established when the circumstances show that causing annoyance was the aim of the entry, rather than merely a likely consequence.
material_facts: The complainant obtained actual physical possession of the land after prolonged litigation and the respondents' resistance to execution of the ejectment decree.
About two weeks after possession was delivered, the respondents entered the land and were found preparing to construct bamboo structures.
The court found no other dominant intention that could explain the respondents' entry.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 441 and 447 of the Indian Penal Code, causing annoyance must be the aim of the entry; it is not enough that annoyance was merely a likely natural consequence known to the entrant. The court must consider all relevant circumstances, including such knowledge and the probability of another dominant intention. The court applied Mathuri and Others v. State of Punjab, [1964] 5 S.C.R. 916, 927.
members.conclusion: The respondents' intention was to annoy the complainant, and the intent required for criminal trespass was established.

rule.if: criminal_trespass_prosecution and prior_possession_recovered_after_dispute and entry_followed_by_construction_preparations and no_other_dominant_purpose

predicates.criminal_trespass_prosecution: The proceeding concerns an alleged entry onto property with the intent required for criminal trespass.
predicates.prior_possession_recovered_after_dispute: The complainant recovered possession of the property after a dispute with the entrants.
predicates.entry_followed_by_construction_preparati: The entrants entered the property and then prepared to construct structures there.
predicates.no_other_dominant_purpose: The circumstances disclose no other dominant purpose that prompted the entry.

members.legal_issue: An entry on property is criminal trespass only when causing an offence, intimidation, insult, or annoyance is the aim of the entry, rather than merely a known natural consequence.
material_facts: The entrants entered land to carry out possession processes that had expired.
They had been armed with the processes and intended to execute them, and the courts considered it reasonable that they did not know the processes had ceased to be executable.
The entrants could have known that their entry would naturally annoy the persons in possession.
The circumstances supported execution of the processes, rather than annoyance, as the dominant purpose of the entry.
members.legal_principle: Section 441 of the Indian Penal Code requires the specified intent; knowledge that annoyance, intimidation, or insult will naturally result is relevant but is not by itself sufficient. The relevant purpose must be the aim of the entry, assessed in light of all circumstances, including whether another purpose was dominant. The Court relied on Bhagwant v. Kedari and approved Emperor v. D'Cunha, Nizamuddin v. Jinnat Hussain, Satish Chandra Modak v. The King, Bata Krishna Ghosh v. State, State v. Abdul Sakur, Queen Empress v. Rayapadaayachi, and Vullappa v. Bheema Rao. It disapproved the contrary approaches in Emperor v. Laxman Raghunath, Sellamuthu Servaigaran v. Pallumuthu Karuppan, and Kesar Singh v. Prem Ballabh.
members.conclusion: The entry was not shown to be criminal trespass, and the defence that the assembly had gathered to resist criminal trespass was rightly rejected.

rule.if: criminal_trespass_assessment and entry_on_another_persons_property and natural_annoyance_was_known and purpose_was_execution_not_annoyance

predicates.criminal_trespass_assessment: The court assessed whether an entry on property amounted to criminal trespass.
predicates.entry_on_another_persons_property: A person entered property occupied by someone else.
predicates.natural_annoyance_was_known: The entrant knew that annoyance to the occupant would naturally result from the entry.
predicates.purpose_was_execution_not_annoyance: The circumstances showed that carrying out an asserted possession process, rather than causing annoyance, was the dominant purpose of the entry.

members.legal_issue: Judges should not make harsh, disparaging findings of misconduct without adequate pleadings and evidentiary support.
material_facts: A judge made strong remarks attributing bad faith, corruption, and improper dealings to the government.
The pleadings did not give adequate particulars or identify the material facts supporting those accusations.
The record did not substantiate the accusations.
members.legal_principle: Judges should exercise sobriety, moderation, and restraint when criticizing parties or witnesses. Allegations of misconduct require adequate particulars and material facts, and unsupported disparaging remarks risk causing injustice.
members.conclusion: The remarks were unjustified and unwarranted and should not have been made.

predicates.judicial_opinion_case: The proceeding involves a judge's written or oral assessment of a party's conduct.
predicates.judge_makes_disparaging_misconduct_findi: The judge makes strongly disparaging remarks accusing a party of misconduct.
predicates.pleadings_or_record_support_finding: The pleadings or evidentiary record provide adequate particulars and support for the misconduct finding.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court should not use extravagant personal criticism or impute corrupt motives to a trial judge without adequate grounds.
material_facts: The High Court reversed the trial court’s decision and used severe language suggesting that the trial judge was biased and influenced by extraneous considerations.
The Supreme Court, after examining the evidence, found those allegations against the trial judge wholly unjustified.
The judgment recognized that a corrupt motive, if established, must be condemned, but emphasized that strong language and such imputations should not be used lightly.
members.legal_principle: Judicial criticism should be temperate and based on an objective assessment of the evidence, with awareness that judges may reasonably differ in their assessment. Strong language and allegations of corrupt motives should not be used lightly; if a corrupt motive is actually shown, it should be condemned and appropriate further steps taken. The judgment cites no earlier case or statutory provision for this principle.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s extravagant criticism of the trial judge and its imputation of improper motives were unjustified.

predicates.appeal_from_trial_judgment: The proceeding is an appeal in which a court reviews a trial court’s judgment.
predicates.appellate_court_uses_extravagant_persona: The reviewing court uses excessive personal language about the trial judge or suggests improper influence.
predicates.corrupt_motive_not_established: The record does not establish that the trial judge acted from a corrupt motive.

members.legal_issue: Income from conducting a business can constitute property held under trust for purposes of the charitable-income exemption.
material_facts: The organization earned income from conducting kuries or chit funds and from money lending.
The governing documents provided for raising funds through those activities to advance the organization’s stated objects.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on section 11(1)(a) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and noted that sections 11(4) and 13(1)(bb) also show that business is property. It followed Commissioner of Income Tax v. Krishna Warrier.
members.conclusion: A business is property within the meaning of the charitable-income exemption provisions, and the business activities here were held under trust; those findings alone did not establish that the income was exempt.

predicates.charitable_tax_exemption_claim: The proceeding includes a claim to exempt income on the ground that it is held for charitable purposes.
predicates.income_earned_from_business: The organization earned income by carrying on a business.

members.legal_issue: Income derived from property dedicated to a public religious purpose is eligible for exemption when the property is subject to a legal obligation for that purpose, even without a formal trust document.
material_facts: The institution was accepted as religious, and its income-tax exemption claim was considered under the provisions governing income from property held for religious or charitable purposes.
Followers’ offerings were used to acquire property for the common purpose of furthering the institution’s religious objects.
The properties were recorded in the name of the Central Council, and the spiritual leader claimed no title or beneficial interest in them.
The properties had been used for the religious community, and revocation of the trust would not return them to the spiritual leader.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 11 and 12 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, exemption requires that the income be derived from property held under a trust or other legal obligation for charitable or religious purposes benefiting the public, and that the income be applied to those purposes as required by the Act. No formal document is necessary to create a trust. The court relied on The Secretary of State for India in Council v. Radha Swami Sat Sang, 13 ITR 520, and applied the test in All India Spinners’ Association v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay, 12 ITR 482. It distinguished the Privy Council’s decision in Patel Chhotahhai v. Jnan Chandra Bask, AIR 1935 PC 97, because that case considered different statutory requirements.
members.conclusion: The income was entitled to exemption under sections 11 and 12 of the Income Tax Act, 1961; the Tribunal was justified in allowing the claim.

predicates.income_tax_exemption_proceeding: A person or institution sought exemption for income derived from property in an income-tax proceeding.
predicates.property_subject_to_religious_legal_obli: The property was subject to an obligation requiring its use for religious purposes.
predicates.property_used_for_public_religious_purpo: The property was used to further religious purposes benefiting a religious community or the public.
predicates.no_private_beneficial_interest: The person managing or leading the institution claimed no personal beneficial interest in the property.

members.legal_issue: Laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule through constitutional amendments made after the basic-structure limitation arose are subject to judicial review for their effect on fundamental rights and the basic structure.
material_facts: The challenged matters concerned laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule by constitutional amendments made after the basic-structure doctrine had been propounded.
Some laws had previously been found unconstitutional, in whole or in part, while others were not connected with agrarian reform.
The challenge concerned whether Article 31B could give those laws complete immunity from review under Part III.
members.legal_principle: Articles 31B and 368 must be read subject to the implied limitation imposed by the basic-structure doctrine. A court applies the direct impact and effect, or rights, test: it first determines whether the law infringes Part III, then whether that infringement damages or destroys the basic structure. The assessment includes the nature and extent of the infringement and the essence of the right, viewed across Part III. The Court relied on Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain, Waman Rao v. Union of India, Minerva Mills v. Union of India, and L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, among other authorities.
members.conclusion: A post-threshold Ninth Schedule insertion does not confer blanket immunity. The law must be tested for infringement of Part III rights and whether the infringement damages or destroys the basic structure; if it does, the law is invalid.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_schedule_insertion and post_threshold_schedule_insertion and law_infringes_part_three and infringement_damages_basic_structure

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_schedule_ins: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a law's inclusion in the protected constitutional schedule.
predicates.post_threshold_schedule_insertion: A constitutional amendment places the law in the schedule after the basic-structure limitation on amendment applies.
predicates.law_infringes_part_three: The law takes away or abridges a right protected by the fundamental-rights chapter.
predicates.infringement_damages_basic_structure: The infringement, assessed by its actual impact and effect, damages or destroys an essential feature of the Constitution.

members.legal_issue: Constitutional amendments adding laws to the constitutional schedule before the basic-structure limit was established are valid, while later additions are open to basic-structure review unless the scheduled law is independently protected.
material_facts: The Constitution’s schedule had been amended over time to include Acts and Regulations that received protection against Part III challenges.
The challenged land-ceiling amendments were added to the schedule after the decision establishing that Parliament’s amending power cannot damage or destroy the Constitution’s basic structure.

The Court held that a scheduled law independently protected by Article 31A or the unamended Article 31C does not require a separate basic-structure inquiry into the amendment adding it to the schedule, insofar as the challenge is based on the rights those provisions protect.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B, read with the constitutional schedule, protects scheduled Acts and Regulations from challenges based on Part III. Applying Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, the Court treated amendments adding laws to the schedule before that decision as valid, but held that later additions are subject to review for compliance with the basic-structure limit. A challenge concerning rights protected by Article 31A or the unamended Article 31C becomes otiose if the scheduled law is saved by either provision.
members.conclusion: Schedule amendments made before the landmark basic-structure decision are valid; later schedule amendments are open to challenge for damaging or destroying the basic structure, but that inquiry is unnecessary where the scheduled law is independently protected by Article 31A or the unamended Article 31C.

rule.if: challenge_to_schedule_inclusion_amendment and law_added_to_constitutional_schedule and (added_before_landmark_basic_structure_ruling or (added_after_landmark_basic_structure_ruling and not independently_protected_law))

predicates.challenge_to_schedule_inclusion_amendmen: A litigant challenges a constitutional amendment that adds a law to a constitutional schedule.
predicates.law_added_to_constitutional_schedule: The challenged law was added to a constitutional schedule by amendment.
predicates.added_before_landmark_basic_structure_ru: The law was added before the judicial ruling establishing the basic-structure limit on constitutional amendments.
predicates.added_after_landmark_basic_structure_rul: The law was added after the judicial ruling establishing the basic-structure limit on constitutional amendments.
predicates.independently_protected_law: The scheduled law is independently protected from the relevant rights-based challenge by a separate constitutional provision.
predicates.pre_landmark_inclusion_valid_and_later_i: An inclusion made before the landmark ruling is valid, while a later inclusion is reviewable for compliance with the basic-structure limit unless the law is independently protected.

members.legal_issue: Extending a central monuments law that lacks a declaration of national importance does not impliedly repeal a valid state law governing ancient monuments that remain within the state’s legislative field.
material_facts: The state preservation regulation was validly made before the central law was extended to the relevant territory.
The central monuments law was extended to that territory, but it did not declare the monument in question to be of national importance.
The state regulation concerned an ancient monument not shown to have been brought within the central law’s national-importance field.
members.legal_principle: Under Entry 67 of List I, Parliament may legislate for ancient and historical monuments declared by or under parliamentary law to be of national importance; under Entry 12 of List II, other ancient and historical monuments fall within the State’s legislative field. Section 3 of the Part B States (Laws) Act, 1951 extended the central law only insofar as it related to matters on which Parliament could legislate. Because the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904 contained no required national-importance declaration for the monument, it did not enter the State’s field. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The central law did not displace the state regulation, which continued to apply to the monument in question.

rule.if: challenge_to_state_monument_notification and valid_state_monument_law and monument_not_declared_nationally_important and central_law_lacks_required_declaration

predicates.challenge_to_state_monument_notification: The proceeding challenges state action taken under a state law to protect a monument.
predicates.valid_state_monument_law: The state law governing protection of the relevant kind of monument was validly enacted.
predicates.monument_not_declared_nationally_importa: The monument has not been declared to be of national importance under parliamentary law.
predicates.central_law_lacks_required_declaration: The central law invoked against the state law does not make the declaration needed to bring the monument within Parliament’s legislative field.

members.legal_issue: Central laws covering only scheduled or expressly notified monuments do not impliedly repeal a state preservation law as applied to a monument outside their coverage.
material_facts: The monument in question was not included in the relevant schedule to the 1951 central law.
The Central Government had not issued the notice or declaration needed under the 1958 central law to bring the monument within that Act.
The state regulation otherwise applied to the monument.
members.legal_principle: The Ancient and Historical Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains (Declaration of National Importance) Act, 1951 applied to monuments specified in Part I of its Schedule. Under sections 3 and 4 of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, monuments covered by the 1951 Act remained declared nationally important, and the Central Government could proceed to declare other monuments through the prescribed process. Since the monument was neither covered by the schedule nor brought within the 1958 Act by the required central action, the state regulation was not displaced. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: Neither central law displaced the state regulation in respect of the monument, and the state regulation continued to apply.

rule.if: challenge_to_state_monument_notification and monument_outside_1951_schedule and no_central_action_covering_monument_under_later_law and state_law_covers_monument

predicates.challenge_to_state_monument_notification: The proceeding challenges state action taken under a state law to protect a monument.
predicates.monument_outside_1951_schedule: The monument is not included in the schedule identifying monuments covered by the earlier central law.
predicates.no_central_action_covering_monument_unde: The Central Government has not taken the action required to bring the monument within the later central law.
predicates.state_law_covers_monument: The state law applies to the monument in question.

members.legal_issue: A special limitation period for acts done or purportedly done in pursuance of a statutory enactment does not govern a contractual claim for non-payment based on breach when the non-payment has no reasonable connection with a statutory duty.
material_facts: A statutory housing body was responsible for carrying out housing schemes and entered into, or was deemed to have entered into, a construction contract for that purpose.
The contractor’s suit sought money allegedly due as damages or compensation for breach of the contract, including non-payment of amounts claimed.
The alleged non-payment was not shown to have a reasonable connection with a duty imposed on the statutory body or its agents by the enactment.
members.legal_principle: Section 64 of the Bombay Housing Board Act, 1948 applied to suits concerning things done or purportedly done in pursuance of the Act. Although sections 19 and 23 and section 24(f) concerned the Board’s statutory housing functions, a claim for non-payment arising from breach of contract was distinct from performance of those functions and lacked a reasonable connection to a statutory duty. The court followed The Trustees of Port of Bombay v. The Premier Automobiles Ltd., approved The Municipal Borough of Ahmedabad v. Jayantilal Chhotalal Patel, and discussed Athimannil Muhammad v. The Malabar District Board and Jalgaon Borough Municipality v. The Khandesh Spinning and Weaving Mills Co. Ltd.
members.conclusion: The contractual claim for non-payment was not an act done or purportedly done in pursuance of the enactment, so the special six-month limitation period did not bar the suit.

predicates.suit_against_statutory_body: The proceeding is a suit against a body established or empowered by statute.
predicates.claim_is_for_nonpayment_due_to_contract_: The claimant seeks payment allegedly due because the statutory body breached a contract.
predicates.nonpayment_not_reasonably_connected_to_s: The alleged non-payment has no reasonable connection with a duty imposed on the body or its agents by statute.

members.legal_issue: The short limitation period for compensation for acts or omissions alleged to be in pursuance of an enactment does not govern a negligence claim where the complained-of failure was not in pursuance of statutory authority.
material_facts: The suit sought compensation for damage caused by a canal breach allegedly resulting from negligence in maintaining the canal banks.
The relevant failure to maintain the banks was not an act or omission alleged to have been done in pursuance of statutory authority.
The canal legislation empowered officials to take certain actions but did not impose a duty to take care of the banks.
The suit was within the period applicable to the tort claim if the short period did not apply.
members.legal_principle: Article 2 of the Limitation Act applies to compensation claims for acts or omissions alleged to be in pursuance of an enactment; an act or omission must be of that character to attract it. Article 36 applied to the tort claim in this case. The Court referred to Mohammad Sadaat Ali Khan v. Administrator, Corporation of City of Lahore and Secretary of State v. Lodna Colliery Co. Ltd., distinguished Punjab Cotton Press Co. Ltd. v. Secretary of State and Commissioners for the Port of Calcutta v. Corporation of Calcutta, and noted that sections 6 and 15 of the Northern India Canal and Drainage Act imposed no relevant duty to maintain the banks.
members.conclusion: The short limitation period did not apply, and the suit was within time under the applicable period for the tort claim.

predicates.tort_compensation_suit: The proceeding seeks compensation for damage allegedly caused by a tortious act or omission.
predicates.complained_of_failure_was_not_in_pursuan: The failure said to have caused the damage was not alleged to have been carried out in pursuance of statutory authority.

members.legal_issue: A conviction remains undisturbed when the appeal raises only the sentence and does not challenge the conviction.
material_facts: The appeals concerned the High Court's reduction of sentence.
The limited issue raised before the High Court concerned sentence, and the conviction for attempted murder was not challenged in the appeals before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the conviction as unchallenged because the issue before it concerned sentence alone, and accordingly confirmed the conviction under Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The conviction for attempted murder was confirmed.

predicates.appeal_limited_to_sentence: The appeal concerns the sentence imposed after conviction and does not raise other issues.
predicates.conviction_not_challenged: The convicted person does not contest the conviction in the appeal.

members.legal_issue: A conviction based on witness credibility is not disturbed on appeal when the challenge concerns only the credibility of witnesses whom the courts below believed.
material_facts: One accused was convicted for his individual act of using a spear to injure the complainant.
The challenge to that conviction concerned the credibility of the witnesses who testified to the act.
The witnesses had been believed by the courts below.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied its usual rule of not interfering on questions of fact, including a challenge confined to the credibility of witnesses believed by the courts below.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with that conviction and dismissed that part of the appeal.

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a criminal conviction.
predicates.challenge_only_concerns_witness_credibil: The appellant's challenge to the conviction concerns only whether the witnesses were credible.
predicates.courts_below_believed_witnesses: The courts below accepted the testimony of the witnesses in question.

members.legal_issue: A court must judicially decide an objection to a document’s admissibility when it is tendered, and merely marking the document subject to objection does not make its admission final.
material_facts: An objection that the document was insufficiently stamped and unregistered was raised when it was tendered in evidence.

The trial court marked the document subject to objection without deciding the objection, and rejected it only later by relying on the rule that an admitted document cannot subsequently be challenged for insufficient stamping.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 35 and 36 of the Stamp Act, the protection against a later challenge applies where the court has judicially admitted the document; a tentative marking subject to objection is not such an admission. The court must determine the objection when the document is tendered and before it is marked. The Court relied on Javar Chand v. Pukhraj Surana, AIR 1961 SC 1655.
members.conclusion: The trial court was required to decide the objection judicially before marking the document as an exhibit. Because it had only tentatively marked the document and had not judicially determined admissibility, the bar against a later challenge did not apply.

predicates.civil_trial_document_admissibility_dispu: A document is tendered as evidence in a civil trial and its admissibility is disputed.
predicates.objection_raised_when_document_tendered: A party objects to the document’s admissibility when it is tendered in evidence.
predicates.court_deferred_decision_by_tentative_mar: The court marks the document subject to objection without judicially deciding its admissibility at that time.

members.legal_issue: An instrument marked only tentatively while an objection to its stamping remains judicially undetermined is not finally admitted so as to bar a later challenge.
material_facts: The court distinguished the situation in which a document is marked subject to an objection that has not been judicially determined from the admission of the agreement in this case, which was made without objection.
members.legal_principle: Section 36 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 applies after an instrument has been admitted in evidence, not where it is merely marked tentatively with an objection left undetermined. Ram Rattan v. Bajrang Lal holds that the objection must be raised when the document is tendered so the trial court can determine it judicially; an unresolved objection means the admission is not final for this purpose.
members.conclusion: A tentative marking of a document with an unresolved stamping objection does not trigger the bar against a later challenge.

members.legal_issue: A contracting party cannot adjudicate a disputed allegation that the other party breached the contract, even when the contract authorizes that party to assess damages for a breach.
material_facts: The agreements authorized the State to assess damages for breach of conditions.
The State alleged that the contractors had breached their agreements and its officers both determined that breaches had occurred and assessed damages.
The contractors disputed the alleged breaches.
members.legal_principle: A power to assess damages is subsidiary and consequential and does not include a power to decide whether a disputed breach occurred. A party to a contract cannot be an arbiter in its own cause; justice and equity require independent adjudication of a disputed breach. Where the breach is admitted or the parties agree that it occurred, the contract may authorize the other party to assess damages. The Court applied the terms of the agreements and relied on no earlier case for this holding.
members.conclusion: The State’s officers could not adjudicate the disputed breaches. The contract authorized them to assess damages only where the breach was admitted or was not in dispute; a disputed breach had to be adjudicated by an independent person or body.

rule.if: contract_breach_proceeding and state_is_contracting_party and breach_is_contested and state_official_decides_breach

predicates.breach_is_contested: The other contracting party disputes that it committed the alleged breach.
predicates.state_official_decides_breach: An official acting for the State determines whether the disputed breach occurred.

members.legal_issue: A forest officer empowered to assess compensation for damage is not thereby empowered to decide a disputed question of whether the contractor caused the damage or breached the contract.
material_facts: The contract required disputes about performance or breach to be referred to the designated senior forest officer for a final decision.
The contractor disputed the allegation that he had cut trees contrary to the contract.
The Divisional Forest Officer found the contractor responsible for damage and assessed compensation without first referring the disputed breach for determination.
members.legal_principle: Rule 15(1) of the Forest Contract Rules makes a contractor liable for damage in a reserved forest and authorizes the Divisional Forest Officer to assess compensation. It does not authorize that officer to decide whether the contractor, servants, or agents caused the damage or breached the contract. Under clause 9 of the contract, a dispute about performance or breach must be referred to the designated Chief Conservator of Forests. Clauses 6 and 9 and Rule 15(1) are consistent: liability is determined by referral, and compensation may then be assessed under Rule 15(1).
members.conclusion: The Divisional Forest Officer could assess the amount of compensation after liability was determined, but could not determine the disputed liability himself; the compensation order could not stand.

predicates.forest_contract_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute arising from a contract for forest produce.
predicates.damage_attributed_to_contractor_is_dispu: The contractor disputes the allegation that the contractor, the contractor’s servants, or the contractor’s agents caused damage.
predicates.contract_requires_referral_of_performanc: The contract requires disputes about its performance or breach to be referred to a designated officer.
predicates.disputed_damage_liability_must_be_determ: The designated officer must determine disputed responsibility for the damage before the amount of compensation is assessed.

members.legal_issue: A prosecution sanction is valid for an offence when the sanctioning authority considered the facts constituting that offence and the sanction is correlated with the offence charged.
material_facts: The sanction order recited that the public servant was entrusted with crops on acquired land, dishonestly or fraudulently allowed the crops to be cut, and misappropriated their value rather than depositing it in government revenue.

The order expressly referred to the offence of misconduct involving property entrusted to a public servant and stated that the government had fully and carefully examined the materials and circumstances before granting sanction.
The public servant was convicted of the entrusted-property offence, although he was acquitted of the separate charge of obtaining a pecuniary advantage.
members.legal_principle: A valid sanction must concern the facts constituting the offence proposed to be charged. It is desirable for those facts to appear in the sanction; if they do not, the prosecution must prove by other evidence that they were placed before the sanctioning authority. The authority must apply its mind, and the sanction must correlate with the particular offence charged or resulting in conviction. Under Section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, misconduct includes dishonestly or fraudulently allowing another person to convert to their own use property entrusted to or controlled by a public servant; Section 5(2) provides the punishment. The Court referred to Bhagat Ram v. State of Punjab, Madan Mohan Singh v. State of U.P., Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King, and Jaswant Singh v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The sanction was valid for the entrusted-property offence because its stated facts and the provision it expressly identified showed that the sanctioning authority had that offence in contemplation and had applied its mind to the relevant facts.

predicates.corruption_prosecution: The proceeding is a prosecution alleging misconduct by a public servant.
predicates.sanction_facts_disclose_entrusted_proper: The sanction records facts that property was entrusted to or controlled by the public servant and that the public servant dishonestly allowed another person to convert it to their own use.
predicates.sanction_authority_considered_relevant_m: The sanction or other evidence establishes that the sanctioning authority considered the relevant materials and circumstances before granting approval.
predicates.sanction_correlates_with_charged_offence: The facts considered by the sanctioning authority relate to the particular offence charged.

members.legal_issue: A prosecution sanction is valid for an offence when the sanctioning authority considered facts that support that offence, even if another offence included in the sanction is not ultimately proved.
material_facts: The sanction described the official’s entrustment with the standing crops, his allowing the crops to be cut, and his failure to deposit the proceeds into government funds.

The sanction expressly referred to the offence of dishonest or fraudulent misappropriation or conversion of entrusted property, and evidence showed that the sanctioning authority had considered the relevant materials.
The official was convicted of the entrusted-property offence but acquitted of the separate offence of obtaining a pecuniary advantage.
members.legal_principle: A valid sanction must relate to the facts constituting the offence charged. Those facts should appear in the sanction, but if they do not, the prosecution may establish by other evidence that they were placed before the sanctioning authority. The facts considered must be correlated with the particular offence charged. The Court applied Section 6(1)(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and relied on Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King and Jaswant Singh v. The State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The sanction was sufficient to support prosecution and conviction for the entrusted-property offence despite the acquittal on the separate charge.

predicates.corruption_prosecution_appeal: The case is an appeal in a prosecution alleging misconduct by a public official.
