predicates.accused_lacked_entrustment_or_dominion: The accused was not entrusted with the property and lacked dominion over it.
predicates.dishonest_disposal_not_proved: The evidence did not prove dishonest disposal or conversion of the property for personal use.

members.legal_issue: A vesting notification may validly take over the portion of an estate within the territorial operation of the abolition law, although another portion of the same estate is outside that operation.
material_facts: The estates included land both within the ordinary territorial operation of the abolition law and within a partially excluded area where the law had not been made applicable.
An initial notification purported to vest the estates in their entirety.
Before the vesting date, the Government modified that notification to exclude the portions in the partially excluded area.
The proprietors did not obtain relief against the vesting of the portions covered by the modified notification.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 1(3), 2(1), and 2(3) of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, read with section 3(2) of the Madras Estates Land Act, an estate within the abolition law may be understood as the portion of a larger estate within that law’s territorial operation. The Act’s purpose of eliminating intermediaries supports taking over land within its operation rather than treating the whole estate as beyond the Act because some land lies outside its reach. The court also observed that the Act does not permit the Government to choose arbitrary portions of an estate to take over.
members.conclusion: The initial notification, as modified, was valid and effective to vest the portions of the estates to which the abolition law then applied.

rule.if: challenge_to_vesting_notification and estate_part_within_lawful_territorial_scope and notification_covers_that_part and notification_excludes_area_outside_scope

predicates.challenge_to_vesting_notification: A party challenged a notification taking over an estate under a land-tenure reform law.
predicates.estate_part_within_lawful_territorial_sc: Part of the estate lay within the territorial area where the law was in force.
predicates.notification_covers_that_part: The notification provided for taking over the part of the estate within the law’s territorial operation.
predicates.notification_excludes_area_outside_scope: The notification excluded the part of the estate outside the law’s territorial operation.

members.legal_issue: A later vesting notification may validly take over the remaining portion of an estate after the law is extended to that portion, where the notifications together carry out the taking over of the estate as a whole.
material_facts: The initial notification, as modified, validly vested the portions of the estates within the abolition law’s original territorial operation.
A later regulation extended the abolition law to the remaining portions situated in the scheduled area.
The Government issued a later notification to vest those remaining portions.
The later notification was challenged on the ground that it took over only part of each estate.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3, 24, and 25 of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act reflect a scheme for taking over an estate as a unit and determining compensation for the estate as a whole. That scheme does not invalidate separate notifications which together take over the whole estate; nor does it authorize arbitrary selection of portions to take over. Once the previously excluded portion came within the Act, taking it over was necessary to complete the whole-estate vesting. No earlier case was relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The later notification was valid because, following the extension of the law, it completed the taking over of the entirety of each estate in conformity with the Act’s scheme.

rule.if: challenge_to_vesting_notification and earlier_notice_validly_vested_first_part and remaining_part_later_brought_within_law and later_notice_vests_remaining_part

predicates.challenge_to_vesting_notification: A party challenged a notification taking over an estate under a land-tenure reform law.
predicates.earlier_notice_validly_vested_first_part: An earlier notification validly took over the part of the estate then within the law’s territorial operation.
predicates.remaining_part_later_brought_within_law: A later legal change brought the previously excluded part of the estate within the law’s operation.
predicates.later_notice_vests_remaining_part: The Government issued a later notification taking over the remaining part of the estate.

members.legal_issue: Consumers may join in a complaint to seek redress for their own grievances without satisfying the requirements for a representative complaint on behalf of numerous consumers.
material_facts: Ninety-one consumers joined in filing the complaint and sought relief for themselves as well as for other purchasers.
The representative application was not maintainable, but the complainants had their own grievances arising from delayed possession.
The complaint could therefore continue as a joint complaint confined to the complainants, rather than being dismissed altogether.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(5), 35(1)(a) and 35(1)(c) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 distinguish a complaint by consumers for their own redress from one brought for numerous consumers. Section 38(11) applies Order I Rule 8 CPC to representative complaints, not to every complaint joined by multiple consumers. Section 13(2) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 provides that the singular includes the plural unless the context requires otherwise. Section 100 of the Consumer Protection Act does not exclude the principle in Order I Rule 1 CPC permitting persons to join as plaintiffs.
members.conclusion: The complaint remains maintainable as a joint complaint by the complainants for their own grievances, notwithstanding the failure of the representative basis.

predicates.consumer_complaint: Consumers have filed a complaint seeking redress in relation to goods or services.
predicates.multiple_consumers_seek_own_redress: More than one consumer joins the complaint to seek relief for their own grievances.
predicates.representative_basis_unavailable: The complaint cannot proceed as a representative complaint on behalf of numerous consumers.

members.legal_issue: A consumer seeking to join an existing joint complaint may be added as a party when that consumer’s grievance is limited to the grievance presented in the complaint.
material_facts: Other purchasers applied to join the complaint after representative-capacity notices had been issued.
The intervenors’ stated grievance was within the grievance projected by the complainants in their complaint.
members.legal_principle: The Court directed that purchasers may join the complaint if their grievance is limited to the grievance projected by the complainants. The direction preserves the complaint as a joint complaint rather than extending it to represent consumers with different grievances.
members.conclusion: Consumers wishing to join may be added if their grievance is limited to the grievance projected in the complaint; the intervenors were to be impleaded.

predicates.joint_consumer_complaint: A complaint is proceeding as a joint complaint by consumers for their own grievances.
predicates.applicant_seeks_to_join: A consumer applies to become a party to the complaint.
predicates.applicant_grievance_matches_complaint: The applicant’s grievance is limited to the grievance presented in the complaint.

members.legal_issue: The notice to quit satisfied the applicable legal requirements in the circumstances of the eviction proceeding.
material_facts: The case was an appeal by a landlord in eviction proceedings.
The landlord had succeeded in three courts, including before a single judge of the High Court.
The Division Bench reversed on the sole question of whether the notice to quit was valid.
The Supreme Court agreed with the single judge that, in the circumstances of the case, the notice complied with the law; the judgment does not state the notice’s terms.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the notice to quit complied with the law in the circumstances of the case. The judgment identifies no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for that conclusion.
members.conclusion: The notice to quit was valid, and the appeal was allowed, subject to the modification concerning recovery of possession.

predicates.appeal_in_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought an appeal arising from eviction proceedings.
predicates.division_bench_reversed_on_notice_validi: A Division Bench reversed the lower-court result on the validity of the notice to quit.
predicates.notice_complied_with_law_in_case_circums: The notice to quit satisfied the applicable legal requirements in the circumstances of the case.

members.legal_issue: The challenged eviction notice was valid.
material_facts: The landlord issued an eviction notice under Section 12(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947.
The tenant challenged the notice’s validity.
The trial and appellate courts considered the challenge, and the Supreme Court agreed with their conclusions.
members.legal_principle: The Court agreed with the trial and appellate courts’ conclusions on the notice under Section 12(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, without setting out a separate general test or further reasoning.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the challenge and upheld the validity of the eviction notice.

predicates.appeal_from_rent_control_eviction_decisi: The tenant appealed from a decision in an eviction proceeding governed by rent-control law.
predicates.eviction_notice_challenged: The tenant disputed the validity of the landlord’s eviction notice.
predicates.lower_courts_found_notice_valid: The trial and appellate courts considered the notice challenge and concluded that the notice was valid.

members.legal_issue: A partition of joint Hindu family property is not a transfer of property in the strict legal sense.
material_facts: A joint Hindu family divided its property among its coparceners.
One coparcener received property worth less than the property allotted to the other members.
The dispute arose in a gift-tax proceeding.
members.legal_principle: A partition transforms joint enjoyment into enjoyment in severalty; each coparcener has an antecedent title, so no new title is conferred by conveyance. The Court followed Commissioner of Income-tax, Gujarat v. Keshavlal Lallubhai Patel, which discussed Gutta Radhakrishnavya v. Gutta Sarasamma, M. K. Stremann v. Commissioner of Income-tax, and Jagan Nath v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The partition did not effect a transfer of property in the strict sense.

predicates.gift_tax_proceeding: The dispute concerns whether a transaction in a gift-tax proceeding is taxable as a gift.
predicates.joint_family_property_partition: Members of a joint family divided jointly held family property among themselves.

members.legal_issue: The allotment of jointly owned family property to an existing coparcener on partition is not an acquisition by transfer for the purpose of the restriction on eviction for a landlord’s personal need.
material_facts: The premises belonged to an undivided Hindu family, and the tenant had been inducted before the family partition.
On partition, the premises were allotted to a coparcener who already had an antecedent title in the family property.
The landlord applied to evict the tenant for bona fide personal need before five years had elapsed from the partition.
The finding that the landlord satisfied the personal-need ground was upheld and was not challenged before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(6), read with section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, prevents a landlord who acquires premises by transfer from seeking eviction for personal need before the prescribed period has elapsed. Its object is to prevent a landlord from using a transfer to enable a new owner, previously without title to the premises, to obtain an eviction advantage. Partition transforms the coparceners’ joint title into separate titles to allotted properties; it does not create title in a coparcener who already had an antecedent title. The Court relied on Girja Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj, 43 I.A. 151, and Commissioner of Income-tax, Gujarat v. Keshavlal Lallubhai Patel, 1965 2 S.C.R. 100. Decisions treating partition as a transfer under section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, or section 17(1)(b) of the Indian Registration Act were not decisive because the meaning of transfer depends on the provision’s context and purpose.
members.conclusion: The allotment on partition was not an acquisition by transfer within the meaning of section 14(6) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, so that provision did not bar the eviction application.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_application_for_pe: A landlord sought to evict a tenant from rented premises for the landlord’s personal need in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.premises_allocated_to_existing_coparcene: A family partition allocated the rented premises to a person who was already a coparcener in the family owning them.
predicates.acquirer_had_antecedent_joint_title: Before the partition, the person receiving the premises had an existing joint title in the family property.
predicates.application_filed_before_waiting_period_: The landlord filed the eviction application before the applicable waiting period had elapsed since the allocation.

members.legal_issue: An appeal relying on a certificate unsupported by reasons is not maintainable when the certificate does not sustain the appeal.
material_facts: One appeal was brought on the strength of a certificate granted by the High Court.
The certificate was unsupported by any reason.
A separate appeal concerning the same judgment was brought by special leave.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the certificate as insufficient to sustain the appeal because it was unsupported by any reason; no earlier case or statutory provision was cited for this procedural conclusion.
members.conclusion: The appeal based on the unsupported certificate was dismissed as not maintainable.

predicates.appeal_based_on_high_court_certificate: An appeal was brought on the basis of a certificate granted by a High Court.
predicates.certificate_unsupported_by_reasons: The certificate supporting the appeal was not accompanied by reasons.

members.legal_issue: A certificate supporting an appeal to the Supreme Court is defective when it does not establish the applicable jurisdictional grounds and the statutory conditions for an appeal are not met.
material_facts: The High Court issued a certificate for an appeal under the constitutional provisions concerning appeals to the Supreme Court and referred to the value and nature of the case without setting out supporting grounds.
The subject matter’s value in the court of first instance was Rs. 5,250, the High Court judgment affirmed the trial court’s decision, and the case raised no substantial question of law.
The appeal was brought under the constitutional provision invoking jurisdiction associated with the former Federal Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that a certificate must set out the grounds supporting its grant. The constitutional provision invoked applies only where the relevant jurisdiction and powers were exercisable by the Federal Court before the Constitution commenced. The conditions under Sections 109 and 110 of the Code of Civil Procedure were not met where the value threshold was not satisfied, the judgment was one of affirmance, and no substantial question of law arose.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the certificate was plainly defective and that the High Court had seriously erred in granting it.

predicates.appeal_under_special_jurisdiction_certif: The proceeding is an appeal to the Supreme Court brought on the basis of a certificate invoking special constitutional jurisdiction.
predicates.certificate_omits_supporting_grounds: The certificate does not state the grounds that support granting it.
predicates.statutory_appeal_conditions_not_met: The required conditions for an appeal, including the applicable value and legal-question requirements, are not satisfied.

members.legal_issue: A special administrative procedure for recovering rent arrears does not permit recovery of a debt that is no longer legally recoverable because a suit to recover it is time-barred.
material_facts: A public authority allotted stalls for a monthly licence fee, and the allottee accumulated arrears.
The authority later sought to recover the arrears through a special administrative procedure.
A suit to recover the arrears would have been barred by limitation when the recovery order was made.
members.legal_principle: The Limitation Act bars the remedy of a suit without generally extinguishing the underlying right, but whether another remedy remains available depends on the statute providing it. The relevant recovery provision supplied only a special procedure and did not create a right to claim a time-barred debt. In that context, “payable” meant legally recoverable, so the officer had to determine arrears in accordance with law. The Court followed Hans Raj Gupta and others v. Official Liquidator of the Dehradun Mussoorie Electric Tramway Co. Ltd., which held that a provision creating a special payment procedure creates no new rights. Section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908 did not apply because no suit for possession of property was involved.
members.conclusion: The special procedure did not create a new right to recover the debt, and the time-barred arrears could not be recovered through it; the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.public_premises_rent_recovery_proceeding: A public authority sought to recover an amount through a special administrative procedure for claims relating to public premises.
predicates.rent_arrears_claimed: The amount sought was unpaid rent or a licence fee for the use of public premises.
predicates.ordinary_suit_would_be_time_barred: A suit to recover the claimed arrears would have been barred by limitation.

members.legal_issue: A summary public-revenue recovery procedure that creates no new substantive right cannot be used to recover a claim that was time-barred when recovery was initiated.
material_facts: The proceedings sought recovery of loans made by banks for agricultural purposes and by a financial corporation, under a law extended to those debts for speedy recovery.
The recovery law provided a method of recovery but did not create a new right to payment.
The statutory scheme allowed a person who paid under protest to seek a refund, and the creditor initiated recovery by a written requisition.
The issue was whether claims already barred by limitation when the requisition was issued could be recovered through that procedure.
members.legal_principle: The Court interpreted Sections 69(2), 70 and 71 of the Kerala Revenue Recovery Act, 1968. A procedure for speedy recovery does not enlarge the creditor’s substantive claim or remove a debtor’s limitation defence unless the law expressly provides for that result. The Court relied on Hansraj Gupta v. Dehra Dun-Mussoorie Electric Tramway Co. Ltd. (AIR 1933 PC 63), which treated ‘money due’ under a special recovery procedure as excluding time-barred claims; New Delhi Municipal Committee v. Kalu Ram (1976 (3) SCC 407), which held that a recovery provision covered only arrears not otherwise time-barred; and The Director of Industries, U.P. v. Deep Chand Agarwal (AIR 1980 SC 801), concerning the speedy-recovery purpose of such procedures. It distinguished Khadi Gram Udyog Trust v. Ram Chandraji Virajman Mandir (1978 (1) SCC 44), which concerned a tenant’s statutory opportunity to avoid eviction, and noted that although limitation ordinarily bars the remedy rather than extinguishing the debt, coercive statutory recovery does not thereby become available for a time-barred claim.
members.conclusion: A claim that was time-barred when the creditor issued the recovery requisition was not an amount legally recoverable through the statutory procedure and could not be recovered under it.

predicates.recovery_through_summary_public_revenue_: A creditor sought to recover a debt through a summary public-revenue recovery proceeding.
predicates.claim_time_barred_when_recovery_initiate: The creditor’s claim was barred by limitation when the recovery process was initiated.
predicates.recovery_procedure_does_not_create_new_s: The recovery procedure provided a method of collection but did not create a new substantive right to recover the debt.

members.legal_issue: An official communication that clearly informs an interested person that an award has been made and the person's claim has been rejected is sufficient notice to start the limitation period for seeking a reference.
material_facts: The land acquisition officer sent a telegram informing the claimant that the award had been declared and that the claimant's demand had been rejected.
The claimant received the telegram but filed the reference application more than six weeks later.
The award had considered and rejected the claimant's claim for compensation.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 12(2) and 18(2)(b) of the Land Acquisition Act, notice need only clearly intimate that the award has been made; it need not set out the award's details or follow a prescribed form. The six-week period runs from receipt of such notice. State of Punjab v. Satinder Bir Singh (1995) holds that notice is an intimation of the award and that limitation does not depend on communication in any particular form where none is prescribed. The rule in Raja Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. Deputy Land Acquisition Officer, which the Court said would otherwise merit consideration regarding knowledge of an award, did not govern because notice under Section 12(2) had been received.
members.conclusion: The telegram was sufficient notice of the award, and the reference application, filed more than six weeks after its receipt, was barred by limitation.

predicates.land_acquisition_reference_proceeding: A person sought a court reference concerning compensation in a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.official_award_communication_received: The interested person received an official communication from the acquisition authority about the award.
predicates.communication_identified_award_and_rejec: The communication stated that the award had been made and that the person's claim had been rejected.
predicates.reference_application_filed_after_six_we: The person filed the reference application more than six weeks after receiving the communication.

members.legal_issue: A notice communicating that an award has been made and stating the compensation awarded is valid even if it omits the detailed basis for calculating compensation, and receipt of that notice starts the limitation period for seeking a reference.
material_facts: A person interested in acquired land received a notice of the award that stated the compensation amount; the acquired area was not disputed.
The notice did not explain the details or method used to determine the compensation.
The person received compensation under protest but applied for a reference after the applicable six-week period had expired.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 11 and 12(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the award determines matters including the land’s area, compensation and apportionment, and is conclusive between the Collector and interested persons. Section 12(2) requires immediate notice of the award to persons not present or represented when it is made; the notice need only communicate that the award has been made and need not include all its details or the method of valuation. A person receiving compensation under protest may inspect the award or obtain a certified copy before stating objections in a reference application under section 18(1). Under section 18(2), the applicable limitation period runs from receipt of the notice; it does not depend on the notice being communicated in a particular form where no form is prescribed. Section 31 is relevant to receipt of compensation under protest. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The notice was valid despite omitting the detailed basis for the compensation. Limitation began when it was received, so the reference application was time-barred; the appeal was allowed and the High Court’s order was set aside.

rule.if: land_acquisition_reference_proceeding and notice_received and notice_identifies_award_and_compensation and award_calculation_details_omitted and compensation_received_under_protest and reference_application_after_deadline

members.legal_issue: An equal pre-emptor cannot obtain a share of the property after another pre-emptor has been substituted for the vendee and the claimant has no superior right.
material_facts: A group of pre-emptors obtained a conditional decree recognizing their pre-emption claim.
Before that group deposited the required balance, another group of equal degree filed a pre-emption suit.
The first group deposited the balance as required and took possession under the decree.
The later claimants had no superior pre-emption right over the first group.
members.legal_principle: A pre-emptor's secondary right is a right of substitution in place of the vendee, not a right to share the property as a matter of general pre-emption law. The claimant must have a superior right to the vendee or a person substituted for the vendee, and that right must subsist when exercised. Sections 4, 13 and 17 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act define and regulate the right but do not create a right to share against a person who has already been substituted; section 17 distributes property among equally entitled claimants only while the right remains to be exercised. Mool Chand v. Ganga Jal and Lokha Singh v. Sermukh Singh were relied on.
members.conclusion: The later claimants could not succeed because, after the first group fulfilled the decree and was substituted for the vendees, the later claimants had no superior right.

predicates.preemption_proceeding: The case is a proceeding to enforce a right of pre-emption.
predicates.first_claimant_substituted_for_vendee: A prior claimant completed the required steps and took the vendee's place in the sale.
predicates.rival_claimant_not_superior: The rival claimant did not have a right superior to that of the substituted claimant.

members.legal_issue: A co-sharer cannot enforce pre-emption over a sale of leasehold land and the house standing on it when the claimant cannot be substituted for the entire bargain.
material_facts: The claimant already owned a share of the property and sought to pre-empt the sale of the remaining share.
The sale included a house and other buildings standing on rent-paying land held on a subordinate, leasehold tenure.
The claimant sought pre-emption of the property sold, while the land interest was not itself subject to pre-emption under the applicable law.

The house could not be separated from the land for the claimed pre-emption without leaving the claimant unable to take the entire bargain; separated from the land, the superstructure would be movable property.
members.legal_principle: Under the customary application of Muhammadan law, pre-emption is an incident of full ownership and does not attach to property held on a subordinate tenure such as a lease. The claimant must take the entire bargain, and the rule operates reciprocally: the vendor must have been in a position to claim pre-emption of the claimant’s whole bargain if the positions were reversed. A house sold with its foundations may be pre-emptible where the land is itself pre-emptible, but a house on leasehold land cannot be detached from that land to permit partial pre-emption; detached, the superstructure is movable property, which is not subject to pre-emption. The Court relied on Bishan Singh v. Khazan Singh for the nature and scope of the right; Gobind Dayal v. Inayatullah, Sakina Bibi v. Amiran, Dashrathlal v. Bai Dhondubai and Shri Audh Behari Singh v. Gajadhar Jaipuria for ownership and reciprocity; and the authorities establishing that leasehold interests are not pre-emptible, including Nathuni Ram v. Gopinath (Full Bench). It agreed with Nathuni Ram’s conclusion that a house on leasehold land cannot be pre-empted separately. The Court also considered the Muhammadan-law texts in Baillie’s Digest and The Hedaya. It rejected the contrary support drawn from Zahur v. Nur Ali because that decision had not addressed the requirement of full ownership in the land, and distinguished Chariter Dusadh v. Bhagwati Pandey because it concerned whether the claimant was a full owner.
members.conclusion: The sale of the leasehold interest was not pre-emptible, and the house standing on that land was not independently pre-emptible; the claimant therefore had no right to pre-empt the sale.

rule.if: customary_preemption_claim and co_sharer_claimant and sale_includes_leasehold_land and sale_includes_attached_structure and claim_cannot_cover_entire_bargain

predicates.customary_preemption_claim: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking to enforce a customary right of pre-emption.
predicates.co_sharer_claimant: The claimant relied on ownership of a share in the property as the basis for claiming pre-emption.
predicates.sale_includes_leasehold_land: The transaction sought to be pre-empted includes land held under a subordinate tenure rather than full ownership.
predicates.sale_includes_attached_structure: The transaction includes a house or other structure standing on that land.
predicates.claim_cannot_cover_entire_bargain: The claimant cannot be substituted for the entire transaction, including because the land interest cannot be pre-empted and the structure cannot be treated as a separately pre-emptible property.

members.legal_issue: A deed that appears to dedicate an entire estate may create only a partial dedication where its terms and circumstances show that the settlor did not intend to dedicate all beneficial interest to the deity.
material_facts: The deed dedicated numerous properties to the deity and specified religious expenses, but made no clear provision for the growing surplus income after those expenses and temple construction.
The settlor retained powers to transfer the property and alter the deed, and a contemporaneous will provided for a relative to receive the trust properties if the deed failed.
The deed could reasonably be construed either as an absolute dedication or as a partial dedication subjecting the properties to a charge for religious purposes.
members.legal_principle: Where a large dedication produces income beyond the religious expenditure specified by the settlor, and the deed's provisions reveal that the settlor did not intend to give the deity the entire beneficial interest, the dedication may be partial, leaving the property with the grantee or secular heirs subject to a trust or charge for religious uses. The Court relied on Sri Sri Iswari Bhubaneshwari Thakurani v. Brojo Nath Dey, 64 Indian Appeals 203, and discussed the reasoning in Surendra Keshav Roy v. Doorga Soondarce Darsee, 19 Indian Appeals 108.
members.conclusion: The Court did not decide which construction was correct; it held that absolute dedication was not clearly and indubitably established as a basis for inferring fraud in the earlier compromise proceedings.

predicates.dedication_dispute_involves_fraud_challe: The proceeding challenged an earlier compromise as fraudulent on the ground that the property had been absolutely dedicated to a deity.
predicates.large_property_income_exceeds_specified_: The property was extensive and its income was expected to exceed the religious expenses specified by the settlor.
predicates.surplus_destination_is_unspecified: The deed did not clearly direct how surplus income would be used after the specified religious expenses and construction work.
predicates.settlor_retained_control_over_property: The settlor retained powers to transfer the property or change the terms governing it.

members.legal_issue: Whether a religious endowment deed creates an absolute dedication or only a charge in favour of the deity depends on the settlor’s intention as disclosed by the deed as a whole.
material_facts: The deed repeatedly stated that the properties were dedicated to the deity, vested absolutely in the deity, and could not be claimed by the settlor or her heirs.
The deed provided for worship and related expenses, accumulation and use of surplus income, and the succession and remuneration of shebaits, including provision for their maintenance and residence.
The deed did not reserve a beneficial interest in the properties to the settlor or her heirs; the directions benefiting shebaits and their descendants operated as charges on the endowed estate.
The evidence did not establish that the endowed property’s income substantially exceeded the specified expenses when the dedication was made.
members.legal_principle: The intention to create an absolute or partial dedication is determined by a conspectus of all the deed’s provisions. If the property is wholly dedicated and no beneficial interest is reserved, the dedication is complete; if the deity receives only a charge and the residue is retained by the settlor, it is partial. Reasonable remuneration, maintenance, and residence for shebaits do not invalidate an absolute dedication. An invalid provision benefiting others does not invalidate the endowment: its benefit enures to the deity if the dedication is absolute, and to the settlor if it is partial. The Court relied on Sri Sri Iswari Bhubaneshwari Thakurani v. Brojonath Dey, L.R. 64 I.A. 203; Sree Ishwar Sridhar Jew v. Sushila Bala Dasi, [1954] S.C.R. 407; and Pande Har Narayan v. Surju Kanwari, L.R. 43 I.A. 143.
members.conclusion: The deed created an absolute endowment for the deity, subject to the specified charges; the properties did not remain beneficially vested in the settlor or her heirs.

rule.if: religious_endowment_deed_case and deed_states_absolute_transfer and no_beneficial_interest_reserved and shebait_benefits_are_charges

predicates.religious_endowment_deed_case: The dispute concerns whether an instrument dedicating property for religious worship gives the deity the whole beneficial interest or only a charge.
predicates.deed_states_absolute_transfer: The settlor’s deed states that the property is dedicated to the deity and belongs to the deity absolutely.
predicates.no_beneficial_interest_reserved: The deed, read as a whole, reserves no beneficial interest in the property to the settlor, the settlor’s heirs, or another person.
predicates.shebait_benefits_are_charges: The deed provides benefits for shebaits or their descendants as charges on the endowed property rather than as a retained beneficial interest.

members.legal_issue: A lessee cannot acquire for personal benefit by prescription an easement of way or water flow over other land belonging to the lessor.
material_facts: The claimant held the property under a lease and used adjacent land belonging to the lessor as a passage and for discharging waste water.
The claimant asserted the easement for personal benefit rather than as a right granted with the lease or on behalf of the owner of the leased property.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882 defines an easement as a right for the beneficial enjoyment of land. Under Section 12, an easement may be acquired by the owner of immovable property or, on the owner's behalf, by a person in occupation; a lessee cannot acquire one against the lessor for the lessee's personal benefit. The court relied on Udit Singh v. Kashi Ram, Jevnath Ali v. Allabudin, Basawangudi Narayan Kamthy v. Lingappa Shetty, Abdul Bashid v. B. Baham Saran, Doma v. Ragho, Girdhar Singh v. Gokul, and Gayford v. Moffatt. The court did not decide a tenant's rights concerning light, air, or support for a building on the leasehold.
members.conclusion: The claimant, as lessee, could not acquire the claimed easement for his own benefit against the lessor.

rule.if: easement_claim_on_appeal and claimant_was_lessee and claimed_way_or_water_easement and servient_land_belonged_to_lessor and claim_was_for_claimants_personal_benefit

predicates.easement_claim_on_appeal: A claimant appealed a decision concerning a claimed easement.
predicates.claimant_was_lessee: The claimant occupied the land as a lessee when the claimed use began.
predicates.claimed_way_or_water_easement: The claimant sought a right of way or a right to discharge water over other land.
predicates.servient_land_belonged_to_lessor: The other land over which the right was claimed belonged to the claimant's lessor.

members.legal_issue: A person who later becomes the owner of leased land cannot add the period of easement use during the lease to the period of use after becoming owner to establish prescription against the former lessor.
material_facts: The claimant used adjacent land belonging to the lessor as a passage and for discharging waste water while occupying the relevant property as a lessee.
The claimant later purchased the reversion and became the owner, then sought to count the earlier period of use during the lease toward acquisition of the easement by prescription.
members.legal_principle: Sections 12 and 15 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882 govern who may acquire an easement and the method of acquisition. Since a lessee cannot acquire an easement against the lessor for the lessee's own benefit under Section 12, the lessee's use during the tenancy cannot be added to the later period of use as owner. The court's reasoning is supported by Udit Singh v. Kashi Ram, Jevnath Ali v. Allabudin, Basawangudi Narayan Kamthy v. Lingappa Shetty, Abdul Bashid v. B. Baham Saran, Doma v. Ragho, Girdhar Singh v. Gokul, and Gayford v. Moffatt.
members.conclusion: The claimant could not tack the period of use as a lessee to the period after becoming owner; prescription could begin only when the claimant became owner.

members.legal_issue: Adverse possession against a female holder of a limited interest does not start limitation against a reversioner who claims from the last male holder rather than through that female holder.
material_facts: The widow held the shebaitship interest as the limited successor to her husband.
A transferee took possession under an alienation by the widow, and that possession was adverse to her.
The claimants sought the interest as heirs of the last male holder, not through the widow, and sued after her death.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 124, read with section 2(8) of the Limitation Act, the defendant’s possession must be adverse to the plaintiff or to someone from or through whom the plaintiff derives the right to sue. A reversioner does not derive title through the widow but claims from the last male holder; accordingly, adverse possession against the widow does not begin limitation against the reversioner before succession opens. The principle that adverse possession against a Hindu widow does not defeat the reversioner is not confined to Article 141. The Court relied on Gnanasambanda v. Velu for the requirement that possession be adverse to the plaintiff or the person through whom the plaintiff claims, and affirmed the principle recognized in Srinath Kuer v. Prosunno Kumar, Banchordas v. Parvati, and Jaggo v. Utsava.
members.conclusion: The adverse possession against the widow did not bar the claimants. For their claim, limitation began when succession opened to them on the widow’s death, so the suit was not time-barred.

rule.if: suit_to_recover_hereditary_office and female_holder_has_limited_interest and claimant_succeeds_from_last_male_holder and possession_is_adverse_to_female_holder

predicates.suit_to_recover_hereditary_office: The claimant brought a suit to recover a hereditary office.

predicates.claimant_succeeds_from_last_male_holder: The claimant’s title arises from the last male holder rather than through the female holder.
predicates.possession_is_adverse_to_female_holder: The defendant or a predecessor possessed the interest adversely to the female holder.

members.legal_issue: An eventual reversioner who claims through the last male holder rather than through a preceding presumptive reversioner is not bound by that preceding reversioner’s admission about the necessity for an alienation.
material_facts: A person who had become the immediate reversioner after the death of the earlier presumptive reversioner made a declaration that the widow’s debts were for legal necessity.
The claimants were that person’s sons, but they claimed as heirs of the deceased property holder, not through their father.
The declaration was not made to the purchasers involved in the challenged transactions.
members.legal_principle: No person has a vested right while the widow is alive, and an eventual reversioner does not claim through a person who merely preceded that reversioner in the line of presumptive succession. The Court considered Rangasami Gounden v. Nachiappa Gounden, which explained the relevant passage in Bajrangi v. Manokarnika.
members.conclusion: The declaration did not bind the claimants.

predicates.reversionary_title_claim_case: A claimant seeks property as an eventual reversioner after the widow’s interest ends.
predicates.prior_presumptive_reversioner_made_admis: A person who preceded the claimant as presumptive reversioner made an admission about the necessity for an alienation.

members.legal_issue: During the statutory accounting period, the government has the exclusive right to collect money due to a coal mine and may use it to meet mine liabilities, while money not collected by the end of that period may be realised directly by the former owner.
material_facts: The management of the mines was taken over before nationalisation, and the former owners alleged that substantial amounts from debtors and coal sales remained outstanding.
The parties disputed whether the government could collect money after the appointed day and whether former owners could directly recover amounts that remained unrealised by the specified date.
The statutory scheme provided a specified date for government collections and payments, and made pre-appointed-day liabilities the former owners’ responsibility.
members.legal_principle: Sections 18(2) and 19(3)–(4) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 form an integrated accounting scheme. Section 19(3) authorises collection up to the specified date notwithstanding that the realisation relates to an earlier period, and section 19(4) authorises discharge of liabilities that could not be discharged by the appointed day. Section 7 leaves pre-appointed-day liabilities with the former owners. The Court also considered the relationship between the Nationalisation Act and the Coal Mines (Taking over of Management) Act, 1973, under which management was taken over while title initially remained with the owners.
members.conclusion: Under sections 19(3) and 19(4), read with section 18(2), the government could exclusively receive mine money realised up to the specified date and apply it to the relevant liabilities. Amounts not realised by the government by that date could be realised directly by former owners to meet their pre-existing liabilities.

predicates.nationalisation_management_accounting_pr: The dispute concerns accounting for a coal mine after government management and nationalisation.
predicates.mine_money_remains_to_be_collected: Money due to the mine remains to be collected after the appointed day.
predicates.pre_transfer_mine_liabilities_exist: Liabilities relating to the mine existed that could not be discharged by the appointed day.

members.legal_issue: A subsidy reimbursement due from the former Coal Board is money due to the mine and may be collected and applied within the statutory mine-accounting scheme rather than paid directly to the former owner.
material_facts: The former owners claimed a subsidy reimbursement from the former Coal Board for hard-rock mining and stowing operations, which remained outstanding in relation to a period before the appointed day.
The High Court had directed the government to pay that subsidy amount to the former owners.
The Supreme Court held that the amount was a due of the mine and set aside that direction.
members.legal_principle: Sections 19(3) and 19(4) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 treat money due to a mine as subject to government collection and use for mine liabilities during the specified period. Relying on Industrial Supplies Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, which construed corresponding provisions of the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, the Court held that a subsidy payable by way of reimbursement is like any other due and is money due to the mine.
members.conclusion: The subsidy was money due to the mine within the meaning of the statutory collection scheme, so the direction requiring direct payment to the former owners was incorrect.

predicates.nationalisation_mine_accounting_proceedi: The dispute concerns accounting for money due to a mine under a nationalisation scheme.
predicates.reimbursement_is_due_to_mine: A reimbursement is payable to the mine for its operations.
predicates.former_owner_seeks_direct_subsidy_paymen: The former owner seeks direct payment of the reimbursement.

members.legal_issue: A timely Letters Patent appeal accompanied by one complete set of required documents is not invalid or time-barred merely because additional sets are filed later.
material_facts: The memorandum of appeal was filed within the prescribed period.
One complete set of the specified documents accompanied the memorandum, and the remaining two sets were filed later, before the appeal was taken up for admission.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI rules 1 and 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure govern the memorandum and accompanying documents for an appeal. The High Court rules on paper books required three typed sets, but, following State of Punjab v. Shamlal Murari, the Supreme Court held that this requirement was directory and that substantial compliance was sufficient. Article 117 of the Limitation Act and the applicable High Court limitation rule governed the time for filing; the High Court’s rule on amendment permitted time for curing procedural defects.
members.conclusion: The requirement to file three sets was directory, and the appeal substantially complied with it; the later filing of the remaining sets cured the irregularity. The appeal was not time-barred.

predicates.letters_patent_appeal: A litigant brought an appeal under a Letters Patent against a judgment of a single judge.

predicates.one_complete_set_submitted: The appellant submitted one complete set of the required documents with the appeal memorandum.

members.legal_issue: An application to extend limitation is unnecessary when an appeal was filed within time and the only deficiency was an irregularity in the accompanying documents.
material_facts: The appeal memorandum was filed within the prescribed period, but it was accompanied by only one set of the required documents.
The remaining sets were filed later, and the appeal was complete before it was taken up for admission.
The Division Bench treated the appeal as late and refused to condone delay on that basis.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act permits extension where an appeal was not preferred within the prescribed period. The Court held that the considerations governing a section 5 application do not apply when the appeal itself was presented within time and the defect is only an irregularity in its presentation. It therefore set aside the limitation ruling founded on the contrary assumption.
members.conclusion: There was no occasion to seek or decide condonation under section 5 of the Limitation Act. The refusal to condone delay, based on the mistaken assumption that the appeal was late, could not stand.

members.legal_issue: Part-performance protection cannot establish title or support an affirmative suit for a declaration of ownership or other rights in immovable property.
material_facts: The claimant relied on a written agreement to sell and possession said to have been given under it.
He sued for a declaration that the land was not liable to attachment and sale and sought injunctions against the sale and interference with his possession.
The agreement had not been registered, although local law required its registration.
members.legal_principle: Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act creates a statutory bar against a transferor enforcing certain rights against a qualifying transferee in possession, but confers no title or interest and is available as a defence, not as an independent cause of action. A contract for sale does not itself create title or an interest in the property under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, and registration requirements arise under Section 17 of the Registration Act. The Court relied on Ram Gopal Reddy v. The Additional Custodian Evacuee Property; Delhi Motor Company v. U.A. Basrurkar; Sardar Govindrao Mahadik v. Devi Sahai; Sheth Maneklal Mansukhbhai v. M/s. Homusji Jamshed-ji Ginwalla & Sons; and Technicians Studio Pvt. Ltd. v. Lila Ghosh.
members.conclusion: The agreement and the doctrine of part performance could not establish title or support the declaration sought; part-performance protection operates as a shield to retain possession, not as a sword to assert title or obtain affirmative relief.

predicates.suit_seeks_affirmative_property_relief: The claimant brought a suit seeking a declaration or other affirmative relief concerning rights in immovable property.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_part_performance: The claimant relied on possession or acts said to have been done under an agreement to transfer the property.
predicates.claimant_seeks_to_establish_title_or_an_: The claimant relied on the agreement and part performance to establish ownership or an independent right, rather than only to resist enforcement against possession.

members.legal_issue: The protection for part performance cannot be used in a suit to establish ownership of property.
material_facts: The claimant relied on an alleged purchase, payment, and possession under an unregistered transfer.
The claimant’s suit sought a declaration that he was the owner and an order requiring a sale deed to be executed and registered.
The transferor was not seeking to recover the property in a proceeding against the claimant.
members.legal_principle: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act affords protection by way of defence in the circumstances to which it applies; it does not enable a claimant to establish ownership through a suit seeking a declaration of title. No earlier cases were relied on for this proposition.
members.conclusion: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act could potentially assist the claimant as a defence if the transferor sought to recover the property, but it could not establish the claimant’s ownership in this suit.

predicates.ownership_declaration_suit: A claimant brought a suit seeking a declaration that the claimant owns the property.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_part_performance_prot: The claimant relied on an alleged transfer and acts of performance to invoke protection based on part performance.
predicates.claimant_seeks_to_establish_title: The claimant sought to use that protection to establish ownership rather than only to resist a recovery claim by the transferor.

members.legal_issue: The rule requiring an applicant to establish lawful possession applies to both the grant and the renewal of a cinema licence.
material_facts: The tenant sought renewal of an existing cinema licence.
The relevant rule appeared in the general part of the rules governing licences.
The Act barred the licensing authority from granting a licence unless satisfied that the rules had been substantially complied with.
members.legal_principle: Rule 13 appears in Part I-A of the Madras Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1957, under the heading “General.” Section 5(2)(a) of the Madras Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1955 requires substantial compliance with the rules before a licence is granted. The Court found no basis for distinguishing a grant from a renewal for this purpose.
members.conclusion: Rule 13 applies to renewal as well as to the grant of a licence.

predicates.cinema_licensing_proceeding: An applicant sought a licence governed by rules regulating cinema licensing.
predicates.application_seeks_renewal: The applicant asked the licensing authority to renew an existing licence.

members.legal_issue: A cinema licence renewal requires the applicant to establish lawful possession even when the renewal provision does not separately repeat that requirement.
material_facts: The applicant sought renewal of a cinema licence after the term of his lease had expired.
The renewal rules required the licensing authority to be satisfied that the rules had been fulfilled.
The initial-licence rules expressly required lawful possession of the site, building and equipment.
members.legal_principle: Rule 11(B)(2) expressly requires lawful possession for an initial licence. Rule 12(B)(1), including its second proviso, requires satisfaction of all the rules for renewal, so the omission of a separate reference to lawful possession does not remove that requirement. The Court approved the Full Bench's interpretation in Smt. Y. Anasuya v. Government of A.P. and rejected the contrary view in M. Kameswara Somayajulu v. State of A.P.
members.conclusion: Lawful possession is required for renewal because the renewal rules require compliance with all applicable rules, including the lawful-possession requirement.

predicates.cinema_licence_renewal_proceeding: The applicant asked the licensing authority to renew a licence to operate a cinema.
predicates.renewal_requires_compliance_with_all_rul: The governing renewal requirements made renewal conditional on compliance with all applicable rules.
predicates.initial_licence_requires_lawful_possessi: The governing requirements for an initial licence required the applicant to possess the relevant property lawfully.

members.legal_issue: A private complaint cannot initiate prosecution for abetting the fabrication of a false court record intended to be used in a judicial proceeding to create an erroneous opinion on a material point.
material_facts: A public servant was alleged to have made a false entry about a case pending in court, intending that the entry be used in the proceeding to create an erroneous opinion about when it was instituted.
The private complainant charged another person with abetting the public servant’s act and filed no complaint from the court concerned.
members.legal_principle: Fabricating false evidence within IPC Section 192 includes making a false entry intended to appear in evidence in a judicial proceeding and cause an erroneous opinion on a material point. The offence is punishable under IPC Section 193, and CrPC Section 195(1)(b) bars cognizance of it, including its abetment, unless the court concerned makes a written complaint. IPC Section 218 does not govern an entry made for that judicial-evidence purpose rather than to save or injure a person or property.
members.conclusion: The prosecution for abetment could not proceed on the private complaint; it required a written complaint from the court concerned.

rule.if: private_complaint_without_court_complaint and prosecution_for_abetting_record_maker and false_record_for_judicial_use and intended_material_judicial_error

predicates.private_complaint_without_court_complain: A private complainant initiated prosecution without a written complaint from the court concerned.
predicates.prosecution_for_abetting_record_maker: The prosecution alleged that a person abetted the maker of a record.
predicates.false_record_for_judicial_use: The record maker allegedly made a false record intending that it be used as evidence in a judicial proceeding.
predicates.intended_material_judicial_error: The record maker allegedly intended the false record to cause an erroneous opinion on a material point in the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A private complaint may proceed for abetting a public servant’s intentional preparation of a false record to save or injure a person or property when the offence does not depend on use of the record in a judicial proceeding.
material_facts: Public servants were alleged to have caused an incorrect land record to be prepared, knowing it was likely to cause loss or injury to the purchasers of the land.
The alleged purpose was to save the property from the effects of the sale, and the offence did not require the record to be used in a judicial proceeding.
The private complainant charged another person with abetting the public servants’ acts.
members.legal_principle: IPC Section 218 creates a distinct offence involving a public servant’s intentional preparation of a false record to save or injure a person or property; it is complete when the record is made with that intention and does not require judicial use of the record. It is not a minor offence included within IPC Section 192 and is not among the offences covered by CrPC Section 195. Accordingly, that section does not bar a private complaint alleging the offence or its abetment.
members.conclusion: The private complaint could proceed against the alleged abettor; the bar on cognizance without a court complaint did not apply.

members.legal_issue: The State is not required by the court to provide alternative accommodation to occupants before releasing requisitioned premises.
material_facts: The occupants sought protection from eviction and relied on the hardship of finding alternative accommodation.
The premises had been requisitioned and the Court required their eventual release.
A separate opinion proposed protective arrangements for certain occupants, but the majority rejected a general requirement to provide alternative accommodation.
members.legal_principle: The majority treated the provision of alternative accommodation as a matter for the State Government's consideration, rather than as a condition that must be satisfied before release of requisitioned premises.
members.conclusion: The State cannot be compelled to provide alternative accommodation to the allottees; whether to provide it is for the State to consider in light of desirability and administrative feasibility. Sawant J. proposed additional protections in a separate opinion.

predicates.requisition_release_proceeding: The matter concerns release of property that has been requisitioned.
predicates.occupants_request_alternative_accommodat: The occupants ask the State to provide other accommodation before they leave the requisitioned property.

members.legal_issue: The State is not generally required to provide an alternative site or flat as a condition of acquiring land for a public purpose.
material_facts: The owner sought protection against the loss of his flat and relied on the right to shelter.
The Court stated that courts may give effect to a State proposal to provide alternative sites, but that such a proposal does not create a condition applicable to every acquisition.
The statutory exception concerning an alternative site did not apply to the petitioner.
members.legal_principle: The Land Acquisition Act, 1894 does not generally require alternative accommodation as a condition of acquisition. A court may give effect to a State proposal to provide alternative sites, and the Court noted the exception in section 31(3), which did not apply in this case.
members.conclusion: The owner was not entitled to require an alternative site or flat as a general condition of the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for fatal accident must be based on a rational, evidence-supported assessment that is just and reasonable, rather than an arbitrary estimate of the deceased’s income.
material_facts: A widow and minor child sought compensation after the death of a young man in a vehicle accident.
The claimants asserted income from farming, cattle trading and milk sales, but produced no material establishing the deceased’s income or the type of land he owned.
The Tribunal estimated monthly income at Rs.4,500 without stating a supporting basis, and the High Court upheld its award.

The Supreme Court assessed monthly income at Rs.3,000, deducted Rs.1,000 for personal expenses, applied a multiplier of 18, and fixed total compensation, including funeral expenses, at Rs.4,34,000; it left the interest rate unchanged.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 168 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, a Tribunal must determine compensation that appears just. Just compensation must be equitable, fair, reasonable and non-arbitrary; although no precise mathematical formula applies, the assessment must be rational and grounded in the evidence and circumstances, not in whim or conjecture. The Court relied on Helen C. Rebello v. Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation, AIR 1998 SC 3191.
members.conclusion: The unsupported income estimate and resulting compensation could not stand. The Court modified the award by fixing compensation at Rs.4,34,000, with interest at the rate previously awarded.

predicates.fatal_accident_compensation_appeal: A party appeals an award determining compensation for a person’s death in an accident.
predicates.income_evidence_absent: The claimants provide no material establishing the deceased person’s income.
predicates.unsupported_income_estimate: The compensation decision-maker estimates income without giving an evidentiary or reasoned basis for that estimate.

members.legal_issue: In a motor accident compensation claim, the deceased’s annual income should be determined from available income tax returns rather than unsupported estimates or other inconsistent material.
material_facts: The claimants sought compensation for the death of a self-employed businessman who had income from several sources, including agricultural land and businesses.
The income tax return for one assessment year recorded the deceased’s house-property, business, and agricultural income.
The Tribunal estimated agricultural income using figures drawn from other judgments, despite the return recording agricultural income.
The claimants relied on other documents to contend that the deceased’s income was higher.
members.legal_principle: Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 provides the basis for the compensation claim. An income tax return is a statutory document on which a court may rely to determine annual income. In New India Assurance Company v Yogesh Devi, (2012) 3 SCC 613, the Court addressed a case without evidence of income from the properties and held that evidence was needed to quantify depletion in income; that decision did not assist the claimants where a tax return was available and no evidence of depletion was adduced.
members.conclusion: The income determination had to proceed on the basis of the available income tax return; the Tribunal’s method of estimating additional agricultural income was unsustainable.

predicates.motor_accident_compensation_claim: The proceeding seeks compensation for a person’s death or injury caused by a motor accident.
predicates.income_tax_return_available: The deceased’s income tax return is available as evidence of annual income.

members.legal_issue: A grant of probate does not determine ownership of property or bar a civil suit seeking a declaration of title and injunction based on claims that the property belongs to a joint family.
material_facts: Probate had been granted for a will bequeathing the disputed properties, and that grant had been affirmed on appeal.
The civil suit alleged that the properties were joint Hindu family properties and that properties had been acquired using income from ancestral agricultural land.
The suit sought a declaration of title and an injunction against alienation; the lower courts dismissed it solely because probate had been granted.
members.legal_principle: A probate court determines whether the will was duly executed and attested and whether the testator had a sound disposing mind; it does not determine the testator’s title to the property or whether the property was joint ancestral or individually acquired. Probate conclusively establishes the will’s due execution and the executor’s legal character, but does not decide title. The civil court may admit the probate as evidence, but it is not decisive of ownership. The Court relied on Ishwardeo Narain Singh v. Smt. Kamta Devi and Chiranjilal Shrilal Goenka v. Jasjit Singh, and distinguished Rukmani Devi v. Narendra Lal Gupta as establishing the conclusiveness of probate as to the will, not as to title.
members.conclusion: The probate grant did not make the civil suit legally unmaintainable. The dismissal was set aside, and the suit was remitted for decision after issues were framed and evidence considered.

rule.if: appeal_from_dismissal_of_civil_title_suit_after_probate and probate_granted and plaint_claims_joint_family_ownership and title_claim_requires_evidence

predicates.appeal_from_dismissal_of_civil_title_sui: An appeal concerns dismissal of a civil suit for title and related relief after probate was granted.
predicates.probate_granted: A competent court granted probate of a will concerning the disputed property.
predicates.plaint_claims_joint_family_ownership: The plaintiff alleged that the disputed property belonged to a joint family rather than exclusively to the testator.

members.legal_issue: A statutory occupancy grant to one member of a joint family does not, by itself, extinguish the other members’ rights to seek partition of the joint property in a civil court.
material_facts: The disputed lands formed part of properties held by a joint family, and the family members claimed shares by succession.
An occupancy right over some of the lands was granted in the name of one family member.
The family members brought a civil suit seeking partition, and the courts below upheld a jurisdictional objection based on the statutory scheme.
members.legal_principle: Sections 10, 24 and 29 of the Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Abolition of Inams Act, 1955 provide for determination of claims to occupancy rights and appeals from those determinations, but do not provide a forum for disputes between members of a joint family claiming under the same title. A statutory ouster of civil-court jurisdiction is strictly construed and extends only to matters the statutory forum is competent to decide. In light of Article 300A, property rights cannot be taken away except in accordance with law; Hindustan Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chenai, (2005) 7 SCC 627, is relied on in this connection.
members.conclusion: The statutory scheme does not oust the civil court’s jurisdiction to decide disputes about the respective rights of joint-family members claiming under the same title; the Act’s forum determines entitlement to occupancy rights, not those inter se rights.

rule.if: partition_suit and joint_family_property and occupancy_right_granted_to_one_sharer and inter_se_family_share_dispute and statutory_forum_does_not_determine_inter_se_shares

predicates.partition_suit: A claimant brought a civil proceeding seeking division of property among alleged co-sharers.

predicates.occupancy_right_granted_to_one_sharer: An authority granted an occupancy right over the disputed property in the name of one family member.

members.legal_issue: A pending review application cannot be bypassed by filing a separate application for recall that raises the same review grounds and seeks an open-court hearing.
material_facts: A review application by the applicant remained pending and had not yet been considered through circulation.
The applicant separately filed an application for recall raising substantially the same issues as the pending review application.
The recall application sought an open-court hearing and included documents offered in support of the same requested relief.
members.legal_principle: Order XL Rule 3 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1966 requires a review application to be disposed of by circulation unless the Court orders otherwise. An application that is in substance a review cannot be used to obtain an oral hearing or to dispose of a pending review application indirectly.
members.conclusion: The recall application was rejected as an attempt to bypass the review procedure, but the applicant was permitted to ask the Registry to list the pending review application in circulation and could submit the documents in that review application.

predicates.review_application_pending: The applicant has a review application in the same matter that has not yet been disposed of.
predicates.separate_recall_application_raises_same_: The applicant filed a separate recall application that substantially repeats the issues raised in the pending review.
predicates.recall_application_seeks_open_court_hear: The recall application seeks an oral hearing outside the ordinary review procedure.

members.legal_issue: A review application should ordinarily be heard by the original bench, and a review should not proceed on an issue already before the appellate court.
material_facts: The review application was heard by a different bench even though a member of the original bench remained available.
The review application sought increased damages based on an affidavit whose filing and consideration were disputed.
An appeal concerning the original order, including the extent of damages, was pending before the Supreme Court when the review was heard.
members.legal_principle: Section 19(4)(f) of the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 gives the Tribunal review powers akin to those of a civil court. Rule 22 of the National Green Tribunal (Practices and Procedure) Rules, 2011 and Order XLVII Rules 1 and 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure support the ordinary requirement that the original bench hear the review, subject to practical impossibility or recusal, and restrict review where the same ground is before the appellate court. The Court relied on Malthesh Gudda Pooja v. State of Karnataka, (2011) 15 SCC 330, and referred to Common Cause v. Union of India, (2017) 9 SCC 499, in discussing improper official clarifications.
members.conclusion: The review order was set aside as illegal.

predicates.different_bench_heard_review: A bench other than the original bench heard the review application.

members.legal_issue: A lease made in breach of statutory letting requirements is not void or unenforceable between landlord and tenant unless the governing law expressly invalidates the agreement.
material_facts: The landlord let the building to a tenant without an allotment order.
The tenant paid rent for three months and then stopped paying; the trial court found the rent and default proved but dismissed the ejectment suit solely because the letting contravened the Act.
The landlord challenged the dismissal, and the Full Bench had held that the agreement was void and unenforceable.
members.legal_principle: Under Nanakram v. Kundalrai, (1986) 3 SCC 83, absent a mandatory statutory provision requiring eviction or declaring the agreement void, the parties remain bound by their agreement as between themselves. The Court held that Waman Shriniwas Kini v. Ratilal Bhagwandas & Co., (1959) Supp. 2 SCR 217, concerned an express statutory prohibition on subletting and was consistent with Nanakram; Sri Krishna Khanna v. A.D.M., Kanpur, (1975) 2 SCC 361, concerned the public authority’s power to allot despite an agreement between the parties; and Mannalal Khetan v. Kedar Nath Khetan, (1977) 2 SCC 424, concerned an agreement contrary to company-law provisions and attachment orders. Those cases did not displace Nanakram. The relevant statutory context included Sections 11, 13, 17 and 31 of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972; the Full Bench’s reliance on Sections 10 and 23 of the Contract Act did not justify disregarding Nanakram.
members.conclusion: The agreement was not void merely because the letting contravened the Act. Unless the statute specifically provides that a contract contrary to it is void, the contract remains binding between the parties and may be enforced between them. The High Court’s contrary ruling was set aside, and the writ petition was remanded for decision in accordance with law.

predicates.landlord_tenant_contract_dispute: A landlord and tenant are disputing the effect or enforcement of their agreement.
predicates.lease_breaches_regulatory_requirement: The landlord let the premises in a way that did not comply with a regulatory requirement governing the letting.
predicates.governing_law_does_not_invalidate_contra: The governing law prohibits the noncompliant transaction but does not expressly make the agreement void.

members.legal_issue: A lease made contrary to statutory controls on letting remains binding between the landlord and tenant when the control scheme does not make the lease void and leaves enforcement to the regulator’s discretion.
material_facts: Landlords sought to treat leases as void because the required vacancy notifications had not been given and the prescribed letting process had not been followed.
The control scheme empowered the regulator to take steps to enforce compliance but did not require the regulator to evict every person who entered into possession contrary to the controls.
The disputes were proceedings between the landlords and their tenants.
members.legal_principle: Under clauses 22, 23 and 28 of the Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, a lease made contrary to the letting controls is not void where the scheme provides discretionary enforcement and does not declare the lease void. The lease remains binding between its parties and cannot be avoided by either in a dispute between them. This follows Murlidhar Agarwal v. State of U.P., which approved Udhoo Dass v. Prem Prakash; Waman Shrinivas Kini v. Ratilal Bhagwandas & Co. was distinguished because it concerned enforcement of a statutory right to evict arising directly from a breach.
members.conclusion: The leases were not void, and neither party could assail them in a proceeding between the parties on the ground that they contravened the letting controls.

predicates.dispute_between_lease_parties: The landlord and tenant disputed the effect of their lease in a proceeding between them.
predicates.lease_made_in_breach_of_letting_controls: The landlord and tenant entered into a lease without following the applicable statutory requirements for letting the premises.
predicates.regulator_has_discretionary_enforcement_: The governing control scheme allowed the regulator to take enforcement steps but did not require it to do so in every case.

members.legal_issue: A tribunal’s finding that a claimed family partition was not genuine and not acted upon could be upheld where it was based on material in the record.
material_facts: The family’s karta claimed that a partition had occurred and sought tax relief and recognition of the partition.
The Income-tax Officer, the appellate authority and the Tribunal rejected the claim; the Tribunal found on the material before it that the partition was not acted upon.
The High Court answered against the taxpayer the referred question whether legal evidence supported the Tribunal’s finding.
members.legal_principle: A tribunal’s finding on whether a partition was genuine and acted upon, when made on material before it, did not give rise to a question of law warranting interference in this appeal. The taxpayer had sought relief under sections 25A and 25(4) of the Income-tax Act, and the matter reached the High Court by reference under section 66(2), following the procedure in section 66(1). No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right to uphold the Tribunal’s finding; no question of law arose for the Supreme Court to decide, and the taxpayer’s appeal was dismissed with costs.

predicates.tax_reference_appeal: The case is an appeal arising from a tax-law reference concerning a tribunal’s finding.
predicates.tribunal_made_finding_on_partition_from_: The tribunal considered material in the record and found that the claimed family partition was not acted upon.

members.legal_issue: A tribunal’s finding that a claimed family partition was genuine could be upheld when additional material before it supported that finding.
material_facts: In a later tax proceeding, the claimed partition was evidenced by a deed different in date from the partition considered in the earlier proceeding.
A civil court had found the deed genuine, fair and binding and found that the joint family had ceased to exist.
The Tribunal had additional material, including sworn statements by the sons and other relevant material, supporting the partition, while making an exception concerning one house.
The High Court found material supporting the Tribunal’s finding, and the Commissioner appealed.
members.legal_principle: A tribunal’s finding that a partition was genuine may stand where additional material supports it, including sworn statements and other relevant material; a finding concerning a differently evidenced partition in an earlier proceeding does not eliminate the support available for the finding in the later proceeding. The later application was under section 25A of the Income-tax Act, and the reference proceeded under sections 66(1) and 66(2). No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right that there was material supporting the Tribunal’s finding that the partition was genuine; the Commissioner’s appeal was dismissed with costs.

predicates.tax_reference_appeal: The case is an appeal arising from a tax-law reference concerning a tribunal’s finding.
predicates.tribunal_considered_additional_partition: The tribunal considered additional evidence and relevant material concerning whether the family partition was genuine.
predicates.sons_gave_sworn_statements: The family members’ sons gave statements on oath supporting the claimed partition.
predicates.asserted_partition_differed_from_earlier: The partition asserted in the proceeding was evidenced differently from the partition considered in an earlier proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A statutory authorization to delegate a power includes the delegation of duties or functions that are necessary for, and integral to, exercising that power.
material_facts: The governing law authorized the State Government to delegate all or any of its powers to specified officers.
The power to resume management of uncultivated land could be exercised only after an inquiry.
The State Government delegated the relevant power to a Deputy Collector, who made the resumption order after an inquiry.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 65(1) and 83 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, a power to delegate includes duties or functions incidental to, and integrally connected with, that power. The Court relied on Edward Liso Mungoni v. Attorney-General of Northern Rhodesia, which treated an interwoven power and duty as incapable of being split between separate persons.
