predicates.private_application_received: A party to the possession dispute applied to the Magistrate for proceedings.
predicates.magistrate_examined_applicant_on_oath: The Magistrate examined the applicant on oath before initiating the proceeding.
predicates.magistrate_satisfied_requirements_exist: The Magistrate was satisfied that a possession dispute existed and was likely to cause a breach of the peace.

members.legal_issue: A pleading that claims continuous possession as owner of property beyond the claimant’s established ownership may amount in substance to a defence of adverse possession even without using that label.
material_facts: The defendant was found to own only a portion of the property but admitted possession of the entire property.
In the written statement, the defendant claimed continuous possession of the property as owner for years and asserted ownership under conveyance and release documents.
The defendant did not expressly plead adverse possession in those words.
members.legal_principle: The substance of a party’s pleaded claim, rather than the use of a particular label, may show that the party has advanced a defence of adverse possession. The Court expressly left open whether the defendant had established a right to title by adverse possession.
members.conclusion: In the circumstances, the defendant’s written statement was in substance a defence of adverse possession, although the Court did not decide whether the defendant was entitled to title on that basis.

predicates.property_title_suit: The proceeding concerns a claim to ownership or possession of immovable property.
predicates.defendant_claims_continuous_possession_a: The defendant pleads continuous possession of the property in the character of owner.
predicates.defendant_claims_more_property_than_esta: The defendant’s claimed possession as owner extends beyond the portion of the property the defendant is found to own.

members.legal_issue: A written defense that expressly claims prescriptive ownership and alleges long, continuous possession raises a specific plea of adverse possession, even if the plea lacks material particulars needed to prove it.
material_facts: The written defense alleged that the defendant’s wife had been in continuous and peaceful possession since the alleged sale and expressly claimed that she had acquired ownership by adverse possession.
The High Court held that there was no specific plea, but the Supreme Court found that the written defense did contain one.
members.legal_principle: A court must assess whether adverse possession has been pleaded from the contents of the written defense. An express claim of prescriptive ownership, read with allegations of long possession, is a specific plea; the sufficiency of the pleading does not establish the claim on its merits.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s finding that there was no specific plea of adverse possession could not be sustained; the written defense did specifically raise that plea, although it lacked material particulars necessary to establish it.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_possession_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree concerning possession of property.
predicates.written_defense_expressly_claims_prescri: The defending party expressly claims that possession has matured into ownership by prescription.
predicates.written_defense_alleges_long_possession: The written defense alleges long-term possession of the property.

members.legal_issue: A person recorded as an occupant in the relevant annual land record may claim statutory occupancy rights without separately proving actual possession, and an eligible occupant dispossessed after the statutory cutoff may regain possession.
material_facts: The claimants were recorded as qabiz, meaning in possession, in the relevant annual khasra, in its remarks column.
The opposing party obtained possession on July 1, 1949, and the record showed no disturbance of the claimants’ possession between the relevant recording period and that transfer.
The land was later attached during criminal proceedings, but the claimants’ statutory occupancy suits rested on the earlier occupant entry.
The claimants were not intermediaries entitled to the land.
members.legal_principle: Section 20(b)(i) and Explanation I to the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 make the relevant annual khasra or khatauni entry the basis for adhivasi status and provide for regaining possession after eviction. Explanation IV excludes an intermediary. An occupant means a person in possession or actual enjoyment; mediate possession is immaterial unless the immediate possessor holds on behalf of the mediate possessor. The section does not require separate proof of actual possession in the recorded year. The court followed Lala Nanak Chand v. Board of Revenue, U.P., Ram Dular Singh v. Babu Sukh Ram, Bhal Singh v. Bhop, and Sugriva v. Mukhi; it noted that The Upper Ganges Sugar Mills Ltd. v. Khalil-ul-Rehman had left the possession question open.
members.conclusion: The claimants did not need to prove actual possession independently of the entry, and, as recorded occupants dispossessed after June 30, 1948, they were entitled to regain possession notwithstanding an order or decree to the contrary.

rule.if: statutory_adhivasi_claim and recorded_occupant_in_relevant_year and not intermediary_claimant and (remained_in_possession or evicted_after_cutoff)

predicates.statutory_adhivasi_claim: The proceeding seeks statutory occupancy status and possession on the basis of an official land-record entry.
predicates.recorded_occupant_in_relevant_year: The claimant is recorded as an occupant in the land record for the year designated by the statutory scheme.
predicates.intermediary_claimant: The claimant claims through an intermediary interest in the land rather than as the recorded occupant.
predicates.remained_in_possession: The recorded occupant continued in possession of the land.
predicates.evicted_after_cutoff: The recorded occupant was dispossessed after the statutory cutoff for eviction.

members.legal_issue: Eligibility for statutory occupant rights based on a land record requires the claimant to be recorded as an occupant throughout the relevant land-record year.
material_facts: The claimant sought occupant rights and possession based on an entry recording her as an occupant from February 24 of the relevant land-record year.
The entry did not establish that she was recorded as an occupant for the entire year.
members.legal_principle: Under section 20(b)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, only a person recorded as an occupant for the whole of the relevant year could claim the rights. The Court declined to read the provision more liberally than its language warranted, noting that the rights could benefit trespassers and that recognizing occupants recorded for only part of the year could encourage lawlessness and make it uncertain which of several temporary occupants qualified. The Court approved Shyam Sunar Lal v. Mangali, Ram Chander v. Chhotu, and Girdhari v. Raghubir Singh.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to the claimed occupant rights, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.claim_based_on_occupancy_record: A person seeks special occupant status on the basis of being recorded as an occupant in a land record.
predicates.record_covers_only_part_of_relevant_year: The record establishes the person's occupant status for only part of the relevant year.
predicates.not_entitled_to_special_occupant_status: The claimant does not qualify for the special occupant status sought.

members.legal_issue: A statutory amendment made after the statute’s inclusion in the protected schedule does not receive protection merely because the original statute was listed.
material_facts: The agricultural tenancy statute had been included in the protected schedule before the challenged amendment was enacted.
The amendment extended the State’s power to take over management to new circumstances, including land held by persons outside the statute’s original landholder scheme.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B protects statutes listed in the Ninth Schedule, but a later amendment that adds new substance cannot be treated as though it had been included when the statute was listed. Treating it as protected would allow a State Legislature indirectly to amend the Ninth Schedule, beyond its competence.
members.conclusion: The amendment was not protected by the constitutional provision protecting laws listed in the schedule.

predicates.ninth_schedule_protection_challenged: A party challenges whether a law receives constitutional protection because it was listed in a protected schedule.
predicates.amendment_after_protected_listing: The law was amended after the original statute had been placed on the protected schedule.
predicates.amendment_adds_new_application: The amendment extends the law to circumstances or property not covered by the original listed law.
predicates.amendment_not_protected_by_prior_listing: The later amendment does not receive protection solely from the original statute’s listing.

members.legal_issue: Amendments made to an enactment after its inclusion in the constitutional schedule do not receive schedule-based immunity merely because they are ancillary to provisions already included.
material_facts: The principal agricultural land-ceiling enactment, including its then-existing provisions, was included in the Ninth Schedule.
Later state amendments added or changed provisions, including provisions concerning the continued cultivation of acquired land by a state-owned farming corporation.
The later amendments were challenged as constitutionally invalid, and the High Court held that some were protected because they were ancillary or incidental to a scheduled provision.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B protects the Acts, Regulations, and provisions specified in the Ninth Schedule against challenges based on Part III rights, but its protection extends only to the enactment as it stood when included, including amendments made by that time. Later amendments must be tested on their own merits; protection cannot be extended to them on the ground that they are ancillary or incidental. The Court relied on Sri Ram Ram Narain Medhi v. State of Bombay, Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan, Ramanlal Gulab Chand Shah v. State of Gujarat, State of Orissa v. Chandra Sekhar Singh Bhoi, and State of Maharashtra v. Madhavrao Damodar Patilchand.
members.conclusion: The amendments made after the principal enactment was included in the Ninth Schedule were not protected by Article 31B, whether or not they were ancillary to provisions already protected.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_later_amendment and principal_enactment_was_previously_listed and amendment_was_made_after_listing and amendment_was_not_itself_listed

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_later_amendm: A party challenges the constitutionality of an amendment to an enactment that had already been placed in a constitutional schedule.
predicates.principal_enactment_was_previously_liste: The principal enactment had been placed in the constitutional schedule before the challenged amendment was made.
predicates.amendment_was_made_after_listing: The challenged amendment was enacted after the principal enactment was placed in the schedule.
predicates.amendment_was_not_itself_listed: The challenged amendment was not separately placed in the constitutional schedule.

members.legal_issue: The presumption arising from a registered document recording an adoption is rebuttable.
material_facts: A registered adoption deed recording the adoption was produced in the dispute over the deceased’s estate.
The deed was signed by the person giving the child and the person taking the child in adoption.
members.legal_principle: Section 16 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, directs the court to presume compliance when a registered document purporting to record an adoption is produced and signed by the giver and taker, but the words “unless and until it is disproved” make the presumption rebuttable. The Court concurred with Modan Singh v. Mst. Sham Kaur & Ors. (AIR 1973 P&H 122).
members.conclusion: The statutory presumption that the adoption complied with the law is rebuttable and does not make the registered deed conclusive.

predicates.adoption_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a claimed adoption was made in compliance with the law.
predicates.registered_adoption_document_signed_by_g: The person giving the child and the person taking the child signed a registered document purporting to record the adoption.

members.legal_issue: Evidence contradicting a claimed adoption may rebut the presumption arising from its registered deed and support rejection of the adoption claim.
material_facts: A voters list prepared before the dispute identified the claimant as the son of his natural father, and he had also described himself that way in proceedings brought by his wife.
The deed recited that the child had been given and taken in adoption earlier, but no specific ceremonies or evidence of that giving and taking were produced.
Several records relied on to support the adoption were created after the suit began; the mutation proceedings occurred without notice, and related records were considered unreliable.
The deed and the later will contained circumstances that the lower courts considered suspicious.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 16 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, contrary evidence may disprove the presumption created by a registered adoption document. Section 11(vi) requires the child to be actually given and taken in adoption with intent to transfer the child from the birth family to the adoptive family. The Court found that the evidence relied on by the lower courts could be considered in assessing whether the presumption had been rebutted.
members.conclusion: The evidence was capable of rebutting the presumption; the concurrent rejection of the adoption claim was not shown to be perverse and was left undisturbed.

rule.if: adoption_dispute and registered_adoption_document_signed_by_giver_and_taker and prior_records_identify_birth_father and adoption_giving_and_taking_lacks_support and post_dispute_supporting_records_are_unreliable

predicates.adoption_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a claimed adoption was made in compliance with the law.
predicates.registered_adoption_document_signed_by_g: The person giving the child and the person taking the child signed a registered document purporting to record the adoption.
predicates.prior_records_identify_birth_father: Records created before the dispute, or statements made independently of the adoption claim, identify the claimant as the child of the natural father.
predicates.adoption_giving_and_taking_lacks_support: The claimed act of giving and taking the child in adoption is not supported by evidence of the relevant event or ceremony.
predicates.post_dispute_supporting_records_are_unre: Records relied on to support the adoption were created after the dispute began or arose from proceedings lacking notice to affected persons.

members.legal_issue: A party waives an objection to a tribunal member’s disqualification by failing to raise it before the tribunal when the party knew the material facts and was aware, or must be treated as aware, of the right to object.
material_facts: The advocate knew that the tribunal chair had appeared for the complainant in the related proceedings.
The advocate did not object to the chair’s participation before the tribunal, but raised the objection later.
The advocate had substantial experience at the Bar and legal assistance in the proceedings; the Court rejected the claim that he was unaware of his right to object.
members.legal_principle: Waiver cannot be inferred merely from failure to object: the party must know the relevant facts and be aware of the right to object. The Court relied on Vyvyan v. Vyvyan and held that the advocate knew the relevant facts and must be deemed conscious of his legal rights.
members.conclusion: The advocate waived the objection and could not rely on the tribunal’s defective constitution to challenge the proceedings.

rule.if: tribunal_member_disqualification_objection and party_knew_relevant_facts and party_aware_of_right_to_object and party_failed_to_object_before_tribunal

predicates.tribunal_member_disqualification_objecti: A party had an objection that a tribunal member was disqualified from participating.
predicates.party_knew_relevant_facts: The party knew the facts giving rise to the claimed disqualification.
predicates.party_aware_of_right_to_object: The party was aware, or must be treated as aware, that they could object to the member’s participation.
predicates.party_failed_to_object_before_tribunal: The party did not raise the disqualification objection before the tribunal.

members.legal_issue: A person who knows the facts supporting an objection to an inquiry committee member and knowingly delays raising that personal objection may waive the right to rely on it to invalidate proceedings.
material_facts: The subject knew that the jurist was a committee member by May 2010 and knew of the jurist’s public opposition to his elevation.
The subject did not object to the jurist’s membership in earlier communications, including a request that the inquiry be expedited.
The subject first objected after receiving the notice of charges and the lists of supporting documents and witnesses.
The objection concerned a right personal to the subject, and the inquiry had proceeded only to the framing of charges.
members.legal_principle: A person may waive a right conferred for that person’s individual protection if the person knows the relevant facts and the right, and no public right or public policy is infringed. Failure to object alone does not invariably establish waiver, but waiver may be inferred where a person knowingly remains silent and raises the objection only after proceedings have advanced. The Court relied on Manak Lal v. Dr. Prem Chand Singhvi, Lachhu Mal v. Radhey Shyam, and Dhirendra Nath Gorai v. Sudhir Chandra. The timing of the objection was also considered in the context of the investigation under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 and the time for submission of the committee’s report under Rule 9(2)(c) of the Judges (Inquiry) Rules, 1969.
members.conclusion: The subject waived the right to object to the jurist’s appointment and could not obtain invalidation of the committee’s proceedings on that basis. The writ petition was dismissed, while the Court requested the Chairman to nominate another jurist and permitted the reconstituted committee to proceed on the charges already framed.

rule.if: judicial_misconduct_inquiry and objector_knew_member_appointment and objector_knew_basis_for_bias_objection and objector_knew_right_to_object and objection_raised_only_after_charges_notice and objection_is_personal

predicates.judicial_misconduct_inquiry: A committee was appointed to investigate alleged misbehaviour or incapacity by a judicial office-holder.
predicates.objector_knew_member_appointment: The person under inquiry knew that the challenged person was a member of the committee.
predicates.objector_knew_basis_for_bias_objection: The person under inquiry knew the facts said to give rise to bias before raising the objection.
predicates.objector_knew_right_to_object: The person under inquiry knew that the committee member’s appointment could be challenged.
predicates.objection_raised_only_after_charges_noti: The person under inquiry first objected after receiving notice of the charges and the supporting materials.
predicates.objection_is_personal: The objection concerns a right for the individual protection of the person under inquiry, rather than a public right.

members.legal_issue: Resumption of land attached to an abolished village office, when expressly subject to re-grant, does not make the land government land excluded from the land-tenancy regime.
material_facts: The disputed lands were emoluments attached to a village office that had been abolished.
The land was resumed subject to statutory provisions allowing re-grant to former office holders or other eligible persons.
The governing provisions distinguished that conditional resumption from a separate situation in which land could vest in the Government free of encumbrances.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(3) of the Karnataka Village Offices Abolition Act, 1961 made resumption subject to Sections 5, 6 and 7, which provided for re-grant. That conditional resumption was distinct from the vesting free of encumbrances described in Section 5(3). Accordingly, the exclusion in Section 107 of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961 for land belonging to the Government did not apply merely because of resumption; Section 110 provided for exclusion from that regime by government notification. The Court also considered that treating the land as government land would defeat the asserted claim to occupant registration under Section 45.
members.conclusion: The lands did not become government lands merely upon resumption and remained within the scope of the Land Reforms Act.

predicates.land_reforms_occupancy_claim: A person claims occupant registration under a land-tenancy regime in respect of the land.
predicates.land_attached_to_abolished_office: The land was attached to a village office that was later abolished.
predicates.resumption_subject_to_regrant: The land was resumed under a scheme that remained subject to possible re-grant to eligible persons.

members.legal_issue: Adverse possession does not defeat the Government’s resumption of land granted as emoluments for village-office service in the circumstances of this case.
material_facts: The lands were held as emoluments for the patel’s office.
A family member who had never performed the service obtained possession through a partition after the prior office-holder’s death.
The Government later resumed the lands and regranted them to the working patel.
members.legal_principle: Once land is found to have been granted as emoluments for an office, the Court held that no question of title by adverse possession against the Government arose in the circumstances considered. The claimant’s success depended on establishing an independent right to a share in the service grant, which he failed to establish.
members.conclusion: The claim of title by adverse possession against the Government did not arise on the facts, and the claimant could not use it to defeat resumption and regrant.

predicates.challenge_to_government_resumption: A person challenged the Government’s resumption of land granted for village-office service.
predicates.land_is_service_emolument_grant: The land was granted as emoluments for performing a village office.
predicates.claimant_possession_arose_through_family: The claimant obtained possession through a partition within the office-holder’s family rather than through performance of the service.

members.legal_issue: When a building is subject to assessment, its first assessment date determines its deemed completion date unless an earlier qualifying completion report or record exists.
material_facts: The shop had been occupied by tenants before its first assessment took effect.
The first assessment took effect on 1 April 1968.
No earlier completion report or record was identified as determining the deemed completion date.
members.legal_principle: Explanation I to section 2(2) provides for the earliest applicable completion report or record and first assessment date; occupation is used only in the absence of such a report, record, or assessment. On the facts, the first assessment date therefore controlled despite earlier occupation.
members.conclusion: The first assessment date, rather than the earlier date of occupation, was the deemed completion date.

predicates.rent_regulation_applicability_dispute: A party to a building-related proceeding disputed the date relevant to whether rent regulation applied.
predicates.assessment_exists: The building was subject to an assessment that had taken effect.
predicates.no_earlier_completion_report_or_record: No completion report or record existed with a date earlier than the first assessment date.
predicates.first_assessment_date_controls_deemed_co: The first assessment date is treated as the building's deemed completion date.

members.legal_issue: The completion date of a building for a new-construction exemption is determined from the specified municipal records and, if those records are absent, from its first actual occupation.
material_facts: The municipal assessment record referred to an “increased assessment,” but its meaning was unclear.
The evidence did not establish whether the building had been newly constructed or whether an existing building had been remodelled, or when the relevant work was completed.
The Court considered municipal records and verification by municipal authorities the best evidence of completion and the nature of the construction.
members.legal_principle: Explanation I(a) to Section 2(2) of the U.P. Act provides that completion is dated by the report or record of the local authority or, for an assessed building, the date the first assessment takes effect, using the earlier date when applicable. In the absence of a report, record, or assessment, completion is dated from first actual occupation, excluding occupation merely to supervise or guard construction. The Court stated that municipal records, rather than witness testimony, are the statutory guide. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The completion date must be determined under the statutory criteria, giving effect to the relevant municipal report, record, or assessment and using first actual occupation only when those records are absent.

rule.if: rent_control_exemption_claim and completion_date_disputed and (municipal_completion_records_exist or (no_municipal_completion_records and building_first_actually_occupied))

predicates.rent_control_exemption_claim: The landlord claims that a building is exempt from rent control because it is a new construction.
predicates.completion_date_disputed: The parties dispute when construction of the building was completed.
predicates.municipal_completion_records_exist: A local authority has a report, record, or assessment relevant to the building’s completion.
predicates.no_municipal_completion_records: There is no relevant local-authority report, record, or assessment for the building.
predicates.building_first_actually_occupied: The building was occupied for the first time for a purpose other than supervising or guarding construction.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition for an integrated public development project constitutes acquisition for a public purpose, and a reviewing court should not substitute its assessment for the government’s absent a basis for interference.
material_facts: The land was acquired for expansion and systematic development of a tourist complex, including a parking area near a fairground.
The project was presented as requiring integrated and planned development of the complex.
The acquisition was challenged on the ground that the stated purpose was not genuinely public.
members.legal_principle: Under Sooraram Pratap Reddy v. District Collector, Ranga Reddy District (2008) 9 SCC 552, an acquisition project must be considered as a whole and assessed for its larger public interest rather than by separating its components. Infrastructure development is a legitimate public purpose; the government is prima facie the best judge of that purpose, although its decision remains subject to judicial scrutiny, and a writ court should not normally substitute its judgment for the government’s.
members.conclusion: The development of the tourist complex, including the adjacent parking area, was a public purpose, and the acquisition was not invalid on that ground.

predicates.acquisition_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of a land acquisition.
predicates.integrated_development_project: The acquiring authority proposed a coordinated project whose components were intended to be developed together.
predicates.identified_public_need: The acquiring authority identified a public need that the project was intended to serve.

members.legal_issue: A court does not substitute its own assessment of individual parcels for the government’s assessment of the land needed for a phased public project when no mala fides are alleged.
material_facts: Some owners argued that their plots were separated from the main proposed market area by a road, were not immediately needed, and could be excluded because other land was sufficient.
The government explained that the plots were needed for access and that the market was planned for development in phases, with future expansion in view.
The owners did not allege mala fides, and the Court considered the proposed project’s phased development and access requirements.
members.legal_principle: The Court will not substitute its judgment for the project authorities’ assessment of which parcels are necessary to a phased public development scheme where the record supports access or future-development needs and mala fides are not alleged.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to decide that the plots were unnecessary or that the remaining land was sufficient, and dismissed the challenges to their inclusion.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and parcel_selection_is_challenged and no_mala_fides_are_alleged and (parcel_needed_for_access or future_project_expansion_is_planned)

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government pursued an acquisition of land.
predicates.parcel_selection_is_challenged: An owner argued that the owner’s particular parcel was unnecessary for the public project.
predicates.no_mala_fides_are_alleged: The owner did not allege that the authorities acted with mala fides in selecting the parcel.
predicates.parcel_needed_for_access: The authorities’ project plan required the parcel to provide access to the development.
predicates.future_project_expansion_is_planned: The project was planned in phases with future development in view.

members.legal_issue: A transferee who purchases property for value in good faith and without notice of an earlier contract is protected from specific performance of that contract against the transferee.
material_facts: The transferees obtained an encumbrance certificate and made inquiries before agreeing to purchase part of the property.
The earlier sale agreement was unregistered and was not disclosed by the encumbrance certificate.
The transferees entered into a subsequent sale agreement, obtained a registered sale deed, and paid consideration for the property.
The Court found that the transferees purchased for value in good faith and without notice of the earlier contract.
members.legal_principle: Section 19(b) of the Specific Relief Act protects a transferee for value who has paid the money in good faith and without notice of the original contract. The Court relied on that provision and found its requirements satisfied on the evidence.
members.conclusion: The transferees were protected as bona fide purchasers, and specific performance of the earlier contract could not be enforced against them.

predicates.specific_performance_claim_against_trans: A plaintiff sought specific performance of an earlier property contract against a person who later acquired the property.
predicates.transferee_acquired_for_value: The later transferee acquired the property in exchange for value and paid consideration.
predicates.transferee_acted_in_good_faith_without_n: The later transferee acted in good faith and had no notice of the earlier contract when acquiring the property.

members.legal_issue: A subsequent transferee who paid value in good faith and without notice of an earlier agreement to sell is protected from specific performance of that agreement.
material_facts: The owner agreed to sell the property to the claimant, and the time for completing the sale was later extended.
Before the extended deadline, the owner sold the property in separate transactions, and the later purchaser acquired the entire interest for value.
The evidence supported the finding that the owner was in financial need and sold in separate transactions for less than the price agreed with the claimant.
The purchaser’s father and guardian had occupied the property as a tenant before the purchase, with that account supported by evidence of an earlier usufructuary mortgage and possession.
The claimant’s evidence that the purchaser or his guardian knew of the earlier agreement was found unreliable, and the guardian’s denial of knowledge was not challenged in cross-examination.
members.legal_principle: Section 19(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits specific performance against a person claiming under a contracting party by a later title, except a transferee for value who paid in good faith and without notice of the original contract. The subsequent transferee initially bears the burden of proving the exception: Bhup Narain Singh v. Gokul Chand Mahraj, AIR 1934 PC 68. Knowledge of facts that would put a transferee on inquiry, where an inquiry would disclose the earlier agreement, amounts to notice: Mohammad Aslam Khan v. Neraze Shah, AIR 1932 PC 228. Once both sides have led evidence, the dispute is decided on the evidence as a whole. Dr. Govindas v. Smt. Shantibai, AIR 1972 SC 1520, was distinguished as depending on its own circumstances.
members.conclusion: The finding that the subsequent purchaser was a purchaser for value without notice was supported by the evidence and was not set aside. Specific performance could therefore not be enforced against that purchaser. The appeal was dismissed, subject to the purchaser’s voluntary additional payment to the claimant in full and final satisfaction of the damages claim, in addition to the damages already decreed against the original seller.

rule.if: specific_performance_appeal and purchaser_paid_value and seller_resold_in_parts_under_financial_pressure and occupancy_as_tenant_preceded_purchase and no_credible_evidence_of_notice

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a claim for specific performance of an earlier agreement to sell against a later transferee.
predicates.purchaser_paid_value: The later purchaser paid consideration to acquire the property.
predicates.seller_resold_in_parts_under_financial_p: The seller resold the property in separate transactions while under financial pressure, for less than the amount agreed with the earlier claimant.
predicates.occupancy_as_tenant_preceded_purchase: The purchaser or the purchaser’s representative had occupied the property as a tenant before the purchase.
predicates.no_credible_evidence_of_notice: The evidence did not credibly establish that the purchaser or the purchaser’s representative knew of the earlier agreement or of facts that would lead an inquiry to disclose it.

members.legal_issue: A family arrangement does not require proof that the participants actually held antecedent title where they asserted claims to rights and the arrangement recognized those claims rather than treating one participant as the sole owner transferring property to the others.
material_facts: The appellant claimed that the properties were his self-acquired property, while the plaintiff claimed a share in them.

Evidence indicated that the landed property had been purchased with the mother’s money, but the document treated the property as joint property of the three brothers and did not recognize any brother as its sole owner.
The arrangement allocated rights and enjoyment among the brothers rather than recording a transfer from a recognized sole owner.
members.legal_principle: The Court explained Sahu Madho Das v. Mukhand Ram as allowing the parties’ antecedent title to be assumed and defined by their arrangement; it distinguished a case in which others receive property by transfer from a participant whose sole ownership they recognize.
members.conclusion: The Court held that actual antecedent title did not have to be established; a claim to such a right was sufficient in the circumstances, and the arrangement did not operate as a transfer by a sole owner.

rule.if: family_property_arrangement_dispute and participants_assert_antecedent_rights and arrangement_recognizes_shared_claims and no_sole_owner_transfer

predicates.family_property_arrangement_dispute: The proceeding concerns an arrangement among family participants about rights in property.
predicates.participants_assert_antecedent_rights: The participants assert claims to rights in the property predating or underlying the arrangement.
predicates.arrangement_recognizes_shared_claims: The arrangement recognizes or defines the participants’ competing or shared claims rather than treating one as the sole owner.
predicates.no_sole_owner_transfer: The arrangement does not recognize one participant as sole owner and provide for that participant to transfer property to the others.

members.legal_issue: A family arrangement may recognize one member’s claim to the whole property and provide for the transfer of allotted portions to other members, subject to the transfer formalities applicable when the arrangement was made.
material_facts: The matriarch had asserted an absolute claim to the properties, while the daughters and grandsons later claimed separate absolute ownership of allotted portions.
The daughters accepted the division and received allotted properties; the grandsons received separate properties while they were minors.
The arrangement was made orally in 1875, when the applicable law did not require a writing for the transfer and the later registration requirement did not apply in the absence of a writing.
members.legal_principle: Ordinarily, a family arrangement acknowledges and defines antecedent titles, with each participant giving up claims to property allotted to others; no conveyance is then needed because the arrangement recognizes the title as already residing in the recipient. The Court extended the principle, in the absence of fraud, to an arrangement in which members relinquish claims and accept gifts or transfers from the family member asserting the whole title. In that situation, transfer formalities must be observed; here, the arrangement predated the Transfer of Property Act and no writing was required, so the Registration Act did not apply. The Court referred to and distinguished Rani Mewa Kuwar v. Rani Hulas Kuwar, [1874] 1 I.A. 157; Khunni Lal v. Gobind Krishna Narain, [1911] 38 I.A. 87; and Ramsumran Prasad v. Shyam Kumari, [1922] 49 I.A. 348.
members.conclusion: The Court upheld the arrangement as sufficient to pass title: the daughters’ allotted interests arose under the family arrangement, and the oral arrangement was sufficient for the transfers made in 1875.

rule.if: family_arrangement_in_property_dispute and one_member_claimed_whole_title and other_members_accepted_allocated_properties and arrangement_was_oral and applicable_law_required_no_writing

predicates.family_arrangement_in_property_dispute: Family members settled competing claims to property through an arrangement allocating separate portions.
predicates.one_member_claimed_whole_title: One family member asserted ownership of the whole property before making allocations to other members.
predicates.other_members_accepted_allocated_propert: Other family members accepted the properties allotted to them in return for giving up claims to other portions.
predicates.arrangement_was_oral: The family members made the arrangement orally rather than in a written instrument.
predicates.applicable_law_required_no_writing: The law applicable when the arrangement was made did not require a writing to transfer the property.

members.legal_issue: Property held by a religious head is not endowed merely because the head acquired it while holding office or failed to distinguish it in documents from endowed property.
material_facts: The successive heads systematically conducted a money-lending business and accumulated property.
They described themselves in property documents as absolute owners and transferred property, including to members of their spiritual community, for consideration or in recognition of claims.
The evidence established little endowed property as a nucleus and did not establish that the disputed properties at issue had been dedicated or given for a charitable purpose.
The Court found that 15 items, including the building used by the institution, were institution property; it could not find that the other properties were not the personal property of the head.
members.legal_principle: The character of property depends on evidence of dedication or endowment; a religious head is legally capable of holding personal property. The Court relied on Parama Nand v. Nihal Chand, 65 I.A. 252, and Raghbir Lala v. Mohammad Said, A.I.R. 1943 P.C. 7, for the principles that succession from guru to disciple does not itself make property religious and religious profession does not make a person incapable of holding property. A head may endow personal property, but the mere absence of a distinction in property documents does not prove dedication where the evidence shows personal ownership and dealings as owner.
members.conclusion: A head could endow personally acquired property, but the evidence did not establish that the disputed properties beyond the 15 identified items had become institution property. The other properties were personal unless a particular item was shown to be subject to an endowment or a gift for a charitable purpose.

rule.if: property_character_is_disputed and mahant_conducted_money_lending_business and mahant_asserted_absolute_ownership and mahant_dealt_with_property_as_owner and specific_endowment_not_proved_for_property

predicates.property_character_is_disputed: The parties dispute whether property held by a religious head belongs personally to the head or to the religious institution.
predicates.mahant_conducted_money_lending_business: The religious head conducted a money-lending or similar business from which property was accumulated.
predicates.mahant_asserted_absolute_ownership: The religious head described or otherwise held himself out as the absolute owner of the property.
predicates.mahant_dealt_with_property_as_owner: The religious head transferred or otherwise dealt with the property as an owner.
predicates.specific_endowment_not_proved_for_proper: The evidence does not establish that the particular property was dedicated to the institution or given for a charitable purpose.

members.legal_issue: Transfers of property held personally by a religious head cannot be invalidated as transfers of institution property when the property is not proved to be endowed.
material_facts: The appeals concerned transfers made by a religious head that had been challenged as transfers of institution property.
The Court found that only 15 items were institution property and could not find that the other properties were not personal property.
The transfers of the properties in that latter class were the subject of the appeals.
members.legal_principle: A transfer cannot be challenged as an alienation of institution property when the property is not shown to belong to the institution; the Court upheld the transfers of the class of properties treated as personal. The Court did not thereby decide the validity of transfers of property found to be institution property.
members.conclusion: The transfers of the properties not established to be institution property were upheld so far as they were before the Court in the appeals.

predicates.appeal_challenges_invalidation_of_proper: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a decision that invalidated a transfer of property.
predicates.property_not_proved_to_be_institution_pr: The evidence does not establish that the transferred property belongs to the religious institution.

members.legal_issue: A land acquisition officer lacks authority to allot acquired land in lieu of monetary compensation under the statutory award-making and compensation-payment powers.
material_facts: Land was acquired for a public purpose.
In a later award, the acquisition officer deducted the value of plots allotted to the landowners in lieu of compensation.
The landowners sought to enforce the allotment of acquired land as part of the award.
members.legal_principle: Sections 11 and 18 confine the acquisition officer’s award and the reference court’s inquiry to matters such as the area acquired, compensation, and its apportionment. Section 31(3) permits, with the appropriate government’s sanction, an arrangement involving other land in exchange for compensation only for a person having a limited interest in the acquired land. Section 31(4) preserves the power to make arrangements with a person competent to contract but does not authorize allotment of acquired land in lieu of compensation. The acquisition scheme, including Sections 4, 6, 16 and 48, does not permit the officer to create a right to reclaim part of acquired land in a way that defeats the public purpose. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The acquisition officer had no power to allot the acquired land in lieu of compensation. The limited power under Section 31(3) to arrange for other land applied only to a person with a limited interest in the acquired land and required prior government sanction; Section 31(4) did not enlarge that power.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land and the determination or payment of compensation for it.
predicates.acquired_land_allotted_instead_of_money: The acquisition officer allotted land that was itself acquired rather than paying monetary compensation for the acquired interest.

members.legal_issue: The acquisition authority cannot award acquired land as compensation to ordinary owners or their purchasers, sub-awardees, or nominees under the limited power to provide land in lieu of compensation.
material_facts: The land acquisition officer included allotments of plots in the award to former owners, sub-awardees, or nominees in addition to compensation.
The respondents claimed plots as purchasers or nominees of a former owner, rather than as holders of a limited interest in land.
The respondents argued that statutory provisions and acquisition rules authorized the allotments and made the earlier decision in Radhey Shyam inapplicable.
members.legal_principle: Section 31(3) of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953 permits, with appropriate government sanction, the allotment of other land or remission of revenue in lieu of money compensation to a person with a limited interest in acquired land. Rule 31 guides that limited power and does not permit forcing an ordinary owner to take land instead of cash. Rule 36 concerns excess land acquired for a company. Neither rule authorizes allotment of the acquired land to ordinary owners or their purchasers, sub-awardees, or nominees. The Court applied Jaipur Development Authority v. Radhey Shyam and held that omission to discuss these rules did not undermine its reasoning.
members.conclusion: The land acquisition officer had no authority to make those allotments. The limited power to provide land in lieu of money compensation applies to persons with limited interests in the acquired land, and the cited rules did not make the earlier decision per incuriam.

predicates.acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns land acquired for a public purpose and compensation for that acquisition.
predicates.ordinary_owner_claims_land_instead_of_co: An ordinary owner seeks acquired land in place of money compensation rather than relying on a limited interest in the land.
predicates.claimant_is_owner_purchaser_sub_awardee_: The person seeking the allotment is an owner, purchaser, sub-awardee, or nominee, rather than a holder of a limited interest in the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: Mortgage money already paid before a conveyance is not added to the stamp-duty consideration as unpaid mortgage money.
material_facts: Before the conveyance was executed, the purchasers had paid a substantial part of the mortgage debt to the bank.
The amount in dispute had been paid by the date of the conveyance.
members.legal_principle: Section 24’s Explanation deems unpaid mortgage money to be part of the sale consideration where the sale is subject to the mortgage; it does not add mortgage money already paid by the date of conveyance. The phrase “subject to a mortgage or other encumbrance” qualifies the sale, not the property. The Court relied on U.K. Janardhan Rao v. Secretary of State and Waman Martand Bhalerao v. The Commissioner, Central Division, and noted that the Stamp Act, as a taxing statute, is to be construed strictly.
members.conclusion: The amount paid before the conveyance was not includible under the mortgage-money explanation to section 24.

predicates.conveyance_stamp_duty_case: A dispute concerns the stamp duty payable on a conveyance.
predicates.mortgage_money_paid_before_conveyance: The mortgage money at issue was paid before the conveyance was executed.

members.legal_issue: An unpaid mortgage amount is not added to stamp-duty consideration where the purchaser is not liable for it, the vendors undertake to pay it, and the property is conveyed free of that charge.
material_facts: A balance of the mortgage debt remained unpaid when the conveyance was executed.
The vendors undertook to pay that balance, and the purchasers did not assume liability for it.
The conveyance provided that the property was sold free from the charge.
The balance formed part of the price allocated to items other than the immovable property conveyed.
members.legal_principle: Under section 24’s Explanation, unpaid mortgage money is deemed part of the consideration where the sale is subject to the mortgage. Article 23 applies to consideration for the conveyance. Because the purchasers were not liable for the balance, the conveyance was free of the charge, and the amount related to other items, it was not added to the consideration for the immovable property. The Court applied the strict construction of taxing statutes.
members.conclusion: The unpaid balance was not includible in the stamp-duty consideration for the immovable property conveyed.

members.legal_issue: A distinct, expedited procedure for correcting revenue records during a compulsory consolidation scheme does not deny equal protection when it provides notice, an opportunity to object and present evidence, and an appeal, and the procedural distinction is reasonably connected to the scheme’s purpose.
material_facts: The challenged procedure applied to villages undergoing consolidation, unlike the procedure for other villages under the general revenue law.
The consolidation officer gave affected persons notice of proposed corrections, heard objections, and allowed them to present evidence.
An appeal was available from the initial correction order.
The petitioners objected that the consolidation procedure differed from the ordinary revenue procedure and barred recourse to civil and revenue courts.
The consolidation scheme was intended to combine scattered plots into compact holdings and was considered to require completion within a reasonable time.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits a procedural classification based on an intelligible differentia reasonably connected to the legislation’s objective. In the circumstances of consolidation, an expeditious procedure is justified if it is not arbitrary or lacking in the essentials of natural justice. The Court relied on sections 7 to 12 and 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, the applicable rules, and the contrast with the U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901. No earlier judicial decisions were relied upon for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The procedure under Chapter II, read with the rules, did not violate Article 14; the challenge to it failed.

rule.if: consolidation_proceeding and (affected_persons_receive_notice and affected_persons_can_present_objections_and_evidence and appeal_is_available) and procedure_is_designed_for_timely_completion and procedural_distinction_advances_consolidation_objective

predicates.consolidation_proceeding: The challenged procedure is used in a proceeding to consolidate agricultural holdings.
predicates.affected_persons_receive_notice: The authority gives notice of proposed record corrections to persons affected by them.
predicates.affected_persons_can_present_objections_: Affected persons may object to the proposed corrections, be heard, and present evidence.
predicates.appeal_is_available: A person aggrieved by the initial correction order may appeal it.
predicates.procedure_is_designed_for_timely_complet: The procedure is structured to complete the consolidation proceeding within a reasonable time.
predicates.procedural_distinction_advances_consolid: The different procedure is reasonably connected to completing consolidation and achieving its agricultural benefits.

members.legal_issue: Expedited procedures for settling principles and proposals in a consolidation scheme, including making an arbitrator’s title decision final and staying related court proceedings, do not deny equal protection when the procedures are reasonably connected to completing consolidation in a reasonable time.
material_facts: The Act provided for publication of statements of principles and proposals, invited objections, and provided for hearings and decisions by consolidation officers.
Disputed questions of title could be referred through a civil judge to an arbitrator, who heard the parties and received oral and documentary evidence.
The arbitrator’s decision was final, and proceedings concerning title to the same land in ordinary courts were stayed.
The petitioners objected that the provisions limited ordinary court jurisdiction and differed from the protections available to tenure-holders outside consolidation.
The procedures were intended to avoid delays that could prevent completion of the consolidation scheme.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits a classification with a rational basis and a nexus to the legislation’s objective. The need to complete consolidation within a reasonable time can justify procedures that limit ordinary appeals and court proceedings, including final arbitration of title disputes. The Court relied on sections 14 to 22 and 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act and the applicable rules. No earlier judicial decisions were relied upon for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The provisions of Chapter III did not violate Article 14; the challenge to them failed.

rule.if: consolidation_proceeding and objections_to_principles_and_proposals_are_heard and title_disputes_receive_a_hearing_and_evidence and finality_and_stays_prevent_delay and procedural_limits_advance_consolidation_objective

predicates.consolidation_proceeding: The challenged procedure is used in a proceeding to consolidate agricultural holdings.
predicates.objections_to_principles_and_proposals_a: Persons affected by proposed consolidation principles and land allocations may object and have those objections heard.
predicates.title_disputes_receive_a_hearing_and_evi: The procedure for resolving disputed land titles includes a hearing for the parties and consideration of evidence.
predicates.finality_and_stays_prevent_delay: The resolution is made final and related ordinary court proceedings are stayed to prevent delay in consolidation.
predicates.procedural_limits_advance_consolidation_: The procedural limits are reasonably connected to completing the consolidation scheme in a reasonable time.

members.legal_issue: Income from property forming part of an impartible estate and transferred by its holder to his wife is included in the holder’s total income when the transfer does not fall within the statutory exceptions.
material_facts: The assessee was assessed as an individual and held an impartible estate.
He directly transferred two premises forming part of the estate to his wife for life as a supplementary maintenance grant.
The transfer was without consideration and was not connected with an agreement to live apart.
The income from the premises was included in the assessee’s total income in the tax assessment.
members.legal_principle: Under section 9(4)(a), the holder of an impartible estate is deemed to be the individual owner of its properties for determining taxable income. That fiction must be given effect when applying section 16(3)(a)(iii), which includes a wife’s income arising from assets transferred by her husband otherwise than for adequate consideration or in connection with an agreement to live apart. Sections 3 and 4, the definition of total income in section 2(xv), and the heads of income in section 6 support treating income from a source as part of total income rather than taxing it separately by head. Section 27(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 made explicit what was implicit in section 9(4)(a). The Court relied on Baijnath Prasad Singh v. Tej Bali, Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Proyad Kumari Devi, and Commissioner of Income-tax v. Dewan Bahadur Dewan Krishna Kishore on the character and incidents of an impartible estate.
members.conclusion: The income from the transferred premises was includible in the assessee’s total income under section 16(3)(a)(iii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.

rule.if: tax_assessment_appeal and holder_of_impartible_estate and transferred_property_part_of_estate and direct_transfer_to_wife and transfer_without_adequate_consideration and not transfer_connected_to_separation_agreement

predicates.tax_assessment_appeal: The proceeding concerns an appeal arising from a tax assessment.
predicates.holder_of_impartible_estate: The taxpayer held an impartible estate.
predicates.transferred_property_part_of_estate: The property transferred by the taxpayer formed part of the impartible estate.
predicates.direct_transfer_to_wife: The taxpayer directly transferred the property to his wife.
predicates.transfer_without_adequate_consideration: The taxpayer made the transfer without adequate consideration.
predicates.transfer_connected_to_separation_agreeme: The transfer was connected with an agreement between the spouses to live apart.
predicates.transferred_property_income_included_in_: Income arising from the transferred property is included in the holder’s total income.

members.legal_issue: Income from property transferred by a holder of an impartible estate to his wife and included in his total income is taken into account when computing the annual value of his residential house under the applicable percentage-based rule.
material_facts: The assessee was assessed as an individual and held an impartible estate.
He transferred two premises from the estate directly to his wife without consideration and not in connection with an agreement to live apart.
The income from those premises was includible in his total income.
The assessment also required computation of the annual value of the assessee’s residential house under the first proviso to section 9(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
members.legal_principle: The first proviso to section 9(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 required the annual value of the assessee’s residential house to be computed by reference to the prescribed percentage of his total income. Because income from the transferred premises was included in that total income under section 16(3)(a)(iii), it was also included in the income base used for that computation.
members.conclusion: The annual value of the assessee’s residential house had to be computed by reference to his total income, including the income from the premises transferred to his wife.

rule.if: tax_assessment_appeal and taxpayer_has_residential_house_annual_value_computed and holder_of_impartible_estate and transferred_property_part_of_estate and direct_transfer_to_wife and transfer_without_adequate_consideration and not transfer_connected_to_separation_agreement
