members.legal_issue: A closed mill can come within the development scheme even without a sickness determination by the specialist board, but a mill claimed to be sick cannot use the special reconstruction provision without referral to that board.
material_facts: The development rule referred to sick and/or closed mills, but some closed mills had not been referred to the specialist board responsible for sick-company proceedings.
The rule’s purpose included reviving or rehabilitating closed mills, and lawful closure could be verified through State processes.
The specialist board, rather than the State planning authorities, was responsible for determining sickness under the sick-company legislation.
members.legal_principle: Purposive and common-sense construction may be used to avoid an interpretation that makes a valuable asset sterile or creates an irrational distinction. The Court relied on the wording and purpose of regulation 58, the Industrial Disputes Act provisions governing lawful closure, and the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, including sections 3, 15, 17, and 32. It also referred to the common-sense construction principle stated in Halsbury’s Laws of England.
members.conclusion: The reference to sick and/or closed mills was disjunctive: a closed mill could qualify without a board recommendation where none was available. However, the special reconstruction provision did not extend to a sick mill that had not been referred to the board.

predicates.mill_development_proceeding: A proceeding concerns the development or redevelopment of mill land under a scheme intended to address mill closure or revival.
predicates.mill_is_lawfully_closed: The mill has been closed in accordance with the applicable legal requirements.
predicates.no_sickness_determination_is_available: The mill has not been referred to the specialist body authorised to determine sickness, so no such determination or recommendation is available.

members.legal_issue: A mill cannot rely on the special reconstruction provision as a sick mill unless its sickness has been determined through the statutory specialist process.
material_facts: The special provision applied to mills described as sick, closed, or requiring modernisation.
The company associated with the mill had not been referred to the specialist body under the sick-company legislation.
The planning authorities lacked statutory authority to determine whether a company was sick or the extent of its sickness.
members.legal_principle: The sick-company legislation is a special statute that governs the determination of sickness and the measures for dealing with it. The State and planning authorities cannot make that determination in place of the body authorised by the statute. The Court relied on the statutory scheme, including sections 3, 15, 17, and 32 of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985.
members.conclusion: The special reconstruction provision did not apply to a sick mill that had not been referred to the specialist body.

predicates.special_reconstruction_proceeding: A proceeding concerns access to a special rule permitting reconstruction of mill structures.
predicates.mill_relies_on_sick_status: The mill seeks the special rule on the basis that it is sick.
predicates.no_specialist_referral: The company or mill has not been referred to the statutory body authorised to determine sickness.

members.legal_issue: The development regulation and the State’s clarification were not shown to be unconstitutional, contrary to the parent planning law, or inconsistent with sustainable and planned development.
material_facts: The State used a statutory process inviting objections and considered reports from planning and expert committees before amending the regulation.
The amendment addressed the failure of the earlier scheme to achieve revival, rehabilitation, or modernisation of mills.
The challenge did not establish that designated green areas had been removed or that the development plan’s basic character had changed.
The regulation provided for land sharing, public housing, open-space measures, and controls on development, and environmental assessment requirements remained applicable where required.
members.legal_principle: Subordinate legislation is presumed constitutional but may be set aside if it is arbitrary, unreasonable, outside the parent Act, or inconsistent with legislative purpose. Environmental protection and sustainable development must be balanced with other public interests and the legislative purpose. The Court relied on sections 22, 37, and 159 of the MRTP Act; Articles 14, 21, 48-A, and 51-A(g) of the Constitution; Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) 5 SCC 647; N.D. Jayal v. Union of India (2004) 9 SCC 362; and T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (2002) 10 SCC 606. It also applied the principles in Sharma Transport v. Government of Andhra Pradesh (2002) 2 SCC 188 and Secretary, Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilizers v. Cipla Ltd. (2003) 7 SCC 1.
members.conclusion: The Court upheld the regulation and clarification against the constitutional and statutory challenges and held that they were not contrary to sustainable or planned development.

rule.if: challenge_to_planning_regulation and statutory_consultation_occurred and no_manifest_arbitrariness_is_shown and no_basic_plan_character_change_is_shown

predicates.challenge_to_planning_regulation: A proceeding challenges a subordinate rule governing land use, development, or planning.
predicates.statutory_consultation_occurred: The rule was made after the prescribed process for inviting and considering objections and suggestions.
predicates.no_manifest_arbitrariness_is_shown: The challenger has not established manifest arbitrariness, unreasonableness, or disregard of relevant environmental and public interests.
predicates.no_basic_plan_character_change_is_shown: The challenger has not established that the amendment altered the basic character of the development plan.

members.legal_issue: A State’s clarification of a planning regulation is not binding on courts, but it is not invalid under the planning statute when it expresses an interpretation already permitted by the regulation and does not alter the development plan’s basic character.
material_facts: The State issued a clarification concerning how the amended mill-development regulation should be read.
Approvals under the State’s interpretation had been granted before the clarification was issued.
The Court independently interpreted the regulation and found that the State’s interpretation was possible to a substantial extent, though it did not accept every aspect of it.
The amendment and clarification did not change the identified reservations or the basic character of the development plan.
members.legal_principle: An executive interpretation may assist a court but cannot bind it or prevent independent judicial interpretation. Whether a planning modification changes the character of a plan depends on whether it alters the plan’s basic features when considered as a whole. The Court relied on section 37 of the MRTP Act, Forward Construction Co. v. Prabhat Mandal (1986) 1 SCC 100, Puran Lal v. President of India (1962) 1 SCR 688, and the principles concerning contemporaneous executive construction in Municipal Corporation for City of Pune v. Bharat Forge Co. Ltd. (1995) 3 SCC 434.
members.conclusion: The clarification was neither ultra vires the planning statute nor unconstitutional, although the State’s interpretation was persuasive rather than binding on the courts.

predicates.state_clarification_of_planning_rule: A State authority issues a clarification about how a planning rule should be interpreted.
predicates.clarification_is_consistent_with_permiss: The clarification expresses an interpretation that the rule can reasonably bear when read as a whole.
predicates.no_basic_plan_character_change_is_shown: The challenger has not established that the clarification changed the development plan’s basic character.

members.legal_issue: A landlord may not continue parallel civil-court and rent-controller proceedings for possession when the pending rent-controller proceeding remains maintainable.
material_facts: The eviction petition remained maintainable before the Rent Controller after the amendment because it was saved as a pending proceeding.
The landlord had also filed a civil suit seeking possession of the same premises.
The landlord was pursuing both proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Because the saved proceeding remained within the Rent Controller’s jurisdiction, the landlord could not continue a parallel proceeding for possession under the general law. The Court ordered the landlord to withdraw one of the two proceedings.
members.conclusion: The landlord could not continue both proceedings and was directed to withdraw one of them.

predicates.saved_rent_controller_eviction_case: An eviction proceeding remained maintainable before the Rent Controller after a legislative change because it had been pending when the change took effect.
predicates.parallel_civil_possession_case: The landlord also brought a civil-court proceeding seeking possession of the same premises.

members.legal_issue: Possession proceedings should not continue in parallel with a pending civil suit concerning possession or title to the same property when the civil court can grant protective relief concerning that property.
material_facts: A civil suit seeking relief concerning title and possession of the property was filed before the possession proceedings began.
The civil court had ordered the parties to maintain the status quo and could grant further protection concerning the property.
The parties’ statements established that both proceedings concerned the same property, and the possession proceedings had not resulted in a final order.
The Magistrate discontinued the possession proceedings because the civil court was already dealing with the matter and had granted protective relief.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, parallel possession proceedings should not continue when a civil suit concerns possession or declaration of title to the same property and the civil court can grant relief protecting it. The Court applied Ram Sumer Puri Mahant v. State of U.P. and distinguished Jhummamal alias Devandas v. State of Madhya Pradesh, which concerned a civil suit filed after a final order in the possession proceedings. The principle avoids multiplicity of litigation and recognizes that civil court orders bind the Magistrate on the matter before it.
members.conclusion: The Magistrate was right to discontinue the possession proceedings, and the High Court’s order requiring them to resume was set aside.

rule.if: parallel_possession_proceeding and pending_civil_property_suit and same_property_in_both_proceedings and civil_suit_concerns_possession_or_title and civil_court_can_protect_property and no_final_possession_order

predicates.parallel_possession_proceeding: A summary proceeding to determine possession is underway while a civil property suit is pending.
predicates.pending_civil_property_suit: A civil suit concerning the property is pending.
predicates.same_property_in_both_proceedings: The civil suit and the possession proceeding concern the same property.
predicates.civil_suit_concerns_possession_or_title: The civil suit seeks a determination concerning possession or title to the property.
predicates.civil_court_can_protect_property: The civil court can grant relief protecting the property while the suit is pending.
predicates.no_final_possession_order: The possession proceeding has not resulted in a final order.

members.legal_issue: The law governing a concealment penalty in a reassessment is the law in force when the original return containing the concealment was filed, rather than the law in force when a return in response to reassessment notice was filed.
material_facts: The assessee filed original returns that omitted profits from land sales.
After reassessment notices were issued, the assessee filed returns again, still omitting those profits, after the penalty law had changed.
The reassessments included the omitted income, and penalty proceedings were initiated for the concealment.
members.legal_principle: Under section 271(1)(c), as interpreted in Brij Mohan v. CIT, the applicable law is the law in force when the offending return is filed. In a case involving multiple returns, the original return, if any, is the relevant return for this purpose. The Court adopted the reasoning in CIT v. S.S.K.G. Arthanariswamy Chettiar and Addl. CIT v. Joginder Singh, and relied on the principles illustrated by Malbary and Bros. v. CIT, Govindarajulu Iyer v. CIT, and Jagan Mohan Rao’s case. Sections 148 and 139(2) did not make the reassessment return the relevant return for choosing the applicable penalty law.
members.conclusion: The original returns determine the applicable law for the penalty proceedings; the later returns filed in response to reassessment notices do not make the amended penalty law applicable. The appeals were dismissed.

predicates.concealment_penalty_proceeding_in_reasse: Penalty proceedings for concealment were initiated in connection with a reassessment.
predicates.original_return_contained_concealment: The taxpayer's original return omitted income that was later assessed.
predicates.original_return_preceded_penalty_law_cha: The original return was filed before a change in the law governing the measure of the penalty.
predicates.reassessment_return_filed_after_penalty_: The taxpayer filed a return in response to reassessment after the change in the penalty law.

members.legal_issue: A penalty imposed during reassessment may be based on concealment in the original return and original assessment proceedings.
material_facts: The assessee omitted land-sale income from its original returns.
The original assessments were completed without including all the omitted income, and reassessments were later undertaken for the same assessment years.
The penalty proceedings were initiated after reassessment, based on the failure to return the land-sale income.
members.legal_principle: Section 271(1)(c) permits a penalty in reassessment proceedings based on concealment in the original return. Malbary and Bros. v. CIT upheld a penalty imposed in reassessment by reference to the original return, and Govindarajulu Iyer v. CIT supports the same principle. The Court also referred to Jagan Mohan Rao’s case in explaining that reassessment reopens the determination of the correct total income for the year.
members.conclusion: A penalty may be imposed in reassessment proceedings by reference to concealment in the original assessment proceedings.

predicates.concealment_penalty_proceeding_in_reasse: Penalty proceedings for concealment were initiated in connection with a reassessment.
predicates.original_return_contained_concealment: The taxpayer's original return omitted income that was later assessed.
predicates.reassessment_redetermined_income_for_sam: The reassessment redetermined the taxpayer's income for the same tax year covered by the original return.

members.legal_issue: Temporary cultivators alike in relevant respects cannot be treated differently in permanent land allotment solely because their temporary leases began in different periods without a rational connection to the allotment objective.
material_facts: The government established separate permanent-allotment regimes for temporary cultivators whose leases began before and after a cutoff.
The earlier-lease group could receive land up to a higher limit, while the later-lease group could be denied further allotment once its existing holding crossed a lower limit.
Both groups’ temporary leases were cancelled, and neither group could acquire tenancy rights in the leased land.
The record did not establish how long before the cutoff the earlier leases had begun, and the difference in occupation length did not justify the different allotment treatment.
An earlier allotment scheme had not distinguished between the two groups.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 requires a classification to rest on an intelligible basis with a rational nexus to the object sought to be achieved. Sections 15 and 15A of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act did not support the distinction: the proviso to section 15 and section 15A excluded tenancy rights for both groups. Sections 7 and 28 of the Rajasthan Colonisation Act provided the framework for allotment and rulemaking but did not make the groups legally different for this purpose. The court also referred to State v. Ramdhan, AIR 1973 Raj 71, which had struck down rules that treated the family unit differently under allotment schemes made under the same Act.
members.conclusion: The temporal distinction had no rational nexus to the allotment objective. The definition of a landless person in Rule 2(1)(xiii) and Rule 3(2) of the post-cutoff rules were discriminatory and void under Article 14.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_land_allotment_rules and allotment_terms_varied_by_lease_period and both_groups_lacked_tenancy_rights and duration_evidence_missing

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_allotme: The proceeding challenged government rules governing permanent allotment of land on equality grounds.
predicates.allotment_terms_varied_by_lease_period: The government prescribed different allotment eligibility or amounts for temporary cultivators according to when their leases began.
predicates.both_groups_lacked_tenancy_rights: The law prevented both groups of temporary cultivators from acquiring tenancy rights in the leased land.
predicates.duration_evidence_missing: The record did not establish a relevant difference in the length of occupation that could explain the different treatment.

members.legal_issue: Allotment conditions cannot provide materially different benefits to temporary cultivators based on the size of their existing holdings without a rational basis.
material_facts: Under the earlier-lease conditions, a cultivator with more than the basic allotment could retain land up to the ceiling and pay for land above the basic allotment.
A cultivator with less than the basic allotment could receive additional land only to reach the basic allotment and had to pay for the newly allotted land.
The court found no justification for the difference in treatment between cultivators with holdings above and below the basic allotment threshold.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits arbitrary differences in treatment between persons within the relevant class; a classification must have a rational nexus to its objective. The court relied on this equality principle in assessing Condition No. 3. Sections 7 and 28 of the Rajasthan Colonisation Act authorized land grants and rules but did not justify the unequal treatment.
members.conclusion: Condition No. 3 of the earlier-lease conditions was discriminatory and void under Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_allotme: The proceeding challenged government rules governing permanent allotment of land on equality grounds.
predicates.allotment_benefits_varied_by_existing_ho: The allotment conditions gave cultivators different retention or additional-allotment benefits according to the size of their existing holdings.
predicates.no_basis_for_holding_threshold: The government offered no justification for the difference in treatment based on the existing-holding threshold.

members.legal_issue: A statutory provision assigning a forum to decide who is the lawful ryot of a holding after an estate is notified is not confined to disputes about arrears of rent.
material_facts: The disputed lands were in an estate that had been taken over by the government under an abolition and ryotwari-settlement scheme.
The parties made rival claims to be the lawful ryots of the holding.
The governing scheme provided for ryotwari pattas for ryots but, under the narrower interpretation advanced, contained no other mechanism for deciding competing claims by ryots.
members.legal_principle: Statutory interpretation, contextual or otherwise, must further rather than frustrate the statute’s object. Read in light of the scheme’s purpose of conferring ryotwari pattas on ryots and abolishing intermediaries, the provision for determining who is the lawful ryot cannot be restricted to the purposes of the rent-arrears provisions. The Court approved the five-Judge Full Bench decision in I. Munuswami Naidu v. R. Venkata Reddy and rejected Cherukuru Muthayya v. Gadde Gopalakrishnayya to the extent it imposed that restriction; the relevant provisions include Sections 55 and 56(1)(a)–(c), read with Sections 3, 11 and 15 of the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948.
members.conclusion: The provision covers disputes over who is the lawful ryot of a holding generally, and is not limited to identifying a person liable for rent arrears that accrued before the estate was taken over.

predicates.notified_estate: The government had formally notified and taken over an estate under a scheme for abolishing intermediaries and introducing ryotwari settlement.
predicates.lawful_ryot_dispute: Two or more claimants disputed who was the lawful ryot of a holding in the estate.
predicates.ryot_pattta_framework_exists: The governing scheme provided for ryots to obtain ryotwari pattas in respect of qualifying lands.

members.legal_issue: A special statutory forum has exclusive jurisdiction over a dispute assigned to it concerning who is the lawful ryot of a holding after an estate is notified, even when that dispute arises in an eviction proceeding.
material_facts: The appellant sought eviction of the respondents for alleged non-payment of rent, claiming to be their landlord.
The respondents claimed that they and their ancestors had occupancy rights and were the lawful ryots of the land, which was in an estate taken over by the government.
The eviction proceedings therefore raised a dispute over who was the lawful ryot of the holding.
The statute assigned disputes about lawful ryot status after notification to a Settlement Officer, provided an appeal to a special tribunal, and made the tribunal’s decision final.
members.legal_principle: The Act is a self-contained code providing specially constituted tribunals to adjudicate specified disputes arising after notification of an estate. On general principles, those tribunals have exclusive jurisdiction over disputes entrusted to them by the statute. The Court relied on Appanna v. Sriramamurthy and approved I. Munuswami Naidu v. R. Venkata Reddy; Sections 56(1)(c) and 56(2) assign the lawful-ryot dispute to the Settlement Officer and provide for an appeal to the Estates Abolition Tribunal, whose decision is final.
members.conclusion: The Settlement Officer and the special tribunal had exclusive jurisdiction to decide the dispute over lawful ryot status; the eviction proceeding could not determine that issue, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and notified_estate and lawful_ryot_dispute and special_forum_assigned_dispute

predicates.eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking to evict an occupant from land on an asserted landlord-tenant relationship.
predicates.notified_estate: The government had formally notified and taken over the estate containing the land.
predicates.lawful_ryot_dispute: The parties disputed who was the lawful ryot of the holding.
predicates.special_forum_assigned_dispute: The governing scheme assigned disputes of this kind to a specially constituted forum and provided for review by a special tribunal.

members.legal_issue: The limitation period for redeeming a valid oral mortgage begins when the mortgage is created, rather than after a later period of possession or registration.
material_facts: The land was mortgaged orally with possession in 1893 for a sum below Rs. 100.
At the time and in the area concerned, an oral mortgage of this kind was legally permissible and enforceable.
The mortgage imposed no restriction postponing the mortgagors’ right to redeem.
The redemption suit was filed in 1980, more than 60 years after the mortgage was made.
members.legal_principle: The Court approved the Full Bench ruling in Sri Chand v. Nathi and rejected the contrary approach in Inder Singh v. Mst. Kishno, which had wrongly relied on Purushottam Dass v. S.M. Dedouza, concerning an invalid unregistered mortgage made when the Transfer of Property Act applied. Before the relevant provisions of the Transfer of Property Act were extended to the area, a mortgage for less than Rs. 100 could be made orally by delivery of possession, and its lack of registration did not make it invalid or defer limitation. Under Article 148 of the Limitation Act, the applicable period was 60 years from when the right to redeem accrued.
members.conclusion: The mortgage was valid from its creation, so the 60-year limitation period began in 1893 and had expired before the suit was filed; the suit was time-barred.

rule.if: redemption_suit and valid_oral_mortgage and no_redemption_restriction and limitation_period_expired

predicates.redemption_suit: A party filed a suit seeking redemption of a mortgage and recovery of the mortgaged property.
predicates.valid_oral_mortgage: The mortgagor created an enforceable mortgage orally, including by delivering possession where that was legally sufficient.
predicates.no_redemption_restriction: The mortgage did not provide a valid restriction postponing the mortgagor’s right to redeem.
predicates.limitation_period_expired: The applicable limitation period had elapsed before the redemption suit was filed.

members.legal_issue: The right to redeem a valid mortgage accrues from its creation unless the mortgage imposes a valid restriction, and it does not await tender of payment, communication that the mortgage has been satisfied, or the enactment of a later summary redemption procedure.
material_facts: The mortgage was validly created in 1893 and contained no restriction postponing redemption.
The mortgagors had not tendered the mortgage amount, and the mortgagees had not communicated that the mortgage had been satisfied.
The mortgagors relied on the Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act, 1913 to argue that the right to redeem had not accrued earlier.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 61(a) of Part V of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, the period runs from when the right to redeem or recover possession accrues. The right accrues when a valid mortgage is made unless restricted by law or by a valid term of the mortgage. C. Beepathumma v. V.S. Kadambolithaya involved a specific restriction and did not support postponing accrual here. The Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act, 1913 provided powers and a summary procedure for redemption; it did not alter the limitation period. The Court also noted that, even if time were counted from that Act, the limitation period had expired before the suit.
members.conclusion: The right to redeem accrued when the valid mortgage was created; neither the absence of tender or communication nor the 1913 Act postponed the start of limitation.

predicates.redemption_suit: A party filed a suit seeking redemption of a mortgage and recovery of the mortgaged property.
predicates.valid_mortgage: The parties created a legally enforceable mortgage.
predicates.no_redemption_restriction: The mortgage did not provide a valid restriction postponing the mortgagor’s right to redeem.

members.legal_issue: Combining adjacent allotted plots and constructing a dwelling on each does not, without more, breach a lease condition prohibiting subdivision, more than one dwelling house on a plot, or commercial use.
material_facts: The lease-cum-sale agreement prohibited subdividing a plot, constructing more than one dwelling house on it, and using any part of the building as a shop, warehouse, or for specified commercial purposes.
The owners had sought permission to amalgamate their adjacent plots, but the request was rejected; the Court found no subdivision of either plot.
There was no finding that more than one building had been constructed on either plot or that any part of a building was being used commercially.
members.legal_principle: The Court interpreted clause 4 of the lease-cum-sale agreement according to its stated prohibitions: subdivision, construction of more than one dwelling house on a plot, or specified commercial use. Amalgamation, even if it occurred, was not itself one of those prohibited acts.
members.conclusion: The alleged plot amalgamation did not violate the relevant lease condition, and the facts did not establish a breach through subdivision, multiple dwelling houses on a plot, or commercial use.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_order and alleged_lease_breach_based_on_plot_combination and plots_not_subdivided and one_dwelling_per_plot and no_commercial_use_established

predicates.appeal_from_writ_order: A party appeals an order finding a breach of a site-related lease condition.
predicates.alleged_lease_breach_based_on_plot_combi: The alleged breach rests on combining or treating adjacent plots as a combined property.
predicates.plots_not_subdivided: The owners did not divide either plot into separate plots.
predicates.one_dwelling_per_plot: No more than one dwelling house was constructed on each plot.
predicates.no_commercial_use_established: The record does not establish that any part of the building was put to a prohibited commercial use.

members.legal_issue: A multi-storeyed dwelling is not prohibited by a lease condition limiting a plot to one dwelling house, provided the building is used for human habitation and complies with the applicable building requirements.
material_facts: The lease-cum-sale agreement defined a dwelling house as a building constructed wholly for human habitation and did not prohibit multi-storeyed construction.
The municipal authority stated that the modified plan was for residential use and that an occupancy certificate would be withheld unless the building complied with the plan and building regulations.
The buildings were incomplete, and commercial use had not been established.
members.legal_principle: The Court construed clause 4 of the lease-cum-sale agreement as regulating the number and use of dwelling houses on a plot, not the number of storeys in a dwelling. Construction remained subject to the sanctioned plan and building regulations and bye-laws. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The lease condition did not prohibit a multi-storeyed building used wholly for human habitation; no objection could be taken to such construction if it complied with the lease and applicable building regulations and bye-laws.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_order and multi_storeyed_building and building_used_for_human_habitation and building_complies_with_applicable_requirements

predicates.appeal_from_writ_order: A party appeals an order challenging the permissibility of a building under a site-related lease.
predicates.multi_storeyed_building: The building has more than one storey.
predicates.building_used_for_human_habitation: The building is used wholly as a dwelling for human habitation rather than for prohibited commercial purposes.
predicates.building_complies_with_applicable_requir: The building conforms to the applicable approved plan and building requirements.

members.legal_issue: Incidental benefits to an organization's members do not prevent its public-utility purpose from being charitable.
material_facts: The organization's work could benefit people engaged in trade and commerce, including its members.
Its stated objects extended to the commercial interests of the country and were not confined to benefits for its members.
The organization's income and property could not be distributed to members as profit.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, does not exclude a public-utility purpose merely because members also benefit in carrying it out; the question is whether personal benefit is so substantial that it cannot be disregarded. The Court relied on Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Yorkshire Agricultural Society and The Institution of Civil Engineers v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue.
members.conclusion: The possibility that members might benefit incidentally did not prevent the organization from being established for charitable purposes.

predicates.income_tax_exemption_claim: The taxpayer sought exemption from income tax for income derived from property.
predicates.public_benefit_is_primary: The organization's main purpose was directed to benefiting the public or a section of the public, rather than serving its members alone.
predicates.member_benefits_are_incidental: Any benefits members received arose incidentally from the organization's pursuit of its public purpose.

members.legal_issue: Ancillary advocacy concerning legislation does not defeat charitable status when the organization's primary purpose is the advancement of a public-utility object.
material_facts: The organization's primary objects were to promote and protect trade, commerce, and industry and their general commercial interests.
One stated object allowed the organization to urge or oppose legislative and other measures affecting trade, commerce, or manufacture.
The legislative advocacy was directed toward achieving the primary objects and was not itself the organization's primary purpose.
members.legal_principle: Under section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, an organization remains charitable where its primary purpose advances an object of general public utility, even if it contemplates incidental political activity to achieve that purpose. The Court relied on In re The Trustees of the Tribune and All India Spinners' Association v. Commissioner of Income-tax, and distinguished Laxman Balwant Bhopatkar v. Charity Commissioner, Bombay, where the primary purpose was political.
members.conclusion: The organization's ancillary advocacy concerning legislation did not prevent its primary public-utility purpose from being charitable.

predicates.income_tax_exemption_claim: The taxpayer sought exemption from income tax for income derived from property.
predicates.public_utility_purpose_is_primary: The organization's principal purpose was to advance an object of general public utility.
predicates.legislative_advocacy_is_ancillary: The organization contemplated urging or opposing legislation only as an incidental means of achieving its principal public-utility purpose.

members.legal_issue: An attachment made while a prior mortgage is subsisting reaches only the mortgagor’s equity of redemption, not the entire property.
material_facts: The owner had granted a simple mortgage over the property before the creditor obtained an attachment before judgment.
When the attachment was made, the mortgage remained subsisting and the owner retained the equity of redemption.
members.legal_principle: A prior subsisting mortgage limits the interest available for attachment to the mortgagor’s equity of redemption. The Court relied on the nature of the mortgage and the interests held by the mortgagor and mortgagee; it cited no earlier cases or statutory provision for this proposition.
members.conclusion: Only the owner’s equity of redemption could be attached; the attachment did not extend to the entire interest in the property.

predicates.money_claim_attachment: A creditor attaches property in connection with a claim for payment of money.
predicates.prior_mortgage_subsisting: A mortgage over the property was created before the attachment and remains in force when the attachment is made.
predicates.mortgagor_retains_equity_of_redemption: The owner of the property retains the right to redeem it when the attachment is made.

members.legal_issue: A creditor attaching mortgaged property can proceed only against the mortgagor’s equity of redemption, or against any sale proceeds remaining after satisfaction of the mortgage claim.
material_facts: The creditor obtained a money decree and sought to sell property that was subject to a prior mortgage.
After the attachment, the equity of redemption was sold in execution of the mortgage decree, and the mortgagee’s claim was to be satisfied from the sale price.
members.legal_principle: An attachment made after a mortgage and while it subsists is subject to the mortgage. The attaching creditor may reach only the mortgagor’s equity of redemption, or any surplus from a sale of that equity after satisfaction of the mortgagee’s claim. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier cases for this proposition.
members.conclusion: While the mortgage subsists, the attaching creditor may sell only the equity of redemption; if that interest has already been sold in execution of the mortgage decree, the creditor may proceed only against any balance remaining after the mortgagee’s claim is satisfied. The mortgagee’s right is not affected.

predicates.money_decree_execution: A creditor seeks to enforce a money decree against property.
predicates.prior_mortgage_subsisting_at_attachment: A mortgage created before the attachment remains in force when the attachment is made.
predicates.attachment_of_mortgagor_interest: The attachment concerns an interest held by the mortgagor in the property.

members.legal_issue: A simple mortgagee without an interest in the equity of redemption cannot use a claim petition to object to attachment of that equity.
material_facts: The claimant held a simple mortgage created before the attachment and had no interest in the equity of redemption when the attachment was made.
The attachment concerned the mortgagor’s equity of redemption.
The claimant was not in possession of the property and filed a claim petition seeking to have the attachment raised.
members.legal_principle: Order 21 Rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for adjudication of a claim or objection that attached property is not liable to attachment. The Court held that a simple mortgagee with no interest in the equity of redemption could not object to attachment of that interest. It cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The simple mortgagee was not entitled to file a claim petition objecting to attachment of the equity of redemption.

rule.if: claim_petition_proceeding and simple_mortgagee and attachment_of_equity_of_redemption and mortgagee_has_no_equity_interest

predicates.claim_petition_proceeding: A claimant brings a proceeding to object to an attachment of property.
predicates.simple_mortgagee: The claimant holds a simple mortgage over the attached property.
predicates.attachment_of_equity_of_redemption: The attachment concerns the mortgagor’s equity of redemption rather than the mortgagee’s interest.
predicates.mortgagee_has_no_equity_interest: The mortgagee has no interest in the mortgagor’s equity of redemption.

members.legal_issue: A person without an independent claim to attached property cannot use an objection to the attachment to execute a maintenance decree against that property.
material_facts: The wife sought to rely on the procedure for objecting to attachment in order to obtain maintenance from the property or its sale proceeds.
The property belonged to her mother-in-law, and the wife had no independent claim to it.
The maintenance obligation, if established, was the husband’s obligation.
members.legal_principle: Section 84 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides a procedure for objecting to attachment, but it cannot be invoked by a claimant who has no independent claim to the property, nor used as a means of executing a decree against attached property.
members.conclusion: The wife could not invoke the objection procedure to claim the property or its proceeds, and that procedure could not be used to execute a decree.

predicates.attachment_objection_proceeding: A claimant invokes a procedure for objecting to the attachment of property.
predicates.claimant_has_no_independent_right_in_pro: The claimant has no independent legal right or interest in the attached property.
predicates.claimant_seeks_to_execute_decree_from_at: The claimant seeks to satisfy a decree by obtaining the attached property or its proceeds.

members.legal_issue: A proved custom treating a river’s deep stream as a constant village boundary can apply when the river changes course suddenly.
material_facts: Both sides accepted that the custom of dhar dhura existed, but disputed whether it covered sudden changes in the river’s course.
The recorded customary statement referred to land gained or lost through river action without specifying whether the action had to be gradual.
Prior official proceedings and a civil judgment recorded instances in which sudden changes were treated as changing the boundary under the custom.
The evidence showed that the custom had been established through local investigation and applied regardless of whether the river changed gradually or suddenly.
members.legal_principle: Section 2 of the Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation, 1825 recognises a clear and definite customary usage under which the main channel remains the boundary despite changes in the river’s course. The party asserting a custom that departs from general law bears the burden of proving it. As stated in Sibt Ali v. Muniruddin, evidence of a custom that transfers land whose character has not changed through river action must be scrutinised carefully, but cogent and satisfactory evidence can establish the custom.
members.conclusion: The evidence established that the custom applied to sudden changes in the river’s course, and the lower courts’ finding on this point was upheld.

predicates.customary_river_boundary_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim to land whose boundary between estates is asserted to be determined by a customary river-channel rule.
predicates.custom_claimed_for_sudden_shifts: A party asserted that the customary boundary rule applied even when the river changed course suddenly.
predicates.cogent_evidence_establishes_sudden_shift: The party asserting the custom produced cogent evidence that the customary rule had been applied to sudden river-course changes.

members.legal_issue: The custom treating a river’s deep stream as a constant boundary is not unreasonable merely because river action can cause accidental gains or losses of land.
material_facts: The custom made gains and losses of land depend on changes in a river’s course, which can be accidental and uncertain.
The custom also provided a convenient way to settle boundaries and avoid disputes between neighbouring estates.
members.legal_principle: A custom must not be contrary to reason, but the relevant standard is legal reason rather than every person’s ordinary conception of reason. The Court referred to Coke on Littleton and noted that preventing quarrels and disputes between neighbouring estates is a community benefit; it also referred to the traditional deep-stream boundary rule discussed in Brihaspati and later commentators, and in Lal Mohan Doss’s work on riparian rights.
members.conclusion: The custom was not unreasonable and was enforceable when established by the evidence.

predicates.customary_river_boundary_dispute: The proceeding concerns a customary rule for determining boundaries between estates divided by a river.
predicates.custom_provides_a_convenient_boundary_ru: The custom provides a practical means of determining the boundary despite changes in the river’s course.
predicates.custom_prevents_neighbouring_estate_disp: The custom helps prevent boundary quarrels and disputes between neighbouring estate owners.

members.legal_issue: A removal power conferred on a supervisory body by an amendment may be exercised on the basis of disobedience that occurred before the amendment took effect.
material_facts: The appellant was a Mutwalli subject to the supervisory body's authority.
The appellant had disobeyed the body's orders and directions before the amendment transferred the removal power to the body itself.
The body removed the appellant after the amendment took effect, relying on the earlier disobedience.
The amendment changed who could exercise the removal power, and the earlier proceedings concerning the alleged misconduct were already underway.
members.legal_principle: A statute is not necessarily retrospective merely because a power conferred by it is based on earlier conduct, where the power is intended to reach that conduct. The Court also held that there was no vested right to continue as Mutawalli after mismanagement and misconduct had been established. It applied the amended removal provision of the Bihar Waqfs Act, 1947, as amended by the Bihar Waqfs (Amendment) Act, 1951.
members.conclusion: The supervisory body could exercise its amended removal power on the basis of orders and directions disobeyed before the amendment took effect.

predicates.waqf_mutawalli_removal_case: The proceeding concerns removal of a Mutawalli in the administration of a waqf.
predicates.amended_law_transfers_removal_power_to_s: A later amendment gives the supervisory body itself authority to remove the Mutawalli.
predicates.prior_supervisory_orders_were_disobeyed: The Mutawalli disobeyed the supervisory body's orders or directions before the amendment took effect.

members.legal_issue: Disobedience of an order issued before an amendment can support removal under the amended power even if the earlier provision referred to directions rather than orders.
material_facts: Before the amendment, the earlier removal provision referred to disobedience of directions.
The appellant contended that disobedience of orders issued before the amendment could not support removal under the amended provision, which referred to orders and directions.
The Court treated orders and directions as expressions of the binding wish of the supervisory body, differing in degree.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that orders and directions both express the binding wish of the supervisory body, although an order is more peremptory. It rejected an interpretation under which disobedience of a direction could lead to removal but disobedience of an order would go unpunished, applying the removal provision of the Bihar Waqfs Act, 1947, as amended in 1951.
members.conclusion: The appellant's distinction between orders and directions did not prevent reliance on disobedience of an earlier order as a ground for removal.

predicates.waqf_mutawalli_removal_case: The proceeding concerns removal of a Mutawalli in the administration of a waqf.
predicates.amended_removal_power_covers_orders_and_: The applicable removal power treats disobedience of orders and directions from the supervisory body as grounds for removal.
predicates.prior_supervisory_order_was_disobeyed: The Mutawalli disobeyed an order issued by the supervisory body before the amended removal power took effect.

members.legal_issue: A suit should not be rejected for a court-fee shortfall without a fair opportunity to make up the deficiency where the litigant could not pay because of financial difficulty and no mala fides are apparent.
material_facts: The litigant paid only part of the court fee when filing a suit seeking relief concerning his property.
He applied for more time to pay the balance, but the trial court rejected the application and closed the suit without giving him an opportunity to pay.
He said he could not pay because of financial difficulties, and the Court found no manifest ground of mala fides.
members.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives the court discretion to allow a party to make up deficient court fees and to validate the deficiency retrospectively. That discretion should ordinarily be exercised in favour of litigants absent manifest grounds of mala fides, while ensuring bona fides; the court should give an opportunity to pay before rejecting a suit for a fee shortfall.
members.conclusion: The trial court’s rejection of the suit was wrong and was set aside.

rule.if: civil_suit and court_fee_shortfall and no_opportunity_to_cure and financial_inability and no_mala_fides_apparent

predicates.civil_suit: A litigant brought a civil suit seeking adjudication of a claim.
predicates.court_fee_shortfall: The litigant paid less than the required court fee when filing the suit.
predicates.no_opportunity_to_cure: The trial court rejected the suit without giving the litigant an opportunity to pay the deficiency.
predicates.financial_inability: The litigant was unable to pay the balance because of financial difficulty.
predicates.no_mala_fides_apparent: The court had no manifest indication that the litigant acted mala fide.

members.legal_issue: Delay in paying deficient court fees may be condoned when financial difficulty prevents payment and rejection would prevent adjudication of a substantive claim, consistent with equal access to justice.
material_facts: The litigant could not pay the balance court fee because of financial difficulty, and the suit was rejected on that ground.
The suit concerned the litigant’s substantive claim to property.
The Court considered that the litigant should have an opportunity to have the claim decided on its merits.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the substantial-justice approach to delay in State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Prasad Singh, Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Mst. Katiji, and N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy. Article 39A, read with Article 21 and State of Maharashtra v. Manubhai Pragaji Vashi, requires attention to equal access to justice and the effect of economic disability. Section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits the court to allow deficient court fees to be made up.
members.conclusion: The delay in payment of the court fee was condoned, and the matter was remanded so the litigant could pay the fee or seek assistance for it.

rule.if: suit_rejected_for_fee_nonpayment and financial_inability and substantive_claim and no_mala_fides_shown

predicates.suit_rejected_for_fee_nonpayment: A trial court rejected a suit because the litigant had not paid the required court fee.
predicates.financial_inability: The litigant could not pay the required fee because of financial difficulty.
predicates.substantive_claim: The suit sought adjudication of a substantive right rather than merely a procedural advantage.
predicates.no_mala_fides_shown: The record did not show that the litigant’s explanation was mala fide or a dilatory strategy.

members.legal_issue: A retired government employee has no entitlement to retain government accommodation or receive alternative government accommodation without a policy authorizing it.
material_facts: A government employee who had been displaced by terrorism retired while occupying government accommodation.

After retirement, he sought to retain that accommodation indefinitely for a nominal licence fee and the High Courts directed that eviction be kept in abeyance and alternative accommodation be provided.
No government policy authorized allotment of government accommodation to displaced retired employees; the accommodation was intended for serving officials.
members.legal_principle: Government accommodation is scarce public property intended for serving officials, not retirees. In S.D. Bandi v. Divisional Traffic Officer (2013) 12 SCC 631, Shiv Sagar Tiwari v. Union of India (1997) 1 SCC 444, and Lok Prahari (I) v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2016) 8 SCC 389 and Lok Prahari (II) v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2018) 6 SCC 1, the Court rejected unauthorized or policy-free allotment and retention of government residences, including by former public officeholders. Compassion does not itself create an entitlement to public property or authorize a court to direct an allotment unsupported by policy.
members.conclusion: The High Court directions were unsustainable. A retired government employee cannot retain government accommodation or demand alternative government accommodation in the absence of a policy authorizing it.

predicates.appeal_challenges_housing_order_for_reti: An appeal challenges a court order allowing a retired public official to retain or receive government housing.
predicates.official_has_retired: The public official whose housing entitlement is at issue has retired from government service.
predicates.official_seeks_to_retain_or_receive_gove: The retired official has sought to keep government housing or obtain alternative government housing.
predicates.no_policy_authorizes_housing_for_retired: No government policy authorizes the allotment of government housing to retired officials in the circumstances at issue.
predicates.government_housing_is_for_serving_offici: The government housing at issue is provided for officials serving in government employment.

members.legal_issue: The right to shelter does not entitle a displaced retired public employee to government housing when the applicable policy provides for transit accommodation or cash assistance.
material_facts: The retired employee had been displaced from his home by terrorism and relied on the right to shelter to seek continued or alternative government housing.
The government policy for displaced persons provided for transit accommodation and, where that accommodation was unavailable, cash assistance toward rental and incidental expenses.
The employee had received a salary, pension and retirement benefits, and the Court noted that the policy-based shelter response did not include government quarters for displaced retirees.
members.legal_principle: Although the right to shelter is a fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution, it does not create an indefeasible right to government accommodation. The Court distinguished the accommodation relief in J.L. Koul v. State of J&K (2010) 1 SCC 371, which concerned a rehabilitation scheme and was granted on its particular facts. It also rejected the broader approach taken in Union of India v. Vijay Mam (2012 SCC OnLine Del 3218): compassion and hardship cannot justify allotting government property without a supporting policy.
members.conclusion: The right to shelter does not extend to a right to government accommodation. The applicable provision of transit accommodation or cash assistance addresses the displaced person’s shelter needs, and hardship alone does not impose a duty on the State to provide government housing.

rule.if: displaced_person_shelter_claim and claimant_is_retired_public_employee and claimant_seeks_government_housing_under_shelter_right and policy_provides_transit_housing_or_cash and no_policy_authorizes_government_housing_for_displaced_retirees

predicates.displaced_person_shelter_claim: A displaced person seeks accommodation on the basis of a claim to shelter.
predicates.claimant_is_retired_public_employee: The person making the shelter claim is a retired government employee.
predicates.claimant_seeks_government_housing_under_: The claimant relies on the right to shelter to seek government housing.
predicates.policy_provides_transit_housing_or_cash: The applicable policy provides transit accommodation or cash assistance toward housing expenses for displaced persons.
predicates.no_policy_authorizes_government_housing_: No policy authorizes government housing for displaced retired employees in the circumstances at issue.

members.legal_issue: A coparcener cannot maintain a suit for a permanent injunction that prevents a family manager from alienating coparcenary property, where the coparcener can challenge the completed alienation and seek recovery of the property.
material_facts: The sons claimed that the house was ancestral coparcenary property and that the proposed sale was neither for legal necessity nor for the benefit of the family estate.
The family manager had agreed to sell the house, and the sons sought a permanent injunction preventing him from selling or alienating it to the proposed purchaser or anyone else.
The sons had an available remedy to challenge the alienation and seek recovery of the property after the sale was completed.
The injunction sought would have barred alienation even if a genuine legal necessity or benefit to the estate later justified a sale.
members.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara Hindu law, a coparcener has an interest by birth but cannot interfere with the manager’s acts of management; the manager may alienate joint family property for legal necessity, benefit of the estate, or to meet an antecedent debt. A coparcener may challenge an unjustified completed alienation, but has no corresponding right to obstruct a proposed alienation. Sections 37 and 38 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 govern perpetual injunctions, and section 41(h) bars an injunction where an equally efficacious remedy is available by another usual mode of proceeding. The Court relied on Hunoomanpersaud Pandey v. Mussumat Babooee Munraj Koonweree and Jujhar Singh v. Giani Talok Singh, and distinguished the contrary view in Shiv Kumar Mool Chand Arora v. Mool Chand Jaswant Singh.
members.conclusion: The suit for a permanent injunction restraining the family manager from alienating the coparcenary property was not maintainable, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.coparcener_seeks_permanent_injunction: A coparcener brings a suit seeking a permanent injunction against the family manager.
predicates.seeks_to_block_manager_alienation: The coparcener seeks to prevent the manager from alienating family property before the alienation is completed.
predicates.post_alienation_challenge_and_recovery_a: The coparcener can challenge a completed alienation and seek recovery of the property through another proceeding.

members.legal_issue: An injunction may be granted against a family manager in a coparcener’s case based on waste or ouster, but not as a blanket restraint on alienation.
material_facts: The sons sought a broad injunction preventing the manager from selling or alienating the house to the proposed purchaser or any other person.
The Court stated that an injunction may be available to a coparcener in a case of waste or ouster, while the suit before it sought a blanket restraint on alienation.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished a specific injunction addressing waste or ouster from a blanket prohibition on alienation. A manager has power to alienate family property for legally recognized family purposes, while the Specific Relief Act’s provisions governing injunctions do not support a blanket restraint that prevents even a justified alienation. The Court discussed sections 37, 38 and 41 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and relied on the Mitakshara principles described in Hunoomanpersaud Pandey v. Mussumat Babooee Munraj Koonweree.
members.conclusion: An injunction may be granted against a family manager at a coparcener’s instance in a case of waste or ouster, but a blanket permanent injunction barring alienation, including alienation for legal necessity, cannot be granted.

members.legal_issue: A municipal rate assessed on land together with tenant-owned huts may be particularized to identify the portion attributable to the huts, which the landowner may recover.
material_facts: The landowner's land was assessed together with huts built and occupied by tenants who owned the huts.
The High Court directed that the assessment be particularized for each portion of land and hut, separately on the consolidated valuation.
The landowner challenged the assessment and recovery of the rate attributable to the tenants' huts.
members.legal_principle: Section 202 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951 is more or less a self-contained code. What is leviable under it cannot be prejudiced by the existence of another provision. The Court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The High Court's direction for particularizing the assessment addressed the complaint, and the landowner could collect the rate attributable to the tenant-owned huts under Section 202 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951.

rule.if: proceeding_is_special_leave_petition and land_is_owned_by_assessing_owner and huts_are_owned_by_tenants and assessment_combines_land_and_huts

members.legal_issue: A rent-control enactment does not bar a landowner from recovering municipal rates attributable to tenant-owned huts when the municipal law separately permits recovery of those rates.
material_facts: The landowner sought to recover from tenants amounts beyond the rent fixed under the Thika Tenancy Act.
The amounts at issue were municipal rates recoverable under Section 202 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished the Thika Tenancy Act, which deals with rents, from Section 202 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951, which deals with rates. The special provision governing rates prevails as to those rates. The Court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The Thika Tenancy Act did not prevent recovery of sums permissible under Section 202 because the former dealt with rents and the latter with rates.

rule.if: proceeding_is_special_leave_petition and landlord_tenant_relationship_exists and rent_is_governed_by_a_rent_control_regime and claimed_amount_is_a_municipal_rate_recoverable_from_the_tenant

predicates.proceeding_is_special_leave_petition: The matter is brought before the court as a petition seeking special leave to appeal.
predicates.landlord_tenant_relationship_exists: A landlord leases land to tenants who occupy structures on it.
predicates.rent_is_governed_by_a_rent_control_regim: A rent-control regime governs the rent payable by the tenants.
predicates.claimed_amount_is_a_municipal_rate_recov: The claimed amount is a municipal rate that the municipal law permits the landlord to recover from the tenant.

members.legal_issue: A municipal authority’s statutory power to establish markets and manage occupancy rights can accommodate a project in which a developer, with the authority’s consent, inducts occupiers into designated accommodation.
material_facts: The project included a vegetable market and commercial complex on municipal land.
The developer was to arrange occupancy of designated accommodation and retain premiums to meet the project’s financial outlays.
The Municipal Council consented to the developer inducting occupiers.
members.legal_principle: Section 272(1) of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965, was capable of supporting the municipal authority’s exercise of power in this project. The Court declined to interpret that statutory power so restrictively as to exclude the enterprise.
members.conclusion: The exercise of power could be fitted within Section 272(1) of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, and the provision did not need to be read restrictively to exclude the project.

predicates.is_appeal_challenging_municipal_project: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a municipal authority’s project decision.
predicates.project_establishes_municipal_market_fac: The project establishes or develops facilities for a municipal market.
predicates.developer_inducts_occupiers_with_council: The developer inducts occupiers into designated accommodation with the municipal authority’s consent.

members.legal_issue: A developer’s induction of occupiers into designated accommodation with the municipal authority’s express consent does not, without more, establish a prohibited lease or disposal of municipal property.
material_facts: The developer could arrange occupancy rights in the accommodation allocated to it under the project.
The Municipal Council expressly consented to the developer substituting occupiers in its place.
Occupiers, including those inducted by the developer, were to pay rent to the Council.
The appellants characterized the arrangement as a prohibited long-term lease, but the Court found that the essential elements establishing a violation had not been shown.
members.legal_principle: Sections 92 and 272(1) of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965, should be applied according to their terms. A statutory power to establish markets and dispose of occupancy rights should not be burdened with restrictions absent from the statute. A developer’s substitution of an occupier in its place is permissible when done with the municipal authority’s express consent.
members.conclusion: The essential elements of a transaction violating Section 92 of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act had not been established; the consensual substitution of occupiers was not impermissible.

predicates.occupiers_pay_rent_to_council: The occupiers pay rent to the municipal authority.

members.legal_issue: A testamentary gift to a named beneficiary and that beneficiary’s heirs, executors and administrators may create a substitutional bequest when the will’s language and circumstances show an intention to benefit those successors if the primary gift fails.
material_facts: The testator’s will gave the estate to a person he described as his mother, followed by words benefiting both her and her heirs, executors and administrators.
The will stated that the beneficiary and those successors were to have the property for their own use and benefit, absolutely and forever.
The testator expressed that he regarded the beneficiary as his mother and that no one could dispute that description.
The primary beneficiary’s husband attested the will, making the gift to her void under section 67 of the Indian Succession Act.
members.legal_principle: A will must be read as a whole, with its parts construed in relation to one another (section 82 of the Indian Succession Act); where a clause can reasonably have effect, that construction is preferred over one that gives it none (section 84); and no part should be rejected as meaningless if a reasonable construction is possible (section 85). The court distinguished and disagreed with the approach in In re McElligott, which did not give effect to the words providing for the beneficiary’s successors’ own use and benefit. The testator’s intention is determined from the language used and the surrounding circumstances.
members.conclusion: The will created a primary bequest to the beneficiary and a substitutional bequest to her heirs, executors and administrators if the primary bequest failed.

predicates.will_gift_dispute: The dispute concerns the meaning of a gift made by a will.
predicates.will_names_beneficiary_and_successors: The will names a primary beneficiary and also refers to that beneficiary’s successors as recipients.
predicates.will_provides_for_beneficiary_and_succes: The will states that the beneficiary and the successors are to hold or use the property for their own benefit.
predicates.testator_expresses_personal_attachment_t: The testator expresses a personal relationship with, or attachment to, the primary beneficiary.

members.legal_issue: Where a substitutional bequest is made to a beneficiary’s heirs and representatives, the beneficiary’s presumptive heirs at the testator’s death may take even if the beneficiary is then alive and no executor or administrator can take.
material_facts: The testator’s will made a substitutional bequest to the primary beneficiary’s heirs, executors and administrators.
The primary beneficiary was alive when the testator died, so the executors and administrators described in the will could not be identified as recipients on the relevant basis.
The primary beneficiary had two daughters, who were her presumptive heirs when the testator died.
The substitutional bequest had already been found to take effect.
members.legal_principle: Although technically no one is the heir of a living person, the word “heirs” may be used in a will to designate those who are presumptive heirs at the relevant time. A failure of the gift to one part of a described class, such as executors or administrators, does not necessarily defeat the gift to another part, such as heirs. The court relied on Halsbury, volume 34, article 358, page 309, for the treatment of presumptive heirs as recipients of a direct gift.
members.conclusion: The two daughters, as the beneficiary’s presumptive heirs at the testator’s death, were entitled to take under the will. The failure of the gift to executors and administrators did not defeat the gift to the heirs; there was no intestacy, and the plaintiffs had no right to maintain the suit as heirs of the testator.

predicates.will_gift_dispute: The dispute concerns the effect of a gift made by a will.
predicates.substitutional_gift_names_beneficiary_he: The substitute gift names the primary beneficiary’s heirs and representatives as recipients.
predicates.beneficiary_alive_at_testator_death: The primary beneficiary was alive when the testator died.
predicates.presumptive_heirs_identifiable_at_testat: People could be identified as the primary beneficiary’s presumptive heirs when the testator died.

members.legal_issue: A Hindu widow who reacquires the same property she had transferred before the relevant legal change becomes its full owner when the transfer is reversed and her original interest is restored.
material_facts: The widow inherited a limited estate in the property from her husband and transferred it before the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
After the Act came into force, the transferee reconveyed the same property to the widow, restoring the interest she had previously transferred.
When her title was challenged, she had reacquired and was possessed of the property.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act provides that property possessed by a female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the Act commenced, is held by her as full owner and not as a limited owner. The Explanation includes property acquired by purchase or in any other manner. Section 4 displaces inconsistent prior Hindu law. The Court approved Chinnakolandai Goundan v. Thanji Gounder, Teja Singh v. Jagat Singh, Ramgowda Aunagowda v. Bhausaheb, and Champa v. Chandrakant; it overruled Ganesh Mahanta v. Sukria Bewa and Medicherla Venkataratnam v. Siddani Palamma. Kotturuswamy v. Veeravva was distinguished because the widow there had obtained possession as a trespasser without title.
members.conclusion: The widow became the full owner of the property under Section 14(1), and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: property_title_appeal and female_had_limited_inherited_interest and female_transferred_property_before_legal_change and transferee_reconveyed_same_property_to_her and reconveyance_restored_original_interest and female_lawfully_held_property_when_title_was_challenged

predicates.reconveyance_restored_original_interest: The return transfer reversed the earlier transaction and restored the interest the female Hindu had transferred.
predicates.female_lawfully_held_property_when_title: The female Hindu had lawfully reacquired and held the property when her title was challenged.

members.legal_issue: A reversioner’s future chance of succession does not defeat a widow’s full ownership when a transfer of her property is reversed and the property is restored to her.
material_facts: The widow temporarily transferred property in which she had inherited a limited estate.
The transferee later reconveyed that property to her, reversing the earlier transaction and restoring her interest.
The competing reversioner had only a possible future chance of succeeding to the property.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that a reversioner has only a spes successionis, or chance of future succession, and that this expectancy is not a present right in the property. When the transaction is reversed and the widow’s interest is restored, Section 14(1) applies to enlarge that interest into full ownership.
members.conclusion: The reversal of the transaction did not affect any existing right of the reversioner, whose mere expectancy could not defeat the widow’s full ownership.

rule.if: property_title_appeal and widow_had_limited_interest and same_property_was_restored_to_widow and reversioner_had_only_future_succession_expectancy

members.legal_issue: Pre-emption rights granted to co-owners are constitutionally valid because co-owners form a distinct class and an outsider's entry may impair common management.
material_facts: The statutory scheme gave other co-owners a pre-emption right in the case of a sale of a share out of jointly owned land or property.
The Court relied on the difficulty of common management when an outsider becomes a co-owner and the benefits of keeping jointly owned property within the existing group of co-owners.
members.legal_principle: A classification of co-owners as a distinct class for pre-emption is reasonable where it protects the practical management and benefits of common ownership. The Court applied Articles 14 and 15 and followed the reasoning in Bhau Ram v. B. Baijnath Singh, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 724, which upheld pre-emption in favour of co-sharers as a reasonable restriction in the public interest. It also referred to Ram Sarup v. Munshi, [1963] 3 S.C.R. 858, in discussing the distinction between kinship-based and co-owner-based pre-emption.
members.conclusion: The co-owner pre-emption category in the relevant clause of section 15(1)(b) was valid and did not infringe Articles 14 or 15.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the constitutionality of a statutory pre-emption scheme in a constitutional proceeding.
predicates.preemption_benefits_existing_co_owners: The statutory right to pre-empt a sale of a jointly owned share was granted to the other co-owners.
predicates.outsider_entry_may_impair_common_managem: The entry of a new outsider as a co-owner could make common management difficult or diminish the benefits of common ownership.

members.legal_issue: Pre-emption rights granted to tenants are constitutionally valid because tenants form a distinct class and the right protects their ability to obtain ownership of the land they cultivate.
material_facts: The statutory scheme granted pre-emption rights to tenants holding the land or property sold, or part of it, under a tenancy from the vendor.
The Court considered the protective purpose of enabling a tenant who tills the soil to obtain proprietary rights and avoid losing possession and livelihood to a superior proprietor.
members.legal_principle: Tenants may be treated as a distinct class for pre-emption where the right advances land-reform objectives by protecting the tiller of the soil from losing possession and livelihood and by enabling the tenant to obtain proprietary rights. The Court applied Articles 14 and 15 and held the tenant categories reasonable and in the public interest.
members.conclusion: The tenant pre-emption categories in the relevant clauses of section 15(1)(a), (b), and (c) were valid and did not infringe Articles 14 or 15.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the constitutionality of a statutory pre-emption scheme in a constitutional proceeding.
predicates.preemption_benefits_a_tenant: The statutory pre-emption right was granted to a tenant holding the property sold, or part of it, under a tenancy from the seller.
predicates.tenant_protection_advances_land_reform: The right protects the tenant's possession and livelihood and advances the objective of enabling the person who cultivates the land to obtain ownership rights.
